Initially created: 2026-03-26T21:58:24.475+09:00 by CH Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Someone said:
A "fu" is a derivative of ancient poetry.
In the past, after the reigns of Chéng and Kāng, praises ceased;
the king's benevolence dried up, and poetry was no longer composed.
At the founding of the Great Hàn,
time was too scarce.
By the time of the reigns of Wǔ and Xuān,
officials of propriety were honored,
and literature was examined.
Internally, the offices of Jīnmǎ and Shíqú were established;
externally, the Music Bureau harmonized and regulated;
to revive and continue what was discarded,
embellishing grand enterprises.
For this reason, the people were joyful,
and blessings were especially abundant.
The songs of the white qilin, red geese, zhī house, and treasured ornaments
were offered at the suburban temple.
Auspicious omens like the divine sparrow, five phoenixes, sweet dew, and the yellow dragon
were used to mark the years.
Therefore, the words and attendants,
such as Sīmǎ Xiāngrú, Yúqiū Shòuwáng, Dōngfāng Shuò, Méi Gāo, Wáng Bāo, and Liú Xiàng,
debated and thought day and night,
contributing every day and month;
and the dukes, ministers,
Yùshǐ Dàfū Ní Kuān,
Tàicháng Kǒng Zāng,
Tàizhōng Dàfū Dǒng Zhòngshū,
Zōngzhèng Liú Dé,
and Tàizǐ Tàichuán Xiāo Wàngzhī,
wrote from time to time.
Some expressed humble sentiments to offer remonstrance,
some extolled superior virtues to fulfill loyalty and filial piety;
gracefully and eloquently,
leaving their mark on future generations,
they approached the elegance and grandeur of hymns.
Therefore, during the reign of Emperor Xiàochéng,
discussions and compilations were made,
with over a thousand compositions presented to the throne,
after which the literature of the Great Hàn
shone brightly, comparable to the three dynasties.
Furthermore, the way has its highs and lows,
learning has its depths and shallows;
thereby establishing virtue according to the times,
without changing principles due to distance or proximity.
Hence, Gāotāo sang for Yú,
Xīsī praised Lǔ,
both recognized by the Confucian school,
included in poems and historical records,
their meanings being one.
Examined in ancient times, it was like this,
reviewed in the Hàn court, it was also thus.
Though small,
it was the old norm of former ministers,
a lingering beauty of the state,
not to be neglected.
I secretly observe the tranquility within the seas,
the court free from affairs,
the capital renovating palaces,
deepening ditches,
erecting gardens and parks,
according to the established system.
The elders of the western lands,
all harbor grievances,
hoping for the emperor's attention,
and greatly praising the old system of Cháng'ān,
compared to the inferior opinions of Luòyì.
Hence, I composed the "Fu of the Two Capitals,"
to fully display what dazzles people,
in comparison with current laws.
Its wording is as follows.
A guest from the Western Capital asked the master of the Eastern Capital:
"I have heard that when the Hàn dynasty first managed the nation,
they considered establishing the capital near the River Luò.
They ceased and did not proceed,
using this to move westward,
building our supreme capital.
Has the master heard the reasons and seen the arrangements?"
The master said:
"Not yet.
I wish for the guest to express old thoughts and reveal ancient sentiments.
Enrich me with the imperial way,
and broaden me with the capital of Hàn."
The guest said:
"Of course."
"The Western Capital of Hàn
is located in Yōngzhōu,
named Cháng'ān indeed.
On the left, it takes support from the barriers of Hángǔ and Erxiáo,
marked by Mount Tàihuá and Zhōngnán.
On the right, bounded by the dangers of Bāoxiá and Lǒngshǒu,
bordered by the mighty River Jīng and Wèi.
Nestled among many streams,
with the Qiān springing from the west.
Among its flowers and fruits,
it is the richest spot in the nine provinces;
as a defensive bastion,
it is the secluded region of the heavens and earth.
Therefore, it spans the universe,
thrice forming the imperial domain.
Zhōu rose like a dragon,
Qín glared like a tiger.
When the Great Hàn received the mandate and settled here,
they astutely comprehended the essence of Dōngjǐng,
and perfectly aligned with the spirit of the Hé图.
Lǐu Hóu planned the schemes,
Līu Hóu elaborated them.
The collaboration between heaven and man marked divine enlightenment.
Thus, they gazed westward,
and indeed established it as the capital.
Then, they looked at Qín Lǐng,
and turned to the northern hills;
embraced the Fèng and Bà rivers,
and rested at Lóngshǒu.
Planned a grand foundation for countless generations,
measured vast plans and magnificently commenced.
Starting lofty and ending plain,
generations adorned to enhance elegance.
Through twelve reigns it extended,
thus reaching prosperity and extremity in luxury.
Built the golden city with myriad towers,
opened Zhōu basin into a deep pond.
Unfurled the wide roads of Sāntiáo,
established twelve thoroughfare gates.
Inside, the streets and alleys spanned boundlessly,
households nearly within a thousand.
Nine markets were opened,
goods varied through lanes and channels.
People could not glance back,
carriages could not turn around.
City overflowed into the suburbs,
flowing beside countless shops.
Red dust enveloped all,
misty clouds joined together.
Then being populous and wealthy,
pleasures were boundless.
The capital's men and women,
differed markedly from the five regions.
Wandering scholars aspired to nobility,
rows of luxurious shops of Jī and Jiāng's level.
Local esteemed and ambitious,
heroes among the roaming knights.
Emulated springs and tasted aspirations,
names next to Chūnlíng.
Formed associations and united,
racing and roaming within.
Now, observing the four outskirts,
floating and wandering nearby counties;
looking south to Dùbà,
north to the five tombs.
Famous cities faced the suburbs,
township residences inherited each other.
A realm of talents and nobles,
where dignitaries arose.
Hats and robes like clouds,
seven ministers and five dukes.
Together with the elite of prefectures and counties,
and the wealth of five capitals.
Three selections and seven transfers,
supplying and serving the tomb cities.
The strategy strengthened the root while weakening the branches,
glorifying the capital while overseeing all nations."
"Within the capital's domain,
the land extends for a thousand li.
It surpasses all the states of Huáxià,
encompassing all they possess.
To the south, there are towering mountains that obscure the sky,
deep forests and vast valleys.
Treasures from land and sea,
and the beautiful jade of Lántián.
Shāngluò winds along its curves,
while Hùdù lies at its base.
Springs and streams irrigate the land,
with ponds and lakes interconnected.
Bamboo groves and fruit orchards,
fragrant grasses and sweet trees.
The richness of the countryside
is said to rival Shǔ.
To the north, it is crowned by Jiǔzōng,
accompanied by Gānquán,
where divine palaces rise among them.
The grandest sights of the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
praised by the likes of Wáng Bāo and Yáng Xióng,
are preserved here.
Below lies the fertile land of Zhèng and Bái,
the source of food and clothing.
The enclosed territory spans fifty thousand [units],
with borders intricately divided.
Canals and ridges are carved like engravings,
and the plains and lowlands resemble dragon scales.
Opening channels brings rain-like irrigation,
and hoes are raised like clouds.
The five grains hang heavy with ears,
while mulberry and hemp spread luxuriantly.
In the eastern suburbs, there are great canals and waterways,
connecting to the Wèi and piercing the Huáng Hé.
Boats sail to Shāndōng,
controlling the Huái and lake regions,
their waves reaching the sea.
In the western suburbs, there are imperial parks and forbidden gardens,
with forests, foothills, marshes, and lakes,
whose ponds stretch to Shǔ and Hàn.
Encircled by walls,
over four hundred li in length.
Detached palaces and separate lodges,
thirty-six in total.
Divine ponds and spiritual pools,
are scattered throughout.
Among them are the qílín from Jiǔzhēn,
horses from Dàyuān,
rhinoceroses from Huángzhī,
and birds from Tiáozhī.
They cross the Kūnlún Mountains,
traverse vast seas,
coming from distant lands and exotic species,
from as far as thirty thousand li away."
"As for its palaces,
their structure symbolizes heaven and earth,
arranging according to yin and yang.
They occupy the rightful place of earth's spirit,
imitating the circular and square forms of the Taìzǐ.
The resplendent towers stand in the middle of the sky,
the vermilion halls crowning the mountains.
Using extraordinary materials to achieve uniqueness,
supporting the rainbow beam of the yìng lóng dragon.
With complex beams spreading like wings,
carrying rafters high above.
Carving jade inlay for the pillars,
setting gold discs as embellishments.
Displaying richly colored hues,
their brilliance is revealed conspicuously.
Thus the left portico and right flank are balanced,
with three tiers of overlapping terraces.
The private rooms are interconnected,
their doors wide open.
Bells are arranged in the central courtyard,
and golden statues stand at the main entrance.
Adding ridges to balance the thresholds,
overlooking steep paths with open gates.
Extending to detached palaces and separate quarters,
complemented by elevated terraces and secluded pavilions.
Shining like a constellation,
surrounded by the Purple Palace.
The climate is clear and cool,
with immortals of long years.
Golden decorations and jade halls,
white tigers and qilin.
The territory is such,
that it cannot be fully described.
Enhancing majestic heights,
ascending and descending in dazzling brilliance.
Unique shapes and curious designs,
each offering a different view.
Riding on velvet and stepping into chariots,
resting and feasting at will.
In the rear palace are the Yètíng and Pepper Chamber,
residences of the empress and concubines.
The walls rise harmoniously,
residing in constant tranquility.
Fragrant as calamus and peppery breezes,
exuding a unique scent.
Orchards and sweet herbs,
where mandarin ducks and luans fly.
Strong and prosperous is Zhāoyáng,
flourishing in Filial Piety.
Roofs do not expose the materials,
walls do not reveal their form.
Covered with embroidered patterns,
interwoven with threads.
The bright moon of Suí Hóu,
scattered within its expanse.
Golden jars holding jewels,
arranged as linked coins.
Kingfisher flames aligned,
shining with brilliance.
Glossy stones and hanging spikes,
the night light is therein.
Thus the dark steps reach the pavilion,
jade staircases and a vermilion courtyard.
Pristine stones and detailed patterns,
exquisite and glowing jade.
Coral and green trees,
growing and surrounding the oasises.
Red silk sash sways,
elegant and intricate brocades.
Brilliant candles and dazzling lights,
looking around like a divine presence.
The rear palace titles,
number fourteen ranks.
Elegant yet luxuriant,
increasingly flourishing and prestigious.
Those occupying these chambers,
number in the hundreds.
In the side courtyards,
are positions for officials of the court.
Xiāo Cāo Wèi Bǐng,
deliberate and plan above.
Assisting the ruler by maintaining order,
supporting and fostering transformation.
Spreading the kindness and benevolence of the great Hàn,
sweeping away the venom of Qín's demise.
Thus these people play harmonious music,
composing songs of enlightenment.
Their merits are renowned among ancestors,
their grace benefiting the common people.
Also, there are the Heavenly Records and Stone Bays,
repositories of classics and books.
Summoning those with profound teachings to advise,
famed scholars serve as tutors.
Discussing the Six Arts,
examining agreements of differences.
Furthermore there is Chéngmíng and Golden Horse,
domains of literature production.
Nobility and grand expression gather,
forming groups here.
Thorough with primary sources,
extensively knowledgeable and widely informed.
Initiating writings,
compiling classified documents.
Encircled by the place of gōu chén,
guarded by strict offices.
Totalling the protocols of ceremonial officers,
exemplary filial piety across all prefectures.
Tiger guards with splendid garments,
eunuchs at the palace gates.
Hundredfold ranks of halberds upon the stairs,
each with specific duties.
Surroundings of a thousand rows of chambers,
winding paths intricately interwoven.
Constructing transport roads,
maintaining and enhancing flying corridors.
From Wèiyāng to Guì Palace,
extending northwards to Míngguāng and spanning Chánglè.
Rising over paths and surpassing the western walls,
reaching Jiànzhāng and connecting with the outer suburbs.
Establishing Phoenix Towers of Jade Gates,
ascending pinnacles where golden sparrows roost.
Internally, are the separate winds of towering heights,
artfully charming and uplifted.
Expanding with a thousand gates,
essential to open and close in accordance with yin and yang.
Presiding Main Hall majestic in elevation,
with multi-tiered high structures,
overlooking Wèiyāng.
It extends vast delights and unprecedented experiences,
reaching great height and joining with heavenly beams.
The roofing arches upwards shading all below,
reflecting sunlight and admitting radiance.
Majestic and outstanding divinity,
moving straight up magnificently.
Surpassing clouds and rain in greater halves,
with rainbows winding around complex cornices.
Though light and swift and untamed,
still stunned and unable to ascend.
Climbing tree trunks yet only halfway,
eyes spinning and minds lost.
Leaving railings to lean back,
seeming to fall but then regain.
Souls bewilderedly wandering beyond bounds,
circling paths then lowering.
Having feared heights from gazing above,
descending and wandering below.
Walking winding paths,
then unseen is the sun.
Passing flying doors and ascending outwards,
watching as if from beyond the sky,
appearing unsupported and leisurely.
In front lies Tángzhōng, behind is the great water of Tàiyè,
viewing the vastness of the blue sea.
Engulfing waves upon Jiéshí,
stirring the grand mountain spirits.
Involving isles of Yíngzhōu and Fānghú,
Penglai rises in the center.
Here divine grasses are verdant in winter,
sacred trees sprout in abundance.
Cliff boundaries elevated and tall,
metals and stones starkly magnificent.
Holding off the dust of the world's chaos,
nurturing pure, bright emanations.
Enabling splendid blessings,
driving the forces of destiny's trials.
Aspiring to resemble the sages of Song Qiáo and their kind,
occasionally visiting and accompanying them in these gardens.
Indeed, the residence of true immortals,
not a place of tranquility for mortals like us.
"Then they engaged in magnificent entertainments and grand spectacles,
unleashing martial prowess in the imperial hunting grounds.
Through this, they awed the Róng and boasted to the Dí,
displaying majestic power while conducting military exercises.
They commanded Jīngzhōu to send forth birds,
and ordered the wilderness of Liáng to drive out beasts.
Furred creatures filled the inner grounds,
feathered flocks covered the skies above.
Wings touching wings, feet treading side by side,
they gathered and crowded within the forbidden forests.
The Water Stewards and gamekeepers
prepared their camps and markers.
By kind and by herd they were divided,
each assigned to its own section and office.
Nets and snares were connected by cords,
enveloping the mountains and covering the plains.
Soldiers were arrayed all around,
scattered like stars, spread like clouds.
Then the emperor mounted his imperial carriage,
equipped with the full ritual procession,
leading his assembled ministers.
Passing through the Fēilián Gate,
they entered the park's entrance.
They circled Fēnghào,
passed by Shànglán.
The six armies set forth in pursuit,
and all beasts were struck with terror.
With a rumbling and flashing,
like thunderbolts and lightning strikes.
Grass and trees were trampled into the ground,
mountains and abysses seemed overturned.
After trampling down two or three-tenths of them,
they restrained their fury and paused briefly.
Then the Jīmén and Cìfēi guards,
with blades arrayed and arrows nocked,
intercepted and chased their tracks.
Birds, startled, struck the silk snares;
beasts, terrified, met the sharp points.
Triggers were not pulled in vain,
bowstrings were not drawn a second time.
Arrows did not kill singly;
each strike surely felled a pair.
Whistling and swirling,
arrows and cords entangled together.
Feathers like wind, blood like rain,
drenching the plains and obscuring the sky.
The plains turned crimson,
the brave warriors grew fierce.
Gibbons and apes lost their trees,
jackals and wolves fled in fear.
Then they shifted forces toward the perilous places,
treading together into hidden thickets.
Cornered tigers dashed and charged,
mad rhinoceroses gored and stumbled.
Xǔ Shǎo applied his skill,
Qín Chéng used his strength to break them.
They seized the swift and cunning,
subdued the fierce and biting.
Horns were torn off, necks broken,
fighting bare-handed, killing alone.
They captured leopards like Shī,
dragged bears and chī-dragons.
Pulled rhinoceroses and yaks,
felled elephants and brown bears.
Leaping over deep ravines,
crossing steep cliffs.
Stumbling on jagged rocks,
giant stones tumbled down.
Pines and cypresses toppled,
groves and forests were crushed.
Not a blade of grass or tree remained,
birds and beasts were utterly annihilated.
Then the Son of Heaven ascended the Zhǔyù Lodge,
passed through the Chángyáng Pavilion.
Surveying the lay of the mountains and rivers,
observing the army's slaughter and captures.
The plains lay desolate,
his gaze reached the four borders.
Birds piled upon each other,
beasts lay heaped together.
Afterwards, they gathered the game and assembled the multitude,
discussed merits and bestowed sacrificial meat.
Light cavalry were arrayed to roast the game,
wine carts were brought forth for pouring and drinking.
Cutting fresh meat, feasting in the wild,
raising beacon fires, ordering toasts.
When the feasting and rewards were done,
toil and ease were balanced.
The grand carriage bells chimed,
leisurely they lingered.
Gathering at the Yùzhāng Palace,
overlooking the Kūnmíng Pond.
To the left the Herd-boy, to the right the Weaving-maid,
like the Milky Way without bounds.
Lush trees cast deep shade,
fragrant grasses covered the banks.
Orchids and zhǐ-flowers displayed their hues,
brilliant and luxuriant.
Like brocade spread out, embroidery displayed,
shining brightly across the slopes.
Among birds were black cranes and white egrets,
yellow swans and jiāoguàn.
Cānggā, bǎoyì,
wild ducks, gulls, wild geese.
At dawn they set off from rivers and seas,
by evening they rested on Jiāng and Hàn.
Sinking and floating, coming and going,
gathering like clouds, dispersing like mist.
Then the rear palace ladies boarded covered carriages,
ascended dragon boats,
unfurled phoenix canopies,
raised flowery banners.
Parting embroidered curtains,
they mirrored themselves in the clear streams.
Ruffled by gentle breezes,
they drifted softly afloat.
Rowing maidens sang,
drums and pipes resounded.
The sound was stirring and piercing,
clamoring up to the heavens.
Flocks of birds soared,
fish gazed from the depths.
They lured white pheasants,
brought down pairs of swans.
Casting patterned rods,
they hauled out flatfish.
Handling great nets,
wielding silk cords.
Paired boats raced together,
bending and rising in utmost joy.
Then like wind lifting, clouds swaying,
they floated about, gazing broadly.
Ahead they passed the Qín Ridge,
behind they crossed the Jiǔzōng peaks.
Eastward they neared the Hé and Huà,
westward they traversed Qí and Yōng.
Palaces and lodges they passed through
numbered over a hundred districts.
Wherever they went, morning or evening,
supplies never failed in provision.
Honoring high and low, connecting with mountains and rivers,
they sought the application of blessings and prosperity.
Collecting the joyful songs of wandering children,
ranking the fine eulogies of attending ministers.
At this time,
capitals gazed upon each other,
towns linked one to another.
The state relied on foundations of ten generations,
families inherited enterprises of a hundred years.
Scholars fed on the reputations of old virtues,
farmers tilled the fields of their forebears' plots.
Merchants followed what their clans had long sold,
artisans used the compass and square of their great-grandfathers.
Brilliant and stable,
each was in his proper place.
"As for me,
I merely observe traces in old ruins,
hear tales from aged elders.
I have not grasped even one-tenth of it,
thus I cannot recount it all."
The host of the Eastern Capital sighed and said:
"How profound is the influence of customs upon men!
You are truly a man of Qín,
boasting of palaces and halls,
guarding boundaries of rivers and mountains.
You may well know of Zhāoxiāng and understand Shǐhuáng,
but how can you perceive the deeds of the great Hàn?
As for the founding of the great Hàn,
rising from commoner to ascend the imperial throne,
within a few years creating a legacy for ten thousand generations—
this is something the Six Classics could not discuss,
nor earlier sages could articulate.
At that time,
achievements were vast and aligned with Heaven,
campaigns against rebels followed the people's will.
Thus Lóu Jìng assessed the situation and presented his plan,
Lord Xiāo adapted to circumstances and expanded the system.
Was that a time of peace and ease?
Plans could not but be carried out.
You, sir, have not witnessed this,
yet gaze upon the later generations' final works—
is this not blindness?
Now I shall tell you of the governance of Jiànwǔ,
the affairs of Yǒngpíng.
Observing the Great Purity,
to change your confused mind."
"In the past, Wáng Mǎng committed treason,
and the mandate of Hàn was interrupted.
Heaven and man brought punishment,
and the six directions were destroyed together.
In the chaos of that time,
the living were nearly extinct,
and ghosts and spirits were obliterated.
Ravines held no intact coffins,
and outer walls enclosed no remaining houses.
The plains were glutted with human flesh,
and rivers and valleys flowed with human blood.
The disasters of Qín and Xiàng
were still less than half of this;
since the beginning of written records,
nothing like it had ever been recorded.
Thus, the people below cried out and appealed above,
and the Supreme Emperor, concerned, looked down and inspected.
Then he entrusted the mandate to the Holy Sovereign.
Thereupon, the Holy Sovereign grasped the heavenly talisman,
revealed the earthly treasures.
He unfolded the imperial charts,
examined the divine texts.
With blazing wrath, he roused himself to action,
responding like rising clouds.
He struck like thunder at Kūnyáng,
relying on fury as fierce as thunderbolts.
Then he crossed the great river,
traversed the northern peak.
He established his reign at Gāoyì,
and founded his capital at Héluò.
He continued the legacy of the hundred kings in times of desolation,
following the cosmic process of cleansing and renewal.
He embodied the primal essence and established institutions,
succeeding Heaven and acting accordingly.
He connected to the lineage of Táng,
and continued the thread of Hàn.
He nurtured and fostered all living beings,
restored the borders and territories.
His achievements combined those of the past,
and his labors rivaled those of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
How could it be said that he merely followed the same tracks and imitated the footsteps,
or that he merely joined the ranks of later rulers,
attending to the tasks of recent antiquity,
treading the perilous and easy paths of a single sage?
Moreover, in the first year of Jiànwǔ,
heaven and earth underwent revolution.
Within the four seas,
husbands and wives were newly formed,
and father and son relationships began.
Ruler and subject were first established,
and human relations truly commenced.
This is what Fúxīshì used to lay the foundation for imperial virtue.
Dividing the lands into provinces,
establishing markets and courts,
creating boats and carriages,
and crafting tools and implements—
this is what Xuānyuánshì used to open the path of imperial achievement.
Carrying out Heaven's punishment,
responding to Heaven and complying with the people—
this is what Tāng and Wǔ used to illuminate the kingly enterprise.
Moving the capital and changing the city—
this follows the model of the revival of the Yīn dynasty;
settling in the center of the land—
this follows the system of prosperity and peace under King Chéng of Zhōu.
Without relying on an inch of land or the power of a single person,
he matched the signs of Gāozǔ.
Restraining himself and returning to propriety,
to uphold the beginning and end—
he was truly reverent like Xiàowén.
Modeling on the ancients and examining antiquity,
sealing Tài Mountain and inscribing achievements—
his ceremonies shone like those of Shìzōng.
Examining the Six Classics to assess virtue,
surveying antiquity to discuss merits—
the affairs of benevolence and sageliness were all encompassed,
and the way of emperors and kings was fully realized."
"During the time of Yǒngpíng,
prosperity flourished with harmony.
The grand ceremonies of the Three Halls were splendid,
and the ceremonial robes with dragon motifs were refined.
The dazzling literature,
the brightness radiated.
The ancestral temples were raised high,
and the ceremonial music was made correct.
The harmony between humans and deities was complete,
and the order among officials was already solemn.
Then the great chariots were set in motion,
following the imperial path.
Inspecting the regions and making tours,
personally observing the wealth and poverty of all nations.
They examined the spread of sound teachings,
disseminating the imperial enlightenment to illuminate the dark.
Thereupon, extending the old customs of the Zhōu,
they maintained the city of Luò.
Magnificence was stirred,
and the wings of dignity were unfolded.
The light of the Hàn capital shone over all of China,
gathering all eight directions as the center.
Within the imperial city,
the palaces were bright,
and the towers and courtyards were divine and beautiful.
Such luxury could not be surpassed,
and frugality could not become extravagant.
Externally, they used the fields to create gardens,
filling flowing springs to become ponds.
Spreading duckweed and algae to hide fish,
enriching the meadows to nurture beasts.
The structures were akin to Liáng and Zōu,
the elegance matched the divine park.
Then according to the seasons, they gathered for hunts,
selecting vehicles and troops to lecture on martial arts.
This must be overseen by the royal regulations,
and tested according to poetry and music.
Traversing like a Cǒuyú beast,
observing the horses of finest iron.
Exquisite vehicles were deployed,
and auspicious days were chosen.
The officers of rites arranged the ceremonies,
and the imperial stages set out.
Thereupon the whales were stirred,
and the bells clamored gloriously.
Ascending the jade chariots,
seizing the time like dragons.
The phoenix canopies were resplendent,
and the harmonious sounds of tinkling chimes.
The heavenly officials followed in splendor,
presenting formidable demeanor and elegant form.
Mountain spirits guarded the fields,
while regional deities oversaw everything.
The Rain Masters sprinkled liberally,
and the Wind Lords cleared the dust.
A thousand chariots sounded like thunder,
and ten thousand horsemen bustled.
The main troops spanned the fields,
spears and lances formed like clouds.
Feathers and banners swept the rainbow,
flags and standards brushed the sky.
Blazing fiercely,
the light and motifs flew high.
The sparks emitted gusts of wind,
devouring the plains and moving mountains.
The sun and moon were dimmed,
and the hills and mounds shook.
Finally gathering in the central park,
deploying the army and setting up camp.
Teams of soldiers formed ranks,
the squads were arrayed.
The three armies were assembled,
and the commanders sworn to their roles.
Then signals were sent by beacons, drums beaten,
orders for three drives issued.
The light chariots dashed like lightning,
and the vanguard cavalry sped like electricity.
Yoū Jī released his arrows,
the Fàn clan executed their strategies.
The bowstrings were unerring toward the birds,
the reins were unwavering against encounters.
The flying creatures could not take flight,
the running creatures could not escape.
With a glance and a moment,
the capture carts were already full.
The joy did not reach its peak,
and not all creatures were destroyed.
The horses pawed the ground with leftover energy,
the warriors' anger was not yet released.
The forefront cleared the way,
and the following vehicles adhered to the cadence.
Thereupon offerings of three sacrifices were made,
and five livestock presented.
Honoring the deities,
placating all spirits.
Paying homage in the Bright Hall,
attending the Bìyōng.
Manifesting radiant harmony,
proclaiming the imperial influence.
Ascending the spiritual terrace,
inspecting auspicious omens.
Looking over heaven and earth,
adopting signs to sanctify the sage's conduct.
Within China spreading benevolence,
overlooking the frontiers while confronting challenges.
To the west halting at the source of the Yellow River,
to the east reaching the seashore.
To the north stirring the remote cliffs,
to the south illuminating the red borders.
Different regions and divided areas,
separated by boundaries and not intersecting.
Places not conquered by Emperor Xiàowǔ,
nor subjected by Emperor Xiàoxuān.
All were frightened and trembling,
hastening to come and pay tribute.
Thereupon pacifying Āiláo,
opening up Yǒngchāng.
In spring, three royal assemblies were held,
convening at the Hàn capital.
On this day,
the Emperor received the maps and documents of the world,
accepting tributes from myriad nations.
Internally overseeing the various Chinese states,
externally pacifying the hundred tribes.
Then grand ceremonies and music were raised,
the banquet was set up in the Cloud Dragon Court.
Presenting all officials to praise the assembly of lords,
fully displaying the imperial rituals and the Emperor's presence.
Thereupon the court was filled with a thousand delicacies,
and ten thousand measures of fine wine.
Rows of golden vessels,
and jade cups distributed.
Precious dishes served,
and a grand feast hosted.
Then the food was brought and the wine cleared,
while the grand master played music.
Displaying metal and stone instruments,
arranging strings and bamboo pipes.
The bells and drums resounded melodiously,
and the flutes and strings shone brightly.
Raising the five tones,
reaching the six pitches.
Singing of the nine virtues,
and dancing the eight ranks.
The Sháo and Wǔ performances complete,
and all the grand antiquities were concluded.
Foreign barbarians performed in intervals,
wherever virtue reached.
Jìmèi and Dōulí,
none were absent.
The myriad of musical pleasures were complete,
and every ceremonial rite combined.
The imperial joy was abundant,
and the ministers were intoxicated.
Smoke descended and spread,
harmonizing the primordial qi.
Then the bell was struck to announce the dismissal,
and all officials withdrew."
"Thus, the Sage Emperor, witnessing the joy and pleasure of all regions,
and being bathed in abundant grace,
feared that extravagant desires would arise,
and that diligence in eastern endeavors would slacken.
Therefore, he reaffirmed the old regulations,
and issued a clear edict.
He commanded the officials
to promulgate laws and standards.
He promoted frugality,
and demonstrated utmost simplicity.
He removed the ornate decorations from the inner palace,
and reduced the carriages and attire of the imperial court.
He restrained the excessive pursuits of commerce and industry,
and promoted the flourishing tasks of agriculture and sericulture.
Consequently, he caused the entire realm to abandon trivialities and return to fundamentals,
to turn away from falsehood and return to truth.
Women cultivated weaving and sewing,
men devoted themselves to plowing and sowing.
Utensils were made of pottery and gourds,
clothing favored plain and dark colors.
They were ashamed of fine and luxurious fabrics and did not wear them,
they disdained the rare and beautiful and did not treasure them.
They discarded gold in the mountains,
and sank pearls into the deep.
Thus, the common people cleansed themselves of flaws and impurities,
and mirrored utmost purity.
Their forms and spirits were tranquil and serene,
their ears and eyes were not distracted.
The sources of desires were extinguished,
and the hearts of integrity and shame were born.
All were leisurely and content,
like jade moistened and metal resonant.
Therefore, within the four seas,
schools were as numerous as forests,
academies were filled to the doors.
Toasts were exchanged in交错,
ritual vessels were abundant.
Below, dances were performed; above, songs were sung,
stepping in virtue and chanting of benevolence.
After the rituals of ascending, descending, feasting, and banqueting were completed,
they sighed together in admiration of profound virtue,
speaking forthrightly and expansively.
All, filled with harmony, exhaled their breath,
and praised, saying:
How magnificent is this age!
"Now, those who discuss only know to recite the books of Yú and Xià,
to chant the poems of Yīn and Zhōu.
They lecture on the Changes of Fúxī and King Wén,
and discuss the Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Kǒng.
Rarely can they discern the purity and turbidity of ancient and modern times,
or investigate the origins of Hàn virtue.
Only you, sir, are somewhat familiar with the old classics,
yet you merely gallop along the minor streams.
It is already difficult to review the old and know the new,
and those who understand virtue are few!
Moreover, being secluded on the border with the Western Róng,
surrounded by perilous barriers and fortifications,
and maintaining its defenses—
how can it compare to being situated in the center of the land,
level and open,
with all regions converging like spokes?
The Qín Mountains and Jiǔzōng,
the rivers of Jīng and Wèi—
how can they compare to the Four Rivers and Five Peaks,
girded by the Hé and facing the Luò,
the deep sources of charts and writings?
The Jiànzhāng and Gānquán Palaces,
where immortals are hosted and served—
how can they compare to the Spiritual Terrace and Bright Hall,
which harmonize Heaven and humanity?
The Tàiyè and Kūnmíng Ponds,
parks for birds and beasts—
how can they compare to the Pìyōng, flowing like the sea,
rich in the Way and virtue?
Wandering knights and excessive extravagance,
violating righteousness and encroaching upon ritual—
how can they compare to treading together within the laws and measures,
reverent and orderly?
You, sir, merely study the towering construction of Qín's Ēpáng Palace,
yet do not know that the capital Luò has its regulations;
you recognize that the Hángǔ Pass can be closed,
yet do not know that the kingly ruler has no outside.
Before the host's words had ended,
the guest from the Western Capital was startled and lost composure.
Hesitantly, he descended the steps,
humbled and downcast,
cupping his hands as if to take leave.
The host said:
"Return to your seat,
for now I shall present to you a poem in five stanzas."
After the guest had finished studying it,
he exclaimed:
"How beautiful is this poem!
Its righteousness surpasses that of Yáng Xióng,
its facts rival those of Xiàng Rú.
It is not only due to the host's love of learning,
but also because he has encountered this era.
I, a reckless and simple youth,
know not how to judge.
Having heard the correct Way,
I beg to chant it for the rest of my life."
The poem says:
Oh, bright is the Bright Hall,
the Bright Hall is greatly luminous.
The Sage Emperor conducts the ancestral sacrifices,
solemn and splendid.
The Lord on High feasts and enjoys,
the Five Positions follow their seasons.
Who is worthy to match Him?
It is Shìzǔ, Emperor Guāngwǔ.
Throughout the heavens and across the lands,
each fulfills his duty.
Oh, how brilliant and glorious,
truly embracing abundant blessings.
Then flows the Pìyōng,
the Pìyōng, vast and mighty.
The Sage Emperor arrives here,
building boats to form a bridge.
White-haired elders of the state,
like fathers, like elder brothers.
Modest and dignified in bearing,
filial, friendly, bright and clear.
Oh, majestic Supreme Sovereign,
show us the Hàn way.
Vast transformation, divine indeed,
forever behold its completion.
Then he ascends the Spiritual Terrace,
the Spiritual Terrace, lofty and high.
The Emperor diligently climbs at times,
to examine auspicious signs.
The Three Lights display their essence,
the Five Elements arrange their order.
Gently blows the auspicious wind,
abundantly falls the sweet rain.
A hundred grains grow lush and thick,
all grasses flourish and abound.
Repeatedly comes the year of plenty,
oh, how joyous and delighted!
The mountains present tribute, the rivers offer treasures,
emitting golden light, exhaling floating clouds.
The precious tripod appears, its colors rich and varied.
Brilliant and shining, adorned with dragon patterns.
Ascend the ancestral temple, offer to the sage spirits.
Display the divine virtue, lasting for a hundred million years.
Open the spiritual texts, unfold the auspicious charts,
obtain the white pheasant, present the plain crow.
Good omens abound, gathering at the imperial capital.
Display white feathers, raise splendid plumes,
pure and bright in appearance, oh, in perfect essence.
Manifest the imperial virtue, equal to Zhōu's accomplishment.
Forever prolonged, receiving Heaven's blessings.
There was a Master of Empty Claims,
whose heart was extravagant and body indulgent,
who greatly loved broad knowledge of antiquity,
studying under the old historians,
and thus knew much of former generations' records.
He spoke to Master Peaceful Dwelling, saying:
"Man, in yang times, is relaxed;
in yin times, is sorrowful—
this is tied to Heaven.
Dwelling in fertile land, he is at ease;
dwelling in barren land, he labors—
this is bound to Earth.
Sorrowful, he lacks joy;
laboring, he is narrow in kindness—
few can avoid this.
If small things are thus,
great things should also be so.
Therefore, the emperor relies on Heaven and Earth to effect transformation,
and the myriad people receive the ruler's teachings to form customs.
The root of transforming customs
shifts with circumstances.
How can this be verified?
Qín, based in Yōng, was strong;
Zhōu, situated in Yù, was weak.
Gāozǔ, with his capital in the west, was prosperous;
Guāngwǔ, dwelling in the east, was frugal.
The rise and fall of governance
always stems from this.
Have you, sir, not seen the affairs of the Western Capital?
Allow me to describe them for you.
"When the Han dynasty first established its capital,
it was on the banks of the Wei River.
To the north lay the lands of Qin,
which was indeed Xiányáng.
To the left were the formidable passes of Yáo and Hán, and the barrier of Táolín.
Adjoined by the two Huà mountains,
the giant spirit Bìxì,
with its towering palms and far-reaching steps,
diverted the winding river,
and its traces remain to this day.
To the right was the narrow pass of Lǒngdǐ,
separating the Huáxià from the western tribes.
Qí, Liáng, Qiān, and Yōng,
where the Chénbǎo and the crowing rooster resided.
To the front stood Zhōngnán and Tàiyī,
lofty and precipitous,
shrouded in mist and mystery.
The ridges connected to Bōzhǒng,
embracing Dù and containing Hù,
drinking from Fēng and spitting into Hào,
and here lay the precious jade of Lántián,
from which it originated.
To the rear were high mounds and level plains,
resting upon the Wei and straddling the Jīng.
Vast and sprawling,
they served as a bulwark nearby.
Farther afield were Jiǔzōng and Gānquán,
where the cold was severe and the ice unyielding.
When the sun reached its northernmost point, the frost persisted,
yet here it provided cool respite in summer.
Then there were the broad, fertile fields,
their soil of the highest grade,
truly the divine and blessed region of the earth.
In ancient times, the Great Emperor was pleased with Duke Mù of Qin and granted him an audience,
feasting him with the universal music of heaven.
The Emperor, in his intoxication,
then bestowed a golden tally,
granting him this land,
and cutting off the portion of the Chúnshǒu constellation.
At that time,
there were six powerful states in all,
yet all under heaven came to dwell in Western Qin—
was this not strange indeed?
"From the time our founding emperor first entered,
the five planets converged,
traveling together in the eastern well constellation.
Lóu Jìng laid down his cart shaft,
and offered his unsolicited advice.
Heaven opened his mind,
and men aided his plans.
When the emperor considered the time,
his thoughts also turned to the spirits and deities.
It was fitting that it should be established as the celestial capital.
How could he not reverently ponder the heavenly thoroughfare?
How could he not yearn to return to his hometown of Fényú?
The mandate of heaven is not to be defied,
who would dare to transgress it!
Thus they measured the diameter and circumference,
examined the breadth and length.
They laid out the city moats,
and built the outer walls.
They drew inspiration from the eight capitals, adopting unique designs—
how could they merely follow old precedents?
They examined the Qin system,
and surpassed the Zhou methods.
Narrowing the humble hundred-wall span,
they expanded the cramped nine-mat hall.
They aligned the Purple Palace with Wèiyāng,
and raised the lofty watchtowers at Chānghé.
They leveled Lóngshǒu to support the halls,
shaping them towering and majestic.
Spanning long beams like mighty rainbows,
they joined rafters and purlins in succession.
Inverted lotuses adorned the caisson ceilings,
with red blossoms spreading in profusion.
Ornamented beams and jade finials,
shimmered with radiant brilliance.
Carved pillars and jade bases,
embroidered brackets and cloud-patterned lintels.
Three-tiered stairs and double eaves,
engraved railings and patterned balustrades.
Leveled on the right, stepped on the left,
with green latticework and crimson steps.
They carved layered platforms and level halls,
setting sharp cliffs and steep banks.
Terraces and ridges scaled like fish,
with perilous paths and jagged cliffs.
High banks and level roads,
long paths and steep dangers.
Multiple gates reinforced for security,
to guard against traitors and villains.
Looking up to the blessings of the imperial abode,
where yang shines and yin hides.
Great bells weighing ten thousand jun,
with fierce stands standing firm.
Bearing the anger of the bell frames,
they spread their wings and soared.
The court hall faced east,
the warm chambers extended north.
To the west stood the Jade Terrace,
connected to Kūndé.
Lofty and precipitous,
beyond comprehension of its rules.
As for the Hall of Longevity and Immortality,
Xuānshì and the Jade Hall.
Qílín and Zhūniǎo,
Lóngxīng and Hánzhāng.
Like stars encircling the pole,
they blazed with dazzling splendor.
The main hall, the imperial resting place,
where all officials were received in audience.
The grand palace stood imposing,
with nine gates wide open.
Fine trees planted in the courtyards,
fragrant grasses piled like mounds.
Tall gates with lofty portals,
where golden statues sat in rows.
Inside were constant attendants and ushers,
fulfilling their duties in service.
Lántái and Jīnmǎ,
took turns lodging and residing.
Next were Tiānlù and Shíqú,
places for collating texts.
Further, Hǔwēi and Zhānggōu,
the offices of strict night watches.
Patrol paths encircled the outer perimeter,
a thousand barracks attached within.
The commandant of guards oversaw eight garrisons,
vigilant by night and patrolling by day.
Planted halberds and hanging shields,
prepared for unforeseen events.
"The rear palaces included Zhāoyáng and Fēixiáng,
Zēngchéng and Héhuān.
Lánlín, Pīxiāng,
Fènghuáng, and Yuānluán.
All exquisitely beautiful and splendid,
a sight to behold within.
Thus their halls and chambers, their lodgings and quarters,
were adorned with intricate decorations.
Wrapped in embroidered patterns,
embellished with vermilion and green.
Kingfisher feathers and fiery pearls,
strung together with beautiful jade.
Flowing Xuánlí and the night-shining pearls,
strung with Suí pearls to serve as candles.
Golden thresholds and jade steps,
crimson courtyards gleaming brightly.
Coral, lin, and jasper,
ruǎnmín and línbīn jade.
Precious objects arranged in abundance,
resplendent as Kūnlún.
Though their scale was not vast,
their extravagance surpassed even the emperor's.
Beyond the Gōuchén constellation,
elevated walkways arched high.
Connecting Chánglè and Míngguāng,
leading north directly to Guìgōng.
They commanded the skilled artisans Bān and Ěr,
to exhaust all variations within.
The rear palaces remained unmoved,
the music never shifted.
Gate guards provided curtains and canopies,
officials supplied according to need.
Indulging in whatever pleased them,
descending from the carriage to feast.
Spending years without returning,
yet still unable to see it all.
Marvels renewed each day,
exhausting what had never been seen before.
"The divine beauty of the imperial sovereign,
fears that distinctions of rank are not made clear.
Though this palace is already spacious,
the heart still feels constrained and not yet at ease.
Thinking to compare it to the Purple Palace,
regretting that Āfáng cannot be inhabited.
Seeking the remnants of past lodgings,
I obtained Línguāng from the remnants of Qín.
Situated in the cool heights of Gānquán,
it rises lofty and spreads wide.
Having newly built Yíngfēng,
added Lùhán and Chǔxū.
Resting the high foundation on the mountain ridge,
straight as a rainbow, it dwells aloft.
Reaching the sky, towering and steep,
a hundred chang in diameter, its stem soaring.
Above, adorned with intricate patterns,
below, carved steeply as if cut.
Soaring kūn birds look up but cannot reach,
let alone bluebirds and yellow sparrows.
Leaning on the balustrade and listening downward,
hearing the thunderclaps clash.
Bǎiliáng having suffered disaster,
Yuè witches presented methods.
Jiànzhāng was thus planned,
to ward off fire omens.
The design of its halls and chambers,
rivals that of Wèiyāng.
Round towers soar to touch the sky,
like twin steles facing each other.
Phoenixes poised to fly from roof ridges,
all facing the wind, ready to soar.
Within the palace gates,
Biéfēng stands lofty.
How wondrous the craftsmanship,
interwoven patterns and spacious windows.
Piercing clouds and mist, reaching upward,
appearing tall and slender.
Shénmíng rises abruptly,
Jǐnghàn stacked a hundred layers high.
Resting wandering beams on floating pillars,
connecting double brackets to support each other.
Layered structures rising step by step,
gazing at the North Star with lofty delight.
Dispelling mists and dust within the central court,
gathering the pure clarity of double yang.
Gazing at the long fins of the curved rainbow,
observing where the cloud master rests.
Ascending to flying gates and looking up,
just seeing Yáoguāng and Yùshéng.
About to venture forth, not yet halfway,
trembling with fear and trepidation.
If not for the agility of Dūlú,
who could ascend and explore such heights?
Sàsuō and Dàidàng,
Dào'ào and Jiéjié.
Yìyì and Chéngguāng,
Kuígū and Xiāohuō.
Rafters layered upon rafters,
towering and majestic.
Upturned eaves grand and lofty,
flying corners soaring high.
Flowing light shining within,
drawing the radiance of sun and moon.
The palace of Tiānliáng,
truly opens high gates.
Banners not removed from their poles,
four-horse carriages aligned side by side.
Wheels brushing against each other, swiftly moving,
accommodated through a single gate.
Long corridors and wide halls,
pathways and pavilions spreading like clouds.
Courtyards strangely varied,
doors and gates numbering in the thousands.
Double chambers and secluded gates,
winding and extending endlessly.
Gazing into deep recesses and straight paths,
losing sight of the way back.
Then, precious towers rise magnificently to their utmost grandeur,
stepped paths winding eastward.
Like the distant slopes of Lángfēng,
crossing western moats and cutting through golden walls.
City guards not slackening their night watches,
yet inside and outside secretly connected.
"Before, opening Tángzhōng,
gazing upon vast expanses.
Overlooking Tàiyè Pond,
its dark waters vast and boundless.
Jiāntái stands in the center,
resplendent and grandly spacious.
Clear abyss, vast and wide,
divine mountains, lofty and steep.
Arraying Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng,
flanking Pénglái, arranged in pairs.
Above, forested peaks piled high,
below, jagged cliffs and rugged rocks.
Strong winds whipping against separate isles,
raising great waves and tossing waters.
Soaking stone fungi along steep banks,
washing spirit mushrooms with crimson stems.
Hǎiruò roaming in dark islets,
whales losing their course and stumbling.
Thus adopting Shàojūn's upright faith,
hoping for Luándà's steadfast constancy.
Erecting immortal palms on slender stems,
catching clear dew from cloud tops.
Grinding jade stamens for morning meal,
surely life's span can be prolonged.
Admiring Sōng and Qiáo of old,
seeking Xiànmén on the heavenly road.
Thinking of the ascending dragon at Dǐnghú,
how could worldly customs be worthy of envy?
If one could live through ages eternally,
why hastily build tombs?
"Merely observing the layout of its walls,
then three gates open on each side,
three roads level and straight.
Twelve carriages abreast,
streets and avenues crisscrossing.
Residential quarters orderly and straight,
roof ridges even and level.
North gate, highest mansions,
facing the road, directly opening.
Employing skill to achieve perfection,
expecting no collapse or decay.
Wood clad in brocade,
earth adorned in vermilion and purple.
Armory's forbidden weapons,
set on weapon racks.
If not Shí or Dǒng,
who could dwell here?
Then opening wide nine markets,
connecting market gates and alleys.
Flag towers five stories high,
overlooking a hundred tunnels.
Zhōu system had great officers,
now only captains remain.
Rare goods arriving in abundance,
gathering like birds and fish.
Sellers reap double profits,
buyers lack nothing.
Then merchants of all kinds,
petty traders, husbands and wives.
Selling good mixed with bad,
deceiving and dazzling border folk.
Why must one toil diligently,
when wicked profits suffice?
Those market men and women,
their beauty and luxury rival Xǔ and Shǐ.
As for Wēngbó, Zhuó, Zhì,
Zhānglǐ families.
Striking bells, dining from tripods,
riding in linked processions.
Dōngjīng's dukes and marquises,
how can their grandeur surpass?
Capital city roving knights,
the likes of Zhāng and Zhào.
Ambitions matching Wújì,
emulating Tiánwén's traces.
Light on death, heavy on spirit,
forming cliques and gathering crowds.
Truly numerous are their followers,
their retinue like clouds.
Yuán of Màolíng,
Zhū of Yánglíng.
Agile, fierce, and bold,
like tigers and like chū beasts.
Over the slightest grievance,
corpses stiffen by the roadside.
The chancellor sought to redeem his son's crime,
Yángshī defiled and Gōngsūn executed.
As for the eloquent debaters from five counties.
Street talks and alley discussions,
criticizing right and wrong.
Analyzing to the finest detail,
dissecting flesh and separating fibers.
What they favor grows feathers,
what they hate becomes wounds and scars.
Within suburbs and outskirts,
villages and towns prosperous and abundant.
Merchants from five capitals,
both migrating and attracting.
Trading caravans linking yokes,
rumbling and rolling onward.
Officials and gentry mingling,
chariots and carriages meeting.
Royal domain spanning a thousand lǐ,
governed by the capital governor.
Commandery and state palaces and lodges,
one hundred forty-five in number.
Right reaching Zhōuzhì,
encompassing Fēng and Hù.
Left extending to Hé and Huà,
reaching even Guó territory.
"The imperial Shanglin Park,
spans valleys and covers hills.
To the east it reaches Dǐnghú,
diagonally bordering Xìliǔ.
It encompasses Chángyáng and connects with Wǔzuò,
winds around Huángshān and touches Niúshǒu.
Its winding walls stretch continuously,
for over four hundred lǐ.
Here plants take root and grow,
animals come to dwell.
Flocks of birds flutter and soar,
herds of beasts gallop and roam.
Scattering like startled waves,
gathering like towering peaks.
Even Bó Yì could not name them all,
nor could Lì Shǒu record their numbers.
The abundance of forests and foothills—
what does it not possess?
Among the trees are firs, cypresses, palms, and nanmu,
catalpas, thorn-elms, rosewoods, and maples.
Fine shrubs and thickets,
lush as the Dèng Forest.
Dense and flourishing,
tall and shady.
They bloom with radiant flowers,
spread leaves and cast cool shade.
Grasses include sedges, club-rushes, and reeds,
ferns, bracken, licorice, and knotweed.
King’s-foxtail, artemisia, and lamb’s-quarters,
hollyhocks and shepherd’s-purse.
Profuse and luxuriant,
covering the marshes and blanketing the slopes.
Bamboo groves spread and extend,
forming dense thickets across the fields.
Valleys, mountains, plains, and lowlands,
vast and boundless without end.
Then there is the Kūnmíng Divine Pond,
with its dark waters and mysterious shores.
Encircled by golden dikes,
planted with willows and wolfberries.
Precious halls of towering timber,
rise prominently in its midst.
The Herdboy star stands to its left,
the Weaving Maid resides to its right.
Here the sun and moon rise and set,
resembling Fúsāng and Méngsì.
Within it dwell giant softshell turtles and alligators,
sturgeons, carps, breams, and snakeheads.
Yellowcheeks, giant salamanders, catfish, and gobies,
with long foreheads and short necks.
Broad mouths and upturned noses,
strange kinds and diverse species.
Birds include spoonbills, swans, cranes, and bustards,
wild geese and brants.
In early spring they arrive,
by late autumn they seek warmth.
Southward they soar to Héngyáng,
northward they roost at Yànmén.
Falcons swoop, ducks return,
with fluttering wings and clamorous cries.
Their forms and sounds are myriad,
impossible to fully describe.
"Then, in early winter, gloom descends,
with chilling winds and harsh cold.
Snow drifts and swirls,
ice and frost bite fiercely.
All plants wither and fall,
fierce insects seize their prey.
Then heaven’s cords are shaken,
earth’s net is stretched.
Rivers and streams are stirred,
forests and thickets are tossed.
Birds are all startled,
beasts are all roused.
Some hide in grass, some perch in trees,
dwelling in nests or burrowing in holes.
Fleeing from there, gathering here,
in chaotic, bustling throngs.
Within that divine hunting ground,
before and behind, no boundary is seen.
The gamekeepers oversee it,
managing its domains.
They burn weeds, level grounds,
clear oaks and cut thorns.
Nets are set for a hundred lǐ,
trails are blocked, paths sealed.
Hinds and stags gather in herds,
crowded together, pressed close.
The Son of Heaven then rides in a carved carriage,
drawn by six dappled steeds.
He wears an emerald cap,
leans on a golden armrest.
Jade-adorned caps and tassels,
shimmer with fleeting radiance.
He raises the dark spear banner,
erects the swaying standard.
Perches the calling kite,
trails the cloud-tipped pennant.
Bowed banners and shooting stars,
rainbow streamers and iridescent plumes.
The jeweled canopy follows the celestial axis,
the Net stars lead the way.
A thousand chariots rumble like thunder,
ten thousand riders surge like dragons.
The auxiliary carriages in train,
carry hounds, fierce and swift.
Not merely for amusement,
but also containing secret texts.
Nine hundred tales of fiction,
originating from Yú Chū.
For leisurely inquiry,
they are stored and ready.
Then Chīyóu grasps his battle-axe,
bristling-maned, clad in tiger-skin.
To ward off malign influences,
and discern supernatural evils.
Demons and goblins,
none dare approach him.
Tiger-warriors are arrayed at Fēilián,
fortifications aligned at Shànglán.
Forming units,
marshaling ranks.
Beacon fires blaze with capital fuel,
thunder drums roar in alarm.
Huntsmen are unleashed,
charging into the deep thickets.
Guards clear the way,
warriors blaze with fury.
In crimson jackets and red knee-covers,
they glare fiercely, arrogant and bold.
Their gleam illuminates the celestial court,
their clamor shakes the coastal shores.
The Hé and Wèi rivers churn with waves,
the Wú and Yuè mountains tremble and crumble.
All creatures are terrified and frantic,
dashing headlong, colliding blindly.
They lose their spirit and soul,
forget their way home, their direction.
Throwing themselves under wheels, between spokes,
unsought, they meet their fate.
Flying nets sweep down,
streaming arrows whistle and thud.
No arrow misses its mark,
no dart is cast in vain.
Trodden underfoot, crushed,
caught by wheels, run over.
Birds and beasts lie stiff and dead,
piled like gravel and stones.
Just observe the snares and nets entangling them,
the poles and clubs striking them down.
Forked spears stabbing and piercing,
bare hands wrestling and grappling.
Before the sun has shifted its shadow,
already seven or eight out of ten are slain.
"As for the pheasants soaring high,
crossing steep pits, leaping over marshes.
Hares darting swiftly,
scaling ridges, vaulting gullies.
Compared to the Eastern Guo’s legendary chase,
none could capture them.
Yet there are swift wings and nimble feet,
tracking shadows, pursuing fates.
Birds have no time to take flight,
beasts no chance to escape.
Blue-taloned hawks seize them from the glove,
Hán Lú hounds tear them at the leash’s end.
And then, the fierce and bristle-maned,
with glaring eyes and lofty brows.
Their might overawes rhinoceros and tiger,
none dare oppose them.
Then the warriors of Zhōnghuáng,
the peers of Yù and Huò,
with crimson headbands and disheveled hair,
their hair standing like poles.
Baring arms, pointing fingers,
striding and pacing with vigor.
They rope red elephants by the nose,
encircle giant wild boars.
Capture baboons and hedgehogs,
seize yǎyǔ beasts and suānní.
Tear through thorny hedges,
burst through bramble fences.
The stubborn woods are torn apart,
the dense thickets are laid waste.
Agile, sharp, cunning, and nimble fellows,
venture into caves,
seek out great foxes.
Scale steep cliffs,
hunt kūntú steeds.
From treetop tips,
catch chánhú monkeys.
Leap over strange thickets,
snatch flying squirrels.
"At this time, the favored beauties of the rear palace, such as the Zhaoyí,
were often second only to the imperial carriage.
They admired the Jia clan's outing to the marsh,
and delighted in sharing the carriage like the north wind.
They indulged in roaming and hunting,
their joy was boundless.
Thus, birds and beasts were exhausted,
and the sights were fully taken in.
Lingering and gazing askance,
they gathered at the Chángyáng Palace.
Resting the footmen,
and halting the chariots and horses.
They collected the game and tallied the carcasses,
counting and assessing the numbers.
Setting up racks and arranging the sacrifices,
distributing the spoils of the hunt.
Cutting fresh meat for a wild feast,
rewarding the diligent and honoring the achievements.
The five armies and six divisions,
arrayed in a thousand columns and a hundred layers.
Wine carts poured sweet wine,
side-by-side carriages delivered the feast.
Raising cups and torches aloft,
after toasting, bells were rung.
The stewards galloped on horseback,
inspecting for duplicates and ensuring nothing was overlooked.
Roasts and broiled meats were plentiful,
clear wines abundant.
The imperial grace was vast,
and great virtue was bestowed.
The charioteers were pleased,
and the soldiers forgot their weariness.
The carriage master ordered the departure,
turning the banners and moving to the right.
Wandering leisurely to the Wǔzuò Lodge,
then resting briefly at the Kūnmíng Pond.
Ascending the Yùzhāng Tower,
selecting fine arrows.
Pú Qiě shot,
striking down the high-flying swans.
Hooking white cranes,
and linking flying dragons.
The stone-tipped arrows never missed their mark,
each shot always brought down a pair.
"Then they ordered the boat masters,
to perform water entertainments.
Floating on the prows of egret-headed boats,
shaded by cloud-like canopies.
Hanging pheasant-feathered parasols,
erecting feathered banners.
Rowing maidens in unison,
singing boat songs freely.
Starting the lead and response songs,
harmonizing with reed pipes.
Playing the Huáinán melody,
and performing the Yáng'ē dance.
Moved by the river god Féng Yí,
and longing for the Xiang River goddesses.
Startling the water spirits,
and frightening the蛟 dragons and snakes.
Then they angled for bream and snakehead fish,
and caught catfish and perch.
Gathering purple cowries,
and capturing aged turtles.
Seizing water leopards,
and tethering submerged buffalo.
The marsh overseer acted recklessly,
what care for spring or autumn?
Probing the clear shallows,
and searching the streams and rivers.
Spreading the nine-fold nets,
setting up fine-meshed traps.
Scooping up昆鮞 fish,
exterminating the aquatic creatures.
Lotus roots were uprooted,
clams and mussels were stripped.
Indulging desires in fishing and hunting,
emulating the capture of fawns and young deer.
Stirring the waters into turmoil,
draining the ponds and cleansing the marshes.
Above, no bird escaped flight,
below, no beast was left running.
Seizing unborn young and gathering eggs,
taking all, down to ant eggs and locust larvae.
Seeking pleasure for today,
who has time to worry about the future?
Once settled and at peace,
how could they foresee collapse and ruin?
"The imperial procession visited the Pínglè Palace,
displaying甲乙 tents and covering them with kingfisher-feathered quilts.
Accumulating treasures and curios,
a profusion of splendor and extravagance.
Facing the vast square for distant views,
presenting marvelous wrestling performances.
Wū Huò lifted the cauldron,
Dūlú performers climbed poles.
Charging through narrow rings and swallow-diving,
chests thrust against sharp blades.
Tossing balls and swords with dexterity,
meeting while walking on tightropes.
Magnificent as Mount Huà's towering peaks,
with ridges and peaks uneven.
Divine trees and magical plants,
their red fruits hanging in clusters.
Gathering immortal performers,
leopards and bears dancing in play.
A white tiger played the sè,
a azure dragon blew the chí.
The goddesses sat and sang long songs,
their voices clear, melodious, and lingering.
Hóngyá stood directing,
clad in feathered garments.
Before the song was finished,
clouds gathered and snow flew.
At first, lightly drifting,
then falling thick and fast.
Multi-storied pavilions and layered towers,
rolling stones sounded like thunder.
The crash of stones echoed and amplified,
booming like the wrath of heaven.
A giant beast a hundred fathoms long,
this was the 'Mànyán' performance.
Divine mountains lofty and steep,
suddenly appearing from behind.
Bears and tigers climbed and wrestled,
apes leaped and reached high.
Strange beasts pranced about,
giant birds paced slowly.
A white elephant walked with its young,
its trunk dangling, coiled like a wheel.
Sea creatures transformed into dragons,
their forms winding and undulating.
The Xīanlì beast opened its mouth,
and turned into an immortal carriage.
Harnessed to four deer,
with a mushroom canopy and nine-petaled flowers.
Toads and turtles,
water people playing with snakes.
Fantastical and sudden transformations,
changing appearances and dividing forms.
Swallowing knives and spitting fire,
clouds and mist enveloping all.
Drawing rivers on the ground,
flowing like the Wèi and connecting to the Jīng.
Dōnghǎi Huánggōng,
with a red knife and Yuè incantations.
Hoping to subdue the white tiger,
but in the end, unable to save himself.
Relying on evil and practicing deceit,
thus his arts did not succeed.
Then they set up performance chariots,
and erected long banners.
Boy performers showcased their talents,
flipping up and down gracefully.
Suddenly falling headfirst, caught by their heels,
as if plummeting to their end, yet reconnecting.
A hundred horses with shared reins,
galloping side by side.
Acrobatics atop poles,
their postures beyond compare.
Bending bows to shoot at the Xīqiāng,
then turning to shoot at the Xiānbēi."
"Thus all transformations cease,
hearts intoxicated and drunk.
Pleasure reaches its peak,
melancholy gathers in the heart.
Secretly warning the palace guards,
incognito, bending to concealment.
Descending from nobility to humility,
concealing the imperial seal and ribbons.
Wandering through the alleys and lanes,
surveying the outskirts and suburbs.
Like the divine dragon's transformations,
manifesting the emperor's supreme dignity.
Then passing through the side chambers,
arriving at the pleasure halls.
Casting aside fading beauty,
following charming grace.
Urging close seating in the central hall,
wine cups circulate without count.
Secret dances alternate in performance,
skilled talents display their arts.
Bewitching allure surpassing Xià Jī,
beautiful voices rivaling Yú Shì.
Slowly advancing with delicate forms,
seeming unable to bear the weight of silk.
Singing the Qīngshāng melody while turning back,
enhancing grace and elegance.
Bodies swirling and swiftly moving,
like startled cranes flocking together.
Shaking vermilion slippers over trays and cups,
waving long sleeves with a rustling sound.
Graceful postures and refined demeanor,
beautiful garments shimmering brilliantly.
Glancing with enchanting eyes,
a single look topples a city.
Even Zhǎn Jì or a Sāngmén monk,
who could remain unmoved?
Ranks of fourteen noble titles,
competing in charm to gain favor.
Prosperity and decline are fickle,
only love determines fate.
Empress Wèi rose for her black hair,
Fēiyàn was favored for her slender form.
Thus indulging desires to the fullest,
exhausting oneself in extreme pleasure.
Heeding the warning of the Táng poem,
'others will take joy.'
Since the ruler sets the precedent,
what rituals can restrain?
Adding Zhāoyí to Jiéyú,
worthy men made dukes and then marquises.
Promising the Zhào clan the highest honor,
wishing to present Dǒng as a tribute to Yǒuyú.
Wáng Hóng argued by the seat,
yet Hàn's records remained secure and unchanged.
"Gāozǔ founded the enterprise,
successors inherited the foundation.
Brief toil for eternal ease,
governing through non-action.
Indulging in pleasure as they pleased,
what worries or thoughts?
Passing through many years,
over two hundred cycles.
Merely due to fertile lands and abundant fields,
all things prosperous and plentiful.
Surrounded by steep cliffs and strong defenses,
easily guarded strategic passes.
Those who gain it become strong,
those who hold it endure long.
Long rivers are hard to exhaust,
deep roots are hard to decay.
Thus extravagance and indulgence,
fragrance and splendor grow ever more.
I, a humble scholar born beyond three hundred years,
hear tales from the unheard.
Vaguely as if in a dream,
unable to glimpse even a corner.
How does this compare to the Yīn people's frequent moves,
eight before and five after?
Dwelling in Xiàng, ruined in Gěng,
never settling their land.
Pángēng issued his proclamation,
leading people through hardship.
Now the sage emperor,
sharing the title of 'Emperor' with heaven,
encompassing all within the seas as his home,
the wealthiest enterprise,
none greater than ours.
Yet regret that splendor cannot adorn the state,
only frugality and stinginess in pettiness,
forgetting what the 'Cricket' poem says?
Is it wanting but unable,
or able but unwilling?
I am secretly perplexed,
wishing to hear an explanation to resolve this.
Master Ānchǔ then seemed unable to speak,
silent for a moment,
then smiled gently and said:
What you, guest, speak of,
is superficial learning and shallow understanding,
valuing hearsay over sight!
If one has a chest but no heart,
unable to restrain with ritual,
no wonder you scorn the present and glorify the past!
Yóu Yú, a lone minister from the Western Róng,
admonished Duke Mù over palaces,
how then can warming the old to know the new,
examining right and wrong,
approach such confusion?
"In the late Zhōu dynasty,
governance failed,
policies grew corrupt.
Starting with palace favoritism,
ending with metal tigers.
The Yíng clan spread its wings,
preying on the western cities.
At that time,
the seven powers contended,
competing in extravagance and splendor.
Chǔ built Zhānghuá earlier,
Zhào erected Cóngtái later.
Qín Zhèng, with sharp beak and long talons,
finally dominated the arena,
seeking to monopolize extravagance,
so none could match him.
Then constructing Ēpáng Palace,
raising Gānquán Palace,
linking cloud towers,
crowning the southern mountains.
Taxes exhausted,
human strength drained.
Then collecting two-thirds levies,
threatening with extermination of three clans.
Treating the people,
like grass cutters mowing weeds,
after piling them up,
setting them ablaze!
Trembling commoners,
not merely cramped under high heaven,
treading carefully on thick earth?
They fought for survival by their necks!
Driven into service,
only strength mattered,
the people could not endure,
thus they rested their burdens on the great Hàn and joyfully supported Gāozǔ.
"Gāozǔ received the mandate and charts,
executing punishment in accord with heaven,
raising the vermilion banner and establishing his reign.
Those he overthrew were doomed to perish,
those he preserved were sure to endure.
Sweeping Xiàng's army at Gāixià,
binding Zǐyīng at Zhǐtú.
Using Qín's palaces,
seizing its treasuries.
The plan to build Luòyáng,
he had no time for.
Thus western craftsmen built palaces,
eyes accustomed to Ēpáng.
Designs exceeding limits,
neither measured nor good.
Reduced and reduced again,
yet still surpassing Zhōu's halls.
Observers deemed them crude and simple,
the emperor already criticized excess and found no comfort.
"Moreover, Gāozǔ, having received the mandate to establish the house,
created our central Xià.
Wén again personally practiced frugality,
achieving peaceful and prosperous virtue.
Wǔ greatly expanded territories,
with solemn achievements in rituals and sacrifices.
Xuān emphasized authority to pacify the Róng and Dī,
Hūhán came to submit.
All recorded ancestors and honored rulers,
sacrifices unceasing,
merits inscribed on bronze vessels,
growing brighter through generations.
Now discarding pure virtue to discuss flawed conduct,
taking what the Spring and Autumn Annals忌讳 as praiseworthy tales,
should raise no issue with the past,
yet you obscure good and promote evil,
merely showing your lack of understanding.
If unrestrained luxury is deemed worthy,
then Huángdì's Hé Palace,
Yǒuyú's Zǒngqī,
surely比不上 Xià Jiǔ's Yáotái,
Yīn Xīn's Qióngshì.
Whom did Tāng and Wǔ overthrow with armies?
Why not look to events of Dōngjīng for enlightenment?
"Moreover, when the Son of Heaven governs well,
his domain is secure overseas.
He maintains his position with benevolence,
not relying on narrow means or causing harm.
If the people's will is not trustworthy,
what use are rugged cliffs and surrounding belts?
Qín relied on the barrier of the two passes,
yet they opened Xiàng and received Pèi.
They occupied a small region and plotted narrowly,
how could this compare to residing at the center and planning broadly?
"In ancient times, when the former kings established cities,
they surveyed the nine regions,
there was no land they did not develop.
They used the gnomon to measure shadows,
neither shortened nor extended.
They considered the intersection of wind and rain,
only then building the royal city.
They carefully examined curves and contours,
with the Luò River behind and the Yellow River as a boundary,
Yi on the left and Chān on the right.
The western barrier was the Nine Hills,
the eastern gate was Yuán.
Mèng Crossing was the rear access,
Tài Valley the front access.
The circuitous way led to Yī Què,
the winding path was swift at Huán Yuán.
The Great Hall was a stabilizing force,
supported by the Xióng'ěr Mountains.
The Dǐzhù River interrupted its flow,
anchored by the Great Píng Mountain.
With warm medicinal springs,
black cinnabar and dark stones.
Wangyǔ Mountain was situated,
capable of supporting a turtle with three legs.
The abode of Mì Fēi,
spiritual power manifested in order.
The dragon's chart was given to Xī,
the turtle's script handed to Sì.
Zhào Bó selected the site,
divining Luò was nourishing.
Duke Zhōu set the initial foundation,
his guidelines were straight.
Cháng Hóng and Wèi Shū,
expanded and defined its limits.
The main path had nine trails,
the city's corners nine fold walls.
The halls were measured with mats,
the chambers with benches.
The capital city was orderly,
a place the four directions observed.
At Han's inception they did not dwell there,
hence the ancestral line was disrupted.
"Great cunning arose among them,
secretly manipulating the divine instrument.
Passing through three cycles of years,
they relied on theft to secure the heavenly position.
At that time the common people,
dared not question or oppose.
Their fear and respect were heavy indeed!
Our illustrious ancestor was angered,
he soared like a dragon to Bái Shuǐ,
like a phoenix to Sān Capital.
He wielded the axe in forty-seven lands,
removing the disorderly officials.
At the start of a fortnight, Āo Xiàng appeared,
leaving no evil remaining.
The universe was secured and peaceful,
he yearned for harmony and sought balance.
With profound wisdom and insight,
he established the palace at Luò.
The timely saying was to halt,
clarity and radiance were harmoniously united.
Having illuminated his military prowess,
benevolence spread and the way was abundant.
He ascended Mount Tài to confer titles,
like the yellow river, he matched in greatness.
"When it came to Xiǎnzōng,
the cosmos was prosperous.
He renewed and exalted virtue,
thus creating Déyáng.
Opening the southern unique gate,
establishing the firm Āngÿing gate.
Extending virtuous kindness to honor the worthy,
raising his righteous reputation to the golden merchants.
Flying dragons in spring paths,
gathering divine tigers in autumn quarters.
Elevating the figures at the twin towers of Èr Wèi,
signifying the reestablishment of the ancient codes.
Internally preserving the virtue at Zhāngtái,
heavenly fortune expressed clearly.
Warm and graciously welcoming spring,
ensuring longevity and perpetual peace.
The flying pavilion with its spiritual form,
none can describe its shape.
Cleanse the dragon's spring, fragrant forest,
nine valleys and eight streams.
Hibiscus covers the waters,
autumn orchids cover the banks.
Fish leap in the islets,
turtles swim in the depths.
Eternal peace in the detached palace,
slender bamboos green in winter.
The shaded pool quietly flows,
the dark spring pure and clear.
The hornbill roosts in autumn,
the hawk sings in spring.
The kuku bird honors the yellow,
chirping resonantly.
To the south stands the forward hall of Líng Terrace,
commanding harmony and blessing.
The arced gate with winding pavilion,
curved and supported by city moats.
Strange trees and rare fruits,
the responsibilities of Hook Shield.
Ascend to the little Huá in the west,
lookout posts refined and commanded.
Within the Nine Dragons,
it is called Good Virtue.
The southwest exits,
without carving or cutting.
Our emperor loved simplicity,
hence he feasted and rested there.
To the east the great pool is clear,
greenish waters gently ripple.
Inside lush with water birds,
outside replete with reeds.
Offering turtles, sea clams, and fish,
providing snails, aquatic chestnuts, and lotus.
To the west lies the fairground of Pínglè,
showing distant spectating.
Dragons and sparrows coil and wind,
celestial horses straddle the sky.
Magnificent and peculiar,
resplendent and bright.
Grandeur not yet extravagant,
frugal yet not crude.
Adhering to kingly measures,
actions always appropriately timed.
"Therefore, when observing the rites,
the ceremonies fully employed.
Starting not in haste,
completion not in a single day.
Yet it's said those who built were weary,
those who dwelled were at ease.
Admiring the thatched homes of Tāng and Yú,
considering the humble rooms of Xià Hòu.
Thus developing three palaces,
distributing teachings and norms.
Overlapping temples with layered roofs,
eight thoroughfares and nine halls.
Measuring the heavens and squaring the earth,
offering the opportunity to guide the locales.
Constructed boats and clear ponds,
only waters vast and wide.
Left controlled by Piyōng,
right established the Líng Terrace.
Advancing as decline approached,
elevating the worthy and simplifying the capable.
Observe the auguries at the shrine,
praying to remove and avert calamity.
"On Mèngchūn's first day,
the many lords stood by the side.
Hundreds of officials conducted themselves properly,
all gathering here.
The vassal states offered gifts,
remote places sent ambassadors.
Every emperor's minister,
presented treasures and carried offerings.
Those who came before the throne,
numbered in the tens of thousands.
Then, the nine guests took precedence,
courtiers were arranged in order.
The honored chariots were arrayed,
bells and drums prepared.
Commanders ordered the ranks,
spears and halberds crossed.
Dragon carriages filled the courtyard,
cloud-like banners waved.
Summer's culmination in three gatherings,
bright torches filled the court.
The great bell tolled,
the sacred drum beat,
vibrating throughout the borders,
echoing with resounding crashes.
It was like swift thunder turning to rumbling and gusty winds."
"At this time, after the announcement of the imperial procession had been made,
the carved carriage descended at the eastern wing.
He wore the Tongtiān crown,
carried the jade seal,
draped the imperial sash,
and girded the Gānjiāng sword.
With his back to the axe-patterned screen,
seated on a layered mat with fine silk borders,
flanked by jade armrests on both sides,
he faced south to hold audience.
Then the various lords entered,
the master of ceremonies distinguished their ranks,
arranging them in order of nobility and humility,
and after the offerings of jade disks, lambs, furs, and silks were presented,
the Son of Heaven greeted them with the ritual of three bows.
Solemn and dignified,
majestic and grand,
orderly and harmonious,
imposing and stately—
truly, it was a magnificent spectacle under heaven.
Then he summoned the dukes, marquises, ministers, and officials,
ascending from the eastern steps,
inquiring into myriad affairs,
consulting on court governance,
diligently sympathizing with the people's hardships,
and removing their afflictions.
If anyone did not find their proper place,
it was as if he himself had cast them into a pit.
Bearing the heavy responsibility of the world,
he did not slacken but remained vigilant and tranquil.
He opened the capital's granaries,
distributed the treasury's wealth.
Rewarding the imperial officials,
down to the lowly servants.
He ordered the kitchen steward to prepare a grand feast,
with provisions overflowing to the households of the attendants.
The spring wine was pure and mellow,
the roasted meats fragrant and savory.
Ruler and ministers rejoiced in harmony,
all intoxicated and merry.
Thousands of ranks and myriad officials,
after their duties were done, withdrew respectfully.
Diligently reflecting and examining,
striving with earnest effort.
