Gazing south to Qí'ào,
where green bamboos grow pure and lush;
facing north to Zhāngfǔ,
where winter and summer differ in their marshes.
Divine drums resound distantly from high ridges,
spiritual echoes occasionally startle the four directions.
Hot springs gush forth with white waves,
Huáqīng cleanses evil and defies aging.
Ink wells and salt ponds,
dark springs and white liquids.
Its fields are of medium grade,
its soil is white.
Plains and lowlands level and even,
mounds and slopes high and broad.
Some towering and with layered plateaus,
some bright and open and expansive.
Heaven and earth interact in harmony and blend in mist,
auspicious signs appear clearly and manifest in advance.
Therefore, portents have stirred since ancient times,
buds and roots existed in the past.
Hidden energies in prophecies and weft texts,
secret images in bamboo and silk.
Silent and profound across changing times,
shining brilliantly in response to destined fortune.
And when the martial sage soared like a dragon,
he began to receive the mandate and shine in residence."
"From its very inception,
auspicious signs were divined.
Consulting both tortoise shell and milfoil,
all proved favorable and true.
Its outer walls were built,
its moats and ramparts fortified.
The design from the beginning
encompassed the wisdom of a hundred kings.
It modeled the dwellings of Yōng and Yù,
replicated the palaces of eight ancient capitals.
It observed the thatched huts of Táng Yáo,
examined the humble halls of Xià Yǔ.
Gǔgōng initiated its creation,
and lofty gates rose majestic;
King Xuān restored its glory,
building chambers by the hundred.
Combining the ways of sages and wise men,
blending refinement and substance in form.
Balancing richness and simplicity with moderation,
measuring according to the standards of the age.
Pondering the hexagrams deeply,
emulating the 'Great Strength' trigram.
Studying Xún Qīng's teachings,
adopting Xiāo Xiàng's methods.
Selecting timber from the forest overseer,
entrusting the master craftsman with the complete blueprint.
People from near and far came joyfully to assist,
artisans debated and showcased their skill.
Applying the principles of the marking line and compass,
following the precise rules of the equinoxes.
Measuring the sun's shadow,
observing the stars' radiance.
Establishing the altars of soil and grain,
erecting the ancestral temple.
Raised palaces encircled the grounds,
aligned with ridges and slopes without deviation.
Constructing the broad hall of Wénchāng,
achieving the grand scale of its beams and rafters.
Lofty as towering mountains rising majestic,
vast as dark clouds stretching high and hanging low.
Rare timbers of immense size,
arranged in harmonious irregularity.
Beams and rafters intricately joined,
brackets and corbels layered in succession.
Vermilion beams arch like rainbows spanning side by side,
crimson rafters densely arrayed in splendid disarray.
Ornate caisson ceilings arranged with hanging stems,
lotus blossoms layered in petals cascading downward.
Dragon-head spouts aligned to gush rainwater,
channeling it into flowing pools.
Rows of pillars stand in orderly grace,
their reflections shimmering and gleaming.
Eaves dark and deep,
steps rugged and layered.
The long courtyard smooth as a whetstone,
bell stands arrayed on either side.
No trace of dust in the wind,
no hint of damp in the rain.
Majestic northern gate towers,
the southern approach follows a stately path.
Twin stone tablets rise steep and tall,
like chariots aligned wheel to wheel.
To the west opens Yánqiū Gate,
to the east unfolds Chángchūn Gate.
Here lords are received in audience,
guests entertained with reverence.
"To the left lies the crimson central court,
where governance and rest reside.
Unadorned and without excess,
avoiding extravagance and extremes.
Wood bears no intricate carvings,
earth wears no silk brocade.
Refined by profound transformation,
embodying the nation's ethos.
Ahead stand Xuānmíng and Xiǎnyáng Halls,
honoring virtue and revering ritual.
Inner gates open wide,
with dignified and orderly presence.
Precious trees lush and graceful,
exotic flowers flourishing abundantly.
Fragrant breezes sweet as incense,
sweet dew pure as fine wine.
Within the forbidden towers and ministerial offices,
interconnected gates face covered corridors.
Direct affairs find their path here,
laws and statutes are stored within.
Rows of attendants stand dignified,
golden cicada ornaments gleaming in unison.
At dawn they attend the imperial canopy,
presenting words with proper form.
Next are the officials behind the pillars,
internal attendants upholding the law.
Keepers of tallies and ushers,
stewards of seals and reserves.
Officers oversee the kitchens,
officials manage medicines and remedies.
Meals and wines follow the seasons,
ensuring bodily harmony and health.
To the rear are Jiāohè and Wénshí Halls,
with long lanes and winding paths.
Catalpa, cedar, and magnolia trees,
quarters arranged in orderly sequence.
Doors face southwest,
completed not in a single day.
Vibrant colors glow brilliantly,
especially within the warm chambers.
Mirroring the cosmos in form,
portraying the images of sages and worthies.
Adorned with a hundred auspicious signs,
embellished with elegant verses.
Through the vastness of ages,
here finds its reflection.
As Yǒuyú created paintings,
here too is a match in splendor."
"To the right are the Garden of Scattered Plots and the Winding Pond,
with terraces below and high halls above.
Orchid islets flourish lushly,
stone rapids rush and roar.
Delicate stems bear fruit,
light leaves stir with fragrance.
Turtles dash and fish leap,
as if at the Lǚliáng Rapids.
Winding carriage paths pass beneath fruit-laden trees,
extended pavilions and connecting halls are meticulously arranged.
Flying stairways and square palanquins lead straight west,
three terraces stand arrayed, lofty and steep.
The lofty Sun Terrace rises from a shaded base,
resembling Mount Huàshān carved sheer.
Above, beams are layered and eaves doubled,
below, ice chambers lie dark and frozen.
Encircling galleries reach to the mid-heavens,
vermilion steps face the whirling winds.
The towering structures rise majestically,
clear dust drifts and swirls.
Cloud-pheasants tread the roof-ridges and raise their heads,
strong wings spread carvings against the azure sky.
Before thunderclouds darken half the sky,
bright sunlight already bathes the patterned windows.
Practicing steps, pausing, ascending and descending,
clad in spring attire, wandering at ease.
The eight extremes can be encompassed in a glance,
all things can be harmonized in a single morning.
Long roads lead to the Mǔshǒu Palace,
patrol paths crisscross each other.
Sundials and water-clocks mark the solemn hours,
day and night follow their measured course.
Attached are racks for spears and halberds,
garrisoned with imperial guards.
Sentinels guard against evil,
the Hooked Array remains unalarmed.
Thus high walls and deep moats,
battlements girded by waterways.
The four gates stand tall and imposing,
grand mansions rise in layers.
Relying on the Great Purity to form a unified whole,
transcending dust and mist to find their origin.
Distant and perilous they soar,
lofty and firm they stand.
Facing the scorched plains without fear,
who could match such strength and agility?
With hills and peaks eternally secure,
not bound by the cycles of worldly sacrifice.
The sun's spirit halts its radiance upon their surfaces,
dark deities dwell shrouded within.
Adorned with the Black Tortoise,
accompanied by deep forests.
Winding walls enclose opened gardens,
viewing pavilions face one another.
Plump fruits among watered thickets,
towering trees rise high.
Bamboo groves embrace the wind,
grapevines form dense shade.
Deep pools whirl and eddy,
accumulated waters run deep.
Reeds and rushes grow thick,
tall grasses stand dense.
Red lotus leaves float on waves, bright and gleaming,
green water caltrops drift on ripples, soaking in the deep.
Feathers flutter up and down,
scales sink and float.
Perching birds choose their trees,
calling birds select their notes.
Like the roars of Bóxiè and Gūyú,
often the crane cries from the shade.
Displaying clear hunting preserves,
inscribing admonitions for gamekeepers.
Thinking of the nation's concerns,
forgetting the pursuit of game.
Woodcutters come and go without hindrance,
deer roam freely, unrestrained.
Lush and fertile are the wild fields,
vast and orderly the plowed acres.
Sweet tea plants stir with life,
grain crops flourish here.
Xīmén irrigated them in earlier times,
Shǐ Qǐ watered them later.
Twelve channeled streams,
sharing one source but different mouths.
Stored, they form massed clouds;
released, they become falling rain.
Water nurtures rice and glutinous rice,
land cultivates millet and broomcorn.
Dark and dense are mulberry and cudrania,
glossy and rich are hemp and ramie.
Fields evenly divided, plots clearly marked,
farmhouses scattered in rows.
Ginger and taro grow thick and full,
peach and plum trees cast deep shade.
Families dwell peacefully in their places,
content with fine clothes and self-delight.
Village homes gaze upon each other,
yet separated for generations.
"Within, streets converge like spokes,
vermilion towers mark the corners.
Stone pillars support flying bridges,
extending to control the Zhāng Canal.
Drains and ditches are cleared to border the roads,
rows of green locust trees shade the paths.
Comparable to the Cānglàng Waters for washing,
surpassing covered walkways for strolling.
Bustling are the officials' caps and canopies,
numerous are the common folk.
The grey-haired carry no burdens,
travelers yield the way.
Offices established, duties divided,
workplaces and residences arranged.
Flanked by government bureaus,
ordered by neighborhoods and wards.
The bureaus hold ranks equal to the Three Ministers,
officials exceed the Six High Officers.
Titles like Fèngcháng,
names such as Dàlǐ.
Grand buildings share one measure,
ornate screens equally splendid.
Solemn are the steps and corridors,
double gates secured with bolts.
Ministers and instructors reside here,
pillars supporting the realm.
The wards include Chángshòu, Jíyáng,
Yǒngpíng, Sīzhōng.
There is also the Qīlǐ quarter,
east of the palace grounds.
Gates open for elders,
lanes embrace the lords.
The Protector-General's hall,
chambers with patterned windows.
Carriages and riders crowd the mornings,
trotting to and fro within.
Guesthouses built around the wards,
adorned as gathering places for visitors.
Majestic is the lofty gate of the Fēng Tower,
first erected in the Jiàn'ān era.
Walls repaired, rooms enclosed,
side-rooms and corridors interwoven.
Carving tools never idle,
craftsmen's skills accumulated.
The lodgings of Guǎngchéng cannot compare,
the mansions of Gǎojiē cannot match.
Expanding three markets, opening shops,
registering level crossroads that reach nine directions.
Rows of stalls arrayed in full display,
market gates set like belts and collars.
Balancing surpluses and shortages,
by midday all gather complete.
Flagpoles of market offices rise high,
boasting the broad vista seen.
A hundred alleys with wheel-hubs clashing,
linked carts worth ten thousand strings.
Leaning on carriage rails, whipping horses,
sleeves and curtains fluttering half-open.
Unifying all regions into harmony,
displaying the utmost in varied splendor.
Contracts fair, exchanges made,
coins and cloth traded beyond count.
Wealth transformed through craftsmanship,
goods circulated through commerce.
Rare and precious items,
here find no place.
Utensils suited for lasting use,
objects shunning flaws, seeking perfection.
No peddling of deceit nor inflated prices,
manifesting the pure customs of honest practice.
The treasury of autumn harvests,
abundant beyond measure.
Equally supplied to the great storehouses,
controlling and drawing upon worldly resources.
Tribal tributes piled high,
precious goods filling to the brim.
Customs-posts harmonize weights and measures,
revenues and taxes handled with care.
Yān bows fill arsenals, stockpiled for strength,
Jì horses crowd stables, sturdy and swift.
"When formidable foes arose in turmoil,
the lands knew no peace.
The sagely martial ruler spoke forth,
to display his awesome might.
Armor and helmets layered thick,
banners and flags waved high.
Bows of polished shell unstrung,
spears and lances gleamed bright.
Armor of triple layers,
coarse silk tassels on helmets.
Drawing bows and selecting arrows,
skillfully matching Gèng Léi.
All clad in practice armor with sharp halberds,
arrayed in flanking formations.
Fully deploying with disciplined order,
employing orthodox and unorthodox tactics in fourfold assaults.
Grand strategies mastered thoroughly,
eyes missing no regulation.
Pushing the vanguard through accumulated years,
the edge of their spirit grew ever sharper.
Three engagements, three victories,
recorded both in books and by the moon.
Subduing those who defied fate,
swallowing the roaring and fierce.
Clouds dispersed rebellion and defiance,
sweeping away plunder and slaughter.
Awe-inspiring power reached the eight directions,
remote and rugged lands all followed.
Washing weapons on sea islands,
grooming horses on river isles.
Returning troops in rumbling chariots,
turning banners homeward, long and leisurely.
Victorious return shared in drinking,
distributing ranks and rewards widely.
Court without wasted seals,
state without lingering expenses.
"After chaos was quelled, feasts could be held;
warriors returned their beasts and ceased war.
Stern axes sheathed blades in scabbards,
rainbow banners furled and rolled up.
Considering the 'Great Plan,'
deliberating on statutes and laws.
Observing the constant,
comprehending its changes.
Above, the ruler governed effortlessly by covenant;
below, officials followed the mean and encouraged themselves.
When the Way arrived, it was esteemed;
when profit was pursued, it was despised.
Prisons empty and silent,
granaries overflowing abundantly.
Then the Eastern Yí were pacified and ordered,
the Western Qīng submitted and followed the way.
Jīngnán cherished kindness,
Shuòběi longed for righteousness.
Long and winding roads,
crossing mountains and fording rivers.
Carrying infants and bearing tribute,
through repeated translation, offering baskets of gifts.
Chieftains with hair tied up,
heroes with earrings of gold.
Wearing their barbarian attire,
tucking robes at the Wèi palace gates.
Setting wine in Wénchāng Hall,
high arrays prepared overnight.
The night not yet deep,
courtyard torches brightly shining.
Guests numerous and grand,
splendid and majestic.
Tall and imposing caps and ribbons,
abundant braided hair.
Clear wine like the Jǐ River,
turbid ale like the Hé River.
Chilled sweet wine flowing freely,
warm fermented liquor leaping in waves.
Rich dishes abundant,
traveling kitchens bustling.
Harmonious feasts with wine,
merry banquets without clamor.
Extending the grand music,
performing the nine movements.
Topping it with 'Sháo' and 'Xià,'
covering it with 'Liù Jīng.'
Sudden sounds arose,
as if shaking thunder.
Heaven's vault startled,
earth's dwellings shocked.
Vast as if the great emperor's creations,
as the two Yíng had once heard.
Constant melodies of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo,
usual tunes of gourd, clay, leather, and wood.
Decorations of shields, axes, feathers, and plumes,
Daily use of hereditary arts,
heard and perceived by ears and eyes.
Blended and interwoven,
comprehensive and extensive.
Music overseen by the Dī Lóu,
tunes of Mèi Mèi, Rèn, and Jìn.
To entertain the lords of the four barbarians,
to harmonize the customs of the eight wilds.
"After plowing and hunting,
then roaming and delighting.
Ceremonial plowing to move with ritual,
grand reviews to act with righteousness.
Preparing the imperial carriage,
arranging the autumn drive.
Displaying the majestic spectacle of civil and martial arts,
surpassing what Liáng Zōu had recorded.
Forests not felling young growth,
marshes not cutting tender plants.
Axes used in season,
nets employed with principle.
Virtue connecting with the pattern of wood,
benevolence causing mushrooms to sprout.
White beasts bred in their marshes,
red fish thrived in their ponds.
Auspicious clouds and soaring dragons,
marsh horses trod the hills.
Mountains depicted their stones,
rivers shaped their treasures.
None blacker than the crow,
three-legged ones came in reverence.
None redder than the fox,
nine-tailed ones came docilely.
Fine grain ears clustered densely,
sweet springs gushed forth abundantly.
Manifesting auspicious signs in subtle completion,
surely touching all things with dual creation.
This too is the response of bright spirits,
the grand omens of excellent portents.
"Gentle and harmonious across the land,
turning to goodness without lack.
Bathed in blessings and responses,
hearts dwelling in richness and purity.
Surplus grain rested in fields unharvested,
songs of praise filled the roads and overflowed.
The Hé and Luò revealed their mysteries,
prophetic mandates emerged.
Graceful yellow birds,
carrying writings came with messages.
What human plans esteemed,
what ghostly plans arranged.
The Liú clan relinquished control,
yielding their sacred vessel.
Consulting jade records in golden caskets,
examining charts and registers in stone chambers.
Examining where the celestial numbers lay,
observing which of the five virtues presided.
Measuring by inches and days,
selecting an auspicious date.
Ascending the central altar,
assuming the imperial throne.
Rectifying the calendar,
changing the ceremonial colors.
Restoring extinct lines,
reviving abandoned offices.
Banners altered accordingly,
instruments reformed.
Manifesting benevolence and assisting brightness,
concealing utility in profound silence.
Few words, substantial deeds,
molding transformation and imbuing learning.
Collating seal and ancient scripts,
all writings fully examined.
Honoring the worthy through illustrious service,
no wickedness appearing among relatives.
Main branch and separate stems,
shielding and protecting the imperial house.
Brave as Rènchéng,
talented as Dōng'ē.
Raising banners, their might sharper than autumn frost;
wielding brushes, their splendor rivaling spring blossoms.
Wise, outstanding, heroic, and bold,
assisting the mandate of the imperial house.
Ministers combining the two eights,
generals fierce as the four sevens.
Majestic and awe-inspiring,
opening affairs with tranquility.
Thus causing the people to see the peace of the Tàijiē,
so that every household could be as one.
"The sacrifices have their cycles,
the heavenly mandate has its end.
Passing on the reign and abdicating the throne,
he humbly bids farewell to all states.
The emperor's grace is vast,
the imperial virtue profound.
Yielding the empire,
his service reaches the utmost impartiality.
Praising his unique conduct,
surpassing the mediocrity of a hundred kings.
Tracing back to the ancient times of rolled collars and knotted cords,
gazing upon Liú Chóng Huá and matching his footsteps.
Zūn Lú, Hè Xū,
Xī, Nóng, Yǒu Xióng.
Though each believed in their own Way,
they considered their grand transformations as lofty.
Generations deeply united in mystery,
why could they not follow in their steps and align with their customs?
Therefore, examine their establishment of states,
analyze their laws and institutions.
Inquire about their construction of palaces,
discuss their actions and measures.
Repeating them without weariness,
extending them with abundance.
Not something refined scholars can master,
nor vulgar words can fully describe.
"As for the majestic and strange mountains and rivers,
the extraordinary and diverse products.
Some are famed for their peculiar names and praised,
some are remarkable in reality and worthy of record.
The richness of life is ever abundant,
the truly beautiful remains unchanged.
Among them are Yuānyāng intersecting valleys,
Tiger Ravine and Dragon Mountain.
Carp-digging marshes,
Gàijié deep pools.
Fluttering Jīngwèi birds,
carrying wood to repay grievances.
Chángshān, Pínggān,
Jùlù, Héjiān.
Immortals are not few,
often emerging from there.
Chāng Róng with refined complexion,
Dú Pèi with connected eyebrows.
Xuán Sú without a shadow,
Mù Yǔ paired with immortals.
Qín Gāo sinking in water without getting wet,
sometimes riding a red carp to roam.
Shī Mén using fire to test his arts,
thus leaving and setting the forest ablaze.
Yìyáng's robust appearance,
Wèi's delicate quality.
Hándān's graceful steps,
Zhào's melodious zither.
Zhēndìng's pears,
Gù'ān's chestnuts.
Strong wine from Zhōngshān,
intoxicating for a thousand days.
Bamboo shoots from Qí Huán,
dates from Xìndū.
Liáng from Yōngqiū,
rice from Qīngliú.
Brocade and embroidery from Xiāngyì,
silk gauze from Zhāogē.
Fine silk from Fángzi,
thin silk from Qīnghé.
Such kinds as these,
abundant and plentiful.
Cannot be fully explored,
thus restrained and not exhausted.
Comparing things with intricate phrases,
describing the serene beauty of the Qing capital.
Though selecting words to simplify the chapter,
merely repeating nine times yet missing the essence.
Reading the 'Great Changes' and 'Spring and Autumn',
distinguishing differences yet converging to one.
Ending with the collapsing wall of Shànglín,
basing on former cultivation to compose the lineage.
"His military bearing does not offend,
trusting in his resolute courage.
Uniting Huá and appeasing Róng,
to support the ducal house.
His great merit matches Guǎn Jìng's achievements,
songs and bells divide the lord's display.
Thus Wèi Jiàng's virtue is renowned.
Dwelling idly in narrow lanes,
the house near but the heart far.
Rich in benevolence, cherishing righteousness,
duty contended, yet not entangled.
A thousand chariots bow at his hut,
lords cease their weapons for him.
Thus Gān Mù's virtue resolves disputes.
Honor not what I esteem,
valuing scholars more than mountains.
Personally attending to gatekeepers,
modestly sharing the carriage.
Pressing Qín, raising Zhào,
awe shaking eight frontiers.
Thus Xìnlíng's name is fragrant as orchids.
Eloquent on rise and fall,
able to save from distress.
Positioned as general and minister,
strategies to fill gaps.
All lands aligned in spearhead,
a single mouth opposing them,
Zhāng Yí,
Zhāng Lù are also worthy of mention.
"Consider Yōng Shǔ sharing nests with magpies,
Gōu Wú sharing burrows with frogs.
One considers itself birds,
one considers itself fish and turtles.
Mountains piled densely and uneven,
springs gushing forth and gurgling.
Lowlands seep and become swampy,
forests and marshes rocky and overgrown.
Remote valleys release clouds,
sun and moon often obscured.
Dwelling lands scorching hot,
borders plagued with miasma.
Thickets sting and prick,
insects poison and bite.
Hàn's criminals exiled for defense,
Qín's remnants relocated to borders.
Appearances petty and ugly,
constitutions hasty and fragile.
Alleys lack those with narrow heads,
villages rarely have the elderly.
Some with coiled hair and leftward speech,
some tattooed skin and drilled hair.
Some sing at dawn,
some float and swim year-round.
Customs consider fierceness and fruit as skillful,
people view harm as an art.
Dignity not restrained,
laws not upheld.
Due to the constraints of heavy mountains,
following the hemming force of long rivers.
Keeping distant passes to spy,
sometimes high perches and tiered controls.
Thin garrisons spread like veils,
no different from spider webs;
weak soldiers in trivial armor,
no different from mantis guards.
"As with former ages always thus,
though truly perilous and cut off.
Measuring past traces,
also the future tracks.
Chéngdū has already fallen,
Jiànyè likewise toppled.
Consider not like piled eggs on stacked chess,
how to observe the form and feel dread!
Borrowing time for fleeting glory,
like morning blossoms lush and dense.
Reading 'Wheat Sprouts' and 'Millet Sorrow',
one can compose ballads in Wú Kuài."
The gentleman's speech was not finished,
when two guests from Wú and Shǔ
were startled and looked at each other,
bewildered and lost.
With an embarrassed expression,
their spirits were dispirited, and their forms wilted.
They relaxed their demeanor and left their seats,
apologizing with humble words.
They said:
"Among our party, we are both extravagant and carefree,
feeling pressured by Mǐn and Pú peoples.
We learn from insects that forget the bitterness of rue,
delighted merely by progress and retreat.
Often sleeping without waking,
we do not see the tracks of the imperial chariots.
We exceed in the solitary cunning of bandits,
experiencing the pure reception of ancient listening.
Bearing perplexity and bestowing error,
ignoring the times and finding no stability.
The gentleman's profound insight,
praised deeply and immeasurably.
Listening to the greatness of superior virtue,
we do not share worries with the wise.
It is like spring thunder sounding,
startling the insects to burst forth and compete.
The dormant dragon emerges from the shadows,
and the hidden spring becomes a shining mirror.
Though stars have preferences in wind and rain,
people have different natures.
Achieving acquaintance with both the hidden and the obvious,
not transforming the world but adhering to righteousness.
Moreover, the cold valley can be rich in millet,
when warmed by blowing bamboo pipes.
Dimmed feelings clear at dawn,
with clear instruction evident.
Though a brilliant pearl spans an inch,
a foot-long jade disk contains fullness.
The chariot shines its two sixes,
toppling three and five cities,
yet it doesn't surpass the enduring tradition and order.
"Liàng said:
The sun does not shine on two lovelies,
nor does the world have two emperors.
Heaven has its rules and Earth its measures,
reasons have their ultimate return.
How can one maintain petty discernments equally? "
In Xiàochéngdì's time,
there was a guest who recommended a talented writer, likening him to Sīmǎ Xiāngrú,
as the emperor was offering sacrifices at Gānquán and Tàizhì,
Fényīn and Hòutǔ,
to seek succession.
Xióng was summoned to await commands at the hall of Chéngmíng.
In the first month,
returning from Gānquán with the emperor,
he presented the "Gānquán Rhapsody" to offer teachings.
Its words said:
During the tenth reign of the Hàn,
preparing to offer sacrifices to Heaven,
establishing Tàizhì,
celebrating the gods' blessings,
honoring the wise title,
aligning with the Three Sovereigns,
recording the accomplishments of the Five Emperors,
comforting descendants with abundant gifts,
expanding paths and opening dominion.
Then ordering court officials,
selecting auspicious days,
coordinating with celestial times,
stars arrayed, while heaven moved.
An edict summoned Yáo and Tàiyīn,
while Fúgōu commanded the warriors.
Aligning the universe with fortifications,
defeating Kuí ghosts and striking mad spirits.
The Eight Gods rushed to clear the way,
resounding with dense military gear.
Those like Chīyóu wield Gānjiàng swords and jade axes,
flying across Mongrong lands.
Distinctive and restrained,
their semblance solid and linked,
billowing clouds racing swiftly,
advancing with purpose.
Lined up in orderly rows,
scaled like fish and congested,
Chái and Sī arrayed unevenly,
fish leap and birds soar.
Effulgent and magnificent,
mist gathers and cloaks,
half-dispersing in radiant splendor,
forming patterns in brightness.
Then the imperial chariot ascended Fènghuáng and shaded Huázhī with glory,
harnessed by green dragons and six white serpents,
gracious and amiable,
with music softly playing.
Leading with hidden closure,
suddenly revealing sunlight,
soaring through clear skies surpassing light,
how gentle are the flags waving splendidly!
Meteor tails illuminate brightly,
while all bear green canopies and phoenix banners.
Thousands of cavalry concentrated in the central camp,
side by side with jade carriages of a thousand chariots.
Sounding alarms softly in splendid fashion,
outracing thunder and scattering winds.
Overcoming majestic heights and depths,
surpassing serene clearness.
Ascending log gates and breaching the heavenly doors,
racing through the celestial gates into icy realms.
At this time, the grand assembly had not yet reached Gānquán,
gazing upon the towered heights reaching the heavens.
Beneath, shadows lurked with a somber chill,
above, vast overwhelm in clash.
Straight and towering, soaring to heaven,
its high celebration beyond measure.
The plain stretched its expansive altar,
arranging fresh fortresses in the forested clearings.
Gathering alleys and clustered cottages,
vastly adorning the absent peaks.
The high hills galloped mightily,
while deep ravines carved valleys.
From palaces to flickering lights at night,
enclosing rocky passes and extending connections.
At that moment, the great hall's clouds twisted fantastically,
forming a captivating sight swiftly.
Gazing upwards with an elevated view,
the eyes lost in distant scenes.
Sweeping expansively with profound detail,
pointing to the vast east and west.
Wandering restlessly about,
the soul lost and bewildered.
Stationed by the carriages to explore around,
suddenly boundless and vast.
Trees of jade emerald green,
jade horses and rhinoceros shining brilliantly.
Bronze men firmly holding tools,
rocky scales mounted grandly.
Emitting radiant brilliance,
suspending images flickering vividly.
Matching heaven's residence in suspended orchards,
symbolizing Tàiyī’s majestic authority.
The grand terrace rose distinctly,
thrusting towards the North Star's summit.
The constellations hung above the flourish,
sun and moon fleeting over the horizon.
Thunder stirred in rocky chambers,
lightning flitted by walls and palisades.
Ghosts could not approach,
half-long journeys overturned below.
Traversing counter-shadows and breaking flying bridges,
floating in mists and soaring to the sky.
Left Chánqiāng and right Xuánmíng,
fiery Zháo Gate ahead and Huò Mén behind.
Shading the Western Sea and hidden capital,
surging with sweet waters forming rivers.
Dragons entwined upon the eastern cliffs,
the White Tiger standing guard at Kūnlún.
Observing curved flows in bright glory,
spreading magnificence in the western purity.
The front palace towering majestically,
with the flawless jade of Hé family.
Towers flying with arching beams,
ethereal spirits supporting the tilted.
Vast and expansive, calming and far-reaching,
like the solemn peaks of the Purple Palace.
Interlaced intricately and gracefully extending,
towering magnificently in entwined embrace.
Riding clouded pavilions ascending and descending,
tangled, shrouded, and solidly formed.
Dragging red hues flowing away,
raising green clouds winding gently.
Enveloping the Mystery Chamber and Leaning Palace,
if climbing high with distant views,
vanished kingdoms solemn over the abyss.
Returning, the storm raging wildly,
the cassia and pepper spreading with yew and poplar.
The fragrant aroma flourished grandly,
striking thickets to reach glory.
Blending scents, swirling profusely,
the sound hampered softly over bells.
Opening jade doors to let golden locks fly,
releasing orchids and aphyllous grasses.
Canopies flutter and stir in streaks,
gradually dimming and darkly serene.
Yin and yang, pure and turbid, harmonizing mutually,
like Kǔiyá tuning the lyre.
Carpenter Bān cast away chisels and axes,
Wang’ěr discarded hooks and ropes.
Though considering Fāng Zhēng and Qiáo and Wòquán,
it still seems dreamlike.
Thus, as events changed and things transformed,
the eyes were astounded and the ears bewildered,
for the Son of Heaven was solemn and serene,
in precious terraces and secluded halls,
with jade-studded rafters and jade blossoms,
amidst intricate and winding corridors.
Only by purifying the heart and clearing the soul,
storing essence and bestowing grace,
moving heaven and earth,
and welcoming blessings from the three deities;
did he seek and select companions,
men like Gāo Yáo and Yī Yǐn,
outstanding in virtue and ability,
bearing the kindness of the Gāntáng tree,
carrying the intent of the eastern campaign,
gathering together at the Yánglíng Palace.
They spread the fragrant vines as mats,
and broke jade branches for their fragrance.
They inhaled the flowing hues of clear clouds,
and drank the dewy blossoms of the Ruòmù tree.
They assembled in the garden for ritual offerings to the gods,
and ascended the hall for praising the deities.
They raised long banners of radiant light,
displaying the majestic splendor of their canopies.
Climbing the celestial pivot to gaze below,
they let their eyes wander to the Sānwēi Mountains.
They arrayed the chariots in the eastern pit,
and set the jade-wheeled carriages racing downward.
Drifting through the Dragon Abyss and circling the nine boundaries,
they peered into the depths of the earth and soared back upward.
The wind whistled as it supported the axles,
while phoenixes fluttered with trailing plumes.
They crossed the Weak Water’s rippling waves,
and trod the winding path of Bùzhōu Mountain.
They envisioned Xīwángmǔ joyfully offering longevity toasts,
while dismissing the Jade Maiden and turning away Fúfēi.
The Jade Maiden had nowhere to cast her clear gaze,
and Fúfēi could not even employ her moth-eyebrows.
Just as they grasped the essence of the Way and its power,
they matched the spirits and drew upon their aid.
Thus, with reverence, they lit the sacrificial fires and prayed,
burning incense to honor the August Heaven,
and invoking Tàiyī with raised arms.
They raised the great ceremonial vessels,
and erected the spirit banners.
The piled firewood ascended upward,
its flames spreading in all directions.
To the east, it illuminated the vast sea,
to the west, it shone upon the flowing sands.
To the north, it brightened the dark capital,
to the south, it blazed upon the crimson cliffs.
The dark jade ladle curved gracefully,
filled with the rich aroma of sacrificial wine.
The fragrance spread abundantly,
sweet and pervasive.
The fiery essence moved the Yellow Dragon, and the blazing phoenix signaled the great unicorn.
They selected Wūxián to call upon the heavenly gatekeeper,
opening the celestial court to welcome the host of deities.
The attendants, solemn and reverent, descended to the pure altar,
and auspicious signs piled up like mountains.
Thus, when the rites were completed and the achievements vast,
they turned the carriages and returned,
passing the three peaks and resting at Tánglí.
The gates of heaven swung open, and the earth’s boundaries parted,
the eight directions harmonized, and all nations were in accord.
Ascending Chángpíng, the thunderous drums resounded,
heavenly voices arose, and the warriors grew fierce.
Clouds flew and rain poured abundantly,
and virtue spread, shining for ten thousand generations.
The finale says:
Lofty is the round mound,
towering and obscuring the sky.
Ascending and descending its winding slopes,
it stands alone, a circular wall.
Its layered palaces rise unevenly,
paired in majestic heights.
Rugged and precipitous,
cavernous without end.
The workings of heaven above,
are profound and boundless.
The sage emperor, solemn and majestic,
truly responds to them.
He comes to offer suburban sacrifices,
where the spirits dwell.
Pacing and swaying,
the divine presence draws near.
Radiant and dazzling light,
descends with its blessings.
For sons and grandsons,
may it last without end.
In the fourth year of the Jìn dynasty,
on the first month, day Dīngwèi,
the emperor personally led the lords to plow the thousand-acre field,
as was the ritual.
Thus, he ordered the field overseers to clear the capital’s outskirts,
and the road officials to sweep the paths.
The border officials raised the altar walls,
and the lodging officers set up the barriers.
The green altar stood majestic like a mountain,
and the emerald canopies spread like clouds.
They laid the foundation of the sacred pedestal,
and opened the four broad approaches.
The fertile fields were rich and lush,
the soil smooth as a whetstone.
The clear Luò River and turbid canals,
channeled and stirred the waters.
The distant paths were straight as ropes,
the nearby lanes like arrows.
The oxen were yoked with pale halters,
and dark blue shafts attached to black plows.
The carriages stood solemnly to the left of the fields,
awaiting the emperor’s personal steps.
The hundred officials were arranged first,
each according to rank and duty.
From high to low,
all were obedient subjects.
They donned the lush garments of spring,
and joined the procession of rumbling carriages.
A gentle breeze arose from the light canopies,
and fine dust stirred beneath the red wheels.
In solemn rows, they held jade tablets,
gazing at the imperial carriage with awe.
Like dew evaporating in the morning sun,
or stars surrounding the North Star.
Thus, the vanguard advanced like fish in formation,
and the following carriages gathered like scales.
The palace gates swung open wide,
and the three roads were filled with teams of four.
The chamberlain accompanied the carriage,
while the grand coachman held the reins.
The empress and consorts presented seeds of early and late crops,
and the minister of agriculture prepared the tools for sowing.
The timekeeper regulated the ascent and descent,
and the palace guard set up barriers at the gates.
The Son of Heaven then mounted the jade carriage,
shaded by the ornate canopy.
Jade pendants chimed clearly,
and fine silks rustled softly.
The golden carriage shone brilliantly,
and the dragon-steeds pranced with vigor.
Red and black banners were displayed for the south and north,
green and white flew for the east and west.
Central yellow blazed gloriously,
and colors mingled in splendid array.
The five carriages rang with bells,
and the nine banners waved their streamers.
Jade ornaments gleamed like flower stamens,
and cloud-patterned canopies cast deep shadows.
Flutes and pipes played with varied tones,
while drums and bells resounded thunderously.
The bell stands rose high and majestic,
and the great bells echoed beyond the region.
With rumbling and shaking,
dust soared to the heavens,
as they proceeded to the sacred field.
Cicada-patterned caps glittered brightly,
and jade-green hues stood solemnly in thousands.
Like night-bright jade cut from Jīng mountain’s stone,
or lush pines clinging to mountain peaks.
Then our emperor descended to the sacred altar,
and took hold of the plow.
He trod the field’s ridges, staining his shoes,
the great plow-line in his hand.
After three pushes, he set it aside,
and the commoners finished the furrows.
Nobles and commoners lined up by rank,
some pushing five times, some nine.
At this time,
there was no distinction between city and countryside,
nor between Huá and Yì peoples.
Old and young mingled and gathered,
men and women, elegant and orderly, all arrived.
Clad in coarse cloth with hems shaking,
with hair tied or flowing loose,
they stood on tiptoe and leaned shoulder to shoulder,
pulling at robes and linking sleeves.
Yellow dust rose and enveloped them,
and sunlight was hidden from view.
Moved to expression and voice, the onlookers
all danced in the broad roads,
singing praises of this sage age.
Their hearts rejoiced in diligent labor,
their minds devoted to planting and cultivation.
None needed supervision to be diligent,
nor required urging to strive hard.
The emperor led by example, inspiring them with joy,
how could harsh laws and strict controls be needed!
There was an elderly villager, a rustic elder,
who stepped forward and declared:
"Increase and decrease follow the times,
for principle has its constant course.
The high is founded upon the low,
and the people regard food as heaven.
To straighten the branches, one must rectify the roots;
to ensure a good outcome, one must be cautious at the start.
If the suitability of the nine soils is not utilized,
and the tasks of the four classes are not unified,
the fields will bear the hue of wild vegetables,
and the court will lack the ranks of those who till in lieu.
With no reserves to prepare for disaster,
one can only hope for a good harvest and trust to fate.
The decline of the three dynasties of old
was all due to this.
Now, our sagely sovereign rises at dawn to illustrious deeds,
and in the evening is vigilant as if in fear.
He plans for scarcity in times of plenty,
and guards against want amidst ease.
Reverently, oh reverently,
he is concerned solely with grain.
He expands the great tasks of the three seasons,
filling granaries to overflowing.
Truly, this is the intent of Yáo and Tāng,
and the essential method for preservation and relief.
As for when there are affairs at the ancestral temples,
and the invocators consult the days,
with the fǔ and guǐ vessels and the widespread offerings,
then these come from this fullness.
The strained aromatic wine and the silvery grass,
also come forth from here.
The millet is fragrant,
the fine wine excellent and pure.
It is fitting that the people are harmonious and the year abundant,
and the spirits bestow auspiciousness.
The ancients had a saying:
'The virtue of a sage
is nothing greater than filial piety!'
Filial piety
is the nature of heaven and earth,
and that by which humans are endowed with spirit.
In ancient times, enlightened kings ruled the world through filial piety,
but those who succeeded them
were rare indeed!
Reaching our august Jìn dynasty,
we truly illuminate this Way.
Our exemplary conduct is trusted by all states,
and love and reverence are fully expressed toward ancestors.
Thus, tilling personally to supply the sacrificial grains
is how filial piety is expressed.
Encouraging agriculture to suffice the people
is how the foundation is secured.
To be able to secure the foundation and be filial—
how supreme is this great virtue and grand enterprise!
This single endeavor
combines two excellences.
Is it not far-reaching,
is it not weighty!
I dare to compose a eulogy, saying:
Delighting in the suburban fields,
we gather its silvery grass.
The great sovereign arrives,
to personally tread the farmland.
The sovereign plows three furrows,
and all directions are reverent.
We hoe our public fields,
and it truly reaches our private plots.
Our fǔ vessels are full,
our guǐ vessels are arrayed.
Our granaries are like hills,
our storehouses like islets.
Thinking of this, being in this,
forever speaking of filial thoughts.
Human effort is everywhere preserved,
invocators and scribes correct their words.
The spirits enjoy the offerings,
and ease and joy know no bounds.
When the sovereign has blessings,
the myriad people rely on them.
The envoy Zǐxū of Chǔ was sent to Qí,
and the king mobilized all his chariots and cavalry to go hunting with the envoy.
After the hunt,
Zǐxū went to visit Master Wūyǒu.
Master Wúshìgōng was also present.
When they were seated,
Master Wūyǒu asked:
"Was the hunt enjoyable today?"
Zǐxū said:
"Enjoyable."
"Did you catch much?"
He said:
"Little."
"Then why was it enjoyable?"
He replied:
"I enjoyed that the king of Qí wished to impress me with the multitude of his chariots and cavalry,
and I responded with tales of Yúnmèng."
Master Wūyǒu said:
"May I hear of it?"
Zǐxū said:
"Yes.
The king's chariots numbered a thousand,
and he selected ten thousand footmen and cavalry,
hunting by the seashore.
Ranks of soldiers filled the marshes,
nets covered the mountains.
They trapped hares and ran down deer,
shot elk and snared qílín.
Galloping over the salt flats,
they cut fresh game and stained their wheels.
Hitting many targets and capturing much,
he boasted and took credit,
then turned to me and said:
'Does Chǔ also have plains and vast marshes for hunting and roaming,
as rich in pleasure as this?
How does the king of Chǔ's hunting
compare with mine?'
I descended from my chariot and replied:
'I
am but a humble man from Chǔ.
I was fortunate to serve as a guard for over ten years,
occasionally accompanying on outings,
roaming in the rear gardens,
observing what is there and what is not,
yet I have still not seen everything,
so how could I possibly speak of the outer marshes?'
The king of Qí said:
'Nevertheless,
briefly tell me what you have heard and seen.'
"I replied:
'As you wish.
I have heard that Chǔ has seven marshes,
and I have seen one of them,
but not the others.
What I have seen
is merely the smallest of them.
It is called Yúnmèng.
Yúnmèng
spans nine hundred lǐ,
and within it there are mountains.
These mountains wind and twist, lofty and dense,
towering and precipitous.
Peaks rise unevenly,
blocking and obscuring the sun and moon.
They intertwine and tangle,
reaching up to touch the blue clouds.
Their slopes are steep and undulating,
descending to connect with rivers.
The soil is of cinnabar, azurite, red ochre, and white clay,
orpiment and white quartz,
tin, jade, gold, and silver.
The myriad colors dazzle,
shining like dragon scales.
The stones include red jade and rose-gem.
Línmín and kūnwú jade.
Jiānlè, dark whetstone,
ruǎn stone, and wǔfū.
To the east, there are orchid gardens,
with thoroughwort, orchids, angelica, and pollia,
and qiōng, sweet flag.
Jiānglí, méiwú,
sugarcane, and plantain.
To the south, there are plains and vast marshes,
with rising and sloping terrain,
broad and expansive.
Bordered by the great river,
and bounded by the Wū Mountains.
In the high, dry areas grow zhēn, xī, bāo, and lì plants,
and xuē, suō, qīng, and fán grasses.
In the low, damp areas grow zāngláng, jiān, and jiā reeds,
dōngqiáng, diāohú,
lotus roots, bottle gourds,
ānlǘ, and xuānyú.
Countless things dwell there,
too many to depict.
To the west, there are gushing springs and clear pools,
with churning waters shifting and flowing.
On the surface bloom lotuses and water chestnut flowers,
while beneath lie huge rocks and white sand.
Within dwell divine turtles, flood dragons, and tuó dragons,
hawksbill turtles and giant softshell turtles.
To the north, there are shaded forests,
with trees like pián, nán, and yùzhāng,
cassia, pepper, and magnolia,
bò, lí, and vermilion poplar.
Hawthorns, pears, yǐng trees, and chestnuts,
oranges and pomelos, fragrant and sweet.
Above, there are yuānchú, peacocks, and luan birds,
téngyuǎn and shègàn.
Below, there are white tigers and black leopards,
mànyán, chū, and àn beasts.
" 'Thereupon he dispatched the likes of Zhuān Zhū,
who grappled with these beasts with their bare hands.
The King of Chǔ then harnessed his team of trained piebald steeds,
and rode in a carriage adorned with carved jade.
He unfurled banners made of whale whiskers on curved poles,
and trailed pearl flags bright as the moon.
He raised the mighty halberds of Gānjiàng,
holding in his left the carved bow of Wūháo,
and in his right the strong arrows of Xiàfú.
Yángzǐ rode as his charioteer,
with Xiān'ē as his driver.
Before the pace had fully quickened,
they were already trampling upon cunning beasts.
They trampled the Qióngqióng,
and crushed the Jùxū.
They outran the wild horses,
and overran the Táotú.
Mounting the swift Yífēng steeds,
they shot the roaming qilin.
Swift as lightning,
they moved like thunder and arrived like whirlwinds,
like shooting stars and crashing thunderbolts.
Not a single arrow was shot in vain,
each strike sure to split an eye socket.
Piercing chests and reaching armpits,
severing the heart's connections.
The game they bagged fell like rain,
covering the grass and blanketing the ground.
Thereupon, the King of Chǔ reined in his pace and lingered,
soaring and gliding at ease.
He gazed upon the dark forests,
observed the fierce rage of his stalwart men,
and the terror of the savage beasts.
He intercepted the exhausted and accepted their surrender,
exhaustively witnessing the myriad transformations of all creatures.
" 'Then, the graceful maidens of Zhèng and the elegant ladies of Màn,
clad in fine silk from Ē,
draped in linen and white silk.
Interwoven with delicate gauze,
they wore veils of mist-like crepe.
With pleats and gathers, folds and wrinkles,
winding and meandering,
deep and twisting like valleys and gorges.
Fluttering and flowing,
lifting their hems, sharply tailored,
with flying sashes and dangling tassels.
Leaning on their carriages, graceful and supple,
rustling and shimmering.
Below, they brushed against orchids and huì grass,
above, they swept the feathered canopies.
Adorned with kingfisher feathers, resplendent and lush,
entwined with jade-tasseled cords.
Ethereal and elusive,
as if immortals in fleeting glimpses.
" 'Thereupon, they joined together for a hunt in the orchid garden,
moving gracefully and slowly,
ascending the golden dike.
They netted kingfishers,
and shot down Jùnyí birds.
Fine arrows were released,
slender silk cords deployed.
They snared white swans,
and brought down wild geese in pairs.
A pair of cāng birds fell,
and black cranes were added to the tally.
Tiring, they later set out,
to roam upon the clear pond.
They floated painted yì boats,
and raised banners on oars.
They spread emerald canopies,
and erected feathered covers.
They netted hawksbill turtles,
and hooked purple cowries.
They struck golden drums,
and blew on sounding panpipes.
The boatmen sang,
their voices flowing and resonant.
Water creatures were startled,
waves surged and foamed.
Springs welled up,
and rushing waters converged.
Stones clashed against each other,
rumbling and crashing.
Like the sound of thunder,
heard hundreds of lǐ away.
" 'When the hunt was about to cease,
they struck the spirit drums,
and lit the beacon fires.
Chariots formed into lines,
horsemen fell into ranks.
Winding in continuous streams,
moving in majestic procession.
Thereupon, the King of Chǔ ascended the Yúnyáng Terrace,
serene in inaction,
calm and self-possessed.
When the seasoned delicacies with peony sauce were prepared,
only then did he partake of them.
Unlike Your Majesty, who gallops all day long,
never once dismounting from your carriage.
Cutting meat on the wheel and searing it,
considering it amusement.
In my humble observation,
Qí is perhaps not equal to this.
Thus, the King of Qí had nothing with which to reply to me.' "
Master Wūyǒu said:
"How excessive are these words!
You, sir, have not regarded a thousand lǐ as too far,
to come and bestow your presence upon Qí.
Our king mobilized all the gentlemen within our borders,
prepared a multitude of chariots and horsemen,
to go hunting with you, the envoy,
wishing only to join efforts in achieving a good catch,
to amuse you, our guest,
how can this be called boasting!
Inquiring whether Chǔ possesses such things or not,
I wished to hear of the great achievements and illustrious customs of your great state,
and the remaining discourses of you, sir.
Now, you, sir, do not praise the profound virtue of the King of Chǔ,
but instead extravagantly extol Yúnmèng as something lofty,
speaking lavishly of wanton pleasures and displaying extravagance and waste.
I humbly believe this is not something you, sir, should adopt.
If what you say were indeed true,
it would certainly not be to the credit of the state of Chǔ.
If it is untrue and you speak of it,
this harms your credibility, sir.
To publicize the faults of your lord,
and injure personal righteousness—
neither of these two is acceptable.
Yet you, sir, engage in them,
and will surely come to be slighted by Qí and burden Chǔ.
Moreover, Qí borders the vast sea to the east,
and has Lángyá to the south.
We gaze from Chéngshān,
and shoot from Zhīfú.
We sail upon Bóxiè,
and roam upon Mèngzhū.
Diagonally, we neighbor Sùshèn,
and to the right, we are bounded by Yánggǔ.
We hunt in autumn at Qīngqiū,
and wander about beyond the seas.
Were we to swallow eight or nine Yúnmèngs,
they would not even cause the slightest hiccup in our bosom.
As for the extraordinary and magnificent,
the exotic and diverse kinds—
rare and marvelous birds and beasts,
myriad in variety, rising like fish scales—
fill our lands to overflowing,
too numerous to record.
Yǔ could not name them all,
Xiè could not count them.
Yet, occupying the position of a feudal lord,
we dare not speak of the pleasures of amusement and sport,
or the vastness of our parks and preserves.
Moreover, you, sir, are a guest,
therefore our king declined to respond further.
How can it be that he had nothing with which to reply!"
Master Wúshìgōng listened and laughed, saying:
"Chǔ is indeed at fault,
but Qí has not acted rightly either.
Now, the reason for requiring feudal lords to present tribute
is not for the sake of wealth and valuables,
but so that they may report on their governance;
and the reason for demarcating borders and drawing boundaries
is not for the sake of defense,
but to restrain excess.
Now Qí is ranked as an eastern vassal,
yet privately associates with Sùshèn beyond its borders,
neglecting the state and overstepping its limits,
crossing the sea to hunt—
this is certainly not permissible in terms of righteousness.
Moreover, the arguments of you two gentlemen
do not strive to clarify the principles of ruler and minister,
nor to rectify the rites proper to feudal lords.
You merely contend over the pleasures of amusement and sport,
and the vastness of parks and preserves,
seeking to outdo each other in extravagance,
and surpass each other in wantonness and excess.
This cannot serve to spread one's name and enhance one's reputation,
but is precisely sufficient to lower one's lord and injure oneself."
"Moreover, the affairs of Qí and Chǔ—what are they worth mentioning?
You have not yet beheld the grand and magnificent,
have you not heard of the Emperor's Shànglín Park?
To the left lies Cāngwú,
to the right the Western Extremity.
The Dān River flows past its south,
the Zǐyuān runs through its north.
It begins and ends with the Bà and Chǎn rivers,
and receives the Jīng and Wèi rivers as they enter and exit.
The Fēng, Hào, Láo, and Jué rivers,
winding and meandering,
course within its bounds.
Vast and mighty, the eight rivers flow in separate streams,
turning away from each other in different forms.
East, west, south, and north,
they race and rush back and forth.
Emerging from the cliffs of pepper hills,
flowing through the banks of islets and marshes,
passing through forests of cassia trees,
crossing boundless wilds.
Surging in merged currents,
they follow the slopes downward,
rushing toward narrow gorges.
Striking against towering rocks,
dashing against piled-up banks,
boiling in violent fury,
roaring and raging.
Gushing and swirling,
pressing and squeezing.
Flowing sideways and bending back,
whirling and churning.
Billowing and splashing,
arching like clouds, bending like rainbows,
twisting and coiling.
Overtopping waves rush into lowlands,
rippling down over shallows.
Splitting rocks and assaulting barriers,
leaping and spraying.
Reaching embankments and pouring into valleys,
splashing and plummeting.
Deep and muffled,
booming and thundering.
Bubbling and gurgling,
seething like a boiling cauldron.
Racing waves and leaping foam,
swift and turbulent,
far-reaching and long-remembered.
Silent and still, without a sound,
they spread out and return to eternity.
Then, vast and expansive,
they glide peacefully and circle slowly.
Gleaming and shimmering,
they flow east into the Great Lake,
overflowing into ponds and pools.
Here,蛟龙 and red chī dragons,
gèngméng and jiànlí fish,
yúyóng, qiántuō,
yúyú, qūtǎ,
raise their fins and thrash their tails,
shake their scales and flap their fins,
dwelling deep among the rocks.
Fish and turtles clamor,
and myriad creatures abound.
Bright moon-pearls,
glittering along the riverbanks,
Shǔ stone and yellow ruǎn jade,
crystal and rock piles.
Glimmering and sparkling,
colors radiant and dazzling,
heaped within them.
Wild swans, cranes, and bustards,
jiā'é geese and shǔyù birds,
jiāojīng and xuánmù birds,
fánwù and yōngqú ducks,
zhēncī and jiāolú birds,
flock and float above.
Drifting and spreading,
swaying with the wind,
rocking with the waves,
gathering by the water's edge.
Pecking at water plants and algae,
chewing on water chestnuts and lotus roots.
"Here, lofty mountains rise high,
towering and majestic.
Deep forests and giant trees,
jagged and precipitous.
The Jiǔzōng peaks steep and rugged,
the Southern Mountains lofty and grand.
Cliffs like yǎn and qí vessels,
rugged and twisting.
Valleys connecting gorges,
winding streams and ditches.
Gaping chasms and wide openings,
separate hills and isolated islands.
Uneven and rugged,
mounds and hollows, piled high.
Hidden and dense,
rising and falling, sloping gently,
with winding pools and marshes.
Overflowing and spreading,
dispersing across level plains.
For a thousand lǐ of flat marshlands,
all are cultivated and built upon.
Covered with green huì orchids,
draped with jiānglí herbs.
Mixed with míwú plants,
interwoven with liúyí flowers.
Spreading jiélǚ grass,
clustering lìsuō plants,
jiēchē, hénglán,
gǎoběn, and shègān.
Zǐjiāng, ránghé,
zhēnchí, ruòsūn.
Xiānzhī, huánglì,
jiǎngzhù, qīngfán.
Spreading widely across vast marshes,
extending over great plains.
Sprawling and expansive,
bending with the wind.
Exhaling fragrance and emitting strong scents,
lush and luxuriant.
All aromas diffuse and rise,
spreading and permeating,
rich and overpowering.
"Here, looking all around and observing broadly,
intricate and dazzling,
vast and bewildering.
To look at it has no beginning,
to examine it has no end.
The sun rises from the eastern pool,
and sets in the western slope.
In the south, even in deep winter, plants grow,
and waters surge with waves.
Its beasts include yōng, máo, mò, lí,
shěnniú, zhǔ, mí.
Red-headed and round-foreheaded creatures,
qióngqí, elephants, and rhinoceroses.
In the north, even in midsummer, freezing cold cracks the earth,
and one wades through ice and lifts river water.
Its beasts include qílín and jiǎoduān,
táotú and tuótuó camels.
Qióngqióng, tuóxī,
juétí, lǘ, luó.
"Here, detached palaces and separate lodges,
cover the mountains and span the valleys.
High corridors extend in four directions,
with layered seats and winding pavilions.
Ornate rafters and jade eaves,
paved paths connecting continuously.
Covered walkways circle around,
with long routes requiring an overnight stay.
Leveling mountain peaks to build halls,
piling terraces and adding layers,
with rock chambers and deep rooms.
Looking down, deep and distant, seeing nothing,
looking up, grasping rafters to touch the sky.
Shooting stars pass through inner doors,
curving rainbows drape over balustrades.
Green dragons coil in the eastern wing,
elephant-drawn carriages move gracefully in the western clear space.
Spirit guardians rest in leisure,
figures like Wòquán bask in the southern warmth.
Sweet springs gush in clear chambers,
flowing streams pass through central courtyards.
Massive rocks shore up cliffs,
steep rocks leaning precariously,
towering and jagged,
carved and precipitous.
Rose-gem and green jade,
coral growing in clusters.
Mín jade spreads broadly,
patterned and scaled like fish.
Red xiá jade streaked and mottled,
mixed and inserted among them,
cháocǎi, wǎnyǎn jades,
and the Héshì jade emerges from here.
"Then the loquats ripen in summer,
the yellow oranges and tangerines.
The loquats, persimmons,
the pears, crabapples, and magnolia.
The jujubes, bayberries,
the cherries, grapes.
The hidden plums and cherries,
the dates and lychees.
They spread throughout the rear palaces,
line the northern gardens.
They extend over hills and mounds,
descend to the plains.
They raise their emerald leaves,
sway their purple stems.
They bloom with red flowers,
hang with crimson blossoms.
Brilliant and resplendent,
they illuminate the vast wilderness.
The sand pears, oaks, and evergreens,
the flowering maples, catalpas, and paulownias.
The willows and coconut palms,
the betel palms and fan palms.
The sandalwood and magnolia,
the camphorwood and privet.
They stand a thousand ren tall,
their trunks so large they require linked arms to embrace.
Their branches stretch straight and free,
their fruits and leaves lush and abundant.
They cluster together, leaning in groups,
twisting and intertwining.
They rise in jagged disorder,
their trunks massive and gnarled.
Their hanging branches spread luxuriantly,
their fallen petals flutter and drift.
Dense and rustling,
they sway with the wind.
Their rustling and whispering
resemble the sounds of metal and stone,
the music of pipes and flutes.
Their forms, varied and wondrous,
encircle the rear palaces.
They layer upon layer,
covering the mountains and lining the valleys,
following the slopes down to the marshes.
To gaze upon them has no end,
to explore them knows no limit.
"Then the black apes and white females,
the gibbons, macaques, and flying squirrels,
the tree shrews, cicadas, and marmosets,
the langurs, badgers, and pangolins,
dwell among them.
They howl long and mournfully,
flitting back and forth across the paths.
They leap nimbly among the branches,
perch atop the highest tips.
They cross broken bridges,
leap over thickets,
grasp hanging vines,
swing through sparse gaps.
Scattered and varied,
they frolic and roam afar.
"Such places number in the hundreds and thousands,
where one may travel for amusement,
lodging in palaces and resting in lodges.
The kitchens need not be moved,
the rear palaces remain in place,
and all officials are fully provided for.
"Then, as autumn turns to winter,
the Son of Heaven conducts a grand hunt.
He rides in a carriage carved of ivory,
drawn by six jade-like dragons.
He trails rainbow banners,
waves cloud-embroidered flags.
Ahead go leather-covered vanguards,
behind follow the guiding outriders.
Sūn Shū grasps the reins,
Duke Wèi rides as attendant.
The guards march in formation,
emerging from among the four divisions.
Drums beat and registers are checked,
then the hunters are unleashed.
The rivers form the enclosures,
Mount Tài serves as the watchtower.
Chariots and cavalry thunder forth,
shaking heaven and earth.
They advance in scattered array,
separating to pursue their prey.
They flow like waves,
along the hills and across the marshes,
spreading like clouds, showering like rain.
They capture panthers and leopards,
wrestle with jackals and wolves.
They seize bears and brown bears with their hands,
trample wild sheep with their feet.
They wear pheasant-tail helmets,
don tiger-striped trousers.
Clad in patterned robes,
they mount wild horses.
They scale the perilous peaks of Sānzōng,
descend the rugged slopes of Qìlì.
They traverse steep paths and brave dangers,
cross ravines and ford waters.
They strike down the Feīlián,
play with the Xièzhì.
They confront the Xiāgé,
spear the Měngshǐ.
They lasso the Yǎoniǎo,
shoot the great boars.
Their arrows never strike without purpose,
piercing throats and shattering skulls.
Their bows never release in vain,
each shot felling its target with a cry.
"Then the imperial carriage slows its pace, wandering about,
soaring and gliding to and fro.
Observing the advance and retreat of the troops,
surveying the changing tactics of the generals.
Then, gradually quickening the pace,
they swiftly vanish into the distance.
They scatter the light birds,
trample the cunning beasts.
They run down the white deer,
outpace the swift hares.
They outstrip red lightning,
leave behind brilliant light.
They pursue monstrous creatures,
venturing beyond the cosmos.
They bend the Fānruò bow,
nock white-feathered arrows.
They shoot the wandering owls,
strike down the Feījù.
They select their target before releasing,
aiming first and naming the spot.
Bowstring and arrow part,
the prey falls dead.
"Then, raising the banners, they ascend and float,
riding the startling winds,
passing through the terrifying whirlwinds,
ascending into emptiness,
joining with the spirits.
They trample the black cranes,
disrupt the Kūnjī.
They corner the peacocks and phoenixes,
press the Jùnyí.
They brush aside the Yìniǎo,
sweep past the fenghuang.
They seize the Yuānchú,
capture the Jiāomíng.
"When the path ends and the road is exhausted,
they turn the carriage and return.
Wandering leisurely and aimlessly,
they descend and gather at Běihóng.
Swiftly heading straight,
dimly returning homeward.
They pass by Shíquè,
traverse Fēngluán.
They pass Zhīquè,
gaze upon Lùhán.
They descend at Tánglí,
rest at Yíchūn,
gallop west to Xuānqǔ,
wash at Niúshǒu.
They ascend Lóngtái,
stop at Xìliǔ.
They observe the diligence and strategies of the officers,
distribute the spoils among the hunters.
The tracks crushed by chariots and foot soldiers,
the trampling of infantry and cavalry,
the places trodden by subjects.
Along with those exhausted and weary,
terrified and prostrate in fear.
Those not slain by blade or spear,
lie heaped in disorder.
They fill the pits and valleys,
cover the plains and blanket the marshes.
"Thus in their amusements and idle pastimes,
they set out wine upon the high terrace of the bright heavens,
and spread music throughout the vast and boundless universe.
They strike bells of a thousand stones,
and set up bell racks of ten thousand stones.
They raise banners of kingfisher feathers,
and set up drums made of alligator skin.
They perform the dances of Yáotángshì,
and listen to the songs of Gětiānshì.
A thousand voices sing,
and ten thousand join in harmony.
The mountains and hills tremble with the sound,
and the rivers and valleys ripple with waves.
The music of Bāyú, Sòng, and Cài,
the 'Gānzhē' of Huáinán,
and the songs of Wénchéng and Diān—
performed in succession by various groups,
with metal bells and drums rising one after another.
Clanging and booming,
they pierce the heart and startle the ears.
The sounds of Jīng, Wú, Zhèng, and Wèi,
the music of 'Sháo,' 'Huò,' 'Wǔ,' and 'Xiàng,'
and the licentious, lingering notes—
Yānyǐng in all its splendor,
'Jíchǔ' with its stirring winds.
Actors and dwarfs,
the performers of 'Dídī'—
all that delights the eyes and ears and gladdens the heart—
spread in gorgeous profusion before them,
with exquisite beauty and dazzling charm.
"As for those like Qīngqín and Fúfēi,
utterly extraordinary and removed from the vulgar,
enchanting and elegant.
Adorned with fine makeup and intricate ornaments,
graceful and delicate.
Soft and supple,
charming and slender.
They trail robes of single cocoon silk,
with long, flowing garments that seem to vanish into thin air.
Graceful and poised,
their attire distinct from the common fashion.
Fragrant and richly perfumed,
intensely sweet and lush.
Their bright teeth gleam brilliantly,
and their lovely smiles sparkle.
Their long eyebrows arch delicately,
and their sidelong glances are tender and distant.
Their beauty captivates the soul,
bringing joy to the heart of the beholder.
"Thus, amid wine and the height of music,
the Son of Heaven grows pensive and reflective,
as if something were missing,
and says:
'Alas,
this is too extravagant!
I have used my leisure from governance,
with no pressing affairs to occupy my days.
Following the way of heaven, I engaged in hunting,
taking rest here in due season.
Yet I fear that future generations, enamored of such luxury,
will become lost in it and never return,
which is no way to establish a legacy for successors and perpetuate our rule.'
Thereupon, he ends the drinking and halts the hunt,
and commands the officials, saying:
'The land may be cleared and cultivated,
all turned into farmland,
to support the common people.
Tear down the walls and fill in the moats,
so that the people of the mountains and marshes may come and go freely.
Fill the ponds and do not restrict them,
leave the palaces and lodges empty and unattended.
Open the granaries to relieve the poor,
and make up for their shortages.
Show compassion to the widowed and solitary,
and care for the orphaned and alone.
Issue benevolent decrees,
and reduce punishments.
Reform the institutions,
and change the ceremonial colors.
Revise the calendar,
and make a fresh start with all under heaven.'
"Then, selecting an auspicious day for fasting and purification,
he dons court robes,
mounts the imperial carriage,
raises the flowery banners,
and sets the jade bells ringing.
He roams in the park of the Six Arts,
and gallops along the path of benevolence and righteousness.
He surveys the forest of the 'Spring and Autumn Annals,'
shoots with the 'Líshǒu' arrow,
and combines it with the 'Zōuyú' arrow.
He shoots down the black crane,
and dances with shield and axe.
He sets up the cloud net,
and captures a flock of elegant birds.
He laments over the 'Fátán,'
and delights in the joy of music.
He cultivates demeanor in the garden of 'Rites,'
and soars freely in the field of 'Documents.'
He expounds the way of the 'Changes,'
and releases the strange beasts.
He ascends the Bright Hall,
and sits in the Pure Temple.
He arranges his ministers in order,
and discusses successes and failures.
Within the four seas,
none fail to receive his bounty.
At this time,
all under heaven are greatly pleased,
turning to the wind to listen,
following the current to be transformed,
swiftly rising to the Way and moving toward righteousness.
Punishments are set aside and not used,
virtue surpasses that of the Three Sovereigns,
and achievements exceed those of the Five Emperors.
If this is so,
then hunting is indeed a joyous affair.
"But if one spends the whole day galloping about,
exhausting the spirit and wearying the body,
wearing out horses and carriages,
and draining the energy of soldiers,
wasting the wealth of the treasury,
without bestowing kindness or generosity,
seeking only one's own pleasure,
with no regard for the multitude,
forgetting the governance of the state,
and coveting the capture of pheasants and hares—
then the benevolent would not follow such a path.
From this perspective,
the affairs of Qí and Chǔ,
are they not lamentable!
Their territories do not exceed a thousand lǐ,
yet their parks occupy nine hundred,
so that vegetation cannot be cleared for cultivation,
and the people have nothing to eat.
For feudal lords, though minor,
to indulge in the extravagance of ten thousand chariots—
I fear the people will suffer the consequences."
At this, the two men changed their expressions, looking solemn,
as if lost in thought,
and withdrew respectfully,
saying:
"We, ignorant and uncultured,
unaware of taboos,
have today received your instruction,
and we humbly accept your words."
During the reign of Emperor Xiàochéng, there was an imperial hunt,
in which Xióng participated.
It was thought that in the times of the two Emperors and the three Kings,
palaces and pavilions,
ponds and parks,
forests and marshes,
wealth sufficed to serve the ancestral temples,
host guests,
and fill the kitchen only,
without taking land of rich grain, mulberry, and catalpa from the people.
Women had surplus cloth,
men had surplus grain,
the state was prosperous and wealthy,
with resources in abundance at all levels.
Therefore, sweet dew fell upon their courts,
sweet springs flowed in their halls,
phoenixes nested in their trees,
yellow dragons roamed their ponds,
and qilins gathered in their parks,
divine sparrows perched in their forests.
In the past, when Yǔ appointed Yì and Yú, there was harmony above and below,
vegetation thrived,
and when Chéng Tāng enjoyed fields, the world had enough to use.
Wén Wáng had a park a hundred lǐ wide,
which the people considered small;
Qi Xuān Wáng had a park forty lǐ wide,
which the people considered large:
this is the difference between benefiting the people and taking from them.
Emperor Wǔ expanded the Shanglin Park,
extending to Yíchūn and Dinghu in the southeast,
dwelling at Kūnwú,
by Mount Nan in the south,
extending west to Zhǎngyáng and Wǔzhuò,
circling north around Mount Huáng,
bordering the Wèi River to the east,
encompassing several hundred lǐ.
He excavated Kunming Pool,
imitating the Dian River,
and built the Zhāng and Fèng Towers,
where divine spirits cavorted,
gradually constructing the Mount Taiyígia Terrace,
resembling the seas surrounding the Isles of the Immortals.
The sights were extravagant and luxurious,
with wonders and beauty pushed to extremes.
Even though some of these endeavors were curtailed,
to aid the people of Qí,
yet on the occasions of imperial hunts, the war chariots, horses, military equipment, and preparations
were still extremely lavish, indulgent, and ostentatious,
not in line with the intent of the sages Yáo, Shùn, Chéng Tāng, and Wén Wáng's three relocations.
There was also fear that future generations would revive old pastimes,
not balancing matters with the resources of springs and terraces,
therefore during the military hunts,
a poetic style is assigned to convey this.
The content of the poem says:
Some praise the sages Fúxī and Shénnóng,
but do these truly embellish the great accomplishments of emperors?
When analysts speak of this,
each time and place is suited to its own needs,
why be bound to the same standard and expectations?
Then, the sealing of Mount Tài,
how does one achieve the seventy and two revisions?
Thus, those who begin endeavor and establish succession,
do not perceive their own lack of clarity,
in the distant and near, the five and three generations,
who knows right from wrong?
Consequently, an ode was composed saying:
Beautiful indeed are the divine beings,
residing in the mysterious palace.
With wealth rivaling the land,
their noble status comparable to the supreme heavens.
To Qí Huán was not enough to assist with the axle,
to Chǔ Yán was not enough to be a riding companion.
Constraining the narrowness of the three kings,
they rose high in great prosperity.
Traversing the vastness of the five emperors,
crossing into the grandeur of the three sovereigns.
Building virtue to be their master,
friend to benevolence and righteousness.
In the somber winter months,
the land and sky were intensely severe,
all things nestled within,
and withered without,
the emperor would then hunt in the sacred parks,
opening the northern boundary,
subject to the constraints of Wūzhōu,
in homage to Zhān Xù and Xuánmíng's rule.
Therefore, he commanded the overseer of parks,
to extend eastward to the neighbors of Kūn,
and race westward to Chānghé.
Provisions were amassed,
soldiers lined the roads.
Bristling thorns were cut,
wild grass leveled.
The protection began from Qiān and Wèi Rivers,
organizing through Fēng and Hào.
Majestic and circular,
exiting and entering like the sun and moon,
the heavens merged with the earth.
Then, the commander for the hunt was stationed at the three mounts of Hǔ Lù,
encompassing a hundred lǐ,
serving as the ceremonial gate.
Externally aligning with the southernmost sea,
and bordering the mysterious abyss.
The vast and nebulous expanse,
projected with towering mountains.
The encampment closed and gathered,
then first set south of the White Poplar,
and east of the Sacred Pool of Kūnmíng.
Such valiant warriors,
bearing shield and feathered projectiles,
wielding dark, sharp weapons and forming ranks in multitudes.
Others bore nets sweeping the sky,
spreading snares over the entirety of the land.
Red poles indistinguishable from sun and moon,
flying banners reminiscent of comets.
Azure clouds tangled,
red rainbows looped,
linked to the emptiness of Kūnlún.
Spreading like celestial stars woven,
vast as waves of the Tao River.
Endlessly unending,
guarding front and back.
Fiery spears formed walls,
the bright moon served as a beacon.
Óu and Huò governed fate,
celestial bows were released.
Flashy as fresh blooms,
in line with matched roads.
Elegant vehicles and light armor,
red pennants and call on the hunt.
Thundering roars,
covering ridges and trailing slopes.
Even at the farthest reaches,
they formed ranks upon highland tops.
The galloping horsemen,
divided in distinct tasks.
Coming and going in disorder,
never-ending turns of the gear.
Appearing and vanishing,
spread below the greenwood.
At this moment the Son of Heaven took Yangchao,
and first emerged from the mysterious palace,
striking the great bells,
raising the nine-layered canopy,
with six white tigers,
mounted the sacred carriage.
Chīyóu accompanied him,
as Lord Méng drove ahead.
Raised the heavenly-banner,
trailing comet-like pennants.
Lightning and thunder shook,
spewing fire applying the whip.
Gather behind in grandeur,
far-flung and expansive,
traversing the eight fronts opening through gates.
Fēilián, master of clouds,
inhales roaring blasts,
scales arrayed and fierce,
collected with dragon feathers.
Chirping haphazardly,
entering the Western Garden,
cutting through divine radiance.
Gazing to the Pleasure Pavilion,
straight through the Bamboo Forest.
Treading through the camphor plots,
trampling through the orchid grounds.
Lifting blazing torches,
drivers displayed their skills,
as they raced in their thousands,
brave riders led by ten thousand.
Assembling the fierce array of tigers,
crossing across thoroughly,
like rolling lightning and thunder,
galloping, turning, and advancing swiftly.
Surging like the rising sun,
heaven shook, earth trembled.
The vast expanse half spread,
and a scattering emptiness thousands of lǐ outward.
As for the valiant knights,
with diverse aspirations and different pursuits,
they gallop east, west, south, and north,
chasing their desires and indulging their passions.
They drag the black boars,
trample over rhinoceroses and yaks,
and trip up swift deer.
They behead giant apes,
wrestle with dark gibbons.
They leap into the void,
and kick at coiled serpents.
They stomp on twisting vines,
and frolic among mountain streams.
In a whirlwind of chaos,
the valleys are swept by gales,
and the forests are stirred into clouds of dust.
And then come the fierce hunters,
who crush pines and cypresses underfoot,
and tread upon thistles and brambles.
They hunt through dense thickets,
and crush light-winged birds.
They tread upon horned beasts,
and wear serpents as belts.
They hook red leopards,
and capture elephants and rhinoceroses.
They cross over rugged hills,
and leap across wide marshes.
Chariots and cavalry gather like clouds,
ascending and descending in dark masses.
Mount Tàihuà serves as their banner,
and Mount Xióng'ěr as its tassels.
Trees fall and mountains tremble,
as if the world beyond the heavens were shaking.
They roam freely across the great marshes,
wandering unrestrained within the cosmos.
Then, with the sky clear and the sun serene,
Féng Méng sharpens his gaze,
and Yì the Archer draws his bowstring.
The imperial chariots gleam darkly,
their radiance illuminating heaven and earth.
The moon-goddess reins in her steeds,
as they glide slowly to Shànglán.
They shift their encirclements and move their formations,
gradually pressing forward in disciplined ranks.
Their troops are firm and dense,
each holding to their positions.
Their fortifications whirl like the heavens,
their divine strikes flash like lightning.
Whatever meets them is shattered,
whatever approaches is broken.
Birds have no time to fly,
beasts cannot escape.
The army is startled, the troops astounded,
sweeping the plains and scouring the earth.
And when the rare chariots soar,
and martial riders dash swiftly,
they trample upon leopards in flight,
and ensnare the roaring beasts.
They pursue the heavenly treasures,
emerging from all directions.
They respond to the thunderous sounds,
striking with flashes of light.
The fields are emptied, the mountains exhausted,
as they capture all, male and female alike.
In vast and flowing multitudes,
they roar across the expanse.
The three armies stand in awe,
exhausted and overwhelmed.
They watch as the swift birds are ensnared,
and rhinoceroses clash in combat.
Bears and panthers grapple fiercely,
tigers and leopards flee in panic.
Horns clash and heads butt,
as fear and trembling take hold.
Souls are terrified, spirits lost,
as they collide with chariot wheels and break their necks.
Arrows fly wildly yet hit their marks,
advancing and retreating, all is captured.
Wounds abound, wheels crush flat,
piling up like hills and mounds.
Then, as the hunt wanes and the game diminishes,
they gather together at the Pavilion of Serene Darkness,
overlooking the Precious Pool.
They channel waters from Qíliáng,
and fill it to overflowing with rivers.
Gazing eastward, the view stretches endlessly,
looking westward, there are no bounds.
Pearls of Suí and Héshì
gleam brightly along its banks.
