Jade and stones rise high,
shimmering with a greenish glow.
Maidens of Hàn dive into the waters,
while mysterious creatures lurk in the darkness,
too numerous to describe.
Black phoenixes and peacocks,
kingfishers displaying their splendor.
Royal ospreys call in harmony,
wild geese chirp melodiously.
They frolic in multitudes,
chirping and singing together.
Ducks, gulls, and egrets
flutter up and down with crashing sounds,
their voices like thunder.
Then come the tattooed divers,
skilled in confronting scaled creatures.
They break through solid ice,
brave the depths of frigid waters,
explore cliffs and push aside rocky banks,
searching for flood dragons and serpents.
They tread upon otters,
grasp giant turtles and alligators,
and seize spiritual tortoises.
They enter deep caverns,
emerge at Cāngwú.
They ride upon giant fish,
mounting colossal whales.
They float across Pénglí Lake,
gazing toward Yǒuyú.
They break apart luminous pearls,
cleave open moonlit oyster shells,
whip the goddess Fúfēi of the Luò River,
and offer sacrifices to Qū Yuán and Péng Xū.
Here, the great scholars and eminent Confucians,
in their lofty carriages and official caps,
mingling in their varied robes,
revise the laws of Táng,
rectify the odes and hymns,
and perform rituals of deference.
Their brilliance shines forth,
mysteriously divine.
Their benevolent reputation spreads to the northern tribes,
their martial righteousness stirs the southern neighbors.
Thus, the kings in felt and fur,
the chieftains of the Hú and Mò tribes,
bring their treasures to offer tribute,
raising their hands in submission.
Some enter through the hunting grounds,
others array themselves before Lúshān.
The assembled nobles, along with figures like Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí,
sigh in unison and exclaim:
"How lofty is your virtue!
Even the glory of Táng, Yú, Dàxià, and Chéngzhōu
cannot compare to this magnificence!
In ancient times, when paying homage to the Eastern Peak,
and performing ceremonies at Liángjī,
who in this world
could match such grandeur?"
Yet the emperor remains modest and unyielding,
intending to seek the flow of the Three Numinous Beings above,
and draw forth the springs of sweet dew below.
He will open the lair of the yellow dragon,
peer into the nest of the phoenix,
approach the park of the qílín,
and visit the grove of the divine sparrow.
He will not indulge in Yúnmèng,
nor boast of Mèngzhū.
He rejects Zhānghuá,
and upholds Língtái.
He rarely visits detached palaces,
and ceases idle excursions.
Earthworks are left unadorned,
wooden structures uncarved.
He guides the people in farming and sericulture,
encouraging them without respite.
He pairs men and women,
ensuring none remain unmarried.
Fearing that the poor may not share in the abundant blessings,
he opens the forbidden parks,
distributes the public stores,
establishes a park of virtue,
and expands the preserve of benevolence.
He roams the divine preserves,
observing whether his ministers possess or lack virtue.
He releases pheasants and hares,
and gathers up nets and traps.
He shares the deer and game with the common people,
for this is how such harmony is achieved.
Thus, he enriches the virtue of profound harmony,
and expands the norms of a flourishing age.
He labors more than the Three Sovereigns,
strives harder than the Five Emperors—
is this not the utmost achievement?
Then, the dignified and solemn disciples
establish the rituals between ruler and subject,
and exalt the deeds of sages and worthies,
with no time for the beauty of parks and preserves,
nor the extravagance of hunting and excursions.
Thus, they turn the chariot around,
leaving Ēpáng Palace behind,
and return to Wèiyāng Palace.
The following year,
the Emperor planned to greatly impress the Hu people with an abundance of wild beasts.
In autumn, he ordered the Right Fufeng region to mobilize people to enter the Southern Mountains,
from Bāoxié in the west,
to Hóngnóng in the east,
driving southward to Hànzhōng,
spreading nets and traps,
capturing bears, brown bears, porcupines, tigers, leopards, monkeys, foxes, rabbits, elk, and deer,
loading them into cage carts,
and transporting them to the Shèxióng Hall of Chángyáng.
Using nets to form an enclosure,
they released the beasts inside,
ordering the Hu people to wrestle them barehanded,
taking what they captured for themselves,
while the Emperor personally observed.
At that time,
the farmers were unable to harvest their crops.
Yáng Xióng followed the Emperor to the Shèxióng Hall,
and upon returning, presented the "Rhapsody on Chángyáng,"
merely using brush and ink to compose a literary piece,
thus borrowing the Hànlín scholar as the host,
and Zǐmò as the guest minister to offer criticism.
The text reads:
Zǐmò, the guest minister, inquired of the Hànlín host:
"I have heard that a sage ruler nurtures the people,
with benevolence reaching all and kindness pervading,
his actions not for personal gain.
This year's hunt at Chángyáng,
first ordered the Right Fufeng region,
with Tàihuá on the left and Bāoxié on the right,
felling Niè'è to make arrows,
winding through the Southern Mountains to set traps.
Deploying a thousand chariots in the forests,
arraying ten thousand cavalry in the mountain corners.
Leading the army to encircle the enclosure,
rewarding the Rong and capturing the Hu.
Seizing bears and brown bears,
dragging porcupines.
Wooden stakes and spear barricades,
serving as defensive barriers.
This is the ultimate spectacle under heaven.
Nevertheless,
it also greatly disturbs the farmers.
For over thirty days,
their toil has been extreme,
yet no achievement is seen,
fearing that those who do not understand will externally view it as a recreational excursion,
internally not regard it as a matter of sacrificial offerings,
how can this be for the people!
Moreover, a ruler should regard profound stillness as divine,
and detachment as virtue,
yet now delighting in distant excursions to display majestic power,
repeatedly mobilizing to exhaust chariots and armor,
is fundamentally not an urgent task for a sovereign,
and I am privately perplexed.
The Hànlín host said:
"Ah,
guest, why do you speak thus!
What you, guest, say shows you know one aspect but have not witnessed the other,
see the exterior but do not recognize the interior.
I have grown weary of discussing this,
unable to detail it point by point,
please allow me to briefly outline the general idea,
and you, guest, may yourself examine its essence.
The guest said:
"Yes, yes."
The host said:
"In the past, there was the powerful Qín,
whose land was like a savage boar,
whose people were like the monstrous Yàyǔ,
and the fanged ones vied with bared teeth.
Heroes seethed like boiling porridge and roiled like clouds,
and the masses suffered unrest.
Then the Lord on High looked favorably upon Gāozǔ,
and Gāozǔ, receiving the mandate,
followed the Dipper and Pole Star,
moved the heavenly pivot.
Traversed the vast seas,
swept over Kūnlún.
Raising his sword and shouting,
wherever he passed, cities were toppled and towns razed,
generals lowered their banners.
The battles of a single day
cannot be fully recorded.
Amid such toil,
his hair disheveled with no time to comb,
hungry with no time to eat.
Helmets bred lice,
armor soaked with sweat.
All to plead for the lives of the myriad people before August Heaven.
Thus he straightened what was bent among men,
relieved what was lacking among men.
Planning for a billion years,
expanding the imperial enterprise.
Within seven years, the world was tightly ordered.
"When it came to the sage Emperor Wén,
following the wind and riding the current,
he turned his attention to utmost peace.
Personally practicing frugality,
his plain silk garments never wore out,
his leather shoes never pierced.
He did not dwell in grand halls,
wooden utensils bore no ornament.
Thus, the rear palace held tortoiseshell cheap and kept pearls distant,
rejected kingfisher ornaments,
eliminated carved and polished artistry.
Disliked extravagance and did not approach it,
spurned fragrances and did not use them,
suppressed the indulgent music of strings and bamboo,
detested hearing the delicate sounds of Zhèng and Wèi,
thus the Jade Balance was aligned and the Grand Steps leveled.
"Afterward, the Xūnyù committed atrocities,
the Eastern Yi rebelled wantonly.
The Qiāng and Rong glared with anger,
Mǐnyuè fell into mutual strife.
Distant lands were unsettled by this,
the Central States suffered their troubles.
Then the martial Emperor erupted in wrath,
and marshaled his troops.
He commanded Piào and Wèi,
like surging Fén and Yún, boiling and swirling,
clouds gathering and lightning striking.
Whirlwinds soared and waves flowed,
crossbows startled and bees darted.
Swift as shooting stars,
strikes like crashing thunder.
Shattered siege vehicles,
smashed felt tents.
Brains spilled on the desert,
marrow in the Yúwú River.
Thus they trampled over the royal court.
Drove off camels,
burned supply stores.
Carved up the Chányú,
dismembered the subject states.
Leveled pits and valleys,
uprooted wild thickets,
sheared mountain rocks.
Trampled corpses and carted the slain,
bound the old and weak.
Those pierced by spears, scarred by arrows,
and wounded by metal arrowheads numbered in the hundreds of thousands,
all knocking foreheads to the ground and raising chins,
crawling and prostrating like ants.
For over twenty years,
they still dared not breathe easily.
When the heavenly troops approached from four directions,
the Dark Capital was first assaulted.
Turning spears and pointing obliquely,
Nányuè warred among themselves.
Without pausing, marching westward,
the Qiāng and Bó raced eastward.
Thus, distant regions with alien customs,
lands of different neighbors and severed factions,
where the highest benevolence could not transform,
where abundant virtue could not pacify,
all raised their feet and lifted their heads,
offering their treasures.
Causing the realm to be tranquil,
forever free from border fortress disasters,
the scourge of weapons and armor.
"Now the imperial court is pure in benevolence,
following the Way and manifesting righteousness,
encompassing all within the literary forest,
the sage's influence spreads like clouds.
The finest blossoms float and sink,
overflowing across the eight regions.
All under heaven, wherever it covers,
none are not moistened by its grace.
If a scholar does not speak of the kingly Way, even a woodcutter would laugh at him.
It is thought that no affair reaches its peak without decline,
no thing flourishes without eventual diminishment.
Therefore, in peace, one does not recklessly court danger,
in safety, one does not forget peril.
Thus, in times of abundant harvests, troops are dispatched,
chariots are readied, and arms are prepared.
The army is roused at Wǔzuò,
horses are trained at Chángyáng.
Testing strength against cunning beasts,
examining martial prowess against swift birds.
Then, gathering, they ascend the southern mountains,
gazing down upon Wūyì.
To the west, subduing the Yuèzhī,
to the east, shaking the realm of the sun.
Yet, fearing that later generations might be misled by temporary affairs,
they often regard this as the great duty of the state,
lest excessive hunting and indulgence,
lead to decline unchecked.
Therefore, chariots do not rest their blocks,
the sun has not yet dimmed the banners.
The followers, as if in a trance,
weary and bent, return.
This is also to uphold the achievements of the great ancestors,
to follow the measures of Wén and Wǔ.
Restoring the hunting grounds of the Three Kings,
returning to the preserves of the Five Emperors.
So that farmers do not cease their hoes,
artisans do not leave their looms.
Marriages are timely,
men and women do not transgress.
Emanating kindness and brotherliness,
practicing simplicity and ease.
Pitying the toilsome,
resting the labors of service.
Seeing to the centenarians,
caring for the orphaned and weak.
Leading and sharing with them,
both hardship and joy.
Only then are the music of bells and drums arrayed,
the harmony of táo and qìng stones sounded,
the stands of jiéxiá erected.
Striking the resonant jades,
performing the dances of the eight rows.
Toasting with pure and splendid wine,
feasting with joyful delight.
Listening to the harmonious sounds in the temple,
receiving blessings from spirits and men.
Songs that match the odes,
winds that harmonize with the elegies.
Such diligence as this,
is why the true spirits reward it.
Awaiting the auspicious signs,
to add to the foundation of Liángfǔ,
to increase the height of Tàishān.
Extending glory to future generations,
matching the honor of past reigns.
How could it merely be for wanton sightseeing and idle viewing,
galloping through fields of jīng rice,
wandering through forests of pear and chestnut trees,
trampling over grass and firewood,
boasting to the common people,
exalting the capture of monkeys and apes,
or taking pride in the catch of deer and elk!
Moreover, the blind cannot see an inch before them,
while Lílóu illuminates the corners of a thousand miles;
you, guest, merely admire the barbarians capturing our birds and beasts,
yet fail to realize that we have already captured their kings and lords.
Before the words were finished,
the ink-scholar descended from his mat,
bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
'How grand is this principle!
Truly, it is beyond what a petty man can attain.
Only today has my blindness been enlightened,
suddenly all is clear!'"
Wandering through the green woods on an excursion,
delighting in the flocking flight of feathered tribes.
Among them, selecting the most splendid plumage,
is the famed pheasant with its five colors.
Fostering a resolute and dedicated heart,
displaying a majestic and beautiful form.
Patrolling the hills and mounds with strategic intent,
marking the boundaries and dividing the territories.
At this time, the season of youth bids farewell,
the crimson brightness begins its reign.
No tree fails to flourish,
no grass lacks lushness.
Fresh stems gleam with new brilliance,
old branches, now sparse, have changed their former state.
The heavens, vast and boundless, hang with clouds,
springs, trickling gently, pour forth their streams.
Wheat, gradually rising, thrusts forth its awns,
pheasants, calling clearly, greet the morning with their cries.
Glancing at cages and pens, they strut proudly,
eyeing the decoy birds, they shift their demeanor.
Stretching strong legs to spar with rivals,
glaring with fierce eyes, casting sidelong looks.
The oriole, with patterned wings, strikes with reddened blows,
the neck, burning like embroidery, and the back, adorned with rolling patterns.
Swelling with rising fury,
longing to cry out and demonstrate their prowess.
Then, they clear the grounds and set up blinds,
pausing amidst the lush verdure.
Green cypresses stand unevenly,
patterned feathers lie like scales in rows.
Dense and flourishing,
supple and agile.
Within, keen and penetrating to discern clearly,
without, pressed close and tightly woven.
Fearing my outing might start too late,
worrying the wild fowl may seldom come.
Willingly tiring my heart with anticipation,
dividing my weary gaze to keep watch.
How harmoniously tuned and lofty,
far surpassing their kind with exceptional talent.
Awaiting the fan's rise to utter a clear call,
the wild, hearing the sound, responds to the lure.
Lifting the fine net to gaze afar,
already they come stumbling slowly forward.
Displaying the crimson crown in its blazing glory,
spreading adorned feathers, full and bristling.
Head adorned with green and white,
body draped with embroidered patterns.
Blue like autumn sedge, sweeping gracefully,
red breast like orchids, clustered finely.
Some strut, some peck,
sometimes moving, sometimes still.
Striped tails raised high,
twin spurs standing prominent.
The skilled hunter calls softly,
drawing them into the designated area.
Startled by a shout, they stand erect,
lifting their bodies, poised and alert.
Holding the yellow crossbow, drawing tight the string,
aiming the sturdy arrow, secretly taking aim.
Birds tumble down in scattered falls,
the mechanism's sound vibrates, not yet ceased.
The mountain pheasant, fierce and harmful,
exceedingly swift and rapid.
Crossing ravines, scaling peaks,
flying and calling, nearing the granary.
Lowering the arrowhead like a whale's tooth,
heart calm, gaze focused.
Feathers and bodies shattered and fallen,
suddenly like scattered brocade.
The outstanding one among the flock,
dominating the field, holding two at once.
Driving off females, jealous of rivals,
coming and going swiftly, suddenly.
Fearing the cutting wind from above,
dreading the dazzling glare of the sun.
Holding breath, restraining movement,
only heart vexed and skill eager.
That righteous bird, responding to the foe,
chirping, seizing the ground, raising a fierce cry.
Hearing the sound, it charges straight ahead,
suddenly crossing spurs, engaging closely.
Red fills the window, beautifully released,
heads fall in disarray, breasts exposed upward.
Or perhaps the high mounds have crumbled flat,
yet farmers have not altered the furrows.
Weeds and beans grow tangled together,
dense and lush, thick and overgrown.
A pheasant crows and shakes its wings,
perched upon its mound.
I descend the hill to chase the foe,
though hidden in form, the grass stirs.
Seeing the drooping ears of grain sway,
I sense a quivering, leaping excitement.
The pheasant emerges from the seedlings into the field,
heightening my alarm and stirring my spirit.
I watch the dark mass merge and obscure the whiteness,
the pheasant shrugs its shoulders and turns on its heels.
Delighted by my keen focus,
I aim for the blue head and strike the neck.
There are also those whose eyes do not follow their bodies,
glancing askance, peering sideways.
Hearing nothing yet startled,
seeing nothing yet flustered.
Circling round and round,
winding and turning, pacing cautiously.
They twist through the cover, spinning to grasp,
winding along the path they tread.
Halting mid-step, hesitating,
then struck by an arrow in mid-flight.
Pierced through the layered breast,
or wings clipped from the side.
As for those who are overly cautious and indecisive,
timid at heart, narrow-minded.
Lacking firm resolve within,
they venture out but avoid engagement.
Approaching like a shy maiden,
fleeing like a sudden flash of lightning.
Peeking through the bean leaves,
glimpsed briefly, then hidden again.
Then I calculate the inches and ounces,
weigh the distance far and near.
Gauge the hanging blade,
unleash my utmost skill.
Like tilting forward or leaning back,
neither too high nor too low.
Aiming at the beak, striking the chest,
tearing the crop, shattering the bill.
Level or rugged, different terrains,
tame or wild, varying behaviors. 𣅳
No time to eat by day,
not weary by night.
In the past, Jiǎshì went to Gāo,
and first smiled at a single arrow.
The ugly man changed his appearance for it,
the resentful wife let go of her grudge.
Those gains from hunting excursions,
all came from daring risks and chasing swiftly.
How tranquil is this art,
yet the fowl are already prepared.
Clearing the path to proceed,
choosing the ground to settle.
Feathers adorn bridles and garments,
meat placed on the altar, forever served.
Not just for the lowly servants,
here even the lord partakes!
If one indulges in pleasure and evades duty,
letting the heart wander, unwavering.
Forgetting to care for oneself,
obsessed with the male and female.
Joyful without restraint,
upright conduct may be compromised.
This is what Lǎozǐ warned against,
what the noble person does not do.
I have encountered an age of upheaval,
suffering the calamity of obstruction and distress.
The old dwellings have turned to ruins,
and I cannot linger even briefly.
So I roll up my sleeves and march northward,
transcending all traces to wander far.
At dawn I set out from the capital,
by evening I lodge at Xuángōng in Húgǔ.
Passing through Yúnmén, I look back,
gazing at the lofty heights of Tōngtiān.
Riding over hills, ascending and descending,
resting in the villages of Xúnbīn.
Admiring the virtuous legacy of Gōngliú,
and the uncut rushes that remain unharmed.
How abundant is life for them,
while I alone suffer these myriad calamities?
Thus, the changes of the times,
are not due to the inconstancy of Heaven's decree.
I climb the long slope of Chìxū,
enter the old city of Yìqú.
Resenting the wanton cunning of the Róng king,
and the disgrace of Empress Xuān's loss of virtue.
Praising King Zhāo of Qín for punishing the traitor,
his majestic wrath as he marched north.
In turmoil, I leave this old capital,
my carriage moving slowly through this land.
Then I loosen the reins and journey far,
pointing toward Āndìng as my destination.
Traversing the long, endless road,
winding far, twisting and turning.
Passing Níyáng, I sigh deeply,
grieving that the ancestral temple lies in disrepair.
I release my horse at Péngyáng,
pausing briefly to reflect.
The sun grows dim as dusk approaches,
I watch the cattle and sheep returning.
Awakening to the sorrow of neglected grievances,
I mourn the poet's lament of the times.
Crossing Āndìng, I wander leisurely,
following the long, endless Great Wall.
Criticizing Lord Méng for exhausting the people,
building resentment for mighty Qín.
Neglecting the pressing worries of Gāo and Hài,
attending to the distant threat of barbarian tribes.
Not displaying virtue to pacify the distant,
but instead fortifying thick walls and repairing borders.
Head and body severed, yet unawakened,
still counting merits and denying faults.
How absurd the master's wild claims,
who speaks of earth's veins causing ruin?
Climbing the beacon tower to gaze afar,
I linger for a moment, swaying gently.
Pitying the Xūnyù for troubling Huáxià,
mourning Wèi Qióng at Cháonà.
Following the sage emperor's humility and yielding,
no armies were sent, only gifts bestowed.
Showing kindness to the elder brothers in Nányuè,
stripping the imperial title from Wèi Tuó.
Bestowing canes and staffs upon the vassal states,
thwarting Wú Bì's rebellious treachery.
Only Tàizōng's magnanimity,
could the former Qín ever envision?
Ascending Gāopíng to survey all around,
gazing at the towering mountain valleys.
The wilderness desolate and vast,
stretching a thousand miles without a home.
The wind howls, blowing fiercely,
valley waters gush, raising waves.
Flying clouds and mist, dark and distant,
traversing piled snow, gleaming white.
Wild geese honk in flocks as they soar,
pheasants crow with piercing cries.
A wanderer grieves for his homeland,
his heart filled with sorrow and longing.
Stroking his long sword, he sighs deeply,
tears streaming down, soaking his clothes.
Wiping away my tears, I sob softly,
mourning the many troubles of the people.
Why does darkness prevail without sunlight?
Alas, the long loss of balance and measure.
Truly, it is the work of fate and circumstance,
to whom can I pour out this eternal melancholy?
Epilogue:
The master remains steadfast in poverty,
wandering in arts and letters;
finding joy to forget sorrow,
only the sage and worthy can do so;
the enlightened person acts,
with principles and rules;
advancing, halting, bending, stretching,
resting with the times;
the noble person upholds trust,
and dwells everywhere;
even among barbarian tribes,
what is there to fear?
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
I followed my lord eastward.
On an auspicious day in early spring,
we chose a favorable hour to depart.
Lifting my feet to board the carriage,
by evening I lodged in Yǎnshī.
Thus leaving the old for the new,
my heart filled with sorrow and grief!
Dawn broke, yet I could not sleep,
my heart hesitant and conflicted.
Drinking wine to ease my thoughts,
sighing, restraining emotions, blaming myself.
Surely, I cannot climb to rob nests or strike at pests,
yet must I not exert my strength and follow?
So I join the crowd and take my place,
heeding the destiny that Heaven decrees.
Following the broad, open road,
to whom should I turn for shortcuts?
Thus I set forth and journey on,
letting my eyes wander and my soul roam free!
I passed through seven cities and beheld the sights,
Encountering many hardships in Gǒng County.
Gazing upon the confluence of the Yellow River and the Luò,
I viewed Xuángāo’s Xuán Gate.
Having escaped the steep and perilous paths,
I passed through Xíngyáng and crossed Juǎn.
I ate and rested my feet in Yuánwǔ,
Lodged amidst mulberry groves in Yángwǔ.
Crossing Fēngqiū and treading the road,
I yearned for the capital and sighed in secret!
Petty men, by nature, cherish their homeland,
As recorded in writings since ancient times.
Thus I advanced along the road, moving slowly forward,
Reaching the northern border of Píngqiū.
Entering Kuāng’s outer walls, I recalled distant times,
Thinking of the Master’s hardships and toils.
In that age of decline and chaos, devoid of the Way,
Even a sage was trapped and imperiled.
Melancholy, I lingered long in contemplation,
Forgetting the passage of day and dusk approaching.
Arriving at the borders of Chángyuán,
I observed the farmers and villagers in the fields.
Beholding the ruins of Púchéng,
Overgrown with brambles and thorns.
Startled awake, I turned to inquire,
Recalling Zǐlù’s awe-inspiring spirit.
The people of Wèi praised his courage and righteousness,
And to this day they still speak of him.
The Qú family lies southeast of the city,
And the people also revere their graves.
Only virtuous deeds are immortal,
The body perishes, but the name endures.
What the classics praise,
Values morality, benevolence, and worthies.
Wú Zhá praised the many noble men,
His words were trustworthy and well-founded.
Later, in decline and beset by calamity,
They fell into decay and did not rise again.
Knowing that life and fate lie with Heaven,
I strive through action to approach benevolence.
Endeavoring to emulate the lofty and follow the virtuous,
Exhausting loyalty and compassion toward others.
Fond of uprightness without turning back,
With sincere devotion reaching the bright spirits.
May the spirits and deities observe and shine upon me,
Blessing the upright and assisting the faithful.
Epilogue:
The thoughts of a noble man,
Must be expressed in writing.
Why not each speak his mind,
Admiring the ancients?
My late father’s travels and halts,
Were recorded in his works.
Though I am not talented,
How dare I not follow his example?
Nobility and baseness, poverty and wealth,
Cannot be sought by force.
Rectify oneself and tread the path,
Awaiting the opportune time.
The span of life, long or short,
Is the same for fools and wise alike.
Composed and reverent, I entrust myself to fate,
Accepting only fortune or misfortune.
Reverent and cautious, never negligent,
Thinking of humility and restraint.
Tranquil and with few desires,
I take Gōng Chuò as my teacher.
The year in Xuánxiāo’s cycle,
The month in Ruíbīn’s journey.
Bǐng and Dīng govern the days,
Yǐwèi presides over the hour.
Master Pān leaned on the chariot rail, traveling westward,
From the capital to Qín.
Then he sighed deeply and said:
From ancient times to the present,
How vast and distant it is!
Boundless and indistinct,
Transforming one breath, shaping the Three Powers.
These Three Powers are:
Heaven, Earth, and the Human Way.
Only life and position
Are called the great treasures.
Life has a fate of long or short span,
Position has fortunes of success or obstruction.
Even ghosts and spirits cannot control it,
Nor can sages and wise men foresee it.
In this bright and prosperous age,
I, with my humble and shallow nature,
Received the bow and banner at Xuántái,
And assisted in the myriad tasks of the imperial court.
Alas, the constant burden of a petty man
Is to worry about loss after gaining.
Lacking Liǔ Xiàhuì’s upright way,
I assisted as a judge and was once dismissed.
Emperor Wǔ suddenly passed away,
The eight tones silenced throughout the land.
The Son of Heaven rested in mourning,
All officials listened to the prime minister.
The burden he bore was exceptionally heavy,
Even Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng would have found it perilous.
Observing the seven powerful families of the Hàn court,
Could a single clan’s survival be assured?
Lacking perilous clarity to secure one’s position,
Only dwelling in oppression to display authority.
Falling into rebellion and receiving execution,
The disaster did not descend from Heaven.
Confucius acted or withdrew according to the times,
Qú Bóyù expanded or contracted with the state.
If one obscures the subtle and errs in action,
The danger of transgression is not far off.
I understand the reclusive scholars hidden in mountains,
Who resolutely departed and never returned.
Ashamed of our own constraints and rigidity,
Drifting like duckweed and turning like tumbleweed.
Official positions rise and fall,
Reputation and integrity crumble and decay.
More perilous than eggs piled high,
Worse than swallows nesting on curtains.
My heart trembles with fear and anxiety,
As if treading on thin ice or facing a deep abyss.
In the evening, I returned outside the capital,
Before midnight, disaster struck.
Not choosing a tree to perch upon,
Few birds survive when the forest burns.
Encountering a rare opportunity of a thousand years,
The emperor united virtue with Heaven and Earth.
Relaxing the stern authority of autumn frost,
Bestowing the abundant grace of spring’s moisture.
Clarifying great righteousness to assign responsibility,
Returning to plain clothes within my private gate.
The emperor discerned my loyalty,
And soon appointed me to a lowly post.
Governing weary people in Western Xià,
I led the old and young into the pass.
Confucius left Lǔ and sighed with longing,
Liú Bāng passed by Pèi and shed tears.
How much more should one cherish one’s hometown,
Grieving the hidden feelings of sages and the wise.
Even an ordinary man feels attached to his land,
How much more when venturing far to Hàojīng.
Like a dog or horse longing for its master,
Secretly I yearn for the imperial court.
Gazing upon Gǒng and Luò, I wipe away tears,
My thoughts linger on the ancestral graves.
Then I crossed Pínglè,
Passed Jiēyóu.
Fed my horse at Gāomén,
And rested my carriage in Western Zhōu.
Distant are the virtues of the Jī clan,
Rising from Gāoxīn.
Thinking of the cultured Hòujì,
Who first gave birth to the people.
Following the western waterside,
His influence spread to Qí and Bīn.
The fortune flourished with Chāng and Fā,
The old state was renewed.
Circling through Mùyě and passing here,
They increasingly upheld gentleness while striving diligently.
Awake all night until dawn,
Worried that Heaven’s protection was not yet secure.
Even Mount Tài seemed precarious,
Yet the sacrifices lasted eight hundred years with lingering blessings.
Reflecting on the fallen king’s arrogance and excess,
He fled to Náncháo to save his life.
Sitting on piled firewood waiting to ignite,
Yet pointing to the sun and comparing its glory.
How divergent are human measures,
How vastly different they are!
Examining the central lands of this city,
they established the capital and built its walls.
Once the tripods were settled at Jiárǔ,
they drilled tortoise shells and opened the oracles.
King Píng, having lost the Way, came to relocate,
relying on the protection of two states.
Was it that the king of the time lacked virtue?
He depended on the wisdom of former sages for lasting prosperity.
Gazing at the two gates north of Yǔ,
I am moved by the aid offered by Guó and Zhèng.
Condemning Zǐ Tuí for delighting in calamity,
especially the treachery west of the pass.
Repeating the punishment of Dài to secure Xiāng,
expanding great harmony to dominate the age.
Líng blocked the river to halt conflict,
Jìn elaborated on righteousness to present arguments.
From Jǐng to Dào until Gài,
governance declined and grew increasingly weak.
Allowing the nobles to plot rebellion,
spanning two kings who usurped the throne.
Passing through ten reigns down to Nǎn,
the state split and became divided.
Ultimately devoured by the tiger’s mouth,
they surrendered the sacred vessels of Wén and Wǔ.
Washing in the Xiào River and rinsing my hat strings,
I praise the fine reputation that lies here.
An infant died at Xīn’ān,
buried in a pit by the roadside.
The pavilion bears the name “A Thousand Autumns,”
but the child did not live seventy days.
Though encouraged by Yán Wú,
I secretly grieve with parental love.
Gazing upon the mountains and rivers, I recall antiquity,
sadly holding the reins midway on the road.
The tyranny of Xiàng’s clan running rampant,
burying surrendered soldiers, innocent and guilty alike.
Inciting the Qín people to return to virtue,
enabling Liú’s rise to bring relief.
Affairs twist and turn, yet retribution returns,
ending with the clan destroyed and himself slaughtered.
Passing Miǎnchí, I ponder deeply,
halting my carriage, refusing to advance.
Qín, a strong state of tigers and wolves,
Zhào, the weakened remnant of invasion.
Venturing into danger for a grand meeting,
relying on the era’s hero, Lìn.
Ashamed of the eastern zither played alone,
he raised the western jar and met the blade.
Humiliating the empty gift of ten cities,
he swiftly took Xiányáng to win acclaim.
Displaying authority beyond the river,
how fierce and roaring his valor!
Submitting with humility to Lián Gōng,
as if limbs had no bones.
Residing in wisdom and courage, profound and great,
compared to the petty anger of Bǐ Mào.
Though days changed and years passed,
no rank could convey such words.
When Guāngwǔ faced peril,

sometimes its peaks hide among a thousand ridges.
One first traverses paths haunted by mountain demons,
and finally treads upon uninhabited realms.
Rarely in the world can anyone ascend it,
and rulers have no means to perform sacrifices there.
Thus, its tales are absent from ordinary writings,
though its name is noted in extraordinary records.
Yet, the emergence of its images
—how could it be without reason?
If not for those who renounce the world and delight in the Way,
who abstain from grains and consume magical herbs,
who could lightly ascend and dwell there?
If not for those with distant aspirations and deep searching,
firm in faith and communion with the divine,
who would be willing to envision it from afar and hold it in mind?
This is why I let my spirit gallop and thoughts flow,
chanting by day and rising at night,
so that in the blink of an eye,
it feels as if I have already ascended twice.
I shall now loosen my silken cords,
and entrust myself forever to this peak.
Unable to bear the utmost depth of my chanted thoughts,
I shall wield my literary talent to disperse my feelings.
The Great Void is vast and boundless,
operating the wondrous existence of spontaneity,
melting to form rivers and streams,
coagulating to become hills and mounds.
How extraordinary and lofty is this Tāiyuè peak,
truly supported by divine spirits.
Sheltered beneath the Ox constellation, its peaks gleam;
resting upon Língyuè, it establishes its foundation.
Its roots spread wider than Huà and Dài mountains,
its direct height surpasses Jiǔyí.
It should match Heaven in the Táng classics,
and equal the lofty extremes in Zhōu poetry.
Remote is that secluded land,
deep, serene, and hidden.
The near-wise cling to their limited views and do not go;
those who go find the paths cut off and remain unaware.
I smile at summer insects doubting ice,
and adjust my light wings, thinking to soar.
No principle remains hidden and unrevealed;
it unveils two wonders as an omen.
Chìchéng’s rosy clouds rise to set a marker,
and the waterfall flies down to demarcate the path.
Witnessing these spiritual signs, I then set forth,
suddenly, I am about to go.
Following the feathered man to Dānqiū,
I seek the blessed court of immortality.
If Tiāntāi’s peaks can be climbed,
why envy the layered city?
Releasing ordinary attachments within the realm,
I express transcendent, lofty feelings.
Clad in a shaggy fur robe,
I shake my metal staff, tinkling.
Pushing through wild, dense thickets,
I ascend steep cliffs, towering and precipitous.
Crossing Yóuxī and advancing directly,
descending through Wǔjiè, swiftly journeying.
Striding across the arched, suspended stone steps,
I face the bottomless abyss of ten thousand fathoms.
Treading on slippery stones covered in moss,
I grasp the emerald screen of sheer cliffs.
Grasping the long vines of twisted trees,
I clutch the flying stems of kudzu vines.
Though once risking the peril of the leaning hall,
I shall forever preserve longevity.
One must pledge sincerity in obscurity,
treading heavy dangers as if level ground.
Having already surmounted the nine bends,
the path, though rugged, now stretches open.
I indulge my heart and eyes in vast clarity,
allowing my leisurely steps to be unhurried.
Resting upon lush, delicate grass,
shaded by tall, sparse pines.
I see soaring luan birds, graceful and elegant,
and hear crying phoenixes, harmonious and melodious.
Passing Língxī, I cleanse myself once,
dispersing vexing thoughts from my heart and chest.
Washing away lingering dust in swirling streams,
dispelling the wandering obscurity of the five hindrances.
Pursuing the lost tracks of Fúxī and Shénnóng,
treading the mysterious traces of the two elders.
Ascending and descending over a couple of nights,
I finally reach the immortal capital.
Twin towers, cloud-piercing, flank the road;
jade platforms hang mid-sky, suspended dwellings.
Vermilion gates, exquisite, among the woods;
jade halls, dimly reflected in high corners.
Rosy clouds, patterned and bright, wing the lattice;
the dazzling sun gleams through ornate windows.
Eight cassias, lush and upright, defy frost;
five magic fungi, containing beauty, bloom at dawn.
Gentle winds linger with fragrance in sunny groves;
sweet springs gush and flow in shaded channels.
Jiànmù trees obscure shadows for a thousand fathoms;
qí trees, resplendent, hang with pearls.
Wáng Qiáo controls cranes to soar skyward;
arhats fly with metal staffs, treading emptiness.
Displaying divine transformations, swift and sudden,
suddenly emerging from existence into non-existence.
Now, having toured completely,
my body still, my heart at ease.
The harmful horse already gone,
worldly affairs all discarded.
Wielding the blade meets only emptiness;
seeing the ox, no whole remains.
Concentrating thought on secluded cliffs,
clearly chanting by the long river.
Then, Xīhé at midday,
wandering vapors lift high.
Dharma drums, clanging, resonate with sound;
various incenses, fragrant, waft smoke.
Freely beholding the heavenly patriarchs,
I then gather with transcendent immortals.
Scooping up the ointment of dark jade,
rinsing with the spring of Huáchí.
Expounding teachings beyond form,
expounding the chapter on non-birth.
Awakening to the incomplete discarding of existence,
perceiving the gap in treading non-existence;
extinguishing form and emptiness to merge traces,
suddenly grasping the profound through existence.
Releasing the two names emerging as one,
dissolving the one non-existence among three banners.
Indulging in joyful discourse all day long,
equal to silent stillness without words.
Blending all phenomena in dark contemplation,
suddenly one body with spontaneity.
Spreading across the plain,
southward galloping to Cāngwú and the swelling sea,
northward running to the Purple Frontier and Yànmén.
Steered by the canal,
axised by Kūngǎng.
Amidst layered rivers and repeated passes’ depths,
at the crossroads of four meetings and five thoroughfares.
In those days of full flourishing,
chariot axles interlocked,
people shouldered shoulder to shoulder.
Marketplaces and dwellings covered the ground,
singing and piping boiled up to the sky.
Wealth multiplied from salt fields,
profit dug from copper mountains.
Talent and strength robust and abundant,
soldiers and horses elite and splendid.
Thus able to surpass Qín’s laws,
exceed Zhōu’s decrees.
Carving lofty walls,
digging deep moats,
planning for enduring ages and blessed fate.
Hence, the earnestness of rammed-earth walls and battlements,
the diligence of watchtowers and beacon towers.
Standards higher than the Five Sacred Mountains,
breadth wider than the three ancient mounds.
Precipitous like a broken bank,
towering like long clouds.
Using lodestone to repel assaults,
plastering with red clay for flying patterns.
Observing the firm fastness of foundations and gates,
it seemed one lord would rule for ten thousand sacrifices.
Passing through three dynasties, over five hundred years,
it finally split like a melon, divided like beans!
Moss clings to wells,
wild vines entangle paths.
Altars swarm with vipers and specters,
stairs host fights between munijacs and flying squirrels.
Tree spirits and mountain ghosts,
field mice and city foxes.
Howling in wind, shrieking in rain,
appearing at dusk, scurrying at dawn.
Hungry eagles sharpen their beaks,
cold owls scare fledglings.
Lurking fierce tigers,
sucking blood, devouring flesh.
Crumbling brambles choke the roads,
ancient highways stand stark and grim.
White poplars shed their leaves too soon,
frontier grasses wither prematurely.
Sharp, biting is the frosty air,
ruthless and fierce the howling wind.
Lone tumbleweeds stir of themselves,
startled sands rise up and fly.
Thickets stretch boundless into the distance,
dense groves tangled and intertwined.
The moats have all been leveled flat,
the towering ramparts now lie in ruins.
Gazing straight for a thousand li,
one sees only swirling yellow dust.
In silent contemplation, hushed and listening,
the heart, wounded, is already broken.
As for those carved doors and embroidered curtains,
the foundations of singing halls and dancing pavilions;
the jade pools and emerald trees,
the lodges for hunting parks and fishing isles;
the melodies of Wú, Cài, Qí, and Qín,
the diversions of fish-dragons, birds, and horses—
all have vanished like extinguished incense, ashes cold,
their light dimmed, their echoes stilled.
The lovely ladies of the Eastern Capital,
the beauties of the Southern Realm,
with hearts of orchids and forms of finest silk,
jade-like faces and vermilion lips—
all have laid their souls to rest in hidden stones,
entrusted their bones to barren dust.
How could they recall the shared carriage's joy and pleasure,
or the bitter toil of the separate palace?
What is the Way of Heaven?
Those who swallow their grief are many!
I take up the qin and compose a melody,
to make a song of the Desolate City.
The song says:
The frontier wind is fierce, the city walls are cold,
the well paths are gone, the mounds and ridges ruined.
For a thousand ages, ten thousand generations,
all ends together—what more is there to say?
The Lǔ Língguāng Diàn [Hall of Numinous Light]
was built by Gōngwáng Yú, son of Emperor Jǐng's consort Chéng Jī.
Initially, when Gōngwáng first established his capital in this subordinate state,
he was fond of constructing palaces and halls.
Thus he built upon the foundation and site left by Lǔ Xīgōng.
During the decline of the Hàn dynasty,
when bandits ran rampant,
from the Wèiyāng and Jiànzhāng Halls of the Western Capital
—all were seen destroyed and ruined—
yet the Língguāng Hall stood firm and alone.
Is it not perhaps that divine spirits relied upon and supported it to preserve the Hàn house?
Moreover, its measurements and design,
correspond above to the constellations,
which is also why it remains eternally secure.
I, a traveler from the southern borders,
came to Lǔ to observe its arts,
and upon seeing this, stood transfixed.
I said: Alas!
When poets are inspired,
they are moved by things and create.
Thus Xīsī praised Xīgōng,
singing of his audience hall,
so that his achievements are preserved in the words,
and the virtue of his fame is made clear in the sounds.
Things are made manifest through the *fù*,
events are proclaimed through the *sòng*.
If not by *fù* or *sòng*,
how shall they be recounted?
Therefore I composed a *fù*, saying:
Examining antiquity, the Imperial Hàn,
its ancestors profound, wise, reverent, and bright.
Flourishing in the pure glory of the Five Emperors' era,
continuing the fiery essence of the Yáo and Táng.
Bearing the Celestial Way, greatly prosperous,
expanding the cosmos to establish its capital.
Spreading the Imperial Norm to found its enterprise,
harmonizing with the Divine Way to achieve great peace.
Then the common people were enlightened,
the nine clans were ordered in harmony.
So they commanded a filial grandson,
to make him Marquis over Lǔ.
Bestowed the great jade tablet as an auspicious token,
dwelt among the vassals and opened his domain.
Then he raised the mysterious hall of Língguāng,
to match the Purple Palace as its support.
It receives the Bright Hall from the east,
shining brilliantly in the division of Kuí.
Observing the form of that Língguāng Hall,
it is lofty and towering,
precipitous and rugged.
Ah! How awe-inspiring, how startling it is to men.
Soaring and unrestrained,
richly splendid, broad and spacious,
profoundly intricate and boundless.
Rare in any age, uniquely outstanding,
marvelously strange and grandly varied.
It stands like a mountain, majestic and dense,
rising lofty into the azure clouds.
Massive and uneven, steep and towering,
jagged and scaled like a dragon's hide.
Glistening bright and resplendent,
brilliantly radiant, illuminating the earth.
Its form is like the clanging of piled stones,
and again seems like the awesome majesty of the Imperial House.
High walls link ridge to ridge in continuous ranges,
vermilion towers stand sheer, a pair erected.
The great gate rivals the Gate of Heaven,
wide enough for two carriages to enter abreast.
Then one ascends the grand steps,
to reach its main hall.
Looking up and down, gazing all around,
east and west, surveying completely.
What purpose have the crimson decorations?
They are but...
Vast and flowing,
glittering and dazzling.
White walls gleam bright as moonlight shines,
red pillars glow vibrant as lightning flashes.
Rosy clouds bloom richly,
now dark, now bright.
Sparkling and shimmering, chaotic and brilliant,
resplendent and glorious.
Hidden in deep shade and summer coolness at its center,
spacious, serene, and towering.
Vast and bright, expansive and open,
yet breezy, desolate, and clear-cool.
The drip-drip forms a sound,
echoing like thunder, startling as if alarmed.
Ears are deafened by the clamor,
eyes are dazed and lose their sight.
Closely set are fine-grained stones and langgān jade,
aligned are jade roof-ornaments and wall-jewels.
Then pushing open the golden door, entering northwards,
the interior is dim and shadowy, dusky and obscure.
Winding chambers, graceful and secluded,
inner rooms, deep and profoundly quiet.
The western wing, winding and leisurely,
the eastern corridor, layered deep and mysterious.
Lofty, dark, and indistinct,
dim, obscured, and profoundly deep.
The soul is startled, alarmed by this,
the heart trembles and palpitates.
Then examining in detail its beams and framework,
observing its construction.
Its measurements correspond to Heaven,
above modeling the constellation Zīzōu.
Jutting forth like rising clouds,
precipitous and interconnected.
Three bays, four external sides,
eight dimensions, nine corners.
Ten thousand pillars cluster together,
massive and piled, supporting each other.
Floating columns soar high, suspended like stars,
swaying, towering, and propped by branches.
Flying crossbeams arch like pointing rainbows,
soaring high and gathering together.
Layered bracket-arms piled perilously high,
curved crossbeams supple and encircling.
Fungus-shaped brackets clustered like gathered halberds,
branching struts splayed and leaning askew.
Beside them, twisting forms thrust out sideways,
intertwining darkly, wrestling and bearing weight.
Below, lush and luxuriant, intricately patterned,
above, steep and perilous, with layered overhangs.
Arranged in rows like fish scales,
scattered and branching, parting ways.
Crisscrossing, continuous and linked,
each with its own direction.
Then there are suspended beams and interwoven rafters,
With celestial windows elegantly spaced.
Round pools and square wells,
With lotus flowers planted upside down.
They bloom and display their splendor,
Lotus blossoms spreading wide.
Green pods and purple seeds,
Drip and hang like pearls.
Cloud-patterned brackets and painted pillars,
Dragon-shaped rafters carved and engraved.
Flying birds and running beasts,
Take form from the wood, full of grace.
A rushing tiger, claws outstretched, leans against a beam,
Fierce and vigorous, with bristling mane.
Coiled dragons soar and writhe,
Their jaws seeming to move, poised and tense.
The Vermilion Bird spreads its wings, perched on a crossbeam,
While a soaring serpent twists and coils around the rafters.
A white deer, solitary and elegant, rests on a bracket,
And a coiled dragon winds gracefully, supporting the lintel.
A cunning rabbit crouches hidden beside a pillar,
While apes climb the rafters, chasing one another.
A black bear, tongue lolling, gnashes its teeth,
Leaning back, bearing a load, and squatting firmly.
All lift their heads and stare with wide eyes,
Silently gazing, fierce and alert.
Barbarians gather distantly on the upper pillars,
Solemn and dignified, kneeling face to face.
Fierce and savage, with carved and glaring eyes,
Wild-haired and staring askance.
Their expressions seem sorrowful in perilous places,
Frowning and pained, bearing a look of distress.
Immortals stand tall between the beams,
Jade maidens peer through windows, gazing down.
Suddenly glimpsed faintly, like echoes and shadows,
As if ghosts and spirits, vague and indistinct.
They depict heaven and earth,
And all categories of living beings.
Assorted strange and wondrous things,
Mountain spirits and sea deities.
Their forms are recorded and portrayed,
Entrusted to vermilion and azure.
With a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations,
Each subject takes its distinct shape.
Following colors to represent categories,
Subtly capturing their essence.
Above, they record the opening of creation,
The very beginnings of antiquity.
The Five Dragons with wings aligned,
The Nine-Headed Human Sovereign.
Fúxī with a scaled body,
Nǚwā with a serpentine form.
The vast wilderness, simple and rough,
Their appearances wild and untamed.
Brilliant and splendid to behold,
Are Huángdì, Táng, and Yú.
Chariots and crowns to mark their service,
Robes and garments distinguished in kind.
Descending to the three later rulers,
Lascivious consorts and chaotic sovereigns.
Loyal ministers and filial sons,
Martyrs and chaste women.
The wise and foolish, success and failure,
All are recorded and narrated.
Evil to warn the world,
Good to instruct posterity.
Thus, connecting pavilions bear the palace halls,
Galloping paths encircle all around.
Sunlit towers gaze outward,
High buildings and soaring observatories.
Long pathways rise and descend,
Balustrades stretch far and wide.
Terraced towers overlook pools,
Layered and winding, nine levels high.
Towering and standing alone,
Distinct and unique in form.
Their height rivals the Huágài constellation,
Looking up, one sees the celestial court.
Soaring staircases rise steeply,
Following the clouds, ascending high.
Seated within, one sees shadows cast down,
Looking down, meteors streak by.
A thousand gates alike in appearance,
Ten thousand doors uniform in design.
Cliffs protrude, caves emerge,
Winding and twisting, bending and turning.
Circling for several miles,
One looks up and sees no sun.
How magnificent and exquisite this grandeur,
Ah, the wondrous effort expended!
Were it not for the brilliant talent, divinely inspired,
Who could have accomplished such a feat?
Based on the precious terrain of the earth’s spirit,
Receiving the pure abundance of the azure heavens.
Encompassing the transformations of yīn and yáng,
Containing the misty vapor of primordial energy.
Dark springs surge and bubble in hidden channels,
Sweet dew covers the eaves, descending abundantly.
Vermilion cassia trees flourish darkly north and south,
Orchids and auspicious grasses sway gracefully east and west.
Auspicious winds gather and rustle gently,
Stirring fragrant scents, ever sweet.
Divine spirits support its beams and halls,
Passing a thousand years, growing ever stronger.
Eternal peace and blessings it bestows,
Long enduring with the great Hàn, ever preserved.
Truly, it is where the supreme sovereign resides,
Ensuring prolonged life and prosperity for descendants.
If such a place can be esteemed thus,
Who would speak of it and not treasure it?
Epilogue:
Vermilion and grand, this divine palace,
Lofty and towering, reaching the heavens,
Vast and magnificent, oh!
Precipitous and steep, rugged and jagged,
High and towering, peaks upon peaks,
Clustered and piled, oh!
Twisted and bending, lofty and proud,
Coiled and winding, rugged and uneven,
Leaning and slanting, oh!
Dark and deep, shrouded in mystery,
Clouds spread thickly, covering all,
Profound and obscure, oh!
Lush green and purple hues,
Majestic and magnificent,
Containing light and shadow, oh!
Utterly wondrous and supremely exquisite,
Since the dawn of beams and halls,
Nothing like it has ever been, oh!
Spirits built it,
Blessing our Hàn dynasty,
Forever enduring, oh!
Great indeed is Wèi,
An age of wise and sagely rulers.
Wǔ laid the founding foundation,
Wén gathered the great mandate.
All modeled on heaven to establish institutions,
Following the times to set governance.
Reaching the emperors,
Successive reigns grew ever brighter and prosperous.
From afar, they followed the natural ways of yīn and yáng,
From near, they rooted in the deepest sentiments of people.
Above, they revered the grand principles of antiquity,
Below, they elucidated the enduring codes of good rule.
All affairs now in order,
Heaven’s hierarchy perfectly clear.
Thus, after two or three reigns,
The state grew rich and punishments light.
In the third month of the year,
The emperor toured eastward,
Reaching Xǔchāng.
He paid homage to mountains and rivers,
Examined the seasons and measured directions.
He inquired after the elderly,
Leading the people in farming and sericulture.
By the sixteenth day of the sixth month,
When the Línzhōng pitchpipe marked the rhythm,
And the great fire star shone at dusk.
Mulberry and catalpa trees flourished lushly,
Heavy rains fell seasonally.
The three ministers and nine directors,
Great Confucians and eminent scholars.
Moved by the oppressive heat’s stifling gloom,
Pondered the balance of life’s fate.
Only Mín and Yuè remained unsettled,
Awakening to campaigns not yet pacified.
Then he spoke eloquently, saying:
"In the past, Lord Xiāo
and Master Xún
were both far-sighted and widely learned,
brilliant, trustworthy, sincere, and earnest.
None failed to believe that without grandeur and beauty,
one could not unify the people and enhance majestic authority.
Without adornment and elegance,
one could not instruct posterity and perpetuate its achievements.
Thus, in their own time, they enjoyed its benefits and efficacy,
and later generations relied on their illustrious reputation.
Moreover, Xǔchāng
is where the great destiny converges,
as indicated by the charts and prophecies.
If virtue and righteousness are thus,
why should palaces and halls not be built?"
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!"
The dark imperial carriage was already harnessed,
and light furs were worn.
He then commanded the officials
to prepare the rituals and ceremonies.
They carefully measured the days and efforts,
and meticulously calculated the expenses and tasks.
They gathered the common people for the commencement,
assembling them during the leisure of agricultural work.
Taking advantage of the eastern army's victory offerings,
and the bribes from the sea rebels,
they erected the mysterious hall of Jǐngfú,
equipping it with the system of the imperial residence.
Then they made the layered roofs deep and imposing,
and built the high foundations grand and majestic.
They arranged the sparse pillars in orderly rows,
and solemnly set the base edges clanging.
Flying eaves spread like wings soaring,
and upturned roof ridges rose high and lofty.
Feather ornaments flowed luxuriantly,
and jade pendants hung like琳琅.
Banners with nine tassels,
fluttered in the wind.
Bright and dazzling,
their crimson colors shone brilliantly.
Thus, the ornamental pillars were resplendent and glittering,
magnificent and radiant,
as if the sun and moon adorned the sky.
Their hidden depths were shaded and obscure,
vaguely indistinct,
like distant stars strung together.
They were arranged like comb teeth and clustered together,
and also broad and spacious.
Embracing vast expanses,
not confined to a single form.
Viewed from afar,
they seemed like spread crimson clouds illuminating the celestial patterns;
observed up close,
they appeared like towering mountains crowned with hanging clouds.
How magnificent and grand they were,
so richly adorned and difficult to distinguish,
this was their general appearance.
As for the high ridges, towering and majestic,
flying eaves caught the rainbows.
Dark and dense,
they blended with the drifting clouds.
Like birds perching on mountains, standing firm,
seeming to soar yet remaining still.
Lofty and steep,
their limits unknown.
Even Lí Zhū, with his utmost keen sight,
would be dazzled and unable to see clearly.
Then they opened the southern end, broad and expansive,
and displayed the bell stands, round and harmonious.
Ornate bells hung high,
and fierce beasts stood boldly in pairs.
Their bodies robust and fiercely resolute,
their sounds rumbling like thunder.
There were distant Dí people,
with splendid forms, round and layered.
Seated in the side halls of the high gate,
they displayed the威严 and divine power of the sage ruler.
Rúruò plants filled the courtyard,
and locust and maple trees covered the imperial grounds.
Adorned with ten-thousand-year vines,
and embellished with purple hazels.
Some gained favor for their auspicious names,
others were treasured for their fine timber.
They bore fruit in late autumn,
and bloomed in youthful spring.
Lush and luxuriant,
fragrant and sweet.
As for their structure,
the long beams were colorfully crafted,
plain below and marvelous above.
Crossbeams overlapped repeatedly,
their forms separate yet forces united.
Vivid like a curved rainbow,
brilliant like a galloping dragon.
To the south, they reached the sunny eaves,
to the north, they extended to the dark cliffs.
Bearing heavy loads over long distances,
their utility was great indeed.
Then they arranged lacquered red carved rafters,
and hung jade-like ornamental tiles.
Undulating like divine dragons ascending and descending,
glowing like bright moonlight flowing.
There were forbidden rafters,
carved and spread like wings.
Supported by yangmǎ beams,
connected with round and square joints.
Patterns interspersed with white,
sparse and dense with order.
Flying brackets leaped like birds,
bearing double rails.
Venturing into peril, soaring into emptiness,
swift and agile, interlocking.
Gleaming white intervals,
neatly arranged like coins.
Morning light shone within,
flowing radiance glittered without.
Intense like钩星 in the Milky Way,
resplendent like cloud beams supporting the sky.
Shifting and increasing in complexity,
turning and suspending to form walls.
Lotus stems inverted and planted,
blooming with lotus flowers.
Encircled by caisson ceilings,
woven with patterned lattices;
red flowers vibrant,
crimson silks intricately patterned.
Lotus buds crimson and gathered,
delicate patterns spreading profusely.
Elaborate decorations and accumulated artistry,
too numerous to record.
Then orchid brackets piled layer upon layer,
and humble rafters set at right angles.
Brackets and capitals each placed to bear weight,
and curved brackets intertwining and interlocking.
Golden pillars stood in neat rows,
jade bases supported the steps.
Blue-patterned doors with silver fittings,
these formed the inner chambers.
Double rafters were already long,
and layered purlins were adorned.
Edge trims bordered the sides,
circling all four extremes.
Like guards in ranks,
and frontier officials at their posts.
Warm rooms lay to the east,
cool chambers were situated to the west.
Opening Jiànyáng brought forth blazing crimson,
unlocking Jīnguāng ushered in clear breezes.
Thus, winter was not bitterly cold,
and summer had no scorching heat.
Harmoniously regulated and perfectly balanced,
one could live long years here.
Walls with patterned foundations,
their brilliance shining brightly.
According to Zhōu dynasty standards, white was used for adornment,
but now it is pale blue.
Falling belts with golden nails,
here there were two grades.
Bright pearls and kingfisher feathers,
were often found here and there.
Admiring the former kings' true fulfillment,
and delighting in Shùn's effortless rule.
He ordered the Minister of Works to create paintings,
displaying the brilliance of the five colors.
Depicting figures of ancient times,
to serve as admonitions and guidelines.
The ranks of the pepper rooms,
were taken as standards and models.
Observing Yú Jī's demeanor,
one learns of the flattering ministers who govern the state.
Seeing Empress Jiāng removing her jade pendant,
one awakens to the ways followed by earlier generations.
Praising Zhōnglí's honest words,
and admiring Chǔ Fán's withdrawal from court.
Commending Consort Bān's refusal of the carriage,
and extolling Mèng's mother's choice of neighbors.
Thus, to broaden wisdom,
one must first hear much.
Hearing much brings variety,
and variety dazzles the truth.
Where does not dazzle lie?
It lies in choosing the right people.
Thus, to establish virtue,
one must first draw near to benevolence.
Wishing this ritual to be without fault,
therefore, they fully followed the ways of the ancients who practiced the Dào.
Observing morning and evening,
how does it compare to inscribing on one's sash?
As for the steps and terraces stretching continuously,
they soar high into the clouds.
The balustrades and railings are widely spaced,
arranged in perfect squares and angles.
The railings resemble soaring serpents,
the brackets are like fine jade blossoms.
Coiled like hornless dragons,
poised like coiling serpents.
Dark verandas interlace as they ascend,
gleaming patterns shining brightly.
Mythical beasts bear offerings,
pure in substance and benevolent in form.
Displaying auspicious signs from heaven,
illuminating distant tribes who come to court.
The northern hall faces the north,
with nine doors on each side.
The right chamber is for quiet repose,
extending east and west.
Connected to Yǒngníng Hall,
Ānchāng Hall overlooks the garden.
Then comes the Bǎizǐ Palace,
where the imperial consorts reside.
Who dwells within?
Graceful and virtuous ladies.
Aspiring to noble virtue,
seeking abundant blessings.
What are these blessings?
That your descendants prosper.
Wise and discerning,
keen and diligent.
Forever granted ageless vitality,
the people rely on them.
To the south stands Chéngguāng Front Hall,
the palace of governance.
Admitting the worthy and employing the capable,
inquiring into the Way to find the mean.
Ordering the cosmos,
molding the nation’s customs.
Like clouds moving and rain falling,
all things are harmoniously blended.
To the west are level grounds on left and right,
a field for practice and training.
Twelve teams face each other,
halls aligned like wings.
Swift evasion seizing advantage,
resembling military maneuvers.
Observing and analyzing before returning,
akin to governance and punishment.
Meant to enforce commands,
not merely for amusement.
Anchored by a lofty tower,
truly called Yǒngshǐ.
With layered pavilions and repeated gates,
awaiting unrestrained revelry.
Stores from the capital granaries,
where nothing is lacking.
Prepared against unforeseen events,
from here they are drawn.
Then raising layered terraces that touch the clouds,
dredging the divine pond of Yúyuān.
Clear dew lies thick,
green waters stretch vast.
Planted with fine trees,
set with fragrant grasses.
Dark fish glide leisurely,
white birds gleam brightly.
Sinking, floating, soaring,
delighting in our emperor’s way.
As for the coiling dragon conduits pouring water,
channels and ditches interflow.
On land, halls and lodges are arranged;
on water, light boats ply.
Bamboo groves shelter phoenixes and egrets;
rapids play with catfish and bream.
Abundant as the Huái River and sea,
rich enough to relieve the hills.
Gathered and piled in masses,
how could one count it all?
Even the grandeur of Xiánchí,
how could it compare?
Then marking with Gāochāng’s lofty observatory,
signifying with Jiànchéng’s steep towers.
Towering peaks stand steep,
lofty ridges reside.
Soaring pavilions pierce the clouds,
floating stairs ride the void.
Gazing afar over the nine wilds,
surveying the long panorama.
Looking down upon the three markets,
what is there and what is not?
Observing farmers weeding and tilling,
understanding the toil of sowing and reaping.
Considering whether harvests are plentiful or scarce,
reflecting on the sighs in “No Idleness.”
Moved by the multitude of things, thoughts deepen;
from this high place, perils are pondered.
Aware that heavenly virtue is unchanging,
yet fearing the world’s ways are hard to know.
Examining whether tools are good or poor,
observing whether customs are sincere or false.
Seeing where nobility and baseness lie,
discerning whether governance and punishment are even or skewed.
This also serves to assess customs and aid teaching—
how could it be merely for pleasure and extravagance?
Barracks and offices arrayed,
thirty-two in number.
Scattered like stars, arrayed like constellations,
intricately interwoven like fish scales.
Named and ordered
by the celestial stems.
Rooms and chambers uniformly aligned,
halls and courtyards all alike.
Going out this door, entering that,
one wishes to return but forgets the way.
So varied are the artisans’ methods,
truly endless in their transformations.
No object is too difficult to craft,
matching Creation itself in grandeur.
Rivaling heaven and earth in laying foundations,
aligning with the constellations in establishing forms.
No detail fails to match the compass and gnomon,
no work, however fine, deviates from the water-level.
Thus its structures rise as if piled high,
planted trees stand like a forest.
Districts joined yet boundaries distinct,
leaves aligned, branches parted.
Separated, facing different directions,
clustered closely, attached side by side.

In the ancient era of Emperor Guī, during the great reign of Táng,
the heavenly order was in turmoil,
bringing decay and calamity.
Vast waves surged and rolled,
boundless for ten thousand miles.
Long billows rose and fell,
stretching and spreading to the eight distant regions.
Then, Yǔ,
leveled the towering cliffs and highlands,
cut through embankments and ponds to connect them.
He opened the lofty cliffs of Lóngmén,
and carved through the mountain ranges with steep chiseling.
Once the mountains were subdued,
all rivers flowed hidden and clear.
The waters, vast and deep,
surged forth with rising momentum.
The rivers and streams now channeled,
countless springs flowed together.
They uplifted the Five Sacred Mountains,
and drained the nine regions dry.
Dripping and seeping moisture,
gathered into mist and clouds.
Tiny streams and swelling currents,
all converged and poured in.
Oh, vast and divine sea,
forever the great reservoir.
Its breadth,
its marvels,
truly make it immense.
As for its appearance,
it is shimmering and glistening,
reaching the sky with no shore in sight.
Vast and boundless,
stretching far and wide.
Waves like continuous mountains,
now merging, now parting.
It inhales and exhales a hundred rivers,
cleansing the Huái and Hàn.
Submerging hills and spreading marshes,
vast and expansive.
When the great sun guides its chariot to the golden pivot's cave,
and the soaring sun dashes swiftly at Fúsāng's ford,
it scatters sand and grinds stones,
sweeping past windy islands and shores.
Then, stirred to fury,
it overflows with waves, lifting and floating.
Crashing against one another,
spray flies and billows rise.
Shaped like a celestial wheel,
twisting and spinning fiercely,
or like the earth's axis,
towering and whirling in contention.
Peaks soar and tumble in turmoil,
the Five Sacred Mountains dance and clash.
Swirling eddies gather and surge,
heaving and falling in tumultuous succession.
Whirling currents strike and form abysses,
swirling waters converge into peaks.
Rippling waves drift and sway,
piled rocks clash and grind.
Terrifying waves thunder forth,
frightening waters gush and gather,
opening and closing, parting and meeting,
surging and splashing endlessly.
Flower-like froth churns and bubbles,
swirling and seething tumultuously.
When gloomy darkness fades away,
nothing stirs or trembles.
Fine dust does not fly,
slender vines do not sway.
Yet still, with gasping sounds,
lingering waves surge alone.
Roaring and rumbling,
like piled-up mountain ridges.
As for its branching streams and deep pools,
they swell and spread into tributaries.
Separating barbarian lands,
intertwining for ten thousand miles.
If urgent news comes from remote borders,
and the king's command must be swiftly delivered,
swift steeds gallop and oars drum,
crossing seas and scaling mountains.
Then, awaiting strong winds,
hoisting hundred-foot sails,
securing long silken ropes,
hanging canvas sheets.
Gazing at distant billows, breaking through,
swift as birds vanishing into the distance.
Startled like ducks losing their mates,
sudden as six dragons pulled by reins.
Leaping three thousand miles at once,
reaching the destination before the day ends.
If one approaches the depths bearing guilt,
with empty vows and broken prayers,
then sea sprites block the path,
and horse-headed demons bar the way.
Tiānwú briefly appears, vague and indistinct,
Wǎngxiàng flickers into sight, then vanishes.
Hordes of monsters converge and oppose,
squinting and leering with sinister gazes.
They tear sails and break masts,
stirring evil winds.
Vast and mystical transformations,
dim and obscure in the dark dusk.
An aura like the celestial firmament,
clouds spreading densely.
Sudden flashes outshine lightning,
a hundred eerie colors revealed.
Gasping and stifled,
glinting and flickering without measure.
Torrents crash against each other,
forces colliding and grinding.
Clouds crumble, rain scatters,
rumbling and gushing endlessly.
Leaping, plunging, swirling, and churning,
boiling, overflowing, and spilling.
Splashing, swirling, and surging,
washing clouds and drenching the sun.
Then boatmen and fishermen,
journey southward or eastward.
Some are crushed and sunk in the lairs of giant turtles,
some are caught and hung on jagged mountain peaks.
Some are dragged and tossed in the lands of naked people,
some drift aimlessly in the realms of black-toothed tribes.
Some float like duckweed, turning with the currents,
some rely on returning winds to find their way back.
They only recognize the many terrors they witness,
but fail to grasp the distance they have traveled.
As for its immense expanse,
it washes against Zhūyá in the south,
sprinkles Tiānxū in the north.
It extends to Xīmù in the east,
and reaches Qīngxú in the west.
The journey through its misty depths,
spans countless miles beyond measure.
It spews clouds and rainbows,
and harbors dragons and fish.
It conceals the scales of giant kūn,
and hides the dwellings of divine beings.
Does it merely accumulate the treasures of Tàidiān,
and the pearls of Suíhóu?
What the world collects is often heard of,
but what remains unnamed seems as if it does not exist.
Moreover, what is rarely heard of in the world,
how can one truly know its name?
Thus, one can only vaguely imagine its colors,
and dimly perceive its forms.
Within its watery palace,
in the deepest of courts,
there are towering islands and giant turtles,
lofty and solitary peaks.
Splitting the vast waves,
pointing to the highest heavens.
Exhausting the bedrock,
providing rest for all spirits.
Riding the gentle southern breeze, sailing southward,
the broad northern winds arrive, journeying north.
Along its shores lie heavenly treasures and aquatic monsters,
the dwellings of jiāo people.
Flawed stones with strange hues,
scales and shells of extraordinary substance.
Where cloud-patterned brocade scatters its patterns on sandy shores,
and silken gauze reflects light on the rings of snails and clams.
Multicolored brilliance radiates splendor,
countless hues conceal their vividness.
Sunlit ice remains unmelted,
while hidden fires smolder silently.
Glowing embers rekindle and blaze,
casting light into the nine springs below.
Vermilion flames and green smoke,
flickering and wavering like cicada wings.
Among its fish is the whale that crosses the seas,
thrusting forward, solitary in its wanderings.
It scrapes against rocky cliffs,
and lies across towering waves.
It devours scales and shells,
and swallows dragon boats whole.
When it inhales waves, vast ripples shrink back,
when it blows spray, all rivers flow backward.
Sometimes, struggling in exhausted waves,
it dies on land in salt fields.
Its giant scales pierce the clouds,
its fins and spines stab the sky.
Its skull becomes a mountain,
its flowing oils form deep abysses.
As for the nooks of rocky islets,
the ruggedness of sand and stone.
Feathers and wings produce fledglings,
eggs are hatched to become birds.
Ducklings are fluffy and downy,
crane chicks are drenched and bedraggled.
In flocks they fly and bathe together,
frolicking in the shallows and floating in the depths.
Soaring through mist in continuous flight,
they spread out and overflow endlessly.
Their flapping wings create thunderous sounds,
disturbing feathers to form a forest.
They call and cry to one another,
with strange colors and diverse voices.
As for when the three lights are clear,
heaven and earth melt into brightness.
Without floating on the waves of Yánghóu,
one rides on clogs to travel afar.
See Ānqī at Pénglái,
behold the imperial image at Qiáoshān.
Groups of immortals, ethereal and distant,
feast on jade by the clear shores.
Treading the left slippers of Fùxiāng,
clad in feathered garments, flowing and graceful.
Soaring over celestial ponds,
playing in the boundless deep.
Distinguishing form within desirelessness,
eternally serene and long-lived.
Moreover, as a vessel,
it encompasses the mysteries of heaven,
and contains the regions of earth.
It is the abode of spirits,
and also the dwelling of deities.
What marvel does it not possess?
What wonder does it not store?
Vast and boundless accumulated streams,
containing forms within emptiness.
How expansive is the virtue of water,
humble in its self-abasement.
Expanding to receive the incoming,
serving as ancestor and capital.
All things are born according to kind,
what exists and what does not!
Consider the combined use of the five elements,
truly the spiritual greatness of water’s virtue.
Only the Mínshān guides the river,
initially originating from a tiny stream.
It begins its course at Luòmò,
gathering myriad streams from Bāliáng.
Rushing through Wūxiá with swift intensity,
ascending Jiāngjīn and swelling with waves.
Reaching immense volume and sea-like motion,
appearing boundless as if flooding the sky.
Encompassing Hàn and Sì,
embracing both Huái and Xiāng.
Swallowing Yuán and Lǐ,
drawing in Jū and Zhāng.
Its source splits at Jūlái,
its flow divides into nine branches at Xúnyáng.
Stirring great waves at Chì’àn,
submerging remaining ripples at Cháisāng.
Networking all streams,
evaluating even the smallest rivulets.
Manifesting divine convergence at Jiāngdū,
mingling flows to meet eastward.
Pouring into five lakes with vast expanse,
irrigating three rivers with roaring force.
Soaking the domains of six provinces,
extending beyond the fiery regions.
Thus forming a boundary for Huá and Yì,
strengthening the perilous barriers of heaven and earth.
Breathing across ten thousand miles,
exhaling and inhaling spiritual tides.
Naturally ebbing and flowing,
sometimes at dusk, sometimes at dawn.
Stirring swift momentum to lead the way,
then roaring with anger to create waves.
Éméi serves as the marker for Quányáng,
Yùlěi stands as the sign for Dōngbié.
Héng and Huò, rugged and lofty, form continuous ranges,
Wū and Lú, towering and steep, stand as neighboring peaks.
Harmonizing with spirits and circulating energy,
surging and pressing, mutually shaping.
Flowing winds steam like thunder,
rising rainbows soar to the heavens.
Emerging from Xìnyáng to journey far,
pouring into the great abyss and Wòjiāo.
As for the gorges of Bādōng,
Xiàhòu dredged and carved them.
Sheer cliffs ten thousand zhàng high,
standing like walls, mottled and variegated.
Hǔyá, steep and towering, rises precipitously,
Jīngmén, lofty and imposing, stands firm and grand.
Circular abysses twist nine times, suspended and soaring,
gushing streams roar like thunder and flash like lightning.
Terrifying waves violently splash,
startling breakers fly and dash.
Swift whirlpools increase turbulence,
surging rapids leap in layers.
Crashing against rocks, they roar into action,
pounding and splashing, churning and foaming.
Swirling and surging, bubbling and gushing,
overflowing and spreading, rushing and flooding.
Gushing and swirling, vast and deep,
churning and seething, swirling and eddying.
Whirling and circling, flowing and swirling,
gathering and falling, spraying and cascading.
Rippling and flowing, dense and continuous,
like dragon scales interwoven.
Green sands drift to and fro,
giant rocks, jagged and rugged, advance and retreat.
Hidden channels churn and swirl,
rushing currents grind and clash.
Cliffs and ledges are carved and eroded,
rocky ridges become jagged and steep.
Deep gullies accumulate obstacles,
rugged stones, rough and uneven.
As for the abodes of layered pools,
the depths of spiritual lakes.
Clear and placid, vast and shimmering,
deep and boundless, profound and swirling.
Deep and still, clear and reflective,
swirling and eddying, rippling and gleaming.
Mingling and blending, radiant and shimmering,
flowing reflections shimmer and glow.
Boundless and vast, endless and deep,
rolling and surging, expansive and wide.
Observe it, and there is no form,
seek it, and there is no boundary.
Misty vapor rises like dense fog,
at times swirling like smoke.
Like chaos before congealing,
resembling the Tàijí forming heaven.
Long waves stretch and spread,
steep rapids tower high.
Whirlpools turn like valleys,
towering waves collapse like mountains.
Yánghóu, majestic and grand, rises from the banks,
great billows curl and swirl like clouds returning.
Swirling and eddying, surging and churning,
now sinking, now piling up.
Gaping like the earth splitting,
opening wide as if heaven parting.
Touching winding cliffs, they coil and wind,
startling collapsing waves that crash together.
Drumming in caves, they surge and swell,
then gush forth and ride the bends.
As for fish, there are river dolphins and sea otters,
sturgeons and giant yellowchecks.
Various carps, breams, and perches,
ling, skate, mullet, and silver carp.
Some with antler-like gills or trunk-like noses,
some tiger-like in appearance or dragon-like in visage.
Scales and armor glitter and interlace,
dazzling and brilliant like brocade patterns.
Raising fins and wagging tails,
spouting waves and spraying foam.
Pushing against currents, breathing and gasping,
following the waves, swimming and extending.
Some shimmer with colors, illuminating the depths,
some gasp with gills among the rocks.
Armored whales ride the waves to come and go,
swordfish and cutlassfish move with the seasons.
As for the strange assortment of aquatic creatures,
there are hidden cranes, fish-cows,
tiger-salamanders, and hook-snakes.
Serpentine fish, horseshoe crabs, and salamanders,
rays, giant turtles, and soft-shelled turtles.
King scallops and sea moons,
sea pork and rock blossoms.
Three-barbeled river fish,
parrot snails and spiral shells.
Boring clams with crabs in their bellies,
jellyfish with shrimp as eyes.
Purple clams as large as ditches,
