giant ark shells filling carts.
Lustrous clams bask in the sun, gleaming with pearls,
stone corals respond to rhythms, waving their blossoms.
Jūzhī insects hang densely with drooping antennae,
black oysters lumpy and uneven, piled and stacked.
Some float shimmering on tidal waves,
some lie buried in mud and sand.
There are dragon carp with a single horn,
strange cāng birds with nine heads.
There are three-legged turtles,
and six-eyed tortoises.
Red turtles leap and spit pearls,
patterned pí fish chime and conceive jade.
Tiáoyóng insects brush their wings and flash with light,
divine lì serpents wriggle and swim deep.
Sea horses surge through waves with stomping hooves,
water rhinoceroses roar like thunder at Yáng Hóu.
Deep-dwelling guests build houses at the cliff base,
jiāo people construct lodges over hanging streams.
Hail-like spread of leftover grain,
star-scattered sandy mirrors.
Green silk threads vie to intertwine,
ornate ribbons compete in shimmering.
Purple seaweed glitters in clustered coverings,
green moss hangs shaggy upon the polished surfaces.
Stone sails loom densely covering the islets,
duckweed fruits occasionally emerge and float.
Below are gold ore and cinnabar gravel,
cloud essence and luminous silver.
Lì pearls, liú gems, xuán jade, guī stones,
aqua jade and hidden mín jade.
Sounding stones arrayed on the sunny islets,
floating chime stones displayed along the shady banks.
Some sparkle with color on gentle ripples,
some gleam brightly near the cliffs.
No forest is not moist,
no shore is not soaked.
Among the feathered tribes,
there are morning owls and heavenly chickens,
yāo, ào, gulls, and piě.
Sun birds soar,
in the dark month.
Thousands of kinds, myriad voices,
clamor cacophonously among themselves.
They wash wings in sparse winds,
flap pinions with a whir.
Flinging and sprinkling pearl-like droplets,
patting and brushing off foamy spray.
Gathering like clouds of sunset hue,
scattering as clouds part wide.
Shedding down, accumulating feathers,
coming and going between Bó and Jié.
Lìn and qǐ trees grow thick along the shores,
lì and lián trees rise densely foresting the ridges and peaks.
Táozhī and yúndāng bamboos,
truly abundant in clusters.
Reeds and cattails spread like clouds,
adorned with orchid-red blooms.
Raising white downy tufts,
thrusting forth purple fluff.
Shading the deep bends of pools,
covering the Long River.
Lush and fragrant hedges of lí,
hidden thickets of water pines.
Shore shrubs verdant and luxuriant,
submerged growth lush and vibrant.
Líng and lú fish huddle at the water's edge,
biān tǎ otters peer alertly from hollows.
Swift wèi monkeys leap through the void with deft skill,
solitary jué apes climb perilous heights with graceful ease.
Kuí and hòu calves kick up heels in the setting sun,
yuānchú phoenixes play with wings east of the mountain.
Following forks, islets form,
meeting gullies, channels open.
Gorges rinsed become inlets,
distinctions made create lakes.
Drained by fán yì floods,
discharged through the wěilǘ drain.
Marked by emerald canopies,
floated upon by wandering wild rice.
Sowing unplanted awn-seeded grains,
raising natural fine vegetables.
Scaled with water lilies and lotuses,
clustered with aquatic melons.
Stems upturned, blossoms gushing,
tips cleansed, husks scattered.
Swaying gracefully with the wind,
rippling along with the waves.
Flowing light shines hidden below,
reflections blaze like sunset clouds aflame.
Nearby lie Yúnmèng and Léichí lakes,
Pénglǐ and Qīngcǎo lakes,
Jùqū, Táo, and Gé lakes,
Zhūchǎn and Dāncháo lakes.
Gazing to the horizon for hundreds [of miles],
vast and shimmering, boundless and bright.
Here are the caverns of Bāo Mountain and Dòngtíng,
the subterranean passages of Bālíng.
Hidden routes run alongside, connecting,
secluded caverns deep and remote.
Gold essence and jade splendor fill their interiors,
yáo pearls and wondrous stones adorn their surfaces.
Black dragons entwine their bases,
cloud-touching treetops crown their summits.
Where the Sea Child patrols and wanders,
where Qín Gāo soars with divine prowess.
Bīng Yí leans on waves gazing arrogantly,
Jiāng Fēi frowns with distant, pensive eyes.
Stroking the ripples, they leap like wild ducks,
inhaling emerald mists, they soar with grace.
And when the cosmos is clear and still,
the eight winds do not stir.
Then boatmen grasp their oars,
ferrymen take hold of poles.
Drifting like flying clouds,
moving yúhuáng vessels.
Sterns and prows linked in succession,
masts connected for ten thousand miles.
Going upstream and down along the flow,
some fishing, some trading.
Heading to Jiāo and Yì,
bound for Yōu and Làng.
Reaching the southern extreme,
exhausting the eastern wilds.
Then they gaze at mists and vapors in the clear dawn,
observe the windsock's movements.
Long winds strengthen and grow in force,
broad and desolate, steady and orderly.
Gentle yet not sluggish,
swift yet not fierce.
Sails drumming, swiftly crossing,
parting swells, cutting through currents.
Riding the waves, rudders wielded freely,
flashing past into distant gloom.
Vivid as morning clouds journeying alone,
tiny as cloud-wings beyond the ridges.
In a blink, hundreds [of miles],
a thousand miles in a moment.
Fēilián could not glimpse their traces,
Qú Huáng could not match their speed.
Then reed-gatherers and fishermen,
cast aside by rivers and mountains,
clad in feathery hemp,
fed only on vegetables and fresh fish.
Stakes set in shallows form weirs,
bamboo traps arrayed amid converging streams.
Bamboo traps and nets linked tip to tip,
lift-nets and seines boat to boat.
Some cast lines from overhanging banks,
some in mid-rapid spin their boats crosswise.
Suddenly forgetting dusk, they return by night,
singing "Gathering Water Chestnuts," beating the gunwales.
Proudly content with a single song,
they seek wind and waves to pass their years.
Then bounded by winding cliffs,
opened by cavernous gorges,
channeled by branching streams,
stirred by morning and evening tides.
Where river currents converge and gather,
where clouds and mists steam and condense.
Where rare marvels transform and are born,
where strange wonders make their dens and dwellings.
Receiving recluses and ranks of perfected beings,
producing extraordinary men of pure essence.
Spreading divine moisture for a thousand miles,
surpassing Dài Zōng's cloud-touching peak.
And when deception and transformation are sudden and elusive,
auspicious signs are not uniform.
Responses in motion know no fixed direction,
stirred by events they emerge.
Ordering heaven and earth,
intertwining human arts.
Too wondrous to be fully captured in words,
affairs impossible to exhaust with the brush.
And when the essence of Mín shines down upon the Eastern Well,
Yáng Hóu conceals his form within great waves.
Qí Xiàng, attaining the Way, dwells as a spirit,
then joins numinous brilliance with the Xiāng River goddesses.
Awe at the yellow dragon bearing the boat,
recognizing Bó Yǔ's upward sigh.
Admiring Jīng Fēi capturing the flood dragon,
finally achieving his spirit through the Tài'ē sword.
Fierce Yāo Lí scheming for reward,
in midstream pushing the spear.
Mourning Líng Jūn bearing the stone,
sighing for the fisherman's rowing song.
Thinking of King Mù of Zhōu ferrying his army,
driving eight steeds across giant turtles.
Moved by Jiāo Fǔ losing his pendant,
pitying the divine messenger ensnared.
Resplendent is the great mass flowing into form,
blending all endings into a single category.
Preserving intactness, eternally firm,
receiving primordial breath from numinous harmony.
Examining rivers and waterways with wondrous gaze,
truly none are more eminent than the Jiāng and Hé.
King Xiāng of Chǔ was strolling in the palace of Lántái,
with Sòng Yù and Jǐng Cuō in attendance.
A wind came soughing forth,
and the king opened his lapels to face it,
saying:
"How refreshing is this wind!
Is this something I share with the common people?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"This is solely the wind of Your Majesty;
how could the common people share it?"
The king said:
"Now wind
is the breath of heaven and earth;
it arrives widespread and unimpeded,
not choosing between noble and base, high and low, to bestow itself.
Now you alone consider it my wind;
surely you have some explanation?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"I have heard from my teacher:
'Where branches fork, birds come to nest;
where there are hollow openings, wind comes through.'
That which it relies upon being so,
then the nature of the wind differs."
The king said:
"Where does the wind begin to be born?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"Wind is born from the earth,
rising from the tips of the green duckweed.
It encroaches upon ravines and valleys,
growing furious at the mouth of earthen caverns.
Following the curves of Mount Tài,
it dances beneath the pines and cypresses.
Swift and fleeting, pounding and crashing,
it whips up blazing fury.
Rumbling like thunder,
it swirls and clashes in confusion.
It overturns rocks and fells trees,
striking down the forest undergrowth.
When it is about to wane,
it scatters and spreads apart,
rushing through holes and moving latches,
glistening and radiant,
dispersing and shifting away.
Thus its clear, cool, majestic wind
soars and rises, ascends and descends.
It mounts the high city walls,
enters into the deep palace.
It alights on flowers and leaves, stirring their fragrance,
lingering among the cassia and pepper trees,
hovering over the rushing waters,
about to strike the essence of the lotus.
It sweeps past the huì grass,
passes by the qín héng.
It levels the xīnyí,
covers the tíyáng.
Swirling through hollows, assaulting hillocks,
it leaves all fragrant plants desolate.
Then it wanders in the central courtyard,
goes northward up to the jade hall.
It ascends into the silk curtains,
passes through the secluded chambers.
Only then does it become the wind of Your Majesty.
Thus the manner in which this wind strikes people
is directly chilling and shuddering,
cool and refreshing, increasing sighs.
Clear and pure, cool and crisp,
it cures illness and dispels hangovers.
It sharpens the ears and brightens the eyes,
calms the body and brings ease to people.
This is what is called the majestic wind of the great king."
The king said:
"Excellent is your discourse!
As for the wind of the common people,
may I hear of it?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"The wind of the common people
suddenly arises from within poor alleys,
stirring up dust from holes and mounds.
Fretful and aggrieved,
it rushes through holes and assails doors.
It disturbs the sand and dirt,
blows on dead ashes.
It startles the foul and turbid,
raises the putrid remains.
Deviously skimming, it enters through jar windows,
reaching the dwelling huts.
Thus the manner in which this wind strikes people
is directly turbid, depressing, and melancholy,
driving in warmth and bringing dampness.
It causes pain in the heart,
breeds illness and creates fever.
Striking the lips, it causes sores;
reaching the eyes, it brings inflammation.
It causes chewing, gnashing, sucking, and gasping,
leaving one between life and death, not reaching either end.
This is what is called the base wind of the common people."
In the fourteenth year of the Jìn,
I being thirty-two years of age,
first saw grey hairs.
Holding the post of Tàiwèi's assistant while concurrently serving as Tiger Guard General of the Household,
I was temporarily assigned to duty in the Imperial Secretariat.
High pavilions connected to the clouds,
where sunlight rarely shone;
men wearing cicada-crested caps and clad in fine silks
moved and dwelled here.
I am a man of the wilds;
my repose was no more than beneath thatched huts and dense woods,
my conversation no more than with guests who were farmers and field elders.
Taking office to fill a vacancy,
I unworthily found myself among the court ranks.
Rising early and retiring late,
I had no leisure to attain peace.
Like a fish in a pond or a bird in a cage,
I longed for the rivers and lakes, the mountains and marshes.
Thus, dipping my brush and taking up paper,
with deep feeling I composed a rhapsody.
It being autumn at the time,
I titled it 'Autumn Inspiration'.
Its words are as follows:
The four seasons swiftly succeed one another;
the myriad things bustle and surge in turn.
Observing the timely growth of flowers and plants,
I discern where flourishing and decline reside.
Moved by winter's desolation and spring's blooming,
I sigh at summer's luxuriance and autumn's falling.
Though it is the flourishing and withering of insignificant plants,
it mirrors the beauty and ugliness of human feelings.
Well said are the words of Sòng Yù:
"How sorrowful is the breath of autumn!
Desolate, ah! plants and trees shake and fall, turning to decay.
Forlorn, ah! as if on a distant journey,
climbing a mountain, facing water, sending one homeward."
Now, sending homeward cherishes the longing of parting;
a distant journey holds the resentment of travel.
Facing a stream, moved by the flow, one sighs at passing time;
climbing a mountain, thinking of the far, one mourns the near.
Those four griefs wound the heart;
encountering even one is hard to bear.
Alas, that autumn days are mournful!
Truly, no sorrow is not fully felt.
In the fields are returning swallows;
in the marshes soar falcons.
Wandering mists rise at dawn;
withered leaves fall at dusk.
Then I put away the light fan,
lay aside the fine summer cloth.
I spread out the mat of sedge and rush,
don the lined garment.
The courtyard trees rustle and shed their leaves;
a fierce wind harshly blows the curtains.
Cicadas chirp shrilly in cold song;
wild geese soar and drift southward.
The sky, bright and clear, grows ever higher;
the sun, lingering and warm, gradually fades.
How brief the faint sunlight's shadow;
I feel the cool night is just growing long.
The moon, hazy and dim, holds its light;
dew, chill and clear, congeals cold.
Fireflies gleam brightly on the steps and doors;
crickets chirp by the porch screens.
I hear the morning cry of departing swans;
gaze at the lingering glow of the Fire Star.
At night, upright and sleepless,
alone I toss and turn in the splendid ministry.
Realizing the year is swiftly ending,
sighing, I bow my head and reflect on myself.
Grizzled temples, hair flowing, bear the cap;
white locks, rustling, hang down to the collar.
I look up at the lofty tracks of the crowd of talents;
I strive to climb the Milky Way to roam and gallop.
They ascend the spring terrace, bustling and bright;
they wear golden sable caps, gleaming and shining.
If our paths of pursuit and rejection differ,
how can one recognize their agitation or calm?
I have heard of the perfect man's noble manner:
he equates heaven and earth to a single finger.
They know safety but forget danger;
thus they go from birth into death.
If one treads only where there is room for a footprint,
one nearly does not step yet gains firm ground.
If one lacks space to set a foot down to the springs,
even monkeys and apes would not tread there.
The turtle, its bones sacrificed in the ancestral temple,
longs to turn its body back to the green waters.
I gather my robes and return,
Suddenly casting off my official sash to soar high.
I plow the fertile soil of the eastern fields,
Paying the surplus tax of millet and grain.
Springs gush swiftly among the rocks,
Chrysanthemums spread their fragrance by the cliffside stream.
I bathe in the trickling autumn waters,
And admire the darting of the swimming fish.
Wandering freely by the mountain streams,
Unrestrained in the world of men.
At ease and carefree,
I pass the days in contentment.
As the year draws to a close,
The hour grows dark.
The cold wind gathers,
And sorrowful clouds multiply.
King Liáng is displeased,
And strolls in the Tùyuán Garden.
He then sets out fine wine,
Summoning guests and friends.
He calls for Zōu Shēng,
And invites Elder Méi.
Xiàngrú has not yet arrived,
But is seated in the place of honor.
Soon, fine sleet begins to fall,
Followed by dense snow.
The king then sings of the north wind from the "Wèi Poems,"
And chants of the southern mountains from the "Zhōu Elegance."
He hands a writing tablet to Minister Sīmǎ,
Saying:
"Draw upon your hidden thoughts,
Unleash your elegant words,
Match the colors and weigh the descriptions,
And compose a rhapsody for me."
Xiàngrú then rises from his mat,
Steps forward and bows.
He says: I have heard that the Snow Palace was built in the eastern state,
And snow-capped mountains stand in the western regions.
Qí Chāng composed verses about the coming thoughts,
Jī Mǎn sang of the yellow bamboo.
The "Cáo Fēng" compares the color to hemp garments,
And the Chǔ ballads pair the "Yōulán" with melodies.
Snow a foot deep heralds auspiciousness for a bountiful year,
While snow many feet deep signifies imbalance in the hidden virtues.
The significance of snow is profound indeed!
Let me speak of its beginning.
When the dark season reaches its end,
The harsh cold ascends.
The scorching streams dry up,
The hot springs freeze.
The fiery wells are extinguished,
And warm springs turn to ice.
Boiling pools no longer surge,
And scorching winds do not rise.
Northern doors are sealed shut,
And naked lands are draped with silk.
Then clouds form over rivers and seas,
And sand flies in the northern deserts.
Layers of mist and haze gather,
Veiling the sun and hiding the clouds.
Sleet patters down first,
And snow, mingled and abundant, follows.
Its appearance is
Scattered and interwoven,
Misty and desolate.
Dense and floating,
Swirling and gleaming.
Fluttering and flying in showers,
Lingering and accumulating.
At first, it clings to the roof tiles and covers the beams,
Finally slipping through curtains and into crevices.
Initially graceful on the courtyard steps,
Eventually swirling onto curtains and mats.
It forms guī tablets where it meets squares,
And becomes bì disks where it encounters circles.
Gazing at the lowlands, ten thousand acres are uniformly white,
Looking at the mountains, a thousand cliffs are all clad in snow.
Thus, the terraces resemble layered jade disks,
And the paths seem strung with connected gems.
The courtyard is lined with jade steps,
The forest stands with jade trees.
The white crane loses its brilliance,
The silver pheasant is stripped of its purity.
Silken sleeves pale in comparison,
And jade-like faces are overshadowed in beauty.
When the accumulated whiteness remains unblemished,
And the morning sun shines upon it,
It glows like the candle dragon,
Holding a torch to illuminate the Kūnlún Mountains.
As for the dripping icicles,
Hanging from eaves and corners,
They sparkle like Féngyí,
Splitting open clams to display bright pearls.
As for the appearance of swirling profusion,
The splendor of dazzling purity,
The patterns of swirling accumulation,
The wonder of flying clusters and gleaming frost—
Truly, it shifts and changes endlessly,
Alas, it is difficult to know it fully.
If one seeks endless delight in its beauty,
The night is quiet and filled with thoughts.
The wind brushes the pillars, echoing softly,
The moon shines through the curtains, casting its glow.
Sip the mellow wine of Xiāng and Wú,
And don the layered robes of fox and raccoon.
Watch the paired dance of courtyard kūns,
Gaze upon the solitary flight of cloud-crossing geese.
Tread upon the mingled frost and snow,
And pity the parted branches and leaves.
Let thoughts wander a thousand miles afar,
Wishing to join hands and return together.
Zōu Yáng, upon hearing this,
Is deeply moved and convinced.
Inspired by the beautiful chant,
He respectfully responds with a final verse.
Then he rises and composes a song of accumulated snow.
The song says:
With my fair one, I part the heavy curtains,
Spread the embroidered quilt and sit on the fragrant mat.
Light the incense burner and bright candles,
Pour osmanthus wine and raise a clear tune.
Then he continues with a song of white snow.
The song says:
The tune is raised, the wine is set,
Rosy cheeks flushed with wine, thoughts turn intimate.
I wish to lower the curtains and lean close on the pillow,
Thinking of removing jade pendants and loosening sashes.
I lament how quickly the years pass,
And grieve that future meetings may never be.
Do you not see the white snow on the steps—
How can it retain its brilliance in the spring sun?
The song ends.
The king then ponders and savors the verses,
Stroking his wrist in contemplation.
Turning to Méi Shū,
He bids him rise and compose the finale.
The finale says:
White feathers may be white,
But their substance is light.
White jade may be white,
But it vainly guards its purity.
They are not like this snow,
Which rises and melts with the season.
The dark cold congeals, yet does not dim its purity,
The sun shines, yet does not fix its constancy.
Constancy is not my name,
Purity is not my virtue.
I rise and fall with the clouds,
Drifting with the wind.
I take form according to objects,
And shape myself according to the land.
Whiteness arises from circumstance,
Stains follow from what I encounter.
With a heart open and bright,
What worries, what schemes?
Prince Chén, having just lost Yīng and Liú,
Is solemn and troubled, with much idle time.
Green moss grows on the pavilion,
Fragrant dust settles on the terrace.
Quietly burdened with sorrow,
Unsettled in the midnight hour.
He clears the orchid-lined paths,
And tidies the cassia garden.
Music rises from the cold mountains,
Carriages halt on the autumn slopes.
Facing the deep gorge, he laments the distance,
Climbing the high peak, he grieves the remoteness.
At this time, the slanting Milky Way marks the left boundary,
The northern star shifts southward.
White dew veils the sky,
The bright moon flows across the heavens.
He ponders the verses of Qí,
And earnestly recites the odes of Chén.
Taking up brush and tablet,
He summons Zhòngxuān.
Zhòngxuān knelt and declared:
I, a humble and obscure man from the eastern borderlands,
grew up in rustic villages,
ignorant of the Way and unlearned,
yet I alone have received your enlightened grace.
I have heard that the deep and hidden follow righteousness,
and the lofty and bright follow the classics.
The sun embodies yang virtue,
the moon embodies yin essence.
It seizes the light of Fúsāng in the eastern pool,
and succeeds Ruòyīng in the western abyss.
It draws the dark hare to the imperial terrace,
and gathers the white lady in the rear courtyard.
Its waxing and waning warn of flaws,
its crescent and full phases show humility.
It follows the celestial order, shining throughout,
and moves with the stars, bringing moisture and wind.
It enhances the splendor of the Táishì,
and radiates brilliance in the Xuāngōng.
When its light shone upon Wú, their enterprise flourished;
when its essence sank upon Hàn, their Way harmonized.
As for when the air clears over the earth,
and clouds gather at the sky’s edge,
the Dòngtíng Lake begins to ripple,
and tree leaves start to fall.
Chrysanthemums scatter fragrance on the mountain ridges,
wild geese convey sorrow over the river shoals.
The pure orb rises slowly,
casting its serene glow downward.
The constellations hide their splendor,
the Milky River veils its shimmer.
The gentle earth is congealed like snow,
the round sky mirrors like water.
Connected terraces gleam like frosty silk,
surrounding steps are pure as ice.
The sovereign, weary of morning pleasures,
delights in nighttime feasts.
He halts the exquisite dances,
silences the clear chimes.
Leaving the candlelit chambers,
he approaches the moonlit hall.
Fine wine is presented,
resonant zithers offered.
If the cool night grows desolate,
and wind through bamboo forms melodies,
with no close kin to accompany,
the lonely traveler advances alone.
Listening to evening calls of marsh birds,
hearing autumn tunes of northern pipes.
Then the silk-strung zithers refine their sounds,
melodies and moods chosen for harmony.
Lingering with “Fáng Lù,”
melancholy with “Yáng Ē.”
The sound-forest empties of its whispers,
the rippling pool stills its waves.
Where shall entangled sorrows find refuge?
He pours them to the bright moon in long song.
The song says:
The fair one is far, her voice and traces cut off,
separated by a thousand miles, we share the bright moon.
Sighing in the wind—how shall it cease?
The river road is long, impossible to cross.
Before the song ends,
the remaining moonlight fades.
The whole hall changes expression,
restless as if lost.
He sings again:
The moon has set, dew about to dry,
the year grows late, with none to return with.
The fine time may yet return,
but light frost dampens one’s clothes!
Prince Chén said:
“Excellent.”
Then he ordered attendants,
to present toast and offer jade.
“I shall treasure these jade-like words,
and repeat them without weariness.”
Jiǎ Yì served as tutor to the King of Chángshā,
for three years,
when an owl flew into Yì’s dwelling,
perching at the corner of his seat.
The owl resembles a xiāo,
an inauspicious bird.
Yì, already exiled to dwell in Chángshā,
where the land is low and damp,
grieved for himself,
thinking his lifespan would not be long,
thus composed a rhapsody to console himself.
Its words say:
In the year of Dān’è,
the fourth month, early summer.
On the Gēngzǐ day at sunset,
an owl alighted in my house.
Perching at the corner of my seat,
its manner quite leisurely.
A strange creature comes gathering—
I privately wonder the reason.
Unrolling the books to divine it,
the prognostication tells its fate.
It says: “When a wild bird enters the room,
the master will depart.”
I inquire of the owl:
“Where shall I go when I leave?
If auspicious, tell me;
if ominous, speak of the disaster.
The measure of delay or haste—
tell me the time.”
The owl then sighed,
raised its head, flapped its wings,
unable to speak with its mouth,
but answered with its mind.
The ten thousand things change and transform—
truly without rest.
Whirling, flowing, shifting—
sometimes pushed forward, sometimes circling back.
Form and energy alternate continuously—
transforming and coiling.
Profound and obscure, without end—
how can it be fully told?
Disaster is where good fortune leans;
good fortune is where disaster lurks.
Worry and joy gather at the same gate—
auspicious and inauspicious share the same domain.
That Wú was mighty and strong—
yet Fūchāi was defeated.
Yuè sheltered at Kuàijī—
yet Gōujiàn ruled as hegemon.
This wanderer achieved success—
Fù Yuè was a convict—
yet became minister to Wǔ Dīng.
Thus disaster and good fortune—
how different are they from twisted ropes?
Fate cannot be explained—
who knows its limit?
Water, spurred, becomes fierce—
an arrow, spurred, flies far.
The ten thousand things surge and press—
vibrating and turning each other.
Clouds rise, rain falls—
tangled and交错, interwoven.
The great potter casts things—
boundless and without edges.
Heaven cannot be forethought—
the Way cannot be pre-planned.
Slow or fast, there is fate—
how can one know its timing?
Moreover, Heaven and Earth are the furnace—
Creation is the craftsman.
Yīn and Yáng are the charcoal—
the ten thousand things are the bronze.
Union, dispersal, waxing, waning—
how can there be constant rules?
A thousand changes, ten thousand transformations—
never with an end.
Suddenly becoming human—
why cling to it?
Transforming into different things—
why worry over it?
Petty wisdom is self-serving—
despising others, esteeming self.
The enlightened see broadly—
nothing is unacceptable.
The greedy die for wealth—
the ardent die for fame.
The boastful die for power—
the common masses cling to life.
Those driven by fear or pressure—
rush east or west.
The great man does not bend—
his mind transforms, equalizing all.
The foolish scholar bound by custom—
constrained like a prisoner.
The perfect man discards things—
alone, he walks with the Way.
The masses are confused—
likes and dislikes accumulate endlessly.
The true man is serene and detached—
alone, he rests with the Way.
Releasing wisdom, forsaking form—
transcending, losing self.
Vast, empty, suddenly desolate—
soaring with the Way.
Riding the current, then drifting away—
finding an islet, then stopping.
Entrusting the body to fate—
not keeping it for oneself.
Life is like floating,
Death is like rest.
Tranquil as the stillness of a deep spring,
Drifting like an untethered boat.
Not treasuring oneself for the sake of life,
Nourishing emptiness and floating.
The virtuous man is unburdened,
Knowing fate, he does not grieve.
Petty matters and trifles,
Why should they cause doubt?
At that time, Huáng Zǔ’s eldest son, Shè, was hosting a grand banquet for guests.
Someone presented a parrot,
And raising a cup before Héng, said:
"Mí Chǔshì,
Today, there is nothing to entertain the guests.
I humbly offer this bird, which has come from afar,
Bright, wise, and clever,
A precious member of the feathered tribe.
I hope you will compose a rhapsody for it,
So that all present may share in its glory.
Would that not be fitting?"
Héng thus composed a rhapsody,
His brush never pausing,
Without revising a single word.
The verses read:
O divine bird from the Western Regions,
You stand with a wondrous natural grace.
Your body bears the exquisite essence of metal,
And blends with the bright radiance of fire’s virtue.
Intelligent and eloquent by nature,
Gifted with wisdom to perceive subtleties.
Thus, you play atop lofty peaks,
And perch in secluded depths.
You never fly without purpose,
And always choose your woods when soaring.
With dark-blue feet and crimson beak,
Green feathers and emerald collar.
Resplendent in your lovely appearance,
Chirping with delightful sounds.
Though of the same feathered kind,
You are uniquely wise and different in heart.
You match the beauty of the luán and huáng birds,
How can common fowl compare in virtue?
Thus, admiring your far-reaching fame,
And marveling at your divine form so praiseworthy,
They ordered the gamekeeper to Lǒng Dǐ,
And summoned Bó Yì from the flowing sands.
They crossed Kūnlún to set their arrows,
And spread nets beneath clouds and rainbows.
Though the snares were fully laid,
It was but a single mesh that caught you.
And yet, your demeanor remained composed,
Calm and steady in your stance.
Unfrightened when pressed,
Unalarmed when stroked.
Preferring compliance to avoid harm,
Rather than defiance and loss of life.
Thus, those who presented you whole were rewarded,
While those who injured you were punished.
Then, in despair, you resigned to fate,
Parted from your flock, bereft of companions.
Confined within a carved cage,
Your wing feathers clipped.
Drifting across ten thousand miles,
Through rugged and repeated obstacles.
Crossing Mín and passing Zhàng,
Enduring cold and heat along the way.
As a maiden leaves home to marry,
Or a servant offers himself to serve his lord.
Even sages, when faced with hardship,
Linger as travelers in distant lands.
How much more a humble creature like a bird,
Can it be tamed to dwell in peace?
Longingly gazing toward the western road,
Yearning for home, standing in prolonged wait.
Considering my foul and humble form,
Why trouble the cauldron and chopping block?
Alas, my fortune is meager and thin,
Why did I encounter such perilous times?
Was it speech that led to chaos,
Or lack of discretion that brought danger?
Grieving the eternal separation from mother and child,
Mourning the living parting of husband and wife.
Not that my remaining years are worth regret,
But pitying the ignorance of my young ones.
Leaving the lowly lands of the barbarians,
To serve in the radiant presence of a noble lord.
Fearing my name does not match reality,
Ashamed my talents hold no wonder.
Admiring the fertile soil of the western capital,
Yet knowing bitterness and joy differ by place.
Harboring the deep longing of Dài and Yuè,
Thus often speaking of this in words.
Then, when Shàohào governs the season,
And Rùshōu prepares the reins,
As harsh frost first descends,
And cool winds rustle bleakly,
You sing long, yearning from afar,
Your mournful cries stir kindred souls.
Your voice, poignant and stirring,
Your appearance, sorrowful and haggard.
Those who hear are saddened,
Those who see shed tears.
Exiled ministers sigh repeatedly for you,
Abandoned wives weep in sorrow.
Recalling companions of bygone days,
Like xūn and chí, harmonizing in need.
Why today are we severed in two,
Like Hú and Yuè in separate realms?
Complying with the cage, I bow and rise,
Peering through windows, pacing hesitantly.
Dreaming of Kūnshān’s lofty peaks,
Longing for Dènglín’s lush branches.
Seeing my six wings broken and ruined,
Though I strive, where can I go?
My heart yearns to return, yet cannot,
Left only to brood bitterly in a corner.
If I devote myself to my duties,
How dare I betray kindness and forget my origins?
Entrusting this humble, insignificant life,
And dedicating this lowly, frail body.
Hoping to remain steadfast in repaying virtue,
Willing to exhaust words in offering my folly.
Relying on past profound grace,
May it endure long without change.
The jiāoliáo
Is a small bird,
Born among weeds and brush,
Raised beneath hedges and fences,
Flying and perching within ordinary bounds,
Yet the way of life is fully satisfied.
Pale in color and plain in form,
It is of no use to humans,
Tiny in shape and lowly in station,
No creature harms it,
It multiplies its kind,
Living in pairs, roaming together,
Fluttering about with self-contained joy.
As for eagles, owls, kūns, swans,
Peacocks, and kingfishers,
Some soar to the edge of crimson skies,
Some dwell beyond the farthest bounds,
Their wings lifting them skyward,
Their beaks and claws enough for self-defense,
Yet all are ensnared by arrows and strings,
Their feathers offered as tribute.
Why?
Because they are useful to humans.
Thus, shallow words can convey deep meaning,
And humble things can illustrate grand truths,
Hence this rhapsody is composed.
How manifold are the works of creation,
Scattering myriad forms among all beings.
The jiāoliáo, a tiny bird,
Also receives life and breath.
Nurturing its plain, fluttering body,
Without dark or yellow hues to deem itself noble.
Its feathers are unfit for tools,
Its flesh unworthy of the sacrificial dish.
Eagles and hawks pass by with barely a glance,
Why then fear nets and snares?
Amid dense, shrouding thickets,
It finds its place to roam and perch.
Its flight is not soaring,
Its glide not swift.
Its dwelling easily accommodates it,
Its needs easily met.
Its nest in the woods needs but one branch,
Each meal requires only a few grains.
Perching without lingering,
Roaming without lingering.
It does not scorn thorns and brambles,
Nor prize zhǐ and orchids.
A flutter of wings brings ease,
A step brings peace.
Resigned to fate, following nature’s course,
Harmless to all things.
This bird, devoid of knowledge,
how does its conduct resemble wisdom?
It does not hoard treasures to invite harm,
nor adorn its appearance to court trouble.
In stillness, it adheres to simplicity without pride;
in motion, it follows nature with ease.
It relies on the natural as its endowment,
unswayed by the temptations of worldly artifice.
The eagle and hawk flaunt their beaks and talons,
the swan and egret soar beyond the clouds.
The pheasant hides in dark and perilous places,
the peacock dwells in distant lands.
Those morning ducks and returning geese,
with wings uplifted, hasten away.
All boast beautiful feathers and plump flesh,
thus, though guiltless, they meet their end.
They merely carry reeds to evade arrows,
yet are ultimately slain in this world.
The fierce hawk is tethered and bound,
the clever parrot is caged.
Their fierce spirits are subdued for care,
confined in deep seclusion within ninefold walls.
They alter their voices to please,
yearning to break their wings for utility.
They long for the forests of Zhōng and Dài,
and pine for the tall pines of Lǒngdǐ.
Though favored today,
they are not as free as in days past.
The sea bird Yuánjū,
seeks refuge from the wind and arrives.
The giant sparrow of Tiáozhī,
crosses mountains to come.
Carried over ten thousand miles,
drifting and trembling in fear.
It is their massive bodies that hinder them,
and their majestic forms that draw admiration.
Yīn and Yáng shape and nurture,
all things in one realm.
Great and small intermingle,
species abundant, kinds diverse.
The tiny Jiāomíng nests on a mosquito’s eyelash,
the great Péng bird fills the corners of the sky.
To compare above, they fall short;
to compare below, they have surplus.
Surveying all between heaven and earth,
how can I discern the measure of great and small?
The steed is not praised for strength alone,
horses are named after dragons,
not merely because the state values majestic demeanor,
and the army requires swiftness and agility,
but truly because they emit radiant light and reveal charts,
symbols of virtue and auspicious signs for sages.
Thus, their divine nature is exalted in speech,
and their arrival is celebrated by the world.
When my高祖 (Gāozǔ) founded the Sòng,
all regions fulfilled their duties,
and distant lands brought tribute.
Rare treasures filled the imperial treasury,
and splendid steeds filled the royal stables.
Among them was the imperial carriage’s Zhěbái horse,
endowed with extraordinary grace,
exquisitely chosen by the emperor’s heart,
granted to the holy stable.
It obeyed commands with ease,
galloped in perfect rhythm,
though its teeth showed age,
its skill and beauty never waned.
Cared for over many years,
showered with deep and constant kindness,
it grew old and its vigor faded,
passing away in the inner stable.
Having served with all its strength,
the compassionate emperor was moved,
and ordered attendants
to convey his inner decree.
I, a humble and obscure servant,
dare to offer this rhapsody.
Its words are as follows:
In the twenty-second year of the Sòng,
glorious achievements shine through successive reigns.
Martial virtue is solemnly displayed,
civil education has spread far and wide.
The steps of peace can be ascended,
the path of a rising king can be joined.
Seeking the state’s glory in ancient histories,
examining records of past deeds.
In ancient times, when Dì Xuān ascended the throne,
the Feīhuáng horse served the stable.
When Hòu Táng received the mandate,
red patterns awaited the sun.
The Hàn dynasty prospered, and heavenly steeds displayed talent;
the Wèi virtue flourished, and marsh horses offered their qualities.
Such extraordinary and marvelous steeds,
have appeared since former times.
All glorified in auspicious records,
celebrated in suburban songs by the Director of Music.
They were used to honor and guard the divine majesty,
to support and protect the imperial procession.
Bright spirits harmoniously followed,
and divine creatures all took their places.
At the beginning of the enlightened mandate,
all nine regions submitted in obedience.
Some braved dangers to pledge allegiance,
others came from afar to present tribute.
Hearing of the king’s assembly in prosperity,
they knew Huánxià was filled with abundance.
Gathering talents from all six domains,
encompassing the seven tribes to obtain fine steeds.
These are the noble kind that ride the wind,
truly the great descendants that precede the light.
Thus they could serve in place of elephants drawing carriages,
and be matched with the constellation Gōuchén.
Their years extended long,
their fame and value highly esteemed.
Truly a lavish gift from the sacred ancestor,
cherished by the emperor and swiftly advanced.
Observe its sinews attached and bones erect,
mane hanging low and hair standing firm.
Double pupils like mirrors set side by side,
two cheekbones harmonious as the moon.
Unique form, peaks arising,
extraordinary appearance, elegance radiating.
Soaring beyond the dust of chariot tracks,
galloping swiftly as if vanishing.
Selected for excellence at the palace gate,
presented in form at the crimson towers.
At dawn, groomed in Yōuyān,
by day, fed in Jīngyuè.
Taught reverence, an unchanging canon,
trained in conduct, a record-worthy act.
For the emperor, for the ancestors,
in leisure, in pleasure.
Light carriages fly ahead to clear the way,
archers on horseback encircle to secure the road.
Commanding five battalions to march in order,
sounding eight bells to pace the steps.
Adorned in golden trappings,
and decorated with red lacquer.
Precious bridles like stars entwined,
carved patterns like clouds spread.
Advancing close to the guard lines,
retreating to join the imperial carriage.
Suddenly rearing up, startling as a wild goose,
at times soaring gracefully like a dragon.
Restraining its majestic bearing to lead,
gentle in heart, awaiting command.
When dew moistens and the moon turns severe,
frost descends and autumn arrives.
The king then speaks,
displaying his awe-inspiring might.
Facing the broad vista,
seated on the hundred-tiered tower.
Assessing martial skills,
judging swift steeds.
Elegant trappings arranged all around,
harmonious bells doubly set.
Glancing at its shadow, it neighs high,
about to leap, then halts midway.
Galloping apart across the distant field,
competing in strength along the long track.
Outshining peers, surpassing the herd,
resplendent and peerlessly distant.
Matching the quick hands of agile men,
keeping pace with the rapid beats of ornate drums.
Passing through dark hooves like hail scattering,
treading white targets like ice cracking.
Chest stained red with foam,
sweat channels flowing with blood.
Hoofprints circling the arena,
pent-up fury not yet spent.
The emperor’s heart is pleased and slightly joyful,
the people look up and rejoice together.
When graceful transformations are complete,
a spirit of urgency takes hold.
Restrained by bit and rein,
confined by the city’s enclosures.
Longingly gazing west, lifting its head,
looking to northern clouds, stamping its feet.
It would make Zǐyàn horses run abreast,
and Lǜshé serpents guard the wheels.
Fine black steeds following step by step,
splendid piebalds pacing together.
To visit the Queen Mother at Kūnqū,
and seek the Emperor’s Terrace at Xuānyuè.
To traverse the tracks of the central plains,
and exhaust the paths of divine journeys.
Yet, indulging in hunting excursions,
he mirrored the former kings.
Reckless upon the people,
he incurred regret from righteous principles.
The Son of Heaven then halted his carriage and reconsidered,
rested his troops and unloaded their gear.
Reflecting on Wǔ Mù,
he emulated Wén Guāng.
He alleviated the people’s sufferings,
and rectified the state’s statutes.
He guarded against the boar that disrupts the chariot,
and was vigilant of the bird that perches on the yoke.
Thus, he revered what is often neglected,
and respectfully prepared for the unforeseen.
The carriage had the stability of double wheels,
the horses were free from the recklessness of straying.
Placed in the depths of Zhuólóng,
entrusted with the rank of abundant grain.
Nurtured with care, they understood benevolence,
following their elders to the end.
Adding worn curtains,
gathering fallen servants.
Heavenly affection was thorough,
imperial grace was complete.
Epilogue:
Only virtue moves heaven,
divine beings respond.
At that time, noble steeds
filled the streets and alleys.
Endowed with the spirit of the moon’s steeds,
ancestral clouds and dragons.
Their majestic will, untrammeled,
their essence, extraordinary.
Both firm and gentle,
they submitted to bridle and rein.
Offering their service to Zhōnghuáng,
sacrificing themselves to gallop.
Wishing for lifelong care,
shading the main branches.
Yet they departed before dawn’s dew,
forever separated.
Scattered through obscure classics to examine things,
marvelous is the immortal bird born from transformation.
Endowed with a floating, expansive elegance,
embracing a clear, distant bright heart.
Pointing to Péng Hú and spreading wings,
gazing toward Kūnlàng and raising its voice.
Circling the sun’s realm in swift flight,
exhausting heavenly steps in lofty search.
Treading divine lands already far,
accumulating spiritual sacrifices now many.
Its essence contains cinnabar, shining like stars,
its crown congeals purple, misty and splendid.
Extending its round throat in delicate grace,
pausing its long toes in grand beauty.
Layered frosty feathers playing with shadows,
shaking jade wings facing the clouds.
Morning play in zhī fields,
evening drink at Yáochí.
Weary of rivers and seas, it roams marshes,
caught in cloud nets and seen restrained.
Leaving the solitude of the imperial realm,
returning to the clamor and lowliness of the mortal world.
Years towering, sorrowful at dusk,
heart melancholy, grieving separation.
Then, deepest yin kills the season,
swift shadows wither the year.
Cold sand shakes the wilds,
the Winnowing Star wind stirs the sky.
Severe, bitter fog,
bright, sorrowful springs.
Ice blocks the long river,
snow fills the mountain ranges.
Soon, the murky night ceases,
scenery clear and vast.
Stars turn, the Milky Way revolves,
dawn’s moon about to set.
Moved by the cold rooster’s early call,
pitying the frost goose leaving the desert.
Facing the bleakness of startling winds,
confronting the shining of flowing light.
Crying clear sounds on vermilion steps,
dancing flying forms in golden towers.
First linked and soaring like phoenixes,
finally winding and leaping like dragons.
Hesitating, pacing back and forth,
shaking swiftly, soaring and breaking.
Startled bodies gather like tumbleweed,
raised wings fly like snow.
Leaving the net, heading separately,
joining threads, relying on each other.
About to rise, then halting,
as if going, yet returning.
Rustling, dignified and looking back,
delaying, lingering till dusk.
Swift wings behind the dust,
soaring ahead on the path.
Pointing to meetings, circling in flight,
approaching forks, stepping with measure.
Grace leaving lingering beauty,
appearance never pausing in delight.
Rushing to the mechanism, meeting the rhythm,
glancing with corners, dividing forms.
Long strides, slow gallops,
wings together, voices joined.
Light traces in disarray,
floating shadows intersecting.
Many changes, myriad postures,
uneven, layered and dense.
Mist intertwining, fog congealing,
as if without feathery substance.
Wind departing, rain returning,
cannot be fully described.
Already scattering souls and dazzling eyes,
bewildered, not knowing where they go.
Suddenly stars scatter and clouds cease,
composing divine demeanor with self-control.
Looking up at heaven’s abode, lofty and cut off,
again melancholy and startled in thought.
At that time,
Yān’s beauties lost their charm,
Bā’s youths felt ashamed.
Scarves and whisks both stilled,
balls and swords both ceased.
Even Hándān dare not compare,
how could Yáng’ē hope to match?
Entering Wèi, they rode in carriages,
leaving Wú’s capital, they overwhelmed the market.
Kept tame for a thousand years,
bound in endless sorrow for ten thousand miles.
Descended from Gāo Xū’s dark lineage,
the clan’s mid-era brilliant spirit.
Swaying in the gentle breeze, shedding like cicadas,
heroic in the northern wilds, spreading fame.
By the tenth reign, soaring like a swan,
bearing feather insignia in the capital.
Great floods overwhelming heaven, extinguishing Xià,
my father met sorrow and sang ballads.
In the end, preserving myself and leaving principles,
dwelling where the highest benevolence resides.
Admirable, the former heroes’ pure virtue,
whether in hardship or success, they surely aided.
Alas, my solitary ignorance, so slight,
on the brink of collapse, without a path.
How could my own body be worth sacrificing?
Yet turning from the family legacy is regrettable.
Quietly dwelling in perpetual thought,
passing days and months, growing more distant.
Not that I dare pick from partisans,
but hope these words remain unblemished.
My lonely soul communes with spirits,
sincerity emerges in night dreams.
Dreaming of climbing mountains, gazing afar,
glimpsing the recluse, faintly visible.
Grasping kudzu vines, handing them to me,
gazing at steep valleys, saying, “Do not fall.”
At dawn’s light, waking and looking up in thought,
my heart dim, still unclear.
The Yellow God distant, without substance,
facing leftover prophecies with conjecture.
Said: “Riding high to meet the divine,
the path far-reaching, yet not lost.
Kudzu vines entwining twisted trees,
singing ‘Southern Wind’ for peace.
Trembling as if facing a deep abyss,
this is what the Two ‘Yǎ’ revere.
Having shown you auspicious signs,
I reiterate with clear warning.
Why not advance early to join the multitude?
Time fleeting, never to return.”
I receive the spiritual instruction, pacing slowly,
Lingering and waiting with patience.
Only heaven and earth are endless,
Rarely do the lives of people endure.
Confusion and hardship abound,
So much difficulty, so little wisdom.
The highest sages suffer before rising,
Though the common people cannot withstand it.
In the past, Wèi Shū drove for Kūn,
Kūn became a bandit and caused his loss.
Guǎn drew his bow to slay his foe,
The foe became a ruler and spared him.
Change transforms the old into the strange,
Who can predict the beginning and end?
Yōng created resentment but was first rewarded,
Dīng followed kindness but was executed.
Lì found mourning in supposed good fortune,
Wáng received blessings in sorrow.
Rebellion twists and turns like this,
The northern elder understood its rise and fall.
Dān governed within but decayed without,
Zhāng adorned the outside but was pressured within.
To attain harmony is nearly possible,
Yet Yán and Rǎn could not achieve it.
Nì beckoned the path to follow himself,
Saying even Kǒngzǐ was not acceptable.
Content in carelessness without restraint,
He finally perished in worldly calamity.
Roaming the sage’s gate yet unsaved,
Even covering the minced meat—what good would it do?
Stubborn persistence surely brings misfortune,
Avoiding banditry and chaos relies on the Way.
Form and energy arise from the root,
Branches and leaves gather, some wither, some flourish.
Fearing the specter’s blame upon the shadow,
How can it be said to have ended?
Lí shone brightly under Gāoxīn,
Mǐ grew mighty by the southern stream.
Yíng gained prestige from Bóyí,
Jiāng’s lineage branched thrice.
Since benevolence truly attains this,
I look up to the heavenly path, following the same track.
The eastern neighbor tyrannized and destroyed the benevolent,
The king aligned his position with the three and five.
The Róng woman was fierce and caused mourning for Xiào,
Bó went forth to meet the dragon and tiger.
Fā withdrew his army to fulfill fate,
Chóng, drunk, acted and paired himself.
The trembling scales’ saliva in the Xià court,
Circled three eras and destroyed Jī.
The Xùn feathers transformed in the Xuān palace,
Filled five reigns and brought disaster.
The Way is long, but the world is short,
Vast, silent, and incomplete.
Xū followed things and consulted ghosts,
Then exhausted time and reached the obscure.
Guī nested Jiāng through youthful divination,
Dàn calculated sacrifices with turtle shells.
Xuān and Cáo’s rise and fall came from dreams below,
Lǔ and Wèi’s names and titles from inscribed songs.
Bǐ heard the cry and indicted the stone,
Xǔ examined patterns and interrogated the branch.
The Way, blended and complete, is natural,
Methods share origins but diverge in flow.
Spirit precedes mind to fix fate,
Fate follows action to wax and wane.
The turning flow shifts without aid,
Thus encountering hardship, expanding and contracting.
Three Luáns in one body,
Though shifting, never err.
Observing disparities in tangled confusion,
This is what bewilders the multitude.
Zhōu and Jiǎ agitated and vented frustration,
Equalizing life, death, fortune, and misfortune.
Raising frank words to feign emotion,
Truly fearing the ox and dreading the owl.
What is valued is the sage’s ultimate discourse,
Following heavenly nature and judging righteousness.
Some things desire but do not dwell,
Others detest but do not avoid.
Holding to Kǒng’s restraint without wavering,
Then virtue is subtle and unburdened.
Three benevolences differ in unity,
Yí and Huì clash yet share the same voice.
The tree recliner multiplied Wèi,
Shēn, with layered calluses, preserved Jīng.
Jì burned himself to guard his lord,
Hào nurtured his will and never faltered.
Awaiting the distinction of plants and trees,
If they bear fruit, they surely flourish.
Seeking immortality beyond this age,
This is what the ancients measured.
Observing heaven’s net vast and covering,
Truly it aids the sincere and teaches mutually.
Planning the great way of former sages,
Also drawing near virtue and aiding trust.
Yú’s Sháo music beautiful, attracting phoenixes,
Kǒng forgot taste for a thousand years.
Plain writings sincere, reaching the qílín,
Hàn hosted blessings from a different age.
Essence connects with spirits and moves things,
Spirit stirs energy and enters the subtle.
Yǎng’s sidelong glance made apes cry,
Lǐ’s tiger roar split stones open.
Without utmost sincerity, how could it connect?
If without substance, who would believe?
Even minor skills must be so,
How much more devoting oneself to the true Way.
Ascending to Kǒng and Hào, up and down,
Weaving through the paths of all dragons.
Morning witnessing truth, evening transforming,
Still ashamed of self and leaving form behind.
Like inheriting Péng and joining the aged,
Appealing to future sages to convey feeling.
Epilogue:
Heaven creates chaos and obscurity,
Establishes nature and life.
Returning to the heart, expanding the Way,
Only sages and worthies can.
Primordial chaos moves things,
Flowing without rest.
Preserving self, leaving a name,
A model for the people.
Giving life for righteousness,
Using it for the Way.
Grieving over premature loss,
Shame, nothing more painful.
Pure your primal simplicity,
Why change color?
Still transcend the subtle,
Sink into the divine realm.
I look up to the profound teachings of former sages,
Though ever lofty, I do not defy.
If not a neighborhood of benevolence, where to dwell?
If not a trail of righteousness, where to follow?
Secretly embracing it, ever observing,
Through long days and months, never fading.
This inner feeling truly cultivated,
Admiring the ancient people’s steadfast virtue.
I straighten myself to follow restraint,
Adhering to rules without stumbling.
Will focused as if responding to suspension,
Sincere heart firm as a knot.
Bannering nature and conduct with crafted pendants,
Wearing luminous pearls and jade branches.
Stringing autumn blooms of secluded orchids,
Also adorning with jiānglí.
Beautiful folds, intense fragrance,
Truly enduring, hard to diminish.
Already splendid and rarely matched,
Not treasured in this time.
Waving my glory unseen,
Spreading my fragrance unheard.
Secluded, guarding this narrow obscurity,
Dare I idle and abandon diligence?
Fortunate the two eights met Yú,
Praising Fù Yuè born in Yīn.
Still admiring former worthies’ legacy,
Pitying later ages unable to reach.
Why this solitary path, desolate,
Alone, not blending, standing apart.
Moved by the phoenix’s solitary perch,
Sad the virtuous rarely unite.
They not uniting—what harm?
Fear the many false ones masquerading as true.
Dàn was slandered by his younger brothers,
Until opening the “Golden Coffer,” then trusted.
Observing the many errors of the masses,
Fear establishing laws to endanger self.
Increasing vexation and confusion,
To whom can I speak?
Privately harboring deep sorrow,
Thoughts tangled, unruly.
Willing to strive to uphold righteousness,
Though poor and humble, unchanged.
Gripping the carved tiger, testing the elephant,
Toe on the edge of the scorched plain.
Hoping to uphold this in all dealings,
Detesting only ceasing after death.
Customs shift, affairs transform,
Blurring the compass and square’s round and square.
Treasuring weeds in layered boxes,
Calling huì and chǎi not fragrant.
Rejecting Xīshī, not employing her,
Tethering swift steeds to pull carts.
Crooked conduct gaining ambition,
Following laws meeting disaster.
Only heaven and earth are endless,
Why are encounters so inconstant!
Not suppressing my integrity to curry favor,
Is like facing a river without a boat.
To seek flattery with a charming smile,
Is something my heart has never tried.
I don the robes of gentle reverence,
And wear the embroidered gown of ritual and righteousness.
I braid loyalty and brightness into my sash,
And mingle skills and arts into my pendants.
I display colorful patterns and carved jade,
So my jade’s sound travels far and grows longer.
Lingering in delay to indulge desires,
The radiant sun suddenly sets in the west.
Relying on my own wisdom to adorn myself,
The cuckoo cries, and fragrance fades.
Hoping for the thrice-blooming plant in a year,
I meet the white dew turning to frost.
Time passes swiftly as seasons change,
Who can stand as my equal?
Alas, the difficulty of matching beauty and virtue,
I think of following Hán to wander in exile.
Fearing gradual decline without achievement,
Staying means obscurity without glory.
My heart hesitates and doubts,
I approach Qízhǐ to reveal my feelings.
King Wén arranged the divination stalks for me,
Advising swift retreat to preserve my name.
Traversing many mountains to roam freely,
Aided by swift winds to spread my voice.
The two maidens moved by the lofty peak,
Some ice breaks, yet they do not linger.
Heaven, though high, becomes a marsh,
Who says the road is not level!
Strive to strengthen yourself without rest,
Tread the jade steps, lofty and steep.
Fearing the diviner’s judgments of length and shortness,
I drill the eastern turtle to observe auspicious signs.
Encountering the noble bird of Jiǔgāo,
I lament my pure intentions unfulfilled.
Roaming beyond the dust, glimpsing the sky,
Perched in dark obscurity, I cry mournfully.
Eagles and vultures compete in greed,
I cultivate purity to increase my glory.
You have ties to the dark bird,
Return to your mother’s clan to find peace.
The divination is auspicious, without regret,
I choose an auspicious day to prepare my journey.
At dawn, I bathe in the clear spring,
And dry my hair in the morning sun.
I rinse with droplets from flying springs,
And savor the flowing essence of stone mushrooms.
Birds soar and fish leap,
I will travel to the eight wildernesses.
Passing Shàohào’s barren wilds,
I ask Jùmáng about the three hills.
How pure and genuine is the true way,
Free from filth and burden, light as a feather.
Ascending Pénglái to wander at ease,
The giant turtle claps but does not tilt.
Staying at Yíngzhōu to gather sacred herbs,
To prolong life for a while.
Riding returning clouds to drift far away,
At dusk, I lodge at Fúsāng.
Drinking jade nectar from green peaks,
Feasting on night dew as my provisions;
Recalling old dreams of the grain tree,
I climb the high ridge of Kūnlún.
At dawn, I journey to Yánggǔ,
Following Bó Yǔ to Jīshān.
Admiring the gods holding jade tablets,
I despise Fángfēng for breaking his word.
Pointing to Chángshā’s winding path,
I pay respects to Chónghuá in the southern lands.
Mourning the two consorts who did not follow,
They flutter by the Xiāng River’s banks.
Gazing afar at Héng’s slopes,
I see Lí’s ruined tomb.
Grieving the Fire Minister’s lack of remembrance,
His lonely soul entrusted to the mountain slope.
Sorrowful and yearning for distant places,
I cross Ángzhōu to wander freely.
Ascending to the sun at Kūnwú,
Resting where fiery flames are molded.
Flames blaze, dyeing the sky crimson,
Waters churn and surge with waves.
Warm winds gather, increasing the heat,
Anguish and depression are hard to bear.
Lonely in travel without companions,
How can I stay here?
Looking toward Jīntiān with a sigh,
I wish to go west to play.
Ahead, Zhùróng raises his banner,
Tying the Vermilion Bird to bear the flag.
Treading the Jiànmù tree in Guǎngdū,
Plucking Ruòhuā flowers, I hesitate.
Surpassing Xuānyuán in the Western Sea,
Striding over Wāngshì’s dragon fish.
Hearing this land has millennia of age,
How could it suffice to amuse me?
Thinking of the nine lands’ different customs,
I follow Rùshōu and proceed onward.
Suddenly transformed, shedding like a cicada,
Companions of pure essence become my fellows.
Leaping through the White Gate, galloping east,
I journey through the central wilds.
Crossing Ruòshuǐ’s murmuring flow,
Lingering at Huàyīn’s rushing isle.
Summoning Féngyí to clear the ford,
Rowing a dragon boat to ferry me across.
Meeting Dìxuān before his return,
I linger, wandering in melancholy.
Gazing at the lush forest by the river,
I admire the “Guānjū” warning to maidens.
The Yellow Spirit examines and inquires of fate,
Seeking how the ways of heaven may be.
It is said: trust the near, doubt the far,
The six classics are silent, unwritten.
The divine way obscure, hard to fathom,
Who can counsel and follow it?
Niú Āi, ill, turned into a tiger,
Even meeting his brother, he would devour him.
Biē Lìng died, his corpse vanished,
He took Shǔ’s throne and prolonged his line.
Life and death交错, uneven,
Even the Director of Fate cannot see clearly.
Dòu wandered the roads of Dài,
Later, his descendants flourished in fortune.
The prince indulged in excess at the Hàn court,
Ending in sorrow, his line cut off.
The commandant with bushy brows languished as a clerk,
Until the third reign, he met Emperor Wǔ.
Dǒng, young, served in high office,
Built a king’s tunnel but did not dwell there.
Good and ill fortune follow each other,
Often shifting, without fixed place.
Mù pleased heaven with an ox,
A servant brought chaos, imprisoning his lord.
Wén cut his sleeve, wary of his uncle,
A eunuch met the villain, bringing peace to the queen.
Even the wise are blind to likes and dislikes,
How can the confused discern clearly?
Yíng heeded prophecies to warn against Hú,
Prepared externally, trouble arose within.
Some carried bribes, avoiding the cart,
A pregnancy while traveling brought retribution.
Shèn and Zào spoke openly of heaven,
Divined water and fire, uttering false omens.
Old Liáng feared the Líqiū ghost,
Mistook his own son, striking with a blade.
Failing to recognize one’s own kin,
How much less trust the unseen realms?
Do not cling to illusions for personal gain,
Lest a hundred worries bring self-harm.
Heaven’s watch is most bright,
It aids the sincere and blesses the benevolent.
Tāng purified himself to pray,
Received great blessings to save the people.
Jǐng pondered thrice to build the state,
Mars dwelled in another constellation.
Wèi Kē, enlightened, followed good governance,
A ghost repaid, causing Qín’s downfall.
Gāoyáo advanced, sowing virtue,
Cultivating abundant virtue in Yīng and Liù.
The mulberry’s end寄托 on rooted life,
Plants wither, yet already sprout anew.
There is no word unrequited,
Nor any journey without return.
Why not roam far to spread one’s name,
Who says time can be stored?
I raise my head and gaze afar,
My soul, bewildered, finds no friend.
Oppressed by the narrowness of the mundane world,
I will journey north to roam and wander.
I tread upon piled ice, jagged and steep,
Clear springs frozen, no longer flowing.
The bitter wind, mournful, ever arrives,
Brushing the lofty peaks with a rustling sound.
The Dark Warrior withdraws into its shell,
The flying serpent coils and twists itself.
Fish, proud of their scales, are locked in ice together,
Birds perched on trees have lost their branches.
I sit in the hidden chamber of the Great Yin,
Sighing deeply, my sorrow grows.
I lament that Gāoyáng chose this dwelling,
And Zhuānxū made his abode in darkness.
How can weaving a path through the four borders
Bring any relief to him or me?
I gaze toward the distant edge of the Cold Gate,
And release my reins toward Bùzhōu.
Swift flames escort me on my way,
Soaring on wings, unrestrained.
I pass through the caverns of deep gorges,
Drifting on the vast river, shimmering and bright.
I traverse heavy darkness in desolate silence,
Pitying the buried sheep hidden deep below.
I pursue the obscure depths beneath the earth,
Transcending formlessness, I float upward.
Emerging from the dark wilds of stony dens,
I know not the path I tread.
I hasten to call the Torch Dragon to hold his torch,
Passing Zhōngshān, I rest midway.
I look down upon the red banks of Yáoxī,
Mourning Zǔjiāng, who met his doom.
I visit the Queen Mother at her silver terrace,
Offering jade mushrooms to cure my hunger.
The Queen Mother, pleased and joyful,
Yet chides me for my tardy pace.
I carry the Jade Maiden of Tàihuà,
Summoning Fúfēi of Luòpǔ.
All are lovely and enchanting,
With charming eyes and moth-like brows.
They sway their slender waists with grace,
Lifting their intricate embroidered sashes.
Parting red lips, they smile softly,
Their radiant faces gleam with light.
They present jade rings and precious silks,
Declaring their affection with dark and yellow gifts.
Though their beauty dazzles and their gifts are fine,
My heart, noble and vast, finds no delight.
Both maidens grieve at my refusal,
And together chant poems in clear song.
Their song says:
"Heaven and Earth in harmony,
A hundred flowers bloom in splendor.
Cranes call, necks entwined,
Turtledoves echo in harmony.
A maiden yearns for spring,
Her soul turns and shifts.
How can one so wise and bright
Forget me so completely?"
I would reply, but have no leisure,
So I prepare my carriage and hasten on.
I gaze upon the towering heights of Kūnlún,
Overlooking the winding river, vast and grand.
The spirit turtle crouches to bear the isle,
While hornless dragons form a flying bridge.
I climb the layered city of Lángfēng,
And fashion a bed of immortality.
I grind jade stamens for provisions,
And ladle white water for my drink.
I summon Wūxián to interpret dreams,
And receive auspicious signs of fortune.
I nurture virtue in its rightful place,
Embracing excellence to spread its grace.
Having borne fruit, I turn to my roots,
And long for my former home.
At peace, serene, and timely in my ways,
I dwell in purity and virtue's abode.
I warn all officers to gather early,
And all attend their duties, full of awe.
The thunder god roars with crashing peals,
Lightning flashes illuminate the night.
The cloud master gathers thick and dark,
Torrential rain pours down upon the road.
I yoke my carved chariot with floral designs,
Harnessing the winged dragon to pull the way.
A host of spirits follows in array,
Riders massed like stars across the sky.
I shake my sleeves and mount the chariot,
My long sword held aloft, now high, now low.
My tall crown gleams beneath the canopy,
My pendants shimmer, radiant and bright.
The coachman solemnly takes the reins,
Eight steeds leap forth, surging ahead.
Banners of mist swirl in the sky,
Rainbow streamers flutter in the wind.
I grasp the rails and glance behind,
My heart boiling like a seething pot.
I envy the splendor of the heavenly capital,
Yet why cling to memories of the old?
To the left, the green dragon bears a sacred fungus,
To the right, the white tiger guards the bell.
Ahead, the long-tailed phoenix fans its feathers,
Behind, the dark lord holds the balance.
I entrust the wind to Jībó,
Cleansing turbidity to make it pure.
I wave cloud banners, flowing and wide,
And ring jade bells, chiming clear.
I cross the clear void, ascending high,
Floating on midges, soaring upward.
In orderly array, I slowly descend,
Flames swirling, displaying divine power.
I call the gatekeeper to open the door,
And see the Heavenly Emperor in his jade palace.
I listen to the grand music's ninefold strains,
Unfolding in harmony, rich and grand;
I examine order and chaos through musical scales,
Pondering beginnings and reflecting on ends.
Though endless pleasures know no satiety,
I fear joy's passing and sorrow's approach.
The plain goddess strums the strings, leaving lingering notes,
Tàiróng chants, saying, "Take heed."
Having guarded against excess and calmed my will,
I take my leisure to soar and roam.
I leave the solemn Purple Palace,
And gather in the vastness of Tàiwēi.
I command Wángliáng to whip the team,
Passing over towering pavilions, grand and strong.
I set up the net carriage, dense and vast,
Hunting in the green forest, boundless and deep.
I bend the mighty bow with force,
Shooting the great wolf of Bōzhǒng.
I observe the ramparts at Běiluò,
Striking the river drum with thunderous sound.
I ride the celestial river, floating free,
Drifting on the Milky Way, vast and wide.
Leaning on Zhāoyáo and Shètí, I wander and flow,
Observing the two eras and five planets, interwoven and grand.
Proud and supple,
Graceful and coiled,
Crowded and clustered,
Swiftly soaring forth.
Swift and streaming,
Abundant and formless,
Resplendent and splendid,
Distant and receding.
I surmount the startling thunder's roar,
Toying with wild lightning's flickering dance.
I pass beyond the vastness of dim obscurity,
Piercing inverted shadows, soaring high.
Vast and boundless, without limit,
Now I gaze beyond the heavens.
Perched on Kāiyáng, I look down,
Facing my old homeland, dim and distant.
I grieve for the toil of a wandering heart,
Filled with melancholy, longing to return.
My soul turns back, glancing often,
My horse leans on the shaft, pacing slow.
Though I wander and delight in fleeting joy,
How can such sorrowful longing be embraced?
I pass through the heavenly gate, descending the sky road,
Riding swift flames, speeding through the void.
Clouds swirl thick around my wheels,
Winds whisper, shaking my banners.
Confused and fluttering, dim and obscure,
Suddenly dazed, I return to the common world.
I gather past delights and ease,
Rolling up wanton thoughts and distant dreams.
I adorn myself in my former robes, swaying gently,
Lengthening my pendants, hanging low.
My garments splendid, shining bright,
Beautifully flowing with the wind.
I harness the precious steeds of the Six Arts,
Roaming the level groves of virtue and Dao.
I weave the classics into a net,
Driving Confucians and Mohists as my prey.
I contemplate the changes of yin and yang,
Chanting the harmonious tones of the "Odes" and "Hymns."
I praise Zēngshì for returning to till the fields,
Admiring the steep slopes of Lìbǎn.
Reverent day and night, unwavering,
Steadfast from start to end in my devotion.
Vigilant at dusk as if in peril, I reflect,
Fearing my self is not yet perfected.
If my inner heart is upright and true,
Unknown to others, I feel no shame.
Silent, inactive, concentrating my will,
I wander freely with benevolence and righteousness.
Without leaving my door, I know the world,
Why must I travel far and toil in vain?
The Preface says:
Heaven is eternal, earth enduring, yet the years do not linger;
To wait for the Yellow River to run clear only brings sorrow.
I wish to travel far for my own pleasure,
Roaming up and down without constancy through all six regions.
Leaping and soaring beyond, transcending the mundane world,
Floating and divinely rising to fulfill my desires.
Heaven cannot be scaled by stairs, immortals are few;
The cypress boat drifts silently, unable to fly.
Sōng Qiáo stands aloft—who can draw near?
Gather your essence, travel afar, and let your heart be your guide.
Turn your will back, come away, and follow the profound plan;
Having attained what I seek, what more is there to ponder?
I lingered in the capital for a long time,
With no brilliant strategy to assist the age.
In vain I stood by the river, admiring the fish,
Awaiting the clearing of the Yellow River, which never came.
Moved by Cài Zǐ's fervor,
I sought Táng Shēng to resolve my doubts.
Truly, the Way of Heaven is obscure and dim;
I followed the Fisherman to share in his joy.
Rising above the dust and grime to depart afar,
I bid a long farewell to worldly affairs.
Then, in the second month of spring, a fine season,
The weather was mild, the air clear.
The plains and lowlands lush and dense,
A hundred grasses flourishing in glory.
The royal ospreys beat their wings,
The orioles sing mournful tunes.
Neck to neck they soar and dip,
Calling "guan-guan," chirping "ying-ying."
Here I wander free and at ease,
Finding solace to delight my heart.
Then came the dragon's chant from the marsh,
The tiger's roar from the hills.
Above, I shot fine arrows into the sky;
Below, I angled in the long stream.
Struck by the arrow, they fell dead;
Lured by the bait, they swallowed the hook.
I brought down the soaring birds from among the clouds,
And hauled up the shā and liú fish from the deep abyss.
As the shining sun cast slanting shadows,
I entrusted myself to the moon's charioteer.
I indulged in the utmost joy of carefree wandering,
Forgetting all weariness though the day turned to dusk.
Moved by the old master's parting admonition,
I turned my carriage back toward my humble hut.
I plucked the wondrous notes of the five-stringed lute,
And chanted the books of Zhōu and Kǒng.
Wielding brush and ink, I composed elegant prose,
Setting forth the models of the Three Sovereigns.
If one can free his mind beyond the material world,
Why care about glory or disgrace?
I once read the biography of Jí Àn,
And came to the part where Sīmǎ Ān rose four times to the rank of Nine Ministers,
Yet the good historian recorded it,
Labeling him as a "clever official."
I could not help but sigh, putting the book aside.
I said: Alas!
Cleverness indeed exists,
But clumsiness is also fitting.
I have always thought that for a scholar's life,
Unless one is a sage of utmost virtue, subtle and mysteriously perceptive,
Then one must achieve merit and accomplish deeds,
Proving useful in his own time.
Thus, with loyalty and trustworthiness, he cultivates virtue;
With refined speech and sincere conduct, he establishes his career.
In my youth, I undeservedly gained some local reputation,
And was honored by the commands of the Minister of Works and the Grand Commandant.
The lord I served,
Was none other than the Grand Steward, Lǔ Wǔgōng.
I was recommended as a Xiùcái and appointed a court gentleman.
Later, I served Emperor Wǔ of the Shìzǔ reign,
As magistrate of Héyáng and Huái counties,
A Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
And a Ping in the Court of Judicial Review.
During the present emperor's mourning period,
I served as Registrar to the Grand Tutor.
When my superior was executed,
I was stripped of my rank and made a commoner.
Soon after, I was reinstated,
Appointed magistrate of Cháng'ān.
I was promoted to Erudite,
But before being summoned to assume the post,
My parent fell ill,
So I resigned and was relieved of duty.
From my capping age to my fiftieth year,
I changed posts eight times but was promoted only once,
Was dismissed twice,
Stripped of rank once,
Declined appointment once,
And was transferred merely three times.
Though fortune and obstruction each had their turn,
This too is the effect of being a clumsy man.
In the past, the wise Hé Chángyú spoke of me,
Firmly saying I was clumsy in employing my many talents.
As for "many," how dare I claim it?
But "clumsy" is indeed true and well-evidenced.
Now, with talented men in office,
And all artisans working in season,
A clumsy man may well give up thoughts of favor and glory.
My aged mother is at home,
Suffering from the frailty of old age.
How can I still leave her side to care for her with a joyful countenance,
And busily engage in petty, lowly duties?
Thus, understanding the bounds of contentment,
Nurturing a lofty, detached ambition,
I built a house and planted trees,
Wandering free and content.
The ponds and pools suffice for fishing,
The grain tax suffices in place of farming.
Watering the garden and selling vegetables
Provide for morning and evening meals;
Herding sheep and selling cheese
Await the expenses of summer and winter sacrifices.
Filial indeed is filial piety,
Friendly indeed are brothers.
This, too, is the governance of a clumsy man.
So I composed the "Rhapsody on Idle Living,"
To sing of my affairs and express my feelings.
The verse says:
Proudly I tread the fields of ancient texts,
Walking the high road of former sages.
Though my face may be deemed thick,
Within, I feel ashamed before Níng and Qú.
When the Way prevails, I do not serve;
When the Way fails, I am not foolish.
Why is my clever wisdom insufficient,
While my clumsy hardships abound?
Thus I retired to live in idleness,
By the banks of the Luò River.
In person, I joined the recluses;
In name, I ranked among the lowly scholars.
Facing the capital, tracing the Yī River,
With suburbs before and markets behind.
A dark floating bridge spans straight across,
The lofty observatory towers high.
I peer into the secret mysteries of astronomy;
I probe the beginnings and ends of human affairs.
To the west lies the imperial barracks,
With dark canopies and green banners.
Xīzǐ and Jùshǔ crossbows,
Different but mounted on the same frame.
Catapult stones thunder like dread,
Arrows fly like fierce gnats.
They march forth to lead the way,
Displaying our emperor's majestic might.
To the east stands the Bright Hall and Circular Moat,
Serene, solemn, spacious, and tranquil.
Encircling woods cast shimmering reflections,
Round waters swirl in deep pools.
Here, filial piety is pursued to honor the father,
Venerating the cultured ancestor to match Heaven.
Reverently, sage respect illuminates obedience,
Nurturing the elderly to honor longevity.
When winter turns to spring,
Yin recedes and Yang spreads.
The Son of Heaven performs the fire sacrifice,
Honoring the ancestors at the suburban altar to display righteousness.
The "Grand Music" of Harmonious Heaven is played,
With a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry arrayed.
Robes flutter in unison, dark and aligned,
Pipes whistle and blow together.
Resplendent,
Echoing,
Such is the grandeur of these ritual displays,
And the magnificent beauty of royal institutions.
Two schools stand side by side,
Twin buildings as if one.
To the right, scions of the state are received;
To the left, worthy recluses are welcomed.
Multitudes of students gather,
Great assemblies of Confucian learning.
Some ascend to the hall,
Some enter the inner chamber.
Teaching knows no constant master;
Where the Way is, there lies truth.
Thus, eminent scholars cast aside their seals,
And famed kings cherish their jade tallies.
Instruction spreads like the wind,
Response bends like grass.
This is why dwelling in benevolence is considered beautiful,
And why Mèng's mother moved three times.
Here, my dwelling is determined,
with rooms built and ponds dug.
Tall willows reflect in the water,
fragrant hedges of zhǐ trees.
Fish swim gracefully,
lotus blossoms unfold.
Bamboos and trees luxuriate,
spiritual fruits unevenly grow.
Zhāng Gōng’s great valley pears,
Liáng Hóu’s ebony persimmons,
Zhōu Wénruò’s slender branch jujubes,
Fánglíng Zhū Zhòng’s plums,
all fully cultivated.
The three peaches mark the separation from the cherry-like hú,
the two nài shine in red and white.
Precious pomegranates and grapes,
scattered and trailing at its side.
Plums and apricots of the lush dí kind,
adorned with vibrant and beautiful ornaments.
Blossoms and fruits are bright and radiant,
beyond words to express.
As for vegetables, there are scallions, leeks, garlic, and taro,
green bamboo shoots and purple ginger.
Mustard greens and shepherd's purse are delicious,
smartweed and artemisia are fragrant.
Curcuma thrives in the shade,
seasonal beans face the sun.
Green amaranth holds dew,
white gourd bears frost.
Then comes the chill of autumn, heat retreats,
spring warms as cold departs.
After light rain, the skies clear,
the universe is serene and bright.
The grand matron then boards the panelled chariot,
ascends the light carriage,
gazes afar at the capital's outskirts,
closely surveys the family gardens.
Her body brings harmony in motion,
medicine is used to ease toil.
Regular meals are enhanced,
old ailments have healed.
Seats stretch with the banquet,
grandchildren lined up.
Willows cast shadows,
carts aligned by tracks.
On land pluck the purple pods,
in water hang the rosy carp.
Some feast in the forest,
others purify by the river.
Brothers’ hair graying,
children with baby teeth.
Toast for a thousand years of life,
all are both fearful and joyful.
The longevity toast is raised,
kind faces in harmony.
Cups overflow, joyful drinking,
strings and bamboo music resound.
Stamp feet, start dancing,
lift voices in high song.
How joyous life is,
who knows what else there is?
Reflection on oneself,
