credibility thin and talents scarce.
Upholding the maxims of Zhōu Rèn,
dare to present my strength and join the ranks.
Nearly unable to protect my humble self,
how can I compare to the wise?
Admiring many wonders, thought ceases,
ending with leisure to nourish my shortcomings.
During the time of Emperor Xiàowǔ and Empress Chén,
she was favored but rather jealous.
She was moved to Chángmén Palace,
where she was in sorrow and deep thought.
Hearing that Shǔ prefecture’s Chéngdū Sīmǎ Xiāngrú excelled in writing,
she sent a hundred catties of gold,
to have Xiāngrú purchase wine for Wénjūn,
thereby delivering words to alleviate her melancholy.
Xiāngrú then composed a piece to enlighten the sovereign,
allowing Empress Chén to regain favor.
His writing said:
How is it that a beauty
strides in leisure and fulfillment?
Her spirit is free and does not return,
her form withers in solitude.
I say I come morning and return at dusk,
forgetting others amid the joys of eating and drinking.
My mind shifts but does not recall the past,
delighting in company and mutual affection.
My thoughts are slow and foolish,
harboring a sincere and honest heart.
Hoping to gain inquiry to advance myself,
to receive the precious words of my lord.
Offering empty words in expectation of truth,
seeking the palace on the south side of the city.
Preparing sparse arrangements myself,
yet you never consent to visit.
Alone, focused in meditation,
heavens drift and winds blow fiercely.
On the orchid terrace, I gaze far,
my spirit in confusion, wandering outside.
Clouds gather densely all around,
heavens vast, shrouded in daytime shadows.
Thunder rumbles and echoes arise,
like the sound of your chariot.
The swirling winds disturb the chambers,
lifting the fine tents.
Cassia trees join in tumult,
their fragrance intensely penetrating.
Peacocks gather together,
black apes howl and sing long.
Kingfishers come, flocking together,
phoenixes fly north and south.
My heart sighs and is not released,
evil spirits strong and attacking within.
Descending from the orchid terrace to survey,
walking leisurely in the deep palace.
The main hall stands solid against the sky,
lush and rising, grand and high.
Restlessly leaning in the eastern chamber,
seeing it stretch endlessly.
Pushing the jade doors makes the bronze fittings clatter,
ringing like the sound of bells.
Carving magnolia as rafters,
decorating with plum as beams.
Draping flowering trees,
supporting towers with parasol trees.
Setting precious timber for eaves,
arrayed unevenly upon the crossbeam.
Occasionally reflecting material illusions,
resembling stacked stones grandly joined.
Five colors now gleaming,
blazing brightly forming rays.
Intricately paved with stone tiles,
resembling tortoiseshell patterns.
Draped with brocade curtains,
hung with silk cords like nets.
Stroking the pillar leisurely,
viewing the curved terrace.
White cranes cry out mournfully,
a solitary female perched on the dead poplar.
As dusk falls, looking endlessly,
longing alone in an empty hall.
The hanging moon self-illuminates,
the pure night in the boudoir.
Playing the elegant zither to change the tune,
expressing sorrows that shouldn’t continue long.
The flowing sign notes are reversed,
the sound young and faintly rises again.
Throughout the displayed repertoire,
my feelings are ardent and uplifted.
Left and right are sad with tears flowing,
tears streaming crisscross.
Heave sighs and increase grumbling,
footsteps rise and wander.
Raising long sleeves to cover oneself,
recounting past misfortunes.
No face to show,
thus thoughts decline and approach the bed.
Twisting fragrant flowers as pillows,
seated in dufting orchids and chài fragrance.
Suddenly sleeping and dreaming,
my soul resembles your presence alongside.
Startled awake, nothing seen,
the spirit wandering as if lost.
Roosters crow and distress me,
rising to view the moon's pure light.
Observing the line-up of stars,
constellation Bì and Mǎo emerge from the east.
Viewing the courtyard's luxuriance,
like late autumn's descending frost.
Night passes slowly like a year,
harboring melancholy unable to renew.
Resting, waiting for dawn,
the desolate courtyard stands bright again.
I am seized by my feelings of sadness,
remembering yearly without daring to forget.
I once lived in close proximity to Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān,
both of whom possessed unbridled talents.
However, Jī’s aspirations were lofty yet detached,
while Lǚ’s heart was broad and unrestrained.
Later, each met his fate due to certain affairs.
Jī was widely skilled in various arts,
and was particularly accomplished in string and wind instruments.
As he faced his execution,
he gazed at the shadow of the sun,
asked for a qín and played it.
I was about to journey westward,
and passed by his former dwelling.
At that time, the sun was setting over Yúyuān,
and the cold ice was desolate!
A neighbor was playing a flute,
its sound clear and resonant.
Recalling the joys of past excursions and feasts,
moved by the music, I sighed,
and thus composed this rhapsody:
I was ordered to go to the distant capital,
then turned back and journeyed northward.
Crossing the Yellow River by boat,
I passed by the old residence in Shānyáng.
Gazing upon the desolate wilderness,
I rested my carriage at the corner of the city wall.
Treading on the traces left by those two men,
I passed through the impoverished alley and the empty house.
Lamenting the millet’s grief for Zhōu,
mourning the wheat’s sorrow at the ruins of Yīn.
Reflecting on the past to cherish the present,
my heart wavers in hesitation.
The beams and rafters remain, not yet destroyed,
but their forms and spirits have departed—where have they gone?
In the past, when Lǐ Sī faced punishment,
he sighed for his yellow dog and chanted long.
Mourning Jī’s eternal farewell,
he gazed at the sun’s shadow and played the qín.
Entrusting fate to understanding,
he placed his remaining life in a fleeting moment.
Listening to the impassioned sound of the flute,
the exquisite music ceased, then was sought again.
Halting my carriage, about to depart,
I then took up my brush to write my heart.
In the past, I often heard elders recounting their lives, their contemporaries, relatives, and old friends,
some already completely fallen,
some barely surviving.
I am just forty years old,
yet among my close relatives,
the dead are many, the living few;
intimate friends,
less than half remain.
Some with whom I once shared a journey,
or feasted together in one room,
after ten years or more,
have all vanished, utterly gone.
Thinking of this brings sorrow,
and the sorrow is palpable!
Thus I composed this rhapsody.
Behold the flow of heaven and earth,
rising and falling in continuous succession.
The sun races across the sky,
seasons follow the void and stand alert.
Alas, the brevity of human life,
who can grasp long years?
Time flits by, never to return,
old age approaches, soon to arrive.
Resenting the lack of proof for the jade stamens,
regretting the difficulty of grasping the morning clouds.
Gazing toward Tānggǔ, I stand on tiptoe,
lamenting that this scene is often hidden.
How sorrowful!
Rivers gather water to become rivers,
water flows ceaselessly, day by day.
Ages gather people to become ages,
people gradually approach evening.
In which age are people not new?
Which age can keep people old?
The fields bloom every spring without fail,
grass never lacks morning dew.
Throughout eternity, it is always thus,
all things follow their inherent nature.
Like the hibiscus on the branch,
though it constantly withers, it does not awaken.
Though it does not awaken, it is pitiable,
my heart grieves and wounds itself!
Clearly, such is the work of creation,
how can I seek lasting permanence?
Grieving that the spiritual root fell early,
lamenting that so many of my kin are lost.
Mourning the collapse and decay of the hall’s framework,
pitying the city towers reduced to mounds and wasteland.
The closer the kinship, the more they have departed,
why should intimate friendships not be forgotten?
Alas, I am now in peril,
why gaze at the vast, obscure heavens?
My heart is wounded, filled with many thoughts,
my face sorrowful, haggard, with little joy.
Hidden feelings arise, forming threads of thought,
stagnant thoughts knock, giving rise to beginnings.
Mourning that this world holds no joy,
I sing of the past in words.
Dwellings filled halls and overflowed rooms,
carriages moved in rows, side by side.
How many years did it last?
Now, wherever I go, all is broken.
Some have vanished into obscurity, completely gone,
some remain in emptiness, barely half.
Truly, when pines flourish, cypresses rejoice,
alas, when orchids burn, huì grass sighs.
If life and fate are not different,
how can waves in the same stream be distinct?
Seeing the overturned cart ahead,
I know this road is truly difficult.
Examining my own limbs with deep grief,
I fear this body will soon be the same.
Poisoned by pleasures, lacking direction,
I resent the many scenes that meet my eyes.
Truly, the many scenes that meet my eyes—
where can my spirit go to find peace?
Seeking my past life in echoes and images,
viewing former things, I cherish them.
Walking through cold woods, filled with sorrow,
enjoying spring blossoms, yet thoughtful.
Touching all things gives rise to grief,
sighing that the same season differs in time.
As years pass, thoughts broaden,
as the road nears dusk, my mind feels constrained.
Relatives grow sparse day by day,
friends dwindle, becoming ever fewer.
Looking back at old intimates among the survivors,
I find but one or two out of hundreds.
Joy, collapsing in the heart, seems forgotten,
sorrow, following emotion, comes to dwell.
Entrusting shallow bonds to later generations,
I will grow old and become a stranger.
Then, reining in my pace, calming my heart,
wondrous thoughts arise from nature’s creation.
Essence floats, spirit sinks,
suddenly beyond the worldly realm.
Awakening to the great night’s shared slumber,
why boast of lateness or resent earliness?
Pointing to that day’s passing,
how can such feelings be enough to disturb?
Moved by autumn flowers on withered trees,
grieving for dew falling on lush grass.
In deep sorrow, I do not turn away,
how then can I speak of knowing the Way?
I shall nourish myself with heaven and earth’s great virtue,
leaving behind the sage’s vast treasure.
Freeing my heart from trivial attachments,
I shall wander at ease, delighting in old age.
At twelve, I was introduced to my father’s friend, Dàihóu Yáng Jūn of Dōngwǔ,
and first became known by name.
Thus, a marriage alliance was arranged,
and Dàoyuán, his heir,
also deepened the affection of our familial bond.
Unfortunately, his life was short,
father and son both withered and perished.
I faced personal hardships,
and was soon engaged in duties abroad,
not setting foot on Sōngqiū’s mountains
for nine years now.
Now passing through again,
filled with emotion, I recall the past and compose this rhapsody:
Setting out at dawn from Kāiyáng,
crossing the clear Luò River directly.
The morning wind, bleak and piercingly cold,
evening snow, white, covering the road.
Wheel tracks hold ice, erasing the path,
water gradually freezes, congealing solid.
The road is arduous, difficult to advance,
the sun dims, nearing dusk.
Looking up, I gaze at returning clouds,
looking down, I mirror the flowing springs.
Ahead, I see Tàishì,
beside, I glimpse Sōngqiū.
Here Dōngwǔ entrusted his remains,
establishing graves, opening fields.
Lofty, the twin markers stand,
orderly, the rows of catalpas.
Gazing at those catalpas,
my thoughts are stirred.
Moved with admiration for Dàihóu,
I also mourn Yuán and grieve for his heir.
Grave mounds, heaped one upon another, connect the ridges,
cypresses, dense and thick, cluster together.
Why do departures and deaths follow one another,
while the old grass shows no change?
In my childhood I was fortunate to meet him,
and received the pure influence of Dài Hóu.
He honored me as a man of state,
and favored me with a fine marriage.
From our ancestors came deep friendship,
and through our two sons, kinship across generations.
We joyfully joined hands to grow old together,
hoping to repay his virtue with a neighborly bond.
Now, after nine years, I return once more,
to an empty house, silent and devoid of people.
Weeds cover the courtyard steps,
the old garden has turned to firewood.
I pace the corridors, wandering back and forth,
tears streaming down, soaking my handkerchief.
At night I toss and turn, unable to sleep,
sighing deeply until dawn.
Alone with pent-up sorrow, to whom can I speak?
So I set down my thoughts in this writing.
Lè'ān Rèn Zǐxián possessed a capacity to withdraw from the world,
and from youth, he and I shared joy!
Even the love between brothers
could not surpass it.
Unfortunately, he passed away at a young age,
my good friend now gone—
what pain compares to this!
His wife is also my aunt,
who lost her parents young,
married, and then her husband too was taken,
leaving a young daughter, just an infant.
This is indeed the utmost hardship in human life,
the extreme grief of bitter suffering.
In the past, when Ruǎn Yǔ died,
Wèi Wén mourned him,
and ordered old acquaintances to compose a "Rhapsody on the Widow."
I thus imitate it,
to express the heart of the orphaned widow.
The words say:
Alas, my life is ill-fated,
grieving that Heaven's trials are not sincere.
Young, orphaned and alone,
anguish and sorrow shatter my heart.
Gazing at the cold spring, I sigh for what remains,
singing the lingering notes of "Lù'é."
Long-lasting sorrow and eternal longing,
thoughts stretch far and grow ever deeper.
As a woman who has married,
I served as a bride in a noble family.
Receiving the radiant cover of auspicious clouds,
bearing the generous kindness of my lord.
Like the creeping vines of kudzu,
I entrusted my frail stem to the sturdy tree.
Fearing my lightness against his heavy gifts,
as if treading on ice or facing a chasm.
Following the clear teachings of righteousness,
heeding the classic admonitions of women's histories.
Offering sacrifices to show obedience,
performing sweeping duties year after year.
What the poets lament,
is but wishing words while hearts ache.
Why is my fate so uniquely thin,
meeting Heaven's calamity, unrepentant?
Splendor once bloomed brightly,
then suddenly my lord departed, leaving me behind.
Quietly shutting the door to live in seclusion,
alone and solitary, with no one to rely on.
Exchanging brocade cushions for straw mats,
replacing silk canopies with plain curtains.
Ordering the nurse to take her place,
looking at the fan and kerchief to ease my grief.
Choking sobs lose their voice,
tears gush forth, soaking my clothes.
To whom can I tell my worries and grievances?
Holding my orphaned child by my side.
As dusk gradually darkens,
the sun fades and sets in the west.
Sparrows flock and fly to the rafters,
chickens roost and fold their wings.
Returning to the empty house, pitying myself,
stroking the quilts and covers, sighing.
Thoughts entangled and confused,
hearts broken and filled with sorrow.
The shining sun swiftly passes,
the four seasons turn and shift.
Heaven condenses dew into frost,
trees shed leaves and branches fall.
Looking up at the vast, empty divine abode,
gazing at the spirit garments fluttering.
Retreating to a corner of the hall in hidden grief,
stepping forward to bow alone by the bedside.
Ears straining to hear the past,
eyes seeing glimpses of former days.
Though dark and unseen,
still lingering, clinging close.
Painful, the separation of life and death,
preparing to move the spirit to its resting place.
The dragon hearse solemnly sets off under stars,
flying banners flutter, opening the way.
Wheels follow the tracks, advancing slowly,
horses neigh mournfully, looking back.
The hidden spirit, distant, never to return,
deep sorrow knots, with no one to tell.
Gazing at his form on the altar,
my soul rushes to the grave mound.
Since mid-autumn, in mourning,
passing through frost, treading on ice.
Snow falls thick and sudden,
winds whistle, rising early.
Eaves drip coldly through the night,
water slowly freezes, barely solid.
Thoughts drifting and fleeting,
spirit rising nine times in a single night.
Hoping distance would lessen grief,
yet sorrow grows deeper, more poignant.
Wishing dreams could connect with the spirit,
eyes wide open, unable to sleep.
Nights long and endless,
cold, desolate, and biting.
Breath stifled, rising in my chest,
tears crisscross, flowing onto the pillow.
The departed soul gone forever,
time and years swiftly come to an end.
Face haggard and worn,
those around me pity my plight.
Moved by the three good men who died for Qín,
I would gladly give my life and follow.
But holding my young child in my arms,
I hesitate, unable to bear it.
Alone, pointing to the shadow, swearing in my heart,
though my body remains, my will has perished.
Again I say:
Looking up at the vast heavens, sighing,
privately pitying myself—where is the end?
Reflecting on my frail, solitary self,
considering my young child, still unknowing.
Like crossing a river without a bridge,
or climbing the sky without wings.
Looking up, I see his lingering image,
looking down, I face the springs and soil.
Dark and hidden, concealed in shadows,
heart remembering, eyes imagining.
Serving the empty seat, solemn and pure,
pleading to the vacant room, open and bright.
Vastly alone, gazing at my shadow,
solitary, speaking to myself, listening for echoes.
Gazing at my shadow, heartbroken,
listening for echoes, grief increases.
Far gone, ever more distant,
remote and long separated.
The four seasons flow, suddenly changing order,
the year grows late, the sun sinks west.
Frost covers the courtyard, wind enters the room,
midnight passes, the Milky Way turns.
Dreaming of my lord coming to visit,
as if the gates of heaven swung open wide.
Startled awake, hearing nothing,
transcending confusion, heart aching.
Heart aching, what can be done?
Speaking of climbing the mountain slopes.
The tomb gate, solemn and still,
the long mound, lofty and high.
A lone bird chirps mournfully,
tall pines rustle, shaking their branches.
Sorrow knots, converging together,
tears stream down, pouring forth;
following Gōng Jiāng's clear vow,
singing "Bǎi Zhōu" in a pure song.
In the end, my bones will return to the mountain's base,
remaining entrusted to what blooms hereafter.
I vow to join my lord in the same grave,
unto death, my resolve will not waver.
Gazing out upon the plain,
creeping vines entwine bones,
arch-forming trees gather souls.
When life reaches this point,
how can one speak of Heaven's way!
Thus I, a man of lifelong sorrow,
am endlessly startled at heart.
I think directly of the ancients,
who died with hidden regrets.
As for the Qín Emperor, pressing his sword,
the feudal lords galloped westward.
He leveled the world,
unified script and shared regulations.
Mount Huà served as his wall,
the Zǐyuān as his moat.
His grand ambitions already overflowed,
yet his martial might was not exhausted.
He was about to harness giant turtles to form bridges,
touring east of the sea to bid farewell to the sun.
But once his soul snapped,
the imperial carriage departed late.
Then there was the King of Zhào, captured,
exiled to Fánglíng.
At dusk his heart stirred,
at dawn his spirit rose.
Parting from lovely consorts and beautiful women,
losing golden carriages and jade chariots.
Setting out wine to drink,
grief came to fill his breast.
For a thousand autumns, ten thousand years,
his resentment is hard to bear.
As for Lǐ Líng’s surrender in the north,
his name shamed, his person wronged,
he drew his sword and struck the pillar,
mourning his shadow, shamed in soul.
His feelings went to Shàngjùn,
his heart remained at Yànmén.
Tearing silk to tie a letter,
he vowed to repay Hàn’s grace.
Morning dew suddenly arrives—
clasping hands, what words to say?
Then, when Míngfēi departed,
she looked to heaven and sighed deeply.
The Purple Terrace grew distant,
frontier mountains without end.
A sudden whirlwind rose,
the white sun hid in the west.
Lǒng’s wild geese seldom flew,
Dài’s clouds lacked color.
Gazing toward her lord—when to expect him?
She ended, withered and cut off, in a foreign land.
Then, Jìng Tōng was rejected,
dismissed, returning to field and village.
He closed his gate, swept no more,
blocked his door, held no office.
Facing his wife on the left,
turning to play with his young child.
Neglecting dukes and ministers,
unrestrained in literature and history.
Bearing his will to the grave,
long harboring endless regret.
And when Jī Kāng was imprisoned,
his spirit stirred and soared.
In the evening, he poured coarse wine,
at dawn, spread his plain qín.
Autumn days bleak and desolate,
floating clouds without light.
Nourishing strange thoughts of azure mists,
he entered the long night without dawn.
Some have isolated ministers shedding perilous tears,
disowned sons with falling hearts.
Exiles by the sea,
banished guards in Lǒng’s shadows.
These men only hear sad winds suddenly rise,
blood dripping to soak their lapels.
Again they swallow bitterness, harbor sighs,
wither away, sink into oblivion.
Then there are overlapping hoofprints,
chariot tracks clustered,
yellow dust covering the ground,
song and music rising on all sides.
All without exception—smoke severed, fire extinguished,
bones sealed in the spring’s depths.
It is finished!
Spring grass fades, autumn wind startles,
autumn wind ceases, spring grass grows.
Silks and gauzes end, ponds and halls vanish,
lutes and zithers perish, mounds and graves level.
Since ancient times, all have death,
none do not drink regret and swallow their voices.
What dims the spirit and melts the soul
is only parting!
Moreover, Qín and Wú are severed states,
again Yān and Sòng are a thousand lǐ apart.
Sometimes spring moss just begins to grow,
suddenly autumn wind briefly rises.
Thus the traveler’s heart breaks,
a hundred feelings mournful and pained.
The wind soughs with an alien sound,
clouds stretch endlessly with strange hues.
Boats linger by the water’s edge,
carriages wind slowly by the mountain’s side.
Dazed, lingering—how to advance?
Horses whinny coldly without cease.
Covering golden cups—who will drink?
Setting aside jade-inlaid zithers, tears stain the carriage rail.
Those who stay lie sorrowful,
dazed as if having lost something.
The sun leaves the wall, sinking its colors,
the moon climbs the balcony, flying its light.
Seeing red orchids receive dew,
gazing at green catalpas touched by frost.
Pacing past layered pillars, vainly closing doors,
stroking brocade curtains, empty and cold.
Knowing the lingering steps of a parting dream,
imagining the wandering soul of farewell.
Thus, though parting is of one thread,
its circumstances are of ten thousand kinds.
As for dragon-steeds with silver saddles,
vermilion carriages with embroidered axles.
Farewell feasts at the Eastern Capital,
seeing off guests at Jīngǔ.
Feather-tuned qín strings spread, pipes and drums arrayed,
Yān and Zhào songs grieve the beautiful ones.
Pearls and jades brighten late autumn,
silks and gauzes grace early spring.
Startling the team’s horses to raise their grain,
stirring deep fish’s crimson scales.
Reaching the moment of parting, they swallow tears,
feeling the solitude, wounding their spirits.
Then there are swordsmen ashamed of grace,
young men repaying patrons.
At Hán’s state, at Zhào’s privy,
in Wú’s palace, at Yān’s market.
Cutting affection, enduring love’s pain,
leaving country, departing village.
Shedding tears together in farewell,
wiping blood as they gaze at each other.
Driving expedition steeds without looking back,
seeing the travel dust rise at times.
Just then, bearing gratitude with a single sword,
not buying fame in the spring’s depths.
Metal and stone tremble, faces change color,
flesh and bone grieve, hearts die.
Or perhaps border commanderies are not at peace,
bearing arrows to join the army.
Liáo River without end,
Yàn Mountain piercing clouds.
In the women’s quarters, wind warm,
on the paths, grass fragrant.
Sun emerges from heaven, shining bright,
dew descends to earth, lifting patterns.
Mirroring red dust’s dazzling glow,
enveloped in azure ether’s misty haze.
Climbing peach and plum trees—unable to bear parting,
seeing off a beloved son—tears stain silk skirts.
As for one going to a severed state,
when to meet again?
Gazing at tall trees of the old village,
parting at the northern bridge forever.
Attendants’ souls stirred,
relatives and guests’ tears flow.
Can spread rushes to share regret,
only with a cup of wine to tell sorrow.
Meeting autumn geese flying days,
facing white dew falling time.
Regret upon regret by distant mountain bends,
going upon going by the long river’s shore.
Or again, if you dwell at Zī’s right,
I, your concubine, at Héyáng,
once sharing jade pendants’ morning glow,
together with golden censers’ evening fragrance.
You tie your official sash a thousand lǐ away,
I grieve that fairy grass blooms in vain.
Ashamed of the secluded chamber’s lute and zither,
dimming the high tower’s yellow silk.
Spring palace seals this green moss hue,
autumn curtains hold this bright moonlight.
Summer mats cool—day does not darken,
winter lamps congeal—night, how long!
Weaving brocade songs—tears already spent,
writing palindrome poems—shadow alone grieves.
Should there be a lofty scholar from Huàyīn,
who, having taken elixirs, returns to the mountains.
Though his arts are wondrous, he still studies;
though his Way is serene, it remains untaught.
He guards the cinnabar furnace, heedless of all else,
and refines the golden cauldron with steadfast resolve.
Mounting a crane, he ascends to the Milky Way;
harnessing phoenixes, he soars to the heavens.
Briefly roaming ten thousand miles,
parting for but a moment, though a thousand years pass.
Yet in this world, farewells are held dear;
bidding farewell to his host, he remains wistful.
Below are poems of peonies,
songs of fair maidens.
Maidens of Wèi among the mulberries,
beauties of Chén in the upper palace.
Spring grass, emerald in hue;
spring waters, rippling with green waves.
Seeing you off at the southern shore,
how heartrending it is!
Then comes autumn dew like pearls,
the autumn moon like a jade disc.
The bright moon and white dew,
as time flows back and forth.
In parting from you,
my longing heart wavers.
Thus, the forms of parting are unfixed,
the reasons for parting number a thousand.
Where there is parting, there must be sorrow;
where there is sorrow, it must swell.
It causes one’s will to falter and spirit to tremble,
heart broken, bones startled.
Even with the exquisite ink of Yuān and Yún,
the refined brushwork of Yán and Lè,
the many talents of the Golden Gate,
the gathered heroes of the Orchid Terrace—
those whose rhapsodies are hailed as soaring to the clouds,
whose debates resound like carving dragons—
who can depict the state of a brief separation,
or write the feelings of an eternal farewell?
Whenever I examine the works of talented scholars,
I privately feel I grasp their intentions.
The expression of ideas and deployment of language
are indeed highly varied;
beauty and ugliness, good and bad,
can be discussed.
Whenever I compose myself,
I especially perceive this truth:
I constantly worry that my ideas do not match the subject,
and my writing fails to capture my ideas.
It is not that understanding is difficult,
but that execution is hard.
Therefore, I write this “Rhapsody on Literature”
to describe the splendid writings of past masters,
and thereby discuss the origins of success and failure in literary composition.
In days to come, it may perhaps be said to exhaustively convey its subtleties.
As for wielding the axe to cut the handle,
though the model is close at hand,
the spontaneous changes of the hand
are truly hard to capture in words.
What can be expressed
is all contained herein.
Standing at the center of the world, I gaze into the profound;
nourishing my emotions and will with the ancient texts.
Following the four seasons, I sigh at their passing;
observing all things, my thoughts grow profuse.
I grieve for falling leaves in the harsh autumn,
rejoice in tender branches in fragrant spring.
My heart, solemn as if bearing frost;
my will, lofty as if facing clouds.
I chant the mighty deeds of worldly virtue,
recite the pure fragrance of ancestors.
Roaming the forest and treasury of literature,
I admire the elegance of beautiful phrases.
Moved, I lay aside the scroll and take up the brush,
to express it all in this writing.
At the beginning,
all sight and hearing are turned inward,
immersed in thought, probing all sides.
The spirit gallops to the eight extremes,
the mind wanders over ten thousand fathoms.
When inspiration arrives,
emotions grow clearer and more vivid,
objects appear distinct and come forth in turn.
I pour out the essence of all writings,
rinse my mouth with the fragrant richness of the Six Arts.
Floating on the Heavenly River, I drift peacefully;
bathing in the lower springs, I immerse deeply.
Thus, sunken words resist,
like fish biting the hook,
emerging from the depths of the abyss;
floating phrases follow in succession,
like a bird ensnared by an arrow,
falling from the heights of layered clouds.
I gather incomplete texts from a hundred generations,
collect lost rhymes from a thousand years.
Rejecting morning blossoms already open,
I unveil evening blooms yet to unfold.
Observing past and present in an instant,
touching all within the four seas in a blink.
Then, selecting ideas and arranging them in order,
testing phrases and assigning them their places.
All that holds substance is struck,
all that contains resonance is plucked.
Sometimes shaking the branches to stir the leaves,
sometimes following the waves to trace the source.
Sometimes moving from the hidden to the manifest,
sometimes seeking the easy and finding the difficult.
Sometimes like a tiger’s transformation, beasts scatter;
sometimes like a dragon’s appearance, birds flee.
Sometimes fitting smoothly and easily applied,
sometimes jarring and uneasy.
Exhausting a clear mind in concentrated thought,
distilling myriad considerations into words.
Encompassing heaven and earth within form,
subduing all things at the brush’s tip.
At first, halting on dry lips,
finally flowing onto moistened brush.
Principle supports the substance to establish the trunk;
writing hangs like branches and bears luxuriant fruit.
Truly, inner feeling and outward expression do not differ;
thus each change shows on the face.
Thinking of joy, one must smile;
speaking of sorrow, one already sighs.
Sometimes taking up the tablet with ease,
sometimes holding the brush, lost in thought.
This matter is indeed delightful,
and thus revered by sages and worthies.
Examining emptiness to demand substance,
knocking on silence to seek sound.
Containing vast distances within a foot of silk,
pouring forth abundance from an inch of heart.
Words expand and grow broader,
thoughts probe and grow deeper.
Spreading the fragrance of fragrant blossoms,
sprouting the lushness of green branches.
Brilliant as wind soaring and whirlwinds rising,
dense as clouds gathering in the forest of letters.
Literary forms are myriad and diverse;
objects have no single measure.
Chaotic and swift,
their forms are hard to depict.
Words compete in talent to display skill;
ideas hold the tally and act as the craftsman.
In being and non-being, strive diligently;
in depth and shallowness, do not yield.
Though departing from square and circle,
aim to exhaust form and capture likeness.
Thus, those who delight the eye favor extravagance;
those who satisfy the heart value aptness.
Those who exhaust words avoid narrowness;
those who discuss breadth prize openness.
Poetry follows emotion and is ornate and delicate;
rhapsody embodies objects and is clear and bright.
Stele inscriptions blend elegance with substance;
elegies are lingering and sorrowful.
Inscriptions are broad yet concise, warm and smooth;
admonitions are rhythmic, clear and vigorous.
Eulogies are leisurely and richly adorned;
discourses are subtle and lucidly fluent.
Memorials are even, penetrating, and refined;
persuasions are brilliant and cunningly deceptive.
Though distinctions lie herein,
also restrain the deviant and curb excess.
Essential is that words convey and principles stand;
thus, verbosity is not to be adopted.
As a thing, it is manifold in appearance;
as a form, it constantly changes.
In grasping meaning, ingenuity is prized;
in deploying language, beauty is valued.
As for the alternation of sounds,
it is like the interplay of five colors.
Though their flow and stop are inconstant,
they are inevitably uneven and hard to arrange.
If one comprehends change and recognizes sequence,
it is like opening a channel to admit a spring.
If one misses the moment and tries to join later,
it is always like attaching the end to the beginning.
Confusing the order of dark and yellow,
thus becoming turbid and lacking freshness.
Sometimes a preceding passage is forced to yield to a later one,
or a later passage is encroached upon by an earlier.
Sometimes the wording is flawed though the reasoning is sound,
sometimes the language is smooth but the meaning is hindered.
Separated, both are beautiful;
combined, both are harmed.
Examine the finest distinctions between the best and worst,
decide what to keep or discard with the utmost precision.
If weighed by the scale of judgment,
it must be aligned with the plumb line of appropriateness.
Sometimes the text is verbose and rich in reasoning,
yet the meaning does not point to a clear goal.
The ultimate cannot have two aims,
the exhaustive cannot be added to.
Place a brief statement at the key point,
and it becomes the driving force of the entire piece.
Though the many words are well-ordered,
they must rely on this to achieve merit.
Clearly, the merits are many and the flaws few,
so it suffices and need not be changed.
Sometimes the ornate thoughts are like brocade woven together,
clear and beautiful, shimmering.
Brilliant as embroidered silk,
poignant as many strings.
If what is conceived is not unique,
it will unwittingly match past writings.
Though woven from my own heart,
I fear others may have preceded me.
If it harms integrity and violates righteousness,
even if cherished, it must be discarded.
Sometimes like a flowering reed or a standing ear,
it stands apart from the crowd, peerless.
Its form cannot be pursued,
its echo cannot be tied down.
Solitary and towering alone,
it is not woven by common sounds.
The heart feels desolate without a match,
the mind hesitates and cannot let go.
A stone containing jade makes the mountain glow,
water holding pearls makes the river charming.
Those unpruned brambles and thorns
also gain glory from the gathering of kingfishers.
To attach a rustic song to a refined melody,
I also enhance its greatness.
Sometimes entrusted to a short verse,
facing sparse traces and solitary inspiration.
Looking down, lonely and without companions,
looking up, vast and unsupported.
Like a single string played alone,
containing a clear song but without response.
Sometimes placing words in a weary tone,
merely elegant in speech but lacking brilliance.
Mixing beauty and ugliness into one body,
tarnishing fine quality with flaws.
Like the lower pipes playing too fast,
though responding, they are not harmonious.
Sometimes abandoning reason to preserve novelty,
merely chasing emptiness and triviality.
Words lacking emotion and scant in love,
language floating adrift without returning.
Like a thin string with urgent frets,
though harmonious, it is not moving.
Sometimes unrestrained to achieve harmony,
striving for clamor and seductiveness.
Merely pleasing the eye and conforming to vulgar tastes,
surely loud in sound but low in quality.
Awake to "Fáng Lù" and "Sāng Jiān,"
again, though moving, they are not elegant.
Sometimes clear and empty, gentle and restrained,
always removing excess and discarding extravagance.
Lacking the lingering taste of the grand broth,
similar to the clear flow of vermilion strings.
Though one sings and three sigh,
surely elegant but not gorgeous.
As for the measure of richness and simplicity,
the form of high and low.
Adapting to change as appropriate,
subtle emotions are expressed.
Sometimes the words are clumsy but the meaning clever,
sometimes the reasoning plain but the language light.
Sometimes following the old yet becoming newer,
sometimes flowing with turbidity yet turning clearer.
Sometimes apparent at a glance,
sometimes requiring study to grasp its essence.
Like dancers moving sleeves to the rhythm,
singers responding to strings with their voices.
This is what Lún Biǎn could not put into words,
and thus not something ornate speech can master.
The universal principles of language and literary rules,
I truly hold them in my heart and abide by them.
Familiar with the common faults of worldly sentiments,
aware of the virtues of past sages.
Though arising from a clever mind,
sometimes criticized by dull eyes.
like beans in the central plains.
Boundless as the bellows,
nurtured together with heaven and earth.
Though abundant in this world,
alas, not enough to fill my handful.
Troubled by the jar often empty,
pained by the difficulty of continuing fine words.
Thus hobbling along a short wall,
releasing mediocre sounds to complete the tune.
Often leaving regret by the end of the piece,
how could I be content and self-satisfied?
Fearful of being dust-covered like a struck earthen jar,
mindful of being laughed at by jade chimes.
As for the meeting of inspiration,
the pattern of fluency and blockage.
Its coming cannot be stopped,
its going cannot be detained.
Hidden like a vanishing shadow,
appearing like a rising echo.
When the natural mechanism is swift and sharp,
what chaos cannot be ordered?
Thoughts like wind arise from the heart,
words like springs flow from lips and teeth.
Abundant and luxuriant, rushing forth,
only the brush and paper can capture them.
Writing brilliantly overflows the eyes,
sounds clear and melodious fill the ears.
And when the six emotions stagnate,
will goes forward but spirit remains behind.
Dull as a withered tree,
empty as a dried-up stream.
Gathering soul to probe the profound,
concentrating essence to seek within.
Reason grows dimmer and more hidden,
thought struggles as if being pulled out.
Thus sometimes exhausting emotion brings much regret,
sometimes following intuition brings few faults.
Though this thing lies within me,
it is not by my effort alone.
So often I stroke my empty heart and sigh,
I do not know the cause of opening and blockage.
As for the function of this writing,
it is surely the basis of all principles.
Expanding over ten thousand miles without obstruction,
connecting through a billion years as a ford.
Looking down, it leaves models for future generations,
looking up, it observes the patterns of the ancients.
Aiding Wén and Wǔ on the verge of collapse,
proclaiming their influence undying.
No distance too far to cover,
no principle too subtle to encompass.
Matching the moistening of clouds and rain,
resembling the transformations of ghosts and spirits.
Inscribed on metal and stone, virtue spreads wide,
flowing through pipes and strings, ever renewed.
Tracing the origin of the xiāo's stem,
from the hills of Jiāngnán.
Hollow, straight, and rarely jointed,
towering, lush, and spreading.
Merely observing its side by the mountain,
then rugged, steep, and towering,
leaning against cliffs, winding and vast,
truly pitiable in its instability!
Gazing far, wild and boundless,
stretching continuously, open and vast,
again delightful in its spacious leisure.
Entrusting its body to the earth,
enduring ten thousand years unchanged.
Absorbing the purest essence, flourishing,
endowed with a verdant color, moist and firm.
Sensing the changes of yīn and yáng,
attaching life to the heavenly sovereign.
The whistling wind passes through its tips,
the circling river flows and irrigates its mountain.
Raising white waves and scattering linked pearls,
the sound rumbling like pouring into an abyss.
Morning dew, clear and cool, falls by its side,
jade-like liquid soaks and nourishes its roots.
A lone female phoenix, a widowed crane,
amuses leisurely beneath it,
spring birds in flocks play,
soaring above its peak.
The autumn cicada eats not,
embracing simplicity and singing long,
the dark ape wails mournfully,
searching within its midst.
Dwelling in seclusion and deep recesses,
densely silent and secluded.
Only by examining its plain form
is it fitting to be clear and quiet, not noisy.
Fortunately named the dòngxiāo,
receiving the generous grace of the sage ruler.
It can be called beneficial without cost,
following the natural disposition of heaven.
Thus, the master craftsman Bān applied his skill,
and Kuí and Fēi set the standards.
Adorned with ivory,
the joints were fitted together.
Carved and engraved with intricate patterns,
crimson lips interwoven in complexity.
Dense and winding,
like overlapping scales, swiftly arrayed.
Tightly compacted and orderly arranged,
pressed and smoothed to perfection.
Then, one whose nature was obscure and profound,
who from birth had never seen the forms of heaven and earth,
and was blind to the appearances of black and white,
was filled with pent-up sorrow and intense grief,
lamenting the loss of light in his eyes.
With few outlets for his thoughts and worries,
he devoted himself entirely to expressing his emotions through music.
Thus, his lips and breath met the notes of gōng and shāng,
harmoniously overflowing in abundance.
His form swayed gracefully as he blew,
his breath sighing deeply with pent-up sorrow.
The air rushed forth and shot out,
scattering and dispersing, then gathering again.
At times, it moved with calm and ease, unhurried,
at others, it surged together in strange and wondrous ways.
Sometimes it was chaotic and flowing gently,
like branches breaking off.
Sometimes it spread out continuously,
overflowing abundantly.
Trembling and dense,
it would suddenly cease and vanish.
Then, with a burst of brilliance,
it would leap forth again.
If one listened carefully to its melodies,
and examined its songs closely,
the chirping and twittering about to burst into song,
moved in harmony, blending together.
Like the wind, vast and unceasing,
gracefully swirling and dancing.
Light and drifting, then suddenly sparse,
floating away, abandoned, and transforming into something else.
It would block the paths,
harmonizing with the songs and ballads.
Thus, listening to its grand sounds,
they flowed everywhere, overflowing,
encompassing and releasing,
like a kind father nurturing his child.
Its exquisite sounds,
were clear, tranquil, and serene,
orderly, humble, and gentle,
like a filial son serving his father.
Its principles and analogies,
truly corresponded to righteousness and reason,
surging and passionate,
how like a heroic warrior!
Gentle and warm,
it also resembled a noble gentleman.
Thus, its martial sounds
were like thunder rumbling,
unrestrained and boiling with agitation.
Its benevolent sounds,
were like a gentle breeze spreading everywhere,
calm and bestowing kindness.
Sometimes they gathered together in convergence,
sometimes they scattered and cast away.
Sorrowful and heartrending, evoking pity,
at times serene and tranquil, relaxed and free.
Drenched and dripping, delicate and soft,
at times bursting forth with radiant clarity.
Melancholy and sorrowful, yet endearing,
truly rich and full of flavor.
Thus, the greedy heard it and became upright,
the fierce and violent heard it and held no resentment.
The rigid and violent returned to benevolence and kindness,
the indulgent and careless were warned of their faults.
Zhōng Qī and Yá Kuàng would be astonished and amazed,
and even the wife of Liáng would be unable to match its spirit.
Shī Xiāng and Yán Chūn dared not display their skill,
Jìn Yín and Shū Zǐ were far from its kind.
The stubborn and foolish, like Zhū and Jūn, were awakened and became wise,
while Jié, Zhí, Yù, and Bó were worn out and haggard.
Blowing the cēn cī, it entered the path of virtue,
thus enduring and precious.
Sometimes playing clever tunes,
it wandered and soared,
sometimes lingering without moving on,
sometimes moving on without lingering.
Confused and scattered,
losing companions and peers.
Searching and gathering together,
the formless sought each other.
Thus, those who understood music found joy and sorrow in it,
while those who did not understand found it strange and marvelous.
Thus, hearing its sorrowful sounds,
none could help but feel sad, sighing heavily,
wiping away tears.
When it played joyful tunes,
none could help but be delighted and cheerful,
swaying gracefully and contentedly.
Thus, even crickets and inchworms,
crawling creatures panting for breath,
ants and lizards,
buzzing and fluttering,
moved slowly and obliquely,
fish gazed and chickens stared.
Beaks drooping, bodies coiling,
eyes wide open, forgetting to eat.
How much more would they be moved by the harmony of yīn and yáng,
and transformed by the customs of human relations!
The finale says:
It appears like a swift warrior,
leaping and soaring, surpassing all,
rapid and skillful.
It is also like flowing waves,
bubbling and surging,
rushing along steep paths.
Roaring and calling out,
rising and falling, connecting and breaking off,
turbulent and chaotic.
Stirring and searching, whistling and sweeping,
carefree and leaping,
as if collapsing and crumbling.
Wandering and drifting,
hesitating and lingering,
it is also captivating.
Declining and fading away,
bidding farewell and drifting far,
floating away, never to return.
Relying on the sage's transformation,
calm and following the middle way,
joyful but not excessive.
Flowing smoothly and penetrating deeply,
it maintains proper restraint.
At the end of the poem and the conclusion of the tune,
lingering echoes remain.
The breath of the chant and the remaining echoes,
continuous and drifting lightly,
give rise to a gentle breeze.
Extending continuously,
transforming endlessly.
King Xiāng of Chǔ, after touring Yúnmèng,
commanded Sòng Yù to compose a fu about the events at Gāotáng.
As he was about to host a banquet with wine,
he said to Sòng Yù:
"I wish to toast my ministers,
how shall we entertain them?"
Yù said:
"I have heard that songs are used to express words,
and dances to convey meaning fully.
Therefore, discussing their poetry is not as good as listening to their sounds;
listening to their sounds is not as good as observing their forms.
The dances of 'Jíchǔ,' 'Jiéfēng,' and 'Yáng'ē,'
are the ultimate spectacle for talented performers,
the most exquisite in the world.
Ah, may they be presented?"
The King said:
"What about their resemblance to Zhèng music?"
Yù said:
"Small and great have different uses,
Zhèng and Yǎ have distinct appropriateness.
The measure of relaxation and tension,
is applied by sages and wise men.
Thus, the 'Record of Music' describes the bearing of shield and axe,
the 'Elegant and Beautiful' praises the crouching dance,
the 'Rites' establish the rule of three cups,
and the 'Odes' contain songs of returning drunk.
As for 'Xiánchí' and 'Liùyīng,'
they are used to adorn the pure temple
and harmonize spirits and people.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi,
is used to entertain in intimate gatherings
and foster joy.
On leisurely days, for pleasure and relaxation,
it is not meant to influence the people;
what harm is there in it!"
The King said:
"Try composing a fu about it for me."
Yù said:
"Yes, yes."
Ah, how bright and clear is this tranquil night,
The radiant moon sheds its brilliant light.
Crimson flames flicker and rise high,
Illuminating splendid halls and inner chambers nearby.
Embroidered curtains are drawn and tied with silken bands,
The door knockers gleam with resplendent, dazzling strands.
Cushioned mats are spread, seats are arranged in rows,
Golden wine vessels overflow, jade cups in order repose.
Goblets and cups are passed around in toasts,
Drunkenness spreads, bringing joy to hosts and guests.
Stern faces soften, glowing with delight,
Inner feelings emerge, shining ever so bright.
The literati cannot conceal their literary grace,
The warriors cannot hide their valor and steadfast pace.
Some grow lazy, leaping and prancing with glee,
Others whirl and tangle in chaotic spree.
Profound and deep, emotions surge and sway,
Breaking from their usual, steadfast way.
Then, the Zhèng maidens step forth, advancing slow,
Sixteen in number, serving in a gentle flow.
Their attire is exquisite, of utmost beauty and grace,
Their demeanor tender, with charm they embrace.
Their looks enchanting, bewitching and fine,
Rosy cheeks radiant, like blossoms that shine.
Their eyebrows slender, delicately curved and long,
Their eyes glance sideways, like waves flowing strong.
Pearls and jade sparkle, shimmering bright,
Embroidered robes flutter, mingling with sheer veils light.
They glance at their shadows,
Adjusting their attire.
Following the gentle breeze,
They waft fragrant scents higher.
Their vermilion lips part,
Their clear voices rise.
Singing high notes, they rejoice under the skies.
The song goes:
I express my thoughts to broaden my view,
Unravel the constraints that bind spirits anew.
Loosen the taut strings of urgency and strain,
Slow the trivial matters, let simplicity reign.
Expand the vastness of generous breadth,
Set aside the petty details, free from dread.
I praise the "Guān Jū" for its restraint and grace,
Lament the "Xī Shuài" for its confined space.
Open the barriers of the primal truth so grand,
Transcend worldly things, rise above the land.
Raise the stirring zhǐ notes,
Unleash the clear jué tones.
Praise the dance's rhythm,
Play the harmonious drones.
Form and spirit harmonize,
Mind and intent unite.
With ease and composure,
Will remains unshaken, bright.
Then, to the beat of drums, they take their place,
Their hearts expand, embracing boundless space.
Minds wander limitless, without a trace,
Thoughts drift far, in a timeless embrace.
As the dance begins to rise,
They bend and lift,
They come and go.
Graceful yet melancholic,
Beyond what forms can show.
As they advance a little more,
They hover and stride,
They stand tall and lean aside.
Movements sudden yet measured,
Gestures matching the sound.
Silken robes flutter in the wind,
Long sleeves crisscross around.
Continuously scattering,
Swiftly merging as one.
Like swallows resting gently,
Like startled swans on the run.
Graceful and leisurely,
Agile and light as air.
Possessing peerless beauty,
With pure and sincere care.
Cultivating demeanor to reveal their aim,
Their thoughts alone roam in the boundless frame.
Like towering mountains high,
Like flowing waters wide.
Changing with their will,
No expression is cast aside.
Clarifying poems to show their intent,
Sighs rise, fervent and ardent.
Spirit like floating clouds,
Will like autumn frost.
Spectators sigh in awe,
No performer is outclassed or lost.
Then, the whole troupe advances in turn,
Waiting in order, each takes their concern.
Competing in skill, vying in art,
Flaunting their beauty, playing their part.
Extraordinary postures emerge untold,
Exquisite forms rise, wondrous and bold.
Glancing at the patterned drum, their clear eyes soar,
Singing lively tunes, their white teeth pour.
Aligning their rows with care,
Planning each move, precise and fair.
As if moved by divine power,
They whirl and hover, standing tall.
Strikes never miss the beat,
Steps never halt or fall.
Lightly they drift away,
Silently they cease to sway.
And when they turn to re-enter,
Pressed by the urgent meter.
Leaping and kneeling in succession,
Tapping toes, rubbing with precision.
Bending forms to reach afar,
Collapsing as if broken, like a falling star.
Fine silk fluttering like moth wings,
Whirling wildly, as if on strings.
Soaring like birds in flight,
Relaxing softly, fading from sight.
Slithering and swaying gently,
Like swirling clouds, drifting lightly.
Bodies like roaming dragons free,
Sleeves like pure rainbows to see.
With a final bow, the dance concludes,
The melody ends, all moods elude.
Lingering with a subtle smile,
They retreat to their ranks in style.
Spectators praise their beauty rare,
All find joy beyond compare.
Thus, the feast reaches its height at night,
The guests are bid farewell, taking flight.
Bustling, they prepare to depart,
Coachmen ready, taking heart.
Carriages and riders press close,
Crowded and dense, as the scene grows.
Fine steeds with swift and graceful pace,
Gallop boldly, winning the race.
Like soaring dragons, they charge ahead,
Bits raised high, froth flying widespread.
Horses differ in their breed,
Each striving to take the lead.
Some dash through dust, following tracks,
Like thunderbolts, leaving no slack.
Stamping the ground, leaving the herd behind,
Leaping in darkness, uniquely designed.
Some, with pent-up fury, hold their ground,
Hesitating, making no sound.
Starting late but arriving first,
They outpace others, as if rehearsed.
Some, proud of their graceful air,
Move with ease, beyond compare.
Adjusting speed to suit the will,
Controlling pace with steady skill.
The sound of wheels like thunder roars,
As horses gallop, closing doors.
Silently they return home,
Scattering like clouds across the dome.
The king feasts with joy and cheer,
Pleasure without excess, ever clear.
Entertaining spirits, forgetting age,
A path to longevity, turning the page.
Leisurely and carefree,
Passing the days with glee.
Since Mǎ Róng was well-versed in classical elegance,
And meticulously studied mathematics and divination,
Moreover, he had a natural fondness for music,
Able to play the qín and blow the dí,
And while serving as a Dūyóu,
With no lingering affairs to attend,
He lay alone in the Wū of Píngyáng in Méi.
A guest from Luòyáng lodged at the inn,
Playing the dí,
Performing "Qì Chū" and "Jīng Liè" in harmony.
Mǎ Róng had been away from the capital for over a year,
Hearing it briefly,
He felt deep sorrow yet found joy in it.
Recalling the odes to the xiāo, qín, and shēng by Wáng Zǐyuān,
Méi Chéng,
Liú Bókāng,
Fù Wǔzhòng, and others,
Only the dí alone had none,
So he casually made up the number,
Composing the "Cháng Dí Fù."
Its words are as follows:
Only the extraordinary zhōnglóng bamboo grows here,
On the northern cliffs of the Zhōngnán Mountains.
Perched upon the solitary peak of Jiǔchéng,
Overlooking the stone ravines of ten thousand fathoms.
Its stems stand tall like arrows and stalks,
Alone listening to the wind at the utmost peril.
Autumn floods wash its lower roots,
Winter snow piles and seals its branches.
Its peak roots stand firm yet precarious,
Stirred by swirling gusts, nearly collapsing.
Facing its sides are layered ridges and added rocks,
Piled rugged and uneven.
Lofty peaks, steep and perilous,
Leaning and tilting, rising and falling.
Deep caverns, cunningly aged,
Gullies and caves, pits and valleys.
Ravines and gorges, mountain streams,
Chasms and cliffs, caverns and hollows.
Winding and twisting, swirling and eddying,
Ridges connected, ranges linked.
Forests of bamboo and sprawling brambles,
Dense groves of oak and plain trees.
Here, mountain waters converge in torrents,
Pools swell, barriers burst.
Waters surge and flow abundantly,
Plunging like pestles into churning holes.
Rushing rapids twist and twine,
Gushing and bubbling, roaring and crashing.
Waves ripple like fish scales,
Depressions and heights, strange and perverse.
Waterfalls spray foam,
Rushing and fleeing, dashing and colliding.
Shaking the mountains,
Disturbing their roots—
Such occurs five or six times a year.
Thus, there are no paths in between,
Rarely trodden by human feet.
Gibbons and monkeys cry by day,
Flying squirrels call by night.
Cold bears shake their jaws,
Solitary stags roam at dusk.
Mountain pheasants flock at dawn,
Pheasants crow at daybreak.
Seeking mates, calling their young,
Lamenting and howling, long and shrill.
Roaming and recognizing paths,
Chirping and clamoring noisily.
Passing by their left and right,
Clamoring before and behind—
There is no rest day or night.
Truly, this is a place of peril and danger,
Where sorrows and griefs accumulate.
Thus, when it responds to the clear breeze,
Its slender tips sway vigorously,
Ringing and resonating, clear and loud.
Like tightened zither strings on close pegs,
Or the high tones of the Hàozhōng bell.
Then, exiled ministers and banished sons,
Abandoned wives and parted friends—
Like Péng, Xū, Bóqí,
Āijiāng, and Xiàojǐ—
Gather downwind,
Focus their spirits, lend their ears.
Sighing like thunder, breathless with sorrow,
Beating their chests, tearing their clothes.
Tears of blood flow freely,
Crisscrossing as they fall.
Awake all night, forgetting sleep,
Unable to restrain themselves.
Then, they sent Lǔ Bān and Sòng Dí,
To construct cloud ladders,
And raise floating pillars.
Treading on slender roots,
Climbing on thin threads.
Chest against steep slopes,
Belly against narrow passes.
Reaching its summit,
Crawling to cut and take.
Trimming the ends,
Measuring with compass and square.
Kuí and Xiāng compared the pitches,
Zǐyě harmonized the modes.
All twelve tones were complete,
With Huángzhōng as the foundation.
Carving and shaping with axes and tools,
Cutting and smoothing, measuring and planning.
Polishing and grinding, discarding flaws,
Outer surface plain, inner lining red.
Named it the flute,
To present to worthy scholars.
Displayed on the eastern steps,
All eight musical instruments joined in.
Feasts concluded with harmony,
To encourage and honor the gentlemen.
Then retired to the high corridor of the Yellow Gate,
Where Chóngqiū, Sòng, Guàn,
Famous masters Guō and Zhāng,
Artisans and skilled craftsmen,
Practiced and refined the music.
Then, leisurely wandering nobles,
Idle royal grandsons,
Hearts delighting in the harmony of the five tones,
Ears attuned to the melodies of the eight sounds,
Gathered together in their courtyard.
Closely observing the rich and varied melodies,
How abundant they were!
Colorful and splendid,
Truly delightful.
Waves spreading far and wide,
Truly remarkable.
Straining and clashing,
Also strange indeed.
Chirping and clamoring,
Like colorful feathers—
Twisting, burning, stirring, and sharpening.
Shaking with suppressed anger,
Roaring and startling, vigorous and unrestrained.
Breath bursting forth, spreading everywhere,
Suddenly pausing, then fiercely rushing.
Like thunder striking the anvil, rumbling—
Clear and chilling as the wind.
Briefly converging, overriding the rhythm,
Rushing ahead, stumbling forward.
Then, listening to the sounds, likening them to forms,
Appearing like flowing water,
Or resembling flying geese.
Vast and boundless,
Grand and expansive.
Gazing far, drawing long,
Whirling and circling back.
Full and winding, dense and coiled,
Tense and clustered, rugged and uneven.
Rich and splendid, open and clear,
Clustered and sprawling, vast and majestic.
Taking and giving, timely and fitting,
Advancing and retreating, with proper measure.
Loud and soft, rising and falling in order,
Sparse and dense, always appropriate.
Gentle breezes, delicate and subtle,
Seeming to exist, then vanish.
Stagnant and cut off,
Pausing midway, then resuming.
Suddenly fading away,
Brilliantly rising again.
Sometimes carefully guarded,
Masterfully skilled and exquisite.
Surpassing strings and reeds,
Overwhelming drums and bells.
Sometimes held steady, coiled and restrained,
Calm and tolerant.
Flutes and pipes all playing,
Metal and stone instruments resounding together.
Not disrupting the order,
To spread the eight winds.
Pitches and modes now harmonious,
Sorrowful sounds descending five times.
The melody ends, the piece concludes,
Remaining strings rise again.
Complex fingerings repeatedly played,
Dense and layered, overlapping.
Pressing and crowding, gathering closely,
Like bees swarming, ants converging.
Many sounds accumulating together,
To send it to its end.
Then, a brief rest, a momentary pause,
Mixed tunes played in intervals.
Easy to hear yet startling to the ear,
Something stirring and evolving.
Peacefully gliding, leisurely swaying,
Calm and unhurried, gentle and slow.
Melancholy and resentful,
Depressed and stifled, suppressed and restrained.
Swiftly seeking and searching,
Now near, now far.
Facing danger, letting go freely,
As if collapsing, then returning.
Twisting and winding, turning and bending,
Coiling and stretching, sinuous and meandering.
Rising and falling, restrained and hidden,
Progressing into various changes.
Twisting and swirling, flowing and merging,
The five tones alternating in succession.
Grasping and pressing, plucking and stopping,
Successively intertwining and shifting.
Returning to shāng, descending to zhǐ,
Each excelling in its own way.
Thus, those who listen to the prelude
observe the method in its rhythm,
examine the variations in its phrases,
and thereby know that ritual propriety must not be transgressed.
Those who hear the interlude
are transported in thought to ancient times,
their minds filled with caution and vigilance,
and thereby know that lasting sorrow cannot be endured in idleness.
Therefore, to discuss and record its meaning,
and harmonize and compare its imagery:
wandering freely and unrestrained,
vast and boundless—
this is the manner of Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ.
Gentle, upright, pliant, and resolute—
this is the way of Confucius and Mèngzǐ.
Stirring, clear, pure, and severe—
this is the integrity of Suíguāng.
Firm, piercing, rebellious, and perverse—
this is the spirit of Zhūbēn.
Sections and phrases clearly demarcated—
this is the system of Guǎnzhòng and Shāngyāng.
Orderly, decisive, intricate, and profuse—
this is the discernment of Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi.
Elaborate, ornate, continuous, and linked—
this is the discourse of Fàn Suī and Cài Zé.
Sharp, incisive, penetrating, and subtle—
this is the wisdom of Xīlóng.
Above, it models itself on the "Sháo Xiāo" and "Nán Yuè";
in the middle, it takes its measure from "White Snow" and "Green Waters";
below, it adopts the form of "Dew-Laden" and "Bǎrén."
Thus, whether noble or base, refined or rustic,
wise or foolish, brave or timid,
even fish, turtles, birds, and beasts—
all who hear it prick up their ears, startled as deer.
Bears stretch, birds extend their necks,
owls stare, wolves glance back.
Clapping, clamoring, leaping, and jumping,
each attains its proper measure.
People's desires are fully satisfied,
all return to harmony and balance,
thereby beautifying customs and mores.
Qū Yuán would go to a land of joy,
Jiè Zhītuī would return to receive his stipend.
Dàntái Mièmíng would carry the corpse home,
Gāo Yú would moderate his weeping.
Cháng Wàn would cease his rebellious plots,
Qú Mí would no longer commit evil.
Kuǎikuì would be able to repel the enemy,
Bù Zhàn would achieve integrity and resolve.
Princes and dukes would preserve their positions,
hermits would dwell peacefully in the woods.
Officials would delight in their duties,
scholars would maintain their family homes for generations.
Sturgeon would gape at the water's edge,
looking up at the team of horses while black cranes dance.
At such a time,
Mián Jū would fall silent,
Bó Yá would break his strings.
Hù Bā would let his bridges fall,
Qìng Xiāng would take down his hanging stones.
They would gaze intently, wide-eyed,
repeatedly praising and lauding.
Losing composure, falling from their mats,
striking and clapping like thunderous applause.
With eyes narrowed and gazing intently,
tears and snivel flowing freely.
Thus, it can communicate with spirits and move things,
express the spirit and convey meaning.
It brings forth sincerity and fulfills intent,
leading to action and initiating affairs.
It washes away filth and impurity,
cleansing grime and dregs.
In ancient times, Fúxī made the qin,
Shénnóng created the sè.
Nǚwā fashioned the huáng,
Bào Xīn crafted the xūn.
Chuí harmonized the bells,
Shū arranged the stone chimes.
Some smelted metal and polished stone,
adorned and carved meticulously.
Shaped, carved, engraved, and polished,
incised, chiseled, drilled, and inlaid.
Exhausting wonder and utmost skill,
spanning days and months.
Only then were the instruments completed,
their sounds as described.
Only the flute, relying on its natural form,
does not alter its material.
Cut and blown,
its sound is as such.
This indeed embodies the principle of simplicity,
the work of a worthy person.
If so,
these six instruments
still benefited from the embellishments of the Two Sovereigns and the sages.
How much more the flute, born in the great Hàn dynasty,
yet scholars do not recognize its ability to enhance and glorify,
neglecting and not praising it—
alas!
A common scholar, Qiū Zhòng, spoke of its origins,
but did not know its vast excellence.
His words say:
In recent times, the double flute arose from the Qiāng,
the Qiāng people cut bamboo without cease.
A dragon's cry in water, unseen by itself,
cut bamboo and blow it, the sound is similar.
Carve holes on top to open passages,
trim it to serve as a mouthpiece, easy to hold.
Yì Jīng Jūnmíng understood tones and rhythms,
so based on four holes, he added one.
The hole Jūnmíng added came later,
this is called the shāng note, completing the five tones.
I have loved music since youth,
and as I grew, I immersed myself in it.
I believe that things have their flourishing and decline,
but this does not change;
flavors can become tiresome,
but this does not weary.
It can guide and nourish the spirit and energy,
express and harmonize emotions and will,
and for dwelling in poverty and solitude without distress,
nothing comes closer than music.
Therefore, if repeating it is not enough,
then chant and sing to express the will;
if chanting and singing are not enough,
then entrust words to broaden the meaning.
Yet among the instruments of the eight sounds,
and the imagery of song and dance,
talented scholars through the ages
have all composed fù and odes for them.
Their styles and elegance
none fail to follow tradition.
Praising their substance,
they take peril and hardship as supreme;
describing their sounds,
they take sorrow and grief as primary;
extolling their transformative power,
they take shedding tears as noble.
Beautiful they may be,
but they have not fully exhausted the principle.
Examining their origins,
it seems they fundamentally did not understand music;
observing their main themes,
they also did not grasp the essence of ritual and music.
Among all instruments,
the virtue of the qin is the finest.
Therefore, I string together my thoughts
to compose a fù about it.
Its words say:
Where the catalpa tree grows,
it rests on lofty peaks and towering ridges.
Breaking through layered soil to emerge and thrive,
it reaches the celestial pole and soars high.
It contains the pure harmony of heaven and earth,
and absorbs the splendid light of sun and moon.
Lush and profuse, it stands alone in luxuriance,
its blossoms flying into the vast azure sky.
At dusk, it gathers shadows into Yúyuān,
at dawn, its trunk is dried by the nine suns.
Passing a thousand years awaiting its worth,
serenely it stands, eternally tranquil.
Moreover, its mountains and rivers, their forms and features,
wind and twist, hidden and deep,
lofty and precipitous, high and steep.
Interlocking ridges, jagged cliffs,
rugged and towering, sheer and perilous.
Crimson bluffs perilous and hazardous,
green cliffs ten thousand fathoms high.
If then layered peaks rise ever higher,
towering aloft, covered by clouds,
far-reaching, lofty and exalted to the utmost grandeur,
soaring majestically, uniquely splendid.
They steam forth numinous vapors to spread clouds,
leaning on divine abysses to spew forth streams.
Then the tumbling waves rush forth abruptly,
wildly racing, contending in their flow.
Striking cliffs, dashing against bends,
pent-up fury, violent and unrestrained.
Surging and swelling, leaping and pounding,
casting spray, raising billows.
Churning and roaring, crashing and booming,
coiling and twisting, intertwined.
Recklessly into the great river,
crossing to the central region.
Peacefully turning, slowly advancing,
silently, ever floating.
Vast and expansive,
winding and embracing the hills.
Observe in detail the products nurtured by this region’s soil,
the treasures fostered within its profound domains.
Rare and marvelous, langgān jade,
yáo and jǐn gems, radiant and crimson.
Gathered in clusters, piled in heaps,
splendidly spreading by its side.
If then spring orchids cover its east,
shātáng trees grow on its west.
Juānzǐ dwells on its southern side,
jade springs gush before it.
Dark clouds shade above it,
soaring phoenixes gather on its summit.
Clear dew moistens its skin,
gentle breezes flow through its spaces.
Towering, solemnly still and tranquil,
densely, subtly, serene and leisurely.
That which is arranged around it,
is surely divinely beautiful by nature,
and fully satisfies longing, love, and delight.
Thereupon, recluses who shun the world,
the likes of Róngqī and Qǐjì,
then together climb flying bridges,
cross secluded ravines,
grasp jasper branches,
ascend steep cliffs,
to wander beneath it.
Circling about, gazing afar forever,
distantly as if soaring in flight.
Looking askance toward Kūnlún,
looking down upon the sea’s shore.
Pointing toward Cāngwú’s distant expanse,
facing the winding river’s meandering course.
Awakening to the many burdens of worldly customs,
looking up to the lingering radiance of Jīshān.
Admiring this mountain’s vast openness,
impassioned, they forget to return.
Emotions relaxed and unfettered, gazing afar,
connecting with Xuānyuán’s legacy of music.
Yearning for Lǎotóng in the Guī corner,
revering Tàiróng’s lofty chant.
Regarding this wú tree and giving rise to thought,
thinking to borrow an object to entrust the heart.
Then they cut a side branch,
measuring precisely its suitability.
The perfected one expands his thoughts,
crafting it into an elegant qin.
Then he had Lízǐ oversee the marking,
Jiàngshí wield the axe.
Kuí and Xiāng presented the methods,
Bān and Chuí displayed their divine skill.
Carving joints, fitting parts together,
clear and dense, adjusted to harmony.
Ornate patterns, carved and polished,
displaying splendor, draping with elegance.
Inlaid with rhinoceros and ivory,
set off with kingfisher green.
Strung with silk from Yuánkè,
markers with jade from Zhōngshān.
Then there are images of dragon and phoenix,
forms of ancient people.
Bóyá raises his hand to play,
Zhōngqī listens to the sounds.
Splendid appearance glowing brightly,
emitting radiance, shining with light.
How beautiful it is!
Línglún compares the pitch-pipes,
Tiánlián handles the playing.
Presented to the noble gentleman,
the new melody clear and bright.
How magnificent it is!
And when it first is tuned,
then jiǎo and yǔ notes arise together,
gōng and zhǐ notes mutually affirm.
Multiple tones issue forth and proceed together,
high and low accumulate in response.
Leaping and tumbling, massive and rugged,
beautiful sounds about to flourish.
Surely harmonious and flowing, fully captivating.
Then he regulates the correct tones,
performs marvelous melodies.
Raises "White Snow",
brings forth "Clear Jiǎo".
Profusely, dripping and flowing,
splendidly overflowing and richly abundant.
Brilliantly, majestically soaring high,
swiftly, urgently connecting one after another.
Abundantly leaping and contending in pursuit,
harmoniously brilliant and richly ornate.
Shaped like lofty mountains,
also resembling flowing waves.
Vast, oh so expansive,
majestic, oh so towering.
Agitated and vexed,
winding and lingering, graceful and swaying.
Soaring and spreading, broadcasting freedom,
suddenly scattering, a profusion of blossoms.
Composing demeanor, imparting rhythm,
responding to changes, conforming to measure.
Striving for fame, mastering the art,
steady on course, advancing slowly.
Vast and sweeping, practiced and fluent,
the sound’s splendor spreads afar.
Containing evident charm to send off the finale,
floating lingering echoes in the primal purity.
If then in high galleries, flying towers,
broad mansions, secluded chambers;
winter nights serene and clear,
bright moon shedding its light.
New robes emerald-bright,
sash tassels flowing with fragrance.
Then the instrument cool, strings tuned,
heart leisurely, hand nimble.
Touching and plucking as the will desires,
only the intention guiding the execution.
First venturing into "Lù Shuǐ",
then performing "Clear Zhǐ".
Elegantly flowing, Táng Yáo,
finally chanting, Wēizǐ.
Broad and bright, expansive and mellow,
leisurely and carefree, pausing and standing.
Stroking the strings, calmly singing,
new melodies arise in succession.
The song says:
Soaring on the whirlwind, oh, resting on Yíngzhōu,
inviting Lièzǐ, oh, to be a good companion.
Feasting on hàngxiè, oh, girdled with morning clouds,
ethereal and graceful, oh, roaming near heaven.
Equalizing all things, oh, transcending to self-contentment,
entrusting life’s fate, oh, accepting departure or stay.
Stirring pure notes to join the gathering,
how intimate are the string songs!
Then, as the prelude draws to a close,
and the various sounds are about to cease,
the melody shifts and the mode changes,
and wondrous strains begin to emerge.
With a serene expression,
and sleeves rolled back to reveal fair wrists,
slender fingers fly and dart,
in a flurry of rapid notes, flowing and spreading.
Sometimes lingering with tender affection,
sometimes restrained and subdued.
Nurturing and cultivating with care,
composed and savoring the hidden depths.
Suddenly bursting forth with vigor,
like a tempest stirring clouds into chaos.
Scattered yet fierce,
spreading and dispersing halfway.
Rich and full, scattering apart,
brilliant and resplendent, dazzling and radiant.
Sublime tones soar and spread,
brilliant and splendid, shining brightly.
Sometimes interwoven with contrasting sounds,
as if cunningly converging.
Two beauties advance together,
running side by side, driving like wings.
At first seeming to diverge,
but ultimately converging on the same path.
Sometimes curved yet unyielding,
straight yet not arrogant.
Sometimes overlapping yet not disordered,
sometimes separated yet not severed.
At times forceful and impassioned,
at times plaintive and hesitant.
Suddenly drifting lightly and swiftly,
then lingering and branching luxuriantly.
Sometimes dense and hurried,
repeated and clustered tightly.
Crisscrossing and continuous,
rushing and pressing urgently.
Pausing for sighs and repeated praises,
with no room even for a breath.
Magnificent, enchanting, wondrous, and grand,
inexhaustible and beyond comprehension.
As for its leisurely grace and elegance,
both grand and delicate are perfectly suited.
Clear and harmonious, smooth and bright,
undulating and variegated.
Gentle and tender, bringing joy and delight,
graceful and compliant, winding and meandering.
Sometimes venturing into perilous passages,
seizing gaps and approaching danger.
Like the cry of a solitary kūnjī bird in a clear pond,
or the wings of a wandering swan soaring over layered cliffs.
With intricate patterns and splendid tails,
delicate and trailing, flowing and cascading.
A gentle breeze carries lingering notes,
soft and graceful, gentle and serene.
Sometimes plucking and strumming,
ethereal and swirling, clear and crisp.
Lightly gliding and floating over the strings,
bright and skillful, sharp and clever.
Swift but not rushed,
lingering but not stagnant.
Fluttering and drifting afar,
subtle tones swiftly fading away.
Listening from afar,
it is like the harmonious cries of luán and fèng birds playing among the clouds;
observing up close,
it is like myriad flowers blooming and shining in the spring breeze.
Rich and abundant in its many forms,
it also excels in both beginning and ending.
How exquisite and magnificent,
how endlessly varied its transformations!
As in the beginning of spring,
when beautiful attire is worn in season.
Then, accompanied by friends,
one wanders and plays.
Crossing orchid gardens,
ascending layered heights.
With dense forests behind,
shaded by splendid flora.
Facing clear streams,
composing new poems.
Admiring the leisurely grace of fish and dragons,
delighting in the flourishing of a hundred plants.
Tuning the ancient melodies of Chónghuá,
sighing with longing and deep contemplation.
As for elegant halls and intimate banquets,
with close friends and honored guests.
Exquisite dishes served together,
fine wine clear and mellow.
Presenting "Nánjīng,"
performing "Xīqín."
Continuing "Língyáng,"
and playing "Bārén."
Varied and mixed, they rise together,
captivating the listeners and astonishing the spirit.
Considering their extraordinary effects and comparing their artistry,
how can shēng and yuè instruments possibly match?
If ranking the melodies suited for preludes,
then "Guǎnglíng" and "Zhǐxī,"
"Dōngwǔ" and "Tàishān."

The king accordingly favored her.
As she departed, she bade farewell, saying:
'I dwell on the sunny side of Mount Wū,
among the rugged heights.
At dawn I become morning clouds,
at dusk I become passing rain.
Morning after morning, dusk after dusk,
beneath the Sunny Terrace.'
At dawn the next day, he looked for her,
and it was as she had said.
Therefore, a temple was built for her,
and she was named
'Morning Cloud.'"
The king said:
"When Morning Cloud first appears,
what is her form like?"
Yù replied:
"When she first emerges,

As she advances a little,

Suddenly she changes appearance,

Chill as the wind,

When the wind ceases and the rain clears,

She lifts her long sleeves to adjust her robe,
Standing hesitantly, unsettled.
Calm and serene, gentle and meek,
Her nature deep and composed, without vexation.
At times she lingers, subtly stirring,
Her intentions impossible to grasp.
She seems near yet already distant,
As if approaching but then turning away.
Lifting my bed-curtain, she offers to attend,
Wishing to devote herself earnestly.
But cherishing chastity and pure integrity,
She ultimately resists me.
Presenting fair words in reply,
Her speech exhales fragrance like orchids.
Through subtle exchanges we interact,
My heart joyful and elated.
Yet our spirits connect without union,
My soul lonely and without direction.
Holding a promise yet undecided,
She sighs aloud with mournful lament.
Frowning slightly in anger, she restrains herself,
Not to be violated or approached.
Then she shakes her jade ornaments,
Rings her jade bells.
Adjusts her garments,
Composes her countenance.
Looks to her matron,
Calls for the tutor.
Before our joyous union is joined,
She prepares to bid farewell and depart.
Drawing back, she retreats,
Beyond intimate approach.
As if leaving yet not gone,
Inwardly as if turning her head.
Her eyes cast a slight glance,
Radiant spirit conveyed in the look.
Expressions and postures abound,
Too many to fully record.
Intentions parting yet not severed,
Heart and spirit fearful and conflicted.
Courtesy leaves no time for conclusion,
Words cannot fully express.
I wish to borrow but a moment,
But the goddess declares haste.
My innards churn, my spirit wounded,
Upset and disoriented.
Darkness falls, and she vanishes,
Suddenly I know not where she is.
Alone with my private feelings,
To whom can I speak?
Despondent, I shed tears,
Seeking her till dawn.
The courtier Dēngtúzǐ attended the King of Chǔ,
And slandered Sòng Yù, saying:
"Yù, in person, is elegant and handsome,
His speech is full of subtle flattery,
And by nature he is fond of women.
I urge Your Majesty not to let him enter and leave the rear palace."
The king questioned Sòng Yù about Dēngtúzǐ's words.
Yù said:
"Elegant and handsome in person—
This I received from Heaven.
Speech full of subtle flattery—
This I learned from my teacher.
As for being fond of women,
I have none of that."
The king said:
"If you are not fond of women,
Can you give an explanation?
If you have an explanation, then stay;
If not, then withdraw."
Yù said:
"The fairest beauties in the world are none like those of Chǔ,
The loveliest in Chǔ are none like those of my village,
