The most beautiful in my village is none like the maiden east of my house.
The maiden east of my house—
Add one inch, and she would be too tall;
Subtract one inch, and she would be too short.
Apply powder, and she would be too pale;
Apply rouge, and she would too red.
Her brows are like kingfisher feathers,
Her skin like white snow,
Her waist like a bound silk sash,
Her teeth like arranged seashells.
With a captivating smile,
She bewilders Yángchéng,
And enchants Xiàcài.
Yet this maiden has peered over the wall at me for three years,
And to this day I have not consented.
Dēngtúzǐ is not like this.
His wife has unkempt hair and crumpled ears,
Protruding lips and gapped teeth.
She walks crookedly, hunched over,
And suffers from scabies and hemorrhoids.
Dēngtúzǐ is fond of her,
And has fathered five children with her.
May Your Majesty examine this carefully—
Who is the one fond of women?"
At that time, the Qín official Zhānghuá Dàfū was at the king’s side,
And stepping forward, he declared:
"Now Sòng Yù lavishly praises the maiden next door,
Considering her a great beauty—
How foolish and misleading!
I consider myself a guardian of virtue,
Yet I dare not compare to him.
Moreover, a humble maiden from a southern Chǔ alley—
How could she be worth mentioning to Your Majesty?
As for my own humble experience,
What these eyes have once beheld,
I have not dared to speak of."
The king said:
"Try to describe it for me."
The official said:
"As you wish."
"In my youth, I once traveled far,
Surveyed the nine regions,
And set foot in five capitals.
I left Xiányáng,
Roamed Hándān.
I lingered between Zhèng, Wèi, Zhēn, and Wěi.
It was toward the end of spring,
Welcoming the sun of early summer.
Orioles sang in harmony,
Groups of maidens emerged to gather mulberry leaves.
The beauties of these outskirts
Radiated splendor and luminous charm.
Lovely in form, enchanting in appearance,
They needed no adornment.
Observing the fairest among them,
I recited a verse, saying:
'Along the broad road, I take your sleeve,
Presenting fragrant blossoms with exquisite words.'
Then the maiden seemed as if expecting yet not coming,
Suddenly as if coming yet not seen.
Intimate in spirit yet distant in body,
Her demeanor shifting with each glance.
Holding joy, she smiled softly,
Stealing glances with wandering eyes.
She then recited a verse in reply:
'Awakening to the spring breeze, fresh blossoms bloom.
Purified and waiting, I long for gracious words.
To receive such a gift—better never to have been born.'
Then she withdrew and declined,
For it was only through subtle words that emotions were stirred,
Spirits connected and relied on each other.
Eyes desired her beauty,
But the heart remembered righteousness.
Raising poetry, upholding propriety,
Never overstepping bounds—
Thus it is truly praiseworthy."
Then the King of Chǔ praised him,
And Sòng Yù did not withdraw.
In the third year of the Huángchū era,
I journeyed to the capital to pay homage,
and on my return, I crossed the Luò River.
The ancients had a saying:
the goddess of this river
is named Fúfēi.
Moved by Sòng Yù's account of the goddess and the King of Chǔ,
I composed this rhapsody.
Its words are as follows:
I depart from the capital domain, returning to my eastern fief.
Leaving Yīquè behind,
crossing Huányuán,
passing through Tōnggǔ,
and ascending Jǐngshān.
The sun already slants westward,
the carriage weary, the horses fatigued.
Then I unharness by the fragrant banks,
tether the steeds in the orchid fields.
I wander leisurely through the sunlit groves,
gazing afar upon the Luò River.
Then, my spirit stirred and startled,
suddenly my thoughts scatter.
Looking down, I perceive nothing,
but raising my eyes, I behold a wondrous sight.
I see a beautiful woman
by the side of the cliffs.
I then grasp the charioteer and ask him:
"Have you glimpsed that one over there?
Who is that person,
so radiantly beautiful?"
The charioteer replies:
"I have heard that the goddess of the Hé and Luò rivers
is named Fúfēi.
Could it be that what my lord sees
is none other than her?
What is her form like?
I wish to hear of it."
I tell him:
"Her form
is light as a startled swan,
graceful as a swimming dragon.
Her splendor outshines autumn chrysanthemums,
her lushness surpasses spring pines.
Dimly, she is like light clouds veiling the moon;
floating, she is like swirling wind driving back snow.
Gazing from afar,
she gleams like the sun rising through morning clouds;
approaching to observe,
she blazes like a lotus emerging from clear waves.
Plump or slender, all is fitting;
tall or short, all is in measure.
Her shoulders are as if carved,
her waist is like bound silk.
Her long neck, her elegant nape,
her fair skin revealed.
No fragrant ointments are added,
no leaden powder is applied.
Her cloud-like chignon towers high,
her long brows curve delicately.
Her vermilion lips bright without,
her white teeth fresh within.
Bright eyes, adept at glancing,
dimpled cheeks supporting lovely contours.
Her rare beauty, radiant and free,
her demeanor calm, her form at ease.
Gentle feelings, graceful bearing,
charming in speech.
Her wondrous raiment, unmatched in the world;
her bone structure matches the paintings.
Draped in shimmering silken robes,
she wears jade pendants of yáobì.
Adorned with golden and kingfisher hair ornaments,
strung with bright pearls to illuminate her form.
She treads in patterned traveling shoes,
trailing light skirts of misty gauze.
Faint is the fragrance of secluded orchids
as she lingers, pacing by the mountain's edge.
"Then suddenly she moves her body freely,
roaming and playing.
Leaning left on colored banners,
shaded right by cassia flags.
Baring her fair wrists by the divine shore,
she plucks dark lingzhī from the rushing rapids.
My feelings delight in her virtue and beauty,
yet my heart stirs, uneasy.
Lacking a good matchmaker to convey my joy,
I entrust my words to the faint ripples.
Wishing my sincere feelings to reach her first,
I untie my jade pendant to pledge to her.
Alas, the fair one is truly refined,
well-versed in ritual and clear in poetry.
She raises a fine jade to respond to me,
pointing to the deep abyss as our rendezvous.
Holding fast to my earnest, sincere devotion,
I fear this divine being may deceive me.
Moved by Jiāofǔ's abandoned vow,
I fret, hesitant and doubtful.
I compose my pleasant expression and calm my will,
upholding ritual bounds to restrain myself.
"Then the Luò spirit is moved,
pacing to and fro, hesitant.
Divine light parts and joins,
now dark, now bright.
She raises her light form, standing like a crane,
as if about to fly yet not taking wing.
Treading on the pungent pepper path,
walking through fragrant sweetgrass thickets.
She chants a long song of eternal longing,
her voice mournful and piercing, ever lengthening.
"Then many spirits gather in throngs,
calling companions, summoning friends.
Some sport in the clear streams,
some soar over divine islets.
Some gather bright pearls,
some collect kingfisher feathers.
Following the two consorts of Nánxiāng,
accompanying the roaming maidens of the Hàn riverside.
She laments the Gourd's lack of a mate,
sings of the Herdboy living alone.
Lifting her light robe, flowing and graceful,
she shelters with long sleeves, lingering in wait.
Her form swift as a flying duck,
floating lightly, as if divine.
Treading lightly on the waves with subtle steps,
her silk stockings seem to stir dust.
Her movements lack constant rule,
now perilous, now safe.
Advance and halt hard to foresee,
now going, now returning.
Turning her gaze, her essence flows,
radiance moistens her jade-like face.
Words contained, not yet spoken,
her breath like secluded orchids.
Her flowery countenance, graceful and supple,
makes me forget to eat.
"Then Píngyì stills the wind,
Chuānhòu calms the waves.
Féngyí beats the drums,
Nǚwā sings a clear song.
Literary fish leap to alert the carriage,
jade bells ring as they depart together.
Six dragons solemnly align their heads,
bearing the cloud-chariot in majestic procession.
Whales and sturgeons surge, flanking the wheels,
waterfowl soar as guards.
"Then she crosses the northern islet,
passes over the southern ridge.
Turning her white neck,
looking back with clear eyes.
Moving her vermilion lips, she speaks slowly,
expounding the great principles of interaction.
She laments that the ways of humans and gods differ,
grieves that in youth's prime they cannot unite.
Raising her silk sleeves to wipe her tears,
tears stream down, soaking her lapel.
Mourning that this fine meeting ends forever,
sorrowing that once departed, they go to separate lands.
Having no slight feeling to offer love,
she presents bright earrings from south of the river.
Though she dwells hidden in the great darkness,
she will forever entrust her heart to the sovereign lord.
Suddenly, unaware of where she has gone,
sadly, the divine light fades and is obscured.
"Then, descending from heights, leaving the lowlands behind,
my feet move on, but my spirit lingers.
Leaving behind emotions, imagining,
looking back, cherishing sorrow.
Hoping the divine form will reappear,
I board a light boat and sail upstream.
Drifting on the long river, forgetting to return,
thoughts continuous, increasing longing.
Night anxious, unable to sleep,
drenched in thick frost until dawn.
I command the servant to ready the carriage,
I shall return to the eastern road.
Grasping the side-horse reins, raising the whip,
sadly I linger, unable to depart."
"Nángāi"
is where filial sons admonish each other to provide support.
Walking along that southern ridge,
I gather its orchids.
Longing for the family courtyard,
my heart finds no peace.
Those who dwell at home,
should not wander or idle.
Fragrant are your evening meals,
pure are your morning repasts.
Walking along that southern ridge,
its grasses lush and glossy.
Those who dwell at home,
their countenance should be gentle in thought.
Longing for the family courtyard,
my heart cannot linger.
Fragrant are your evening meals,
pure are your morning delicacies.
There is an otter, an otter,
by the river’s edge.
It dives through the waves into the depths,
devouring bream and catching carp.
The cawing forest crows,
are fed by their young.
Nurture is abundant, reverence scant—
only akin to beasts.
Strive to increase your devotion,
to invite great blessings.
“White Blossoms”
speaks of the filial son’s purity and whiteness.
White blossoms with crimson calyxes,
spread over the secluded thickets.
Brilliant are the young men of noble houses,
polished as if ground and honed.
Throughout the day, thrice they reflect,
never lax in their reverence.
White blossoms with scarlet stems,
on the slopes of the hills.
Fresh and vibrant are the scholars,
unstained and unchanging.
Exhausting sincerity and utmost respect,
diligently, forgetting their toil.
White blossoms with dark bases,
in the curves of the mounds.
Noble and dignified are the recluses,
without worldly pursuits or desires.
Rare as morning flowers,
none can taint or disgrace them.
“Glorious Millet”
speaks of harmonious times and bountiful years,
suitable for millet and grain.
Dark and dense are the layered clouds,
gentle and mild the harmonious winds.
Millet blooms on hilltops,
wheat ears flourish in the valleys.
No field is left unsown,
the nine grains thus abundant.
Vast and lofty is the dark sky,
drizzling sweet rain.
Millet sprouts with dense blooms,
also standing tall and elegant.
No field is left uncultivated,
the nine grains thus lush.
No height is left unplanted,
no lowland left uncultivated.
Boundless are the crops,
abundant the harvests.
Storing the king’s bounty,
filling the people’s food.
The jade candle shines brightly,
the illustrious plan is majestic.
“Following the Path”
speaks of all things attaining their proper way.
Vast and level is the great path,
all things follow it.
Teeming multitudes of beings,
the king also nurtures them gently.
The Way is thus followed,
transformation is thus gentle.
Trees shed leaves in autumn,
grasses sprout in spring.
Beasts roam in the grass,
fish leap with the current.
The four seasons alternate in succession,
the eight winds take turns blowing.
Xiān’ā adjusts the sundial,
stars change their courses.
The five constants are not violated,
the six qi do not alter.
Tranquil is our king,
continuing the legacy of Wén.
“Lofty Mounds”
speaks of all things reaching their utmost height and greatness.
Gaze upon those lofty mounds,
their forests lush and dense.
Plants grow tall here,
moving creatures grow large.
The Zhou customs are harmonious,
the king’s rule truly peaceful.
Vast is the square earth,
immense the heavenly canopy.
What kind does not multiply,
what life does not flourish?
Things fulfill their nature,
people enjoy long life.
Vast is the great circle,
boundless the nine regions.
Sustaining life, looking up to transformation,
what is not nurtured?
People do not die untimely,
things reach their limit and grow.
“Following Proper Form”
speaks of all living things
each attaining its proper form.
Solemn and dignified are the noble men,
following proper form according to their nature.
Brilliant and enlightened are the rulers,
governing with benevolence.
Fish swim in clear ponds,
birds gather in peaceful woods.
Washing scales and flapping wings,
their sounds resonant and harmonious.
Guests express their sincerity,
hosts exhaust their hearts.
The times are harmonious,
what more to think or cultivate?
Culture flourishes within,
military achievements extend afar.
The enlightened value the self,
lofty sentiments belong to the heavens and clouds.
Embracing both the nature to aid others,
yet not entangled by worldly defilement.
Duàn Shēng protected the state of Wèi,
Zhǎn Jì saved the people of Lǔ.
Xián Gāo feasted the Jìn army,
Zhòng Lián repelled the Qín forces.
Facing the official ribbon, he did not fasten it,
confronting the jade tablet, he would not accept division.
Benefiting others, he declined rewards,
striving with purpose, thus surpassing ordinary men.
Towering through a thousand years,
afar spreading pure dust.
Pure dust—who ultimately inherits it?
The wise, in their time, manage state affairs.
Setting aside lectures, ceasing discourse on the Way,
changing attire to bring peace to the world’s troubles.
Troubles once pacified,
honoring the ruler, elevating the people.
In the Central Plains, chaos once reigned,
chaos that knew no end.
Turmoil erupted by the end of Yǒngjiā,
oppression began with Tàiyuán’s start.
Beyond the river, no return to order,
by the Yangtze, collapse and ruin.
All states trembled in fear,
the raging flood relied on noble men.
Saving the drowning through moral sentiment,
quelling violence with divine principle.
Qín and Zhào rejoiced in revival,
Yān and Wèi delayed in adopting cultural norms.
The worthy minister resigned as fate turned,
grand plans halted with events.
Withdrawing proudly beyond the seven provinces,
brushing off his robes within the Five Lakes.
Following mountains, dredging deep pools,
by cliffs, planting elms and catalpas.
Casting off worldly attachments, forsaking material dust,
steadfastly observing the beauty of hills and valleys.
Mèng served as tutor to King Yuán,
tutoring his son King Yí and grandson King Wù.
Wù was licentious and did not follow the Way,
so he composed a poem to admonish him.
It said:
Solemn and revered is our ancestor,
Whose state began with Shǐwéi.
Robed in embroidered black and crimson,
With four steeds and dragon banners.
Vermilion bows set forth on campaign,
To pacify and soothe distant wilds.
He unified the many states,
To support and aid the great Shāng.
Alternating with the great Péng,
His merits and achievements shone brightly.
Reaching the time of the Zhōu,
Through generations they joined in assembly.
The king lent ear to slander,
And truly severed our state.
Our state once severed,
Its governance thus grew lax.
The execution of rewards and punishments,
Did not stem from the royal house.
The many officers and lords,
Neither supported nor defended.
The five domains collapsed and scattered,
The ancestral Zhōu thus fell.
Our ancestor then declined,
And moved to Péngchéng.
As for me, a humble youth,
Toiling and sighing through this life.
Oppressed by this arrogant Qín,
With plow and share I tilled the soil.
Distant, arrogant Qín,
Heaven showed it no peace.
Then turning its gaze southward,
It bestowed Hàn upon the capital.
Oh, glorious was the Hàn,
Marching forth to the four directions.
No place it went was not embraced,
The myriad states were thereby pacified.
Then it commanded his younger brother,
To establish a marquis in Chǔ.
Making us, his minor officials,
Solely to assist as tutors.
Cautious and reverent, the first king,
Respectful, frugal, calm, and unified.
He cherished these common people,
And accepted those who aided and advised.
He enjoyed the state for a generation,
Leaving a legacy for posterity.
Then came King Yí,
Who was able to uphold his heritage.
Alas, his mandate was not long,
Only the king’s sacrificial line continued.
The attendants and ministers,
These were the royal officers.
How is it that our king,
Does not think to guard and preserve?
He does not tread on thin ice,
To continue the ancestors’ legacy.
State affairs are neglected,
Leisure and wandering are his amusement.
Dogs and horses roam freely,
They are released and driven.
Engrossed in these birds and beasts,
He neglects these crops and seedlings.
The people are left in want,
While our king indulges in pleasure.
What he promotes is not virtue,
Those he draws close are not worthy.
Only his parks are expanded,
Only flattery is trusted.
Fawning, sycophantic men,
While the outspoken elders with yellowed hair.
How is it that our king,
Has never examined this?
Disdaining his lower officials,
He pursues desires and unrestrained indulgence.
Insulting that illustrious ancestor,
Lightly regarding this reduction and dismissal.
Alas, alas, our king,
Kinsman of the Hàn.
Never day or night,
To cultivate a fine reputation.
Majestic is the Son of Heaven,
Shining upon the lands below.
Bright and clear are the many officers,
Upholding the law without partiality.
Correcting the distant begins with the near,
Peril lies in relying on this.
Alas, alas, our king,
Why does he not think on this?
Without thought, without reflection,
His successors will have no model.
Increasingly his indolence grows,
Perilously his state stands.
Ice forms not from frost alone,
A fall comes not from arrogance alone.
Behold, our king,
At times nothing is not practiced.
Reviving the state, saving its decline,
Who would reject repentance and reform?
Reflecting on the yellow-haired elders,
Duke Mù of Qín thereby achieved hegemony.
The years and months pass by,
Age approaches oldness.
Oh, glorious gentleman,
May you be illustrious to posterity.
How is our king,
That he never reviews this?
Not drawing near the yellow-haired,
Why does he not take timely warning!
The great mechanism turns and moves,
Heaven revolves, earth travels.
The four seasons follow like scales,
Cold and heat cycle round.
The star Fire having set at dusk,
Suddenly it is pure autumn.
Cool winds shake the falling leaves,
Fireflies gleam in the night stream.
The noble man thinks on autumn,
Truly moved by the transformation of things.
Day and month,
Gradually they alternate and pass.
What passes is like this,
Ceaseless day and night.
Alas, you many officers,
Why do you idly abandon yourselves?
The way of benevolence is not distant,
Virtue is light as a feather.
Seek it and it arrives,
Yet few among the multitude can uphold it.
The great plan is profound and silent,
I shall draw out its threads.
The ancients had their deeds,
Bequeathing to us lofty standards.
Though one may have fine qualities,
If the heart is let loose and unrestrained.
Indulging in wandering and amusement,
Dwelling in many idle days.
Like that catalpa timber,
If not diligently painted with cinnabar and lacquer.
Though laboriously carved and polished,
In the end it betrays its plain substance.
Yǎng Yóu adjusted his arrows,
Beasts cried out in the forest.
Pú Lú twirled his silk cord,
With spirit he moved the flying birds.
The subtle skill’s marvel,
Moves creatures in response to the heart.
Delving deep, immersed in the Way,
What depth is there that cannot be reached?
Settle the heart in calm and openness,
Lodge aspirations among floating clouds.
Embodied through substance,
Adorned through culture.
Like those southern fields,
Where strength and plow have been diligent.
Weeding and covering lead to great achievement,
There must be abundant harvest.
Water accumulates to form deep pools,
Now turbulent, now clear.
Earth accumulates to form mountains,
Steam rises, dense and dark.
Mountains do not refuse dust,
Rivers do not decline fullness.
Strive to embrace with breadth,
To magnify the sound of virtue.
Height is based on lowness,
Vastness arises from the fine.
Wide rivers begin from a source,
Becoming a complete person starts at the beginning.
Accumulating the subtle to become manifest,
This is the principle of things.
The length of a tethered rope,
Indeed accumulates over a thousand lǐ.
Returning to ritual all day long,
The world turns to benevolence.
Like metal tempered on a whetstone,
Like clay shaped on the potter’s wheel.
Advancing virtue, cultivating deeds,
Radiance and light renew daily.
Xí Péng looked up in admiration,
What kind of person am I?
Your subject Zhí states:
Since I embraced blame and returned to my fief,
carving into my flesh and bones,
I have reflected on my offenses and transgressions,
eating only at midday,
and resting only at midnight.
Truly, because the net of Heaven cannot be re-encountered,
and the sage’s grace is hard to rely on again,
I secretly felt the lesson of the poem “Xiàng Shǔ,”
which says that without propriety one should quickly die.
My form and shadow alone console each other;
my five emotions are ashamed and flushed.
To abandon life because of my crimes
would violate the ancient worthies’ exhortation to reform by evening;
to endure disgrace and barely preserve myself
would incur the poet’s ridicule of “how dare I show my face?”
I humbly consider that Your Majesty’s virtue mirrors Heaven and Earth,
your grace towers like that of parents,
your beneficence flows like the spring breeze,
your favor is like timely rain.
Thus, not distinguishing between thorns and brambles
is the kindness of auspicious clouds;
nourishing the seven young equally
is the benevolence of the cuckoo;
pardoning faults and demanding achievement
is the action of an enlightened ruler;
pitying the foolish and loving the capable
is the grace of a compassionate father.
Therefore, this foolish subject lingers within your grace,
not daring to abandon myself.
Previously, having received the imperial edict
that we, your subjects, were to cease attending court,
my heart was severed and my will cut off;
I reckoned myself already aged and hoary,
forever without hope of holding the jade tablet.
I never imagined that a sage edict
would condescend to summon me by name.
On the day I arrived,
my heart raced toward the imperial carriage,
but dwelling in a secluded western lodge,
I have not yet attended at the palace gates.
My leaping heart,
gazing longingly and turning restlessly,
cannot surpass the affection of a dog or horse longing for its master.
Reverently I present this memorial along with two poems.
Their words and ideas are shallow and slight,
unworthy of your perusal,
but I value revealing my humble feelings,
braving shame to make them heard.
Your subject Zhí is truly fearful and trembling,
kowtowing and kowtowing again,
worthy of death, worthy of death.
Oh, solemn and illustrious father,
who in his time was Wǔ Huáng.
He received the mandate from Heaven,
to pacify and succor the four quarters.
Where the vermilion banners swept,
the nine regions were cleared and ordered.
His mysterious transformation flowed abundantly,
and the distant regions came to acknowledge the king.
Surpassing Shāng and exceeding Zhōu,
he matched the tracks of Táng.
Truly he begat our emperor,
generations succeeding in wisdom.
In martial affairs, stern and fierce;
in civil affairs, harmonious and timely.
Receiving the abdication from Hàn,
he became sovereign over all states.
All states now transformed,
he followed the old rules.
Broadly appointing close kin,
to protect and guard the royal domain.
The emperor said, “You, marquis,
rule this Qīng territory.
Encompassing the seacoast,
comparable to Lǔ in Zhōu.”
Carriages and robes have splendor,
banners and insignia have order.
Numerous are the talented and virtuous,
assisting and supporting me.
But I, this petty fellow,
relied on favor and grew arrogant and full.
My actions caught in the net of the times,
disturbing and confusing the state’s laws.
As a bulwark and screen,
I first ruined the established tracks.
I scorned the imperial envoy,
violated the court’s rituals.
The state has canonical punishments;
I was demoted and dismissed.
About to be handed to the judiciary,
as leader of the chief culprits.
Brilliant and enlightened Son of Heaven,
truly generous and kind.
Unable to bear my punishment,
exposing me in the morning market.
Contravening those who upheld the law,
he pitied this petty subject.
Changing my fief to Yǎn,
by the river’s banks.
Without aides and assistants placed,
having a ruler but no ministers.
For the faults of my wantonness,
who will assist my person?
Lonely and solitary, my attendants
are in that Jì region.
Alas, I, this petty fellow,
have met with this calamity.
Majestic and awe-inspiring Son of Heaven,
whose grace leaves nothing behind.
He capped me with the dark crown,
girded me with the vermilion ribbon.
Glorious and splendid, the great envoy
brings me honor and splendor.
Receiving the tally and accepting land,
the royal rank is added.
Looking up, I touch the golden seal;
looking down, I hold the sage’s decree.
The imperial grace is excessively abundant;
I receive it with fear and trembling.
Alas, I, this petty fellow,
am afflicted with obstinacy and ill fate.
In death, ashamed before the imperial tombs;
in life, ashamed before the palace gates.
I dare not scorn virtue,
but truly rely on this grace.
If your majestic spirit changes and adds more,
it would suffice till the end of my days.
Vast Heaven is boundless;
life and fate are unforeseeable.
I have often feared stumbling and falling,
embracing guilt in the yellow springs.
I wish to receive arrows and stones,
and raise banners on Dōng Yuè.
Hoping to establish even a hair’s breadth,
redeeming myself with a tiny merit.
Offering my endangered body, giving my life,
knowing it suffices to escape blame.
Willing to go to Jiāng and Xiāng,
and wield spears in Wú and Yuè.
Heaven opened its heart,
letting me meet at the capital region.
Longing to attend the sage’s countenance,
like thirst, like hunger.
My heart’s admiration,
how sorrowful, how sad.
Heaven is high yet hears the lowly;
would the emperor deign to shine on the insignificant?
Reverently receiving the bright edict,
I respond to the summons to the imperial capital.
Under the stars I set out at dawn,
feeding the horses, greasing the chariots.
Commanding those in charge of followers,
to make my journey orderly.
At morn I depart from Luán Tái,
at eve I lodge at Lán Zhǔ.
Vast and boundless, plains and marshes;
multitudinous, the gentlemen and ladies.
Passing by those public fields,
I delight in their millet and grain.
Here are the bending trees,
their layered shade not for rest.
Though there is dry provisions,
hungry, I have no leisure to eat.
Gazing at cities, I do not pass through;
facing towns, I do not wander.
The coachman urges with the whip;
the level road is what I follow.
Dark steeds, lush and numerous,
raise bits, froth flying.
Flowing winds assist the yoke;
light clouds bear the canopy.
Fording the streams’ banks,
skirting the mountain’s bends.
Following those riverbanks,
the yellow slopes are my steps.
Westward crossing Guān Gǔ,
sometimes descending, sometimes ascending.
Team horses weary on the road,
resting again, rising again.
I am to attend the sage emperor;
I dare not be late or tranquil.
Reining in, yet galloping long,
pointing to the sun, swiftly journeying.
The vanguard raises torches;
the rear carriage hoists banners.
Wheels never cease turning;
bells never stop sounding.
Then reaching the imperial residence,
I lodge at this western wall.
The gracious edict not yet bestowed,
court attendance cannot be followed.
Looking up, I gaze at the city gate;
looking down, I think of the palace gates.
Longing, forever yearning,
my anxious heart as if intoxicated.
O glorious Jin of this age,
Your mandate is firm and secure.
The three ancestors in heaven above,
The sage emperor continues the throne.
Virtue vast, transformation bright,
Punishments simple, wrongs set right.
A tiny spark left unguarded,
Spread to our treasured storehouse.
Stupid are those Róng and Dí tribes,
Cunningly thinking to run wild.
Observing our country's distress,
They spy upon our sharp weapons.
Mountain and pasture officials think differently,
Might and kindness, two ways of rule.
Generals lack special strategies,
Soldiers are not trained in advance.
Lofty and eminent Prince Zhào,
Requested to lead thirty thousand.
Court discussions were full of doubt,
This wish could not be fulfilled.
Majestic was the Liáng campaign,
High banners were then raised.
Flags and canopies looked at each other,
Auxiliary troops served as support.
Tiger-like, glaring fiercely,
Their might shook Hàozhì.
White armor shone like the sun,
Dark tents rose like clouds.
Who followed after them?
Xiàhóu, the high minister.
Only tying and stationing,
Forming camps like chess pieces.
Was it truly without planning?
The warriors enjoyed peace.
Defense had complete outer walls,
But in battle, no intact troops.
Blades clashed, soldiers fled,
Who could avoid Mèng Míng's fate?
Swift dispatches flew to Qín's outskirts,
Reporting defeat to the capital.
Zhōu died for his army's command,
His body fattened the Dí axes.
When a man is lost,
His steadfast virtue shines forth.
Lú Bō disobeyed orders,
Cast into the northern lands.
Suffering evil for the law's sake,
Who says bitter herbs are bitter?
Pity these common people,
Without crime, without guilt.
Livers and brains smeared the ground,
White bones filled the crossroads.
Husbands gone, wives widowed,
Fathers departed, children orphaned.
Making our Jìn people
Turn into Dí captives.
This misery of chaos and separation,
Days and months grow ripe with sorrow.
The Son of Heaven grieves for this,
Dining late, sleeping little.
The lord worries, ministers labor,
Who does not feel awe and fear?
Ashamed I have no offerings to give,
Holding position idly, deeply so.
The emperor blazed with anger,
Then marshaled the finest troops.
Commanded those from Shànggǔ,
Pointing at the sun, swiftly gone.
Personally following established plans,
Awe-inspiring might spread far.
First they stormed Zhōngtíng,
Boasting of tens of thousands.
War is indeed the way of deception,
First sound, then substance.
The officials heard of it,
Taking ten thousand as one.
Zhòu's wickedness,
I do not necessarily affirm.
Falsely brightening Nǎndé's virtue,
Wrongly displaying Jiǎjí's armor.
Yōngmén's gates did not open,
Chénqiān faced peril and pressure.
Guānsuì fought like a tiger,
Grateful, he exerted his strength.
The heavy siege was broken,
The endangered city regained color.
Can it be said there were no faults?
Yet the achievement was immeasurable.
Human affairs are indeed myriad,
What among them does not exist?
Confusion reigned with Qí Wàn,
Also greatly shameful.
Some said accept their surrender,
Some said behead their leader.
Which truth can be concealed?
Which falsehood can last long?
Having examined your words,
Having heard your disputes.
Should clarify the facts,
Otherwise, evidence is empty.
Fine ranks are already bestowed,
Severe punishments also follow.
Have you not seen Dòu Lín,
Lying dead in Hàn's domain!
The Zhōu people's poem,
Is truly called "Cǎiwēi".
Northern troubles from Xiǎnyǔn,
Western worries from Kūnyí.
Comparing ancient times to now,
How can it suffice to display might?
Only pitying these people,
My heart feels sorrow and grief.
How are these people?
Poisoned by Qín.
Armies having been sent,
Famine followed because of this.
Epidemics spread wantonly,
Thorns and brambles became thickets.
Jiàngyáng's grain,
Floated on the Wèi River's banks.
Brilliant Son of Heaven,
Looks upon the people as if injured.
Repeatedly commands all officers,
Protect your borders.
Do not oppress the masses,
Do not bully the strong.
The timid, few, and weak,
Like basking in spring sunlight.
The noble lord, respectful and fond of guests,
At banquet's end knows no fatigue.
In clear night, roaming the western garden,
Flying canopies follow one another.
Bright moon purifies clear scenes,
Constellations arrayed unevenly.
Autumn orchids cover the long slope,
Red blossoms crown the green pond.
Hidden fish leap in clear waves,
Fine birds sing on high branches.
Divine gusts meet red carriage wheels,
Light chariots move with the wind.
Drifting freely, releasing heart's intent,
A thousand autumns ever thus.
Vast heaven sends down rich dew,
All plants stand lush and splendid.
Cool winds dispel stifling heat,
Clear clouds repel blazing sun.
Grand gathering in the gentleman's hall,
Sitting together shaded by ornate rafters.
Fine dishes fill round and square vessels,
Sweet wine brims in golden jars.
Pipes and strings emit harmonious notes,
Melodies clear and yet sorrowful.
All seated share the same joy,
Only lament the slow passing of cups.
Often heard the poet's words,
"If not drunk, do not return."
Today if joy is not utmost,
Holding feelings, for whom to wait?
Your favor truly beyond measure,
Keeping to my lot, how could I disobey?
The ancients left a saying,
"A gentleman's fortune lies in peace."
May my worthy host,
With heaven enjoy lofty heights.
May you match Duke Zhōu's deeds,
Through generations, unsurpassed.
All day engaged in play and wander,
Joy and pleasure not yet ended.
Lingering thoughts in the dark night,
Together again we soar and roam.
Carriage flies with plain canopy,
Followers fill the roadside.
Moon rises, shines upon the garden,
Precious trees lush and deep green.
Clear stream passes stone channel,
Flowing waves form fish barriers.
Lotus flowers scatter their blooms,
Lotuses overflow the golden pond.
Divine birds dwell by water's edge,
Benevolent beasts roam the flying bridge.
Splendid lodge rests upon flowing waves,
Open and broad, welcoming cool breeze.
In all my life never before heard,
How can singing fully describe it?
Laying down brush, long I sigh,
Such beauty cannot be forgotten.
Morning geese cry amidst the clouds,
How mournful their echoes sound!
I ask them, "Where do you wander?"
They fold their wings, hesitating.
They say, "We come from the cold gates,
Heading to Héngyáng to rest.
Last spring we flew to northern lands,
This winter we lodge in southern Huái.
Our long journey endures frost and snow,
Our feathers wither day by day.
We fear our bones and flesh will break,
Our bodies sink into yellow mud.
A precious pearl fallen in sand and stone,
How can it harmonize within?
We wish to ride the clouds and rain,
Wash our wings and climb the lofty stairs.
But noble encounters are hard to find,
Where is the path to raise our brows?"
The noble lord honors his guests,
Joyful drinking knows no weariness.
His gentle face brings ease and cheer,
He deigns to notice humble folk.
He gifts a poem to show his care,
Unworthy though this lowly one may be.
For now, let us indulge in joy,
Not drunk, we shall not return.
All must revere your station,
To satisfy this thirsting heart.
The Three Corrections succeed each other,
The Great Sage opens fortune's course.
Since ancient wise kings,
They followed Heaven's will.
Lords rose and fell in reverence,
Down to recent ages.
Yellow radiance once faded,
White spirit received the blessing.
With tender regard,
Fortune dwelled in this land.
Three rulers laid the foundation,
Shìwǔ greatly continued.
Harmonious winds spread awe,
Heaven's sun shone clear above.
Pure light filled the six directions,
Imperial blessings arose.
From those Héfén rivers,
They aligned the Seven Governors.
The age's culture belongs to Jìn,
Each generation deep in sageliness.
Revering the vast heavens,
They answered and upheld the mandate.
The nine regions were all in harmony,
Songs and chants resounded.
The Emperor inherits glory,
Expanding teachings, broadening the Way.
In transformation, richness abounds,
In governance, achievements are examined.
He oversees myriad deeds below,
And reaches the great creation above.
Modeling ancestors and forebears,
He secures Heaven's protection.
Truly born is our sovereign,
Bright and outstanding.
His form shines with double radiance,
Following rules, embracing fate's number.
His abundant virtue runs deep,
His heavenly bearing, jade-like grace.
A petty minister like me,
Far in distant wilderness.
Laying down my burdens,
I lift my tassels, serve at Chénghuá.
Not by my initial wish,
But by the grace of command.
Majestic is Heaven's blessing,
Giving rise to a noble mandate.
Four ancestors rectified the house,
Heaven's fortune secured stability.
Wise and profound is Jìn,
Generations bear bright sages.
Like the sun and moon,
All scenes are rightly ordered.
Lofty, bright, and sage,
The Way prospers from Heaven.
Clarity distinguishes brightness,
Observing signs, penetrating mysteries.
Winds align with order,
Brilliance illuminates the depths.
Solemn harmony spreads afar,
Fortune and blessings arrive.
In the past, treacherous ministers
Stirred chaos in the Purple Palace.
Divine winds secretly arose,
With awe-inspiring might.
Spirit flags raised banners,
Like lightning, they swept forth.
Bringing Heaven's judgment,
To the banks of the river.
The mandate gathered once more,
The imperial carriage returned in triumph.
The fallen net was restored,
All things found their proper order.
The divine way revealed simplicity,
Casting off ornament, returning to essence.
Sun and shadows shine doubly bright,
Harmonious winds answer the pitch pipes.
All within the realm is without dust,
Beyond the seas, there is peace.
Vast and boundless cosmos,
Heaven and earth in prosperous union.
The king in his splendid hall,
Holds a feast, a joyous gathering.
Dark radiance stern and clear,
Emerald clouds rise in lofty layers.
Crowns and caps with swaying tassels,
Robes adorned with hanging sashes.
Numerous ministers and officials,
Arrive in harmonious grace.
Humbly they present their offerings,
Bowing beneath his countenance.
Looking down upon honored guests,
Gazing up at jade-like faces.
Giving of oneself with restraint,
Yet in ritual, richly adorned.
Heaven grants agelessness,
Like mountains, lofty and enduring.
Vast and distant is the Supreme Ancestor,
From whom the people first arose.
The Great Norm was established,
And constant principles were laid out.
The Five Virtues alternated in succession,
Receiving the mandate and the tally.
When Táo Táng had already declined,
The Heavenly Calendar rested with Yú.
At that time, the Supreme God
Turned His gaze and showed favor.
He illuminated our Jìn dynasty’s fortune,
Accepting the abdication in due time.
The throne was ascended like a dragon soaring,
Civil governance transformed like a tiger’s stripes.
Profound grace flowed abundantly,
Benevolent influence spread silently.
Within the realm, hearts found peace,
And distant corners turned to face the center.
Heaven displayed its signs,
Earth revealed its patterns.
The phoenix sang at morning’s sun,
The dragon soared amid radiant clouds.
Auspicious grain bore double ears,
The calendrical plant flourished with fragrance.
All under heaven were in order,
And every person was joyful.
Expansive was the imperial measure,
Majestic was the sage’s demeanor.
In speech, he sought harmony,
In appearance, he embodied reverence.
In seeing, he was perceptive,
In hearing, he was discerning.
He advanced the worthy by virtue,
And tested them clearly by merit.
What was his reverence like?
He rose before dawn to glorify his duties.
No principle was left unexamined,
No righteousness was left unpracticed.
In conduct, he discarded ostentation,
In speech, he avoided clever rhetoric.
His mind wandered in utmost emptiness,
Aligned with the rule of simplicity.
The six treasuries were well managed,
The nine regions were thus pacified.
No land was left unblessed by his grace,
No transformation was left unapplied.
His teachings reached southward,
And spread west to the flowing sands.
Reclusive men ventured through dangers,
Distant lands forgot their remoteness.
Yuèshāng sent repeated envoys,
To fill our royal court.
Lofty stood the various lords,
Resplendent were the tiger-like ministers.
Within, they harmonized the five relationships,
Without, they awed the four guests.
They fulfilled their tribute duties in season,
And came to court to see the heavenly-appointed one.
They received commands and gifts in full,
With feathered canopies and crimson carriages.
Banquets were held for joyful gatherings,
Not limited in their frequency.
What the divine heart received,
Was understood without words.
At that time, archery was practiced,
Bows and arrows were wielded.
They shot at the five targets,
And wine was poured in abundance.
The ways of civil and martial arts,
Their strategies never declined.
In the past, the former kings
Used these tools of archery and charioteering.
Displaying martial prowess to avert neglect,
Excess, too, was a fault.
All you lords and rulers,
Do not slacken in your posts.
When the wind arrives, cold garments are bestowed,
When frost descends, all labors cease.
Dense forests lose their sunny hues,
Lush gardens shed their blossoms.
No swallows linger in nest-covered eaves,
By the islets, wild geese arrive.
Light clouds crown the autumn sun,
Swift west winds brush the clear sky.
The sage’s heart cherishes this fine season,
Raising carriage bells to the traveling palace.
At the four feasts, fragrant wine is shared,
In the central hall, silk-stringed music rises.
The setting sun approaches the western stream,
Joy remains though the feast must end.
Gone now is the guest about to depart,
Nurturing simplicity to achieve completion.
By the flowing stream, regret for what cannot be followed,
A joyful heart sighs like drifting tumbleweed.
Grandeur returns to the court,
Tranquil solitude remains by river and hill.
The mountain ridge aligns with Confucius’ nature,
The yellow canopy is not Yáo’s heart.
The imperial carriage, not yet solemnly arrayed,
The literary park receives its shining visit.
Flowing clouds rise like a moving canopy,
Morning winds guide the carriage bells’ sound.
Plains and marshes are lush and level,
Terraces and gullies are layered and deep.
Orchid ponds clear the summer air,
Long curtains hold autumn’s shade.
Following islets, climbing through dense growth,
Ascending mountains, traversing rugged paths.
Gazing afar, the view reaches its limit,
Wandering thoughts seek no nearby paths.
Though knowledge has accumulated,
Age and strength decline in turn.
Examining myself, I decline the crimson robes,
Moved by events, I long for the deep woods.
Late autumn on the northern frontier is harsh,
Migrating geese flee frost and snow.
Withered are the sunny plants,
Gleaming pure is the cold pond.
This fine hour stirs the sage’s heart,
Cloud-like banners rise in the late season.
Reed pipes sound at the vermilion palace,
Orchid wine is offered to the wise of the time.
The farewell feast shines with sincerity,
Harmony and joy fill what was lacking.
Governing with leniency brings order to all under heaven,
Inspiring the myriad regions to rejoice.
The departing guest heads for the sea’s edge,
Removing his cap, he bids farewell to the court.
Mooring the boat by the winding islet,
Watching the shadows, awaiting the music’s end.
The river’s flow has urgent waves,
The galloping team has no slow pace.
Is it only the river journey that brings thought?
My long-held heart feels shame at parting.
O, the noble way of hills and gardens,
I sigh, wounded by my own frailty.
The Way lies hidden in the formless,
Governance manifests only after disorder.
The Emperor’s traces hang in balance,
The imperial stream flows in unity.
Only the King creates things,
Eternally bestowing grand designs.
Benevolence firmly opened the Zhōu,
Righteousness elevated the ascent of Hàn.
Blessings fuse with worldly wisdom,
Achievements illuminate successive sages.
The Supreme One assumes the rightful position,
Heaven oversees the sea-mirror.
Institutions adapt through transformation,
Establishing form and nature.
Kindness soaks the sprouting lives,
Trust extends to flying and swimming creatures.
Emptiness revered is without proof,
Accumulated substance has no equal.
How could it be merely human harmony?
Truly, it is the spirits’ gift.
The sun completes its phases,
The moon does not obscure its fullness.
Treasures sail across waters,
Tribute carts cross barriers.
The Emperor’s form is radiantly bright,
Marking time as the heir.
He rules that Eastern Court,
Gold gleaming, jade pure.
Virtue moistens the self,
Ritual does not err in vessels.
Gentle within, deep reflections,
Fragrant plans, orchid secrets.
Once there was Wénzhāo,
Now there is Wǔmù.
Oh, glorious royal minister,
Fāngdàn residing as uncle.
With bright wisdom, a vassal,
Thus he treads, pacifying the pastures.
Tranquil utmost, harmonizing scales,
Guarding the capital, maintaining service.
Crescent and full moon both intersect,
Lunar qi thrice transforms.
Blossoms open, sprinkling dew,
Rainbows stretch, lightning flashes.
Transformation knows no interval,
The imperial heart shows affection.
He thinks of Hào’s feasts,
Often recalls Luò’s banquets.
Suburban farewells have altars,
The lord’s actions follow ritual.
Curtained tents in orchid fields,
Painted streams flow from high steps.
Courtyards divided, music offered,
Waves parted, floating sweet wine.
Joy as in Xià’s proverbs,
Affairs combine with crossing waters.
Looking up, I see abundant gifts,
Looking down, I am but a humble thing.
Thrice hindered as a servant,
Five times dusting court robes.
Path peaceful, fate beset,
Favor full, repayment lacking.
Regrets can be mended,
Stubborn flaws hard to wipe away.
The state honors the master’s position,
Families revere Confucian gates.
Receiving the Way, nurturing virtue,
Discussing arts, establishing words.
Clear brightness at dawn,
Understanding righteousness dispels darkness.
Eternal gaze on the early awakened,
Looking back to later generations.
The great man nurtures things,
Continuing Heaven, connecting with sages.
Times of hardship must turn prosperous,
Fate obscured then rectified.
Martial arts laid to rest,
Civil orders proclaimed.
All scholars lean to the wind,
Ten thousand streams mirror upward.
Yúxiáng adorned halls,
Wise plans brightly manifest.
Cherishing benevolence, crowds gather,
Embracing wisdom, they come like deer.
Approaching the gate, presenting books,
Treading lightly, offering vessels.
Cleansing body in dark depths,
Dwelling mind in Dao’s secrets.
In ancient times, Zhōu’s heir,
Shed light on past records.
Thinking of royal worldly wisdom,
Embracing origin as successor.
Relying on this early knowledge,
Descending to follow classic will.
Distancing from former texts,
Compass of Zhōu, square of value.
Main hall empty of mats,
Officials select the day.
Honored seats hold staffs,
Assistants present scrolls.
Attendants speak with eloquence,
Sincere historians hold brushes.
Subtle understanding of subtle tones,
The royal record has its account.
Extensive discussion, fragrant news,
Great teachings fully clear.
Reverently performing sacrificial rites,
Offering libations to sage spirits.
Ritual belongs to viewing ablutions,
Music presents songs and sheng.
Bright service is solemn,
Sacrificial meats are not the fragrance.
Offerings end, auspiciousness follows,
Entering palace for grand feast.
Hall set with ivory mats,
Courtyard hung with golden chimes.
Ministers and guardians share emblems,
Imperial relatives match in excellence.
Food dried, wine clear,
Robes straight, caps tidy.
Six offices oversee commands,
Nine guests assist in ceremony.
Sashes and tablets fill the order,
Turbans and scrolls crowd the streets.
Capital’s dignity moves like clouds,
Country roads race like wind.
Ordered as Zhōu, ranked as Hàn,
Transcendent, far-reaching, ah!
Clear radiance in the sky,
Any light must shine.
Things follow their nature,
Principle reveals its depths.
Presumptuous before state heirs,
I overhear the nation’s teachings.
Only ashamed of my obscurity,
Finally declining wisdom’s effect.
At dawn, the Chānghé Gate opens,
On the imperial way, phoenix flutes are heard.
Tender grass bears the jade carriage,
Fine blades cushion the dragon steeds.
Wind lingers, mountains still echo,
Rain ceases, clouds yet gather.
Nests empty, early birds fly,
Duckweed tangled, new fish play.
Truly, the North Gate is weighty,
If not kin, who can be entrusted?
Varying thoughts arise,
Solemn grace spreads its waves.
This humble servant is truly fortunate,
Could my life ever repay this duty?
Dānpǔ did not delight in war,
Bearing the burden, pressing the lord’s approach.
Our Emperor holds utmost virtue,
Forgetting self, using Yáo’s heart.
Pitying this realm within,
Fish and birds lose flight and dive.
Pushing chariots through Èrxiáo’s passes,
Raising banners at Jiǔhé’s south.
Superb riders all in triple armor,
Chosen warriors worth a hundred gold.
War chariots leave Xìliǔ,
Farewell feast at Shànglín’s cups.
Commanding armies to punish late submissions,
Giving laws to spare the forward prey.
Hánhuán just loosens its belt,
Yáowǔ begins to open its lapels.
Punishing crime at Mángshān’s bends,
Consoling people by Yīshuǐ’s banks.
I shall accompany the victory rites,
Awaiting this, not yet removing my hairpin.
Climbing the Běimáng slope,
Gazing afar at Luòyáng’s mountains.
How desolate Luòyáng is,
Palaces all burned to ashes.
Walls crumbled and split,
Thorns and brambles reach the sky.
No sight of old elders,
Only seeing new youths.
Feet sidelong, no paths to tread,
Wild fields no longer tilled.
Wanderer long not returned,
Knows not the lanes and byways.
Mid-plains so bleak and drear,
A thousand li without smoke of men.
Thinking of my usual abode,
Breath choked, unable to speak.
Peaceful times are hard to come by often,
Joyous gatherings cannot last forever.
Heaven and earth have no end,
But human life is like morning frost.
I wish to express my heartfelt affection,
For my friend heading to the northern lands.
Close friends gather to see him off,
Setting wine by the northern bank of the river.
Is the feast alone insufficient?
Guests drink, yet cups remain unfilled.
Love runs deep, hopes run bitter,
How can I not feel shame in my heart!
Mountains and rivers block the distant way,
Parting is swift, reunion days seem long.
I wish to be a pair of lovebirds,
Spreading wings to soar high together.
Morning winds blow over forked roads,
Drizzling rain falls on autumn grass.
The whole city comes to bid farewell,
Feasting me on the thousand-mile journey.
Three fates all have their limits,
Alas, how can one be preserved?
None greater than a child’s untimely death,
Even Péng Zǔ and Lǎo Dǎn are cut short.
Fortune and misfortune twist like ropes,
Worry and joy tangle together.
Heaven and earth are my furnace,
How small are the ten thousand things!
The enlightened possess broad vision,
Admonishing this bitterness not to come early.
Separation lies on the long road,
Melancholy fills my embrace.
Who can discern my heart?
Let the azure sky be its mirror.
Our shared vow is made today,
To keep it until we grow old together.
Wáng Shēng harmonizes the tripod’s substance,
Shí Zǐ guards Hǎiyí’s shores.
Friends and family each speak of departure,
My heart is saddened by the parting.
How to express these parting thoughts?
Hand in hand we stroll the outskirts.
At dawn we leave Jìnjīng’s sunny side,
By dusk we rest at Jīngǔ’s banks.
Winding streams curve through obstacles,
Steep slopes make the path treacherous.
Green ponds ripple gently,
Willow trees sway gracefully.
Gushing springs churn like dragon scales,
Surging waves scatter like pearls.
In the front courtyard grow shātáng trees,
In the back garden stand wūbēi trees.
The royal park blooms with pomegranates,
The lush woods array fragrant pears.
We drink by the splendid pond,
Move seats to climb the high mound.
Dark wine dyes our faces red,
Only lamenting the slow passing of cups.
Raising drumsticks, we beat the sacred drum,
Flutes and pipes sound clear and mournful.
Who does not admire spring’s glory?
But enduring winter’s cold is rare indeed!
Entrusting my bond to a steadfast friend,
Together we return, white-haired, to the same end.
Summoned back to the northern capital,
Returning to official duties in the southern region.
Boats carry old and new friends,
Feasting with the wise governor after long absence.
Raising cups, we proudly drink farewell,
Pointing the way, I think of lodging ahead.
Tomorrow’s dawn holds no fixed course,
Parting moments hasten to their end.
The setting sun shines on the open ferry,
Evening shadows darken the flat plain.
Boatmen prepare the traveling vessel,
Light carriages order the return journey.
We part at the eastern city gate,
Setting sail from the western river bend.
Though parting and meeting bring closeness,
Can the flowing river ever return?
Who says feelings can be written?
Full expression is not in letters.
On duty, I leave the imperial city,
Hoping to rest in Ōuyuè together.
Untying the cable as the tide flows,
Nostalgia holds me back from departure.
Rustling, I approach the fading woods,
Bright and clear shines the autumn moon.
Emotions easily overflow within,
Encountering things, they are hard to cease.
Long illness dismisses worldly cares,
Few desires leave little lacking.
With this, I dwell forever in seclusion,
Not merely parted for years.
Let each strive for daily renewal,
May news comfort this lonely silence.
Dòngtíng, land where music once resounded,
Xiāoxiāng, where imperial daughters roamed.
Clouds drift from the Cāngwú wilderness,
Waters flow back to Jiānghàn’s streams.
Halting my carriage, I gaze in sorrow,
You cease your oars, lingering in hesitation.
Guǎngpíng’s hearing may yet be recorded,
Màolíng will seek an audience.
Heartfelt matters are all finished now,
Only parting sorrow remains on the river.
In the days of youth and vitality,
Parting easily promised future meetings.
Now that we share the twilight of age,
It is no longer a time for farewells.
Do not speak lightly of this cup of wine,
Tomorrow it may be hard to share again.
If in dreams I cannot find the way,
How then to comfort this longing?
Since ancient times, none should die for the dead,
As the enlightened well know.
Duke Mù of Qín killed three good men,
Alas, a futile deed it was.
From youth they served a bright sovereign,
Receiving kindness beyond measure.
At death’s door, he demanded their lives,
How could they not follow?
Wives and children weep at the gate,
Brothers cry by the roadside.
At the tomb they call to heaven,
Tears fall like unending streams.
Each person has their own will in life,
Never to be swayed by this.
Knowing well the agony of burial,
Their hearts still had a purpose to fulfill.
In life, heroes among a hundred men,
In death, models for all brave souls.
The “Yellow Birds” poem sings their sorrow,
Its voice remains undimmed to this day.
Fame and merit may not be attained,
But loyalty and righteousness are my peace.
Duke Mù of Qín departed first,
Three ministers ended their own lives.
In life they shared glory and joy,
In death they share worry and hardship.
Who says sacrificing oneself is easy?
To give one’s life is truly hard alone.
Wiping tears, I climb my lord’s tomb,
At the grave, I sigh to heaven.
How dark and deep the long night?
Once gone, never to return.
Yellow birds sing mournful songs,
Alas, it wounds the heart and lungs!
At twenty, I wielded the soft brush,
Outstanding, I perused many books.
My essays followed “Guò Qín” as standard,
My rhapsodies imitated “Zǐ Xū.”
Border towns suffer whistling arrows,
Urgent dispatches fly to the capital.
Though not a warrior in armor,
I once studied the strategies of Ráng Jū.
A long whistle stirs the clear wind,
My ambition acts as if Dōng Wú did not exist.
A leaden blade values its one cut,
Dreaming to gallop with noble plans.
Glancing left, I clear Jiāng and Xiāng,
Looking right, I pacify Qiāng and Hú.
Achieving merit, I’ll accept no rank,
With a deep bow, return to field and hut.
Lush, lush, the pines at the ravine’s base,
Sparse, sparse, the seedlings on the hilltop.
With their inch-thick stems,
They shade these hundred-foot boughs.
Nobles occupy high positions,
Talents remain in lowly posts.
Circumstances make it so,
This has been true since ancient times.
Jīn and Zhāng relied on old merits,
Seven generations wore Hàn’s sable hats.
Was Féng Gōng not great?
White-haired, he was never summoned.
I admire Duàn Gān Mù,
Who reposed yet shielded Wèi’s lord.
I revere Lǔ Zhòng Lián,
Who with talk and laughter repelled Qín’s army.
Valued in his time for being unbound,
In crisis, he could resolve disputes.
Achieving merit, he accepted no reward,
His lofty integrity stood unmatched.
Facing the official seal, he would not buckle it,
Facing the jade tablet, he would not share it.
Linked seals gleamed in the front courtyard,
But to him, they were like floating clouds.
In the capital city, thronging and grand,
Reside the illustrious princes and lords.
Their canopies shade the four thoroughfares,
Their crimson carriages vie on the long avenues.
By day they gather at the mansions of Jīn and Zhāng,
By night they lodge in the halls of Xǔ and Shǐ.
To the south, neighbors strike bells and chimes,
To the north, lanes blow shēng and yú.
Silent and still is Yáng Zǐ's dwelling,
Its gate without carriages of ministers or chancellors.
In its vast, empty chambers,
What is discussed lies in the profound and abstract.
His discourse follows Xuānní's standards,
His rhapsodies emulate Xiàngrú's style.
Through the distant passage of a hundred generations,
His noble name reigns across the eight regions.
The bright sky spreads the white sun,
Its radiant light shines upon the Divine Land.
Row upon row of mansions within the Purple Palace,
Their soaring eaves float like clouds.
Within those towering, lofty gates,
Gather in abundance kings and marquises.
Since I am no climber of dragons,
Why should I suddenly come to wander here?
Clad in coarse cloth, I leave the Chānghé Gate,
With lofty strides, I pursue Xǔ Yóu.
Shaking my robe on the thousand-ren peak,
Washing my feet in the ten-thousand-mile stream.
Jīng Kē drank in the markets of Yān,
In his wine-induced fervor, his spirit soared even higher.
Singing mournful songs with Jiànlí,
He acted as if no one stood beside him.
Though lacking the integrity of a true hero,
He was still extraordinary among his contemporaries.
Gazing loftily, he looked down upon the Four Seas;
What are the powerful and noble worth mentioning?
The noble may deem themselves noble,
But I regard them as mere dust.
The humble may deem themselves humble,
But I value them as weighty as a thousand jūn.
Zhǔfù failed to attain office,
And even his own flesh and blood looked down upon him.
Jiǎ Chén, reduced to gathering firewood,
Found no peace in his marital home.
Chén Píng possessed no property or estate,
Returning to dwell by the city wall, hidden and obscure.
Chángqīng returned to Chéngdū,
His home bare and desolate, with walls standing empty.
Were these four worthies not great?
Their glorious deeds illuminate the pages of history.
Yet when they had not yet met their time,
Their worry was to fill the ditches and gullies.
Heroes face trials and tribulations,
A truth that has existed since ancient times.
In which age are there no extraordinary talents?
Left abandoned in the wilds and marshes.
Fluttering, the bird in its cage,
Lifts its wings only to strike the four corners.
Isolated, the scholar in the impoverished lane,
Holds his shadow, guarding his empty hut.
Stepping out, he finds no open road,
Thorns and brambles block the middle of his path.
His plans and strategies are cast aside, unaccepted,
Lonely as a fish stranded in a dried-up pond.
Looking outward, he holds not an inch of official salary;
Looking inward, he has not a peck of grain in storage.
His relatives still scorn him,
His friends grow more distant day and night.
Sū Qín traveled north to persuade,
Lǐ Sī went west to present his memorial.
In an instant, they gained glory and splendor,
In a breath, they withered and fell again.
Drinking from the river, one only hopes to fill his belly;
Valuing sufficiency, he desires no surplus.
Nesting in the forest, perched on a single branch—
This can serve as a model for the enlightened man.
In former times, during the Western Capital's era,
Both court and commoners knew much joy and pleasure.
At the bustling eastern capital gate,
The assembled lords bade farewell to the two Shū.
Vermilion carriages gleamed in the golden city,
Banquet tents lined the long avenues.
The enlightened man knows when to stop, knows contentment,
Casting aside glory as if it were nothing.
Pulling out his hairpin, shedding his court robes,
Letting down his hair, he returns to the coastal corner.
Passersby shed tears for him,
How virtuous was this great man!
Spending gold freely, he delighted in his time,
Leaving no savings as the year drew to a close.
Turning to the guests seated all around,
He said: "Excessive wealth only burdens the foolish."
His pure breeze stirs ten thousand generations,
His name endures as long as heaven and earth.
Ah, you officials in cicada-winged caps,
You, gentlemen with sashes, ought to read of this.
The Zhào clan possessed the Hé jade,
Under heaven, none failed to hear of it.
The people of Qín came seeking to purchase it,
But their offered price was mere empty words.
To give it would mean being sold out,
Not to give it might bring disaster.
Selecting talent to prepare the envoy's retinue,
Hoping to ensure the state's fate remained intact.
Lìn Shēng, though in a lowly position,
Was praised by Miào Zǐ for his worthiness.
Bearing his charge, he galloped beyond the borders,
Leaning on the carriage rail, he went straight through the pass.
The King of Qín sat upon his hall's throne,
The envoy of Zhào, holding his tally, stepped forward.
Flicking his sleeve, he glanced sidelong at the golden pillars,
Ready to sacrifice both body and jade.
The chain of cities was falsely offered,
Yet the jade of Jīng returned truly intact.
Then at the meeting in Miǎnchí,
The two rulers managed to establish friendly relations.
Zhāoxiāng sought to rely on his might,
But Xiàngrú broke his arrogant intent.
Blood from his glaring eyes dripped onto his lapel,
His furious hair stood on end, lifting his cap.
In the end, the western fou was struck twice,
The eastern sè was not plucked alone.
Is it not easy to sacrifice one's life?
But to face death truly is uniquely difficult.
His awe-inspiring might atop the Zhāngtái Terrace,
Even the strong and oppressive dared not interfere.
Bending his principles within Hándān's walls,
Lowering his head, he endured turning the carriage back.
And Lián Gōng—what manner of man was he?
Bearing thorny branches, he apologized for his fault.
Wisdom and courage surpassing their generation,
Their tension and release make me sigh in admiration.
The royal airs, mournful and pensive,
The way of Zhōu, turbulent and without order.
Divining at Luòyì reveals rise and fall,
Where turmoil arises, none escape ruin.
Forces vying for power swallowed the Nine Tripods,
Harsh evils exposed the three untimely deaths.
Shouldering burdens, the people's thoughts entwined,
Divine insight gathered at the Vermilion Light.
That man, sensing the work of his age,
Came forth to support the rising king.
Gracefully planning within the tent,
Brilliantly, the heavenly enterprise prospered.
At Hóngmén, the eclipse of power dissolved,
At Gāixià, the baleful star fell.
Ennobling an enemy, establishing Xiāo as minister,
Securing the capital, protecting the heir apparent.
Beginning with trust, joining the reclusive elder,
Soaring and flying, pointing toward the imperial city.
A benevolent heart striving for a thousand ages,
Pure dust spreading boundlessly.
Divinely martial, harmonizing the three correct principles,
Establishing order, covering the eight wilds.
The bright pair illuminates the north of the river,
Auspicious clouds approach Fényáng.
Imperial banners pass by the crumbling resting place,
Adorned images offered in fine sacrifice.
The sage's heart is not merely for display,
Only virtue lies in never forgetting.
If the departed could rise again,
I would measure myself, yearning for the way of Zhōu.
Numerous are the chariot attendants,
Resplendent is the arena of brush and ink.
I, a blind man, miss the splendid sight,
Standing on tiptoe, gazing toward that direction.
Though the four roads are level and straight,
My halting steps feel ashamed, lacking goodness.
Partaking of harmony, forgetting the subtle and distant,
Craning my neck, I sing of Tàikāng.
The phoenix tree leans tall, awaiting the phoenix,
The cold valley awaits the singing pitch-pipes.
How can one not cherish echoes and shadows?
From afar, they often match each other.
Gentle is that secluded, graceful maiden,
Who becomes a bride in the nobleman's home.
Her lofty integrity pierces autumn frost,
Her bright beauty rivals the morning sun.
Since fortune now follows me,
My joyful wishes are fulfilled from this moment.
Before peaceful dwelling could be enjoyed,
My good husband looks upon departure.
Removing his headscarf a thousand miles away,
He fastens his official sash and ascends to the royal domain.
The journey begins at dawn,
Attendants gather closely around.
Driving the carriage beyond the suburbs,
The road ahead is long and winding.
Alive, we face long separation,
In death, eternal absence.
Alas, I lament this journey of duty,
Three ascents exhaust dawn and dusk.
The harsh carriage braves wind and cold,
Unhitching the saddle, he faces frost and dew.
Plains and marshes are filled with sorrow,
Whirling winds sweep through tall trees.
Stray beasts rise on desolate paths,
Startled birds scatter in all directions.
How sorrowful, you wandering official,
Toiling along these mountain and river roads.
Far, far away the traveler goes,
Time twists and turns, years pass by.
A fine moment for this parting,
Sun and moon move toward their decline.
Who knows the accumulation of cold and heat?
Striving, one sees glory and decay.
Year's end, facing an empty room,
Cool winds rise from the corner of my seat.
Sleeping and rising, the day grows cold,
White dew forms on the courtyard weeds.
Toiling in service, I follow my wish to return,
Retracing the road along mountains and rivers.
Once, autumn had not yet turned pale,
Now, the year again bears blossoms.
In silkworm month, observing leisure time,
Through mulberry fields I often pass.
The fair lady tends to her tasks,
Gracefully reaching for high branches.
Who would not gaze upon such beauty?
Reining in, I pause at the midslope.
Years gone by, truly longing and toil,
Matters distant, severed from sight and sound.
Though parted for five years,
We meet as if strangers in life.
Leaving the carriage, I follow the old road,
Ducks and algae hasten, eyes meet in understanding.
Is southern gold not precious?
Yet I lightly regard what I value.
A righteous heart bears many bitter tunes,
Closely resembling the sound of gold and jade.
Lofty integrity cannot long linger,
Departing again, leaving empty words.
Slowly, the road ahead ends,
Reluctantly, I arrive at the gate's foundation.
Entering the hall to pay joyful respects,
Stepping into the chamber, I ask, "Where is she?"
At dusk, returning from gathering herbs,
The scene is of mulberry and elm time.
The fair lady gazes toward evening's arrival,
Shyly sighing, she approaches to hold me.
Who can cease such deep feelings?
Let me briefly express these hardships.
Living apart for many years,
A single separation blocked by rivers and passes.
Spring comes without moments of joy,
Autumn arrives, ever early cold.
Dawn stirs a sorrowful heart,
In the chamber, long sighs arise.
Bleak and dreary, the year draws to its close,
Sunset colors the wanderer's face.
High tension snaps the severed string,
Urgent sound arises from the tuning.
Since ancient times, I have wronged your radiant dust,
Our pledged words were firm from start to end.
How, after such long separation,
Do a hundred actions fault oneself?
If the nobleman loses clear righteousness,
With whom shall I grow old?
Ashamed before the poem "Walking Through Dew,"
I would gladly drown in the long river's stream.
Though Ruǎn Jí sank into obscurity,
His insight was profound, his discernment piercing.
Deep in drink as if burying his light,
His verses often carried hidden satire.
His long whistle seemed to yearn for someone,
Transgressing rites, he startled the crowd.
Matters past cannot be discussed,
At road's end, could he not wail?
Jī Kāng did not conform to the world,
By nature, he was one who feasted on mist.
His bodily liberation proved silent transcendence,
His discourses revealed concentrated spirit.
Standing apart from customs, he opposed popular opinion,
Seeking mountains, he befriended recluses.
The luan's wings may sometimes be clipped,
But who can tame the dragon's nature?
Liú Líng excelled at closing his gates,
Concealing emotions, extinguishing sight and sound.
Bells and drums brought no joy,
Could glory and beauty dazzle him?
Veiling his essence, daily sinking into drink,
Who knew it was not mere wild feasting?
Though his "Ode to Wine" is a short piece,
His deep heart is revealed therein.
Ruǎn Xián possessed the makings of the blue clouds,
Truly endowed with the finest of human gifts.
Why need profound understanding of music?
He discerned subtleties in golden harmonies.
Guō Yì was already captivated in heart,
Shān Táo's admiration was no empty glance.
Though recommended repeatedly, he did not enter office,
With one wave of the hand, he went out to govern.
Xiàng Xiù embraced simplicity and plainness,
His deep heart entrusted to brush and silk.
He loved exploring profound mysteries of the Way,
Reading books, he disdained mere commentary.
His friendship with Lǚ Ān soared like a swan,
Climbing with Jī Kāng, he rose like a phoenix.
Lingering in travels along the river,
Sorrowful, he composed the "Fù of Shānyáng."
The five capitals boasted of wealth and power,
The three rivers nurtured fame and profit.
A hundred in gold could not buy off death,
Mastery of classics brought high position.
In the capital's twelve thoroughfares,
Flying eaves lined up like fish scales.
Officials fluttered ornate tassels,
Travelers tightened light reins.
Morning stars still sparse,
Carriage canopies already arrive like clouds.
Guests and attendants bustle noisily,
Saddled horses shine upon the ground.
Cold and heat converge in one season,
Splendor and spring's charm abound.
Jūn Píng alone dwelled in solitude,
Rejecting both world and self.
Holding the banner as Hàn's general,
Sweating horses marched beyond the Great Wall.
The Great Wall's terrain perilous,
Stretching ten thousand lǐ to meet the clouds.
In the cool eighth and ninth moons of autumn,
Barbarian cavalry invaded Yōubīng.
Fēihú Pass dimmed in daylight,
The vast sea grew somber with gloom.
Feathered dispatches sometimes cut off,
Watchmen's clappers alarmed day and night.
Mounting the rampart, brandishing precious swords,
High banners blotted out the sun.
Clouds gathered, seven elite troops,
Fish-scale formation, six commandery soldiers.
Hújiā melodies stirred thoughts beneath the pass,
Qiāng flutes sounded atop the Lǒng hills.
The Gǔdū chieftain first trembled in fear,
The Rìzhú leader next lost his spirit.
The Yùmén Pass dismissed its scouts,
Mansions began construction anew.
Rank ascended, granaries piled high,
Merit established, a hundred deeds accomplished.
Heaven long, earth enduring,
Human affairs know wax and wane.
Before the stirring Chǔ music ended,
Already the high tower was seen toppling.
Let it be that upon the Lín gé,
For a thousand years, his heroic name remains!
Lowly places are not fit to dwell;
A noble man is cautious at the start.
High renown does not linger long;
Easily it invites slander and harm.
Having left my official post before,
Someone came to visit my humble home.
In my rustic house, I had nothing to offer,
So I brewed sweet wine and grilled dried fish.
He asked me what merits I had achieved,
To serve three times in the Chéngmíng Hall.
The land I occupy here,
Is said to be where the wise and benevolent dwell.
My writings cannot govern the state,
Nor do my boxes hold official documents.
How can I be praised for talent and learning,
When such praise is often heard?
I rose from my mat and knelt to explain:
"This humble man is truly empty inside.
Like the man of Sòng meeting a visitor from Zhōu,
I am ashamed and know not where to turn."
Lush are the pines on the hilltops,
Tall and straight, the cypresses on high peaks.
Their radiance thrives in winter and summer,
Their roots never wither or fall.
A virtuous man holds a steadfast heart,
Awakened by things, he thinks of distant refuge.
He lifts his aspirations to the dark clouds' edge,
And turns his gaze to gaze upon the cliffs.
I admire the ancient Prince Wángzǐ Qiáo,
Whose friendship began in Yīluò.
Far he journeyed over steep mountains,
Swiftly riding flying cranes.
His traces left behind for ten thousand miles,
How could he cling to mortal joys?
Long have I yearned for immortal kin,
Dazzled, my heart drifts far and wide.
In the capital, roving knights gather,
In mountains and forests, recluses dwell.
What glory is there in vermilion gates?
Better to entrust oneself to Pénglái.
By the source, I draw clear waves,
On the ridge, I pluck crimson sprouts.
In the spirit stream, one may hide and wander,
Why seek to climb the cloud ladder?
In Qīyuán there was an arrogant official,
In Láishì there was a transcendent wife.
Advancing, one may preserve the dragon's sight,
Retreating, one becomes a ram butting the fence.
Soaring beyond the dusty world,
I bow deeply, bidding farewell to Yí Qí.
The green stream spans a thousand rèn,
Within it dwells a Daoist priest.
Clouds drift between the beams and pillars,
Wind whispers through the window frames.
I ask, who might this be?
They say it is Guǐgǔzǐ.
He yearns for the traces of Yǐngyáng,
By the river, he thinks of washing his ears.
The western gate of heaven arrives from the southwest,
Hidden waves ripple, scales arise.
The spirit maiden glances at me with a smile,
Brightly she reveals her jade-like teeth.
But the matchmaker is no longer here,
To whom shall I entrust my plea?
Kingfishers play among orchid tips,
Their colors shine more vividly together.
Green vines entwine the tall woods,
Lush and dense, they cover the mountain.
Within dwells a silent hermit,
Quietly whistling, strumming a clear string.
Releasing his spirit beyond the heavens,
He chews on petals and sips from flying springs.
Chìsōng appears upstream,
Riding a swan through purple mist.
On the left, he tugs at Fúqiū's sleeve,
On the right, he pats Hóngyá's shoulder.
I ask the mayfly-like crowd,
How could they know the years of turtle and crane?
How can the six dragons be halted?
The flow of fate has its cycles.
Changing times stir human thoughts,
Though autumn comes, I long for summer again.
In Huáihǎi, tiny birds transform,
Yet my life alone does not change.
Though I wish to soar to the cinnabar stream,
The cloud-dragon is not my steed.
Ashamed I lack Lǔyáng's virtue,
To turn back the sun three houses away.
By the river, I mourn my advancing years,
Clutching my heart, alone in sorrowful lament.
The soaring wing longs to brush the sky,
The swift foot envies distant travels.
Clear springs have no swelling waves,
How can they carry a ship that swallows the sea?
Though jade tablets are specially esteemed,
A bright pearl is hard to give in darkness.
Hidden buds lament the spring sun,
Hilltop reeds mourn the pure autumn.
Grief strikes my crimson heart,
Tears fall, streaming down my tassels.
The záxiàn bird dwells at Lǔ's gate,
Warm winds foretell disaster.
A ship-swallowing fish surges from the sea's depths,
High waves carry Pénglái.
Immortals emerge, parting the clouds,
Revealing only towers of gold and silver.
Língyáng draws cinnabar dew,
Róngchéng wields a jade cup.
Héng'é raises her wondrous voice,
Hóngyá nods his chin in approval.
They rise and fall with the long mists,
Drifting and playing across the nine realms.
Their wondrous age surpasses the five dragons,
A thousand years still like an infant.
Yānzhāo lacked the numinous energy,
Hànwǔ was no talent for immortality.
Dark and bright moons cycle like a ring,
The full moon already shows its waning light.
Rùshōu clears the western sky,
The red sun will turn pale.
Cold dew brushes the hilltop reeds,
The dodder vine parts from pine and cypress.
The hibiscus blooms not through the morning,
How can the mayfly see the evening?
Yuánqiū holds wondrous herbs,
Zhōngshān yields spirit elixirs.
Noble sons display eight delicacies,
Ānqī refines the five minerals.
I bow deeply to those in power,
Then come and go as a mountain forest guest.
Staff in hand, I summon the recluse,
Wild paths stretch across past and present.
The cave has no built structure,
Yet within the hill, a lute sings.
White snow rests on the shaded ridge,
Crimson flowers gleam in the sunlit woods.
Stone springs rinse jade-like rocks,
Tiny fish float and sink within.
Not necessarily strings and bamboo,
Mountains and streams have clear sounds.
What need for singing and whistling?
Shrubs themselves chant mournfully.
Autumn chrysanthemums serve as provisions,
Hidden orchids adorn the layered collar.
Hesitating, my feet grow weary,
I long to cast aside my official pin.
I began building a hut on the eastern hill,
Fruit trees grew wild into thickets.
Before it lies a cold spring well,
Enough to cleanse my heart and spirit.
Amidst steep cliffs and verdant hues,
Bamboo and cypress reveal their true nature.
Tender leaves endure frost and snow,
Flying blossoms drift with lingering dew.
Rank and robes are not constant joys,
Likes and dislikes have their ebb and flow.
Tying the official sash brings entanglement,
Brushing off the hat removes the dust.
Huìlián did not bend my will,
Shǒuyáng did not shape my virtue.
Let us observe what is esteemed,
Wandering freely, choosing fine days.
At dawn, my heart is not at peace,
I shake my robes, pacing to and fro.
Pacing, where shall I go?
The recluse dwells in the deep valley.
At morn, I gather algae in the southern stream,
At eve, I rest at the western hill's foot.
Slender branches form cloud-like structures,
Dense leaves create emerald canopies.
Stirring songs linger in orchid groves,
Fragrant breezes brush the fair woods.
How clear and cold the mountain stream,
Flying springs rinse jade-like stones.
Mournful notes cling to spirit waves,
Fading echoes reach the layered curves.
Supreme joy needs no pretense,
Why dilute the pure and simple?
If wealth and honor are hard to attain,
I shall retire and follow my desires.
The small recluse hides in hills and marshes,
The great recluse hides in court and market.
Bó Yí fled to Shǒuyáng,
Lǎo Dān served as archivist.
In the peaceful times of old,
There were also dwellers in nests.
Now, though in a bright and prosperous age,
Can there be no hermits in the woods?
Releasing spirit beyond the azure clouds,
Vanishing traces deep in remote mountains.
The pheasant crows before dawn,
The mournful wind rises to meet the night.
Frost withers the rosy face,
Cold springs injure the jade-like feet.
Universal talent is trusted to the crowd,
Partial wisdom is left to oneself.
Accepting one’s lot gains heavenly harmony,
Forcing one’s nature loses the highest principle.
What can one hope for upon return?
To be one with all things, from beginning to end.
Riding a carriage, I roam by night,
