Strolling freely through the western garden.
Two canals irrigate each other,
Fine trees surround the flowing stream.
Low branches brush the feathered canopy,
Tall boughs rub against the azure sky.
A sudden wind lifts the wheels,
Flying birds soar before me.
Crimson clouds flank the bright moon,
Brilliant stars emerge from between the clouds.
Heaven bestows radiant splendor,
How vivid are the five colors!
Lifespan is not like pine or fungus,
Who can attain immortality?
Roaming freely delights the heart,
Preserving oneself to a hundred years.
The four seasons follow like fish scales,
Each with its own principle and measure.
Only the clear autumn day
Can exhaust my lofty joy.
The scenery is bright and distant,
The wind and things are bleak and sharp.
Clear sounds awaken hidden rhythms,
Mournful ravines echo hollow valleys.
In cold years, no early blossoms,
Floating glory willingly withers early.
How to mark steadfastness and frailty?
Briefly, entrust to pine and mushroom.
The wise craftsman feels the bleak dawn,
Solemnly halts beyond worldly dust.
A grand feast spreads universal love,
Noble cups extend fine company.
I delight in loving benevolence,
Doubts dispelled, stinginess vanishes.
Humbly heading the court of Ā Héng,
I’ll earn the Xiongnu’s scorn.
Understanding the cricket’s song,
Believing this laborer’s chant.
What comes is never slow,
But fine journeys often falter.
Roaming freely beyond city markets,
I wish to pass by often.
Winding paths lead to hills and towers,
High terraces gaze at flying clouds.
Gentle winds sway lush gardens,
White clouds gather on layered slopes.
Sunlight dims, singing birds gather,
Water and trees gleam clear and bright.
Lifting robes along orchid shores,
Wandering, I pluck fragrant branches.
The fair one delays the years,
What can be done in late twilight?
Do not be bound by longing thoughts,
Nán Róng warns of their excess.
Sunset floats on clear waters,
Stars scatter as light oars row.
Resting in pavilions facing winding streams,
Facing the flow against returning tides.
Laying aside whips, sharing feasts,
Sitting together, inviting companions.
Mournful geese cry on sandy isles,
Sad apes echo on mountain peaks.
Tall and straight, reflecting on river moon,
Gently flowing, valley gusts emerge.
Misty air veils the peaks,
Glistening dew fills the branches.
Close gaze dispels hidden gloom,
Distant view scatters noisy clamor.
Enlightened talk knows no end,
From dusk till clear dawn.
The jade seal warns of sincerity,
The yellow canopy shows loftiness.
Deeds serve the teachings of names,
The Way transcends through divine principle.
Once heard of Fénshuǐ excursions,
Now see bridles beyond the dust.
Reeds sound from spring isles,
Dismounting to climb mountain peaks.
Unfurling banners gaze at inverted reflections,
Setting feasts watch returning tides.
Distant cliffs reflect on orchid thickets,
Bright sun beautifies riverbanks.
Plains and marshes sprout green willows,
Village gardens scatter red peaches.
The imperial heart praises sunny grace,
All things are bathed in light.
Reflecting on my own vain bonds,
Consoling ambition, ashamed of field sprouts.
Skill and clumsiness each have their place,
In the end, returning to forest nests.
Once entangled in old thoughts,
Viewing things, I sing a long chant.
Stepping out the western city gate,
Gazing afar at the western hills.
Ranges of peaks layer upon layer,
Green and deep, dark and profound.
Morning frost reddens maple leaves,
Evening glow darkens mountain mist.
Seasons pass, sorrow not shallow,
Feelings arise, thoughts run deep.
A caged hen longs for old companions,
A lost bird yearns for former woods.
Holding affection, still toils with love,
How to part from a joyful heart?
Facing the mirror, dark strands turn gray,
Holding the belt, loosening tight collars.
Arranging fate is but empty words,
In solitude, relying on the lute’s song.
The hidden dragon charms with secluded grace,
The flying swan echoes with distant cries.
Near clouds, ashamed to float,
In rivers, ashamed to sink deep.
Advancing virtue, wisdom falters,
Retiring to farm, strength fails.
Pursuing salary to distant seas,
Lying ill, facing empty woods.
Ears inclined, listening to waves,
Eyes raised, gazing at rugged peaks.
Early light dispels lingering winds,
New sun changes old shade.
Ponds grow spring grass,
Garden willows change singing birds.
Lush growth grieves the Bīn song,
Luxuriance moves the Chǔ chant.
Solitary dwelling feels eternal,
Apart from others, hard to settle heart.
Holding integrity not just in ancient times,
No distress is proven today.
As evening clears after rain,
Clouds return, sun races west.
Dense woods hold lingering freshness,
Distant peaks hide half the sun.
Long ill from damp gloom’s bitterness,
From inn gazing at suburban paths.
Marsh orchids gradually cover paths,
Lotuses begin to bloom in ponds.
Not yet tired of youth’s beauty,
Already seeing bright summer shift.
Sorrowful, sighing at things,
Streaks of white hair hang down.
Medicine halts by affection,
Aging illness suddenly here.
Soon to await autumn waters,
Resting shadow by old cliffs.
Who understands my aspiration?
Joyful heart only with true friends.
Early summer still clear and mild,
Fragrant grass not yet faded.
Living on water, lingering dawn to dusk,
Dark clouds rise and vanish repeatedly.
Touring weary of shores,
How much more the barren lands.
River gods sometimes calm the flow,
Heavenly Wú still does not stir.
Hoisting sails to gather stone flowers,
Raising mats to collect sea moons.
Vast seas without bounds,
Empty boats freely surpass.
Zhòng Lián disdained Qí’s honors,
Zǐ Móu longed for Wèi’s palace.
Boasting fame lacks the Way,
Suiting oneself, things can be ignored.
Heed Rèn Gōng’s words,
Finally avoid heaven’s punishment.
Dawn and dusk shift the weather's hue,
Mountains and waters hold clear light's view.
Clear light can delight the heart,
A wanderer lingers, forgetting to depart.
Leaving the valley, the sun still early,
Boarding the boat, the sun's glow faintly.
Woods and ravines gather twilight's shade,
Clouds and mist collect as evening fades.
Lotus and water chestnut gleam in turn,
Reeds and weeds in mutual embrace yearn.
Brushing aside, I head southward along the trail,
Joyful, I rest by the eastern gate, without fail.
With calm thoughts, worldly things seem light,
Content in mind, reason aligns with delight.
To those who seek to nurture life, I say,
Try using this way to guide your day.
At dawn, I seek the cliffs with my staff in hand,
At dusk, I rest in a mountain dwelling, so grand.
Sparse peaks oppose the lofty hall,
Facing ridges, near winding streams, I recall.
Tall woods line the cave's entrance wide,
Piled stones embrace the steps with pride.
Continuous cliffs block the path ahead,
Dense bamboos make the trail mislead.
Newcomers forget the fresh route they tread,
Departing souls are confused by the old path instead.
Gurgling, the evening stream flows fast,
Chirping, the night apes' cries last.
In deep seclusion, is there another truth to find?
Holding to the Way, I leave no doubt behind.
My heart bonds with the autumn tree's core,
My eyes play with spring sprouts, I adore.
Living in constancy, awaiting life's end,
Following nature's course, all things blend.
Alas, no kindred spirit shares my quest,
To climb the ladder of blue clouds, abreast.
At dawn, I depart from the sunny cliff's height,
As shadows fall, I rest on the shaded peak's site.
Leaving the boat, I gaze at distant isles,
Halting my staff, I lean on lush pines, with smiles.
Side paths are winding and deep,
Encircling isles are delicate, secrets they keep.
Looking down, I see treetops high,
Looking up, I hear deep ravines' sigh.
Rocks block, waters divide and flow,
Dense woods, trails vanish, no trace to show.
What feeling does growth's mystery bring?
Rising and thriving, all things in beauty spring.
Young bamboos sheath in green, so new,
Fresh cattails hold purple down, in view.
Seagulls play on spring shores with glee,
Heavenly chickens sport in gentle breeze, free.
Embracing change, my heart never tires,
Viewing nature, my affection inspires.
I regret not being far from worldly strife,
But lament having no companion in life.
Solitary wandering is not a sigh of despair,
If appreciation ends, who understands to care?
Apes' cries truly herald the dawn,
Though the valley's dark, light is not yet drawn.
Clouds gather beneath the cliff's embrace,
Dew still glistens on flowers, with grace.
Winding along bends and coves, I tread,
Ascending ridges and peaks, ahead.
Crossing streams, I brave the swift flow,
Climbing plank paths, to heights I go.
Rivers and isles twist and turn,
Riding currents, I watch waters churn.
Duckweed floats on deep pools, serene,
Reeds emerge from clear shallows, green.
Standing on rocks, I scoop flying springs,
Climbing trees, I pluck curled leaves, nature sings.
I imagine a hermit in the mountain's fold,
Vines and creepers before my eyes, untold.
Holding orchids, my efforts in vain,
Breaking hemp, my heart feels the strain.
Emotion finds beauty in appreciation's art,
But obscure matters, who can impart?
Seeing this, worldly worries fade,
In one awakening, all burdens are laid.
Zhōu's chariots traced every track,
Xià's records crossed mountains, forth and back.
Storing grief, was it wise or bright?
Skilled travelers were saints, in holy light.
The emperor's glory followed motion's decree,
Clear roads patrolled the wide city, free.
Towers viewed abundant harvests near,
Golden carriages mirrored pines, clear.
Rushing like streams, they moved in line,
Crimson wheels replaced in circles fine.
Divine travel matched floating light,
Competing radiance filled mid-sky's height.
Winter's start pities fading things,
Decay fills transformation's springs.
Sunny slopes gather essence's might,
Shaded valleys drag cold mist, white.
Clustered white forms dense and grand,
Accumulated green stands lush, across the land.
Resting feasts report the good year's grace,
Easing hardship warns of famine's trace.
Warmth reaches even servants low,
Kindness graces the later banquet's glow.
Observing customs, long have I composed,
Presenting poems, my lack of skill exposed.
Weary and weak, I decline haste's call,
Burdens not from bonds, I recall.
Xuán Tiān high in the northern row,
Rì Guān overlooks the eastern sea's flow.
Entering the river, rising from Yáng Xiá's might,
Treading Huà Shān, carved by nature's light.
Cliffs and dangers leave Hàn's domain,
Guards and defenses move to Wú's reign.
Flowing pools form by nature's hand,
Mountain passes built by gods' command.
Garden counties reach to farthest sight,
Village shrines gather earth's spirit bright.
Dwellings align with stars' design,
Birth's glow answers divine sign.
Wise thoughts linger in homeland's embrace,
Imperial tours circle old fields' space.
Ascending peaks, carriage paths soar,
Seeking clouds, jade rooftops roar.
Spring rivers swell with winds and waves,
Orchid fields flourish with sprouts, nature saves.
Spreading journeys aid the world below,
Reaching far, holy thoughts grow.
Mountains and seas have harmonious meet,
Auspicious practice in divination's feat.
Zhōu Nán mourned the elder of old,
Lingering, I feel the remnant folk's cold.
Empty meals tire the court's display,
Returning taxes, to cliff farming I sway.
Yú's winds carried imperial hunt's might,
Xià's proverbs praised royal travels bright.
Spring's season stirs the celestial ride,
Hopes for favor pour from five lands wide.
Mountain spirits guard the ridge's way,
Water gods alert the sea's sway.
Divine chariots from jade axles start,
Heavenly vessels with carved boats part.
Ten thousand axles follow the guard's line,
A thousand sails float, in flight they shine.
Carved clouds adorn the jeweled canopy,
Lucky breezes bear colored flags, free.
Jiāngnán presents Jīng's beauty rare,
Hé Jī offers Zhào's songs in air.
Golden light shines on coastal shores,
Reed drums shake the sea's deep roars.
Gazing afar, I see green cliffs tall,
Drifting, I view green fields, overall.
Human spirits soar over city and wild,
Scales and feathers rise from deep and mild.
Virtue and rites spread far and near,
Rivers and mountains feel kindness clear.
Roosters crow, border guards arise,
Drums beat early, morning's ties.
Stern chariots face distant lanes,
Extended gaze crosses city domains.
Creeping weeds climb high corners' might,
Tall willows flank broad ferries, light.
Swift winds blow from dawn's first breath,
Level roads choke with flying dust's death.
Restless wanderers seeking posts,
Busy market folks, bustling hosts.
Clutching gold, drawn to profit's call,
Gripping swords, leaving kin, they fall.
Racing for miles on endless trails,
Each tending to life's hundred-year tales.
Blossoms open in youth's tender phase,
Holding beauty, grudging spring's amazed gaze.
Honoring worth, forever bright and clear,
Lonely and lowly, long hidden in fear.
Loveliness fades while sitting still,
For whom is this bitter toil, with will?
Sorrowful, with no joy in sight,
Hand in hand, we seek delight.
Chasing clouds, ascending layered towers,
Following hills, viewing mushroom-like bowers.
Distant trees dim in lush array,
Rising mist spreads in hazy gray.
Fish play, new lotus leaves sway,
Birds scatter, leftover blossoms decay.
Not facing spring wine's fragrant cheer,
Still gazing at green hills, far and near.
Guǎngchéng loved the divine cauldron,
Huáinán was fond of alchemical scriptures.
This mountain is adorned with phoenixes and cranes,
Where immortals and spirits come and go.
Jade-like plants glow with vibrant colors,
Jade trees truly flourish in lush green.
Crimson mists descend and linger low,
White clouds ascend into the distant haze.
Sitting midway, I gaze upon the winding rainbow,
Looking down, I watch the shooting stars.
Without seeking the extremes of distant wonders,
One knows how startling they are to the senses.
The sun sets over the isle of Chángshā,
Layers of darkness spread for ten thousand miles.
Leaning on orchids, I harbor many thoughts,
Facing the wind, I silently contain my emotions.
I aspire to learn the seclusion of pines and cypresses,
Ashamed to chase after fame in the bustling streets.
Fortunate to receive the end of your radiant recitation,
I humbly think of entrusting myself to your trailing banner.
The sacred mountain records the virtue of the earth,
The perilous terrain relies on the spirit of the peaks.
Zhōngnán marks the vantage of Qín,
Shǎoshì is near the royal city.
Emerald phoenixes soar over Huái and the sea,
Like a sash, they encircle the divine outskirts.
How steep the northern hills are,
With forests deep and lushly green.
Rising from the earth are many wondrous ridges,
Reaching the clouds in varied forms.
Converging and overlapping, they hide the sky,
Uneven and staggered, they gaze at one another.
Majestic structures form crimson cliffs,
Towering peaks rise like azure screens.
Their might rivals the height of Jiǔyí,
Their aura matches the grandeur of the Three Mountains.
The scene itself is already beautiful,
The view from afar is even more extraordinary.
Looking south, I see the Chǔxū Observatory,
Gazing west, I behold the Kūnmíng Pond.
All within the mountains bring joy,
Appreciation shifts with the four seasons.
Spring light emerges from the ridge’s head,
Autumn wind stirs among the cassia branches.
Often I meet companions who calm the heart,
Building dwellings at the mountain’s foot.
The eight liberations echo in the flowing streams,
The four meditations hide within winding cliffs.
Profound and obscure, they remain unseen,
Desolate and still, with nothing to desire.
My wish is to wander with them,
With this, my heart is content.
The sovereign displays transcendent interest,
Feathered banners approach the lofty base.
White clouds follow his jade steps,
Azure mists mingle with cassia flags.
Lingering, he seeks the five medicinal herbs,
Pausing to gaze upon the three divine fungi.
Here I look up to his carriage and steeds,
Hoping to meet by year’s end.
King Chén’s cockfighting path,
Ānrén’s wood-gathering road.
The eastern suburbs are no different from before,
A place to leisurely stroll.
Wild paths wind and twist,
Desolate trails crisscross.
Hibiscus hedges sparse and dense,
Thorn gates new and old.
Wind howls atop the trees,
Frost and dew gather at the grass roots.
Startled deer do not rest,
Migratory birds occasionally glance back.
Owls hoot from thatched roofs,
Cold hares dart across flat ridges.
Evening shadows cloak the layered hills,
Long mists draw out light silks.
Fleeting light suddenly urges me on,
How can I stop as the year draws to a close?
If I could obtain the western mountain’s herb,
Perhaps my declining years could be prolonged.
Emperor Qín ruled the universe,
Emperor Hàn expanded military achievements.
When human pleasures were exhausted,
Their inner nature remained unfulfilled.
Eagerly they turned to the Three Mountains,
Placing hopes in the Nine Heavens.
They built the Qínián Observatory,
And also erected the Wàngxiān Palace.
Was it truly a love for the Way,
Or merely boundless desire?
As for me, I know contentment,
This wish requires no abundance.
Wherever I find a place to linger,
I desire to rest my humble self.
Distant peaks layer upon layers,
Nearby bamboo and trees are lush and dense.
Opening my collar, I bathe in cold water,
Loosening my belt, I face the clear breeze.
My burdens are not external things,
My thoughts dwell in emptiness.
When friends come, we grasp stone marrow,
When guests arrive, we ride light swans.
All human paths are cut off,
Only the cloud road remains open.
Soaring at once above the inverted shadows,
With no need to seek Huà or Sōng.
I send word to those who appreciate beauty,
At year’s end, come join me here.
Gānquán alerts with beacon fires,
Shànggǔ holds back Lóulán.
This river is famed for its perilous expanse,
These mountains are again lush and winding.
Inside and out, the terrain is supremely strategic,
Like a sash, it embraces all cliffs and ridges.
Tall bamboos strengthen the lower slopes,
Precipitous towers soar upward.
Ascending the battlements, I gaze afar,
Turning my head, I see Cháng’ān.
Golden canals flow toward Bà and Chǎn,
Paved paths lead to Yuānluán.
Gleaming carriages race with ornate wheels,
Sweating steeds leap with silver saddles.
In youth, bearing heroic spirit,
Upright and noble, standing with bristling hair.
Holding memories of Yānshān’s stones,
Thoughts of breaching Hángǔ’s pass.
How could it be like the games at Bàshàng,
Ashamed to be a roadside spectator.
I send word to those seeking nobility,
Fate’s odd twists are truly lamentable!
In the night, unable to sleep,
I rise and sit, strumming the resonant qín.
Thin curtains reflect the bright moon,
A clear breeze blows through my lapel.
A lone goose cries in the wilds beyond,
Northern birds call in the northern woods.
Pacing back and forth, what will I see?
Only sorrowful thoughts wound my heart.
Two consorts wandered by the riverbank,
Carefree, they followed the wind in flight.
Jiāofǔ cherished the pendant gifts,
Graceful and lovely, fragrant and fair.
Entwined in tender affection,
For a thousand years, never to forget.
Their beauty captivated Xiàcài,
Lovely appearances stirred the heart.
Deep emotion gave rise to melancholy thoughts,
Planting forgetfulness herbs in orchid chambers.
For whom are the ointments and washes applied?
Longing for rain, resentful of the morning sun.
How can a bond firm as metal and stone,
Suddenly bring such parting sorrow?
Beneath fine trees, a path naturally forms,
In the eastern garden, peaches and plums.
Autumn wind blows the flying leaves,
From this begins their withering fall.
Splendor gives way to decay,
Thorns and brambles grow in the hall.
Driving my horse, I leave it behind,
Going up to the foot of the western hills.
If I cannot protect myself,
How can I care for wife and children?
Hard frost covers the wild grass,
By year’s end, all is said to end.
In former days, men of splendor,
Ānlíng and Lóngyáng.
Blossoming peach and plum flowers,
Brilliant and radiant with light.
Joyful as the nine springs,
Bowing low like autumn frost.
Glancing eyes emit charming grace,
Words and laughter exude fragrance.
Hand in hand, sharing equal affection,
Night and day, sharing the same clothes.
Wishing to be a pair of flying birds,
Wing to wing, soaring together.
Paintings record their solemn vows,
Never to forget for all eternity.
Heavenly steeds emerge from the northwest,
From ancient times, they come from the east.
Spring and autumn have no fixed abode,
How can wealth and honor last forever?
Clear dew bedews the marsh orchids,
Hard frost moistens the wild grass.
In morning, a charming youth,
By evening, turned ugly and old.
Unless one is Prince Jìn,
Who can remain forever fair?
Ascending high, overlooking the four wilds,
Gazing north toward the green mountain slopes.
Pines and cypresses shade the ridge and hill,
Flying birds call as they pass one another.
Moved by emotion, I harbor bitterness and sorrow,
Resentment and poison are often all too many.
Lord Lǐ grieved at the eastern gate,
Master Sū felt confined by the three rivers.
Seeking benevolence, one attains benevolence—
Why then sigh and lament again!
The onset of autumn heralds cool air,
Crickets chirp by the bed curtains.
Touched by things, I brood with deep worry,
Silently, it makes my heart grieve.
Much to say—but to whom can I tell it?
Profuse words—to whom shall I pour them out?
A gentle breeze stirs my silken sleeves,
The bright moon shines with clear radiance.
Morning crows cry from the tall trees,
I order the carriage and set off to return.
In my youth, in the prime of life,
Frivolous, I loved strings and songs.
Traveling west to Xiányáng,
I mingled with Zhào and Lǐ.
Pleasures not yet at their end,
The bright day suddenly slipped away.
Driving my horse, I come back again,
Looking back toward the three rivers.
A hundred yì of gold all spent,
Resources and means often bring much trouble.
Northward, facing the Tàiháng road,
Having lost my way, what shall I do?
Long ago I heard of the Dōnglíng melons,
Close by, outside the Qīngmén gate.
Carts lined up along the paths and fields,
Mother and child melons clinging together.
Five colors gleaming in the morning sun,
Honored guests gathering from all sides.
The flame consumes itself by burning,
Great wealth becomes a source of harm.
A plain cloth gown can last a lifetime—
Can favor and salary be relied upon?
Strolling out of the Shàngdōng gate,
Gazing north toward the Shǒuyáng ridge.
Below are the scholars picking ferns,
Above, a fine grove of trees.
Where is the auspicious time?
Frost congeals, dampening my lapels.
Cold wind shakes the mountain ridge,
Dark clouds gather, bringing heavy shade.
Wild geese cry, flying southward,
The cuckoo utters its mournful sound.
Pure essence wanders with the autumn tones,
Desolation wounds my heart.
In past years, at fourteen or fifteen,
My aspirations inclined to books and poetry.
Clad in coarse cloth, yet harboring pearls and jade,
I sought companionship with Yán and Mǐn.
Opening the window overlooking the four wilds,
Ascending high, gazing toward my thoughts.
Grave mounds covering the mountain ridges,
Ten thousand generations all in one time.
A thousand autumns, ten thousand years hence—
Where will glory and fame then be?
Thus I envy Xiànménzǐ,
And now, in my clamor, mock myself.
Wandering by the Péngchí pond,
Turning back to gaze toward Dàliáng.
Green waters surge with great waves,
The vast wilds stretch boundless and bleak.
Running beasts crisscross in gallop,
Flying birds follow one another in flight.
At this time, the Quail Fire is at its zenith,
Sun and moon are precisely facing each other.
The north wind blows with severe cold,
The yin energy descends with light frost.
A traveler with no companion,
Looking up and down, I harbor sorrow.
Petty men calculate their gains,
Noble men uphold their constant way.
Why regret ending in weariness?
I chant and compose this verse.
The blazing heat belongs to this summer,
Three ten-day periods about to pass.
Fragrant trees hang with green leaves,
Clear clouds stretch winding afar.
The four seasons alternate in succession,
Sun and moon race in turn.
Pacing in the empty hall,
Distressed, none knows me.
I wish to witness lasting joy and harmony,
Not to see the sorrow of parting.
Blazing, the sun sinks in the west,
Its remaining light shines on my clothes.
A swirling wind blows against the four walls,
Cold birds cling to one another.
Zhōuzhōu still carries twigs in its beak,
Qíongqíong also thinks of hunger.
How can those in high positions
Bow so deeply they forget their return?
Is it for the sake of vainglory and fame,
That they let weariness grieve their hearts?
Better to soar with swallows and sparrows
Than follow the yellow swan in flight.
The yellow swan roams the four seas—
Midway, where will it return?
Sitting alone in the empty hall,
With whom can I share joy?
Going out the door, facing the long road,
I see no carts or horses passing.
Ascending high, gazing over the nine provinces,
Vast and distant, divided by wild expanses.
A lone bird flies northwest,
A stray beast descends southeast.
At dusk, I think of dear friends,
Meeting in conversation to ease my heart.
In Běilǐ there are many wondrous dances,
From Púshàng come subtle melodies.
Frivolous, idle wanderers
Rise and fall, now floating, now sinking.
Taking shortcuts down narrow paths,
They strive toward wanton excess.
Where can one see Wángzǐqiáo,
Riding clouds, soaring over Dènglín?
Only the art of prolonging life
Could comfort my heart.
Deep and clear, the long Yángzǐ River,
Above it, groves of maple trees.
Marsh orchids cover the paths,
A black steed speeds swiftly away.
Gazing afar brings sorrow,
Spring’s breath stirs my heart.
In Sānchǔ there are many talented men,
But “morning clouds” lead to wantonness.
Vermilion blossoms exude fragrance,
In Gāocài they pursue one another.
Once moved by the yellow sparrow’s lament,
Who can hold back their tears?
All my life without great ambition,
From youth beset by care and trouble.
How to bear this bitter heart,
Especially when autumn deepens?
Bright and clear, the sky’s moon shines,
Resplendent, the river stars gleam.
The wind carries the cicada’s desolate song,
Lonely cries of geese crossing the clouds.
The cold autumn stirs the quiet chamber,
A lone lamp dims the dark curtain.
Upright and troubled, worries accumulate,
Tossing and turning through half the long night.
Peace and peril are hard to foresee,
Rise and fall obscure former plans.
Though I admire Xiàngrú’s broad-mindedness,
I differ from Chángqīng’s negligence.
I rather like Zhèngshēng’s ease,
But do not seek office in plain clothes.
Not knowing the hearts of the ancients,
I follow my nature’s delights.
When guests arrive, wine may be poured,
When friends come, we may take up the brush.
High terraces I often climb,
Clear shallows I sometimes cross in disarray.
The waning moon will not be full again,
The setting sun knows no second dawn.
Metal and stone will fade away in the end,
Vermilion and azure only briefly glow.
Let each heed the sigh of dark-haired youth,
Lest white-haired age bring regret.
Thus, singing, I compose this rhapsody,
To share with close companions.
Bóyáng went to the western tribes,
Confucius wished to dwell among the nine barbarians.
If one cherishes ambitions for the four directions,
Any place can be a land to roam and linger.
Moreover, encountering hardship and distress,
Tossed about and meeting with calamity.
The ancients understood signs of opportunity,
Spurring their horses to roam near the passes.
Alas, I am young and ignorant,
Holding responsibility as a minor official.
Secret plans were already laid in the shadows,
Forming the beginning of this fortune and misfortune.
Vast and boundless between heaven and earth,
How wide the four seas are!
Heaven’s net spreads its threads and cords,
No step can find peace.
Pine and cypress wither in deep winter,
Only then do we know the year’s cold.
Without traversing the peril of Tàiháng,
Who would know the difficulty of this road?
Truth and falsehood are revealed through events,
Human feelings are hard to foresee.
Poverty and success are fixed by fate,
What use is there in passionate sighs?
Above, I have failed my kind mother’s grace,
Pain and cruelty shatter my heart and liver.
Below, I look upon my beloved daughter,
Grieving, my heart aches with sorrow.
My two sons abandoned as if discarded,
Thinking both met with cruel misfortune.
I do not regret my own death,
Only this cycles like a wheel.
Holding paper, my five emotions are blocked,
Wielding the brush, tears flow like streams.
Alas, my blessings are meager,
In youth I met with misfortune.
Orphaned and ignorant,
Still in swaddling clothes.
Mother and elder brother nurtured me,
With kindness, without sternness.
Relying on love, I acted willfully,
Without discipline or teacher.
When I reached the age of capping,
I indulged myself, relying on favor.
My heart aspired to antiquity,
Following what I esteemed.
I took delight in Lǎo and Zhuāng,
Despising things, valuing the self.
My will was to preserve simplicity,
Nourishing plainness, keeping whole the true.
I say I am not clever,
Fond of goodness, yet ignorant of people.
The failure of Zǐyù,
Repeatedly added dust to my path.
The great man embraces vastness,
Hiding filth, bearing shame.
The people are many in their perversity,
Governance does not come from oneself.
Only this narrow heart of mine,
Clearly distinguished right from wrong.
Awakened, I reflect on my faults,
Painful as wounds and sores.
Wishing to lessen my errors,
Slander and criticism boil over.
My nature does not harm others,
Yet often incurs resentment and hatred.
Once I was ashamed before Liǔ Huì,
Now I feel愧 before Sūn Dēng.
Within, I betray my long-held heart,
Without, I shame my good friends.
I admire Yán and Zhèng,
Who delighted in the Way, living in leisure.
Having no dealings with the world,
Their spirit and energy were tranquil.
Alas, I am not virtuous,
Burdened with many troubles.
It did not descend from heaven,
Truly it came from my stubbornness and negligence.
Reason failed, troubles knotted,
Finally leading to prison.
Facing base interrogations,
Bound in this secluded confinement.
Truly ashamed to plead for exoneration,
The times are not with me.
Though called righteous and upright,
My spirit is shamed, my will crushed.
Cleansing myself in the blue waves,
How could it mend anything?
Honking, honking, the wild geese cry,
Flapping wings, flying north.
Moving with the seasons,
Finding joy, forgetting sorrow.
Alas, my indignant sighs,
Cannot match them at all.
Events go against my wishes,
Meeting this prolonged delay.
Poverty and success are fated,
What more is there to seek?
The ancients had a saying,
Goodness should not approach fame.
Follow the times, be reverent and silent,
Faults and regrets will not arise.
Wàn Shí was cautious and prudent,
Securing his kin, preserving glory.
Worldly affairs are tangled and chaotic,
Only disturbing my feelings.
In peace and joy, be vigilant,
Then ultimately benefit and steadfastness.
Glorious, glorious, the divine mushroom,
Three times it blooms in a year.
Why alone am I thus,
With aspirations unfulfilled?
Punished by hardship, thinking of return,
My heart within feels remorse.
Hoping to strive in the future,
Without fragrance, without odor.
Gathering ferns on the mountain slopes,
Letting hair flow free on cliffs and peaks.
Forever whistling, long chanting,
Nourishing nature, prolonging life.
Bright moon shines on the high tower,
Flowing light lingers and drifts.
Above, a sorrowful thinking woman,
Lamenting with lingering grief.
May I ask, who is the one sighing?
She says she is the traveler’s wife.
My lord has been gone over ten years,
I, the lonely concubine, often dwell alone.
My lord is like clear road dust,
I am like turbid water mud.
Floating and sinking, each with different circumstances,
When will our meeting be harmonious?
I wish to be the southwest wind,
Long gone, entering my lord’s embrace.
My lord’s embrace truly does not open,
What then shall this humble concubine rely on?
The western capital in chaos, without order,
Jackals and tigers just bringing calamity.
Again I leave the central plains,
Going far to dwell among the Jīngmán.
Relatives face me with sorrow,
Friends chase after, clinging.
Going out the gate, I see nothing,
White bones covering the plain.
On the road, a starving woman,
Holding her child, abandons it in the grass.
Turning back, hearing cries and sobs,
Wiping tears, she alone does not return.
Not knowing where she herself will die,
How can both be kept whole?
Urging the horse, I leave them behind,
Unable to bear hearing these words.
Southward, ascending Bàlíng’s bank,
Turning back to gaze toward Cháng’ān.
I understand the man of “Xiàquán,”
Sighing deeply, wounding heart and liver.
Jīngmán is not my homeland,
Why linger here so long?
A double boat sails up the great river,
Dusk saddens my heart.
The mountain ridges hold lingering light,
Cliffs and hollows deepen the shadows.
Foxes dash toward their dens,
Birds fly back to old woods.
Flowing waves stir clear echoes,
Monkeys and apes chant by the shore.
Swift wind brushes my sleeves,
White dew moistens my collar.
Alone at night, unable to sleep,
Adjusting my robe, I rise to play the qin.
Silk and paulownia move human feelings,
For me, it emits mournful sounds.
A traveler’s journey has no end,
Worries and thoughts, strong and hard to bear.
How densely clustered are the northern hills,
Four or five lofty mounds rise there.
I ask whose tombs these might be,
And all reply: "The lords of Hàn."
Gōng and Wén gaze afar at one another,
Yuánlíng mound lush and overgrown.
In the age's decline, chaos arose,
Bandits and thieves like wolves and tigers.
They destroyed more than a handful of earth,
Opened the hidden doors of side chambers.
Pearl caskets parted from jade bodies,
Precious treasures plundered and stolen.
Garden tombs turned to wastelands,
Circular walls without a trace left.
Thick thorns and brambles grow wild,
Paths trodden only by shepherd boys.
Foxes and hares burrow within,
Overgrown and never swept again.
Crumbling mounds are plowed and dug,
Seedlings planted for fields and gardens.
Once they were lords of ten thousand chariots,
Now they are but earth of the hills.
Moved by those words of Yōngmén,
Sorrowful, I mourn for times past.
Autumn winds exhale the breath of shāng,
Rustling, they sweep the woods ahead.
Sunlit birds cease their harmonious songs,
Cold cicadas leave no lingering sound.
White dew congeals at midnight,
Leaves fall, branches stand stark.
Red light hastens to the northern land,
Floating shadows suddenly sink west.
Gazing around, I see nothing,
Only the shade of pines and cypresses.
Solemn, tall paulownia branches,
Fluttering, a lone bird perches.
Looking up, I hear the departing wild goose cry,
Looking down, I hear the cricket's chirp.
A sorrowful man is easily moved to grief,
Touching things only deepens his sadness.
Mounds and hills grow more distant each day,
Entangled thoughts grow ever deeper.
Sorrow comes and turns hair white,
Who says one can bear such grief?
Pacing to and fro in the long wind,
Tears fall and soak my robe.
Slowly, winter and spring fade,
Cold and heat suddenly shift.
My beloved has returned to the deep spring,
Layers of earth forever keep us apart.
Who can understand my private thoughts?
What good does lingering here bring?
Striving to obey the court's command,
I turn my heart back to my former duties.
Gazing at the house, I think of that person,
Entering the room, I recall past moments.
No shadow on curtains or screens,
Only traces of ink remain.
Her lingering fragrance has not yet faded,
Her keepsakes still hang on the wall.
Lost in reverie, as if she still lives,
Restless, startled, anxious, and fearful.
Like birds in a wooded grove,
Once paired, now one alone.
Like fish swimming in a stream,
Side-by-side, parted mid-journey.
Spring wind slips through the cracks,
Morning dew drips from the eaves.
Resting, when can I forget?
Deep sorrow grows day by day.
Perhaps in time it will lessen,
Like Zhuāngzǐ, I may yet strike the pot.
Bright, bright the moon at the window,
Shining on the southern end of my room.
The clear shāng tone answers autumn's arrival,
The humid heat fades with the season.
Chilly, chilly, the cool wind rises,
Only then I feel the summer quilt thin.
It's not that I lack a heavy quilt,
But who will share the winter's cold with me?
No one to share the winter's cold,
How dim the bright moon seems.
Tossing and turning, I gaze at pillow and mat,
The long mat lies empty across the bed.
The empty bed gathers clear dust,
The vacant room invites mournful winds.
Alas, I lack Lǐ's spiritual power,
To glimpse your likeness faintly.
Stroking my robe, I heave a long sigh,
Unaware, tears soak my chest.
Soaking my chest, how can it cease?
Grief rises from within.
Awake or asleep, your form stays in my eyes,
Your voice still lingers in my ears.
Above, I shame Dōngmén Wú,
Below, I愧 Mèng Zhuāngzǐ.
I write poems to express my thoughts,
Yet these thoughts are hard to fully convey.
Fate, what can be done?
Constant sorrow makes me despise myself.
The shining sun moves by heaven's design,
The four seasons alternate and pass.
Chilly, chilly, morning dew congeals,
Fierce, fierce, the evening wind blows harsh.
How can I mourn my virtuous spouse?
Her grace and form forever hidden.
Thinking of this as if yesterday,
Who knew a full year has passed?
Changing clothes to attend court duties,
My grieving heart clings to private rites.
Blankets and curtains spread in the old room,
On the first and fifteenth, I come to offer sacrifice.
How long will these sacrifices last?
The first and fifteenth suddenly end again.
Quilts and robes once removed,
For a thousand years they will not be used again.
Slowly, a full month cycles round,
Sorrowful, ever more pitiable.
Grief stirred by things that come,
Tears fall in response to feeling.
I ride to climb the eastern hill,
Gaze at the tomb, thoughts winding and pained.
Pacing among the ruins and graves,
Wishing to leave, yet unable to bear it.
Pacing, unable to bear leaving,
Wandering, steps hesitant and slow.
Fallen leaves lie by the tomb path,
Withered roots cling to the grave's corner.
A lone soul, solitary and forlorn,
Who knows if spirit exists or not?
Committing my heart to obey the court's command,
Wiping tears, I force myself into the carriage.
Who says the imperial palace is far?
The road ends, yet sorrow remains.
Dawn moon departs from Yúnyáng,
Setting sun rests at Zhūfāng.
Bearing grief, I sail the broad river,
Shedding tears, I gaze at the linked ridges.
With fond remembrance, I think of the noble one,
Deep pain knots within my heart.
When the Way fades, resentment gathers,
When fortune opens, sorrow is expressed.
Her spirit seems ever present,
Her virtuous words never forgotten.
Passing away so easily seems eternal,
Pines and cypresses already stand dense.
Yánzhōu kept his heartfelt promise,
The Chǔ elder cherished orchid fragrance.
What use was unbuckling the sword?
Stroking the tomb only brings self-sorrow.
All my life I doubted such people,
Clarity and obstruction hinder each other.
Reason moved, deep feeling grieves,
Surely not what ordinary understanding grasps.
Fragile and brief, truly pitiable,
Premature death exceeds the common lot.
Once gone, transformed to nothingness,
What use is empty fame?
Raising my voice, tears already shed,
A long sigh, verses left unfinished.
The Zhōu dynasty esteemed bright sacrifices,
The Hàn way revered radiant spirits.
Mournful reverence flourished in ancestral temples,
Revered trees were added to garden tombs.
When I first served under auspicious mandate,
I set foot upon the steps of the royal court.
Attending in retinue, I received heaven’s gaze,
At morning feasts, the sage’s affection flowed.
Early in service, duty to the body weighed heavily,
Late in attainment, life’s caution felt light.
When adversity came, the king’s favor dried up,
When prosperity passed, men repented their forms.
I reproached myself, ashamed of accumulated simplicity,
Yet again I joined with flourishing fortune.
Favor united, not by gradual soaking,
Glory met through chance encounters.
Long I drove under strict, pure regulations,
Morning chariots guarded the forbidden city.
Girded sashes entered the western chambers,
Bowed carriage shafts emerged from eastern fields.
Robes and caps finally sank into darkness,
Tombs and mounds turned lush and green.
Pine winds rushed along the road,
Mountain mist rose over the ridges.
The imperial heart relied on accommodating things,
The people’s thoughts were clothed in songs.
Ten thousand ages recorded in strings and pipes,
A thousand years entrusted to banner tassels.
Not different from the distant age of emperors,
Already joined with the sprouts of decay and transformation.
Young and sturdy, trapped in lonely integrity,
In late twilight, declining secluded chastity.
Setting forth, I lost the easy path,
Returning, cautious of steep inclines.
Silk curtains fluttered by the well’s railing,
Ritual wine as if in life.
Lush, lush are the trees at Xīlíng,
How can one hear songs and pipes?
Fragrant lapels stained with traces of tears,
Graceful sorrow, empty again with feeling.
The jade seat still lies in silence,
How much more so my humble self!
All my life, ritual propriety severed,
I look up to the nation’s pillars.
One morning, all transformations cease,
Still, my old friend’s feelings remain.
Awaiting the time, belonging to rising fortune,
The king’s aide awaits the people’s hero.
Bound in friendship for thirty years,
One bond of life and death.
Hand in hand, we escaped decline and calamity,
Facing the light, we served in prosperous times.
When fortune blocked, honest words were cast aside,
When times were peaceful, jade steps lay level.
Jùn Chōng obtained the talented Yàn,
While you, sir, met a madman.
That man has his clear and muddy waters,
It is not for me to stir up turbidity or clarity.
Parting unwillingly, unable to bear farewell,
Wishing to dispel the sorrow of separation.
Unable to bear a moment’s feeling,
A thousand ages, ten thousand regrets arise.
Enough—the affairs of a lifetime,
Songs and poems fill boxes and baskets.
Along with mutual teasing and jesting,
Often meeting with empty boats.
When will I see Lord Fàn again,
To recount the thoughts of a lifetime?
How many days since parting from you,
The journey’s path not yet a full week.
Not seeing your rosy face changed,
Only imagining the person of a lifetime.
How could I know the day of peaceful song
Was not the morning you laid aside the sè?
Enough—what more have I to sigh?
Ceasing the mortar, mourning the nation’s balance.
Graceful, graceful flying phoenix,
Now flying, now eastward bound.
My friend has gone,
They say, to the old land.
Boats glide gracefully,
To sail up the great river.
Lush, alas, the desolate road,
At times traveled, yet impassable.
Sighing, I cherish and yearn,
As does the noble man.
Long, long the world’s road,
Chaos and separation, many obstacles.
Crossing Dài, traveling the Jiāng,
Far apart in different places.
Wind scatters, clouds disperse,
One parting like rain.
Life is truly hard,
May it not be so for you.
Gazing at the distant road,
Truly I stand on tiptoe, waiting.
Fierce, fierce the winter sun,
Solemn, solemn the chilly wind.
Hidden scales in the deep,
Returning geese soar aloft.
If not the swan or eagle,
Who can soar and fly?
Though I pursue and yearn,
My thoughts find no expression.
Gazing at the eastern road,
Sorrow and grief increase my sighs.
Following those river currents,
Ah, gone without a set time.
The noble man’s sincere oath
Does not change with the times.
And you, my colleague,
In life and death, steadfast.
What to give as parting gift?
I offer this poem.
My heart deeply mourns,
Tears and snivel flow freely.
Alas, you noble man,
How can I not think of you!
Heaven sent down chaos and ruin,
No state was left unsubdued.
I and my friend,
From that capital city.
Ancestral guardians lost and scattered,
Fleeing, we used escape and avoidance.
Moving to Jīngchǔ,
By the banks of the Zhāng.
By the banks of the Zhāng,
We could also feast and dwell.
Harmonious as chí and xūn,
Virtue matched as chariot and sideboard.
Having measured ritual and righteousness,
We finally gained laughter and talk.
May these long days
Not err in their course.
Though said to be without error,
Time does not wait for me.
Hearts united, affairs apart,
Thus there is departure and halt.
Crossing this great river,
Submerging that southern shore.
My thoughts cannot reach,
Now sitting, now rising.
Only that southern shore,
Where the noble man resides.
Long, long is my heart,
Faintly I yearn for him.
People also have a saying,
Not a day without thought.
How much more for one so graceful,
How can I not grieve?
Morning breeze, evening gone,
Entrusting to it our meeting time.
Looking up to the royal house,
Sighing, I heave a long lament.
The good man is abroad,
Who will aid the heavenly officials?
The four regions still blocked,
Sending you back to your fief.
You, returning to your fief,
Become a model for lower states.
Do not say “barbarian border,”
And not revere your virtue.
Be careful in what you preside over,
Follow the excellent rules.
Though the dragon is unused,
Its will is also without error.
Long, long the Dàn and Lǐ rivers,
Lush, that Táng forest.
Though in the same region,
Far, its depths remote.
White colt, distant ambition,
Admonished by the ancients.
Truly, noble man,
Do not distance your heart.
Whether coming or going,
Do not withhold your news.
Graceful are the wild geese,
Flocking by the riverside.
The nobleman sets forth on his journey,
To visit the western neighbor.
Approaching these vast isles,
He thinks of Liáng and Mín.
Your journey is far and distant,
How can you not be diligent?
The nobleman respects beginnings,
Cautious in whom he serves.
Counsel must be wise,
And misguided words corrected with support.
Yánlíng had his deeds,
Aligning with Qiáo and Xī.
The traces left by ancient people,
Are models for future generations.
Since you are cautious in your service,
You also understand subtle signs.
Probing emotions to see their brilliance,
Observing the obvious to know the subtle.
With clear sight and keen hearing,
There is nothing you do not consider.
Dǒng Hè bore a reputation,
How could one not learn from him?
The multitude cannot be concealed,
Do not overly esteem my words.
The Wú Palace led to debate,
Qí and Chǔ brought about calamity.
Success has its essentials,
In the joy of the people's thoughts.
People harbor many taboos,
Concealing them is truly difficult.
Gaze upon that Black River,
Its waters surging and flowing.
The Jiāng and Hàn have their bends,
Truly bringing their blessings.
If the two states falter,
The responsibility lies with you.
Distant are those travelers,
Few can linger long.
Noble indeed is the gentleman,
Different from other adversaries.
Who among men is not diligent?
Do not deepen my worries.
I compose this poem as a gift,
Daring to chant it in the boat.
In the past, I followed the great sovereign,
Arranging the carriage to the southern lands.
Passing by the capital of Fēng and Pèi,
I soared freely with you.
The four seasons push and repel each other,
The late winter wind is cold.
Many guests gather in the grand hall,
Bright lamps shine with fiery light.
Clear songs create wondrous sounds,
A myriad of dances fill the central hall.
Golden vessels hold sweet wine,
Feathered cups pass around freely.
Through the long night, we forget to return,
Briefly indulging in great joy.
Four steeds gallop toward the road,
Sighing with regret, truly endless.
I am burdened with a chronic illness,
Withdrawing to the banks of the clear Zhāng River.
From summer through to deep winter,
Over a hundred days have passed.
Often fearing to wander to Dàizōng,
Never to see old friends again.
How sincere are my dear ones?
They come on foot to comfort me.
Engaging in refined talks day and night,
Sharing feelings and recounting worries and toils.
Soon we must part with farewell words,
As your carriage returns to the western neighbor.
Plain leaves rise with the wind,
Dust flies on the broad road.
Those who depart are like flowing water,
Mourning this separation.
Asking when we will meet again,
You promise me in the bright spring.
Longing and admiration knot unresolved,
I leave you with new poems.
Strive to cultivate noble virtue,
Face north and cherish yourself.
Autumn days bring many sorrows,
Sighing with deep emotion.
All night long, unable to sleep,
I express my thoughts with a wet brush.
Bright lamps shine in the chamber,
The clear wind turns cold and bleak.
White dew coats the front courtyard,
The main gate is tightly closed.
The four seasons push and repel each other,
The year suddenly nears its end.
The brave soldier marches far to war,
Military affairs will be uniquely difficult.
Tears soak my clothes,
How can I not miss my beloved?
The cool wind blows sand and gravel,
The frosty air is gleaming white.
The bright moon shines on crimson tents,
Ornate lamps scatter fiery radiance.
Composing poems in continuous verses,
Through the deepest night, unaware of returning.
The lord is full of bold thoughts,
Elegant writings soar freely.
I, a humble servant, am truly dull,
How can I strive to keep up?
Who says we are far apart?
Only this western palace wall separates us.
Confined by strict prohibitions,
My inner feelings have no way to express.
Thoughts of you sink into my heart,
Long sighs, unable to speak.
Rising and sitting, losing all order,
Three or four times a day, unsettled.
Stepping out of the northern temple gate,
Gazing afar at the western garden park.
Slender willows line the road,
Square ponds hold clear springs.
Light leaves swirl with the wind,
Flying birds, how they flutter!
A troubled heart is easily moved,
Tears fall, mingling with my lapel.
Looking up at the white sunlight,
Bright and high, suspended.
Illuminating all within the eight directions,
All things without bias.
Alone, I harbor deep feelings,
Unable to share in this.
Flowing eastward, the endless water,
Gleaming stones within the stream.
Duckweed and algae grow on its banks,
How delicate and vibrant their beauty!
Gathered to offer in the ancestral temple,
They can be served to honored guests.
Are there no sunflowers in the garden?
Yet these excel, emerging from deep marshes.
Tall and straight, the pine on the mountain,
Rustling, the valley wind.
How fierce the sound of the wind!
How resilient the pine branches!
Ice and frost bring desolation,
Yet it remains upright all year round.
Does it not face severe cold?
The pine and cypress have their inherent nature.
The phoenix gathers on the southern peak,
Lingering by the solitary bamboo roots.
In its heart, it is never satisfied,
Soaring on wings into the purple heavens.
Is it not always toiling hard?
Ashamed to mingle with yellow sparrows.
When will it come as an auspicious sign?
Awaiting a wise and enlightened ruler.
The swift wind sweeps the white sun,
Suddenly it sets behind the western hills.
The round moon's light is not yet full,
Stars gleam brightly in multitude.
The determined man builds a legacy for the ages,
The petty man is also never idle.
Let me wander by night for a while,
Roaming between the twin towers.
The Wénchāng Pavilion rises like clouds,
Facing the wind, towering in the mid-sky.
Spring doves call from flying rafters,
Swift gusts beat against lattice windows.
Thinking of the scholar in his humble hut,
Poor and lowly, truly pitiable.
Wild herbs fail to fill his emptiness,
Even coarse clothes are incomplete.
Filled with passionate sorrow,
He composes writings into verses.
Who is to blame if treasure is discarded?
Héshì bears the fault.
Brushing off his hat, he awaits a true friend,
But who among true friends is not the same?
Fertile fields never yield late harvests,
Rich soil brings abundant years.
Truly, he cherishes the beauty of jade,
Virtue grows and shines over time.
Kinship and friendship lie in sincerity,
What more can be said in these verses?
In early autumn, cool air arises,
In the courtyard trees, leaves slightly fall.
Frost condenses on the jade steps,
Clear winds drift through the flying towers.
Morning clouds do not return to the mountains,
Continuous rain turns into rivers and marshes.
Millet and grain lie fallen in the fields,
How can the farmers gain their harvest?
Those in high places often forget the lowly,
Who can bestow kindness broadly?
Fox-fur robes suffice to ward off winter,
Who then thinks of the clothless guest?
I admire Yánlíngzǐ,
Who did not begrudge his precious sword.
May you calm your heart,
For kinship and friendship’s bond is not shallow.
Sitting upright, tormented by sorrowful thoughts,
I gather my robes and rise to wander west.
Trees burst with spring blossoms,
Clear ponds churn with long-flowing streams.
Among them, a lone mandarin duck,
Cries mournfully, seeking its mate.
I wish to hold this bird,
But alas, I have no light boat.
Wishing to return, I forget the old path,
Looking back, I am filled with sorrow.
A mournful wind whistles by my side,
Xīhé passes, leaving no trace.
Heavy clouds moisten all things,
Why fear the dew’s uneven spread?
Who makes you dwell on so much,
Causing you to harbor countless worries?
Joining the army, I cross Hángǔ Pass,
Driving my horse past the Western Capital.
Mountain peaks rise without limit,
Jīng and Wèi rivers churn clear and muddy.
How grand the imperial abode,
Splendid beyond a hundred cities.
Round towers pierce the floating clouds,
Dew-collectors scrape the pure sky.
The imperial assistant spreads Heaven’s grace,
Throughout the realm, no conflicts arise.
Though strategists love victory,
Preserving the whole state brings noble fame.
A gentleman in lowly position,
Cannot sing praises of virtue.
Dīng Shēng resents serving at court,
Prince Wáng delights in his own pursuits.
Joy and resentment are not true principles,
Harmony and balance truly guide the way.
I visit the emperor at Chéngmíng Lodge,
Then depart to return to my old land.
At dawn I leave the imperial city,
By dusk I pass Shǒuyáng Mountain.
Yī and Luò rivers, broad and deep,
I wish to cross, but there is no bridge.
Boating over great waves,
I lament the long eastern road.
Looking back, I yearn for the city gates,
Stretching my neck, my heart aches within.
Tàigǔ Valley, how vast and empty,
Mountain trees lush and verdant.
Continuous rain muddies my path,
Floodwaters surge and sprawl.
The crossroads are utterly trackless,
I change course and climb the high ridge.
The long slope reaches to clouds and sun,
My horse turns dark and sallow.
Dark and sallow, yet it can advance,
But my thoughts grow tangled and knotted.
Tangled and knotted, progress is hard,
My dear ones are left behind.
I had planned to journey together,
But midway, we could not stay united.
Owls screech at the carriage yoke,
Jackals and wolves block the road.
Flies confuse black and white,
Slander and cunning estrange the close.
Wishing to return, there is no path,
I grasp the reins and halt in hesitation.
What is this hesitation for?
Longing knows no end.
Autumn wind brings a slight chill,
Cold cicadas chirp by my side.
How desolate the plains,
The white sun suddenly hides in the west.
Returning birds fly to tall woods,
Fluttering, beating their wings.
A lone beast runs seeking its herd,
Carrying grass, no time to eat.
Moved by these sights, my heart grieves,
I press my chest and heave long sighs.
What use are these long sighs?
Heaven’s decree goes against me.
How can I forget my own brother,
Gone forever, his form never to return?
His lonely soul hovers over the old city,
His coffin rests in the capital.
The living suddenly pass away,
The departed decay on their own.
A person lives but one lifetime,
Departing like morning dew drying.
Years reach the mulberry and elm,
Echo and shadow cannot be pursued.
I know I am not metal or stone,
Sighing and gasping, my heart grieves.
Heart’s grief stirs my spirit,
Cast it aside, speak no more.
A true man’s will spans the four seas,
Even ten thousand miles is like next door.
If affection does not wane,
Distance deepens the bond day by day.
Why must we share quilt and curtain,
To show earnest care?
Worry and longing breed illness,
Is that not childish tenderness?
In haste, the bond of flesh and blood,
Cannot but hold bitterness and hardship.
What thoughts amid bitterness and hardship?
Heaven’s decree is truly doubtful.
Vainly seeking immortality,
Sōngzǐ has long deceived me.
Sudden change can come in a moment,
Who can hold onto a hundred years?
Parting means never meeting again,
When will we clasp hands once more?
May you cherish your jade-like body,
Together we’ll reach hoary old age.
Wiping tears, I take to the long road,
Taking up my brush, I bid farewell here.
Honored guests fill the city towers,
Sumptuous feasts emerge from the central kitchen.
I and a few companions,
Hold a private feast at the city corner.
Qín zithers evoke western airs,
Qí lutes raise eastern songs.
Dishes come not in vain,
Wine arrives, none remains.
Am I one to fraternize with strangers?
Friends are with me.
A great state has many fine talents,
Like the sea yielding bright pearls.
A gentleman’s righteousness is abundant,
A petty man’s virtue is meager.
Accumulating goodness brings lasting fortune,
Glory and decay soon appear.
Vast and free, that is great integrity,
The worldly are often constrained.
A gentleman comprehends the great Way,
He does not wish to be a worldly scholar.
A fine horse, already trained,
Beautiful robes gleam.
Left hand grasps Fánruò,
Right hand holds Wàngguī.
Wind-swift, lightning-fast,
Treading shadows, chasing flight.
Sweeping across the central plains,
Glancing around, full of grace.
With my beloved companion,
I ride my light carriage.
Southward, scaling long ridges,
Northward, passing clear canals.
Looking up, startling geese fall,
Looking down, I lure deep fish.
Roaming and hunting at leisure,
Such joy, such delight.
Light carriage speeding swiftly,
I rest in those tall woods.
Spring trees bear blossoms,
Leaves spread, casting shade.
Gentle valley breezes,
Blow over my plain zither.
Chirping yellow birds,
Turn to companions, trilling notes.
Moved, my feelings gallop,
Thinking of those I admire.
My heart is sorrowful,
I sigh and chant long.
Vast, mighty river,
Encircles my homeland.
Lush green woods,
Bloom gloriously, shining bright.
Fish and dragons frolic,
Mountain birds flock and fly.
I harness my carriage to roam,
From dawn till dusk, forgetting return.
Thinking of my good friends,
Like thirst, like hunger.
My wishes go unfulfilled,
How sorrowful, how sad.
I rest my troops in the orchid garden,
And graze my horses on Mount Huà.
I shoot my arrows over the level marsh,
And cast my line into the long river.
My eyes follow the returning geese,
My hands strum the five-stringed lute.
Looking up and down, I find contentment within,
My mind wanders in the vast mystery.
I admire that old fisherman,
Who, having caught the fish, forgets the trap.
The man of Yǐng is gone,
With whom can I speak my heart?
In the quiet night, serene and clear,
The bright moon shines upon the porch.
A gentle breeze stirs my robe,
The curtains are drawn high.
Fine wine fills the cup,
But there is none to share the joy.
The lute lies ready to play,
But who will pluck its strings?
I yearn for those of like mind,
Whose fragrance is like orchids.
The fair one is not here,
How can I not sigh forever!
Tall and lofty stands the catalpa tree,
Parasitic upon the southern peak.
Above, it reaches the azure clouds and rainbows,
Below, it overlooks a thousand-fathom valley.
Its place is lonely and perilous,
Where can I set my feet?
Once it faced the morning sun,
With bending branches awaiting the phoenix.
Now it is cut off from worldly use,
Harassed and constrained.
Master Bān and the craftsmen do not regard me,
Yá and Kuàng do not record me.
How then can I become a lute or zither,
By what means can I play wondrous tunes?
Swiftly the three lights race,
How fast the passing of time!
At midnight I cannot sleep,
Grasping my sword, I rise and pace.
Moved by the sigh of Confucius,
I grieve at the brevity of life.
Biàn Hé lies hidden in darkness,
Who can attest to the rare jade?
I hope the divine dragon will come,
Raising its light to shine upon me.
How oppressive is the way of officialdom!
I am confined, sitting in distress.
The tassels and ribbons become fetters,
How can the laws and regulations be overstepped?
Tranquility and leisure are painfully lacking,
Worry and haste are ever abundant.
A good friend presents me with new poems,
Showing me the joys of wandering.
Gracious as a clear breeze sprinkling,
Brilliant as spring blossoms unfolding.
Since ancient times, we shared the same office,
Now we are neighbors in garden cottages.
In declining years, near disgrace and peril,
Perhaps we should both retire our carriages.
With hair unbound beneath dense shade,
Holding a staff by the clear stream.
Attentively listening to orioles singing,
Letting my eyes play with darting fish.
Leisurely nurturing my remaining days,
Finding joy in the evening of life.
The great potter molds all things,
The vast earth endows all living beings.
Brightness and darkness truly differ in appearance,
Stillness and agitation also take distinct forms.
Since I gained awareness,
My ambition has never been fame or merit.
Emptiness and tranquility are what I secretly love,
Literature and learning I have seldom pursued.
Undeservedly bearing duties beyond my capacity,
The sun has already set in the west.
The path is long, but my wisdom is short,
Responsibilities heavy, but my talent light.
Zhōu Rén left behind his rules,
His words are clear and bright.
“Carrying a burden on a carriage” serves as my warning,
At dusk I am vigilant, sitting in alarm.
Thus moved by your kind gift,
I pour out my heartfelt sincerity.
Though the opening lines are warm and beautiful,
Are they not contrary to my true feelings?
The four seasons alternate in succession,
The hanging images roll and unfold in turn.
Suddenly late spring returns again,
With gentle winds accompanying the season.
Looking down upon clear springs gushing,
Gazing up at fine trees spreading.
I wander around my humble garden,
Looking west toward the cottage of Guǎngwǔ.
Though noble, one should not forget frugality,
In possession, one can preserve emptiness.
To steady customs lies in simplicity,
Why imitate blocking the view with screens?
In the past, we served together in the same office,
Now we both dwell in garden ruins.
My private wish is to join you in old age,
Roaming freely, harmonizing lute and books.
Raising cups beneath lush shade,
Hand in hand, we linger together.
Why need we discard our physical forms?
Forgetting the trap lies in catching the fish.
Oh, glorious sage-like age,
The literature of the time belongs to Jìn.
Receiving the mandate from Heaven,
It embraces all the worthy and wise.
The gates of heaven have opened,
Chénghuá Palace is rebuilt again.
Brilliantly above,
Gathered are only the talented.
Splendid is Féng Shēng,
His wise words truly guide.
Heaven protects and stabilizes you,
No virtue fails to shine.
Your heart strides into profound vastness,
Your will soars to lofty heights.
Following that Chénghuá,
Your countenance is radiant.
Alas, people like me,
Fold our wings by the riverbank.
By fate, we gather here,
Flying up from the south.
Emerging from the deep valley,
To join you in the same grove.
Our mutual feelings reflect each other,
Transcending things, we understand each other’s hearts.
People also say,
True friendship is indeed hard to find.
There is the cap with its tassels,
A tune played once in a thousand years.
Now you and I,
Across ages, share this joy.
Our bond can cut metal and stone,
Our spirit fragrant as autumn orchids.
The multitudes are not yet pacified,
The Emperor therefore toils diligently.
I seek virtuous governance,
To extend it over a hundred li.
All say you are harmonious,
To bring order to the people.
Thus you turn your gaze northward,
To respond and extol the Emperor’s blessings.
In past travels,
Our affection was deep and enduring.
Though it is said not yet fully blended,
It has already been three years.
At court, accompanying the splendid canopy,
On outings, following the vermilion carriage.
Side by side like steeds with matched bits,
Treading the same path, sharing the dust.
Since you received your command,
The four steeds stretch their necks.
Following the road, striding far,
Soaring on tracks, galloping high.
Auspicious clouds support your substance,
Clear breezes bear your shadow.
Alas, I long for you,
Your journey stretches far and wide.
Fortune and misfortune differ,
Adversity and success part ways.
I am like spring blossoms,
You follow like autumn sunlight.
You are about to leave me,
Ascending to the northern frontier.
If not for thoughts of you,
For whom would my heart grieve?
I formerly served as Tutor to the Crown Prince,
Jiǎ Chāngyuān served for many years as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary in the Eastern Palace.
I went out to fill the post of Chief Steward to the Prince of Wú,
And in the sixth year of Yuánkāng entered the capital as Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat.
Duke Lǔ presented me with a poem,
And I composed this poem in reply.
In ancient times there were sovereigns,
Who first succored the common people.
They preceded heaven in creating things,
And received the glorious mandate.
Descending to the many lords,
They alternately declined and rose.
Far distant is the ancient past,
Yet the rise and fall have their signs.
In the final years of the Hàn,
The imperial order was torn asunder.
The great stars hid their light,
The metal tiger practiced its nature.
Brave ministers galloped forth,
Righteous men rushed to uphold their integrity.
They left their posts and brandished spears,
Speaking of plans to aid the royal house.
The chaos of the royal house,
Left no state unruined.
Like those falling shadows,
They could never be raised again.
Then he looked upon three sages,
To govern these people.
Though opening the land was difficult,
They changed things and received heaven’s favor.
Thus came the Wèi,
Establishing palaces in the heavenly capital.
Wú indeed soared like a dragon,
Liú also stood firm as a mountain.
Weapons of war were raised high,
Ritual vessels were stored away.
The people toiled, armies rose,
The state grew lax, yet victory entered.
Heaven wearied of hegemonic virtue,
The yellow mandate announced its flaw.
Litigation turned away from Wèi,
Songs of praise went to Jìn.
Chénliú returned to its fief,
Our emperor ascended to the throne.
Yōng and Mín bowed their heads,
The three rivers changed their tribute.
Glorious and grand was Jìn,
Vastly dwelling over all the land.
Responding to heaven and man,
There was orderly blessing.
Only you, Grand Steward,
Brilliantly assisted the two founders.
You gave birth to a great heir,
Continuing the legacy in Lǔ.
The eastern court was established,
Your fine reputation towered high.
I sought virtuous brilliance,
To aid in harmony and unity.
The Duke of Lǔ arrived,
His ceremonial robes flowing gracefully.
Thinking fondly of the crown prince,
He strode high into Chénghuá.
In the past I reached this place,
A time when I was a lowly official.
And you lingered here,
Same forest, different branches.
Different in age, alike in will,
Different in dress, close in righteousness.
Roaming across three springs,
Affection firm as two autumns.
Reverently receiving the imperial command,
Going out and coming in without fault.
Going to serve in the feudal court,
Returning to walk in the purple palace.
Ascending and descending the secret pavilion,
My garments shone with glory.
Who says I was not fearful?
Looking up, I revered the bright majesty.
Parting is easy,
But joining hands is truly hard.
Thinking of those fine past wanderings,
Here I sigh forever!
Your words are moving,
Leaving behind this literary piece.
Luxuriant are those lofty phrases,
Like jade in its brilliance.
Only the Hàn had trees,
That never crossed the border.
Only the south has gold,
All states sing of it.
The people’s likes and dislikes,
The reckless and the cautious sharpen the sage.
Models exist in the past,
I have heard your command.
Dragged by the world, entangled in the net of the times,
I harness words to journey far.
Is the farewell drink with different clans?
Kinsfolk, younger and elder brothers.
Gentle and lovely, the thoughts of those who stay,
Twisted and heavy, the feelings of the wanderer.
At dawn I leave peaceful sleep,
Awake, words bring tears to my collar.
Parting ways by the side of the tall forest,
Waving sleeves at Wànshǐ Pavilion.
Gazing long for distant scenes,
Inclining my ear to savor the lingering sounds.
Returning south, I rest at Yǒng'ān,
Heading north, I pause at Chéngmíng.
Yǒng'ān has tracks of yesterday,
Chéngmíng, you abandon me.
Looking up and down, I grieve in the sparse woods,
Filled with emotion, bearing bitterness.
Recalling past joys, the end is severed,
Mourning what comes, worries form threads.
Feeling the sorrow of parting, wings slacken,
Thinking of return, joy follows the shore.
The great fire holds crimson light,
Accumulated brightness shines from the south.
The moon leaves the metal tiger,
Píngyì exhales heavy shadows.
A bleak wind opposes the season’s order,
Bitter rain becomes a downpour.
Morning outings forget light feathers,
Evening rest recalls heavy quilts.
Moved by things, a hundred worries arise,
Entangled, they seek each other.
With you separated by the screen wall,
The screen wall is deep and divides.
Form and shadow, vast and unconnected,
What I rely on are voice and sound.
Voice and sound grow distant day and night,
How can they comfort my heart?
Morning outings in layered cities,
Evening rest returning to duty lodgings.
Swift thunder stirs at midnight,
Startling lightning flashes through the night.
Dark clouds drape the vermilion pavilion,
Shaking winds press on carved windows.
Heavy rain overflows long gutters,
Yellow floods soak the steps.
Lingering shadows knot unresolved,
Broad roads turn into channels.
Sunken crops drown in Liáng and Yǐng,
Refugees flee against Jīng and Xú.
With tender thoughts of my homeland,
Might I not become a fish!
Lord Gù embodies bright virtue,
Pure winds have already swept by.
Beginning your path assisting the feudal lord,
Changed appointment to pacify the southern borders.
Beating drums beyond the Five Ridges,
Raising banners ten thousand miles away.
Distant achievements do not scorn the small,
Establishing virtue does not lie in greatness.
How can high mountains be scaled?
Vast seas are still like winding belts.
Melancholy, I gaze at your flying carriage,
Craning my neck, watching your returning banners.
A lone beast longs for its old marsh,
A parted bird grieves for its former forest.
Gracefully wandering officials,
Toiling hard, for whom is the heart?
As if by the north bank of Gǔshuǐ,
Lovely at the south of Kūnshān.
Soul and spirit cherish this land,
Vigor and spirit like flying and sinking.
Awake or asleep, no peace or joy,
Wishing to speak of what I admire.
Feeling the hardship of your return journey,
Makes my longing and admiration deep.
How can I get forget-return grass,
To plant on my back and lapel?
These words are not empty,
For the longing bird has a mournful song.
Purifying myself, I ascend the secret pavilion,
The secret pavilion, lofty and profound.
All morning managing documents,
By dusk, no time to close my eyes.
Harnessing words to tour bright sacrifices,
Paying respects in prayers for the year.
Wandering free in the spring king’s garden,
Pacing back and forth through a thousand acres of fields.
Winding channels curve along narrow paths,
Flowing waves support straight ridges.
Fine grains hang with heavy ears,
Fragrant trees burst into bloom at the top.
I am truly a man of water country,
Reining my horse by the clear abyss.
Sorrowful, many distant thoughts,
Step by step, they become this piece.
I left home to travel far,
A long, long journey of three thousand miles.
The capital is full of wind and dust,
My plain robe has turned to black.
I cultivate myself, mourning sorrow and hardship,
Thinking of those who share my feelings.
Deep thoughts leave my heart,
Buried joys remain unstirred.
Buried joys are hard to revive,
A troubled heart—who will soothe it?
I wish to borrow the wings of returning geese,
To fly back to the shores of the Zhèjiāng River.
In the southeast, there is a longing wife,
Her long sighs fill the secluded chamber.
If asked why she sighs,
Her beloved is far at the edge of the sky!
Long has he been away as an official, not returning,
The mountains and rivers are vast and distant.
Like the stars Shēn and Shāng, we are apart,
No news reaches across the void.
Partings and reunions are not constant,
Like the bowstring and its notch.
May you preserve your body like metal or stone,
To comfort my long hunger and thirst!
Once, with a few companions,
We roamed south of Chénghuá.
Flapping wings on the same branch,
We flew off to different pursuits.
Without wings to ride the wind,
I linger, guarding the old grove.
Who will share my fervent feelings?
I wish to express my admiration.
Setting off from the clear Luò River’s bend,
Driving my horse north of the great river.
I stand gazing at the northern road,
Long, distant, deep, and far.
Parting has always brought sorrow,
Men of purpose often bear bitter hearts.
Sad feelings knot by the river,
Bitter words drift with the wind.
Ashamed I have no ornate jade to give,
Let good news replace precious gold.
You, sir, excel in far-reaching plans,
With sincere words, send kind tidings.
Onward, I lament the long road,
Grieved by the haste of parting.
Pointing the way, sorrow abounds,
Facing the cup, joy falls short.
I am like water flowing west,
You stand firm as an eastern peak.
Fervent departures stir emotions,
Lingering stays nurture affection.
How can we walk hand in hand,
Through hardships, side by side?
From the beginning of creation,
Heaven and Earth were in chaos.
Then came humankind,
Fúxī was the first ruler.
He used knotted cords to spread culture,
The eight trigrams formed writing.
Vast were the nine regions,
Divided into territories.
Shénnóng succeeded as king,
Xuānyuán continued the line.
He demarcated lands with borders,
And enfeoffed his many sons.
Xià and Yīn followed in succession,
The Zhōu dynasty carried on the sacrifices.
Like continuous melon vines,
The six states stood opposed.
The strong Qín annexed them all,
Swallowing the four corners.
Zǐyīng faced the coffin in surrender,
Hàn’s founder received the mandate.
Líng and Xiàn were weak and feeble,
In darkness, they declined.
Three heroes stood like a tripod’s legs,
Sūn opened the southern Wú.
What was southern Wú?
A usurper who claimed kingship.
The great Jìn unified the realm,
Its benevolent influence spread far.
The false Sūn offered jade in surrender,
Presenting his land and returning to the border.
Graceful and long-winged,
It soared over the river.
Who is this long-winged one?
I speak of you, Lù Shēng.
A crane cries in the nine marshes,
Its voice still carries far.
How much more from a coastal corner,
Your fame spreads to the capital.
Answering the summons with banners,
You spread your wings in the ministerial court.
Chosen for the crown prince’s service,
Truly selected for excellence.
Brilliant like a scarlet phoenix,
You came from southern hills.
Shining in lofty righteousness,
In dark crown and crimson robes.
Like orchids and iris,
You exude their fragrance.
A feudal lord guarding the realm,
Aiding our capital’s house.
Returning to your homeland,
The emperor’s brother acts as support.
Some say a state official
Loses the path of purity.
But you are serene,
Calm and at ease.
The court is pure,
Talented men are invited.
Selected for a fine post,
You moved from the state.
Joining ranks with many dragons,
Gloriously assisting the advisor.
Leisurely in the palace offices,
With brush at ear in splendid halls.
In the past, you and I,
Were close in the eastern court.
Though treated as guests by protocol,
Our bond was like friends and colleagues.
We delighted in strings and pipes,
Beating drums, dancing to Sháo music.
On bright days and clear moons,
We strolled hand in hand, carefree.
Since I left the group,
Two years have passed.
Though we seldom meet face to face,
Our deep affection remains.
You soar high,
Truly comforting my heart.
I speak these words as a poem,
Awaiting your kind reply.
To elevate its height,
Its layers must be solid.
The handle of virtue’s establishment
Is none other than peace and constancy.
Sweet in the south,
Cross north, it becomes bitter orange.
I admire your sharp brilliance,
Unfalling, unbroken.
The beauty of the southeast,
Once was Yánzhōu.
Illustrious and sincere, Lù Shēng,
Now has few peers.
Stirring scales in the southern sea,
Washing wings in clear streams.
Graceful in the literary forest,
At ease among ancient texts.
Jade gains luster from polishing,
Sui jade shines with radiance.
You rose to the capital,
You served in the crown prince’s palace.
Savoring your pure elegance,
Tasting your fragrant style.
The more I swim in it, the wider it becomes,
The more I draw from it, the deeper it flows.
What does Kūnlún Mountain hold?
It holds jade and min stone.
With you as colleagues,
We are all close ministers.
I tread through pale autumn,
You ascend into spring’s youth.
Ashamed I lack maturity,
I stand among the ever-new.
Vast and great is this nation,
Our homeland, our mulberry and catalpa.
Noble and serene is this man,
A model for the southern land.
The emperor said, “You are harmonious,”
A lord among kings and ministers.
Bowing to follow the command,
What care, what joy?
My carriage is readied,
My horses are harnessed.
Stars arrayed, I set off at dawn,
Greasing axles, fitting linchpins.
Graceful in the two palaces,
Pacing through hall gates.
Clear wine remains unsavored,
Who will soothe hunger and thirst?
Once, in private favor,
You gave me orchids and iris.
Now you go east,
What shall I give in return?
Every moment is precious,
Could it be without fine jade?
That admirable Lù Shēng,
With whom I can converse heart-to-heart.
Mì Shēng was born in Shànfù,
Zǐ Qí governed Dōng'ē.
Tóngxiāng established enduring deeds,
Wǔchéng spread the sound of lute and song.
Swift steeds gallop on level roads,
Hidden dragons leap in vast waves.
At twenty, stepping into high office,
At thirty, governing Sānhé.
Their fame fragrant as autumn orchids,
Their writings radiant as spring blossoms.
Merely admiring their natural grace,
How could one speak of worldly honors?
Kūnshān accumulates jade and gems,
Great halls are built with many materials.
Swimming fish gather in divine ponds,
Spreading wings, they aspire to heavenly steps.
Who can melt the fragrant orchids?
Good governance relies on the worthy and able.
Kings and nobles weary of lofty rites,
Turn their steps to the pure Xiàntái.
The inchworm's bend is but a small retreat,
The dragon's soar heralds great arrival.
Unite hearts to assist the sage's age,
Exert all strength to praise prosperity!
Lǎnglíng Duke Hé Jìngzǔ,
Is Xián's maternal cousin;
National Academy Chancellor Wáng Wǔzǐ,
Is the grandson of Xián's paternal aunt,
Both esteemed in the world for their illustrious virtue,
Xián respects and honors them,
Affectionate as siblings,
In principle, they are teachers and friends.
After Duke Hé became Palace Attendant,
Wǔzǐ soon also attained office,
The two worthies delighted in each other,
And Xián also celebrated for them.
Yet I regret my own dullness and inadequacy,
Though I wish for their close bond,
I have no means to follow them;
Repeated attempts proved futile,
And there are family hardships besides.
I compose a poem to express my feelings,
To present to them thus.
Sun and moon illuminate the great purity,
Constellations shine in the Purple Palace.
Glorious is the great Jìn court,
Brilliantly opening the imperial gates.
My brother has soared like a phoenix,
And the prince has taken flight like a dragon.
