Twin phoenixes roam orchid isles,
Two suns cast clear radiance.
Hand in hand ascending jade steps,
Seated together attending crimson curtains.
Golden earrings adorn wise caps,
Resplendent, displaying noble grace.
Such honor is not for the common,
The close bond is what my heart desires.
Do I not aspire to lofty traces?
But the unicorn's hoof is distant, hard to follow.
By the river, no fragrant bait is cast,
Why vainly guard the islet?
Withered leaves await the wind to scatter,
Soon I shall part from you.
Parting from you, how can I not grieve?
Useless, I should speak of returning.
Returning to my humble thatched hut,
Finding joy in the Way, forgetting hunger.
Advancing, I bring no remedy,
Retreating, I care for my private concerns.
I only hope for magnified beauty,
The royal rule daily grows clear and peaceful.
Gleaming white silk threads,
Woven into cold maiden's garments.
Though the cold maiden is exquisitely skilled,
She cannot hold the shuttle and loom.
Cold weather tells of time's swift passage,
Especially when wild geese fly south.
The tailor takes up knife and ruler,
Abandoning me suddenly as if discarding.
If others do not seek from themselves,
What can the world's scholars hope for?
Moreover, having already breakfasted at court,
How would they know my hunger?
Far, far you journey on,
Lonely, I remain alone.
How can mountains and rivers be crossed?
The long road stretches ten thousand miles apart.
The capital abounds with glamour,
Resplendent are the city's daughters.
Elegant steps sway slender waists,
Artful smiles reveal bright teeth.
Such beauty is truly admirable,
Faded and lowly, how could I compare?
From afar, I receive your caring words,
Grateful for kindness beyond expectation.
After crossing the sea, water is hard to admire,
After roaming forests, sights are hard to marvel.
Beauty values timeliness,
Morning blossoms fear the day's late hour.
Bright and fair is that lovely maiden,
Glowing with spring's radiant bloom.
Xīchéng excels in elegant dances,
Zǒngzhāng abounds with clear melodies.
Reed pipes sound from crimson lips,
Vermilion strings circle pale wrists.
Light skirts flutter like lightning,
Double sleeves scatter like mist.
Splendid countenance fills embroidered tents,
Melancholy notes rise to the Milky Way.
A true connoisseur is rare in this world,
Who but you can appreciate this?
Abandoning the North Star,
I inquire of this dark dragon's brilliance.
At dusk, what more can be said?
Flowers fallen are destined to be cheap.
Distant roads may have an end,
Brief parting breeds longing for long reunion.
Cherishing kindness, I linger on your journey,
Raising thoughts while facing the wine cup.
The southern ford has no ferry,
The northern shore lacks bridge or beam.
Spirit flies together with the departed,
Body remains grieving like Shēn and Shāng.
If paths and tracks diverge,
The Oxherd cannot pull the cart.
Journeying across long rivers,
Drifting, braving wind and dust.
Flowing waves strike winding shores,
Sorrowful winds press upon hillside brush.
Long roads leave endless traces,
Wells and towns follow one another.
A hundred cities each with different customs,
A thousand households, none good neighbors.
Old joys are hard to reunite,
How can native soil be falsely dear?
Longing for the mulberry and catalpa town,
Faintly seeing familiar faces before my eyes.
Slowly, day and night grow distant,
Yearning, I harbor bitterness and toil.
Kǔn bows his head:
Your letter and poems,
filled with bitter words of sorrow,
express the profound meaning of enduring hardship.
I hold and ponder them repeatedly,
unable to put them down.
I sigh with grief,
yet rejoice with delight.
In my youth,
I never restrained myself.
I admired from afar Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ's doctrine of equalizing all things,
and praised from nearby Ruǎn Jí's unrestrained freedom.
I wondered how distinctions of favor and neglect could arise?
How could sorrow and joy come about?
But since recent turmoil,
I have been trapped in rebellion and chaos.
The state is shattered, my family lost,
relatives and friends have perished.
Leaning on my staff, I wander and chant—
then all sorrows descend upon me.
Sitting alone in solitude,
grief and indignation gather together.
Occasionally, we still raise cups together, knees touching,
turning tears into laughter,
dispelling a lifetime's accumulated misery,
seeking a moment's fleeting joy.
It is like suffering from a chronic illness for years
and hoping to cure it with a single pill—
how could that be possible?
Talent is born into the world,
and the world truly needs talent.
The jade of Héshì,
how could it shine only in the hands of Yǐng?
The pearl of night radiance,
how could it be enjoyed solely in the palm of Suí?
The treasures of the world
should be shared with all under heaven.
But on the day of parting,
I cannot help but feel regret and sorrow!
Only then did I realize that Lǎodān and Zhuāng Zhōu's teachings were empty and false,
and that Sìzōng's actions were reckless.
In the past, the swift steed leaned against the shaft on the slopes of Wú,
neighing loudly to Liáng and Yuè—
it was a matter of being understood or not.
Bǎilǐ Xī was foolish in Yú but wise in Qín—
it was a matter of meeting the right opportunity or not.
Now you have met your opportunity,
so strive forward!
I have not paid attention to literary pursuits for over twenty years.
Long neglect leads to lack of order,
but I imagine you wish for a response,
so I present a piece in accordance with your intent,
merely to highlight the added beauty of your coming poems.
Kǔn bows his head again and again.
When misfortune first arrived,
the yang line was at six.
The heavenly signs showed the pillar collapsing,
the earthly vessel overturned.
Conflict and chaos spread wildly,
hordes of demons vied fiercely.
Fire ravaged the divine land,
great floods swept the Huá region.
That millet grows dense,
that grain sprouts lush.
I mourn for our august Jìn,
pain piercing my eyes.
Heaven and earth have no heart,
all things share the same path.
Disaster for the wicked goes unproven,
fortune for the good proves empty.
Rebels hold entire cities,
the righteous lack a single intact capital.
Blossoms fall in summer,
poisonous weeds flourish in winter.
Like that tortoise-shell jade,
stored in a box yet destroyed.
The talk of straw dogs—
is it not most fitting?
Alas, I am weak,
unable to bear the burden.
Faults and offenses remain clear,
yet honors and favors are repeatedly added.
Authority I could not establish,
calamity spread and evil multiplied.
Loyalty perished for the state,
filial piety failed at home.
These accumulated sins
are like those mountains and rivers.
These deep offenses
can never be erased.
Harmonious old marriages,
charming new unions.
Carrying provisions, leading the weak,
crawling and rushing like stars.
Before your carriage halted,
my gate had already fallen.
Two clans both perished,
three evils took root together.
Forever shamed before the old orphans,
eternally bearing the wronged souls.
Tall and solitary trunk,
standing alone without companion.
Green leaves lush and dense,
tender branches slender and rare.
In morning I pluck your fruit,
at evening I strip your stems.
Stems emerald and abundant,
pearls overflowing the bowl.
Truly they dispel my sorrow,
easing urgent grief with respite.
Must you depart?
The courtyard empty, emotions full.
What is emptiness and fullness?
Orchids and cassia transplanted.
Flourishing that spring grove,
withering these autumn thorns.
There is a bird soaring in flight,
with no leisure to rest.
It perches only on paulownia,
eats only from bamboo.
Forever folding eastern wings,
grooming western pinions.
I respect and honor it,
abandoning joy and leaving duty.
Music is played for appreciation,
flavors prized for rarity.
Writing clarifies speech,
speech expresses spirit.
With your departure,
the four beauties do not arrive.
Clear wine overflows the cup,
strings and flutes gather dust.
Plain scrolls remain unopened,
curtains lack conversational guests.
My virtue left solitary,
my neighbors missing.
Glorious Duàn Shēng,
emerging from obscurity, ascending to heights.
Endowed with loyalty, walking in trust,
martial valor and literary brilliance.
Banners and bows gleaming,
carriages and horses lofty.
Then wielding long reins,
these are the bridles and bits.
What shall I give you?
Devote your heart to the public court.
How to express my feelings?
Lifting my head, I sing a long ballad.
In my hand is a hanging jade,
originally from the Qióng of Jīngshān.
Only that Tàigōng Wàng,
once an old man by the Wèi river.
How inspired was Dèng Shēng,
traveling a thousand lǐ to seek him.
At Báidēng, he was fortunate to have Qū'nì,
at Hóngmén, he relied on Liú Hóu.
Chóng'ěr employed the five worthies,
Xiǎobái made Shègōu his minister.
If one can honor the two overlords,
why ask about faction or enmity?
At midnight I stroke my pillow and sigh,
longing to roam with those few men.
I have long been in decline,
why do I not dream of Zhōu?
Who says the sage understands limits,
knowing fate thus free from worry?
Xuānní grieved at catching the qílín,
weeping at the western hunt, Kǒngqiū.
Achievements not yet established,
the sunset suddenly flows west.
Time does not wait for me,
passing like floating clouds.
Vermilion fruit falls in fierce wind,
lush blossoms drop in pure autumn.
On narrow roads the canopy tilts,
startled steeds break the twin shafts.
Who would have thought steel tempered a hundred times
could become soft enough to wind around a finger.
Your former subordinate, Attendant Gentleman of the Ministry of Works Lú Chén, bows his head in deepest guilt, deepest guilt!
Chén is by nature weak and inadequate,
rarely fit for the responsibilities of the present age.
Following his natural disposition,
he has always preferred quiet and withdrawal.
Among trees, he lacks the quality of useless timber;
among geese, he is wanting in the gift of a fine cry.
He differs from Qú Bóyù in his reluctance to serve;
he is more foolish than Níng Wǔzǐ in his simplicity.
Though the master craftsman occasionally glanced his way,
he could not avoid being cast aside like the worthless guest.
I have often reflected on this myself:
by a turn of fortune and opportunity,
I was fortunate enough to be received into your service.
Since I began attending upon your noble presence,
five years have now passed.
No illustrious achievements have been shown,
yet the ridicule of those who watch for faults has become evident.
Your great and refined nature is all-embracing,
your capacity vast as mountains and marshes.
Moreover, the treatment and reception you have granted me have been increasingly generous;
your sincere affection has grown ever more intimate.
You have included me in strategic deliberations,
and admitted me to the joys of private feasts.
The depth of your regard,
has been like that for your own flesh and blood.
To be your intimate friend—
even the ancients had no greater example.
In the past, Niè Zhēng gave his life in response to Yán Suì's regard;
Jīng Kē was drawn by Yān Dān's righteousness.
Moved by such spirit and resolve,
they did not regret laying down their lives.
Though they did not attain the highest principle of integrity,
one may say they came close.
And if it is said they had feeling,
then who, having such feeling, would not cherish it?
Therefore, from the day I entrusted myself to you,
I resolved to share both peril and safety with you.
But affairs have gone against my wishes.
I am about to disgrace myself by taking up a post abroad,
and thus must depart from your side,
withdrawing from your court and administration.
When the root is the same but the branches differ,
Yáng Zhū was moved to sorrow;
when what begins in plain white ends in deepest black,
Mò Dí shed tears.
At the moment of separation and parting,
all is cause for sighs and lament.
The path that leads to such emotion
is perhaps forced upon one here.
Must one wait until standing by the roadside to then cry out long and loud,
or see the parting silk before one can sob and sigh?
Therefore, looking up, I recall past affection;
looking down, I consider my present circumstance.
Moved by what remains, mindful of what is lost,
touching things, I am filled with longing.
The *Yì* says:
"Writing does not fully express speech;
speech does not fully express ideas."
Thus, writing is not the instrument that fully conveys speech,
nor is speech the tool that fully conveys ideas.
How much more, then, may speech fail to reach the fullness of meaning,
and writing fail to reach the fullness of speech?
I cannot bear this oppressive distress!
I respectfully offer a poem,
though it is hardly sufficient to extol your great virtue,
but only to pour forth what is in my heart.
If you, my lord, would generously bestow great kindness,
and thus fulfill your profound grace,
granting me the sound of your cough or spit—
to console me in this feeling of separation—
then it would be as if the music of Xiánchí were repaid with the songs of Běilǐ,
or luminous pearls required with fish eyes.
This is Chén's wish,
though not what he dares to hope for.
Chén bows his head in deepest guilt, deepest guilt.
Profound and wise is the emperor,
Continuing the glory of the Jìn dynasty.
He revives what had slackened,
Illuminating and expanding distant harmonies.
Those who come are met with grace,
Those who arrive find peace and order.
The Three Terraces shine brightly,
The Four Peaks rise even loftier.
Yī Zhì assisted the Shāng,
Shān Fǔ aided the Zhōu.
They greatly relieved hardships,
Responding to and extolling the king’s virtue.
If not for their exceptional virtue,
How could they be peers across generations?
Adding loyalty and steadfastness,
They displayed their splendid plans.
My humble clan,
Once received great kindness.
Bound by marriage ties,
Established for generations.
Our righteousness shared joys and sorrows,
Our affections rose and fell together.
Who says it was not harmonious?
Like music in perfect accord!
The royal house lost its armies,
Private families were scattered and displaced.
We hoped for your return,
Seeing danger but disregarding hardship.
This wish was not fulfilled,
Midway hindered and overturned.
Looking up, I grieve for past intentions,
Looking down, I reflect on my own faults.
The great wheel of fate turns,
Fine days pass by.
Gazing at the sun and moon,
Swiftly they rise and set.
Reflecting on the present, I recall the past,
Words remain, thoughts linger.
Speaking of it as if yesterday,
Suddenly it becomes the distant past.
What is the distant past?
Those who are gone grow ever more distant.
Gentle and respectful people,
Careful to the end as at the start.
Reading their遗留 words,
Pitying the orphaned and destitute.
Like that bent tree,
Creepers spread over it.
Wonderful are the creepers,
Finding support on the bent tree.
Leaves not like clouds spreading,
Flowers not like stars shining.
Though likened to Biàn Hé,
My substance is not the jade of Jīng.
Cherished like Yóu Liáng,
Yet lacking the steeds Jì and Lù.
Support has been sincere,
Affection has been close;
Praising this clumsy and lowly one,
Matching him with fine steeds.
Harmony in assistance was not achieved,
Good plans were not presented.
Not hoping to match Hú and Zhào,
But to be among the five ministers.
What of the five ministers?
Through hardships and countless trials.
Personally experiencing dangers,
Treading dark and distant paths.
Righteousness born of deep kindness,
Bonds strengthened by intimacy.
Devoted and wholehearted,
Identifying as one, not as another.
In past leisurely days,
I sought profound principles.
Admiring their spirit,
Making them men of integrity.
Emotions arise from the body,
Feelings stir from emotions.
Choices without essential aim,
Poverty or success ends here.
By Yóu Yú’s few words,
The Qín people were awed.
Jīn Rìdī’s loyal service,
Made his fame ring in the Hàn.
Majestic was the Fǔjūn,
A crown among ancient worthies.
Coming to govern Yōudū,
Relieving its extreme suffering.
Suffering relieved,
Enemies defeated, people prosperous.
Erroneously placing this weary servant,
In a high court position.
Above, I fear the great responsibility,
Below, I rejoice in the generous favor.
Truly revering the lofty and bright,
How dare I forget my duty?
Observe the returning crow feeding its parent,
Even among flying birds.
Who are these people,
Who can bear such a heart?
Often relying on mountains and seas,
Hoping to glimpse heights and depths.
Gazing afar at survival and demise,
Remotely forming flights and sinkings.
The long tether already fastened,
I shall depart and move on.
Gathering traces westward,
Bearing sorrow looking east.
How can the road be far?
Yet not a step away.
How not to travel day and night?
But the path is full of dew.
The delicate dodder vine,
Clings to the pine’s tip.
Receiving moisture from the great trunk,
Basking in sunlight on lush branches.
Shallow roots hard to secure,
Weak stems easily wither;
Holding that delicate nature,
Facing this rushing storm.
Delicate nature truly frail,
The rushing storm encountered,
Who says words are refined?
Their essence lies in appreciated meaning.
Not seeing the fish caught,
Also forgetting the bait.
Leaving the physical form behind,
Entrusting it to deep understanding.
Ancient people nurtured their will,
Retreating to mountains, hidden by benches.
Gazing up at red cliffs,
Bathing below in green waters.
Not seeking harmony,
Naturally aligning with all beauty.
My passionate distant traces,
Feel ashamed before lofty aims.
Thus creating divergent views,
Liver and gall as distant as Chǔ and Yuè.
Only with broad perspective,
All differences follow one track.
Since life and death are equal,
What distinction between glory and shame?
Dwelling at the mysterious root,
Vast and without entanglements.
Fortune is the start of misfortune,
Misfortune becomes fortune’s step.
Heaven and earth wax and wane,
Cold and heat revolve.
Fūchāi’s line ended,
The flaw lay in defeating Qí.
Gōujiàn became hegemon,
His fortune rose from Kuàijī.
Far-reaching is great understanding,
Relying solely on the Dào.
The form may not be at ease,
But the spirit is ever free.
Like a river’s flow,
Like an abyss’s capacity.
Above, expanding the pillar’s strength,
Below, meeting the people’s hopes.
Strolling leisurely by the city wall,
On a leisurely day, wandering at ease.
Gazing north to the desert’s edge,
Looking south to the old capital’s road.
Level plains drawing long streams,
Ridges and peaks raising lush trees.
The central plains swept by swift winds,
Mountain hollows rising with clouds and mist.
A wanderer always grieves in heart,
Lifting eyes increases eternal longing.
Good companions not obtained together,
To whom can I express my feelings?
Thinking of the ways of worthy men of old,
Thus preserving ancient duties.
The northern borders abound with knightly spirit,
Is it only due to the land’s firmness?
Lǐ Mù guarded the border city,
Barbarians from the wilderness feared the south.
Zhào Shē secured the frontiers,
The Qín people abandoned northern plans.
A traveler under lenient rule,
Offering service as time allows.
Regretting my clumsy and slow nature,
Vainly troubling the flying son’s carriage.
Already relieved of burdens,
Shamefully positioned to govern the common people.
If barely avoiding blame,
What leisure to seek people’s praise?
Ní Kuān was demoted for poor performance,
Yet finally excelled in tax collection.
Hé Wǔ was not illustrious,
But his benevolent legacy remained after departure.
Not hoping to match the ancients,
My own weakness is innate.
Why compose these words?
Only because of those two men.
A lofty tower is not built from a single timber,
A precious fur robe is not made from one fox's armpit.
Many talents accomplish great deeds,
A host of worthies achieve grand merits.
By chance, I met with the times' favor,
And briefly aligned with the traces of courtly talents.
Looking at these feathers on my belly and back,
I feel ashamed before those who soar on empty wings.
I entrust my body to the shade of the four peaks,
And rely on the support of three beneficial friends.
Though our meeting was but a brief encounter,
Our great bond surpasses the past.
In danger, we shared perils together,
In safety, we remained unchanged in ease.
Together we endured the hardships of Jìnchāng,
And shared the perils of Fēihú.
Kindness arises from shared trials,
Righteousness accumulates through mutual support.
How could I have imagined the praise of my hometown,
Would mistakenly lead me to serve in my native province?
Separation fills me with emotion,
Both sorrow and joy stir my feelings with caution.
Reason connects through spirit,
Not merely through physical presence.
Your exquisite poem expresses deep affection,
Pure meaning penetrates the profound and obscure.
I regret not having the pearl of Suí Hóu,
To repay the jade disc of Jīng Wén.
Evening clears, the air turns cool,
The quiet room holds lingering freshness.
Opening the window, I extinguish the splendid candle,
Moonlight and dew gleam in fullness.
Alone at night, free from worldly duties,
Even sleepers speak of peace.
Suddenly, I receive your song of melancholy rain,
Bearing the toil of your accomplished composition.
I sigh at the hardships of your journey,
Deeply moved by the affection in your words.
Though I find little solace,
My heavy worries are momentarily lightened.
Hastily, I respond to your elegant verses,
Bowing deeply, ashamed of my own life.
Branches abundant, the forest grows denser,
Waves clear, the source runs deeper.
From a glorious clan, you, my outstanding one, are born,
Succeeding the legacy of your forebears.
Bound closely by noble demeanor,
Warmly conveying fragrant tidings.
Like a wild goose ascending with changing affairs,
Like the Cloud Terrace growing lofty with years.
Blossoms and calyxes adorn each other,
Chirping birds delight in harmonious calls.
Cherishing kinship, you urge me on,
Admiring virtue, I appreciate you.
Compared to the scenery, later brilliance fades,
Facing the years, a single day grows long.
Withered leaves cherish flourishing branches,
Dried-up streams long for broad rivers.
Devoted to my duty, I decline accomplished conduct,
Returning to propriety, I am ashamed of my humble joy.
Fortunate to meet, I indeed till another's field,
Holding office by the southern bend of the river.
Treading fate, I grieve the fleeting time,
Following the road, I sigh at its vast distance.
Laying bare my heart, I hold dear what I admire,
How deeply I toil!
Though beginnings align with the same rule,
Soaring flight differs in each case.
Far beyond the capital's borders,
Deep within the Chéngmíng Palace.
Seeking the path, the way already diverges,
Approaching reason, principle already confronts.
The path of silk holds constant sorrow,
How much more when it lies with my beloved?
Walking slowly with measured steps,
With clipped wings circling a few fathoms high.
Do I not recognize the heights and distances?
Straying from the right path leads to regret.
In winter's cold, frost and snow are severe,
Past the midpoint, the road grows steeper.
Measuring myself, I fear my friends,
Bravely retreating, not daring to advance.
Go forth and strive for noble deeds,
Writing sincerely in response to your message.
My journey points to early spring,
Yet mid-spring has not yet arrived.
The road ahead is long, with a set date,
Thoughts of separation never cease.
Packing done, awaiting an auspicious day,
Rowing the boat under the lovely moon.
Gazing at the road, my spirits low,
Looking back, my heart filled with longing.
My wise elder, moved by parting,
Escorts me beyond the suburban woods.
Farewell feast in a countryside pavilion,
Parting ways by the shaded shore of the clear lake.
Sad words linger as I stay,
The wandering guest's heart filled with attachment.
Around the pond, boats and oars disappear,
Gazing into the distance, sight and sound fade.
Slowly, I embark on the long road,
Heavy with distant sorrow.
Distant sorrow must be quelled alone,
On a long road, whom can I tell?
Walking on, the road grows farther,
Going away, feelings grow more delayed.
Yesterday I departed from Pǔyáng's bend,
Tonight I lodge by the Zhèjiāng's shore.
Gathering clouds obscure layered peaks,
Fierce winds churn flying currents.
Drizzling rain moistens marshlands,
Falling snow sprinkles forested hills.
Floating mists darken cliffs and ridges,
Accumulated white confuses plains and fields.
By the winding bay, a brief halt for the traveler,
The open river halts all passing boats.
Facing the ford, unable to cross,
Halting the oar, hindered by wind and waves.
Desolate at the islet's edge,
The atmosphere lacks harmony.
Looking west, I sigh with wandering thoughts,
Gazing east, I stir with mournful song.
Accumulated grief turns to sickness and sorrow,
Without the daylily, what can be done?
Resigning from office—is it for high rank?
Pleading illness, not waiting for the years.
By chance, I align with Zhāng and Bǐng,
Long wishing to return to the Eastern Hills.
In the past, the sage's favor turned to me,
But my humble aspirations went unexpressed.
Who would have thought a violent storm would stir,
Fierce flames unleashing blazing smoke?
Jade burned, emitted from Kūnlún's peak,
The remaining fire then forced my move.
Cast into the sands, reason pressed upon me,
Like Qióng, my wishes also went astray.
Long parted from joy and love,
Forever severed from lifelong bonds.
Floating boats in thousand-fathom gorges,
Gripping reins on ten-thousand-fathom peaks.
Churning foam poses no danger,
Stone forests are no hardship!
How can one dwell in Mǐnzhōng?
Day and night, I yearn to return.
Affairs stumble, two seem straight,
Heart content, thrice avoiding the worthy.
Entrusting myself to the blue clouds above,
Perching on cliffs, drawing from flying springs.
Bright prosperity dispels gloomy haze,
Pure virtue brings peace through adversity.
Distant lands all receive grace,
Even the smallest things are selected and chosen.
Deeply moved, my resolve is not firm,
Weak in substance, easily entangled.
Once I returned to my former garden,
Speaking of the past, truly heartfelt.
The old foundation was already built,
The former pond not dug anew.
Fruit trees stand in their old rows,
Soil and stones not extended far.
Though not a place of rest and leisure,
I take it for long days of idleness.
Nurturing life has its own classics,
Resting in shade, I decline all entanglements.
You, my master, illuminate true feelings,
Reaching into my heart, you offer past writings.
In late autumn I seek distant mountains,
The mountains far, my journey not yet near.
With you I part at the mountain's bend,
Bearing sorrow I set off on the long carriage track.
Midstream our sleeves are about to part,
Wishing to go, yet feelings cannot bear it.
Looking back, my neck not yet weary,
By the winding shore the boat is already hidden.
Hidden shore, despairing of the boat.
Swift oars chase the startled current.
Wanting to suppress a lifetime's joy,
Together we rush on a thousand-mile journey.
Sunset calls for rest and shelter,
Mooring ropes tied by the riverside tower.
Not only evening feelings gather,
Recalling how we lingered together.
Lingering on past joys,
Adds further to today's sighs.
This feeling already divides my thoughts,
How much more when joined with sorrow's onset.
Autumn springs sing in northern streams,
Mournful apes echo on southern peaks.
Grieving, the heart of new parting,
Desolate, long-held thoughts accumulate!
Accumulated thoughts assail the parting heart,
At dawn departing from Qīngxī's shade.
At dusk I lodge in Shànzhōng,
At dawn I climb Tiānmǔ's ridge.
High, high into the clouds and rainbows,
The hoped return—how can it be found?
Should I meet Fúqiū Gōng,
Forever cut off from your virtuous words.
Lying ill, I decline company,
Erasing traces, entering cloud-capped peaks.
Cliffs and valleys occupy my eyes and ears,
Joy and love severed from voice and face.
Forever cut off from heart's delight hopes,
Long harboring what none can share.
At life's end I meet my noble younger brother,
My face brightens, my heart opens wide.
Since my heart is thus opened,
All satisfaction lies here.
Crossing streams to seek my dwelling,
Unrolling scrolls, asking what I know.
Evening worries flow with dawn's moon,
Morning fears race with setting sun.
Awake together, never weary of rest,
Gathering and parting become separation.
Separating, we leave Xīchuān,
Turning shadows, returning to Dōngshān.
Parting's sorrow already extreme,
After parting, feelings stretch even longer.
Longing, I await your fine words,
And indeed receive your "Crossing the River" piece.
Toilsome winds and waves affairs,
Sincere words of isles and shores.
Since shores and isles have lingered long,
Winds and waves delay your journey.
Striving to match Huájīng thoughts,
How could empty valley hopes remain?
Yet again you favor me with coming lines,
Only enough to stir my thoughts.
If indeed your words of return prove true,
Together we'll rejoice in late springtime.
Late spring though not yet joined,
Mid-spring is fine for wandering.
Mountain peaches bloom red buds,
Wild ferns gradually purple sheaths.
Warbling already brings delight,
Secluded dwelling still feels gloom.
Dreaming, I await your returning boat,
To release my regret and toil.
Jade waters record square currents,
Jasper sources bear rounded bends.
Treasured gems often keep silent,
Though hidden, still shine clear.
Hearing dragons in deepest springs,
Catching phoenixes at crimson caves.
How many skilled have I heard?
Only thus have I met a sage of the age.
Spreading culture, broadening the nation's splendor,
Spreading words far in courtly ranks.
Virtue's glow illuminates the state's glory,
Fragrant winds reach village elders.
Aside, like a recluse dwelling,
Country gates often closed by day.
Woods and lanes sometimes open late,
Often turning back elders' carriage tracks.
Courtyard dim, seeing wild shade,
Mountains bright, gazing on pine-clad snow.
Quietly pondering all transformations,
Passing life into season's end.
Anticipating going, joy indeed ceases,
Sorrow comes, not pleasure's end.
Entrusting beauty to many brushes,
Distant thoughts in brief letters.
Sweltering skies full of dust and gloom,
Summer's end halts dusty turmoil.
Alone in stillness, lacking companion's seat,
Facing the hall under divided stars.
Listening aside to wind brushing trees,
Gazing afar as moon parts clouds.
Night cicadas hasten in summer,
Shaded insects foretell autumn's sound.
Year's cycle just past its half,
How long can fragrant plants last?
Retired life grieves at nature's change,
Yearning for kindred, holding deep feeling.
Nine departures not empty thoughts,
Seven weavings yield no finished pattern.
Imperial seat embodies the world's pole,
Natural defenses set by Heaven's work.
Two palaces block connecting tracks,
Facing gates limit clear winds.
On tiptoe I lodge in eastern halls,
Singing alone by southern walls.
Resting and rising, gloom unending,
Rising to gaze at stars and Milky Way.
Flowing clouds veil blue towers,
Bright moon mirrors crimson palace.
Hesitating by tight clear defenses,
Wandering, always as water-clock runs dry.
Noble one sends fragrant tidings,
Moved by things, pitying my heart.
Pity no hills-and-gardens excellence,
Admiring conduct, those tall pines.
Knowing words has sincere thread,
Fine value hard to fully fill.
How to inscribe your fine gift?
Planting mulberry and paulownia trees.
Weak plant admires upright conduct,
Struggling steps fear early straying.
Standing alone, not choosing direction,
Determined, relying on poor dwelling.
In past days encountering much fortune,
Holding brush, serving two palace gates.
Though ashamed of vermilion and blue applied,
Never thought dark and plain would part.
Only met with fine times' distortion,
Kingly way shrouded in dark haze.
Human and divine, dark and bright severed,
Friends' goodwill like clouds and rain parted.
Mourning Qū Yuán at Tīngzhōu's shores,
Paying homage to emperor at Cāngshān's path.
Leaning on cliffs, listening to lingering winds,
Climbing woods, plucking remaining shoots.
On tiptoe I gaze at Héng and Qiáo peaks,
What month to see Qínjī?
Imperial sage reveals Heaven's virtue,
Rich grace stirs sunken mud.
Pity no pheasant transformed by rank,
What use to fill seas and Huái?
Leaving state, returning to old village,
Secluded gate overgrown with weeds.
Gathering thatch to mend former dwelling,
Cutting thorns to open old fields.
Things fade, season already late,
Years pass, aspirations not aligned.
Kinship and benevolence spread affectionate closeness,
Rising to compose, exhausting lyrical dwelling.
Fragrance fades from orchids and indigo,
Clear tones surpass jade and gem.
Exhausting words is not a return piece,
Just to lay out what I hold dear.
Chángqīng crowned in Huáyáng,
Zhònglián renowned by sea's shade.
Jade tablets already in cultural store,
Essence and principle also in Dao's heart.
Noble one raises high carriage,
Dusty tracks indeed form a forest.
Lofty feelings match distant traces,
Clear breath overflows plain lapels.
Forming friendship, briefly years' meaning,
Sincere care discards floating and sinking.
Cold glory shared in resting and sunning,
Spring brew timely offered and poured.
Then comes year's sequence warm,
Light clouds emerge from eastern peaks.
Wheat ridges rich in lovely hues,
Willow gardens flow with fine sounds.
Joy in this ride of daylight leisure,
Suddenly forgetting passing shadows' encroach.
How to comfort hidden heart?
Brush and ink long chant and sing.
Perching phoenix, hard to be a branch,
Fine gift not what approaches.
Chanting to eternally revolve,
Boxing to replace double gold.
How far-reaching is the structure,
Gazing out to the utmost heights and depths.
Distant peaks arrayed beyond the window,
Towering forests overlooked from the courtyard’s edge.
At sunrise, flocks of birds scatter,
At mountain dusk, a lone ape cries.
Already there is wine by the pond,
And again, the zither in the breeze.
Were it not for your matchless grace,
Who would trouble this heart of mine?
Kind and able to cherish me,
You inquire with jade-like words.
If you abandon the steps of the Golden Gate,
Come visit the peaks of Jade Mountain.
The guardian of Huáiyáng, a trusted minister,
Still reclines in peace here.
Moreover, in the winding southern hills,
How different from a hermit’s retreat?
Continuous clouds enrich the farming season,
Bamboo hats gather in eastern fields.
The high pavilion often shut by day,
The wild steps seldom hear disputes.
Fine mats cool the summer chamber,
Light fans stir the cool breeze.
Fine bream may be offered as tribute,
Green wine I alone hold.
Summer plums sink with crimson fruit,
Autumn lotus breaks with delicate threads.
Where is the fine day after all?
Long ago I dreamed of a joyful meeting.
Sitting and whistling, time merely accumulates,
A year has passed in governing the land.
Songs with strings will never be chosen,
Stroking the desk, I mock myself.
The great river flows day and night,
The traveler’s heart grieves without end.
In vain I think the mountain pass is near,
Finally knowing the return road is long.
The autumn river dawns bright and clear,
Cold islets stretch vast in the night.
Turning my gaze, I see the capital’s halls,
The palace walls stand facing each other.
Golden waves gleam on the Zhīquè Palace,
The Jade Rope star lowers over Jiànzhāng Hall.
Driving my carriage outside Dǐng Gate,
I long to see the sun over Zhāoqiū.
The galloping sunlight cannot be reached,
How much more when separated by two lands?
Through wind and clouds, birds have their paths,
But Jiāng and Hàn have no bridge to cross.
Often I fear the hawk’s strike,
As autumn chrysanthemums wither in harsh frost.
Send word to the snare-setter,
The vast sky is already soared high.
Slender branches grow strong early,
Dew lingers late, drying slowly.
In the south, oranges and pomelos flourish,
How would they know the wild geese fly?
Brushing through mist, I enter the green pavilion at dawn,
Sitting in the crimson gates till dusk.
Sadly gazing, the road is blocked,
Uneven thoughts gather in hundreds.
Spring grass turns greener in autumn,
Yet the noble lord has not returned west.
Who can long stay in Jīngluò?
Black dust stains plain white robes.
Favored grace received from the imperial son,
Treading respectfully in service to the prince’s grandson.
Once attached to the Jīnmǎ Office,
Then appointed to the Tónglóng Gate.
Entering and leaving Píngjīn’s mansion,
Once meeting the honored Méng Cháng.
Returning to shade of mulberry and oak,
Morning and evening differ in warmth and chill.
Decline is indeed as it is said,
Silence and neglect persist from start to end.
Closing the gate, clearing three paths,
Sitting by the railing, facing the winding pond.
Wild ducks and cranes call to their companions,
Lotus and water chestnuts begin to spread unevenly.
Though there are no broad lotus leaves,
With you I drift on rippling waves.
Spring blossoms and autumn fruits,
The prince’s sons and household ministers.
The royal gate is thus esteemed,
Since ancient times, many talents gather.
The detached palace collects fine timber,
Splendid halls abound with Xú and Chén.
At dawn, the Shànglín Park,
At sunset, the banks of the Yī River.
The secretary’s writing is elegant,
Songs and rhapsodies achieve wondrous perfection.
Xiàng Rú would blush at such gentle beauty,
Zǐyún would feel ashamed of his brushwork.
A swift steed longs for the long slope,
A humble cart fears the perilous track.
Ashamed of this Shānyáng feast,
Vain is this Héyáng farewell.
Ten days of drinking on the plains,
Zhōngsǎn’s thousand-mile journey.
Bóhǎi is now flooded and stagnant,
Who in Yíchéng offers toasts?
Secluded beneath the southern hills,
Facing this season just as autumn arrives.
Alas, the time is not with me,
At dusk, there is no light boat.
The farmer goes to gather firewood,
Returning only at twilight.
Hearing from his young child’s tale,
A guest knocked at the rustic gate.
Attendants all adorned with pearls and jade,
Furs and horses all sleek and fine.
Carriages and canopies shine upon the village,
Official tokens gleam with radiance.
Suspecting it is the governor of Xúfāng,
Yet again doubting it is not.
Recalling old friendships, once spoken of,
This way is now rarely seen.
Human nature discards the flawed and lowly,
Why alone care for my humble gate?
Regretting not having chicken and millet prepared,
To share with an old friend.
In vain, feelings stir restlessly,
Tears fall in a steady drizzle.
Sending a letter with wild geese among the clouds,
Fly northwest for me.
Holding office at the Green Lattice Gate,
Gazing from afar at the Phoenix Pond.
Who says the distance is far?
Yet affection is blocked by sight and form.
Dài Mountain abounds with spiritual wonders,
Yí River is rich in heroes and talents.
Soaring wings cross the Northern Sea,
Taking flight from Nánpí.
Encountering a sage and enlightened ruler,
Coming to perch on the branches of the paulownia tree.
How lush are the bamboo flowers,
How dense are the paulownia leaves!
They offer both a perch and food,
What more is needed beyond this?
How could it compare to the wren,
With a single grain, it has surplus wealth.
At dawn, departing from Fùchūn Isle,
Holding back feelings, enduring longing.
The governor of Zhuō returns from spring inspection,
Carriages and caps overflow the riverbanks.
After long gazing, they finally gather,
Joy and sorrow hard to contain.
The dark river road ends here,
Rapids and perils begin from this point.
Layered peaks easily echo with sound,
Added to by the night ape’s mournful cry.
The traveler’s heart finds its own solace,
Midway meeting a kindred spirit.
Close friendships end from this point,
Solitary wandering begins henceforth.
My humble self is lighter than cicada wings,
In youth, I was graced by a noble summons.
In sorrow, I hindered the path of worthies,
Then rose again to the court of the chief minister.
Unworthily bearing Gōng Shū's recommendation,
I repeatedly attended among the royal officials.
With a long whistle, I returned to the Eastern Hills,
Holding the plow to weed the seasonal sprouts.
In secluded valleys, delicate vines flourish,
On steep cliffs, glorious branches spread.
Fallen blossoms drift to the forest's edge,
Soaring stems rise splendid on lofty hills.
High and low—what constancy is there?
Rising and falling can happen in a single morning.
I only regret that in times of peace,
The way of petty men fades away.
Like wild field thistles,
Whirling and flowing, they drift with the wind.
Once weary of roaming the capital city,
Now I oversee corvée labor in Hé Shuò.
Ascending the walls, I gaze southward with longing,
The south wind lifts fine silk gauze.
The river's mighty flow vast and mighty,
Long ridges lush and towering high.
Who says Jìn's capital is distant?
The dwelling is near, yet the body is truly far.
Who says a county magistrate is insignificant?
A good reputation fears not shining bright.
Humans dwell between heaven and earth,
Who can demand a full century of life?
Bright as a spark from flint,
Swift as a whirlwind cutting across the road.
In Qí's capital, no legacy remains,
In Tóng Xiāng, enduring ballads still echo.
Blessings favor the pure and restrained,
Harm comes to the proud and arrogant.
Though lacking a ruler's virtue,
I regard the people with no frivolity.
At dusk, dark clouds gather,
I climb the walls to gaze at the mighty river.
River mist veils the mountain ridges,
Raging rapids strike the rocky cliffs.
Returning geese reflect in orchid marshes,
Swimming fish stir rounded ripples.
Cicadas shrill with chilly notes,
Seasonal chrysanthemums gleam in autumn splendor.
Craning my neck, I gaze toward the capital,
The southern road lies in felling an axe-handle.
The great hall remains unseen from afar,
Lofty peaks rise rugged and steep.
Busy, bustling city folk,
Restless, customs corrupted and flawed.
By the water, like floating duckweed,
On pine trees, like hanging vines.
Zhū Bó rectified laxity and sloth,
Chǔ's customs spread to Láng Yé.
How can a bent mugwort grow straight?
It relies on dense hemp for support.
What constancy do the common people have?
Good governance lies in the people's harmony.
My position equals that of Shàn Fù's magistrate,
Yet I feel ashamed, lacking Zǐ Jiàn's songs.
How dare I scorn this humble office?
Only fear I may disgrace what I bear.
The southern path welcomes the long sunlight,
Zhū Míng sends off the fading twilight.
The first fu-day heralds a new season,
The height of summer blazes fiercely.
Mornings envision auspicious clouds rising,
Evenings linger as the white sun shifts.
Wiping sweat, I leave the central courtyard,
Climb the walls to overlook the clear pool.
Cool breezes gather from afar,
Light robes flutter in the wind.
The divine garden glows with splendid fruits,
Broad avenues lined with tall catalpas.
Melon vines spread with long buds,
Ginger and taro fill wide plots.
Rice seedlings stand in neat rows,
Millet sprouts lush and abundant.
Empty and shallow, lacking timely use,
My position lowly, my name grows humble.
Driven to govern two counties,
Yet in governance, no achievements made.
Since I left the capital's carriage,
Four years have passed until now.
My vessel unfit for courtly halls,
Repeated departures are surely fitting.
In vain, I cherish the southern bird's intent,
Longingly yearning for the southern branch.
Spring and autumn alternate in passing,
The four seasons' changes bring much delight.
Favor and disgrace—why not remain unperturbed?
Attachment to roots makes reflection hard.
I arrived when ice had not yet thawed,
Now summer's heat suddenly blazes fiercely.
Moved by this, I linger past my expected stay,
Sighing at the swift passage of years.
Climbing the walls, I gaze upon the suburbs,
Letting my eyes roam past morning temples.
A small state with few people's duties,
All day silent, without affairs.
White waters rush past the courtyard,
Green locusts planted flanking the gate.
Truly lovely, yet not my homeland,
Only stirring my longing to return.
Suddenly I turn toward Gǒng Luò,
Mountains and rivers distant and apart.
I wish to return to my old hometown,
But fear the prohibitions of official documents.
I merely uphold my duty to guard the altars of state,
Residing恪守 in my official post.
Southern mountains loom rugged and steep,
Luò River swift and urgent.
Green pines shade the long ridges,
Green ferns cover the wide lowlands.
Morning sun along the long road,
Evening dusk with nowhere to gather.
Returning clouds ride on floating canopies,
Chilly winds seek entry through curtains.
On the road, I meet a deeply perceptive scholar,
Raising his hand, he bows to me.
The world's troubles are not yet pacified,
Xiáo and Hán passes remain perilous and rough.
Foxes flank the carriage shafts,
Jackals and wolves block the road ahead.
Soaring phoenixes trapped in cage bars,
Steeds of legend bound by tethers seen.
Ritual vessels I once heard of,
Military affairs I never learned.
Please halt your carriage awhile,
Slowly wait for spears and shields to be sheathed.
No lofty tally for this rare age,
No fierce heart in pursuing the Way.
Quiet and upright, I solemnly receive my mandate,
Borrowing an oar to cross the river's deeps.
Family and friends bid me farewell,
Wiping tears by the broad river's shade.
Clutching my chest, I release their hands,
Eternal sighs form lingering echoes.
No traces, yet something lies hidden,
Silent and still, sound must sink away.
Straining my eyes to what cannot be reached,
Remotely as if both have submerged.
Gazing south, I weep by the dark islet,
Heading north, I traverse the long forest.
Valley winds brush through sparse thickets,
Oily clouds shroud the high peaks.
Weary, a lone beast dashes forth,
Chirping, longing birds sing.
Moved by things, I yearn for home's halls,
How deep this parting thought!
Standing still, I sigh with emotion,
Awake or asleep, tears soak my lapel.
Alas, I lack the will to return home,
Who will share the toil in my heart?
A traveler far from home, serving as an official,
I entrust myself by Chéng Huá's side.
Grasping my sword, I follow the bronze carriage,
Adjusting my cap strings, utmost in reverence.
How swiftly the years pass,
Cold and heat suddenly alternate.
Long separation brings much sorrow,
Moved by things, feelings turn mournful.
Passionately I cast aside ease and comfort,
Eternal sighs abandon food and drink.
Seeking joy—joy is hard to lure,
Speaking of return—return is not achieved.
What purpose in worry and suffering?
Entangled, filling chest and heart.
Looking up at the sky-soaring birds,
I envy your wings flying home.
Gathering the reins, I ascend the long road,
Sobbing, I bid farewell to close kin.
May I ask, sir, where are you bound?
The world's net ensnares my body.
Eternal sighs along the northern shore,
Lingering thoughts knot at the southern ford.
Walking on, I have gone far indeed,
Wild paths empty, without a soul.
Mountains and marshes twist and wind,
Woods and thickets dim and sprawling.
Tigers roar from deep valley bottoms,
Roosters crow atop tall trees.
Mournful winds flow through midnight,
Lone beasts cross before me.
Sad feelings stirred by things encountered,
Deep thoughts tangled and entwined.
Standing still, I gaze toward my hometown,
Looking at my shadow, pitiful and alone.
Traveling afar across mountains and rivers,
the mountains and rivers stretch long and wide.
I raise my whip to climb lofty hills,
and rein in my horse to follow the flat wilderness.
At dusk I rest, embracing my shadow to sleep,
at dawn I set off, carrying thoughts as I go.
I halt my horse, leaning against a high cliff,
and listen sideways to the mournful wind’s sound.
Clear dew falls with pure radiance,
how bright the bright moon is!
I stroke the table, unable to sleep,
shake my clothes, alone in long reflection.
In the past, blessed by good fortune,
I raised my steps to enter Chóngxián.
Borrowing wings from the phoenix’s branch,
I washed my feet in the dragon’s abyss.
Black caps hide no ugly men,
fine robes make me handsome.
A light sword brushes the belt’s ornaments,
long tassels, splendid and fresh.
Who says my service has been shallow?
Through hardship, it has passed three years.
Humbly I received later commands,
changed robes to become a frontier vassal.
At dawn I set off, seeking the pure path,
traveling afar across Liáng and Chén.
Moved by things, many distant thoughts arise,
with fervor I cherish the ancients.
In youth I entrusted myself beyond worldly affairs,
devoting my heart to lute and books.
Clad in coarse cloth, I delighted in contentment,
often empty yet always at peace.
When the time came, if it suited the occasion,
I reined in my horse to rest at the crossroads.
I cast aside my staff, ordering the morning journey,
temporarily parting from garden and field.
Alone, a tiny boat drifts,
endless thoughts of return wind and twist.
Is my journey not far?
Ascending and descending over a thousand miles.
My eyes weary of the long, strange road,
my heart longs for mountain and marsh dwelling.
Gazing at clouds, I shame the high-flying birds;
facing water, I blush before the swimming fish.
True thoughts first dwell in the heart—
who says form and traces confine?
Let me follow the changes of transformation,
and in the end return to Bān Shēng’s hut.
Leisurely living for thirty years,
I then merged with worldly affairs in obscurity.
Poetry and books deepened old delights,
woods and gardens held no worldly sentiments.
Why abandon this to go away,
far, far to the Western Jīng?
Rowing under the new autumn moon,
by the flowing stream I bid friends farewell.
Cool winds rise as dusk approaches,
night scenes clear, empty and bright.
Vast and bright, the sky stretches wide,
glistening, the river lies calm.
Burdened by duties, no time for sleep,
at midnight I still journey alone.
Singing for office is not my affair—
lingering thoughts lie in paired plowing.
Cast off my cap, return to the old village,
not for the glory of fine rank.
Nurture truth beneath a thatched hut,
hoping to make a good name for myself.
Reporting for duty as summer heat wanes,
preparing the oar as seasons turn to gold and white.
Autumn banks clear in evening shade,
fiery sky gathers morning dew.
Toil and hardship—for whose sake?
A wanderer meets declining years.
Love resembles Zhuāng’s remembrance of old,
long respect, as Zēng preserved the past.
How can this homesick heart
thank Yuǎndù with this?
Lǐ Mù would shame his long sleeves,
Xì Kè blush at his limping gait.
Fortunate times do not discard me,
ugly form not deemed repulsive.
I too am fragmented and incomplete,
yet early on admired the proper way.
Born lucky in an enlightened age,
personally honored by wise and noble regard.
Vainly ranked with Zhào’s jade disk,
uselessly strayed like Wèi’s gourd.
From then, gradually two cycles passed,
only now finding the road home beside me.
I will exhaust traces of mountain and sea,
forever cut off from enlightened joy.
Since youth, I cherished integrity,
chasing things, I then drifted and changed.
Turning from my will seems like yesterday,
two cycles have reached this year.
Stained, I decline pure expanse;
weary and frail, I shame steadfast strength.
Clumsiness and illness lean close together,
yet I regain the quiet one’s ease.
Appointed to guard the blue sea,
my boat detours past old mountains.
Mountain travel exhausts climbs and halts,
water journeys end with twists and turns.
Steep cliffs, ridges dense and layered,
islands winding, sandbars linked in chains.
White clouds embrace secluded rocks,
green bamboos charm clear ripples.
Thatching a hut facing the winding river,
building a lodge on a layered peak’s base.
Waving my hand, I bid the village farewell,
in three years I vow to return.
For now, plant elms and catalpas,
do not let my wish go unfulfilled!
Night crossing at Yúpǔ Pond,
by dawn I reach Fùchūn’s walls.
Dìng Mountain veiled in clouds and mist,
Chìtíng offers no lingering stay.
Rowing upstream, I meet startling rapids,
facing jagged banks, blocked and uneven.
Clearly lacking Bó Hūn’s composure,
the danger surpasses Lǚliáng’s gorge.
Repeated trials should bring familiarity,
double mountains value stopping and reliance.
All my life I’ve yearned for secluded times,
yet stumbled and trapped in frailty.
Long exposed, I sought official salary,
only now fulfilling the distant travel vow.
Long-held wishes gradually unfold,
all things have withered and fallen.
My heart now clear and open,
external things are but dragon and inchworm.
A traveler’s heart gathers on autumn morn,
morning’s accumulation unfolds in wandering gaze.
A lone guest grieves at rushing currents,
fellow travelers suffer steep, crumbling cliffs.
Shallow stones, water murmuring flow,
sunset, mountains shining bright.
Wild woods lush and flourishing,
mournful birds cry and call.
Facing things, I lament exile and rejection,
yet in preservation lies essential subtlety.
Since I hold the heart of the highest sovereign,
why heed the scorn of latter days?
Gazing upon Yánzǐ’s rapids,
my thoughts turn to Rén Gōng’s fishing line.
Who says ancient and modern differ?
Different eras can share the same tune!
South of the river, weary of touring,
north of the river, long absent from wandering.
Anxious thoughts make the road seem longer,
seeking wonders, time does not extend.
Chaotic currents head straight for the cut-off,
a lone isle charms the midstream.
Clouds and sun shine on each other,
sky and water share clarity and freshness.
Manifesting numinous beauty, things go unadmired;
holding truth within, who will transmit it?
Imagining Kūnlún Mountain’s grace,
distant and remote from worldly ties.
Now I believe Ānqī’s art,
can fulfill the years of nurturing life.
Péng Xiǎn and Xuē Guāng merely knew shame,
Gòng Yǔ did not yet forsake glory.
Perhaps they can surpass the greedy and contentious,
But how can they be called masters of a carefree life?
As for me, I hold to humble aspirations,
Clumsy and reticent, I decline empty fame.
A cottage garden serves as my cliffside dwelling,
A lowly post replaces tilling the soil myself.
Though I consider myself self-sufficient,
My heart and actions are still not in harmony.
Having no talent, I emulate Zhōu Rèn,
Afflicted by illness, I resemble Sīmǎ Xiàngrú.
Completing marriage duties like Shàng Zǐ,
Traveling lightly like Bǐng Hàn.
Reverently following the ancients’ intent,
I pack hastily to return to my humble home.
I took office during the Yuánxīng era,
And resigned my seal in the Jǐngpíng years.
For twenty years I betrayed my heart,
And now I cease welcoming and seeing off guests.
Preparing the oars, I hasten the return date,
Following the islets, I speed through long fields.
Up the stream I finally cross the waters,
Ascending the ridge, I begin the mountain trek.
The wilds are vast, the sandy shores clean,
The sky is high, the autumn moon bright.
Resting on rocks, I scoop the flying spring,
Climbing through woods, I pluck fallen blossoms.
Conquering desires, the lean grow stout,
Halting the mirror, the flowing waters still.
This is the transformation of Fúxī and Táng Yáo,
Granting me the song of beating the earth!
A white jade disc can still be polished,
But these words once stained are hard to cleanse.
Though I embrace the hexagram Zhōng Fú’s sincerity,
I am still wearied by slanderous verses.
If this inch of heart is not clear,
My faint life hangs by a thread.
The sun and moon shed their radiant light,
Granting success and encompassing this.
Departing, I lodge near the capital outskirts,
At dawn, I pack, riding the Lǔ breeze.
Once more enduring lifelong partings,
Again bidding farewell to friends and acquaintances.
My native hills grow farther each day,
Winds and waves—when will they bring me back?
Vast, the sail of ten thousand miles,
Boundless—where will it end?
I shall wander to Luófú Mountain,
And rest must be at Lúshān and Huòshān.
Crossing the sea, I ascend the Three Immortal Peaks,
Roaming the Xiāng River, I pass the Jiǔyí Mountains.
Admiring the sages as if dawn to dusk,
Yearning for the wise also fills me with sorrow.
Pure and bright, my heart at daybreak,
Undeceived by the year’s cold.
The tune of “Gathering Water Caltrops” grows urgent,
The song of “South of the River” does not slow.
The hearts of Chǔ people long ago were severed,
The traveler from Yuè’s heart now breaks.
Though severed thoughts differ,
Both are filled with longing for return.
You accumulate thoughts of your homeland,
I brood with resentment for the mountains.
Recalling times of rest and dwelling,
Lying reclined, indulging in abandon.
Finding one’s nature is not sought externally,
Self-mastery—for whom is it compiled?
I do not lament the long autumn nights,
But often suffer the short summer days.
Washing in the stream, stirring the swift currents,
Resting in shade, leaning on dense bamboo.
Cherishing the past, rejecting new joys,
Holding sorrow, forgetting spring’s warmth.
Mournful, the melody of “Bright Moon,”
Sorrowful, the “Guǎnglíng Melody.”
Earnestly pouring out on trembling strings,
With fervor, commanding the swift pipes!
Travel-weary, I lodge by water,
Winds and tides—hard to fully describe.
Isles and sandbars swiftly converge and part,
Banks and shores repeatedly crumble and rush.
Beneath the moon, I listen to mournful gibbons,
Drenched in dew, I savor fragrant herbs.
Spring ends, green fields are splendid,
Cliffs high, white clouds gather.
A thousand thoughts collect day and night,
Ten thousand feelings fill dawn and dusk.
Climbing cliffs, I gaze at the Stone Mirror,
Pulling leaves, I enter the Pine Gate.
Affairs of the Three Rivers are mostly past,
The principle of the Nine Tributaries exists in vain.
Revealing things, I prize the rare and strange,
Secretive beings hide their essence and soul.
Golden nectar extinguishes bright light,
Aquatic jade interrupts flowing warmth.
Vainly composing the song of a thousand miles,
The strings snap, longing grows stronger.
The southern region truly has fiery virtue,
Cassia trees tower over cold mountains.
Copper ridges reflect in emerald streams,
Stone steps cascade with crimson springs.
Here dwell reclusive wanderers,
And also rest noble hermits.
Precipitous paths cannot be measured,
Celestial roads are not mere trails.
Thus I ascend the foremost of clustered peaks,
Remote as if rising through clouds and mist.
Feathered immortals are utterly beyond semblance,
Dānqiū is but an empty trap.
Charts and records again wear away,
Stone tablets—who hears their tales?
Unable to discern a hundred generations hence,
How can we know a thousand years before?
For now, I express my solitary intent,
Playing with murmuring streams beneath the moon.
Constantly fulfilling momentary needs,
How could it be for the sake of past or present!
Changing clothes, I prepare the traveling party,
Setting out on the road, constrained by peril and hardship.
Raising oars, I depart from Wúzhōu,
Mounting horses, I ascend Chǔ mountains.
The route passes through Liáng and Sòng outskirts,
The path goes between Zhōu and Zhèng.
Ahead, I climb the Yángchéng road,
At dusk, I gaze toward Sānchuān.
In the past, destiny was interrupted,
From the beginning, sages were distant.
The Yī and Gǔ rivers lack ferries,
Towers and halls lack a single rafter.
Palace steps host many nests,
City gates give rise to clouds and smoke.
The royal way ascends to the eight directions,
Alas, my journey begins in twilight years.
Icy winds shake the desolate wilds,
Flying snow blurs the boundless sky.
On the road, not yet having set forth,
Setting out wine, somber and wordless.
Hidden grief—attendants and drivers mourn,
Weary and slow, fine horses grow restless.
Wandering duties take me from fragrant seasons,
Returning, I often encounter past faults.
My fickle heart is already done,
Drifting lightly is also just the same.
Vast and silent, the road is long,
Haggard, the toil of campaign and garrison.
In the past, I marched with the vanguard,
Now I return after the army.
Wielding my whip, I gaze toward the eastern road,
Stumbling, I fail to keep pace with the group.
Resting my party, I watch as dusk falls,
Straining my eyes where Liáng and Chén divide.
My homeland has many tall trees,
The empty city congeals with cold clouds.
Mounds and graves fill the outer walls,
Inscriptions and records vanish without trace.
Wood and stone bar the secluded gates,
Millet sprouts stretch over high tombs.
Only that Yōngménzǐ,
Lamented Mèngcháng Jūn.
Foolish and lowly alike are buried and forgotten,
Who alone hears of the noble and honored?
Why be a long-time wanderer?
Worries and broodings grow intense of themselves.
The Jiāng and Hàn rivers divide Chǔ’s vistas,
Héng and Wū mountains secure the southern land.
The Three Xiāng sink into Dòngtíng Lake,
The Seven Marshes flourish in Jīng’s pastures.
The route extends along old tracks,
Ascending battlements, I seek out rivers and land.
The water-country’s terrain is perilous all around,
Rivers and mountains truly fold upon themselves.
Leaning back against the forests of Yúnmèng,
Looking ahead to the gardens of Jīngtái.
Clear air clears over Yuèyáng,
Layered sunlight nears the rippling shores.
Desolate, the wind from afar,
Grieving, the view of a thousand miles.
Ten thousand ages present comings and goings,
A hundred generations toil in rise and fall.
Survival and demise—who after all?
Integrity lies in brightness and goodness.
I beg to follow the people of high antiquity,
Returning to tend mulberries and bamboo.
Last night I lodged at Nánlíng,
This morning I entered Lúzhōu.
A traveler grieves at the passing of sun and moon,
Surging waves cannot be detained.
Before the stars fade, I hasten on the early road,
Chasing after my companions till daylight ends.
Fish-scale clouds rise at dusk,
The whistling dawn wind grows fierce.
Swirling sand chokes the air with yellow mist,
Rolling waves toss white gulls.
Boarding the ship, I gaze toward Huái’s plains,
Covering my tears, I look toward Jīng’s streams.
As far as the eye reaches, plains stretch to the end,
Now and then distant smoke floats into view.
Suddenly sorrow sits and gathers within,
In a moment, thoughts grow deeper than autumn.
Never before have I strayed from my courtyard gate—
How could I journey a thousand miles?
Who made me lack the ancient integrity
That brings this sorrow of leaving my homeland?
The river road stretches long southwest,
The homeward current races northeast.
At sky’s edge I recognize returning boats,
Amid clouds I discern riverside trees.
Travel thoughts weary, unsteady,
Solitary journeys I’ve made many times before.
Now gladdened by thoughts of official salary,
Yet also in tune with recluse’s delight.
Bustling dust from now is kept away,
Joyful heart here finds its meeting.
Though I lack the dark leopard’s noble bearing,
At last I’ll hide in South Mountain’s mist.
This mountain spans a hundred miles,
Layered peaks rise level with the clouds.
Hermits have already entrusted themselves here,
Spirits and marvels all dwell within.
Above, it blocks the bright sun,
Below, it connects with winding streams.
Intertwined vines grow wild and spreading,
Curved branches tower then droop low.
A lone crane cries at dawn,
Hungry flying squirrels wail through the night.
Scattered clouds already stretch endlessly,
Frequent rains also fall chill and drear.
Though my journey is for official duties,
I also get to seek secluded paths.
Following the stream’s source, still not reaching the end,
The way back is dark and bewildering.
I long to pursue wondrous delights,
Right here, climbing the crimson stairs.
The emperor’s favor, after all, is gone,
This principle, I hope, will not be betrayed.
A modest outing, but I must report my return,
Yearning for leisure, I wish to retire and go back.
Returning to Qióng, I’ll sing rhapsodies like before,
Resting at Rǔ, my carriage and horsemen will not be wrong.
Bà’s pool I cannot bear to leave,
Yī River’s banks are hard to part from again.
Riverside reeds gradually sway softly,
River rushes again cling tenderly.
Field cranes call from afar,
Sand plovers suddenly vie in flight.
Above the clouds, Chǔ mountains appear,
Beyond the forest, Wú peaks loom faintly.
Trying to gaze with fellow travelers,
Hometown tears soak all my clothes.
Relying on this full cup of wine,
Holding the view, I gaze at fragrant blooms.
You ask what wearies me so?
Bathing in dew, I look up to pure eminence.
My ambition narrow, I slight carriage and crown,
Deeply favored, I long for the inner chambers.
Spring wine marks the passing years,
In plain attire I rest by the suburban gate.
From Bà’s bank I gaze toward Cháng’ān,
From Héyáng I look toward the capital county.
Sunlight glints on soaring eaves,
Uneven rooftops all come into view.
Lingering clouds scatter into brocade,
Clear river lies still like a silk ribbon.
Noisy birds crowd the spring islets,
Mixed blossoms fill the fragrant fields.
I depart, yet linger here,
Longing for home, I end the joyful feast.
When will the happy reunion be? Sadly, who knows—
Tears fall like streaming sleet.
Sentient beings know the ache of gazing toward home,
Who can keep dark hair from turning white?
Restlessly I pack my gear through the night,
Solemnly I prepare for the journey at dawn.
Morning stars still sparse and faint,
Daylight again spreads vast and dim.
Still damp with leftover dewdrops,
Gradually I see morning clouds rise.
Hometown, distant and far removed,
Mountains and rivers, long and wide.
Official documents pile up before me,
Missing loved ones, my heart loses its joy.
Bowing in service, often anxious and constrained,
Gazing on favor, only trembling with awe.
Onward I go, weary of the long road,
With no way to unharness and return.
Upholding duty, I reached Jiāng and Hàn,
Only then learned how long Chǔ’s frontiers stretch.
Southern pass winds around Tóngbǎi,
Western peak rises from Lǔyáng.
Cold fields leave no lingering shadows,
Autumn sun hangs with clear light.
Sad wind bends the dense woods,
Clouds and haze chill the rising streams.
Year grows late—how are you, my lord?
Falling tears soak my clothes.
Jade pillars stand bare, veiled in dew,
Golden cups sit holding frost.
Once I hear the “Bitter Cold” melody played,
Even more the love songs wound my heart.
Fishing pool’s mist not yet cleared,
Chìtíng’s wind already blows strong.
Rowing songs rise from midstream,
Drumbeats echo through layered cliffs.
Village children suddenly gather,
Country elders now and then gaze out.
Bizarre stones form strange shapes,
Precipitous peaks take wondrous forms.
Dense, dense, wild trees stand even,
Sifting, sifting, cold sands rise.
Vines hang, islands easy to climb,
Cliffs tilt, islets hard to approach.
Truly a place for eternal seclusion,
Not merely a brief escape to clarity.
Sitting and whistling—some in the past had such grace,
Governing while reclining—today it may still be honored.
From youth I loved distant valleys,
In later years I encounter wondrous mountains.
Peaks marked beyond rainbow hues,
Ridges placed amid white clouds.
Sheer cliffs suddenly slant and stand,
Summit again solitary and round.
Toward the sea, flowing waters stretch far,
Out of the inlet, shallow streams ripple.
Wild pears bloom, not yet fallen,
Mountain cherries burst, about to blaze.
Forgetting return, drawn by orchids and asarum,
Longing for salary, yet entrusting to fragrant herbs.
Fondly speaking of gathering magic mushrooms,
Lingering, I gaze toward the Nine Immortals.
Fondly speaking to the boat-passing visitor:
This river truly is to be treasured.
Clear through, following depth and shallowness,
Bright mirror, no difference of winter or spring.
From a thousand fathoms, tall trees are reflected,
At a hundred yards, swimming fish are seen.
The Cānglàng sometimes turns muddy,
The clear Jǐ runs dry, leaving no ford.
How could it compare to riding this stream away,
Looking down on glistening, rocky shallows?
Separated as I am from the noisy world’s grime,
Why would I need to wash my clothes and scarf?
Yet I wish with this murmuring water
To moisten the dust upon your cap-strings.
In military service there is both hardship and joy,
But it all depends on whom you follow.
If you follow a leader divine and mighty,
How could the troops long suffer toil?
The Prime Minister campaigns west of Hángu Pass,
His majestic wrath shakes heaven’s might.
With one strike he annihilates the Xūn barbarians,
With another he subdues the Qiāng tribes.
Pacifying bandits in the western borderlands,
Swift as bending to pick up a lost item.
Rewards piled high surpass hills and mountains,
Wine and meat overflow rivers and banks.
The soldiers are fully sated and enriched,
Men and horses all grow plump and stout.
Returning on foot and with mounts to spare,
They come back empty-handed yet with surplus wealth.
Expanding territory for three thousand lǐ,
The round trip swift as flying.
With song and dance they enter Yèchéng,
All their wishes fulfilled without fail.
Spending whole days in the grand court,
At dusk they briefly speak of returning.
Outwardly participating in enlightened governance of the time,
Inwardly not neglecting family affairs.
Even beasts fear being chosen as sacrifice,
The fine seedlings have truly been scattered.
Unable to emulate Jǔ and Nì,
Following them to grasp plow and hoe.
Whoever reads the Master’s poem,
Truly knows his words are wrong.
The cold wind sharpens in autumn’s season,
The Minister of Justice proclaims detailed punishments.
My lord follows the season to launch the campaign,
Majestically marching southeast in expedition.
Boats cover the long river,
Troops deployed across marsh and field.
The soldiers long for their kin,
Who can be without feelings of attachment?
Clutching my robe, leaning on the boat’s mast,
Yearning with deep affection for Yèchéng.
Pitying those men of the Eastern Hills,
Sighing with emotion at the crane’s cry.
The sun and moon find no rest,
How can any man attain constant peace?
In ancient times, men followed the Duke of Zhōu,
Once gone, it took three years.
Now our divine and mighty army,
Though briefly gone, will swiftly bring peace.
Abandoning the kindness of close bonds,
I devote my strength, exhausting loyalty and steadfastness.
Fearing I may be of no use even as one man,
To repay my sincere devotion despite idleness.
Day and night I stir myself to action,
Thoughts of departure twist like a drawn thread.
I shall take up the vanguard’s feather banner,
How dare I heed the gong’s retreat signal?
On military campaign to distant roads,
To subdue those southeastern tribes.
Double boats sail down the broad river,
By dusk not yet anchored at shore.
The white sun half behind western hills,
Mulberry and catalpa trees hold lingering light.
Crickets chirp along both banks,
A lone bird flutters in flight.
The soldier’s heart is full of longing,
Sorrow and sadness make me grieve.
Disembarking, climbing the high embankment,
Dew on grass soaks my clothes.
Turning back to seek my bed for rest,
To whom can I tell this sorrow?
Personally engaged in warfare,
How can I dwell on private concerns?
In battle, one receives the command,
This principle cannot be defied.
At dawn we depart from Yèdū Bridge,
By dusk we cross Báimǎ Ford.
Strolling freely on the riverbank,
Looking left and right at our army.
Linked vessels exceed ten thousand ships,
Armored soldiers number tens of millions.
Leading along the southeastern road,
We shall achieve merit in one decisive strike.
Strategies are planned within the tent,
All from our sagely lord.
I regret having no timely plans,
Like those officials who merely fill posts.
Bowing within the central ranks,
With minor schemes, nothing to present.
Xǔ Lì was a common soldier,
With one word alone he defeated Qín.
I bear the blame of idleness,
Truly ashamed before the woodcutters of “Tán.”
Though I lack the use of a leaden knife,
I may still strive with my humble self.
Long and far we journey on desolate roads,
Slowly my heart fills with sorrow.
Looking around, no sign of smoke or fire,
Only forests and hills in view.
City walls overgrown with brambles and thorns,
Paths and trails with no way through.
Reeds and rushes cover the vast marshes,
Bulrushes and reeds line the long streams.
As evening falls, the cold wind rises,
Gently drifting my boat along.
Cold cicadas sing in the trees,
Storks and cranes soar to the sky.
The traveler is filled with sorrow,
Tears fall, unstoppable.
At dawn we enter Qiáo Jùn’s borders,
Suddenly, worries melt away.
Roosters crow across the four frontiers,
Millet and grain fill the plains and fields.
Houses and mansions fill the villages,
Men and women crowd the roads.
Unless it were a land of sages,
Who could enjoy such peace?
Poets praise the happy land,
Even a traveler wishes to stay.
Reverently upholding the precious mandate,
Solemnly honoring the imperial ancestors.
Brilliant as the sea, manifest at Tài,
Descended from Táng, heirs of Chǔ.
Divine insight, wise in culture,
The people look to martial wisdom.
Vastly receiving widespread blessings,
Centered in dwelling, expanding territory.
Across the earth hailed as emperor,
To the heavens’ limit made sovereign.
From the moon’s cavern come guests,
To the sun’s edge offer land.
Initiating the primal era, first rectification,
Rituals exchanged, music performed.
Six codes link affairs,
Nine ministers arrayed in order.
Pure beasts in the cleansing pool,
Clean offerings on the altar.
Presented to please the king’s heart,
To answer the gods’ blessings.
The sage honors the emperor,
The filial honor their kin.
The emperor’s preparations are complete,
Rituals performed in early spring.
Rites performed in ancestral temple,
Reverence extends to suburban sacrifice.
Golden branches planted in the center,
Grand music arrayed on four sides.
Ascending to match in the capital,
Descending virtue among the people.
Rushing spirits illuminate the night,
High flames blaze at dawn.
Yīn and Yáng glow and shimmer,
Deep sacrifices sink into the depths.
Announcing completion, great reward,
Receiving blessings from the primal spirit.
The moon’s charioteer regulates pace,
Star drivers support the wheels.
Far rising, distant journeying,
Radiant and resplendent.
Green, green the grass by the river,
Long, long my thoughts of the distant road.
The distant road cannot be pondered,
Last night I dreamed of it.
In the dream, you were by my side,
Suddenly I wake in a foreign land.
A foreign land, a different county,
Tossing and turning, I cannot see you.
Withered mulberry knows the sky’s wind,
Seawater knows the sky’s cold.
Entering the gate, each cherishes their own,
Who is willing to speak for me?
A traveler comes from afar,
Bringing me a pair of carp.
Calling my child to cook the carp,
Inside is a letter on plain silk.
Kneeling long, I read the plain letter,
What does the letter finally say?
Above, it says “Eat more food,”
Below, it says “Long remember me.”
Bright, bright the white moon shines,
Its radiant light illuminates my bed.
The sorrowful one cannot sleep,
Restless, how long the night!
A gentle breeze blows through the chamber door,
The silk curtains flutter on their own.
Gathering my robe, I pull the long sash,
Slipping on shoes, I descend the high hall.
East or west, where shall I go?
Pacing back and forth, wandering aimlessly.
Spring birds turn and fly south,
Soaring alone, graceful and free.
Their mournful calls seek companions,
Their plaintive cries wound my heart.
Moved by these sights, I think of my beloved,
Suddenly, tears soak my garments.
Standing still, I utter a lofty chant,
Releasing my anguish, I complain to the vast sky.
Lush, lush the sunflower in the garden,
Morning dew awaits the sun to dry.
The spring sun spreads its virtuous warmth,
All things glow with radiant light.
Often I fear the arrival of autumn,
When flowers wither, yellow and faded.
All rivers flow east to the sea,
When will they ever return west?
If youth does not strive,
Old age brings only sorrow.
Freshly cut Qi silk, pure and white,
Gleaming bright as frost and snow.
Made into a lovers’ fan,
Round and full like the bright moon.
Carried in my lord’s sleeve,
Waving gently to stir a breeze.
Often I fear the arrival of autumn,
When cool winds steal away the heat.
Discarded into a box,
Affection cut off midway.
Facing wine, one should sing,
How long does a human life last?
Like morning dew,
Past days are bitterly many.
Moved with deep emotion,
Worries are hard to forget.
How to dispel sorrow?
Only Dùkāng can.
Blue, blue your collar,
Long, long my heart yearns.
But for your sake,
I ponder still.
Calling, calling the deer cry,
Eating the wild mugwort.
I have fine guests,
Playing lutes and blowing pipes.
Bright, bright as the moon,
When can I grasp it?
Sorrow rises from within,
Unceasing, unbroken.
Crossing paths and fields,
You honor me with your visit.
Reunited, we talk and feast,
Remembering past kindness.
The moon bright, stars sparse,
Crows and magpies fly south.
Circling the tree three times,
Which branch can they rely on?
Mountains never tire of height,
Seas never tire of depth.
The Duke of Zhōu spat out his food,
And all under heaven turned to him.
Northward, ascending Tàiháng Mountain,
How rugged and towering!
The winding goat-gut slope,
Shatters cart wheels.
How desolate the trees,
The north wind’s sound so mournful.
Bears and brown bears crouch before me,
Tigers and leopards roar along the road.
Few people in the valleys,
How thickly the snow falls.
Craning my neck, I sigh long,
Far journeys bring many thoughts.
How troubled my heart,
Wishing to return east.
Deep waters, bridges broken,
Midway, I wander aimlessly.
Confused, I lose the old road,
Dusk falls, no place to rest.
On and on, the day grows distant,
Men and horses both grow hungry.
Carrying bags, gathering firewood,
Chopping ice to make porridge.
Saddened by that “Eastern Hills” poem,
Long, long it makes me grieve.
Autumn winds rustle, the weather turns cold,
Plants wither, dew becomes frost.
Swallows depart, wild geese fly south,
Thinking of you, a traveler, breaks my heart.
Longing to return, yearning for home,
Why linger in distant lands?
I, humble wife, lonely in an empty room,
Worried, thinking of you, I dare not forget,
Unaware, tears soak my clothes.
Taking the lute, plucking clear notes,
Short songs, soft chants, cannot last long.
Bright, bright the moon shines on my bed,
The Milky Way flows west, the night not yet over.
The Cowherd and Weaver Girl gaze from afar,
Why are you alone, wronged, barred by the river bridge?
Climbing the mountain to gather ferns,
At dusk, suffering hunger.
Valleys full of wind,
Frost and dew soak my clothes.
Wild pheasants call in flocks,
Monkeys and apes chase each other.
Looking back toward my homeland,
Gloomy, layered with sorrow.
High mountains have cliffs,
Forests have branches.
Sorrow comes without reason,
No one knows it.
Life is like a sojourn,
Why so much worry?
Now I am not joyful,
Years and months race by.
Surging river flows,
In it, a boat travels.
Turning with the waves,
Like a traveler’s journey.
Whip my fine horse,
Don my light fur robe.
Galloping and driving,
To forget my sorrows for a while.
Setting wine in the high hall,
Kin and friends follow me in revelry.
The kitchen prepares a lavish feast,
Cooking lamb, slaughtering fat cattle.
How impassioned the Qín zither,
The Qí lute harmonious and gentle.
Yáng’ē presents wondrous dances,
Jīngluò offers famous songs.
Merry drinking past three cups,
Loosening belts, enjoying delicacies.
The host offers a thousand in gold,
The guest pledges ten thousand years in return.
Old promises must not be forgotten,
Ending lightly is a fault in righteousness.
Humble, humble the virtue of a gentleman,
Bowing low, what does he seek?
Startling winds sweep the white sun,
Light and shadow race westward.
Prime years cannot return,
A hundred years suddenly press upon me.
Born in splendid mansions,
To wither and return to hills and mounds.
Which of the ancients did not die?
Knowing fate, why worry!
A beautiful woman, enchanting and graceful,
Picking mulberry leaves by the fork in the road.
Soft branches sway gently,
Leaves fall, how gracefully.
Rolling up sleeves reveals fair hands,
White wrists adorned with golden bracelets.
