On her head, golden sparrow hairpins,
At her waist, emerald green jade pendants.
Bright pearls adorn her jade-like body,
Coral and wood-difficulty gems interspersed.
Silk robes flutter lightly,
Light skirts swirl with the wind.
A glance leaves behind radiant light,
A long sigh, breath like orchids.
Travelers halt their carriages,
Resting men forget their meals.
May I ask where the lady lives?
She dwells at the southern end of the city.
A green tower faces the main road,
Tall gates secured with double bolts.
Her beauty outshines the morning sun,
Who does not admire her lovely face?
What do matchmakers busy themselves with?
Betrothal gifts not timely arranged.
The fair one admires noble virtue,
Seeking a worthy mate is truly difficult.
Why do the crowds clamor so?
How can they know what she values?
In her prime, confined to her chamber,
At midnight, she rises with long sighs.
A white horse adorned with a golden bridle,
Gallops swiftly toward the northwest.
May I ask whose son this is?
A wandering knight from Yōubīng.
He left his hometown in his youth,
And made his name known at the desert frontier.
He has long wielded a fine bow,
With arrows of thornwood, how uneven they seem!
Drawing his bow, he pierces the left target,
Shooting to the right, he shatters the yuèzhī.
Raising his hand, he catches flying monkeys,
Bending low, he scatters the horse-hoof targets.
Agile and cunning, surpassing apes and monkeys,
Brave and fierce, like leopards and dragons.
The border towns face many alarms,
The northern tribes frequently shift and move.
Urgent dispatches arrive from the north,
He spurs his horse and climbs the high embankment.
Charging far to trample the Xiōngnú,
Glancing left to subdue the Xiānbēi.
He casts himself upon the edge of blades,
How can he cherish his own life?
Not even his parents can he care for,
Let alone his children and wife.
His name is enrolled in the roster of warriors,
He cannot turn his thoughts to private matters.
He offers his life to answer the nation’s peril,
And looks upon death as a sudden return home.
Famous cities abound with enchanting women,
The capital Luòyáng produces young gallants.
Precious swords are worth a thousand in gold,
Their garments shining and splendid.
They fight cocks on the eastern suburb road,
And race horses among the tall catalpas.
Before the gallop is halfway done,
A pair of hares dash before me.
I seize my bow and swiftly fit a whistling arrow,
Charging far up the southern hills.
Drawing left, I shoot to the right,
One shot pierces both birds.
Before I can display further skill,
I raise my hand and catch a flying kite.
All onlookers praise my skill,
The many experts acknowledge my excellence.
I return to feast at Pínglè,
Where fine wine costs ten thousand per dou.
Sliced carp and stewed fetal shrimp,
Chilled turtle and roasted bear paw.
Calling companions and summoning friends,
We sit in rows along the long banquet mats.
Swiftly we play ball and throw clods,
With skill and agility in countless ways.
The white sun races toward the southwest,
Its light and shadow cannot be grasped.
The clouds disperse as we return to the city,
At dawn we will come again.
Wáng Míngjūn,
Originally named Wáng Zhāojūn,
Was renamed to avoid the taboo of Emperor Wén.
The Xiōngnú were powerful,
And requested marriage from the Hàn.
Emperor Yuán matched Zhāojūn, a good family girl from the rear palace, to them.
In the past, when a princess married the Wūsūn,
She ordered pipa music to be played on horseback,
To comfort her thoughts on the journey.
Those who escorted Míngjūn
Must have done the same,
And the new melodies they composed
Often carried tones of sorrow and lament,
Hence I record them on paper.
I am originally a child of the Hàn,
Bound for the court of the Chányú.
Before my farewell words are finished,
The vanguard has already raised their banners.
Servants and drivers shed flowing tears,
The carriage horses whinny in sorrow.
Grief and melancholy wound my innermost being,
Tears soak the crimson tassels of my hat.
Journeying on, day by day growing farther,
I finally reach the Xiōngnú city.
They welcome me into a felt tent,
And bestow upon me the title of Yānzhī.
A different kind is not where I find peace,
Though honored, it brings no glory.
Father and son both humiliate me,
Facing them, I am ashamed and shocked.
To end my life is truly not easy,
So silently I endure a wretched existence.
What solace is there in such a life?
Accumulated thoughts often swell with indignation.
I wish to borrow the wings of a wild goose,
To ride them on a distant journey.
But the wild goose pays me no heed,
I stand still, lost and anxious.
Once I was jade in a casket,
Now I am a flower upon dung.
Morning blossoms bring no joy,
I would rather join the autumn grass.
Tell those who come after me,
That marrying far away is hard to bear.
When thirsty, do not drink from the bandit’s spring;
When hot, do not rest in the shade of a foul tree.
Does the foul tree lack branches?
But the resolute man is full of earnest care.
I prepare my carriage, heeding the command of the times,
Taking up my staff to seek afar.
Hungry, I eat in the tiger’s den,
Cold, I roost in the wild sparrow’s grove.
The day returns, yet merit remains unbuilt;
Time passes, and the year grows dark.
Towering clouds loom over the banks, awe-inspiring;
Swaying branches sing with the wind.
Silently I speak in the depths of a secluded valley,
And give a long cry on the high mountain’s peak.
A taut string has no timid sound,
A bright integrity is hard to voice.
Life truly is not easy,
How can one open this heart?
I cherish my steadfast and upright heart,
Yet looking up and down, I feel shame before past and present.
The way of heaven is level and simple,
The way of man is treacherous and hard.
Fortune and misfortune tread upon each other,
Turning over and over like waves.
To rid oneself of illness, one must not go far;
Doubt and suspicion indeed give rise to calamity.
Near fire, one is bound to feel heat;
Treading on ice, how can one dislike cold?
Plucking the bee destroys heavenly principle,
Picking up dust confuses Kǒngzǐ and Yán Huí.
What more can a banished minister have?
And what sigh is enough for a forsaken friend?
Good fortune always has its omens,
Disaster gathers not without cause.
Heaven’s diminishment is not easily refused,
Man’s increase can still bring joy.
A bright mirror is not far to borrow,
One need only tilt one’s cap to see it.
Being too close to emotion, one suffers from self-trust;
A gentleman guards against what has not yet occurred.
Bitter, ah, are those on distant campaigns,
Drifting and wandering to the four far reaches.
South, they climb the peaks of the Five Ridges,
North, they garrison the curves of the Great Wall.
Deep valleys stretch without bottom,
Lofty mountains rise steep and towering.
Straining their arms, they climb tall trees,
Lifting their steps, they cross flowing sands.
The height of summer is already cruel,
The chill wind is severe and harsh.
Summer branches gather fresh moss,
Winter ice congeals rushing waves.
Hú horses gather like clouds,
Yuè banners also spread like stars.
Flying blades leave no unbroken shadows,
Whistling arrows answer one another.
At dawn they eat without removing helmets,
At dusk they rest still bearing spears.
Bitter, ah, are those on distant campaigns,
Stroking their hearts, how they grieve!
Boating on the clear river islet,
Gazing afar at the mountain’s shadow.
River and land are different paths,
Yet beloved kin will seek afar.
Three jīng trees joyfully share one trunk,
Four birds sorrow in separate woods.
Joyful meetings have been rare since ancient times,
Mournful partings are not unique to today.
How long does one dwell in this world?
The sun sets, and shadows do not pause.
The road ahead is already long,
The path behind fades with the years.
Hastening, hastening, the twilight scene,
Weary, weary, few can withstand it.
Why again be troubled by this?
Truly, I have harbored a bitter heart.
Lofty integrity is lightly touched by worldly things,
Close emotions, how can they not run deep?
Go now, and preserve your blessed fortune,
When the light is cut off, let word follow.
Northward I journey to Yōushuò's town,
Where cold wilds hold many perils and hardship.
I bend down into deep valley floors,
And climb up winding mountain heights.
Frozen ice seals the layered streams,
Accumulated snow cloaks the long ridges.
Dark clouds rise beside the cliffs,
Mournful winds wail through treetops.
No glimpse of the bright sun's light,
Only the clamor of cold birds I hear.
Fierce tigers roar deep in the woods,
Black apes sigh by the riverbanks.
At dusk I rest beneath tall trees,
Sorrowful, seldom any joy.
Thirsty, I drink from solid ice,
Hungry, I wait for scattered dew as meal.
Long have I borne this parting grief,
Waking or sleeping, none to speak with.
How bitter the life of a traveler,
Forever suffering, constant bitter cold.
Driving my horse up Yīnshān's slopes,
The mountain high, my horse won't advance.
I go ask the Yīnshān sentry,
"The fierce foe is at Yānrán."
War chariots know no halted tracks,
Banners and flags march on and on.
Looking up, I rely on snow‑piled cliffs,
Looking down, I cross solid ice rivers.
Winter comes, autumn not yet returned,
Far, far away from home I roam.
The Xiǎnyǔn clearly not yet pacified,
How can we soldiers simply turn back?
With virtue low, men race to be first,
Tools of slaughter leave none unscathed.
If the army wins, scant rewards are given,
If the army falls, our humble bodies are lost.
I shall follow the tracks of Gān and Chén,
And win merit under the Chányú's banner.
Returning troops, reward the homecoming men,
Receive noble rank, spread fame in Gǎojiē.
At the gate there is a guest with carriage and horse,
Who says he has come from my old hometown.
Thinking of you, long gone without return,
I traced your steps across Jiāng and Xiāng.
I fling my sleeves, rush to the gate path,
Grab my robe, not waiting for my skirt.
Clutching my breast, I take the guest's hand and weep,
Wiping tears, we speak of warmth and cold.
I ask of our clan and kinsmen,
With sorrow we discuss who lives, who died.
Most relatives and friends are scattered and lost,
The elders of former days have all passed away.
Marketplaces and courts have changed places,
City walls and towers lie in ruins or wilderness.
Grave mounds grow more with each passing day,
Pines and cypresses loom thick and vast.
Heaven's way indeed knows rise and fall,
How can human life be long?
Filled with emotion over my whole life,
Looking up and down, alone in grief.
I order my carriage, climb the northern hill,
Lingering, I gaze at the city walls.
How thriving the neighborhoods and lanes,
Streets and alleys stretch wide and dense.
Grand mansions rise with lofty gates,
Deep chambers link with soaring towers.
How clear the winding pools,
Pure streams girdle flowery shores.
Deep halls display latticed windows,
Orchid rooms adjoin silken drapes.
Fair faces here rise in status,
Mournful tunes follow their expressions.
Human life truly moves on,
Beauty fades as years pass.
Excellent indeed, you men of fine grain and meat,
Your livelihoods are profound and broad.
Ease and comfort consume the spirit's root,
Such poison should not be indulged.
Do not, with your meat‑eater's wealth,
Mock the mallows and beans.
Yíngqiū lies curved along the sea,
Its fertile plains crisp and level.
Great rivers command Hé and Jǐ,
Lofty mountains pierce the high gloom.
East, it borders Gūyóu's side,
South, it bounds Liáoshè's town.
Sea creatures intermingle, myriad kinds,
Land products still number a thousand names.
Mèngzhū swallows Chǔ's dream‑like lakes,
Its strategic might rivals Qín's capital.
Only the teacher restored the eastern realm,
Duke Huán steadied Zhōu's decline.
Heaven's way has its alternations,
Human affairs know no lasting fullness.
Petty, that sigh on Niúshān,
It does not reach the perfect man's sentiment.
If even Shuāngjiū has passed away,
How can you, my friend, expect to stay?
On and on, I shall go again,
Eternal preservation is not our aim.
At Yīluò there are forked roads,
Forked roads where crimson wheels cross.
Light canopies catch the splendid sunlight,
Swift steps tread on flying dust.
Those who wear jade pendants are no plain scholars,
Those who lean on chariot rails are all outstanding men.
Fierce hearts sharpen in the brisk autumn,
Gorgeous robes glow in fragrant spring.
I am but a weary wanderer,
Yet many gallant talents are old friends.
Meeting by chance, I receive fragrant news,
If one is to crow, it must be at dawn.
Clinging to one way is not worth pride,
Forked roads are truly worth following.
Walking by compass leaves no wide tracks,
Stepping by square surely cannot catch others.
Once you set foot, the thread is already spun,
The four seasons need not be followed.
Though we take different paths and tracks,
We are asked to reach the same ford.
Gone, the sun that crosses the sky,
Sorrowful, the rivers that gird the earth.
Not a moment's pause in the inch of shadow,
How can a foot of wave merely swirl back?
Years pass swift as a strong arrow,
Time comes bright as a taut bowstring.
Distant hopes are rarely achieved,
Full numbers are seldom wholly kept.
Beauty withers night and day,
Vitality fades as I sit.
If even this cannot be halted,
How can my lifespan be prolonged?
In a glance, it will all have passed,
How brief, the span between.
What use to pour out my fervor?
Heaven's way is simply thus.
I only regret my merits and fame are thin,
No record on bamboo or silk to proclaim.
While the year is not yet at its end,
I sing a long song to fill my leisure.
A wanderer in fragrant spring woods,
Spring's fragrance wounds the wanderer's heart.
Gentle winds waft clear echoes,
Fresh clouds hang in light shade.
Huì grass brims with gentle air,
Seasonal birds offer lovely songs.
Gracefully, the turtledove's wings flutter,
Chirping, the oriole sings.
Dark orchids fill the open valley,
Tall beauty clothes the high ridges.
Even the dodder has something to cling to,
Even the creeping vine has somewhere to seek.
How sorrowful, the wandering scholar,
How deep his anxious thoughts!
His eyes grieve with the grass that follows the season,
His ears mourn the songs of timely birds.
Waking or sleeping, many distant thoughts,
Far‑flung, like things flying or sinking.
I wish to entrust my words to the returning wind,
To send a message to the one I admire.
Lady of Chǔ, cease your sighs,
Maid of Qí, hold your songs.
All seated here, listen quietly,
As I sing of Wú’s pathways.
Wú’s pathways have their origins,
Let us begin from Chāngmén.
How towering is Chāngmén,
With flying pavilions spanning flowing waves.
Layered brackets bear the wandering rafters,
Curved galleries open to winding slopes.
Luminous auspicious clouds spread,
Cool, gentle breezes pass by.
Mountains and marshes nurture many treasures,
The local customs are pure and fine.
Tàibó guided with benevolent virtue,
Zhòngyōng carried forth his influence.
Solemn and dignified, Yánlíngzǐ,
Brilliantly shone among the Huá.
Royal traces declined in troubled times,
Imperial deeds rose across the four directions.
Dàhuáng from Fùchūn,
Raised his hand to order the world’s web.
Talented men of the state rose with fortune,
Bright as blossoms in spring woods.
Every city had its scholars,
But Wú’s towns were the most abundant.
Eight clans were not enough to boast,
Four surnames truly renowned families.
Civil virtue flourished with pure excellence,
Martial achievements matched mountains and rivers.
How abundant were the rites and courtesies,
Transforming influence flowed like surging waters.
Their virtue and beauty are hard to fully recount,
I deliberate and compose this song.
Wine set in the high hall,
Singing sorrowfully before the cup.
How long does human life last?
It passes like morning frost.
Time never returns,
Flowers do not bloom twice.
Duckweed thrives in spring light,
Orchids fragrance in autumn.
Days to come are painfully short,
Days gone by are painfully long.
If I do not seek joy now,
Crickets chirp in the room.
Joy arises from gatherings,
Sorrow emerges from partings.
How can I say I feel nothing?
Worries are forgotten for your sake.
My wine is already fine,
My dishes are already good.
Short songs are to be chanted,
Long nights are not to be wasted.
Some say it is Luófū’s beautiful song.
The rising sun ascends over Fúsāng,
Shining upon this high terrace’s edge.
The high terrace holds many enchanting beauties,
From deep chambers emerge fair faces.
Lovely countenances gleam like the bright sun,
Kind hearts pure and serene.
Beautiful eyes radiate jade-like luster,
Delicate brows resemble kingfisher feathers.
How smooth and fresh their skin,
Lovely colors as if one could feast upon them.
Graceful and elegant in demeanor,
Charming and skilled in sweet speech and laughter.
In late spring, spring attire is complete,
Brilliantly adorned in silk and gauze.
Golden hairpins hang with ornate plumes,
Jade pendants fastened with precious gems.
Carriages side by side raise fine dust,
Feet washed in the waves of Luòshuǐ.
Gathering like wind and clouds,
How numerous are these fair ladies.
Southern cliffs fill with silk curtains,
Northern shores overflow with carriages.
Clear streams reflect shimmering scenes,
High cliffs adorned with brilliant red.
Fragrant sleeves waft sweet scents,
Cool, slender fingers pluck strings.
Sorrowful songs emit clear sounds,
Elegant dances spread orchid-like grace.
Vermilion lips hold autumn’s essence,
Graceful movements surpass the seven platters.
Responding to melodies swift as startled swans,
Treading rhythms like gathering phoenixes.
Exquisite postures change with expressions,
Profound grace never lacking source.
Bowing and rising, all graceful,
Every glance and step brings joy.
Lingering fragrance ties to flying gusts,
Floating reflections mirror clear rapids.
Alluring beauty is not enough to sing of,
Spring outings are truly worthy of praise.
Immortals gather, a divine assembly,
Grand meeting at the layered city’s slopes.
Long winds rise for ten thousand miles,
Auspicious clouds cluster toweringly.
Fúfēi rises from Luòpǔ,
Wáng and Hán emerge from Tàihuà.
Summoning maidens from northern jade towers,
Inviting goddesses from southern Xiāng River.
Solemn night journeys begin to move,
Fluttering emerald canopies spread.
Feathered banners perch jade phoenixes,
Jade ornaments emit harmonious sounds.
Tàiróng strums high strings,
Hóngyá sings clear songs.
Toasts and offerings now complete,
Lightly ascending, riding purple clouds.
Reining at Fúsāng’s branches,
Washing feet in Tānggǔ’s waves.
Clear radiance overflows the heavenly gate,
Bestowing blessings upon the royal house.
Jiānglí grows by secluded isles,
Its faint fragrance not enough to proclaim.
Covered by the meeting of wind and clouds,
Moved to dwell by Huáchí’s edge.
Unfolding splendor beneath the jade terrace,
Casting shadows upon Cānglàng’s spring.
Moistened by dew already ample,
Roots entwined deep and firm.
Four seasons pass without pause,
Flourishing blooms cannot stay fresh long.
Gentle aura fades with time,
Remaining fragrance scattered by the wind.
Heaven’s way has shifts and changes,
Human affairs lack constancy.
Men’s joy: wisdom overcomes folly,
Women’s love: fading avoids beauty.
I do not regret my humble retreat,
But fear the flies that come before.
I wish you would extend your lingering light,
To shine upon my twilight years.
Six melodies slow the clear singing,
Three modes await the rich sounds.
All rows of feasts fall silent,
Together listening to the gathering chant.
The gathering chant has its beginnings,
Let us start from Wénmìng’s achievements.
His deeds began in Hújì,
Clearing woods to the Jiāng’s shores.
Constellations blaze in heaven’s patterns,
Seas stretch across the earth’s layout.
Peak after peak vies in thousand-ren heights,
Rivers flow apart for hundred-mile courses.
Biāochí irrigates rice paddies,
Light clouds shade pines and medlars.
Two capitals pale in comparison to this beauty,
How could three cities ever match?
Layered terraces point to mid-heaven,
High walls pile lofty battlements.
Flying swallows leap on broad roads,
Painted prows play on clear islets.
Shops display graceful charms,
Roads shine with lovely maidens.
Since ancient times, across ages,
Wise and virtuous too many to record.
Gōujiàn knew rise and fall,
Yuè elder understood advance and halt.
Fàn Lǐ left rivers and lakes,
Méi Fú entered city markets.
Dōngfāng sought wandering ease,
Liáng Hóng left his mulberry homeland.
I string together records of local customs,
Words exhausted, meaning not yet spent.
Host, please do not speak,
This humble one sings a word:
I was originally a man of cold lands,
My start owed to Hàn’s grace.
First following Colonel Zhāng,
Enlisted to reach Héyuán.
Later pursuing General Lǐ,
Chasing foes to the frontier walls.
Secret routes spanned ten thousand miles,
Peaceful years still saw seven rushes.
Muscle strength spent on saddle and armor,
Mind endured cold and warmth.
The general has since passed away,
His troops also rarely remain.
Times change in a single morning,
Who now speaks of lone achievements?
In youth I left home,
In poor old age I return to the gate.
Sickle at waist, cutting mallows and beans,
Leaning on staff, herding chickens and pigs.
Once like a hawk on the glove,
Now like an ape in a cage.
Only bearing a thousand-year regret,
Vainly carrying a lifetime’s sorrow.
The discarded mat longs for the lord's tent,
The weary horse yearns for the lord's carriage.
May the grace of the Jìn lord descend,
To be worthy of Tiánzǐ's soul.
Urgent dispatches rise from border posts,
Beacon fires reach Xiányáng.
Mounted troops gather at Guǎngwǔ,
Forces divide to rescue Shuòfāng.
In harsh autumn, bows and arrows are strong,
The enemy formations, skilled and mighty.
The Son of Heaven grasps his sword in anger,
Envoys are seen far and wide.
Geese in rows follow stone paths,
Fish in file cross soaring bridges.
Flutes and drums carry Hàn thoughts,
Banners and armor clad in Hú frost.
Fierce winds rush through the fortress,
Sand and gravel swirl and fly.
Horsehair bristles like a hedgehog's spines,
Horn bows cannot be drawn.
In perilous times, a minister's integrity shows,
In chaotic ages, loyalty is known.
Offering life to repay a wise lord,
Death for the state, a martyr's fate.
A dappled horse with golden bridle,
Brocade sash bearing a Wú hook.
Disheartened amid cups of wine,
Bright blades rise in enmity.
Pursuing troops arrive at once,
Carrying swords, he roams afar.
Thirty years away from home,
At last returning to old hills.
Ascending heights, overlooking four passes,
Surveying the imperial city, within and without.
Nine roads level as water,
Twin towers floating like clouds.
Palaces flanked by generals and ministers,
Paths lined with princes and nobles.
At noon, markets and courts are full,
Carriages and horses flow like rivers.
Bells chime, tripods set for feasts,
Carriages side by side seek each other.
Now, why alone do I remain,
Trapped in gloom, burdened with countless cares?
Wounded birds dread the bowstring's twang,
Weary travelers loathe parting songs.
Parting songs sever the traveler's heart,
Guests and attendants all shed tears.
Tears fall, hearts break,
About to leave, yet turning back for farewell.
A moment apart feels unknown,
How much more parting in a foreign land?
The distant journey stretches far,
The fading sun sinks slowly.
Those at home shut doors and lie abed,
The traveler dines in the dead of night.
Wild winds blow through autumn trees,
The traveler's heart is torn with grief.
Eating plums, one often finds them sour,
Wearing hemp, one often feels the cold.
Though strings and flutes fill the seats,
The sorrowful find no relief in smiles.
Singing long to console myself,
Only stirs deeper wells of regret.
Chìbǎn stretches as a western barrier,
Huǒshān blazes with southern might.
Bodies fevered, heads throbbing with pain,
Birds fall, souls return home.
Hot springs steam from cloudy pools,
Scorching mists rise from rocky shores.
Sun and moon are ever dim,
Rain and dew never dry.
Crimson snakes exceed a hundred feet,
Black wasps swarm ten arm-spans wide.
Sand-shooters aim at flowing shadows,
Poison-blowers pain the traveling light.
Miasma fumes by day soak the body,
Dews of Wǎng by night dampen clothes.
Hungry apes find no food to eat,
Morning birds dare not take flight.
The poisoned Jīng still claims many deaths,
Crossing the Lú, how can limbs be spared?
Living bodies tread on deadly ground,
Lofty ambitions mount the engines of doom.
Gēchuán's glory is meager,
Fúbō's rewards are slight.
If even light wealth is cherished by lords,
How can scholars hope for more?
Straight as the red silk cord,
Pure as jade pot ice.
Why feel shame for past intentions,
When suspicion and resentment persist?
Human feelings scorn old kindness,
Worldly judgments follow rise and fall.
A hair's breadth flaw,
Becomes a mountain too heavy to bear.
Grain-eating truly are the giant rats,
White stains indeed come from blue flies.
Ducks and cranes, distant, are deemed fair,
Firewood and fodder, nearby, are trodden down.
Shēn was dismissed, Bāonǚ advanced,
Bān departed, Zhàojī rose.
The Zhōu king daily sank in delusion,
The Hàn emperor ever sighed in praise.
Even heartfelt admiration is hard to rely on,
Outward deference, how easily feigned?
Since ancient times, it has been thus,
Not you alone beat your breast in despair.
Knotweed worms avoid mallow and violets,
Accustomed to bitterness, they speak no blame.
Petty men are narrow and mean,
How can they know the mind of a free spirit?
Roosters crow within Luòchéng's walls,
Palace gates open at break of dawn.
Officials and nobles arrive in throngs,
Carriages and riders come from all directions.
Plain sashes trail in long gusts,
Ornamented tassels gather distant dust.
At midday, how can they cease?
Even when bells chime, they have not returned.
An age of peace is hard to meet,
A wise lord truly loves talent.
Clear judgment comes from heaven's decree,
Unswayed by outside doubt or suspicion.
A single word grants jade tokens and rank,
A slight virtue lifts one from the wilds.
Not just the gift of white jade,
But the raising of the Golden Terrace.
Now, what ailment holds you back,
Lingering alone on the road?
My family home lies near the passes,
I served as an official in the royal city.
Well-versed in tales of ten emperors,
Intimate with affairs of both capitals.
Weary of seeing things rise and fall,
Startled by the shifts of peace and turmoil.
Swift as a turning palm,
Vague as morning glory's bloom.
At road's end, regret short-sighted plans,
In later years, value long life.
Following a master into distant peaks,
Befriending immortals, serving divine spirits.
The Five Charts unfold from golden records,
The Nine Keys conceal the Cinnabar Classic.
Dining on wind, resting beneath pines,
Lying on clouds, roaming the heavens at will.
Wearing rainbows, ascending colored towers,
Removing jade, drinking in pepper-scented courts.
Briefly wandering beyond ten thousand miles,
A short parting spans thousands of years.
From the Phoenix Terrace, no returning carriage,
Only the lingering sound of flutes and pipes.
When shall I with you, my friends,
Peck at rot and swallow foulness together?
Jiāngnán, land of beauty and grace,
Jīnlíng, capital of emperors and kings.
Winding along with emerald waters,
Stretching afar with vermilion towers.
Flying eaves flank the imperial way,
Weeping willows shade the royal moat.
Still pipes escort high canopies,
Layered drums send off ornate carriages.
Present memorials at Yúntái's court,
Merit and fame are surely within grasp.
In life, roaming the nation's capital,
In death, cast aside in the wilds.
At dawn, departing from lofty halls,
By dusk, lodging beneath the Yellow Springs.
The white sun sinks into Yúyuān,
Chariots halt, teams of horses rest.
Though creation holds divine intelligence,
How can it preserve me once more?
Form and appearance slowly fade,
Teeth and hair will soon fall away.
Since ancient times, all have been thus,
Who can escape this fate?
Divination selects an auspicious day for the funeral,
The favorable decree is all set here.
At dawn, the carriage startles the attendants,
Reins are tied, halting at the heavy foundation.
Dragon banners draped over broad willows,
The vanguard raises light flags high.
How clamorous the funeral hall,
Mournful sounds boil within the inner gates.
The inner gates, do not clamor yet,
Listen to my "Song of the Dew on the Shallots."
Life and death each follow different paths,
The ancestral send-off must have its time.
Setting aside wine vessels at the two pillars' place,
Opening the coffin to advance the spirit carriage.
Farewell drinks, cups cannot be raised,
Departing to lodge, return has no date.
Curtains and mats lie empty, leaving only shadows,
The house and beams bid you farewell.
Close relatives all rush to gather,
Friends come from afar on their own.
Gracefully fly the light carriages,
Swiftly urged on are the plain black steeds.
Reins in hand, follow the long thicket,
Escorting you to the long night terrace.
Calling you, you do not hear,
Weeping for you, you do not know.
Sighing heavily beside the double coffin,
Remembering our times of old.
Three autumns may still be gathered,
But ten thousand ages—how can they be pondered?
To follow in death, the body easily perishes,
Saving you is beyond my power.
Words held back choke in the throat,
Wiping tears, they stream down ceaselessly.
How towering the heavy mound,
The dark lodge hides within it.
Vast and majestic, it stands to the four extremes,
Arched and lofty, it mimics the azure sky.
Listening sideways to the dark ditch's surge,
Lying down to watch the sky-well suspended.
How vast and boundless the wide heavens,
The great dusk—how can it dawn again?
Others leave but have returning years,
My journey has no year of return.
Once dwelling in the homes of the four peoples,
Now entrusted to be neighbor to ten thousand ghosts.
Once a seven-foot body,
Now turned to ash and dust.
Gold and jade, once worn always,
Now lighter than a goose feather, never to rise again.
Plump flesh feasts the ants,
Fair beauty forever vanishes.
The hall of longevity invites demons,
Emptiness and nothingness host each other.
Ants, what grievance do you hold?
Demons, what kinship have I with you?
Beating the breast in agony of bitter suffering,
Long lamenting, none to tell it to.
Drifting apart, thoughts of kin and friends,
Melancholy, the spirit finds no peace.
Plain steeds wait by the hearse carriage,
Dark teams gallop with flying canopies.
Mournful cries rise from the funeral hall,
Lingering sorrow in the wilds outside.
The soul carriage silent, without a sound,
Only caps and sashes are seen.
Objects prepared mirror his lifetime,
Long banners—who will wave them now?
Sad winds brush the traveling tracks,
Tilted clouds form flowing mists.
Whip raised pointing to the spirit mound,
Driving the carriage, from here I depart.
How vast the wild grasses,
White poplars too rustle desolate.
In the harsh frost of the ninth month,
They escort me beyond the distant outskirts.
On all sides, no human dwells,
High graves stand jagged and steep.
Horses crane necks and neigh to the sky,
Winds themselves turn bleak and dreary.
Once the dark chamber is sealed,
A thousand years will not see dawn again.
A thousand years will not see dawn again,
Even the wise and accomplished can do nothing.
Those who came to see me off,
Have each returned to their homes.
Some relatives may retain lingering grief,
Others have already turned to song.
What more is there to say about death?
Entrust the body to the same mountain slopes.
Crown Prince Dān of Yān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the King of Qín,
Dān held a farewell ceremony for him on the banks of the Yì River.
Gāo Jiànlí struck the zhù,
Jīng Kē sang,
Sòng Rúyì harmonized with him,
Saying:
The wind soughs, oh! the Yì River is cold,
The brave man once gone, oh! never returns!
Emperor Gāozǔ returned,
Passed through Pèi,
And stayed. He set out wine in the Pèi Palace,
Summoned all his old friends, elders, and young men to join the drinking,
Gathered over a hundred and twenty youths from Pèi,
And taught them a song.
When the wine was at its height,
The Emperor struck the zhù and sang himself:
A great wind rises, oh! clouds fly and scatter,
Might imposed across the seas, oh! I return to my hometown,
How to get fierce warriors, oh! to guard the four directions!
At dawn I set out from Guǎngmò Gate,
At dusk I lodge at Dānshuǐ Mountain.
Left hand bends the Fánruò bow,
Right hand brandishes the Lóngyuān sword.
Looking back, I gaze at palace towers,
Bending and straightening, I ride the flying carriage.
Leaning on the saddle, I heave a long sigh,
Tears falling like flowing springs.
Tethering the horse under tall pines,
Removing the saddle atop the high mountain peak.
Fierce, fierce, the mournful wind rises,
Cold, cold, the stream waters flow.
Waving my hand in lasting farewell,
Choked with sobs, unable to speak.
Floating clouds gather for me,
Returning birds circle for me.
Days since leaving home grow ever farther,
How can I know survival or death?
Filled with emotion in the deep forest,
Clasping my knees alone, heartbroken.
Deer roam before me,
Monkeys play beside me.
Supplies and provisions now exhausted,
How can ferns and bracken suffice to eat?
Taking the reins, I command my companions,
Chanting and whistling amidst the sheer cliffs.
The gentleman's way is faint indeed,
The Master thus knew hardship.
Remembering Lǐ Líng of old, who overstayed his term,
Left stranded in the Xiōngnú court.
Loyalty and trust instead brought guilt,
Emperor Hàn Wǔ did not see clearly.
I wish to finish this song,
This song sorrowful and long.
Lay it aside, do not repeat it,
Repeating it only wounds the heart.
Rú Jī slept within the inner chamber,
Bān Jiéyú once shared the carriage seat.
Great waves accompany the drinking tent,
Forest light feasts on Qín's remnants.
Year's end, cold gusts arrive,
Autumn waters shed the lotus blooms.
Zǐxiá deceitfully followed the rear carriage,
Ānlíng wept for the former fish.
This lowly concubine is finished forever,
My lord, how will you fare!
Walking on, walking on, again walking on,
From you, my lord, in life we part.
Separated by over ten thousand miles,
Each at the horizon of the sky.
The road is hazardous and long,
When can meeting again be known? Northern horses lean into the north wind,
Southern birds nest on southern branches.
Days since parting grow ever farther,
My belt grows daily more loose.
Floating clouds obscure the bright sun,
The wanderer does not turn to return.
Thinking of you makes one grow old,
The years and months suddenly grow late.
Cast aside, speak of it no more,
Strive instead to eat more, eat your fill.
Green, green, the grass by the riverbank,
Lush, lush, the willows in the garden.
Radiant, radiant, the lady upstairs,
Bright, bright, she faces the window.
Lovely, lovely, her rouged and powdered makeup,
Slender, slender, she stretches forth her pale hands.
Once she was a singing-girl,
Now she is a wanderer's wife.
The wanderer travels and does not return,
An empty bed is hard to guard alone.
Green, green, the grasses on the mound,
Piled, piled, the rocks within the stream.
Man’s life between heaven and earth,
Is sudden as a traveler from afar.
With a dipper of wine we entertain each other,
Though meager, let it not be thought too thin.
Driving the carriage, urging the worn-out horse,
We roam and play in Wǎn and Luò.
How flourishing is Luò within,
Officials and nobles seek each other out.
Long avenues lined with narrow lanes,
Many mansions of princes and lords.
Two palaces gaze at each other from afar,
Twin towers over a hundred feet high.
Feasting to the fullest gladdens the heart,
Yet what sorrow presses upon me?
Today’s splendid feast,
Its joys are hard to fully tell.
Strumming the zhēng, stirring extraordinary sounds,
New melodies wondrously divine.
Virtuous men sing lofty words,
Those who understand the tune hear its truth.
Hearts aligned in shared desire,
Yet meanings held within, unexpressed.
Man’s life is but a sojourn in this world,
Swift as a gust of wind-blown dust.
Why not urge on the swiftest steed,
First seize the crucial ford and road?
Do not cling to poverty and lowliness,
Long suffering in hardship and distress.
In the northwest stands a lofty tower,
Its top level with the floating clouds.
Lattice windows adorned with silk patterns,
A pavilion with triple-tiered stairs.
From above come sounds of strings and song,
How mournful is the melody!
Who could have composed this tune?
Surely it is Qǐ Liáng’s wife.
The clear shāng notes drift with the wind,
Midway through the song, it lingers and turns.
Once plucked, again and again it sighs,
Full of passionate, lingering sorrow.
I grieve not for the singer’s pain,
But saddened that understanding ears are few.
I wish to be a pair of calling cranes,
Spreading wings to soar on high!
Wading the river to pick lotus flowers,
In orchid marshes, fragrant grasses abound.
Picking them, to whom shall I give them?
The one I long for is on a distant road.
Turning to gaze toward my old home,
The long road stretches vast and endless.
Hearts united, yet living apart,
In sorrow we shall grow old.
Bright, bright, the moonlight of the night,
Crickets chirp by the eastern wall.
The Jade Balance points to early winter,
How clear and distinct the myriad stars.
White dew moistens the wild grasses,
The season suddenly changes once more.
Autumn cicadas sing among the trees,
The dark swallows depart—where will they go?
Once I had friends from the same school,
Soaring high, shaking their six wings.
They do not recall our hand-in-hand closeness,
Abandoning me like discarded traces.
The Southern Winnow and Northern Dipper,
The Oxherd does not bear the yoke.
Truly, there is no firmness like solid rock,
What use is empty fame?
Slender, slender, the lone bamboo growing,
Its roots entwined at Tài Shān’s slope.
With you I became newly wed,
Like dodder clinging to maidenhair vine.
Dodder has its time to grow,
Husband and wife should meet in due season.
A thousand miles to marry from afar,
Far, far apart by hills and slopes.
Longing for you makes me age,
Why so slow your carriage’s coming?
I grieve for those orchid flowers,
Holding blossoms, glowing with splendor.
If not plucked in their season,
They will wither with autumn’s grass.
If you truly hold to noble virtue,
What then can I, your humble wife, do?
In the courtyard stands a wondrous tree,
Green leaves burst with blooming flowers.
Climbing the branch, I pluck its blossoms,
To give to the one I long for.
Fragrance fills my sleeves and bosom,
But the road is far, I cannot send them.
This thing—what worth has it as a gift?
Only feeling the long time apart.
Far, far away, the Herdboy Star,
Bright, bright, the Weaving Maid of the River Han.
Slender, slender, she lifts her pale hands,
Click-clack, she works the loom’s shuttle.
All day she weaves, yet completes no pattern,
Tears falling like rain.
The River Han is clear and shallow,
How far apart are they, after all?
Across the shimmering stream of water,
Gazing silently, unable to speak.
Turning the carriage, I set out on my way,
Far, far, I journey the long road.
Looking all around, how vast and boundless,
The east wind sways the hundred grasses.
All I meet are not the things of old,
How can I not quickly grow old?
Flourishing and fading each have their season,
Establishing oneself—alas, too late.
Man’s life is not like metal or stone,
How can it last for long years?
Suddenly it follows things and transforms,
Honor and fame are what I treasure.
The eastern wall is high and long,
Winding and stretching, connecting itself.
Whirling winds rise shaking the earth,
Autumn grasses lush, already green.
The four seasons change and turn,
How swift the year’s end comes!
The morning wind bears a bitter heart,
The cricket grieves at confinement.
Cleanse and release your heart’s desires,
Why bind yourself in restraint?
In Yān and Zhào are many fair ladies,
Lovely ones with faces like jade.
Clad in silken robes and garments,
By the door they practice clear tunes.
How mournful is the melody, the strings urgent,
Knowing the pegs are tightened.
With racing heart, I straighten my inner sash,
Pondering, I pause and hesitate.
I long to be a pair of flying swallows,
Carrying mud to nest in your house.
Driving the carriage to the Upper East Gate,
Gazing afar at the tombs north of the walls.
How rustling the white poplars,
Pines and cypresses flank the broad road.
Below lie the long-dead,
Deep, deep in eternal night.
Sleeping hidden beneath the Yellow Springs,
For a thousand years never to awaken.
Vast, vast, yīn and yáng shift,
Life’s span is like morning dew.
Man’s life is sudden as a sojourn,
Longevity lacks the firmness of metal or stone.
Ten thousand years pass in succession,
Even sages and worthies cannot transcend.
Taking elixirs, seeking immortality,
Often misled by such medicines.
Better to drink fine wine,
Clad in fine silks and white gauze.
Those gone grow more distant day by day,
The living grow closer day by day.
Stepping outside the city gate, gazing straight ahead,
I see only mounds and graves.
Ancient tombs plowed into fields,
Pines and cypresses felled for firewood.
White poplars in mournful winds,
Rustling, sorrow enough to kill.
Longing to return to my old village,
But no way to go back on the road.
One’s years of life do not fill a hundred,
Yet often harboring worries of a thousand years.
The day is short, the night long and bitter,
Why not hold candles and roam?
Seek joy while it is timely,
How can one wait for the coming years?
Fools cherish and hoard their wealth,
Only to be mocked by later generations.
The immortal Wáng Zǐqiáo,
Is hard to equal or await.
The year draws to a close, stern and cold;
In the evening, the mole crickets chirp mournfully.
The chilly wind has grown fierce and harsh,
And the wanderer shivers without warm clothes.
The brocade quilt was left by the Luò River’s shore,
My comrade has parted from me.
Alone I lodge through the long, long nights,
Dreaming I see his radiant face.
My good man remembers our past joy,
He came in person, handing me the front reins.
I long to keep his charming smile forever,
Hand in hand, returning together in his carriage.
But he came only for a fleeting moment,
Nor did he stay within the inner chambers.
Truly, I lack the wings of the morning wind—
How could I soar upon the wind and fly?
I gaze afar to ease my heart,
Craning my neck, peering into the distance.
Pacing to and fro, my heart is filled with sorrow,
Tears falling, dampening the double doors.
In early winter, the cold air arrives;
How bitter and piercing is the north wind!
With many sorrows, I know the night is long;
I look up and see the host of stars arrayed.
On the fifteenth, the bright moon is full;
On the twentieth, the hare in the moon wanes.
A traveler came from a distant land,
And brought me a letter.
It began speaking of enduring longing,
And ended speaking of long separation.
I placed the letter within my bosom and sleeves,
For three years the words have not faded.
With all my heart I cherish this devotion,
Yet fear you do not perceive or understand.
A traveler came from a distant land,
And brought me a bolt of damask silk.
Though we are separated by ten thousand miles,
The heart of my beloved remains thus constant.
Patterned with a pair of mandarin ducks,
I shall cut it to make a “union of joy” quilt.
Stuff it with enduring longing,
And border it with knots that cannot be undone.
Like glue thrown into lacquer,
Who can separate these two?
How bright, how bright is the moonlight,
Shining on the silk curtains of my bed.
Anxious with sorrow, I cannot sleep;
I pull on my robe and rise to pace about.
Though travel may be called pleasurable,
It is not as good as an early return.
I go out the door and wander alone,
To whom can I tell my sorrowful thoughts?
Craning my neck, I return to my room;
Tears fall, dampening my robes.
The good time will not come again;
Parting is but a moment away.
Anxiously we linger by the roadside,
Holding hands, hesitating in the wilds.
Looking up, I see the fleeting clouds race,
Suddenly they pass and overtake each other.
Once scattered by wind and waves,
Each will be at a corner of the sky.
We must part forever from this moment on,
Yet let us stand here a little while longer.
I wish to ride the morning wind,
And send you off with my humble self.
A joyful gathering is hard to meet again;
Three years seem like a thousand autumns.
By the river I wash my long cap-strings,
Thinking of you, my sorrow stretches far.
Gazing into the distance, a mournful wind arrives;
Facing the wine, I cannot drink a toast.
The traveler thinks of the road ahead;
What can console my grief?
Only a brimming cup of wine,
To bind us in close intimacy.
Hand in hand we climb the river bridge;
Wanderer, where will you go at dusk?
Pacing back and forth by the path’s side,
In anguish, I cannot say farewell.
The traveler cannot linger long;
Each speaks of enduring longing.
How do we know it is not like the sun and moon,
Which have their times of waxing and waning?
Strive to uphold bright virtue,
Till white-haired age we shall meet again.
Flesh and bone are like branches and leaves;
Forming friendships also follows this principle.
All within the four seas are brothers—
Who then is a stranger on the road?
Moreover, we are like interlocking trees,
Sharing the same body with you.
Once we were like mandarin ducks,
Now we are like Shēn and Chén, stars apart.
In the past we were always close,
Now distant as the Hú and Qín.
Only thinking of this impending parting,
Our bond of affection grows ever new.
The deer’s call longs for the wild grass;
It can be used to welcome honored guests.
I have a jar of wine,
Wishing to present it to one far away.
I hope you will stay and drink your fill,
And recount this lifelong kinship.
The yellow swan, once parted far,
Looks back and lingers for a thousand miles.
The northern horse that loses its herd
Longs for its companions, ever yearning.
How much more for a pair of flying dragons,
Whose wings are about to part?
Fortunately, there are songs of strings,
That can express what is in my heart.
Let me sing the “Wanderer’s Song,”
How clear and cold, and full of grief!
Strings and bamboo raise a pure sound,
Passionate and laden with lingering sorrow.
The long song reaches its peak of intensity,
My heart is grieved and crushed.
I wish to perform a clear Shang melody,
But thinking of you, I cannot return.
Looking down and up, wounded within,
Tears fall that cannot be wiped away.
I wish to be a pair of yellow swans,
And send you off, flying far together.
Since we bound our hair and became husband and wife,
Our love and affection have never doubted each other.
Joy and delight are for this very night,
Harmonious and gentle in this fine hour.
The soldier thinks of the road ahead,
He rises to see what time of night it is.
Shēn and Chén stars have both set,
Go, go, and take your leave from here.
You go to serve in the battlefield;
The day we meet again is uncertain.
We clasp hands and heave a long sigh,
Tears flow for this parting in life.
Strive to cherish the bloom of youth,
Do not forget the times of joy.
If I live, I will surely return;
If I die, I will forever long for you.
Bright, bright is the morning moon;
Fragrant, fragrant are my orchid’s scent.
Sweet fragrance arises in the fine night,
Carried by the wind, it reaches my hall.
The soldier thinks of the distant road,
The wanderer yearns for his native land.
In the twelfth month of cold winter,
At dawn I rise and tread on severe frost.
Looking down, I see the Jiāng and Hàn rivers flow;
Looking up, I see the fleeting clouds soar.
Good friends are parting far away,
Each at a corner of the sky.
Mountains and seas separate the central plains;
The distance between us is vast and long.
Joyful gatherings are hard to meet twice;
Happiness is far from reaching its end.
I hope you will uphold noble virtue,
And cherish the shining light according to the times.
Zhāng Héng was not content to remain long in confidential duties.
During the Yángjiā era,
He was sent out to serve as Chancellor of Héjiān.
At that time, the king of the principality was arrogant and extravagant,
Disregarding laws and regulations,
And there were many powerful families that monopolized and annexed land.
As soon as Zhāng Héng took office,
He established authority and severity,
And was able to thoroughly investigate the subordinate counties.
Crafty and deceitful individuals who committed plunder through trickery
Were all secretly identified by name.
Subordinate officials arrested them,
And they all submitted and were captured.
All the local strongmen and wandering knights
Fled in fear beyond the borders.
The commandery was greatly well-governed,
Disputes and lawsuits ceased,
And no prisoners were held in jail.
At that time, the empire was gradually declining,
And he, feeling depressed and unable to fulfill his ambitions,
Composed the “Poem of Four Sorrows.”
Qū Yuán used the beautiful woman to represent the noble man,
Used precious treasures to represent benevolence and righteousness,
And used deep waters and snowy mists to represent petty men.
He wished to offer the Way and its methods in return,
Presenting them to the ruler of his time,
But feared that slanderers and evil men would block their communication.
His words say:
The First Longing says:
The one I long for is on Tàishān Mountain,
I wish to go to her, but Liángfǔ is arduous.
Turning eastward, I gaze, tears soaking my collar.
The fair one gave me a gold-inlaid dagger,
With what shall I repay her? Fine jade and qióng.
The road is far, I cannot reach it, leaning idly,
Why harbor sorrow, heart troubled and toiled?
The Second Longing says:
The one I long for is in Guìlín,
I wish to go to her, but the Xiāng River is deep.
Turning southward, I gaze, tears soaking my lapel.
The fair one gave me gold-inlaid lánggān,
With what shall I repay her? A pair of jade plates.
The road is far, I cannot reach it, leaning melancholy,
Why harbor sorrow, heart troubled and wounded?
The Third Longing says:
The one I long for is in Hànyáng,
I wish to go to her, but the Lǒng slopes are long.
Turning westward, I gaze, tears soaking my robe.
The fair one gave me a sable cloak,
With what shall I repay her? A bright moon pearl.
The road is far, I cannot reach it, leaning hesitant,
Why harbor sorrow, heart troubled and knotted?
The Fourth Longing says:
The one I long for is at Yànmén,
I wish to go to her, but snow falls thick and fast.
Turning northward, I gaze, tears soaking my kerchief.
The fair one gave me a brocade segment,
With what shall I repay her? A blue jade tray.
The road is far, I cannot reach it, leaning with added sighs,
Why harbor sorrow, heart troubled and grieved?
At dusk I stroll in the western garden,
Hoping to pour out my sorrowful thoughts.
The winding pond ripples with white waves,
Rows of trees spread crimson blossoms.
Above, a solitary perched bird,
Yearning for spring, sings toward me.
Lifting my robe, I wish to follow it,
But the road is perilous, I cannot journey.
Pacing back and forth, unable to leave,
I stand still, gazing at your form.
The gusty wind raises swirling dust,
The bright sun suddenly turns dark.
Turning back, I enter the empty room,
Entrusting my dreams to convey sincere feelings.
If human desires do not defy Heaven,
Why fear we shall not be reunited?
Official duties pile up and press upon me,
Documents and writings scatter in disarray.
Rushing with brush, no leisure to eat,
The sun sets, unaware it grows late.
Immersed in the ledgers and records,
Round and round, I grow confused and disordered.
Leaving this behind, I go out the western city gate,
Climb high and wander to gaze about.
The square pond holds clear water,
In it are ducks and geese.
How can I gain swift wings?
To follow you floating on the waves.
Long, long is the autumn night,
Fierce, fierce the north wind, cold.
Tossing and turning, unable to sleep,
I don my robe and rise to wander.
Wandering, suddenly it has been long,
White dew soaks my robe.
Looking down at the clear water's ripples,
Looking up at the bright moonlight.
The Milky Way turns westward flowing,
The stars Three and Five crisscross the sky.
How mournfully the grass insects chirp,
A lone goose flies south alone.
Heavy with sorrowful thoughts,
Endlessly longing for my old home.
I wish to fly, but how gain wings?
I wish to cross, but the river has no bridge.
Facing the wind, I heave a long sigh,
Severing my innermost heart.
In the northwest there is a floating cloud,
Towering like a carriage canopy.
Alas, it meets no timely opportunity,
But happens to encounter a whirlwind.
Blowing me southeastward,
Southeastward to Wú and Kuàijī.
Wú and Kuàijī are not my homeland,
How can I linger here long?
Cast aside, speak no more of it,
A wanderer often fears others.
Facing that northern wind,
I cherish the thought of Wèi's capital.
I wish to gallop on Dàimǎ steeds,
Swiftly northward to go.
The south wind forever arrives,
Thinking of those southern regions.
I wish to follow Yuè birds,
Fluttering and flying southward.
The four seasons alternate,
Sun and moon revolve in cycles.
Parting seems but a moment,
Yet feels like three autumns apart.
When I first moved away,
Vermilion blossoms were not yet sparse.
Now that I return and stay,
White snow flies like clouds.
Descending a thousand fathoms,
Ascending to heaven's barriers.
The wind scatters tumbleweeds flying,
Bearing separation through cold and heat.
A thousand fathoms are easy to climb,
Heaven's barriers can be crossed.
Those who once shared my robe,
Now are forever parted.
You love fragrant grasses,
How could I forget your gift?
Luxuriant blooms about to flourish,
Autumn frost withers them.
If you show no care,
How can sincerity be spoken?
Autumn orchids may serve as metaphor,
Cassia trees flourish in winter.
Strumming and singing dispel thoughts,
With whom to ease my worries?
By the river at dusk, thinking,
Why go boating?
Is there no harmony and joy?
But those wandering are not my neighbors.
Who forgets to go boating?
Ashamed I have no boatman.
High towers harbor much mournful wind,
Morning sun shines on northern woods.
That person is ten thousand miles away,
Rivers and lakes distant and deep.
How can a double boat reach that far?
Parting thoughts are hard to bear.
A lone goose flies southward,
Passing the courtyard, long mournful cries.
Raising thoughts, I yearn for the far-off one,
Wishing to entrust a remaining message.
Form and shadow suddenly vanish,
Fluttering away, wounds my heart.
Tumbleweed leaves its root,
Drifting and whirling with the long wind.
Unexpectedly, a whirlwind lifts,
Blowing me into the clouds.
High above, without limit,
The heavenly road, how can it be traversed?
Like this wandering traveler,
Who gives his life, far away following the army.
Coarse garments cannot cover his form,
Ferns and beans often do not fill him.
Go, go, speak no more of it,
Deep sorrow makes a man grow old.
In the northwest there is a weaving woman,
Gauze and plain silk, how profuse.
At dawn she holds the shuttle,
By sunset, no pattern is formed.
Sighing through the long night,
A mournful whistle enters the azure clouds. I guard the empty chamber,
My good man has gone with the army.
He promised to return in three years,
Now already nine springs have passed. Birds circle the trees flying,
Crying clearly, seeking their flock.
I wish to be the south-flowing light,
Racing its rays to see my lord.
In the southern land
there is
a fair lady, her beauty like
peach and plum blossoms.
Morning she wanders north of the river,
Evening she lodges on Xiāng's islet.
The times disdain rosy faces,
For whom to reveal white teeth?
In a moment, the year will end,
Splendor is hard to long maintain.
The groom early prepares the carriage,
I am about to travel far.
Far traveling, to where shall I go?
Wú is my enemy.
I shall gallop ten thousand miles,
The eastern road, how can it suffice?
Between the rivers, much mournful wind,
Huái and Sì race with swift currents.
I wish to cross lightly once,
Alas, I have no boat.
Idle living is not my aspiration,
Willingly I go to serve the nation's worry.
The soaring tower rises over a hundred feet high,
By the window I lean on the railing, gazing far and nigh.
Looking out, a thousand miles stretch before my eyes,
Morning and evening, the plains under vast skies.
A noble heart is often filled with sorrow and pain,
While petty men idly seek pleasure and gain.
The nation's enmity remains unavenged, I know,
Willing to sacrifice my life, to the foe I'd go.
Gripping my sword, I gaze toward the southwest land,
Longing to march to Tàishān, sword in hand.
The tightened strings release a mournful sound,
Hear my impassioned words, profound.
A faint shadow dims the sun's bright ray,
A clear breeze gently lifts my robe to sway.
Fish swim deep in the emerald water's flow,
Birds soar high, brushing the sky as they go.
A traveler, distant and alone, I roam,
On a far-off duty, unable to return home.
When I left, harsh frost had begun to form,
Now I return, white dew dries in the morn.
The wanderer sighs over the millet's decline,
Those left behind sing of hardship's sign.
With noble guests, I speak with fervent heart,
Yet inwardly, sorrow tears me apart.
A gentle breeze fans clear and cool,
Clouds disperse, the sky's a tranquil pool.
Bright and gleaming, the moon shines so fair,
Adorning the high corner with its glare.
I urge the noble lord, with grace,
To join me in the carriage, face to face.
Steeds like dragons, majestic and grand,
Raise their bits, pausing as they stand.
Solemnly we travel through the night,
To my friend's abode, bathed in moonlight.
Lamps emit a radiant glow,
Silken curtains hang long and slow.
Phoenix cups filled with sweetest wine,
Sacred cauldrons cook fish so fine.
Strings surpass Zǐyě's skill in song,
Laments outdo Mián Jū, deep and strong.
Chanting of the primal essence, pure and vast,
Praising the mysteries of the void, unsurpassed.
Who among the worthy and wise,
Shall share with you the official ties?
The determined grieve the day's swift flight,
The sorrowful know the endless night.
Adjusting my robe, I stroll the courtyard near,
Gazing up at southbound geese appear.
Dark shadows follow forms in motion,
Echoing sounds return to the empty room's notion.
How the clear wind flutters and sways,
A faint moon rises in the western haze.
Stars cling to the azure sky so deep,
Constellations in their ordered rows keep.
Cicadas chirp among the lofty trees,
Wild birds call from the eastern breeze.
Wispy clouds at times seem to appear,
Dew soaks my robe, drawing near.
Good times pass, no scene will stay,
The Dipper suddenly dips and sways.
Often I fear the cold season's arrival,
When freezing air turns to frost, a survival.
Leaves fall, by the wind they're torn,
Cut off like a fleeting beam, forlorn.
The sun's course follows heaven's decree,
The four seasons succeed in harmony.
The Eastern Wall marks dusk's embrace,
As deepening cold ascends in place.
Heavy frost descends at night's fall,
A mournful wind rises, answering the call.
Vermilion flames lose their fiery light,
Orchid oil congeals, cold and white.
Layered quilts hold no warmth within,
Wrapped in padding, ice seems to begin.
Lying on my pillow through the distant night,
Awake, my words meet no reply in sight.
Ever pondering rise and fall's design,
With a sigh, alone, I beat my breast in line.
A clear breeze stirs the curtain's lace,
The morning moon lights the secluded space.
My fair one dwells in a distant land,
No radiant beauty graces the orchid room, unmanned.
My bosom holds a spiritual scene,
Light covers drape the empty bed, serene.
In joy, nights seem hurried and brief,
In sorrow, the night brings endless grief.
Patting my pillow, I sigh alone,
Moved and wounded to the heart, unknown.
My gaze roams over the wilds outspread,
Free and alone, I linger, ahead.
Orchids and iris line the clear stream's side,
Lush blossoms shade the green isle with pride.
My fair one is not here with me,
Whom shall I give these to, whom shall I see?
Nest-dwellers know the wind's chill breath,
Burrowers sense the rain before death.
If never parted by distance vast,
How could one yearn for companions past?
I planted sunflowers in the northern garden's ground,
They grow in lush profusion, all around.
At dawn, they lean toward the northeast light,
By dusk, their heads face southwest, bright.
Fresh dew drips with a glistening sheen,
The bright moon casts its radiance, serene.
Gentle winds cease as time slips away,
Year's end brings the autumn gale's swift sway.
Layered clouds hold no warming rain,
Harsh frost wields its凝固 power, plain.
Favored by the high wall's virtuous shade,
Dark shadows shelter the white blooms, arrayed.
Lush stems flourish with spring's full might,
Leaves fall after autumn's decline, in sight.
Rejoicing in late-blooming fortune's grace,
Forgetting this lonely life's sorrowful trace.
Thick clouds obscure the sun's bright ray,
Torrential floods swamp the courtyard's way.
Harsh frost withers the emerald grass,
Cold winds shake the slender, withered mass.
The air is clear, with a biting chill,
Sparse and scattered, plants on the hill.
Moved by the season, I sing of crickets' cry,
Longing for worthies, the white colt's sigh.
My feelings stagnate with the dark shade's hold,
My heart whirls with the turning wind, bold.
What thoughts does my heart contain?
I think of my friend Ōuyáng, again.
Profound meanings probe divine mystery,
Clear insight sparks wondrous theory.
Since we parted months ago,
Subtle words have ceased to flow.
Lifting my robe is not too hard a task,
But clear sunlight I cannot ask.
Stretching my neck beyond the eaves' line,
Standing still, my longing thoughts entwine.
In wealth, others gather near,
In poverty, even kin disappear.
Lián Pō and Lìn Xiàngjū's gates changed their course,
Tián Fén and Dòu Yīng fought with force.
Morning winds gather in lush woods deep,
Roosting birds leave branches dry and steep.
Now I am trapped in ignorance and plight,
Scholars turn their backs, taking flight.
Yet villagers uphold virtue's way,
Gathering to honor, bright as day.
Facing guests, I praise "The Guest's" song,
Raising cups, "Dew on the Grass" prolong.
At joyful feasts, what do I sigh for?
White silk and forked roads, evermore.
Autumn wind rises with evening's breath,
Bright moon shines on the tall tree, beneath.
The quiet room fills with fresh air,
The broad courtyard gleams, bright and fair.
In stillness, a mournful sigh I release,
Melancholy, I step out, seeking peace.
Looking up at grass on the wall high,
Looking down at dew on the steps, nigh.
With heart empty, body feels light,
Floating as if in immortal flight.
Gazing at the tomb mound's height,
I long to meet a divine sprite.
The Way is deep, hard to attain,
Subtleties are not my desire's domain.
Diligent thoughts last through the distant night,
Eternal words pour out my heart's plight.
North winds stir the autumn grass,
Border steeds yearn for home, alas.
Why must we be parted so long?
Slowly, time has drifted along.
Royal duties distract my mind,
Separated farther than stars aligned.
When I left, orioles sang their tune,
Now I return, crickets chirp 'neath the moon.
The heart longs for the homeland old,
A guest bird misses its nest of gold.
Shī Juān's music has long ceased to play,
Who can express what my heart would say?
The Wú rebels not yet quelled,
Chaos encroaches on the borderlands.
The Son of Heaven commands the chief minister,
To serve as protector in Hànyáng.
Establishing a state, founding a new domain,
With jade and silk, the worthy are courted.
I am not the uncut jade of Jīng Mountain,
Yet mistakenly enter Hé Shì’s workshop.
A sheep’s nature with a tiger’s stripes,
A swallow’s wings pretending to be a phoenix’s flight.
Already fearing I am unfit for the task,
I lament that southern road’s great length.
A thousand miles, so vast and distant,
The journey halted by passes and bridges.
My servants weary from the long trek,
Carriages and horses exhausted on the hills.
Deep valleys descend without bottom,
High cliffs reach up to the azure sky.
Lush grasses soak in the moisture,
Mist and dew dampen my clothes.
Dark woods gather gloomy air,
Windless, yet cold and chill.
Looking back, emotions cut deep,
Sorrowful, my heart grieves.
A man is born with a bow hung,
His duty lies across the four directions.
How can one always wander free,
Sitting idly within the women’s quarters?
Upholding duty, I sever worldly ties,
Yet inner feelings are truly hard to forget.
How biting the autumn wind,
White dew becomes morning frost.
Tender branches soon grow tough,
Green leaves turn yellow day and night.
The bright moon emerges from clouded cliffs,
Gleaming, it streams with pure light.
Pushing open the window, I face the front courtyard,
Honking, morning geese soar.
High ambitions confined within the world,
Alone, I guard an empty hall.
Youth does not linger forever,
Year’s end often brings sighs.
Late spring’s mild air arrives,
White sunlight shines upon the garden groves.
Green twigs seem gathered emeralds,
Yellow blossoms scatter like gold.
Lovely flowers truly a sight to behold,
But seeing this, I cannot linger long.
Craning my neck, no good path in sight,
Stamping my feet, I entrust myself to seclusion’s depths.
Glory and vigor both depart,
Lowliness and old age come seeking.
Joy does not light my face,
Grief and sorrow give rise to song.
What use is singing and sighing?
The ancients alone can comfort the heart.
Autumn night, cool winds rise,
Fresh air clears away sultry murk.
Crickets chirp beneath the steps,
Moths flutter past the bright candle.
The gentleman travels far on duty,
The fair lady remains in lonely solitude.
How long since we lived apart?
Drilling wood for fire, the kindling wood has changed.
No traces in the rooms and corridors,
Courtyard grass grows lush and green.
Green moss clings to empty walls,
Spiders weave webs in the four corners.
Moved by things, many thoughts arise,
Deep sorrow knots within my heart.
Great Fire Star flows in the earth’s corner,
The white sun speeds through the western sky.
Floating sunlight gleams on emerald woods,
Whirling winds fan the green bamboo.
Flying rain sprinkles morning orchids,
Light dew rests on clustered chrysanthemums.
The dragon hibernates, warm air congeals,
The sky is high, all things turn solemn.
Weak twigs will not entwine again,
Fragrant blooms shall not regain their scent.
Life within this vast sea,
Suddenly like a bird passing before the eyes.
The sigh by the river for things passing,
The ancient sages used to spur themselves.
Golden winds fan the pure season,
Crimson clouds herald the overcast days.
Soaring clouds like billowing smoke,
Dense rain like scattered threads.
Cold flowers bloom with yellow hues,
Autumn grass holds green vitality.
Living in leisure, I admire all things,
Apart from the crowd, I yearn for my beloved.
No letters from Xiāo on my desk,
No traces of Gòng in my courtyard.
Noble, aloof from kings and lords,
The Way accumulated forms its own foundation.
The perfect man is not entangled by things,
His remaining influence can still sway the age.
Morning clouds greet the white sun,
Crimson aura nears Tāng Valley.
Gloomy, dense clouds gather,
Profuse, they scatter abundant rain.
Gentle winds break the sturdy grass,
Congealing frost stiffens the tall trees.
Dense leaves thin by day and night,
The grove of trees stands bundled tight.
In former days I lamented time’s slowness,
In later years I grieve life’s brevity.
Year’s end, harboring a hundred cares,
I shall go to seek Jì Zhǔ’s divination.
Once I brought ceremonial caps,
Hoping to suit the land of Yuè.
Journeying into deep wilderness,
Ōu and Luò tribes with shorn hair.
All year, of no use to them,
Where could such goods be placed?
Common tiles boast of being jade,
Fish eyes laugh at the bright moon.
Have you not heard the songs of Yǐng,
How high and low are clearly distinct?
“Yángchūn” finds none to harmonize,
“Bārén” all sing in lower key.
Common custom is mostly blind,
Who can discern this principle?
At dawn I climb Lǔyáng Pass,
The narrow path steep and deep.
Flowing streams drop ten thousand zhàng,
Encircling trees reach thousands of xún.
Roaring tigers echo through barren hills,
Crying cranes clamor in empty woods.
Bitter winds howl for me,
A hundred sounds sit and chant alone.
Moved by things, many feelings arise,
In danger, one’s constant heart changes.
Coming here, wary of the unforeseen,
I grip the reins, cross soaring peaks.
Wáng Yáng drove through Nine Bends,
Zhōu Wén fled through jagged cliffs.
Facing obstacles, haste is unwise,
This truth is clear for ages to come.
This land
is not my place,
This town is not my city.
A traveler with no settled heart,
Fluttering like a hanging banner.
Outside, I see armies and horses arrayed,
Inside, I hear drums of war.
Often fearing urgent dispatches fly,
The Divine Martial One will summon once.
Long swords clang in their sheaths,
Beacon fires line the border posts.
Leaving my humble gate behind,
Again I don the warrior’s tasseled cap.
Once I cherished modest aims, Secretly studying within the tent.
Why must one wield spear and shield, When in the hall there are
Marvelous strategies?
Victory won between the wine cups,
Triumph decided between the pillars.
Clever delays earn no praise,
Swift simplicity achieves lasting fame.
Reporting for duty, I head to the border town,
Bound and confined among the troops.
Descending from the carriage as if yesterday,
Yet the moon has waxed four or five times.
May I ask what season this is?
Butterflies flit through the southern garden.
Flowing waters long for the old shore,
Wandering clouds yearn for former hills.
Mǐnyuè folk wear patterned serpents,
Northern steeds wish to cross to Yān.
How can one adapt to local ways?
From the start, it has always been thus.
I built my hut at the bend of a barren ridge,
Plowing in pairs in the shade of a secluded marsh.
The desolate courtyard is silent and idle,
The secluded peaks steep and deep.
A chill wind rises from the eastern valley,
Rain clouds gather over the southern hills.
Though not the season for the Jī and Bì stars,
A slight moisture forms its own downpour.
Marsh pheasants ascend the ridges and call,
Cold apes cling to branches and cry.
No human trace in the streams and gorges,
Wild thickets lush and desolate.
I lay down my plow and walk along the bank,
Sometimes hearing the sound of woodcutters.
The layered hills can match my resolve,
The winding abyss can compare to my heart.
Nurturing truth, I honor non-action,
The Way prevails, valuing reclusion.
My thoughts wander in the garden of bamboo and silk,
My words entrusted to the forest of brush and ink.
The black Li serpent leaps in the deep abyss,
The Shāngyáng bird dances in the wild courtyard.
Fēilián answers the southern winnowing basket,
Fēnglóng meets the roaring screen.
Cloud roots reach the eight extremes,
Rain feet sprinkle the four seas.
The downpour lasts over twenty days,
Its spread rivals the nine-year flood.
Springs surge beneath the steps,
Water moss grows upon the hall.
Vast deluges wildly carve the land,
People harbor muddled, drowning feelings.
Sinking waters wash over old roots,
Green leaves rot on autumn stems.
No curling chimney smoke in the village,
No sound of cart wheels on the road.
Surrounding walls crumble on their own,
Fences and gates no longer conceal.
An inch of ash outweighs cassia,
Red grains more precious than jade.
The nobleman holds fast to steadfast poverty,
In hardship, he does not falter in virtue.
Though honored by Tián Fāng’s gift,
Ashamed to be named for ditches and gullies.
I take my resolve from Yúlíng’s son,
Compare my lot to Qián Lóu’s life.
Ceaselessly the round heavens revolve,
Vast and endless the square earth expands.
Suddenly, suddenly, the year says it is late,
I roam the plains gathering mugwort and beans.
Northward crossing the Máng and Hé rivers,
Southward approaching the Yī and Luò rivers.
Frozen dew moistens creeping grass,
A mournful wind shakes woods and thickets.
Rustling, fragrant leaves fall,
Drooping, sweet blossoms drop.
The lower spring rushes clear and cold,
The wild fields grow more desolate and vast.
Climbing high, I gaze at distant wastelands,
Looking to the horizon, no cliffs or peaks.
Form changes with the times,
Spirit stirred by things arises.
Serene is the heart of the ultimate man,
Tranquilly preserving mysterious silence.
I built my hut within the human realm,
Yet hear no clamor of carriage or horse.
You ask how this can be so?
With heart remote, the place grows secluded.
Picking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge,
Serenely I gaze upon the southern mountains.
Mountain air is lovely at dusk,
Flying birds return together.
In this return lies true meaning,
Wanting to explain, I’ve forgotten words.
Autumn chrysanthemums have lovely hues,
Dew-drenched, I pluck their blossoms.
Floating on this worry-forgetting thing,
I distance myself from worldly affairs.
Though I drink alone, cup after cup,
When the cup empties, the pot pours itself.
As the sun sets, all movement ceases,
Returning birds hasten to the woods, chirping.
Whistling proudly beneath the eastern eaves,
I find this life once more.
All creatures have their place to rest,
Only the lone cloud drifts without support.
Dimly fading in the empty sky,
When will its lingering glow be seen?
Morning clouds clear the night mist,
Flocks of birds fly together.
Slowly, a wing emerges from the woods,
Returning before evening falls again.
Measuring my strength, I keep to the old path,
How could I avoid cold and hunger?
If a kindred spirit does not exist,
Let it be—what is there to grieve?
In early summer, grass and trees grow tall,
Trees surround my house with spreading branches.
All birds rejoice in having a perch,
I too love my humble hut.
Having plowed and already sown,
I return to read my books.
Deep ruts stay far from my poor lane,
Often turning old friends’ carriages away.
Joyfully we drink spring wine,
Plucking vegetables from my garden.
A light rain comes from the east,
A gentle breeze accompanies it.
I browse through King Zhōu’s legends,
Skim over the maps of mountains and seas.
In a glance, I traverse the universe—
If this isn’t joy, what is?
The setting sun hides behind eaves and pillars,
The rising moon shines through blinds and lattices.
Round, round, dew fills the leaves,
Soughing, soughing, the wind shakes the branches.
I stroll along the broad steps,
Blinking, I gaze at the layered sky.
In the Milky Way, a divine pair,
For years apart, unable to meet.
Distant rivers veil their tender love,
Long isles stretch with clear, lonely grace.
Weaving at the loom, no pattern forms,
Reining the carriage, chasing former traces.
Once parted, autumn had passed twice,
Now reunited, no evening matches this.
The tilting river easily turns its course,
But sincere joy is hard to prolong.
Lush and vibrant, the divine carriage departs,
Silent and empty, the cloud canopy remains.
Lingering feelings gaze upon the splendid chamber,
A distant heart pursues the galloping dragon.
Pondering deeply, moved by this,
Deep emotion grows ever stronger.
The celestial measures do not linger,
The sun’s course hurries as if urged.
White dew nourishes garden chrysanthemums,
Autumn wind sheds leaves from courtyard locusts.
Rustling, rustling, the katydid’s wings,
Fierce, fierce, the cold cicada’s cry.
Evening shadows gather like empty curtains,
Night moon shines bright within the inner chamber.
The fair lady prepares her robes,
Adorned properly, she goes to meet him.
Hairpins and jade from the north room,
Golden ornaments step on southern stairs.
High eaves, the pounding block sounds,
Long pillars, the pestle’s mournful note.
Faint fragrance rises from both sleeves,
Light sweat stains both temples.
Fine silk is already woven,
But my lord has not yet returned.
Cutting with the knife from the chest,
Sewing into a robe for ten thousand miles.
The full chest comes from my own hands,
Sealed secretly, awaiting your opening.
The waistband measured as before,
Not knowing if it fits you now.
Dim, dim, the sun sinks in the west,
Long, long, the road presses close.
Ascending the tower, for whom do I yearn?
By the river, awaiting the late-coming guest.
When we parted, we set a date,
The date was the fifteenth night.
The full moon has long been round,
Yet my beloved has not arrived.
This matter grieves our separation,
Moved by things, I feel deep sorrow.
Early summer nights are not long,
Yet dusk to dawn feels like years apart.
Jade flowers are not yet ready to pluck,
Orchid shoots have been picked again and again.
The road is blocked, no gifts or questions sent,
How then to soothe this parting pain?
Scratching my head, I ask the travelers,
Craning my neck, hoping for a good meeting.
Woodcutters and recluses both dwell in the mountains,
Yet their pursuits have always been different.
Different not in just one matter,
I too nurture my illness within the garden.
Within the garden, screened from worldly clamor,
The clear expanse beckons distant winds.
I built my hut leaning against the northern hill,
Opened the door facing the southern river.
Rushing streams replace drawing water from the well,
Planted hibiscus hedges serve as walls.
Many trees now surround my door,
And numerous mountains also face my window.
Winding paths lead down to the lower fields,
From afar I gaze upon the lofty peaks.
With few desires, I do not seek toil,
In my affairs, I rarely rely on others' labor.
Only opening the path like Jiǎng Xùn,
Forever cherishing the traces of Qiú and Yáng.
The joy in my heart cannot be forgotten,
Hoping to share in subtle goodness.
In the past, I roamed the capital's splendor,
Yet never abandoned hills and valleys.
How much more now, returning to mountains and rivers,
Where mind and traces both dwell in solitude.
Empty halls free from disputes and lawsuits,
The vacant courtyard visited by birds and sparrows.
Lying ill, I have ample leisure,
Occasionally dabbling in brush and ink.
Embracing thoughts, I observe past and present,
In rest and meals, I indulge in playful banter.
I laugh at the hardships of Jǔ and Nì,
And smile at Zǐyún's tower.
Serving as a guard also brings weariness,
How could farming and sowing be called joy?
All things under heaven cannot bring simultaneous delight,
Fortunately, the philosophy of "Dáshēng" offers solace.
Climbing perilous heights to build a secluded dwelling,
Parting clouds to lie within a stone gate.
Who can tread on the slippery moss?
How can one grasp the frail kudzu vines?
The gentle autumn wind passes by,
Lush spring grasses grow abundant.
The fair one travels afar, never to return,
How can our cherished meeting be fulfilled?
Fragrant dust settles on the jade mat,
Clear wine fills the golden goblet.
The Dòngtíng Lake lies empty, its waves stilled,
In vain I reach for the cassia branches.
My thoughts ascend to the Milky Way,
A solitary shadow, with none to console.
Bending to wash in the pool beneath the rocks,
Looking up to see monkeys on the branches.
Early I hear the evening gale's urgency,
Late I witness the morning sun's glow.
Cliffs lean, sunlight hard to retain,
Deep forests, echoes easily rush forth.
Moved by the past, I fear recurrence,
When reason comes, emotions fade away.
I wish to hold the sun-chariot's reins,
Thereby to comfort my restless soul.
Not for the multitude do I speak,
But hope to discuss with the wise.
The pining wife ascends the high tower,
Longing, leaning on the ornate railing.
Strumming the strings, she cannot complete a tune,
A mournful song conveys her bitter words.
Broom and dustpan remain by the riverbank,
Her beloved husband is at Yànmén.
Does he recall the hardship of lacking clothes?
Only knowing the warmth of fox-fur white.
As dusk falls, cattle and sheep descend,
Wild sparrows fill the empty garden.
In early winter, the cold wind rises,
The eastern wall faces the deepening gloom.
