A lone crimson lamp illuminates her,
Holding her shadow, she drowns in sorrow.
Who knows the turmoil in her heart?
Her thoughts are beyond words.
Alone, I serve west of the pass,
My family fills the lands east of the mountains.
For two years I followed the imperial carriage,
Observing fasts and rituals at Gānquán Palace.
After the three-day national celebrations ended,
On leave, I returned to my homeland.
Four steeds gleam on the long road,
Light canopies like flying swans.
Five nobles bid me farewell,
A grand gathering at Xīnfēng.
Six musical strains arrayed in the wide hall,
Silken curtains flutter in the spring breeze.
Seven-plate dance, long sleeves rising,
In the courtyard, rows of singing bells.
Eight delicacies fill carved vessels,
Exquisite dishes layered in profusion.
Nine clans all gaze with admiration,
Friends and guests look up to my noble bearing.
Ten years of study brought no achievement,
Skill in office, once attained, brings instant success.
First appearing at the southwest tower,
Slender as a jade hook.
Finally shining on the northeast steps,
Delicate like moth eyebrows.
Moth eyebrows hidden behind beaded lattices,
Jade hooks separated by intricate windows.
On the fifteenth and sixteenth nights,
A thousand miles apart, yet sharing the same moon with you.
Night shifts, the Dipper and Han River set,
Pacing back and forth within curtains and doors.
Falling petals wither first from dew,
Parting leaves depart early in the wind.
A traveler weary of bitter toil,
An official tired of drifting dust.
On rest days free from public duties,
Feasting and comfort extend to private hours.
Shǔ qín plays "White Snow,"
Yǐng melodies sing of "Spring Sunshine."
Food dries, wine not yet depleted,
Golden pot marks the evening's descent.
Turning the carriage, halting the light canopy,
Lingering over drinks, awaiting my beloved.
Only in the past, encountering enlightened times,
For ten years I attended the cloud-wrapped steps.
Once registered in the golden gate's records,
Again I drank from jade feasts' sweet wine.
Imperial favor wearied of shining upon,
Dark winds overwhelmed the successor's reign.
Chaotic rainbows disrupt the morning sun,
Muddy rivers defile the clear Jì.
Guarding speech still counted as lenient rule,
Eating bitter herbs seemed sweet as shepherd's purse.
Illustrious ministers expanded human plans,
Civilized governance truly heaven-sent.
Green essence aids the purple carriage,
Yellow banners reflect on vermilion mansions.
Again I witness the Commissioner's insignia,
Once more see the eastern capital's rites.
The central region all at peace,
Lightly regarding life, I find clarity.
Hastening to duties, I leave the palace gates,
Carrying brush, I accompany banners and halberds.
Villages and hamlets turn sparse and wild,
Cold streams run clear and pure.
Withered willows still hang heavy,
Condensed dew lies thick and muddy.
Falling leaves grieve for friends,
Joyful feasts entertain brothers.
Holding a heart of cinnabar stone,
How could I shed tears of plain silk?
Riding this to ultimate detachment,
I'll fish with rod by the deep ravine's base.
Purple halls solemn and shadowy,
Vermilion courtyards grand and spacious.
Wind stirs the ten-thousand-year branches,
Sunlight bathes the dew-collecting palms.
Exquisite knots form patterned coins,
Deep shadows reflect on crimson nets.
Red peonies flutter by the steps,
Green moss creeps up along the walls.
Here they speak of the Phoenix Pond,
Where jade pendants chime with clear sounds.
Truly fine, but not my home,
In the central garden, I long to recline.
Friendship's feelings lie pent-up,
Spring things now ripple and sway.
How can I gain wings to ride the wind,
To freely enjoy mountain and spring?
Northern winds blow flying rain,
Desolate, it comes over the river.
Already sprinkling the Hundred-Pace Tower,
Again gathering on the Nine-Tiered Terrace.
Misty and vague like thin fog,
Scattered and spread like light dust.
At dawn, I shake my robe and sit,
Layered gates still not opened.
Ears and eyes briefly free from disturbance,
Believing in antiquity, truly remote.
Folding wings, hoping to lift my head,
Riding the current, fearing to expose my gills.
Action and rest cannot both succeed,
At crossroads, much hesitation.
Just like the victor in inner struggle,
I go to clear the northern mountain's weeds.
I ask when I shall leave my carriage behind,
Not just because the moon is full and bright.
I gaze afar from the cold city wall,
Where trees on the plain stretch in endless green.
Mountains pile up, blocking Língyáng’s path,
Streams flow with springs from Chūngǔ’s vale.
Winding and distant, far from the suburbs,
Jagged peaks touch the distant sky.
Soughing, the gloomy wind blows at dusk,
Mulberries and thorn-trees raise cold mist.
Melancholy, my heart is overwhelmed,
Dazed, my soul drifts time and again.
Since youth I’ve wearied of life as a traveler,
All my life I’ve served early at the frontier.
Who seeks the splendor of lavish feasts?
Would I ever crave fox-fur’s white warmth?
I’ll renounce the promise of Rǔnán,
And speak of tilling fields in Liáodōng.
The flame’s spirit left sword and seal behind,
Dāngtú trembled at the dragons’ war.
The sage’s era lacked in the central land,
The hegemon’s deeds rose in the counties.
The magpie soared, ascending Wú Mountain,
The phoenix glided over Chǔ’s plains.
Belts and girdles reached steep cliffs and dangers,
Curtains and tents were filled with chosen plans.
Northward, they drowned steeds and bridles in resistance,
Westward, they gathered armored troops in triumph.
Since rivers and seas held no more waves,
Looking up and down, they cast heroic glances.
Fur robes and crowns resembled suburban sacrifices,
Divinations exalted the distant palaces.
By the fishing terrace, they reviewed troops,
At Fán Mountain, they held grand feasts.
Cultural relics flourished together,
Fame and brilliance shone lush and bright.
The three lights tired of divided radiance,
Writing and tracks sought to be united in offering.
Uneven, the generations’ sacrifices passed swiftly,
Silent, the markets and courts transformed.
Dancing halls show remnants of their foundations,
Singing beams recall lingering turns.
In old groves, withered trees lie level,
By desolate ponds, autumn grasses spread everywhere.
Grand ambitions fade sadly like this,
Wise governors gaze deeply into the distance.
A recluse lingers by the riverbank,
Following pleasures, yet straying from official caps.
Clear wine is hindered from toasts and sharing,
Fine books are limited in what they reveal.
Fortunately, fragrant words abound,
Receiving the breeze, I gather remaining splendor.
If duty should have a set time,
At Èzhǔ we may wander together.
Two separations block the Hàn River’s shores,
Twin peaks gaze toward the Hé River’s bend.
This ridge again rises steep and lofty,
Dividing regions, securing the Huái’s domain.
East bounded by Lángyé Terrace,
West reaching Mèngzhū’s land.
Dense and mingled, varied trees arise,
Fine bamboos cast shade, tall and graceful.
The sun hides, streams congeal in emptiness,
Clouds gather, peaks seem layered and doubled.
Appearing and vanishing, I gaze at tower battlements,
Far and near, I send my springtime gaze.
Róng tribes once brought chaos to Huá,
Pure scenes sank in Yī and Gǔ valleys.
Peril was averted by the ancestral robe,
Subtle governance entrusted to enlightened shepherds.
The long serpent could indeed be severed,
The fleeing whale since then basked in the sun.
The path lofty, fragrant dust flows,
Achievements distant, years and fortune fleeting.
All my life I’ve admired noble plans,
Alas, fate has not been kind.
Vast and boundless, I part from kin and friends,
In succession, I prepare the journey’s axle.
Again far from the Wáwa Palace,
Twice leaving Héyáng Valley.
Wind and mist invade through four seasons,
Frost and rain bathe morning and night.
Spring’s beauty has truly faded,
Autumn’s fields may yet be tilled.
Wǎn and Luò are fine for wandering,
Spring hues fill the imperial region.
Halting the carriage on green suburban roads,
Looking back at the dark river’s flow.
Sunlight shimmers on the water’s surface,
Scenery floats amid the grasses.
Peach and plum form hidden paths,
Mulberry and elm shade the roadside.
The eastern capital has begun its labors,
Speaking of return, I gaze at green fields.
The inner court sent envoys to distant lands,
Chángmén Palace lost its joyful feasts.
Meeting, they sang of the língwú herb,
Leaving favor, they grieved like Bān Jiéyú’s fan.
Among flowers, butterflies flit in disorder,
Through the wind-blown curtain, a pair of swallows enter.
Only causing the spring sash to grow long,
Sitting to lament the fading of rouge and powder.
A single glance in life held great weight,
In past times, a thousand gold seemed cheap.
The old friend’s heart remains thus,
Yet the old friend’s heart is unseen.
Wáng Qiáo flew on his duck-sole shoes,
Dōngfāng Shuò at the Golden Horse Gate.
Serving office, yet not among official companions,
Avoiding the world, yet not avoiding noise.
Considering myself under the emperor’s discernment,
With short wings, I’ve fluttered repeatedly.
At dawn I hasten to court at Jiànlǐ Hall,
At dusk I bathe and rest in the suburban garden.
When guests arrive, I lower the dusty couch,
When sorrow comes, I summon the green goblet.
Ancient worthies matched timely rain,
Today’s guardians are fragrant like orchids.
Spiritual communion wearies dreams,
Long roads separate thoughts and memories.
Clumsily drawn, I err in the eastern marsh,
Floating idly, I reach the western heights.
Looking back, I follow what is humble and slight,
How can I match jade and precious stones?
I shall follow the vast sea away,
Preen my feathers and float on clear springs.
Moonlight descends on the still night,
The quiet night clears away dust and haze.
Square radiance enters through the door,
Round shadows come through the cracks.
High towers grieve the longing wife,
Western gardens entertain talents.
Net-curtained windows gleam with pearl strands,
The main gate illuminates green moss.
The inner chamber is not yet dawn,
The clear light truly lingers on.
When Lián Pō lost power and influence,
His gatehouse saw emptiness and fullness.
If high and low are thus,
How much more when winding pools lie level?
Tall carriages’ dust has not yet settled,
Pearl-adorned shoes still leave echoes.
Guest steps are overgrown with green coins,
Visitor seats sprout purple moss.
Who now upon the Jiǔyuán heights,
Lushly gazes toward the fine tomb?
Autumn wind blows across the broad road,
Desolate, it enters the southern gate.
The sorrowful person lies with shutters closed,
High windows now and then stir the door.
The empty lodge fills with clear shade,
The divine dwelling dims faintly.
Spiderwebs hang woven across the door,
Evening birds fly by the eaves.
Official regalia are worn in vain,
Rivers and seas affairs often go awry.
In the mountains there are cassia trees,
At year’s end I may speak of return.
White water fills the spring pond,
Traveling geese often circle and soar.
Nibbling streams, they tug at tender algae,
Folding wings, they carry lingering frost.
In flocks they float on gentle waves,
Alone they drift, chasing solitary light.
Hovering in flight, they never descend,
Rising in disorder, not yet in formation.
Preening feathers together, swaying and rippling,
With one ascent they return to their homeland.
The bright sun belongs to the third day of the third month,
the year's blossoms are all here at this time.
Flowers have fully encircled the trees,
and singing birds again fill the branches.
The dashing youths of Luòyáng,
the frivolous gallants of Cháng'ān.
They venture east to the Qiānjīn Weir,
and approach west the Yànwù Marsh.
Gossamer threads shimmer as they twirl in the air,
tall poplars brush the ground with hanging boughs.
Green headbands gleam with patterned brilliance,
purple swallows shine in dazzling array.
At dawn they sport by the Yī River's waters,
by dusk they lodge amidst orchid ponds.
Ivory mats resound with precious zithers,
golden vessels float with feathered winecups.
Who then recalls the spring silkworms rising,
as dusk falls and the mulberries wilt?
Long sleeves are often brushed aside,
while fine rice is just being cooked.
Loved yet unseen,
night after night her beauty fades.
Better to go forgetting all passion,
why sigh alone in vain?
Far, far the journey stretches,
deep, deep the sorrowful thoughts.
What thoughts are these I think?
Thoughts of your grace and voice.
Your voice and grace grow distant day and night,
remote as flight or sinking deep.
The royal sturgeon yearns for river caves,
the morning breeze longs for northern woods.
The wanderer is lost at heaven's edge,
distant hopes cannot be sought.
Sudden storms disrupt returning messages,
though homeward clouds may carry word.
Standing still, I envision ten thousand miles,
heavy sorrow gathers in my heart.
Gathering my robe, the sash hangs loose,
following my form, the lapel does not fill.
Away, away, cast off emotional burdens,
settle peacefully and stroke the clear-toned qin.
On a leisurely night I summon joyful friends,
set out wine at the Welcome Breeze Hall.
A Qí lad chants "Liángfǔ's Lament,"
a Qín maiden plucks the "Zhāng's Daughter" melody.
Mournful notes wind round the beams and eaves,
lingering echoes enter the Milky Way.
All four seats share the same intent,
feathered winecups cannot be counted.
How elegant their lofty discourse!
Lush as morning clouds' radiant glow.
Human life does not last long,
joyful moments often come too late.
Like those birds awaiting dawn,
they raise their voices just at daybreak.
Why always dwell in worry and distress,
clinging to this poverty and low estate?
Bright, bright shine the clear Han's stars,
brilliant, brilliant light the heavenly steps.
The Herd Boy turns to the northwest,
the Weaving Maid looks toward the southeast.
How radiant her flowery countenance!
Waving her hand as if shaking plain silk.
Resenting that the river has no bridge,
grieving that the year draws to its close.
Standing on tiptoe, no good chance arises;
gazing longingly, she cannot cross.
Craning her neck, she gazes at the great river,
twin streams of tears like dew-drops falling.
Climbing the mountain to gather jade stamens,
deep valleys abound with fragrant orchids.
Gathering, gathering, not filling a handful,
far, far away, I long for my beloved.
How vast my homeland lies!
Mountains and rivers block and bar the way.
Deep in thought, focused on ten thousand miles,
hesitating, alone I chant and sigh.
Luxuriant grows the jiānglí grass,
glittering bright by the river's side.
Fair, fair is that lovely maiden,
graceful, she weaves before the window.
Brilliant, brilliant her enchanting form,
radiant, radiant her beautiful features.
Her good man wanders, not returning,
she roosts alone with but one wing.
Empty rooms admit the mournful wind,
at midnight she rises with a sigh.
Resting peacefully in the northern hall,
the bright moon enters my window.
Shining, it leaves lingering light,
grasping it, it does not fill my hand.
Cool winds wind through winding chambers,
cold cicadas chirp in the tall willows.
Hesitating, moved by seasonal sights,
my journey has been long indeed.
Wandering in office brings no success,
parting thoughts are hard to bear forever.
Fine trees grow facing the morning sun,
congealed frost seals their branches.
Holding fast to heart, awaiting the season's promise,
in year's cold they never wither.
How distant is the beautiful one!
Radiant, she dwells beyond the clouds.
Profound longing spans the months and years,
a long whistle enters the flying whirlwind.
Craning my neck, I gaze to heaven's edge,
like that plant turning toward the sun.
Softly swaying duckweed on the high mound,
fluttering gently with the wind's wings.
How long does human life endure?
Like those ripples on turbid water.
Sorrowful, many stagnant thoughts,
I set out wine to feast my beloved.
Side by side, carriages shake flying reins,
traveling far, we enter Cháng'ān.
How splendid the famous capital!
City walls and towers rise majestic, coiled.
Flying pavilions girdled with rainbow sashes,
layered terraces crowned with cloud-like caps.
High gates arrayed by the northern gate-towers,
mansions grand with pepper and orchid.
Knights-errant rein in peerless steeds,
city folk drive jade-adorned carriages.
Roaming free, indulging heart's desires,
for whom do they sigh with fervent passion?
How steep the Western Mountains are!
Layer upon layer, towering and lofty.
Falling dew fills the sky as it descends,
huì leaves rely on the woods to wither.
Cold and heat follow one another,
time passes suddenly like collapse.
The Sānlǘ official tied his flying reins,
the great elder sighed at the setting sun.
Why be entangled in worldly affairs,
when the heart feels as if against its will?
Jīng and Luò have many enchanting beauties,
jade faces rivaling jade flower stamens.
On a leisurely night she strokes the singing qin,
graceful notes, clear and mournful.
Long songs keep pace with hurried rhythms,
sorrowful sounds follow high pitches.
One singing makes ten thousand men sigh,
singing again makes dust fly from the beams.
Longing to be birds by the winding river,
swimming in pairs along the Fēng River's banks.
How lofty the tall tower is!
Soaring high, steep yet secure.
Lattice windows emerge from dusty gloom,
flying stairways tread upon cloud banks.
A fair lady strokes the qin and sè,
slender hands, clear and leisurely.
Fragrant breath gathers with the wind,
mournful notes sweet as orchids.
Who may behold her jade-like face?
The city-toppling beauty lies in one pluck.
Standing still, I watch the setting sun,
hesitating, sighing again and again.
I do not resent standing long,
but only wish the singer joy.
Longing to ride the returning wild geese's wings,
wing to wing in paired flight.
Joyful friends went in orchid season,
far, far away, their voices and grace hidden.
Yúyuān draws the last sunlight,
the four seasons pass like flight.
Fragrant grass has long been lush,
yet the fair one never returns.
Hesitating, I walk by woods and shores,
a gentle breeze enters my bosom.
Moved by things, I yearn for my beloved,
gathering these, for whom shall I give them?
Year's end, cool winds arise,
the vast sky, clear and bright.
The Dipper points to the northwest,
the Milky Way tilts to the southeast.
The bright moon shines on the quiet room,
crickets chirp within the courtyard.
Fluttering, returning geese gather,
chirring, cold cicadas sing.
Former companions of shared feasts,
soared on wings to the high heavens.
Fine robes changed the sound they hear,
pleasant dwellings left old feelings behind.
The Weaving Maid has no loom and shuttle,
the great beam does not rest on pillars.
Where my thoughts lie is in Yíngzhōu,
I wish to go there, but the road is rugged and long.
Climbing the cliff, gazing afar, tears and snivel flow,
My heart is filled with sorrow and grief.
The fair one left me a green qǐn zither,
What shall I give in return? A pair of southern gold.
I wish to ride the flowing waves across the deep abyss,
Yet in the end, I cannot reach it, only adding to my eternal lament.
At dusk, the sky is cloudless,
The spring breeze gently fans a mild warmth.
The fair one delights in the clear night,
Until dawn, she drinks deeply and sings.
When the song ends, she heaves a long sigh,
Holding this, it moves people deeply.
Bright and clear is the moon among the clouds,
Brilliant and radiant are the flowers among the leaves.
How could there not be a moment of beauty?
But soon, what will become of it?
At the end of the Jiàn'ān era,
I was then in the Yè palace,
Roaming by day and feasting by night,
Reaching the pinnacle of joy and pleasure.
Fine times and beautiful scenes under heaven,
Delightful hearts and happy events,
These four are rarely combined.
Now, with my brothers and friends,
Two or three outstanding talents,
We have exhausted them all.
Since ancient times, such pleasures
Have not been recorded in books.
Why?
In the time of King Xiāng of Chǔ, there were Sòng Yù
and Táng Jǐng;
In the time of Prince Xiào of Liáng, there were Zōu,
Méi, Yán,
and Mǎ. The travelers were splendid,
but their lords were not cultured;
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn had talents like Xú Yuè,
fully equipped with the ability to respond,
but he was suspicious and jealous—
how could they attain the comfort of candid conversation?
Without disparaging the future,
perhaps it must be better than today.
Time flows like a river,
scattering and nearly exhausted.
Composing writings, thinking of people,
I reflect on the past and feel increased sorrow.
The words say:
All rivers flow to the great sea,
All stars circle the North Star.
Shining brightly through the Milky Way,
Distant and far, rising from long shores.
Heaven and earth were in turmoil,
Our royal house saved the people.
Once the realm was cleansed,
All heroes were sure to gather.
I, unworthy, admire the virtuous nature,
Always having cherished benevolence.
Moreover, meeting these many gentlemen,
Devoted hearts flourish daily anew.
Discussing things without empty talk,
Analyzing principles, truly expounding.
How could detailed accounts lack words?
Profoundly exploring heaven and humanity.
Clear wine fills golden vessels,
Connected couches spread with splendid mats.
Urgent strings stir flying listeners,
Pure songs brush dust from the beams.
How can one say meeting is easy?
This joy is truly precious.
My family originally from Qínchuān,
Descendants of noble lords,
Encountering chaos, drifting in exile,
I grieve deeply for myself.
In the past, Yōu and Lì brought collapse and chaos,
Now Huán and Líng cause turmoil and unrest.
Yī and Luò are already scorched by smoke,
Hán and Xiáo vanish without trace.
Packing my belongings, I leave Qínchuān,
Galloping my horse toward Chǔ lands.
Jǔ and Zhāng are naturally beautiful,
But the traveler's heart is not lured by externals.
Often I sigh at the poet's words,
"How can one go in decline?"
The high minister upholds the imperial spirit,
Lords and nobles all revere the elder.
Cloud-like cavalry disrupts Hànnán,
Jìyǐng is all swept clean.
Pushing aside fog, facing the bright glory,
Parting clouds, meeting clarity and light.
Fortune and peace desire to overlap,
The lord specially appreciates first.
Not expecting the wish to rest my shoulders,
Suddenly I encounter the bright pair.
Together we travel to the capital Yè,
Side by side boats sail the broad river.
Intimately engaged in clear feasts and pleasures,
Silent echoes in the beams and pillars.
Since we indulge in all-night drinking,
How could we care for nurturing by daylight!
Yuán Běnchū's secretarial scholars,
Thus recounted many events of chaos and loss.
The great Hàn encountered hardship,
The world suffered from ominous evils.
The Dǒng clan fell in Guānxī,
The Yuán family held Héběi.
A lone man easily panics,
A distressed body submits to restraint.
Who would have thought affairs would turn against me?
Forever I cherish longing for my homeland.
The lord truly toiled for the king,
Truly able to pacify the traitors.
Again I see the splendor of the eastern capital,
Once more behold the laws of the Hàn court.
My remaining life is fortunate indeed,
Moreover, I encounter enlightened virtue.
Loving guests without wearying,
Feasting and drinking, forgetting the passage of time.
At night, listening until the stars fade,
By day, roaming until dusk turns dark.
Melancholy tunes stir dust on the beams,
Urgent cups dispel silent gloom.
Just enjoy a day's pleasure to the full,
Heed not the perplexities since ancient times.
From youth, I had no desire for officialdom,
Harboring the heart of Jī and Yǐng,
Thus my words in the world were often plain.
In the past, my home was in Línzī,
Holding hands, playing the Qí sè.
Setting out wine to drink in Jiāodōng,
Lingering and resting in Gāomì.
This joy I thought could last forever,
But external matters are hard to conclude.
Swaying with the sentiments of Jī and Pú,
All year long pressed by worry and fear.
Fortunately, in later years, encountering enlightened rule,
I perch and gather, relying on my meager quality.
Already spared the hardship of carrying firewood,
I still wander in chambers of pepper and orchid.
Clear discussions explore myriad matters,
Fine words truly are not few.
Passing cups, performing mournful songs,
All night long, tied to the bright day.
Magnificent houses are not thatched huts,
How could the fashionable be my match?
Mid-drink, I reflect on my past heart,
Melancholy, as if having lost something.
Outstanding yet eccentric,
But his writing is most spirited,
What he gains is rather extraordinary.
Living in poverty, tranquil in the neighborhood,
From youth, I grew up in Dōngpíng.
Hé and Yǎn are at a strategic point,
Drifting and wandering, I approached Xǔjīng.
The broad river has no countercurrent,
Recruiting and admitting, I mingled among the heroes.
Northward, crossing the Líyáng ford,
Southward, ascending the walls of Jìyǐng.
Having observed affairs past and present,
I somewhat understand the conditions of order and chaos.
Joyful friends understand and support each other,
Expounding and presenting, exploring a lifetime.
Moreover, bearing the regard of the wise,
Knowing deeply, I feel life is light.
By day, roaming until cattle and sheep descend,
By night, sitting as crickets chirp.
All year long, not just a single day,
Passing cups, playing new tunes.
Since affairs are hard to harmonize,
Joyful wishes now combine.
Only envying the solemn swan,
Colorful and disorderly, soaring to the high heavens.
Scholars of Rǔ and Yǐng,
Drifting and displaced by worldly affairs,
Often have sighs of wandering and drifting.
Crying geese in the clouds,
Raise wings from Wěiyǔ.
Seeking cool by Ruòshuǐ’s banks,
Fleeing cold at Chángshā’s isles.
Thinking of my time in Liángchuān,
Strolling slowly, gathering at Yǐngxǔ.
Once encountering worldly troubles,
Drifting and wandering, ever a traveler.
In times when the world was unsettled,
I found refuge early on.
At Guāndù, among the soldiers,
At Wūlín, facing hardships.
In later years, meeting many worthies,
Gathered together under heaven’s shelter.
Seated in rows beneath ornate rafters,
Golden cups filled with clear wine.
First playing the Yánlù melody,
Then conversing into the night.
Banter exchanged in response,
Jests and teasing without shame.
Pouring oneself out, leaving no hidden worries,
In the heart, all is well expressed.
The duty of managing records,
Holds words of generous favor.
The river isle full of sand and dust,
Wind mourns, yellow clouds rise.
Golden bridles racing each other,
Fluttering endlessly, without cease.
Auspicious clouds bestow generous favor,
Humbly climbing among many scholars.
Recalling the past in Bóhǎi times,
Playing by clear waters at Nánpí.
Now roaming again by the river bend,
Sounding reeds, floating on orchid streams.
Treading steps up crimson stairs,
Sitting side by side, attending gentlemen.
Elegant talk gladdens the heart,
Melancholy tunes truly please the ear.
Pouring wine tied to fragrant brew,
Toasting words, how could they ever end?
Since eating duckweed,
Only today seems beautiful.
The nobleman cares not for worldly affairs,
Only delights in wandering,
Yet often sighs with worry for life.
Morning outings ascend the phoenix tower,
Evening gatherings at the splendid pond.
Leaning branches pull tender twigs,
Climbing vines to pick huì grass.
Wandering freely, gazing afar,
Eyes reaching the limits of exploration.
Looking west at Tàiháng Mountain,
Peering north toward Hándān road.
Level roads long and straight,
White poplars truly tall and slender.
The crown prince orders a feast,
Joy and pleasure pour out heartfelt feelings.
Fine wanderings know no day or night,
How can one speak of late or early?
All guests are exquisite and refined,
Pure words sprinkle orchid-like elegance.
Mournful notes descend like circling swans,
Remaining echoes pierce the clear sky.
Zhōngshān knows no drunkenness,
Drinking virtue alone brings fullness.
Wishing for the age of white hair,
Nurturing life, mindful of approaching old age.
How gallant the sword-bearing riders!
Among Cháng’ān’s five imperial tombs.
Qín land, pivot of the world,
Talents from eight directions converge.
Jīng and Wèi have many brave men,
Yuān and Luò abound with youths.
Proud spirits deeply self-assured,
Who would serve the power of commanderies?
Renowned from beyond the pass they come,
Carriages and followers fill the capital’s outskirts.
Five marquises vie with letters and gifts,
All nobles hasten to speak for them.
Righteousness clearer than frost,
Trust and conduct straight as a bowstring.
Making merry beneath Chíyáng,
Lingering at feasts west of Fényīn.
Once pledging a promise to others,
How can one sit idly and abandon it?
Waving banners, leaving Hángǔ Pass,
Casting pendants, departing Gānquán.
Alas, this pursuit of distant plans,
The heart suspended for all under heaven.
Only striving to fulfill one’s will,
How can one weigh immediate gains?
Chivalrous and fierce, truly renowned,
Since ancient times, all have known this.
Questioning this weary traveler,
His native home from Liáodōng.
Once served under General Lǐ,
Ten years in western campaigns.
Halting carts beneath high watchtowers,
Gazing afar to see Yúnzhōng.
Four sides each a thousand miles,
Crisscrossed by fierce winds rising.
Cold and heat, how can they follow seasons?
Frost and rain, often different and alike.
Sleeping at night north of the river’s shade,
Dreaming of returning to Gānquán Palace.
Hard service not yet ended,
Prime years wasted in vain.
Then I know why people of old,
Lamented the turning tumbleweed.
Distant, ascending the long road,
Far, far away traveling onward.
Turning the carriage, leaving the capital behind,
Waving hands, bidding farewell from here.
Dust gathers in the hall,
Green grass thrives in the courtyard.
Autumn cicadas soar over winding waters,
Autumn hares cling to mountain bases.
Blossoming years have splendid moons,
The fair one has no return date.
Evening brings cool breezes rising,
Facing wine, enduring longing.
Sorrow sings the Jiāngnán melody,
Worries entrusted to verses on the lapel.
Lying awake, bright lamps grow dim,
Sitting up, light silk turns dark.
Tear-stained face cannot be adorned,
Dark mirror hard to restore.
May the twilight scene descend,
Shine upon me in my sunset years.
Setting lodgings half a distant city,
Floating clouds veil layered towers.
Jade eaves bring clear breezes,
Silk curtains extend the autumn moon.
Thoughts entwined, longing for that person,
Deep sorrow harbors dawn’s clarity.
Who, as a traveler so long,
Often sees fragrant blooms fade?
Rivers wide, streams without bridges,
Mountains high, roads hard to cross.
In youth, fond of gallant chivalry,
Traveling in office, roaming pass sources.
Treading ancient traces of old,
Briefly inquiring of rise and fall.
Glorious Zhōu turned to marshes,
Imperial Hàn became mountain fences.
Long lost, the detached palace grounds,
How recognize Shòulíng’s garden?
Mid-autumn, border winds arise,
Lone tumbleweed rolls frosty roots.
White sun lacks brilliant light,
Yellow sand dims for a thousand miles.
Clear tracks share no different path,
Dark roads, how could souls differ?
Sages and worthies are long gone,
Embracing fate, what more to resent?
Yōu and Bīng value mounted archery,
Youths fond of galloping pursuits.
Felt belts bear double quivers,
Ivory bows tucked in carved cases.
Beasts plump, spring grass short,
Flying reins cross level plains.
Morning outings at Yànmén Pass,
Evening returns to Lóufán to rest.
Stone bridge has leftover strength,
Startled birds lose their whole eyes.
Hàn and foes not yet at peace,
Border towns repeatedly overturned.
Leaving me a white-feathered arrow,
To share the tiger-tally command.
A Lǔ guest serves the King of Chǔ,
Carrying gold, clad in red and white.
Having received the master’s favor,
Also honored by the minister’s regard.
Day ends, leaving court return,
Saddled horses crowd the road.
Clan and faction bask in glory,
Guests and servants admire from afar.
Wealth and honor, what all desire,
Virtue and morals, what is there to fear?
In southern lands, a Confucian scholar,
Lost in ways, alone sinks in error.
Cutting wood by Qīngjiāng’s banks,
Setting traps to guard against crafty hares.
At fifteen I chanted the Odes and Documents,
No piece of writing was beyond my grasp.
In my youth I joined the company of many scholars,
And strode swiftly to visit the palaces of Qín.
I glimpsed the discourses of noble men,
And foresaw the manner of the ancients.
Two arguments exhausted the tip of my tongue,
Five cartloads of books blunted my writing’s edge.
Ashamed to accept the gift of a white jade disc,
I felt disgrace at receiving merit like that of Liáochéng.
In later years I followed worldly affairs,
Riding to distant barriers to make peace with the Róng.
I removed my jade pendants and donned rhinoceros-hide armor,
Rolled up my scrolls to serve with bow in hand.
My initial hopes—strength fell short;
How could I know where I would end today?
Northern winds blow the snow from the frontier,
A thousand miles across the Dragon Mountains.
It gathers in your jade terrace,
Dancing and flying before the two pillars.
This season is beautiful in itself,
But should yield to the radiant years.
In the radiant season of peach and plum blossoms,
Pure whiteness cannot match their splendor.
Westward I climb the Sparrow Terrace,
Eastward I gaze at the cloud-wreathed palace gates.
Tiered pavilions solemnly house the heavens,
The imperial road stretches straight as a hair.
Embroidered ridgepoles knot flying clouds,
Jade lintels admit the traveling moon.
Hills are built to resemble Pénglái and Húliáng,
Ponds dug to mimic the vast ocean.
Beauties selected from all over Qí and Dài,
Singers summoned from every corner of Qióng and Yuè.
Bells are arrayed for evening feasts,
Music and song await the break of dawn.
Youth and appearance cannot return,
Body and spirit will surely wane and cease.
Ants can breach mountains and rivers,
Silken tears can corrode golden bones.
Vessels fear being full and tipping over,
Things dread thriving too much and perishing.
How wise are the many scholars,
Who follow reason and discern clarity from obscurity.
Cold sand stretches flat on all sides,
Flying snow startles for a thousand miles.
Winds break the trees of the Yīn Mountains,
Fog obscures the city of Jiāohé.
By day we charge the Zuǒxián’s formation,
By night we press close to the Xiūtú’s camp.
Once I served in the vanguard’s tent,
Now I follow Piāoyáo’s troops.
Losing the way brings heavy punishment,
Lingering delay is not lightly judged.
What we rely on is the Son of Heaven today,
The Hàn way grows ever brighter and more prosperous.
Far from you, my lord, I part,
All the way to Yànmén Pass.
Yellow clouds cover a thousand miles,
When will you, wanderer, return?
Seeing you off feels like yesterday,
Yet dew already gathers before the eaves.
I do not regret the late-blooming huì grass,
But grieve for the cold of the long road.
You are at one end of the sky,
I remain in lasting separation.
I long to see your face just once,
No different from a branch of jade trees.
Like dodder and duckweed,
Where I cling, I shall never shift.
With a cup of wine I send off the traveler,
Hesitating at the farewell feast.
As dusk falls, floating clouds thicken,
Washing my hands, tears fall like sleet.
Long flows the clear river water,
Where fine bream find their place.
But I am ten thousand miles away,
Bound by marriage yet never to meet.
In my sleeve is a short letter,
I wish to entrust it to a pair of flying swallows.
A silk fan like the full moon,
Comes from plain cloth on the loom.
Painted with the daughter of the King of Qín,
Riding a phoenix into mist and haze.
Colors and beauty are prized by the world,
But the new cannot replace the old.
Secretly I fear the cool wind’s arrival,
Blowing the trees by my jade steps.
Before my lord’s favor is fully spent,
I shall wither and fall midway.
Setting wine, I sit in the soaring pavilion,
Carefree by the splendid pool.
A divine breeze arrives from afar,
Lotus flowers sway left and right.
Green bamboo lines the clear water,
Autumn orchids cover the secluded banks.
The moon rises, shining on the garden,
Caps and pendants follow one another.
A guest comes from southern Chǔ,
Playing the shēng pipes for me.
Deep-water fish still lurk in the shallows,
Listeners show no sign of weariness.
How elegant is this lofty writing,
What can a petty scholar accomplish?
Vast and solemn, the great hall lies in shadow,
Sparrows’ cries grieve in the northern woods.
All the guests have returned to the city,
What can console my heart?
The monarch honors the worthy and wise,
Not sparing treasures of gold and jade.
Twin towers point to the imperial road,
Vermilion palaces line the mansions.
Leisurely at the Ice Well Terrace,
Clear pools reflect lush foliage.
Cool winds scatter fragrant scents,
Green trees shed leaves before autumn.
At dawn I await my fair one,
At dusk I gaze toward the blue pavilion.
Lifting my robe to pluck bright pearls,
Wandering to gather huì and ruò herbs.
Cherishing my two or three companions,
Whose words and meanings gleam like gold and cinnabar.
Yánlíng valued his precious sword lightly,
Jì Bù held his promise in high regard.
In wealth, do not forget poverty,
The true way lies in sunflowers and beans.
Lush and verdant, the cassia of Zhōngshān,
Round and full, colored by frost and dew.
How severe are frost and dew?
Yet the cassia branch grows straight by nature.
Oranges and pomelos in the southern lands,
Rely on you for wings of support.
Undeservedly favored by the sage ruler,
I entrust myself to a post of letters and ink.
Since my red talent has already been recognized,
How dare I not refine and adorn myself?
Bright moonlight shines on the square pool,
We sit in rows beside the golden hall.
This humble servant has indeed received grace,
Such vast favor is truly beyond measure.
In those past days, encountering a world in chaos,
I mounted my horse and left the imperial capital.
Grieving at parting like tangled weeds,
I then understood the sentiment of the lone pear tree.
Xiáo and Hán again became mounds and ruins,
Jìquè’s towers lay distant and crisscrossed.
Leaning on the oar, I floated on the Jīng and Wèi rivers,
At dusk, mountains and rivers grew clear.
Crickets cling to the mulberry fields,
Harsh winds blow the ruò stems.
Storks and grebes hide in the deep grass,
The traveler’s tears have already fallen.
Thirty years since leaving my homeland,
Fortunately, I meet a world at peace.
A worthy lord bestows fine rewards,
Golden sable caps and dark-tasseled robes.
Attending feasts by the river’s bend,
Riding in swift carriages to tour Yèchéng.
How long does morning dew last?
Suddenly like duckweed on water.
A nobleman steadfast in kindness and righteousness,
His branches and leaves will never droop.
Since fortune and stability are secured,
A fine name will endure for a thousand years.
I say, I did not follow the teachings,
But secretly aspired to leave the worldly dust.
My thoughts reached far beyond the vast realm,
My steps strode high above ordinary men.
The divine phoenix shakes its feathered majesty,
Hiding its light by the Western Sea’s shore.
By morning it eats from the lánggān tree,
By evening drinks from the jade pool’s springs.
Following the natural course, thus free from burdens,
Nurturing virtue, one enters the divine.
How boundless is the cosmos’ favor,
Cloud nets spread out in all directions.
The wise value understanding righteousness,
The great and elegant clearly protect themselves.
Zhuāngzǐ awakened to non-action,
Lǎozǐ guarded his authenticity.
All under heaven attained the One,
Name and substance long complemented each other.
The Xiánchí music feasted the yōujū bird,
But bells and drums may bring sorrow.
Liǔ Xiàhuì excelled in uprightness,
Sūn Dēng nearly understood men.
Expressing my feelings is not far off,
Moved by your gift, I inscribe it on my sash.
The bluebird roams over the sea,
The grackle flies beneath the mugwort.
Sinking and floating are not suited,
Each with its own wings returns to its place.
Drifting and fluttering may last a year,
How can one discern right from wrong in the vast expanse?
Morning clouds ride on transformations,
Their radiant brilliance is rare in the world.
Jīngwèi carries twigs and stones,
Who can fathom the hidden subtleties?
The autumn moon shines on the curtained window,
Its suspended light enters the crimson steps.
The fair lady strums the singing qin,
In the clear night, she guards the empty chamber.
Few footprints mark the orchid path,
Spiderwebs grow on the jade terrace.
The courtyard trees burst with red blossoms,
The boudoir grasses hold verdant moisture.
Lingering, I adjust my silken robes,
To send them ten thousand miles to the one I long for.
May the grace of heavy dew descend,
Believe in my promise as bright as the sun.
Youth speeds like the heavenly mechanism,
The plain autumn gallops with the white sun.
The beauty has returned to the deep springs,
Grief and sorrow know no end.
The burial chamber is already solemn and still,
The pines and cypresses turn desolate.
Looking up and down, I cannot cease,
Reflecting on memories, not just one.
Clutching my robe, I mourn the solitude,
Lost in a trance as if something is missing.
The bright moon enters the patterned window,
Vaguely, I recall her orchid-like purity.
To dispel sorrow, not the daylily,
Eternal longing, how can dreams bring peace?
Dreams are but darkness upon darkness,
How can I behold your form again?
I am ashamed of the arts of Běihǎi,
You lack the spirit of the Emperor’s daughter.
I ride forth from the distant mountains,
Pacing and weeping by the pine-carved epitaph.
Rain ceases, no returning clouds,
Flowers fall, can they retain their blossoms?
Sun and moon alternate in their course,
When will rest and rise find peace?
The Crown Prince bestowed a gracious command,
The favor reached my humble self.
At dawn, I yearn for my homeland,
Sighing forever, missing close kin.
My thoughts flow as I leave the southern shore,
Bearing resentment, parting from the western ford.
Galloping my horse along the Huái and Sì rivers,
Morning and evening, I see Liáng and Chén.
Upholding duty, I follow the ranks above,
Adjusting my steps among the palace officials.
Red insignia adorn all the talented scholars,
Long tassels grace the outstanding men.
In hardship, I served within Chénghuá,
Bound closely for years beyond count.
At dusk, I gather my carriage for leisure,
Wandering freely, gazing at the Luò River.
Many are gone, buried beneath arched trees,
Old grasses rise through the cold mist.
A wanderer easily feels sorrow and sighing,
Hesitating, I pity myself.
I wish to send word with the three birds,
Parting thoughts are not in vain.
Hán Gōng sank to selling medicine,
Méi Shēng hid by the market gate.
A hundred years pass swiftly indeed,
Why torment the soul with anguish?
One should learn from generals like Wèi and Huò,
To achieve merit at the river’s source.
Jade tablets and silk sashes, the wise lord’s gaze,
Blue and purple robes, the enlightened ruler’s grace.
Zhōng Jūn’s talent just began to flourish,
Jiǎ Yì’s position then grew honored.
Jīn and Zhāng wore sable crowns,
Xǔ and Shǐ rode in splendid carriages.
Kings and nobles value a single counsel,
Dukes and ministers weigh a single word.
In times of peace, much joy abounds,
Flying canopies at the eastern capital’s gate.
Yet I think of Zhāng Zhòngwèi,
With weeds overrunning his garden.
Crimson clouds veil the sun’s light,
Green springs gush from shaded isles.
Water storks nest on layered eaves,
Mountain clouds moisten the pillar bases.
Some rejoice in spring’s festival,
Others grieve through autumn’s rainy season.
Rustling, cool leaves fall away,
Fierce, sharp winds rise high.
Discussing loftily, I ponder the four seasons,
Living alone, I yearn for past companions.
Green moss turns yellow day and night,
Fragrant blooms become withered thickets.
At year’s end, a hundred worries intertwine,
Nothing to comfort my lingering gaze.
The great Jìn encountered the ninth yang calamity,
The world was shrouded in chaotic fog.
Qín and Zhào faced eclipses of light,
Yōu and Bìng met tiger-like usurpers.
I, bearing the grace of favor,
Moved with gratitude, rushed to serve.
Though lacking the six wondrous strategies,
I hoped to meet with Zhāng and Hán.
Níng Qì struck his ox horn and sang,
Duke Huán encountered and raised him high.
Xún Xī braved peril and hardship,
Truly for loyalty’s sake.
In vain, I let the sun and moon pass,
Ashamed, without the ancients’ measure.
Watering my horse beyond the city moat,
Gazing north toward the desert road.
A thousand miles, how desolate and bleak,
The white sun hides behind cold trees.
Shaking my sleeves in frustration and wrath,
Resting on my pillow, a hundred cares arise.
Fame and merit, alas, remain unachieved,
My dark hair has already turned white.
If by chance the time brings opportunity,
Order and chaos depend on hidden fate.
A great hall requires exceptional timber,
The court and temple need no common vessel.
Heroes establish merit for the age,
Many scholars fill these positions.
Favored regard leads to close bonds,
Thus matching with the finest of the time.
Marriage ties long held true,
Hardships shared, not just once?
Meeting adversity already together,
Facing danger, we do not fear.
Often I admire the bearing of past worthies,
Observing antiquity, discussing gain and loss.
Mǎ Fú served as Zhào’s general,
The borders gained peace and calm.
Xìnlíng wore Wèi’s seal of office,
Qín’s troops dared not march forth.
Sighing, I lack strategies from the tent,
Only ashamed of my plain silk nature.
A traveler leaving my old homeland,
Feeling our bond, like qin and sè in harmony.
Reflecting, I am no catalpa or lacquer tree,
Yet I strive without respite.
Moreover, I fear my friends,
Blowing falsely, straying from name and reality.
Mount Yān has many spiritual herbs,
The seashore abounds with wondrous stones.
Proudly I seek the azure clouds,
In seclusion, I anchor my essence.
Taoist priests read cinnabar scriptures,
Alchemists refine jade elixirs.
Vermilion clouds enter the window lattice,
The shining sun illuminates the gaps.
Proudly gazing, I pluck the tree fungus,
Crossing waves, I gather water jade.
Vastly roaming ten thousand miles,
Raising my palm, I gaze at misty wanderers.
Eternally attaining Ānqī’s arts,
Why worry about Méngsì’s approach?
Since the Primal Simplicity divided,
The breath of ten thousand things took form.
If stillness and movement have a source,
Then we say the child who dies young is cut short.
The Way lost for a thousand years,
Who can comprehend the ferry and bridge?
Wishing to ride the soaring wings of the whirlwind,
Towering aloft, against the wind I rise.
Quietly observing the principle of the foot-long staff,
Reason suffices, never lacking.
Bright, bright, the autumn moon shines,
Leaning on the balcony, I sing of Yáo and Lǎo.
Roaming without care for ugliness or beauty,
Then the way of the nobleman emerges.
Comprehending, returning to unity,
In the southern mountains dwells the elegant elder.
Arms linked, long transformed by change,
Passing the fire, it becomes fuel and grass.
Profound thoughts flow clear and steady,
From the chest, all cunning departs.
Object and self both forgotten,
One can befriend the gulls and birds.
Zhāng Zǐ discerns inner mysteries,
Dān Shēng obscures outer appearances.
For a time, I cast aside worldly snares,
Serenely enjoying the emptiness.
Shedding this sentiment of weak attachment,
I rely on spirit to wander alone.
Gathering herbs by the winding white clouds,
I leisurely nurture my being.
Crimson blossoms shine with fragrant splendor,
Green bamboo shades the tranquil expanse.
Lofty thoughts find solace here,
Unaware, I ascend the ethereal heights.
Curved lattice stirs the fresh breeze,
The stone chamber echoes with secluded sounds.
Departing to follow my desires,
Gain and loss are not external rewards.
Sublime is the master of the axe,
Whose clarity has long been bright.
The five difficulties now washed away,
Transcending traces, beyond the dusty net.
Morning wanderings follow where they gather,
Serenely holding true delight.
The cloudy sky stretches vast and bright,
At times meeting with a joyful heart.
Green pines stand with elegant buds,
Graceful hues emerge from tall trees.
Gazing afar at the deep clear waves,
Reflecting upon the plain stone cliffs.
Purified feelings leave no residue,
Brushing off robes, releasing worldly duties.
Seeking benevolence lies within myself,
Why yearn for the mystic wind outside?
Simply placed, forgetting all control,
Tranquil and free, shedding lingering cares.
Truly, the toil of transformation wearies,
The anxious heart remains unsettled.
Briefly following the suburban road,
Reining the horse, leaving the court offices.
Chill and desolate, the season lofty,
Vast and silent, the mind’s insight eternal.
Seasonal chrysanthemums gleam on rocky slopes,
Clouds and mist crown the autumn ridges.
Fondly cherishing the fine hour,
Lingering, treading the fading light.
Rolling and unfolding, though myriad threads,
Movement returns to stillness.
Once pressed by the setting sun,
In year’s end, I follow what I hold.
The boat and valley cannot be climbed,
Entrusting forgetfulness to the craftsman of Yǐng.
Planting seedlings in the eastern fields,
Sprouts fill the paths between.
Though weary from hoeing,
Rough wine brings solace.
At dusk, covering the firewood cart,
The road darkens as light fades.
Returning folk gaze at hearth smoke,
Young children wait by the eaves.
Ask, what is your purpose?
A lifetime has its duties.
Only hope the mulberry and hemp thrive,
In silkworm month, spinning and weaving.
A simple heart is just like this,
Opening the path, hoping for worthy friends.
Rivers and seas wind through twists,
Mountain peaks bear fullness and lack.
The divine realm truly lingers,
Joyful hearts are not in vain.
At dawn, ascending cloud-capped peaks,
Far removed from Lú and Huò.
Emerald barriers flow endlessly,
Golden pools ever clear and pure.
Tung forests clad in morning mist,
Stone cliffs reflect the first light.
Milk caves drip and trickle,
Cinnabar wells lie vast and deep.
Cliffs and crags shift in wondrous beauty,
Peaks and summits hide each other.
Red jade hides in jade streams,
Brocade clouds cover sandy shores.
At night, hear gibbons cry,
At dawn, see flying squirrels vanish.
Southern climate warm,
Vermilion blooms defy white snow.
Fortunate to wander in Jiàndé’s land,
Marvel at wonders, pass Yǔ’s cave.
Body and fame—who will discern?
Charts and histories fade in time.
Drifting on Guì River’s tide,
Moonlit, roaming the sea’s edge.
Nurturing life values harmony,
To be shared with the wise.
The Tàiwēi star solidifies the imperial realm,
Yáoguāng shines upon the divine domain.
Measuring the sun, bright in written histories,
Observing capitals, splendid in lore.
Arrayed stars form immortal palaces,
Opening heavens, crafting treasure halls.
Cassia beams retain summer breezes,
Orchid rafters halt winter sleet.
Green woods gather in misty depths,
Crimson cliffs draped in lush verdure.
Mountain clouds hold noble grace,
Pond flowers display spiritual change.
Double sunlight gathers pure energy,
Descending chariots, joining mystic feasts.
Gazing afar, dividing the world’s paths,
Scanning eyes cover capital and fields.
Mists rise from river and mountain shades,
Smoke clears, Huái and sea appear.
Seated among, adorned with crimson sashes,
Strolling corridors, jade caps in rows.
Rituals ascend, awaiting wise sentiments,
Music ends, prolonging imperial gaze.
Measuring grace, surpassing ease,
Following documents, ignorant of lowly state.
Honor brings gifts of double gold,
Circling splendor, surpassing full gems.
Dare I adorn the commoners’ songs?
Shamed by the green waters’ offering.
Yesterday departed from Chìtíng’s isle,
Tonight lodged at Pǔyáng’s shore.
Just as cloud peaks differ,
How could a thousand li part us?
Fragrant dust still on the mat,
Streaming tears linger on sleeves.
Halting oars, gaze at distant banks,
Resting paddles, hindered by wind and snow.
Wind and snow persist through time,
Long nights stir longing thoughts.
Drifting on Běi Lake’s wanderings,
Awaiting Nán Tower’s lofty pavilion.
Dipping brush, singing new delights,
Opening scrolls, clarifying doubts.
Plucking blossoms, loving fragrant air,
Gathering petals, cherishing vibrant hues.
Vibrant hues fear lushness,
Human affairs also melt away.
Your heart grieves, do not go,
Valley wind mocks fickleness.
Together holding Yánzhōu’s trust,
Unashamed of Zhònglù’s promise.
Gazing at língzhī, hoping for triple bloom,
Solitary bamboo, where feelings rest.
Where feelings rest, earnest and true,
Only enough to stir the longing heart.
Now traveling beyond Tū and Shèng,
Bearing thoughts to the seaside.
Seeing you, distant and untimely,
When will our earnest gaze meet?
Mixed pendants may be gifted,
Sparse blossoms find no display.
No display, heart weary and troubled,
The traveler—is this wandering joy?
Fortunate that wind and snow clear,
Youth fills the riverbanks.
Loosening ropes, awaiting former companions,
Looking back, still heavy-hearted.
Misty scenes seem far removed,
Last echoes sent as jade gifts.
Secluded and vast, Xiāo and Xiāng empty,
Emerald streams, tranquil and faint.
Silent and desolate, hundred grasses dim,
Suddenly, the pheasant’s mournful cry.
Clear shadows come and go afar,
Moonlight scatters on front steps.
Refining elixirs, gazing through sheer curtains,
Playing the zither, lying in distant drapes.
Water’s jade tested, not defiled,
Golden ointment’s spirit, never tarnished.
On northern isle, the emperor’s child,
Drifting and vast, beyond reach.
Melancholy in mountain dusk,
Bearing illness, I compose this poem.
In palace and temple, rites are solemn and reverent,
In the town of Fényì, the way is stern and profound.
Reverence and purity arise from bright sacrifices,
The solemn procession seeks blessings for the year.
Summoning followers to ascend in the final month,
Adorning the phoenix banners to journey across the river.
Cloud-like banners move like the Milky Way,
The imperial net hangs like stars suspended.
Crimson oars gleam on cold islets,
Golden bridles reflect on autumn mountains.
Feathered guards gather in flowing light,
Colorful music shakes the deep abyss.
Debating poetry to gauge the capital,
Treading records to examine the city’s markets.
Folk songs echo like jade pitch-pipes,
Town praises are strung on crimson strings.
Literary carriages reach the Cassia Sea,
The sound of teachings illuminates the icy heavens.
Harmony and grace bestow the upper tablets,
Kindness and favor soak the lower mats.
Fortunate to attend the viewing of Luò after,
How could one envy the river inspection before?
Upholding righteousness remains untainted,
Unfolding songs yet to be fully expressed.
The solemn boat departs the outskirts,
Music lingers by the river’s southern bank.
Emerald mountains are lush and serene,
Green shores lie deep and tranquil.
Cool leaves shine on sandy isles,
Autumn blooms adorn the water’s edge.
Wind scatters over perilous pine frames,
Clouds gather on deep stone paths.
Silent mirrors stretch across vast fields,
Gazing around at layered peaks in disarray.
Clear air heralds wild geese leading,
Dew’s brilliance recognizes the gibbon’s cry.
Cloud attire truly sheds official robes,
Mist carriage can forsake gold.
First refining the art of Dānquán,
Finally glimpsing the heart of purple fragrance.
Traveling light naturally sways with ease,
Let no weak thoughts intrude.
Proud men waste a foot of jade,
Petty men value favor’s glow.
Dying for duty, not for gain,
Holding the reins, lightly leaving home.
In the month of winter suburban sacrifices,
A killing chill brings severe frost.
Warhorses find no warmth in grain,
Soldiers drink ice as broth.
At dawn ascending Chénggāo slope,
Gravel and stones twist like sheep’s guts.
Cold shadows shroud the white sun,
The great valley darkens, vast and gray.
Resting troops, halting the campaign carriage,
Leaning on swords, facing the eight wilds.
The jiāomíng cannot fly,
Xuánwǔ hides beneath river bridges.
Broken wings come with the times,
Moved by things, I sorrow alone.
Pedantic scholars cling to one classic,
Unable to grasp action and withdrawal.
The northwest autumn wind arrives,
The Chǔ traveler’s heart grows wistful.
At dusk, azure clouds gather,
Yet the fair one has not come.
Dew’s radiance just begins to shimmer,
Moonlight starts to linger.
Precious books I close for you,
How can the jade lute be played?
Longing for the shores of Wūshān,
Gazing wistfully at Yángyún Terrace.
Incense burners extinguish deep flames,
Brocade mats gather floating dust.
Guì River flows a thousand miles daily,
Carrying with it lifelong thoughts.
I am a descendant of the ancient Emperor Gāoyáng,
My late father was called Bóyōng.
When Shètí pointed to the first month,
On the Gēngyín day, I was born.
My father, observing my natal aspect,
Bestowed upon me a fine name.
He named me Zhèngzé,
And styled me Língjūn.
Abundant are the inner virtues I possess,
To which I add cultivated talents.
Clad in river thoroughwort and secluded angelica,
I string autumn orchids as adornments.
Swiftly I press on, as if lagging behind,
Fearing time will not wait for me.
At dawn, I pluck magnolias on the hill,
At dusk, gather perennial herbs on the isle.
Sun and moon swiftly pass without lingering,
Spring and autumn alternate in succession.
Seeing plants and trees wither and fall,
I fear the fair one’s fading beauty.
Not seizing youth to discard the foul,
Why not change this way of yours?
Mounting swift steeds to gallop forth,
Come, I will lead the way ahead!
The ancient three kings were pure and perfect,
Truly where all fragrant herbs gathered.
Mingling pepper and cassia,
Not just stringing huì and chǎi.
Those Yáo and Shùn were upright and bright,
Following the right path, they found the way.
Why were Jié and Zhòu so reckless and wild,
Preferring shortcuts to stumble and fall!
The faction seeks only pleasure,
Their path dark, perilous, and narrow.
Do I fear disaster for myself?
I dread the royal chariot’s ruin.
Hastening to rush ahead and behind,
To follow in the former kings’ footsteps.
The prince does not discern my loyal heart,
Instead believes slander and rages at me.
Well I know plain speech brings trouble,
Yet I endure and cannot desist.
I call the Nine Heavens to witness,
All for the sake of the Divine One.
At first, he pledged his word to me,
Later turned away, seeking another.
Parting from him is not hard for me,
But I grieve his constant changes.
I have nurtured orchids over nine acres,
And planted huì over a hundred more.
In plots, I grow liúyí and jiēchē,
Mingled with dùhéng and fragrant zhǐ.
Hoping their branches and leaves grow lush,
I wait for the time to reap the harvest.
Though they wither, what harm is there?
I mourn that fragrant herbs turn to weeds.
All vie for advancement, greedy and covetous,
Insatiable in their pursuit of gain.
Forgiving themselves while judging others,
Each harbors jealousy in their hearts.
Rushing madly in pursuit of power,
Is not what my heart seeks.
Old age approaches gradually,
I fear my fair name will not be established.
At dawn, I drink the falling dew from magnolias,
At dusk, I dine on autumn chrysanthemum petals.
If my heart is truly fair and steadfast,
Long hunger and gauntness matter not.
I pluck tree roots to knot with chǎi,
Stringing fallen stamens of bìlì.
Twisting cassia, threading huì,
Braiding húshéng into long strands.
I emulate the ancient sages,
Not what the vulgar world admires.
Though out of step with people today,
I wish to follow Péngxián’s example.
Long I sigh, wiping away tears,
Grieving life’s many hardships.
Though I love beauty and restrain myself,
Morning reproach brings evening dismissal.
Dismissed for wearing huì sachets,
And further for gathering chǎi.
Yet this is what my heart holds dear,
Even nine deaths would bring no regret.
I resent the Divine One’s recklessness,
Never discerning people’s hearts.
Many women envy my fine brows,
Slandering me as licentious.
Truly, the vulgar are skilled in cunning,
Defying rules, altering measures.
Abandoning the line to chase crookedness,
Competing in flattery as their standard.
Gloomy, despondent, and distressed am I,
Alone in hardship at this time!
Rather die suddenly or wander in exile,
I cannot bear such demeanor!
The fierce bird does not flock with others,
Since ancient times, it has been so.
How can square and circle fit together?
Who of different ways can find peace?
Bending heart and suppressing will,
Enduring blame, bearing insults.
Embracing purity to die for righteousness,
Was truly valued by the ancient sages.
I regret that I did not examine the path clearly,
I linger and hesitate, about to turn back.
I turn my chariot to retrace the road,
While the straying journey is not yet far.
I walk my horse on the orchid-covered bank,
Gallop to the pepper hill and there rest awhile.
To advance brings no entry but invites blame,
I will retreat and restore my former attire.
I fashion lotus leaves into a robe,
And gather lotus blossoms to make a skirt.
If no one knows me, so be it,
As long as my heart is truly fragrant.
I raise my hat high and towering,
Lengthen my pendant, shimmering and bright.
Fragrance and luster mingle together,
Only my pure essence remains undiminished.
Suddenly I look back and gaze afar,
I will go to observe the four distant lands.
My adornments are dazzling and abundant,
The fragrance grows ever more radiant.
Each person in life has their own joys,
I alone take refinement as my constant practice.
Even if my body is torn apart, I will not change,
How could my heart be punished?
Nǚ Xū, graceful and concerned,
Admonishes me again and again.
She says, "Gǔn, stubborn and upright, lost his life,
And perished in the wilderness of Yǔ.
Why are you so outspoken and fond of refinement,
Alone possessing such noble virtues?
Weeds fill the room in abundance,
Yet you alone stand apart and refuse to wear them.
You cannot explain to everyone door to door,
Who will understand our innermost feelings?
The world flocks together and loves factions,
Why are you so solitary and refuse to listen to me?"
Following the moderation of ancient sages,
I sigh in distress as I face this.
I cross Yuán and Xiāng to journey south,
To seek Chóng Huá and present my plea.
Qǐ performed the "Nine Songs" and "Nine Changes,"
Xià indulged in pleasure and gave free rein to himself.
Heedless of hardship and planning not for the future,
His five sons lost their home and roamed.
Yì roamed wantonly and hunted excessively,
And loved to shoot the great foxes.
Such disorderly ways seldom end well,
Zhuó coveted and took his household.
Ào, clad in strength and armor,
Indulged his desires without restraint.
Daily lost in pleasure and forgetting himself,
His head thus fell in ruin.
Xià Jié constantly defied the norm,
And thus met with calamity.
Hòu Xīn minced and pickled his foes,
So the Yīn dynasty did not last long.
Tāng and Yǔ were stern and reverent,
Zhōu upheld the Way without error.
They promoted the worthy and appointed the capable,
Adhering to the rule without deviation.
The August Heaven shows no partiality,
It observes virtue and aids accordingly.
Only the sagely wise with splendid conduct
May thus rule over this land.
Looking back and gazing forward,
I observe the ultimate principles of human affairs.
Who can be employed without righteousness?
Who can be followed without goodness?
Though I stand on the brink of danger and death,
Looking back at my beginnings, I have no regret.
Not measuring the mortise before fitting the tenon,
Was why the ancients were minced and pickled.
I heave sighs of sorrow and depression,
Grieving that my time is ill-suited.
Gathering soft orchids to wipe my tears,
Which soak the front of my robe in streams.
Kneeling, I spread my lapels and present my plea,
Enlightened, I have now found this middle path.
Harnessing jade dragons, riding the phoenix,
I soar on the dusty wind, ascending swiftly.
At dawn I set off from Cāngwú,
By evening I reach Xuánpǔ.
Wishing to linger at this divine gate,
The sun hastens, soon to set.
I command Xī Hé to slow his pace,
Gazing at Yānzī, urging him not to rush.
The road stretches long and far,
I will search high and low.
I water my horse at Xiánchí,
Tie my reins at Fúsāng.
Breaking Ruòmù branches to brush the sun,
I linger awhile, wandering freely.
I send Wàng Shū ahead as my vanguard,
Order Fēi Lián to follow behind.
The phoenix warns ahead for me,
But Léi Shī says preparations are incomplete.
I command the phoenix to soar high,
Continuing day and night without cease.
Whirlwinds gather and converge,
Leading clouds and rainbows to welcome me.
In swirling masses they part and join,
Shimmering and shifting up and down.
I command the heavenly gatekeeper to open,
But he leans against the gate and stares at me.
The light dims, the day draws to a close,
I knot orchids and linger in wait.
The world is murky, confounding right and wrong,
It loves to obscure beauty and harbor envy.
At dawn I will cross the Báishuǐ,
Ascend Lángfēng and tether my horse.
Suddenly I look back and shed tears,
Grieving that the high hill has no fair maiden.
Swiftly I wander to this spring palace,
Plucking jade branches to add to my adornments.
Before the blossoms have faded,
I seek a maiden below to present them to.
I command Fēng Lóng to ride the clouds,
To seek the dwelling of Fú Fēi.
I untie my pendant to pledge my word,
And send Jiǎn Xiū as my envoy.
In swirling confusion, she wavers and hesitates,
Suddenly capricious and hard to sway.
At night she rests at Qióngshí,
At dawn she washes her hair at Wěipán.
Proud of her beauty, she acts with arrogance,
Daily indulging in pleasure and wanton roaming.
Though truly fair, she lacks propriety,
So I turn away and seek another.
Surveying and gazing to the four extremes,
I roam the heavens, then descend again.
Beholding the lofty jade tower,
I see the fair maiden of Yǒusōng.
I send a zhèn bird as matchmaker,
But the zhèn tells me she is not good.
The male dove chirps and flies off,
But I dislike its frivolous cunning.
My heart wavers with doubt,
Wishing to go myself, yet I cannot.
The phoenix has already borne the gift,
I fear Gāo Xīn will precede me.
Wishing to go far, yet finding no place to rest,
I wander aimlessly, drifting freely.
Before Shào Kāng had taken a wife,
There remained the two Yáo maidens of Yǒuyú.
My envoy is weak, my matchmaker unskilled,
I fear the proposal will not hold firm.
The world is murky and envious of the worthy,
It loves to obscure beauty and praise the vile.
The inner chambers are deep and distant,
The wise king remains unawakened.
Holding my feelings within, unexpressed,
How can I endure this forever?
I gather sacred grass and bamboo stalks,
Commanding Líng Fēn to divine for me.
He says: "Two beauties are bound to unite,
But who is truly refined and will admire you?
Think of the vastness of the Nine Regions,
Is it only here that there are maidens?
He says: "Strive to go far without doubt,
Who seeking beauty would reject you?
Where is there no fragrant grass?
Why do you cling to your old home?
The times are dark and dazzlingly confused,
Who will discern our beauty or ugliness?
People's likes and dislikes differ,
But these partisans alone are peculiar.
They wear mugwort, filling their waists,
And say the dark orchid cannot be worn.
They cannot even judge plants rightly,
How could they assess the beauty of jade?
They stuff their sachets with dung and soil,
And say the pepper of Shēn is not fragrant."
I wished to follow the auspicious divination of Líng Fēn,
Yet my heart hesitated and was filled with doubt.
Wū Xián was about to descend at dusk,
I held pepper and rice to welcome him.
A hundred spirits shaded the sky as they descended together,
The nine peaks of Jiǔyí welcomed them in splendor.
Brilliantly they displayed their divine power,
And told me of auspicious reasons.
They said: Strive to ascend and descend, to rise and fall,
Seek the measure and rule that aligns with yours.
Tāng and Yǔ were solemn in seeking harmony,
Zhì and Gāo Yáo were able to harmonize.
If the inner feelings are truly fond of refinement,
Why must one rely on matchmakers?
Yuè labored with a builder’s tool at Fù Yán,
Wǔ Dīng employed him without doubt.
Lǚ Wàng wielded his butcher’s knife,
Encountering Zhōu Wén, he was raised up.
Nìng Qì sang his songs,
Qí Huán heard him and made him an assistant.
While the years are not yet late,
And time is still not exhausted.
I fear the cuckoo will sing first,
Causing all the fragrant plants to lose their scent.
Why is my jade pendant so lofty,
Yet the crowd obscures it with envy?
Only these partisans lack integrity,
I fear jealousy will break it.
The times are chaotic and ever-changing,
How can I linger here any longer!
Orchids and angelica have changed and lost their fragrance,
Quán and huì have transformed into weeds.
Why have the fragrant plants of old,
Now become mere wormwood and mugwort?
Is there any other reason for this,
Than the harm of not loving refinement?
I thought the orchid could be relied upon,
Yet it bore no fruit, only a fair appearance.
It abandoned its beauty to follow vulgar ways,
Merely to be counted among the fragrant ones.
Pepper is flattering and deceitful in its arrogance,
And shā seeks to fill the perfume pouch.
Since they strive only for advancement and entry,
How can any fragrance be revered?
Truly, the customs of the time flow with the current,
Who then can remain unchanged?
Seeing how pepper and orchid are like this,
What more of jiēchē and jiānglí?
Only this pendant is truly precious,
Yet its beauty has been abandoned to this state.
Its fragrance is rich and hard to diminish,
Its scent remains undiminished to this day.
I harmonize my steps to amuse myself,
Wandering freely in search of a fair one.
While my adornments are still in their prime,
I shall journey and observe all around.
Since Líng Fēn told me the auspicious divination,
I choose a lucky day to set out on my journey.
I break jade branches to make delicacies,
And refine jade dust to prepare my provisions.
For me, harness flying dragons,
And adorn the chariot with jade and ivory.
How can hearts at odds be united?
I shall go far away to distance myself.
I turn my path toward Kūnlún,
The road is long and winding.
I raise cloud-banners that darken the sky,
And the jade bells chime with a gentle sound.
At dawn I set off from Tiānjīn,
By evening I reach the western edge.
Phoenixes spread their wings to bear my banners,
Soaring high with majestic grace.
Suddenly I travel through the shifting sands,
Following Chì Shuǐ, I linger at ease.
I command the flood-dragons to make a bridge at the ford,
And bid the Western Sovereign to ferry me across.
The road is long and fraught with hardship,
I order the many chariots to wait along the path.
Passing Bùzhōu, I turn to the left,
Pointing to Xī Hǎi as my destination.
I assemble my chariots, a thousand in number,
Align their jade hubs and race them side by side.
Driving eight dragons in winding motion,
Bearing cloud-banners that flutter and sway.
I restrain my will and slow my pace,
My spirit soars high into the vast distance.
I play the Nine Songs and dance to the Sháo music,
Taking this time to indulge in joy.
Ascending to the brilliant splendor of the imperial heights,
Suddenly I look down upon my old homeland.
My driver grieves, and my horses yearn,
Crouching and turning, they refuse to go on.
Epilogue:
Enough, it is over!
In this land, no one understands me,
Why should I long for the old capital?
Since none are worthy to share in virtuous governance,
I shall follow Péng Xián to his dwelling.
Auspicious day, oh fine hour,
Reverently we please the Supreme Sovereign.
Grasping the long sword with its jade hilt,
The jade pendants chime with a clear sound.
Jade mat and jade weights,
Why not grasp the fragrant jade flowers?
Huì meat steamed upon orchid mats,
Offer cassia wine and pepper brew.
Raise the drumstick and strike the drum,
With gentle rhythm, sing peacefully,
Arrange yú and sè, and sing loudly.
The spirit, majestic in splendid attire,
Fills the hall with rich fragrance.
The five notes mingle in complex harmony,
The lord is joyful and at ease.
Bathe in orchid-scented water, wash with fragrance,
Adorn colorful robes like blooming flowers.
The spirit lingers, coiled and lingering,
Radiant and bright, never fading.
Peacefully dwelling in the Hall of Longevity,
Shining with the sun and moon.
Dragon-drawn chariot, imperial robes,
Wandering freely, circling around.
The spirit, resplendent, has descended,
Swiftly soaring high into the clouds.
Gazing beyond Jìzhōu, far and wide,
Crossing the four seas, boundless and endless.
Thinking of my lord, I sigh deeply,
My heart is weary with anxiety.
My lord does not come, lingering in doubt,
For whom does he tarry in the midstream isle?
Fair and graceful, adorned with care,
I swiftly ride my cassia boat.
Command Yuán and Xiāng to have no waves,
Make the river waters flow peacefully.
Gazing for my lord to return,
Playing the panpipes, for whom do I yearn?
Driving flying dragons northward,
I turn my course toward Dòngtíng.
Bìlì vines for banners, huì for silk,
Quán for oars, orchids for streamers.
Gazing toward Cényáng’s distant shore,
Crossing the great river, displaying divine power.
Displaying divine power, yet not reaching the end,
The maiden, graceful, sighs for me.
Tears flow freely in streams,
Secretly thinking of you, my heart aches.
Cassia oars and orchid rudders,
Chop through ice and pile up snow.
Plucking bìlì from the water,
Picking lotus blossoms from treetops.
Hearts not aligned, the matchmaker’s labor is in vain,
Affection not deep, parting comes lightly!
Over stone rapids, shallow and swift,
Flying dragons, graceful and light.
Friendship without loyalty brings lasting resentment,
Appointments broken, claiming no time.
At dawn, galloping along the riverbank,
By dusk, resting at the northern isle.
Birds roost upon the roof,
Water encircles the hall below.
I cast my jade ring into the river,
Leave my pendant at Lǐpǔ’s shore.
Gather dùruò on the fragrant isle,
To give to the maiden below.
Time once gone cannot be regained,
I wander freely, at ease and content.
The princess descends to the northern isle,
Gazing afar, she fills me with woe.
Gently blows the autumn breeze,
On Dòngtíng's waves fall the leaves from the trees.
I climb the white sedge and gaze around,
For our tryst at dusk the feast is spread.
Why should birds gather on duckweed ground?
Why should nets be spread over trees overhead?
Yuán has sweet grass and Lǐ has orchids fair,
Longing for my lord, I dare not declare.
Gazing afar in a trance, I sigh,
To see the water flowing by.
Why should deer seek for food in courtyard bound?
Why should water dragons haunt the shallow ground?
At dawn I gallop my steeds by rivershore;
At dusk I cross the western stream.
I hear my princess call me o'er;
I'll drive my chariot with her in my dream.
I'll build a bower in water clear,
Roofed with lotus leaves overhead.
With iris walls and courtyard paved with shells,
The hall with fragrant pepper will be spread.
With cassia beams and orchid rafters fine,
With magnolia lintel and lotus white,
Woven with fig leaves for curtains fair,
And screens of melilotus set left and right.
With white jade weights the mats are pressed down;
The fragrant stone-orchids are strewn around.
The lotus roof is thatched with iris leaves,
Bound with asarum, sweet and fair.
All fragrant plants are grown in the courtyard,
And sweet flowers bloom by corridor and stair.
The gods from Jiǔyí Mountain come down in throngs
To greet the princess like clouds in the sky.
I throw into the river my sleeves so long,
And leave on Lǐ's shore my under-robe high.
I pluck sweet flowers on the riverside
For my beloved one far away.
The happy hour cannot be back with the tide;
Let me wander at ease while I may!
Sweet orchids and fragrant thoroughwax grow
In rows beneath the hall.
Green are their leaves and white their flowers,
Their fragrance permeates all.
Every man has his own good children;
Why should you, my lord, worry at all?
Sweet orchids grow in green,
With green leaves and purple stems.
The hall is full of beauties fair,
But you have singled me out of them.
You come without a word and go without goodbye,
Riding the whirlwind with cloud banners high.
No grief is greater than parting when alive;
No joy is greater than making friends anew.
In lotus coat and melilotus belt,
You come all at once and go as soon.
You lodge at dusk on heaven's frontier;
For whom do you wait on clouds high?
I'd roam with you by rivers nine,
When wind and waves together rise.
I'd bathe with you in the sun's pool,
And dry your hair on the sun's rise.
I look for my princess, but in vain;
Singing aloud, I'm drowned in pain.
With pheasant-plume canopy and flags of kingfisher plume,
You mount the ninefold heaven with Broom star in hand.
You draw your long sword to protect the young and fair;
You are fit to be our lord of the land.
In mountains deep appears a lass
With creeping vines and belt of grass.
Her smiling eyes and pearly teeth beam;
She is slender and fair, a fragrant dream.
She rides a red leopard, followed by striped civet cat;
Her chariot of magnolia with banners of cassia sweet.
With stone-orchids as robe and belt of asarum,
She gathers sweet flowers for her lover discreet.
I dwell in dark bamboo grove where I see not the sky;
The way is steep and dangerous, so I come late.
Alone I stand on mountain high,
Clouds gather below in a dense state.
It's dark by day in the deep, deep dell;
The east wind brings showers from gods' spell.
I'd wait for my lord, forgetting to go away;
What can restore my youth when I grow old and gray?
I gather magic herbs in mountains high,
Where rocks are rugged and vines run wild.
I complain of my lord and forget to go by;
Do you think of me when you are not beguiled?
The mountain maiden is fair as sweet flowers;
She drinks from fountain and rests under pine bowers.
Do you think of me? I doubt and believe by turns.
Thunder rumbles and rain darkens the sky;
Monkeys chatter and cry all night long.
The wind whistles and trees sigh;
I think of my lord and feel sad forlorn.
From youth I've been fond of curious dress,
And now old, I love it none the less.
I carry a long sword trailing on the ground,
And wear a cloud-piercing hat on the crown.
I'm adorned with bright moon and precious jade.
The world is muddy; none knows me, I'm afraid.
I'll ride high without looking back.
I drive green dragons with white serpents on either side;
I'll roam with Shùn in gardens of jade.
I'll climb Mount Kūnlún to eat jade fruits;
My life will be as long as heaven and earth;
My light will shine like sun and moon.
Alas! Southern tribes know not my worth;
At dawn I'll cross the riverside.
On Èzhǔ I look back with a sigh
For the autumn and winter wind high.
I let my horse walk by rivershore;
I rest my carriage in woodland before.
I sail upstream in a boat;
The oars keep time and beat the tide.
The boat goes slowly and won't advance;
It lingers in whirlpool as in a trance.
At dawn I leave Wǎngzhǔ, the bay;
At dusk on Chényáng I stay.
If my heart is upright and true,
What does it matter if I'm far from you?
I come to Xùpǔ and linger there,
Not knowing where to go, I'm in despair.
The forest is dark and drear;
It's the haunt of apes and monkeys here.
The mountains are so high they shut out the sun;
It's dark and rainy below when day is done.
There is no end of sleet and snow;
Cloud on cloud hangs as far as eye can go.
Alas! I find no pleasure in life;
Alone I dwell in mountains rife.
I cannot change my heart and follow the base;
So I'll be sad and poor all my days.
Jiē Yú shaved his head to show his disdain;
Sānghù went naked to show his disdain.
The loyal are not always employed;
The wise are not always employed.
Wǔ Zǐ met disaster and died;
Bǐgān was minced and fried.
