Since all were like this in days gone by,
Why should I complain of men today?
I'll hold to my principles without regret;
I'll be obscure and poor till my dying day.
Qu Yuan had been exiled for three years,
unable to see the king again.
He had exhausted his wisdom and loyalty,
yet was obstructed and slandered.
His heart was troubled and his mind confused,
not knowing which way to turn.
So he went to see the Grand Diviner Zhèng Zhānyǐn,
saying:
"I have doubts,
and wish to have them resolved by you, sir."
Zhānyǐn then straightened his divining stalks and brushed his turtle shell,
saying:
"What would you have me do?"
Qu Yuan said:
"Should I be sincere and earnest,
simple and loyal?
Or should I bustle about socializing,
endlessly accommodating?
Should I clear away weeds,
and labor at farming?
Or should I seek out the powerful,
to build my reputation?
Should I speak truthfully without concealment,
even at risk to myself?
Or should I follow the crowd for wealth and honor,
to live a life of ease?
Should I rise above it all,
to preserve my true nature?
Or should I cringe and fawn,
whispering and flattering,
to serve a woman?
Should I be honest and upright,
to keep myself pure?
Or should I be smooth and slippery,
like grease or soft leather,
to polish the pillars?
Should I be noble like a thousand-mile steed?
Or float aimlessly like a duck in water,
rising and falling with the waves,
just to preserve my body?
Should I pull the yoke alongside noble steeds?
Or follow in the tracks of worn-out nags?
Should I soar wing-to-wing with the yellow swan?
Or fight for food with chickens and ducks?
Which is auspicious, which is ominous?
What should I abandon, what should I follow?
The world is murky and unclear:
a cicada's wing is deemed heavy,
a thousand jun is deemed light.
The bronze bell is cast aside,
the earthen pot thunders.
Slanderers are exalted,
worthy men go unnamed.
Alas, in silence,
who knows my integrity and loyalty?"
Zhānyǐn then set aside his divining stalks and declined,
saying:
"A foot sometimes falls short,
an inch sometimes exceeds;
things have their shortcomings,
wisdom has its blind spots;
numbers have their limits,
spirits have their mysteries.
Use your own heart,
follow your own will.
The turtle shell and stalks truly cannot know this matter."
Qu Yuan, having been exiled,
wandered by the river's deep pools,
walking and chanting along the marsh's edge,
his countenance haggard,
his form withered.
A fisherman saw him and asked,
saying:
"Are you not the Sānlǘ Dàfū?
What brings you to this state?"
Qu Yuan said:
"All the world is muddy, I alone am clear;
all men are drunk, I alone am sober.
Therefore I am exiled."
The fisherman said:
"The sage is not rigidly attached to things,
but can move with the world.
If the world is all muddy,
why not stir up the mud and ride the waves?
If all men are drunk,
why not eat the dregs
and drink the weak wine?
Why dwell so deeply and hold yourself so high,
bringing exile upon yourself?"
Qu Yuan said:
"I have heard:
one who has just washed his hair must flick his cap;
one who has just bathed must shake his clothes.
How can I, with my clean body,
endure things that are sullied?
I would rather plunge into the Xiāng River,
be buried in the bellies of its fish,
than let my pristine whiteness
be covered by the world's dust!"
The fisherman smiled faintly,
paddled his boat and left.
He then sang:
"When the Cāngláng's waters are clear,
I can wash my hat-strings;
when the Cānglàng's waters are muddy,
I can wash my feet."
He then went away
and spoke no more.
How sorrowful is the breath of autumn!
Desolate, the plants and trees wither and decay.
Forlorn, as if on a distant journey,
climbing mountains, facing waters, sending off the departing.
Vast and empty, the sky high and the air clear;
still and quiet, the floods recede and the waters clear.
Heart-rending sighs increase as the slight chill strikes a man;
desolate and dejected, leaving the old for the new.
Frustrated, the poor scholar loses his post, his will unfulfilled.
Lonely, a traveler with no companion.
Melancholy, I privately pity myself.
Swallows, fluttering, take their leave;
cicadas, silent, make no sound.
Wild geese, honking, journey south;
pheasants, chirping shrilly, cry mournfully.
Alone, I await dawn without sleep,
grieving for the crickets' nightly march.
Time passes swiftly, past its midpoint;
stalled, I linger and achieve nothing.
Sorrowful, distressed, and destitute, alone in emptiness;
there is a beautiful person whose heart finds no joy.
Leaving home and village, coming as a distant guest;
wandering aimlessly, where shall I go now?
Wholly thinking of my lord, I cannot change;
my lord does not know me, what can I do!
Storing resentment, accumulating thoughts,
my heart troubled, I forget to eat.
I long to see him once to convey my meaning,
but my lord's heart differs from mine.
The carriage has departed and returned,
I cannot see him, my heart grieves.
Leaning against the carriage rail, I sigh deeply;
tears stream down, soaking the yoke.
To cut off ties resolutely, I cannot;
my mind is bewildered and confused.
Privately pitying myself, where will it end?
My heart pounds, honest and upright.
Heaven evenly divides the four seasons,
yet I secretly grieve for this harsh autumn.
White dew has already descended on the hundred plants;
suddenly these wútóng and qiū trees shed their leaves.
Leaving behind the bright shining sun,
entering the long, endless night.
Parting from the flourishing fragrance of prime youth,
I, frail and weak, am filled with sorrow.
Autumn first warns with white dew,
winter then adds severe frost.
It gathers up the expansive vigor of early summer,
then leaves it stifled and hidden away.
Leaves, withered and colorless;
branches, tangled and crisscrossed.
Their appearance, overgrown, is about to fade;
their boughs, seemingly, turn sallow.
The sparse, bare twigs are pitiable;
their forms wasted and bruised.
Seeing them mixed and about to fall,
I regret they missed their season and are out of place.
Reining in my team and slowing the pace,
I wander idly to and fro.
The year hurries swiftly to its end;
I fear my lifespan will not be long.
I mourn that my life is ill-timed,
meeting this age of chaos and strife.
Calmly lingering, I lean alone;
crickets chirp in this western hall.
My heart is fearful and agitated;
how many are the sources of my worry!
Gazing at the bright moon, I sigh deeply;
walking among the stars until dawn.
I lament that the orchid flowers once bloomed so profusely,
In splendid array within the grand chamber.
Why did their blossoms bear no fruit,
Scattered by wind and rain?
I thought you alone wore this orchid,
Yet it proved no different from common flowers.
Grieving that my noble thoughts remain unheard,
I shall leave you and soar high.
My heart aches with sorrow and pain,
Longing for a meeting to make my case clear.
Though blameless, I face separation,
My heart knots in deepening grief.
How could I not yearn for you in melancholy?
But your gates are ninefold barred.
Fierce dogs bark fiercely to greet me,
Barriers and bridges closed, impassable.
Heaven pours down endless autumn rains,
When will the earth ever dry?
Alone I linger in this marshy land,
Gazing at floating clouds with endless sighs.
Why is the world so skilled in deceit,
Turning from the straight rule to alter measures!
They reject fine steeds, refusing to ride them,
And whip worn-out nags to tread the road.
Is there no fine steed in this age?
Truly, none can master their handling.
Seeing the reins held by unfit hands,
They bolt and gallop far away.
Ducks and geese peck at grain and weeds,
While the phoenix soars ever higher.
A round tenon in a square mortise—
I knew well they would not fit.
All birds find perches to rest,
Only the phoenix drifts with nowhere to alight.
I wish to hold my tongue in silence,
Yet ever remember your deep kindness.
Lǚ Shàng gained glory at ninety,
Truly, he met no fitting match before.
Where shall the fine steed return?
Where shall the phoenix perch?
Changing ancient ways, customs decay as the world declines,
Today’s judges pick only the fat.
Fine steeds hide, unseen,
Phoenixes fly high, never descending.
Even birds and beasts know to cherish virtue,
Why say worthy men find no place?
The steed does not rush forward seeking to be tamed,
Nor does the phoenix greedily eat just any fare.
You cast me aside, unheeding,
How can I offer loyalty, though willing?
I wish to withdraw in silence, severing all ties,
Yet dare not forget your initial deep virtue.
Alone in sorrow, it wounds the heart,
Bearing this gloom, where will it end?
From youth, I was pure and uncorrupt,
Devoted to righteousness, never fading.
Upholding this noble virtue,
I was dragged by vulgar customs into filth.
Above, none examined this noble virtue,
Long have I suffered calamity and sorrow.
The Emperor told Wū Yáng:
"There is a man below,
I wish to aid him.
His soul has scattered,
You, divine and restore it!"
Wū Yáng replied:
"Master of Dreams!
The Heavenly Emperor's command is hard to follow!
If I must divine to restore it,
I fear delay will bring decay,
And then Wū Yáng can be of no use."
So he descended and summoned:
O soul, come back!
Why leave your constant abode,
To wander the four directions?
Forsake your joyful dwelling,
And encounter such ill omens.
O soul, come back!
The east is no place to trust.
Giants a thousand ren tall,
Seek only to seize souls.
Ten suns rise in turn,
Melting metal, scorching stone.
They are accustomed to it,
But any soul going there will dissolve.
Come back, come back!
It is no place to trust.
O soul, come back!
The south is no place to stay.
Tattooed foreheads, blackened teeth,
Take human flesh for sacrifice,
Using bones to make paste.
Vipers swarm thickly,
Giant foxes roam a thousand miles.
Male
They dart back and forth swiftly,
Devouring men to nourish their hearts.
Come back, come back!
Do not linger long there.
O soul, come back!
The west brings perils,
Shifting sands for a thousand miles.
Whirled into the Thunder Abyss,
Shattered and scattered beyond stopping.
If by chance you escape,
Beyond lies a vast wilderness.
Red ants large as elephants,
Black wasps like gourds.
No grains grow there,
Only clumps of reeds to eat.
The soil rots men,
Nowhere to find water.
Wandering with no support,
Vast and boundless, no end in sight.
Come back, come back!
Lest you bring ruin upon yourself.
O soul, come back!
The north is no place to stay.
Piled ice towers high,
Flying snow for a thousand miles.
Come back, come back!
Do not stay long there.
O soul, come back!
Do not ascend to heaven.
Tigers and leopards guard the nine passes,
Pecking and harming those below.
A giant with nine heads,
Uproots nine thousand trees.
Jackals and wolves with glaring eyes,
Swarm back and forth in throngs.
They dangle men for sport,
Then cast them into deep abysses.
Only after reporting to the Emperor,
Can they then close their eyes in death.
Come back, come back!
Going there endangers your life.
O soul, come back!
Do not descend to this dark capital.
The Earth Lord, nine-coiled,
His horns sharp and jagged.
Thick back, bloody thumbs,
Chasing men in frenzy.
Three-eyed, tiger-headed,
His body like an ox.
All these relish human flesh.
Come back, come back!
Lest you bring disaster upon yourself.
O soul, come back!
Enter the Gate of Splendor.
The master priest calls for you,
walking backward to lead the way.
A Qin basket and Qi silk cord,
with Zheng netting woven fine.
All summoning tools are ready,
long cries and calls resound.
O soul, come back!
Return to your old abode.
Heaven and earth, the four directions,
harbor many thieves and traitors.
Your image is set in your chamber,
tranquil, peaceful, and serene.
Lofty halls and deep dwellings,
with tiered railings and layered balconies.
Storied terraces and layered pavilions,
overlook the high mountains.
Latticed doors with vermilion adornments,
carved square patterns interlinked.
In winter, there are warm retreats;
in summer, the rooms are cool.
Streams and valleys wind and return,
their waters murmuring softly.
Sunlit breezes stir the huì orchids,
and spread the fragrance of lofty lán.
Through the hall into the inner chamber,
vermilion dust mats are spread.
Polished rooms with kingfisher plumes,
hung with curved jade hooks.
Kingfisher-feathered pearl quilts,
dazzling with shared radiance.
Soft silk covers the walls,
gauze curtains are drawn.
Braided silks and patterned damasks,
tied with precious jade pendants.
The sights within the chamber,
are many rare and wondrous things.
Orchid-scented oil in bright candles,
adorned with splendid faces.
Sixteen maidens attend through the night,
taking turns in service.
Noble ladies from nine domains,
numerous and swift in multitude.
Luxuriant hair in varied styles,
fill the palace in reality.
Their beauty and grace are comparable,
surpassing all generations.
Gentle faces, firm in bearing,
sincere and full of intent.
Lovely features and graceful forms,
fill the inner chambers.
Delicate eyebrows and soft glances,
eyes gleaming with light.
Smooth complexions and fine skin,
lingering gazes, tender and deep.
In distant pavilions and long tents,
they attend you in leisure.
Kingfisher curtains and emerald drapes,
adorn the lofty hall.
Crimson walls and sandalwood panels,
beams of dark jade.
Looking up at carved rafters,
painted with dragons and serpents.
Sitting in the hall, leaning on the railings,
overlooking the winding pool.
Lotus flowers begin to bloom,
mingled with water caltrop and lotus leaves.
Purple-stemmed water shields,
ripple patterns on the waves.
Guards in leopard-skin attire,
stand watch on the slopes.
Carriages and chariots have halted,
foot soldiers and horsemen are arrayed.
Orchids planted by the door,
jade trees form the hedge.
O soul, come back!
Why wander far away?
The household honors you as ancestor,
with food of many varieties.
Rice, millet, early wheat,
mixed with yellow grain.
Bitter, salty, sour,
spicy and sweet are all served.
The tendons of fattened oxen,
tender and fragrant.
Blended sour with bitter,
presented as Wú broth.
Stewed turtle and roasted lamb,
with sugarcane syrup.
Braised swan and duck stew,
fried wild goose and crane.
Marinated chicken and turtle soup,
rich but not cloying.
Fried dough and honeyed cakes,
with sweet malt sugar.
Jade-like wine and honeyed ladles,
fill the feathered cups.
Strained dregs, chilled for drinking,
cool and refreshing wine.
Ornate wine vessels are set out,
with jade-like nectar.
Come back, come back to your old home,
revered and without hindrance.
Before the feast is fully served,
female musicians are arrayed.
Strike the bells and press the drums,
perform new songs.
Crossing the river to pick water chestnuts,
and gather lotus blossoms.
their rosy cheeks flushed.
Playful glances, sidelong looks,
eyes like layered waves.
Clad in patterned robes, wearing fine silk,
lovely but not garish.
Long hair and flowing locks,
dazzling in splendor.
Sixteen dancers in matching attire,
begin the Zhèng dance.
Skirts swirling like crossed bamboo poles,
they lower their hands to the mats.
Yú pipes and sè zithers wildly join,
drums thunderously beat.
The palace courtyard shakes with sound,
stirring the passionate Chǔ melodies.
Wú songs and Cài ballads,
played to the Dàlǚ mode.
Men and women sit mingled,
disorderly and indistinguishable.
Belts and hat strings cast aside,
strewn in tangled disarray.
Seductive entertainers from Zhèng and Wèi,
come to mingle in the display.
The finale of the passionate Chǔ tune,
stands out uniquely, leading all.
Ivory chess pieces with jade boards,
there is the game of Liùbó.
Divided sides advance together,
fiercely pressing each other.
Achieving xiāo and móu,
they call for "five white!"
Jìn-made rhinoceros-horn dice,
consume the daylight hours.
Bells clang, stands tremble,
zǐwood sè zithers are plucked.
Wine and revelry never cease,
sinking into day and night.
Orchid-scented oil in bright candles,
ornate lamps intricately placed.
Composing with deepest thought,
borrowing the fragrance of orchids.
Each person reaches their limit,
chanting in shared heart.
Drinking fine wine, joy is complete,
delighting ancestors of old.
O soul, come back!
Return to your old home.
Epilogue:
The year begins, spring emerges,
and I journey southward in haste.
Lǜ grass and duckweed leaves unfurl,
while white zhǐ herbs sprout.
The road crosses Lújiāng, leftward lies the vast thicket,
leaning by marsh and islet, gazing far and wide.
Black steeds harnessed in fours, a thousand chariots aligned,
torches raised in succession, dark smoke billows high.
On foot or galloping, the guide leads the charge,
racing with the king toward Mèng, vying to be first or last,
the king himself releases the arrow, striking down the blue rhinoceros.
Dawn succeeds night, time does not linger,
marsh orchids cover the path, this road grows faint.
Deep and clear the river waters, above them maples stand,
eyes straining over a thousand miles, grieving the spring heart,
O soul, come back! Lament for Jiāngnán!
Cassia trees cluster in the mountain's secluded depths,
Twisting and coiling, their branches intertwined.
Mountain mists rise dense, rocks tower jagged and steep,
In ravines with rugged cliffs, waters surge in layers of waves.
Gibbons and apes howl in groups, tigers and leopards roar,
Climbing the cassia branches, I linger here awhile.
The noble wanderer roams, never to return,
Spring grasses grow, lush and dense.
As the year draws to its close, I find no solace,
Cicadas chirp with a mournful, endless drone.
Vast and boundless,
The mountain paths wind and twist,
My heart lingers here, lost in a daze of wilderness.
Confused and obscure,
Trembling with fear.
Tigers and leopards crouch in their lairs,
In thickets and deep woods, men tremble with dread.
Precipitous peaks and jagged rocks, rugged and towering,
Tree trunks twist and entangle, the forest dense and wild.
Green sedge mingles with trees, duckweed sways and spreads.
White deer and stags, some leaping, some resting.
Their forms lofty and majestic,
Fresh and glistening, damp with dew.
Macaques and bears,
Yearning for their kind, filled with sorrow.
Climbing the cassia branches, I linger here awhile.
Tigers and leopards fight, bears roar fiercely,
Birds and beasts flee in terror, scattering from their kin.
O noble wanderer, return!
The mountains are no place to linger long.
The Crown Prince of Chǔ was ill,
And a guest from Wú came to inquire after him,
Saying:
"I have heard that Your Highness's jade-like body is unwell,
Has it improved somewhat?"
The Crown Prince replied:
"Weary!
I thank you, guest."
The guest then remarked:
"Now the world is at peace,
The four quarters are harmonious.
Your Highness is in the prime of youth,
Yet I suspect you have long indulged in pleasures,
Day and night without restraint.
Evil influences have invaded,
Causing congestion within.
Confused and unsettled,
Sighing and groaning, troubled and intoxicated.
Anxious and fearful,
Unable to find rest in sleep.
Weak within and hard of hearing,
Averse to the sound of human voices.
Spirit and energy dissipated,
All manner of ailments arise.
Eyes and ears dazzled and confused,
Joy and anger unbalanced.
If this persists without relief,
Your very life will be endangered.
Does Your Highness suffer from such symptoms?"
The Crown Prince said:
"I thank you, guest.
Thanks to the sovereign's grace,
Such symptoms occur from time to time,
But they have not yet reached that point."
The guest said:
"Now the sons of noble families
Dwell in palaces and inner chambers,
Attended by nurses within,
And tutors without,
With no opportunity to socialize.
Their food is warm, rich, sweet, and tender,
Rich and fatty meats.
Their clothing is layered, soft, and warm,
Hot enough to scorch in summer.
Even if one were as strong as metal or stone,
One would still melt and weaken.
How much more so between the sinews and bones?
Thus it is said:
Indulging the desires of the eyes and ears,
And giving free rein to bodily comfort
Harms the harmony of blood and vessels.
Moreover, riding in carriages and litters
Is called the trigger for paralysis and atrophy;
Deep chambers and cool palaces
Are called the medium for fevers and chills;
Beautiful women with pearly teeth and moth eyebrows
Are called the axe that hacks at one's vitality;
Sweet, crisp, rich, and creamy foods
Are called the poison that rots the intestines.
Now Your Highness's complexion is pale and delicate,
Your limbs limp and feeble,
Your sinews and bones slack and weak,
Your blood and vessels swollen and sluggish,
Your hands and feet idle and useless.
Maidens from Yuè attend you in front,
Beauties from Qí serve you behind.
You come and go, feasting and reveling,
Indulging freely in secluded chambers and hidden rooms.
This is like savoring poison as a delicacy
Or playing with the claws and teeth of fierce beasts.
The roots of this run deep and far,
Lingering long without relief.
Even if Biǎn Què were to treat you internally
And Wūxián were to treat you externally,
What could they do now?
For an illness like Your Highness's,
Only a gentleman of the world,
Widely learned and strong of memory,
Seizing opportunities to speak of matters,
Changing your habits and altering your thoughts,
Constantly at your side,
To serve as your wings,
Could prevent the pleasures of indulgence,
The wild and extravagant heart,
And the will to escape and neglect
From ever taking hold!"
The Crown Prince said:
"Very well.
Once I am recovered,
I shall follow this advice."
The guest said:
"Now Your Highness's illness
Can be cured without medicine, needles, or moxibustion,
But with essential words and wondrous principles to persuade and dispel it.
Would you care to hear them?"
The Crown Prince said:
"I am willing to listen."
The guest said:
"The paulownia tree of Lóngmén
Stands a hundred feet tall without branches.
Its trunk is knotted and gnarled,
Its roots spread wide and separate.
Above, it faces peaks a thousand ren high;
Below, it overlooks ravines a hundred zhang deep.
Torrents and countercurrents
Wash against it.
Its roots are half-dead, half-alive,
In winter, lashed by fierce winds, sleet, and flying snow;
In summer, shaken by thunder and lightning.
At dawn, orioles and cuckoos sing there;
At dusk, lost hens and wandering birds roost there.
A lone swan cries at dawn above it,
And pheasants mournfully call and circle below it.
Thus, from autumn into winter,
Qín Zhì is made to fell it and craft it into a zither,
With silk from wild cocoons for strings,
The hook of an orphan for the pegs,
And the earrings of a nine-times-widowed woman for the bridges.
Shī Táng is made to play 'Chàng,'
And Bó Zǐyá to sing.
The song goes:
'Wheat sprouts lush, pheasants take flight at dawn,
Facing empty valleys, turning from withered locust trees,
Leaning against perilous cliffs, overlooking winding streams.'
Birds hearing it
Fold their wings and cannot leave;
Beasts hearing it
Droop their ears and cannot move;
Insects and ants hearing it
Probe with their mouths and cannot advance.
This is the utmost sorrow in the world.
Can Your Highness rouse yourself to listen?"
The Crown Prince said:
"I am ill,
And cannot."
The guest said:
"The fat of a stall-fed ox,
Cooked with bamboo shoots and cattails.
A stew of fat dog,
Topped with mountain fungus.
Rice from Chǔmiáo,
And Ānhú grains,
Formed into balls that do not crumble,
Dissolving with a single sip.
Then Yī Yǐn is made to simmer and stew,
Yì Yá to blend and season.
Bear's paw braised till tender,
With peony sauce.
Thin slices of grilled rib meat,
Fresh carp sashimi.
Autumn-yellow perilla,
White-dew vegetables.
Orchid-blossom wine
To rinse the mouth.
Pheasant from the mountain ridge,
And the fetus of a leopard raised in captivity.
Small meals and large draughts,
Like hot water melting snow.
This is the utmost delicacy in the world.
Can Your Highness rouse yourself to taste it?"
The Crown Prince said:
"I am ill,
And cannot."
The guest said:
"The stallions from Zhōng and Dài,
carriages drawn by horses in their prime,
their front like flying birds,
their rear akin to Jùxū.
Fed on juē mài and kept in stables,
they are restless within and agitated without.
Harnessed with strong reins,
they tread on smooth roads.
Then Bólè inspects them from front to back,
Wáng Liáng and Zàofǔ drive them,
Qín Quē and Lóu Jì serve as their outriders.
These two men,
can halt runaway horses,
and right overturned carriages.
Thus, they are made to race for a thousand yì in wagers,
competing in a chase of a thousand lǐ.
This too is the finest steed in all the world.
Can Your Highness rouse yourself to ride them?"
The crown prince said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The guest said:
"Having ascended the Jǐngyí Terrace,
gazing south toward Jīngshān,
north toward Rǔhǎi,
with the river on the left and lakes on the right,
there is no greater joy.
Then we summon eloquent scholars,
to trace the origins of mountains and rivers,
exhaustively name the plants and trees,
compare and categorize things,
arranging phrases and linking categories.
Drifting and sightseeing,
we then descend to set out wine in the Yúhuái Palace.
Connected corridors extend in four directions,
terraced walls rise in layered structures,
a profusion of dark and green.
Paths for palanquins crisscross diagonally,
yellow pools wind and curve.
Hùnzhāng and white egrets,
peafowl, kūnhú, and swans,
yuānchú and jiāojīng,
with emerald crests and purple tassels.
Chī dragons and démù birds,
gather and sing in harmony.
Yang fish leap and surge,
flapping fins and shaking scales.
Jìliáo and chóuliǎo plants,
creeping grasses and fragrant líng.
Young mulberries and river willows,
with plain leaves and purple stems.
Miáo pines and yùzhāng trees,
their branches reach up to the sky.
Wútóng and bìnglǘ trees,
stretch as far as the eye can see, forming forests.
All fragrances rich and lush,
mingled by the five winds.
Leisurely and graceful,
they wax and wane with the sun and shade.
Seated in rows, we drink freely,
our hearts delighted by unrestrained music.
Jǐngchūn assists with the wine,
Dù Lián arranges the music.
Flavors of all kinds are arrayed,
dishes and delicacies intermingled in abundance.
Elegant colors please the eye,
flowing melodies gladden the ear.
Then we strike up the stirring melodies of Jíchǔ,
and raise the pure music of Zhèng and Wèi.
We have Xīshī, Zhēng Shū, Yángwén, Duàngān, Wúwá, Lǘjū, Fùyǔ, and their like,
with mixed skirts and trailing sāo,
their glances enticing, hearts yielding,
sleeves flowing like rippling waves,
adorned with dùruò herbs,
veiled in fine dust,
anointed with orchid unguents,
dressed in finery and attending.
This too is the most extravagant, luxurious, and grand pleasure in all the world.
Can Your Highness rouse yourself to partake in it?"
The crown prince said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The guest said:
"I shall prepare for Your Highness trained qíjì horses,
a carriage with flying líng,
mounted on a team of stalwart steeds.
On the right, strong arrows from Xià's quivers,
on the left, carved bows of Wūháo.
Roaming through cloud-topped forests,
galloping around orchid marshes,
halting by the river's edge.
Treading over green duckweed,
bathing in the clear breeze.
Basking in the yang energy,
stirring the heart of spring.
Chasing cunning beasts,
gathering light fowl.
Then exhausting the skills of hounds and horses,
wearing down the feet of wild animals,
draining the wit and craft of guides and drivers.
Tigers and leopards are terrified,
birds of prey are cowed.
Horses race with ringing bits,
fish leap and elk clash.
Trampling over jūn and hares,
stamping on jīng and deer.
Sweat flows and foam falls,
creatures lie trapped and overwhelmed,
those dying without a wound
are enough to fill the following carriages.
This is the grandest of hunting spectacles.
Can Your Highness rouse yourself to join?"
The crown prince said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
Yet a yang glow appeared between his brows,
spreading gradually upward,
nearly filling his entire countenance.
Seeing the crown prince's pleased expression,
the guest pressed further and said:
"Dark flames brush the sky,
war chariots rumble like thunder.
Banners wave and flutter,
feather ornaments stir in orderly profusion.
Racing and vying in pursuit,
all crave the taste and strive to be first.
The hunting grounds are vast and broad,
the viewing area marked by boundaries.
Pure and unblemished whole sacrifices,
are presented at the ducal gate."
The crown prince said:
"Excellent,
I wish to hear more."
The guest said:
"It is not yet over.
Then in dense forests and deep marshes,
where smoke and clouds darken the gloom,
rhinoceroses and tigers arise together.
Fierce and powerfully brave,
men bared their bodies and closed in.
Gleaming white blades,
spears and halberds interlocked.
Harvesting game and recording merits,
rewards of gold and silk bestowed.
Spreading duckweed and displaying ruò grass,
a mat is laid for the herdsmen.
Fine wine and excellent dishes,
delicacies, roasts, minced meat, and grilled fare,
are offered to entertain the guests.
Passions surge and arise together,
stirring the heart and startling the ear.
Sincere and resolute, without regret,
decisions firm, promises kept.
The hue of loyalty and trust,
manifest as metal and stone.
Loud songs are raised in chorus,
'Long life!' without cease.
This is truly what would please Your Highness.
Can you rouse yourself to join this excursion?"
The crown prince said:
"I very much wish to accompany you,
only I fear being a burden to the gentlemen."
Yet now a look of eagerness had risen in him.
The guest said:
"We plan to gather on the fifteenth day of the eighth month,
with feudal lords and traveling companions from distant lands, brothers all,
and together go to watch the tidal bore at the winding river of Guǎnglíng.
Upon arriving, we had not yet seen the form of the tide.
But merely observing the reach of the water's force,
was enough to shock and terrify.
Watching how it surged and raced,
how it rose and towered,
how it churned and swirled,
how it gathered and swelled,
how it scoured and cleansed—
even with keen perception and eloquent speech,
one could never fully describe the reasons for its appearance.
Vague and indistinct,
fearful and trembling,
turbulent and rushing,
sudden and bewildering,
unexpected and unrestrained,
vast and boundless,
vast and limitless.
Its intent seems fixed upon the southern mountains,
its gaze reaching toward the eastern sea.
Arching to touch the azure sky,
one's thoughts are strained to the water's edge.
Gazing endlessly upon the flow,
the spirit returns to the mother sun.
Then it swiftly rides the current downward,
and none know where it will stop.
Sometimes chaotic, its flow twisting,
suddenly veering away, never to return.
Approaching Zhūsì, it recedes into the distance,
leaving emptiness, vexation, and increasing weariness.
Not dispersing until dawn breaks,
one holds it in mind, maintaining composure.
Thereupon, it cleanses the chest within,
washes and purifies the five viscera,
rinses hands and feet,
and bathes hair and teeth.
It casts off lethargy and idleness,
expels turbidity and filth,
resolves doubts and uncertainties,
and refreshes ears and eyes.
At such a time,
even those with chronic ailments and lingering diseases
would straighten their hunched backs and rise from lameness,
open blind eyes and unstop deaf ears to gaze upon it.
How much more so for those merely afflicted with minor vexations,
hangovers, or drunken ailments!
Thus it is said: to enlighten the benighted and dispel confusion,
words are insufficient."
The crown prince said:
"Excellent,
but then, what manner of energy is this tidal bore?"
The guest said:
"It is not recorded.
However, I have heard from my teacher:
three things make it seem divine, yet it is not:
the sound of sudden thunder heard for a hundred lǐ;
river water flowing backward,
seawater flooding inland;
mountains exhaling and inhaling clouds,
ceaselessly day and night.
Spreading, overflowing, swift and fierce,
waves surge and the bore arises.
When it first begins,
it pours down like a torrential rain,
as if white egrets were swooping down.
As it advances a little,
vast and towering,
like the spread canopy of a plain carriage with white horses.
Its waves surge like chaotic clouds,
tumultuous as an army preparing for battle.
When it rises and dashes from the sides,
it flutters like light chariots marshaling troops.
Six dragons draw it,
following the Great White Star.
Purely racing like a vast rainbow,
in an endless procession front and rear.
Lofty and towering,
firm and unyielding,
multitudinous and majestic.
Like layered, solid fortifications,
crowded as marching troops.
With a roaring, thunderous clamor,
rolling and surging, spreading afar,
its force truly irresistible.
Observing its flanks,
they swell and seethe with suppressed force,
dark and obscure, thrusting fiercely,
striking above, dragging below.
Like brave, robust soldiers,
bursting with rage and fearless.
Treading on walls, charging at fords,
penetrating every bend and corner,
surmounting banks, leaping over islets.
Those it meets perish,
those it strikes are destroyed.
It first emerges from the banks of Huòwéi,
where valleys part and ridges twist.
It wheels above Qīngmiè,
silent as troops with gagged mouths at Tánhuán.
Halting briefly at Wǔzǐ's mountain,
it passes swiftly through Gǔmǔ's grounds.
It sweeps past Chì'àn,
brushes against Fúsāng,
and races sideways like thunder.
Truly, it exerts its martial might,
as if enraged, as if shaking with fury.
Chaotic and tumultuous,
its form like galloping horses.
Roaring and rumbling,
its sound like thunderous drums.
In furious outbursts it gathers force,
clear surges leap and bound,
mighty waves rise and shake,
joining battle at the mouth of Jièjiè.
Birds have no time to fly,
fish no time to turn,
beasts no time to flee.
In chaotic, sweeping profusion,
waves surge, clouds scatter.
It batters the southern mountains,
strikes back against the northern shore.
It overwhelms and diminishes hills and mounds,
levels the western banks.
Perilous and treacherous,
it collapses embankments and ponds,
only ceasing when victory is decided.
Gurgling and murmuring,
splashing and streaming.
At the peak of its violent fury,
fish and turtles lose their footing,
tumbling and flailing sideways,
struggling and floundering,
crawling and sprawling in succession.
Strange and wondrous things,
too numerous to tell.
It simply makes men stumble,
dazed, gloomy, and sorrowful.
This is the world's most extraordinary and bizarre spectacle.
Can the crown prince rouse himself to watch it?"
The crown prince said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The guest said:
"I shall then recommend for the crown prince masters of esoteric arts, men of talent and insight,
such as Zhuāng Zhōu, Wèi Móu, Yáng Zhū, Mò Dí, Biàn Yuān, Zhān Hé, and their like.
Have them discuss the subtleties of the world,
and adjudicate the rights and wrongs of all things.
Let Confucius and Lǎozi examine and judge,
Mèngzǐ hold the counting rods and calculate it all,
with not one error in ten thousand.
This, too, is the world's essential discourse and wondrous doctrine.
Would the crown prince wish to hear it?"
Thereupon, the crown prince leaned on his armrest and rose, saying:
"Clear and bright, as if hearing the words of sages and debaters."
Suddenly, sweat poured forth,
and abruptly his illness was cured.
In the past, Méi Chéng composed the "Seven Stimuli",
Fù Yì composed the "Seven Exhortations",
Zhāng Héng composed the "Seven Discriminations",
Cuī Yīn composed the "Seven Imitations",
each with beautiful language.
I admired them,
and thus composed the "Seven Openings".
And I also ordered Wáng Càn to compose one.
Xuánwēizǐ dwells in seclusion in the courtyard of the vast wilderness,
soaring in retreat, detached from the mundane world,
purifying his spirit and calming his soul.
He scorns wealth and disdains nobility,
and has no worldly ambitions.
He delights in emptiness and cherishes tranquility,
yearning for this eternal life.
Alone, his thoughts roam the edges of the sky and clouds,
where no material forms can sway him.
Upon hearing this, Jìngjīzǐ sets out to persuade him.
He harnesses steeds that gallop across the wilds,
and rides in a carriage swift as the chasing wind.
Crossing distant deserts,
emerging from shadowy ruins,
he enters the boundless wilderness,
and finally arrives at Xuánwēizǐ's dwelling.
His abode is
flanked by rushing waters on the left,
and towering peaks on the right.
Behind it lie cave-fed streams,
facing fragrant woods.
Wearing a leather cap,
draped in an embroidered fur robe,
he emerges from a hidden cave in the mountain,
leaning against a steep cliff as he wanders in delight.
His spirit soars aloft,
lofty and sublime,
as if the six directions and nine provinces were too narrow for him.
Like one about to take flight yet not departed,
or with wings raised but lingering midway.
Thereupon, Jìngjīzǐ climbs by grasping vines,
stands firmly upon the rocks,
and proclaims with the wind:
"I have heard that a gentleman does not flee the world and abandon his name,
nor does a wise man turn his back on society and obliterate his achievements.
Yet now, you forsake the splendor of the Way and its arts,
and cast aside the essence of benevolence and righteousness.
You exhaust your spirit in the void,
neglecting the order and principles of human affairs.
It is like painting a form without an image,
or creating a sound without a voice.
Have you not considered this?
Why is your vision so obstructed?"
Xuánwēizǐ bows his head and replies:
"Ah,
such words indeed!
In the beginning of the Supreme Ultimate,
chaos was yet undivided,
the myriad things entangled in confusion,
rising together with the Way.
For all that has form must decay,
all traces must come to an end.
The vast primordial energy—
who knows its finality?
Fame sullies my being,
status burdens my person.
Secretly, I admire the aspirations of the ancients,
and revere the legacy of Lǎo and Zhuāng.
Borrowing the spirit turtle as a metaphor,
I would rather wag my tail in the mud."
Jìngjīzǐ says:
"The beauty of eloquent speech
can make barren marshes flow with water,
and withered trees burst into bloom.
If it can stir spirits and rouse the divine,
how much more so the hearts of men nearby.
I shall describe for you the ultimate pleasures of travel and sightseeing,
perform the enchanting allure of music and beauty.
Discuss the utmost marvels of transformation,
and expound the grandeur and beauty of virtue.
Would you care to hear?"
Xuánwēizǐ says:
"You, sir, have disciplined yourself and wearied of the world,
delving into the hidden to rescue the submerged.
Not deterred by the distant journey,
I am honored by your radiant presence.
I shall respectfully cleanse my ears,
to listen to your jade-like words."
Jìngjīzǐ says:
"Fragrant wild rice, refined white grains,
frost-nurtured greens, dew-fed mallows.
The dark bear's pale skin,
the plump swine's tender flesh.
Sliced as thin as cicada wings,
carved with fine and delicate precision.
Layered like folded silk,
scattered like drifting snow.
Lightly carried by the wind,
the blade never turns in its cut.
Mountain partridges and quails,
treasures of pearls and kingfisher feathers.
Chilled nests of fragrant water-lilies with turtle,
minced flying scales from the Western Sea.
Braised river otters from Jiāngdōng,
stewed singing quails from Hànnán.
Blended with fragrant sourness,
sweet harmony, rich and mellow.
Xuánmíng adjusts the saltiness,
Rùshōu tempers the spiciness.
Purple orchids and red peppers,
applied with measured harmony.
The flavors are distinct,
their lingering fragrance wafts afar.
Then there is the clear spring wine of pale green,
crafted by Kāng and Dí.
It transforms in response,
taking shape when touched by the ether.
Pluck the zhǐ note, and bitterness arises;
strike the gōng note, and sweetness is born.
It is then served in jade-green goblets,
poured into carved wine vessels.
Floating bubbles seethe like a boiling cauldron,
intense and richly aromatic.
It can harmonize the spirit,
and delight the senses.
Such are the wonders of these delicacies—
will you follow me and partake of them?"
Xuánwēizǐ says:
"I am content with coarse greens,
and have no leisure for such feasts."
Jìngjīzǐ says:
"The Bùguāng sword,
adorned with intricate, lavish patterns.
Embellished with patterned rhinoceros horn,
carved with kingfisher green.
Studded with pearls from the black dragon,
inlaid with jade from Jīngshān.
It can sever rhinoceros and elephant on land,
yet this is not deemed remarkable.
It slices through swans upon the waves,
leaving the water undiminished by the blade.
The crown with nine tassels,
scattering radiance, draped with elegant patterns.
The silken cords of the cap's ties,
flutter in the wind, a riot of colors.
Pendants of Jiélǜ and Xuánlí jade,
treasures of exquisite subtlety.
Their luminous brilliance shines resplendently,
flowing light casting radiant glow.
Robes of embroidered ceremonial patterns,
skirts of sheer silk gauze.
Golden-flowered shoes,
whose movement leaves trails of light.
Ornaments varied and manifold,
delicate and fresh as frost.
Sash pendants intricately entwined,
some carved, some inlaid.
Perfumed with secluded herbs,
their fragrance spreads freely.
Strolling with dignified ease,
turning and shining as one moves.
Nánwēi would loosen her stern expression for this,
Xīshī would offer her artful smile.
Such are the wonders of this attire and adornment—
will you follow me and wear them?"
Xuánwēizǐ says:
"I prefer coarse woolens,
and have no leisure for such garments."
Jìng Jīzǐ said:
"Galloping can dispel cares,
hunting excursions can delight the heart.
I shall drive for you the flying steeds of cloud-dragons,
adorn the jade carriage with tasseled trappings.
Dangling the long ribbons of the curving rainbow,
raising the splendid banner of the Dipper.
Swift arrows that forget to return,
grasping the mighty Fánruò bow.
Suddenly treading on shadows and lightly racing away,
outrunning swift steeds and surpassing the swiftest winds.
Then ravines are filled and valleys blocked,
thickets and marshes leveled and smoothed.
Setting traps along the mountains,
spreading nets across the wilderness.
Below, no tracks escape;
above, no birds fly free.
Birds gather and beasts crowd together,
then the encirclement is joined.
Hunters spread like clouds,
mounted warriors scatter like mist.
Vermilion banners blaze across the fields,
spears and halberds gleam bright.
Dragging the patterned fox,
covering the cunning hare.
Sweeping down the sùshuāng birds,
brushing aside the startled egrets.
Those in the path are trampled,
those underfoot are crushed.
Flying chariots flash like lightning,
beasts tumble beneath the wheels.
Wings have no time to spread,
feet no chance to leap.
Moving, they touch flying blades;
rising, they catch in light nets.
Searching forests, scouring perilous places,
probing thickets, exhausting hidden obstacles.
Leaping over mountains, plunging into valleys,
like wind whipping, like flames rising.
Arrows never miss their mark;
when they strike, feathers drink deep.
Then, with people dense and nets close,
the land confined, the situation pressing,
roaring beasts,
baring fangs, bristling manes,
intent on charging forth,
fierce spirits undaunted.
Then men like Běigōng and Dōngguō
tear off leopard tails alive,
split the shoulders of chū beasts.
Forms cannot withstand their hands;
bones cannot hide from their fists.
Splitting bears, shattering paws,
pulling apart tigers, crushing their stripes.
In the fields, no furred creatures remain;
in the woods, no feathered flocks.
Piled beasts rise like hills,
flying pinions form clouds.
Then, with drums and bells resounding,
banners furled, pennants relaxed,
nets lowered, meshes released,
the hunting party turns back.
Fine steeds prance together,
raising bits, flying foam.
Leaning down on golden yokes,
reaching up to stroke emerald canopies.
Composed and leisurely,
delighting the mind beyond worldly cares.
This is the wonder of the feather hunt;
can you follow me to witness it?"
Xuán Wēizǐ said:
"I delight in tranquility;
I have no leisure for such sights."
Jìng Jīzǐ said:
"Leisurely palaces, spacious and bright,
cloud-like halls gleaming radiantly.
Raising high foundations on scenic peaks,
welcoming clear winds to erect viewing towers.
Vermilion galleries, purple pillars,
carved rafters, ornate beams.
Ornate ceilings hold blooming flowers,
golden steps, jade cabinets.
Warm rooms where winter clothes are sheer gauze,
cool chambers where midsummer holds frost.
Magnificent pavilions touch the clouds,
flying stairways ascend the void.
Looking down, shooting stars are glimpsed;
gazing up, the eight directions are seen.
Climbing dragons cannot reach such heights;
dwelling loftily at the edge of the sky.
Intricate marvels, divine wonders,
changing names, strange forms.
Bān Shū would have no place for his axe and adze;
Lí Lóu would lose his keen sight before them.
Beautiful grasses planted in rows,
rare species, exotic kinds.
Green leaves, crimson blooms,
shining upon heaven, dazzling the sun.
Clear water fills the ponds,
dense trees form forests.
Winged creatures soar on high,
scaled beings hide in the depths.
Then, wandering at ease,
suddenly as if forgetting to return.
Have Rénzǐ cast his fishing line,
Wèishì set his mechanical crossbow.
Fragrant bait sinks into the water,
light lines shoot flying birds.
Bringing down birds soaring through cloudy screens,
hauling up spirit turtles from the ninefold depths.
Then gathering water lily blossoms,
plucking duckweed from the streams.
Playing with pearl-bearing clams,
sporting with mermaidens.
Reciting the odes of 'Hàn Guǎng,'
beholding roaming maidens by the water's edge.
Their divine radiance shines on midstream islets,
clad in sheer gauze of fine silk.
Leaving fragrant traces as they stroll calmly,
raising fair hands to sing clear songs.
The song says:
Gazing toward the clouds, there is a beloved one,
but the heavenly road is long, no way to go.
Wearing orchids and fragrant herbs, for whom do I adorn myself?
Sweet meetings cut short, my heart grieves.
This is the wonder of palaces and lodges;
can you follow me to dwell here?"
Xuán Wēizǐ said:
"I am devoted to rocky caves;
I have no leisure for such dwelling."
Jìng Jīzǐ said:
"Having toured the central plains,
wandered through leisurely palaces,
passions unleashed, will set adrift,
excessive pleasures not yet ended.
There will also be talented performers, marvelous courtesans,
transcending the world, surpassing custom.
Spreading the flowing melodies of Běilǐ,
continuing the exquisite tunes of Yáng'ē.
Then ride in ornate carriages,
approach Dòngtíng Lake.
Qins and ses alternate in playing,
chí on the left, shēng on the right.
Bells and drums all resound together,
flutes and pipes join in chorus.
Then beauties don patterned gauze, splendid gowns,
shaking light silks that flutter and sway.
Wearing golden hairpins that shimmer and gleam,
raising kingfisher feathers in twin crests.
Waving flowing scents,
shining with flying patterns.
Passing through drum arrays,
brilliant and multicolored.
Long robes follow the wind,
mournful songs enter the clouds.
Nimble as if flying,
treading emptiness, stepping far.
Leaping and soaring,
undulating and swirling.
Soaring like wild geese rising,
suddenly vanishing like diving ducks.
Releasing light bodies to swiftly advance,
shadows chasing forms but never catching up.
Flying notes stir the dust,
wavering and piercing echoes.
Talents nimble as gods,
forms hard to capture in image.
Then, as joy remains unspent,
the white sun slants westward.
Music disperses, attire changes,
taking light steps to inner chambers.
Dark brows relaxed, lead powder fallen,
tidy disordered hair, apply orchid ointment,
graceful forms in fine robes, wafting subtle fragrance.
Rosy faces suited to smiles,
glancing sidelong, light flowing in eyes.
At times with you, my friend,
hand in hand we stroll together.
Treading flying steps,
approaching quiet rooms.
Splendid candles blaze,
curtains and canopies spread.
Moving vermilion lips,
issuing clear shāng notes.
Raising silken sleeves,
shaking splendid robes.
On an autumn night,
joy knows no end.
This is the wonder of music and beauty;
can you follow me to revel in it?"
Xuán Wēizǐ said:
"I desire clarity and emptiness;
I have no leisure for such revelry."
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"I have heard that the gentleman delights in exerting his integrity to manifest righteousness,
and the determined scholar willingly endangers his body to achieve benevolence.
Therefore, men of valor and talent
form alliances and establish bonds.
They value spirit and disregard life,
moved by duty, they forsake their persons.
Thus Tián Guāng fell upon his sword in Northern Yān,
and Gōngshū met his end in Western Qín.
Resolute and decisive, swift in judgment,
they stride like tigers, stirring gales in the valleys.
Their might awes rulers of ten thousand chariots,
and all under heaven proclaims them heroes."
Before his words had finished,
Xuánwēizǐ said:
"Excellent."
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"These are but wandering knights;
they cannot yet be called sublime.
As for men like Tián Wén and Wújì,
they were the brilliant lords of high antiquity.
All spread benevolence and exalted righteousness,
soaring in the ways and arts.
Their minds roamed without bounds,
their aspirations rose to the clouds.
They overawed the feudal lords,
and galloped across the age.
A wave of their sleeves stirred winds across the nine wilds;
in their fervor, their breath formed rainbows in the sky.
If you, sir, lived in such times,
could you follow me and befriend them?"
Xuánwēizǐ said:
"I truly desire it.
But in relation to the Great Way,
would this not be a burden?"
Jìngjīzǐ said:
"There is a sage ruler in the world,
assisting the emperor and dominating the age.
His measure equals heaven and earth,
his brilliance matches the sun and moon.
His mysterious transformations join with the divine,
and he is in harmony with the numinous.
His beneficent grace spreads to the common people,
his majestic power shakes all within and beyond.
He surpasses the peace of Yīn and Zhōu,
treads in the steps of Fúxī and equals Tàihào.
His court is illustrious and pure,
the Kingly Way extends evenly far and wide.
The people look to him as grass to dew,
our grace falls upon them like spring.
By the riverbanks, there are no men washing their ears;
upon the high peaks, no people dwell in nests.
Thus men of talent come to serve,
beholding the glory of the state.
No talent is overlooked in recommendation,
advancement comes from every quarter.
Rituals and ceremonies are praised in the Pìyōng,
civil virtue is discoursed in the Mingtáng;
the ornate theories of vulgar customs are corrected,
and the ancient statutes of Master Kǒng are synthesized.
Music is diffused to transform manners,
the state is enriched, the people prosper.
Divine responses and blessings arrive,
auspicious signs are repeatedly obtained.
Thus sweet dew descends profusely at dawn,
and the radiant star shines forth at night.
One sees the roaming dragon in the divine abyss,
and hears the crying phoenix on the high ridge.
This is the utmost flourishing of the Hegemonic Way,
the glorious age of harmony and joy.
Yet our sovereign still deems his deep grace insufficiently broad,
fears that his teachings and influence are not yet vigorous;
he seeks the extraordinary from obscurity,
and proclaims the imperial brilliance even in mountain caves.
This is the season for Nìngzǐ's merchant song,
and the reason why Lǚ Wàng cast his line and departed.
You, sir, are a subject of this great peace;
do you not wish to serve in the age of Táng Yáo?"
Then Xuánwēizǐ pushed up his sleeves and rose, saying:
"How brilliant are these words!
Earlier, sir,
your descriptions were ornate and excessive,
intending to incite me,
but only disturbed my heart.
Now I hear that all under heaven is serene and pure,
an enlightened ruler governs the state,
observing the proper principles of fullness and emptiness,
and understanding the delusions of stubborn simplicity.
Now I am suddenly enlightened,
my body feels light as if flying.
I wish to return to my original garb,
and follow you back."
Chōngmò Gōngzǐ,
embracing splendor, concealing his light.
Joyous in retreat, coiling like a dragon,
disporting in the world, treading the high path.
His mind roamed in vastness,
his will amused itself among the myriad subtleties.
He dwelled beyond sight in the remote barriers of the great wilderness,
and swallowed sound in the deep recesses of secluded mountains.
Then Xùnhuá Dàfū heard of him and came to visit.
He ordered cloud-carriages,
harnessed flying steeds.
Crossed rushing sands,
crushed flowing frost.
Soared on the whirlwind,
trod the ford of solid ice.
Banners brushed the edges of the sky,
wheel-tracks emerged from the azure bounds.
The heavens clear and chill, without rosy clouds;
the wilds open and bright, without dust.
Facing layered peaks, he gathered the reins;
looking toward the stone chamber, he turned his chariot.
Thus he reached the dwelling of Chōngmò.
His dwelling
was lofty and dimly vast,
desolate and void, mysterious.
The murky sea, turbulent and surging, lay behind it;
the ravine valley, rugged and steep, spread before it.
Tall bamboos, raising their stems, shaded its gullies;
the chorus of a hundred sounds deafened its mountains.
Fierce gales arose and turned back the sun;
flying stones rose and sprinkled the sky.
Then he climbed the sheerest peak,
faced the long wind.
He set forth arguments to dispel delusion,
and addressed the公子 in the midst of the crags, saying:
"I have heard that the sage does not roll up the Way and turn his back on the times,
nor does the wise man abandon his person and conceal his traces.
In life, one must make one's glorious name shine in the jade tablets;
in death, then inscribe one's great deeds in the golden records.
Now you,公子, withdraw from the world, sinking into obscurity,
fleeing the earth, hiding alone.
The joys of living are extinguished,
the duty owed to one's father is abandoned.
Sorrow fills a hundred years,
bitterness overflows a thousand ages.
How is this different from tiny fish swimming in puddles,
or short-winged birds nesting in thickets?
Now I shall honor you with the great treasure of heaven and man,
and delight you with the ultimate pleasure of following your nature.
Roam to the ends of the earth,
dwell at the center of the sky.
Pour out the joys of the four seas,
exhaust the richness of the nine provinces.
Bore through the gourd of Qūgǔ,
loosen the bonds of Shūshǔ—
do you desire this?"
The公子 said:
"You,大夫, have not forgotten me,
coming to gather here in the wilds beyond.
Though I am untalented,
I reverently listen to your fine words."
The Grand Master said:
"The paulownia tree of the cold mountain,
originates from the Great Abyss.
It contains the Yellow Bell and sprouts its trunk,
standing alone on the azure peak.
Then there are jade cliffs towering high,
golden banks steep and sheer.
To the left, it faces the windy valley,
to the right, it overlooks the cloud-filled stream.
Above, there are no nests in the empty sky,
below, no paths tread by creatures.
Shaking and towering, rugged and upright,
lofty and distant, soaring high.
It basks in the overflowing dew of the three springs,
and faces the howling winds of the nine autumns.
Scattered snow adorns its roots,
drifting frost seals its branches.
The trees flourish and then turn green,
the grass withers before turning pale.
Then we build cloud ladders,
ascend the rugged heights.
We cut the sunny branches of Ruíbīn,
split the shady stems of Dàlǚ.
The craftsman carves its simplicity,
Líng Lún harmonizes its sounds.
The instruments are raised, music is played,
with urgent tunes and high tension.
The sound is clear like the Hàozhōng bell,
the melody pure, lingering around the beams.
It chases the lingering echoes of the eight winds,
gathers wondrous harmonies from Guīchāng.
It opens the Shǎogōng of Zhōnghuáng,
releases the Biànshāng of Rùshōu.
When the dragon fire declines in the west,
the warm air begins to fade.
Flying frost welcomes the season,
high winds send forth autumn.
Those wanderers longing for home,
the drifting souls afflicted by countless sorrows.
Stroking the tightened strings brings a sour nose,
plucking the high-pitched strings brings flowing tears.
If one pursues the clear melodies,
and follows the strict rhythms.
Playing 'Lǜshuǐ',
singing 'Báixuě'.
Stirring Chǔ tunes to return,
the flowing wind gathers.
Lamenting the morning fall of the míngjiá,
mourning the evening wane of Wàngshū.
The lonely widow beats her breast in grief,
the aged widow sobs and weeps.
Prince Wángzǐ brushes his tassels and leans to listen,
the six horses exhale to the sky and raise their heads to chew.
This is the utmost wonder of musical melodies.
Can you, sir, follow me and listen to it?"
The Young Master said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The Grand Master said:
"The secret halls of the orchid palace,
carved halls with ornate windows.
Cloud screens shimmer brilliantly,
jade walls verdant and lush.
The main gate has eight layers,
the jade terrace nine stories high.
Marked by the hundred-cháng tower,
encircled by the ten-thousand-zhì wall.
Then the lofty pavilion greets the wind,
elegantly rising to the mid-heaven.
Emerald towers stand tall and green,
carved pavilions connect like rosy clouds.
Long eaves reach the clouds,
flying stairs ascend the mountains.
Gazing at the Yùshéng star to set the roof,
facing the inverted light to open the windows.
Crimson and white shine brightly,
beams and brackets rise high.
Dark dragons bear the eaves,
sun horses support the corners.
Adorned with jade blossoms,
carved with golden flowers.
Square lattices hold elegance,
round wells bloom with flowers.
Heavy halls rise in layers,
ornate curtains face each other.
The secluded hall is dim by day,
the bright room luminous at night.
Tiny insects fly and stir the wind,
inchworms move and create sound.
If the eyes tire of common sights,
the body wearies of curtains and canopies.
Take the young master for a stroll together,
and enjoy the view in the forested foothills.
Ascend the emerald hill,
approach the crimson valley.
Flowers and grass flourish like brocade,
flying colors twinkle like stars.
Sunny leaves are green in spring,
shady branches verdant in autumn.
Blossoms and fruits renew in turn,
following one's whims to indulge in joy.
Look up and pluck the divine xiāo herb,
bend down to gather morning orchids.
Follow the huì wind through the thickets,
gaze at the pepper path on the jade altar.
Then float on three-winged boats,
play in the midstream isle.
Hidden gills startle,
startled feathers rise.
Sink the silk lines,
release the flying arrows.
Hang the returning wings beyond the crimson sky,
draw the splendid scales from the purple abyss.
Then row the oars with the wind,
rest the paddles and ride the waves.
Blow the lone bamboo flute,
strum the Yúnhé zither.
The river singer chants the Huáinán tune,
the boatman plays the 'Cǎilíng' song.
The song goes:
Ride the duck boat for water play,
approach the fragrant isle to pluck the divine mushroom.
Joy makes one forget sorrow,
wandering to pass the time.
Turn night into day,
spend the year as if it were a season.
This is the grand beauty of leisurely dwelling,
can you, sir, follow me and dwell here?"
The Young Master said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The Grandee said:
"When the white autumn season arrives,
the moon signals the time to distribute winter garments.
Heaven congeals and earth closes up,
winds sharpen and frost flies.
Supple branches grow stiff by evening,
dense leaves thin by morning.
We shall harness this energy to enact slaughter,
and upon the Metal Suburb muster our troops.
Then we array light warriors,
marshal armored might.
Raise cloud-tasseled banners,
unveil fierce spear-points.
Harness the flying steeds of Hóngyáng,
team the Sùshuāng steeds of Tánggōng.
Mass feathered arrows in the outer woods,
release swift wings into the central wilds.
Then we spread flying nets,
stretch long snares.
Scale yellow ridges,
hang over green peaks.
Mark the long gorge as our boundary,
girdle the flowing stream as our gate.
Thus within, no sparse trail remains;
without, no trace escapes.
Beat gongs to count the troops,
raise flags to signal the kills.
Draw golden crossbows.
Loose singing arrows.
Shear tough bristles,
strike down powerful pinions.
Chariots and cavalry vie in galloping,
moving abreast, tracks aligned.
Swift and sudden, flickering fast,
like clouds swirling, wind fierce.
Raised halberds dense as a forest,
brandished blades flash like lightning, then vanish.
Looking up, they topple cloud-nests;
gazing down, they exhaust earth-burrows.
Then there are round-patterned lynxes,
striped-forehead tigers.
Manes bristling, raising wind;
furious eyes flashing lightning.
Jaws snapping at frosty blades,
paws batting flying spear-points.
They shake the woods, stumble on rocks,
stamp and trample the deep thickets.
Then fleet steeds exert their sharpness,
strong warriors display their skill.
They press the giant boar,
overthrow the rampant swine.
Drag down striped tigers,
break the xièzhì beast.
Hooked claws are shattered,
saw-teeth are wrenched apart.
Scattered in disarray,
filling ravines, toppling thickets.
Carcasses hang on hills,
fallen bodies cover the marshes.
The marsh becomes a forest of fur,
the lowland a crimson thicket.
Then we withdraw the encirclement, gather the nets,
furl the banners, retrieve the kites.
The gamekeepers count the beasts,
the forest officers tally the fresh kills.
Prizes are awarded for the highest scores, the diligent are feasted,
horses are rested, bows unstrung.
Meat-laden carriages are linked bit to bit,
wine-carts stand side by side.
A thousand cups are drained like lightning,
ten thousand torches blaze like stars.
Hills and mounds are moist with flowing fat,
streams and valleys sated with fragrant smoke.
When joy peaks and pleasure is spent,
we turn our reins and return.
This too is a grand spectacle of field excursions;
could you, sir, follow me and do this?"
The Young Noble said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The Grandee said:
"The Yang Sword of Chǔ,
wrought by Ōuyě.
The ore from Yéxī,
the essence of Chìshān.
Smelted surpassing Yángtóu iron,
forged exceeding Duànchéng steel.
Refined and tempered,
folded a myriad times, quenched a thousand.
Fēnglóng wielded the hammer,
Fēilián fanned the coals.
Thus the divine weapon was formed,
with raised patterns and sunken lines.
Flowing damask like linked stars,
floating colors brilliantly displayed.
Its light like scattered lightning,
its substance like gleaming snow.
Its frosty edge congealed like water,
its icy blade pure as dew.
In form it surpasses Háocáo,
in fame it outvalues Jùquē.
Point it at Zhèng, and three armies turn white-haired;
brandish it at Jìn, and a thousand lǐ run with blood.
How could it merely be said to sever jiāo and hóng in water,
or scatter galloping teams on land,
or be deemed skillful for slicing floating feathers,
or praised as sharp for piercing heavy armor?
As for its numinous power,
it expands and contracts without limit,
with strange edges and extraordinary form.
Its shape astounds Xuē Zhú,
its light startles Fēnghú.
Its worth equals three districts,
its fame outshines two capitals.
Some, renowned, overwhelmed Qín;
some, flying by night, left Wú.
Thus its merit crowns ten thousand ages,
its awe shines endlessly.
He who wields it has no equal before him,
he who holds it becomes a hero himself.
With it one can subdue the nine states,
control the eight barbarian tribes.
Claws and teeth flock to its shadow,
all Xià receives its influence.
This is a divine weapon rare in the world;
could you, sir, follow me and wield it?"
The Young Noble said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The Grandee said:
"The noble steed, Heaven's charger,
its graceful form surpassing.
It receives its vital breath from the numinous deep,
its essence from the bright moon.
Its pupils shine with dark light,
its black coat gleams with a purplish sheen.
Its foam is like flung rouge,
its sweat like shaken blood.
Qín Qīng could not discern its exact measurements,
Fāng Yīn could not perceive its vanishing speed.
Then caparisoned with cloud-canopied chariots,
treading the morning mist.
They speed along spring roads,
arrayed for autumn drives.
Like coiling dragons leaping, hornless dragons soaring,
like qílín surpassing, dragons ascending.
Seeing a mountain, they charge toward it;
seeing a forest, they rush to it.
Spirit soaring, fury unleashed,
like stars flying, lightning startling.
Ambition overawes the Nine Provinces,
momentum crosses the Four Seas.
Their shadow cannot keep up with their form,
dust has no time to rise.
Before the floating water-clock's arrow has moved,
they have twice covered a thousand lǐ.
Then they pass heaven's border,
cross earth's barriers.
Traverse where even Hànmàn never roamed,
tread where even Zhāng and Hài left no trace.
The Sun Crow folds its wings for them,
Kuāfù casts aside his staff for them.
These are the finest mounts under heaven;
could you, sir, follow me and drive them?"
The Young Noble said:
"I am ill,
and cannot."
The Grandee said:
"The millet of Dàliáng,
the grain of Qióng Mountain,
the seeds sown by Táng Jì,
the blossoms tasted by the Divine Farmer.
Then there are the rare treasures of the six domestic fowl,
the diverse delicacies of the four seasonal meals.
The exotic foods from the farthest seas,
the finest produce from the utmost lands.
Yī Gōng tends the cauldron,
the master chef wields his knife.
Flavors enriched through nine boilings,
harmonized with peony and spice.
Morning wild ducks and dew-fed swans,
frost-partridges and yellow sparrows.
Round trays arrayed like scattered stars,
square zhang mats adorned with floral patterns.
The paws of the sealed bear,
the feet of the crowing fowl.
Swallow thighs and gorilla lips,
yak tail remnants and elephant marrow.
Turtles from the numinous abyss,
blowfish from Láihuáng.
Phoenixes from Dānxué,
womb of the black leopard.
Sautéed with autumn oranges,
seasoned with spring plums.
Served with King Zhòu's chopsticks,
presented in Emperor Xīn's cups.
Fàn Gōng's scale-fish,
emerging from the nine streams.
Crimson tail and scarlet gills,
purple fins and azure mane.
Then he commands Zhīlí,
to wield the frost-sharp blade.
Red flesh unfolds like brocade scattering,
white skin falls like snow drifting.
The fine hair of the Lóu rat cannot compare to its delicacy,
the wings of autumn cicadas are not enough to match its thinness.
When the lavish feast concludes,
there are also chilled delicacies.
Fruits from Shāng Mountain,
hazelnuts from Hàngāo.
Split open the casings of longan,
cleave apart the shells of coconuts.
Exquisite flavors selected ten thousand times,
presented successively to please the guest.
Then there is Wūchéng from south of Jīng,
Zhúyè from north of Yù.
Floating bubbles starry and boiling,
flying froth like duckweed connecting.
Xuán Shí once tasted its flavor,
Yí Shì presented its method.
Empty the jar in a single morning,
and one can remain intoxicated for a thousand days.
A single jar of unstrained brew poured into the river,
can make the three armies declare victory.
These are what gods and men admire and envy,
what sight and hearing find dazzling and splendid.
Could you, sir, force yourself to rise and partake of them?"
The Young Master said:
"To indulge in flavors that corrupt the palate,
to relish tastes as poisonous as dried meat.
To consume medicines that rot the intestines,
to employ vessels that ruined states.
Though these may be what you, Grandee, consider glorious,
they are precisely what we people fear.
I am ill,
and cannot do so."
The Grandee said:
"It is because the Jìn dynasty has melted into the imperial aura,
the golden splendor initiating its reign,
that the great man has arisen.
Continuing the bright dynasty's radiance,
matching Heaven's light and dwelling in virtue.
Its foundational virtue,
is loftier than when Duke Jī dwelled in Qí.
Its bestowed benevolence,
is richer than when the Yīn dynasty was in Bó.
The winds of the Southern Winnowing Basket,
cannot fully convey its transforming influence.
The clouds gathering near the Moon,
are insufficient to enrich its blessings.
The imperial way shines brilliantly,
the sovereign's achievements accumulate brightly.
Guiding the vital breath with music,
proclaiming virtue with poetry.
Teaching purer than in the age of the Cloud Officials,
governance more harmonious than in the era of the Bird Annals.
The kingly way extends to the four borders,
all within the passes is tranquil and peaceful.
Red frontiers extinguish their beacon fires,
green borders lay down their alarms.
Horses are turned back to pull manure carts,
virtue is inscribed on the Kun-Wu tripods.
The multitudes return to simplicity,
the literature of the age flourishes richly.
Ploughmen yield the field borders,
fishermen cede the dry land.
Woodcutters are ashamed of tall-hat ornaments,
servants and grooms laugh at short-jacket garments.
The six directions are constantly harmonious,
lofty and vast.
Black-haired children sing in the lanes,
yellow-haired elders beat the earth in rhythm.
Untying the cords of Fúxī's reign,
erasing the penal symbols of Táng Yáo's time.
As for the barbarians of Hua and Yi,
the Mo tribes of distant wilderness.
Whose language is not recorded by light-carriage envoys,
whose lands do not receive the imperial calendar.
None fail to gallop forth and knock their foreheads to the ground,
presenting themselves through repeated translation.
At this time, even insects and reptiles sense the kindness,
no thought remains unsoothed.
Parks sport nine-tailed birds,
enclosures perch three-legged crows.
Singing phoenixes in the forests,
more numerous than in Huángdì's gardens.
Dragons swim in the deep pools,
filling Kǒng Jiǎ's ponds.
All things blend in harmony,
Heaven and Earth communicate in peace.
Righteousness embraces without inner exclusion,
transformation reaches without outer limit.
In the woods, none wear coarse cloth,
in the mountains, none gird leather belts.
All images are carved by the hundred craftsmen,
omens arise from the numinous tortoise shells.
Officials gather in great numbers,
carriages and caps spread in profusion.
Achievements compete in flow with the Creator,
virtue matches in greatness the Two Forms (Heaven and Earth)."
Before his words concluded,
the Young Master sprang up abruptly,
and said:
"This rustic man, stubborn and ignorant,
clings to this wild and unrestrained nature.
For there are principles that, when criticized,
resolve disputes over contending treasures;
words that, when anger is expressed,
cure the illness of the King of Qí.
Earlier, you tempted me with deafening music,
sheltered me in a house with matted windows.
Hunting excursions and unrestrained galloping,
sharp blades and swift steeds.
These are what Lǎozi warned against,
not what we people desire.
Therefore, I could not respond to you.
But now I hear the imperial aura is truly splendid,
the sagely way of the time is pure.
Substantial achievements are like autumn harvests,
literary embellishments bloom like spring.
Below are people deserving of enfeoffment,
above is a sovereign truly great.
Though I am not clever,
I beg to follow in your footsteps."
The Edict said:
"To achieve extraordinary merit,
one must await extraordinary men.
Thus, some horses may kick and gallop yet cover a thousand lǐ,
some scholars may bear the burden of vulgar criticism yet establish merit and fame.
Those horses that bolt from control,
those scholars who are dissolute and unrestrained,
also depend on how they are managed.
Let the commanderies and counties examine officials and commoners for outstanding talent and exceptional ability,
those who can serve as generals, ministers, or envoys to distant states."
We have heard that in the times of Táng and Yú of old,
symbols were drawn and the people did not offend.
Wherever the sun and moon shone,
none failed to follow and obey.
In the Chéng and Kāng reigns of Zhōu,
punishments were set aside unused,
virtue reached even birds and beasts;
teaching extended throughout the four seas,
beyond the seas was Sùshèn.
Běifā and Qúsōu to the north,
Dī and Qiāng came to submit.
Stars did not stray from their paths,
sun and moon were not eclipsed,
mountains and hills did not crumble,
rivers and valleys did not clog.
Qílín and phoenixes dwelled in the suburban marshes,
the Hé and Luò rivers produced charts and writings.
Alas!
What deeds achieved such a state?"
Now that I have been able to serve the ancestral temple,
I rise early to seek,
and ponder late into the night,
as if treading upon deep waters,
not knowing how to cross.
How magnificent! How grand!
What actions can I take to manifest the great achievements and splendid virtues of the late emperor?
To emulate Yáo and Shùn above,
and match the Three Kings below—
I am not intelligent,
and cannot extend virtue afar.
This is what you, my ministers, have witnessed and heard.
The virtuous and worthy, well-versed in the principles of governance throughout ancient and modern times,
having received the edict and considered the questions,
shall all respond in writing.
Record them in scrolls,
and I shall personally review them.
Imperial Edict:
To the Commissioner with Imperial Authority, Chancellor, and Governor of Jìzhōu, Marquis of Wǔpíng:
I, lacking virtue,
encountered misfortune in my youth,
and was far away in the western lands,
moving to Táng and Wèi.
At that time,
I was like a dangling ornament,
with the ancestral temple lacking sacrifices,
and the altars of state without a rightful position.
Numerous villains coveted the throne,
dividing up the various states of Xià,
so that not a single person or an inch of land
was under my control.
Thus, the mandate of our exalted ancestor
was on the verge of falling to the ground.
I therefore rose early and slept fitfully,
trembling with grief in my heart.
I said: “O ancestors, O forefathers,
ministers and former officials,
who will take pity on my person?”
Then Heaven’s heart was moved,
and gave birth to the Chancellor.
To protect and assist our imperial house,
and deliver us from hardship and peril—
I truly rely on him.
Now I shall confer upon you the rites and ceremonies;
reverently heed my command:
In the past,
when Dǒng Zhuó first raised the calamity against the state,
and the various lords lost their positions,
you plotted for the royal house.
You then stepped forward,
first leading the military campaign.
This was your loyalty to the imperial court.
Later, when the Huángjīn [Yellow Turbans],
rebelled against the natural order,
invaded our three provinces,
and extended to the common people,
you again campaigned against them,
wiping out their traces,
and bringing peace to the eastern Xià.
This was again your achievement.
Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng,
wielding authority arbitrarily,
were again subdued by your merit,
and their threat was removed.
Thus Xǔdū was established,
creating our capital region,
setting up offices and conducting sacrifices,
so that the old ways were not lost.
Heaven, earth, and the spirits
thereby found peace.
This was again your achievement.
When Yuán Shù usurped and rebelled,
running rampant in Huáinán,
he was awed by your might,
and you employed a brilliant strategy.
In the battle of Qíyáng,
Qiáo Ruí lost his head;
your awe-inspiring power spread southward,
and Shù perished in collapse.
This was again your achievement.
Turning your spears eastward,
Lǚ Bù was slain;
as the chariots were about to return,
Zhāng Yáng was thwarted and died;
Suī Gù confessed his crime;
Zhāng Xiù submitted in obeisance.
This was again your achievement.
When Yuán Shào defied the natural order,
plotting to endanger the altars of state,
relying on his multitudes,
and raising troops to insult us from within,
at that time,
the royal forces were few and weak,
the world was filled with dread,
and none held firm resolve.
You upheld the great principles,
your essence piercing the white sun;
rousing your martial fury,
and deploying divine strategies,
you brought the battle to Guāndù,
and annihilated the vile horde,
enabling our state
to be rescued from peril and ruin.
This was again your achievement.
Crossing the troops over the great river,
you pacified and secured the four provinces;
Yuán Tán and Gāo Gàn
both lost their heads.
Pirates fled in disarray,
and the Hēishān bandits submitted to order.
This was again your achievement.
The three tribes of Wūwán,
creating chaos for two generations,
and Yuán Shàng relying on them,
forcing their occupation north of the frontier—
you bound the horses and suspended the chariots,
and with one campaign destroyed them.
This was again your achievement.
When Liú Biǎo turned treacherous,
failing to offer tribute,
the royal forces set out,
and your awesome might preceded them;
the hundred cities and eight commanderies
joined hands and bent their knees in submission.
This was again your achievement.
Mǎ Chāo and Chéng Yí,
sharing wickedness and aiding each other,
occupied the banks of the Hé and Tóng,
seeking to fulfill their desires.
You annihilated them south of the Wèi,
presenting tens of thousands of severed left ears;
thus securing the border cities,
and pacifying the Róng and Dí tribes.
This was again your achievement.
The Xiānbēi and Dīnglíng,
arriving through multiple translations,
in their felt tents and plain huts,
requested officials and led their duties.
This was again your achievement.
You have the merit of stabilizing the world,
and are further endowed with illustrious virtue.
You bring order throughout the land,
spreading beautiful customs,
extensively applying diligent instruction,
and showing care and caution in criminal cases.
Officials impose no harsh governance,
and the people harbor no wickedness.
You honor and exalt the imperial clan,
supporting and continuing extinguished lines;
old virtues and former merits
are all properly ordered.
Even Yī Yǐn, who reached up to August Heaven,
and Zhōu Gōng, whose light shone across the four seas,
are far inferior when compared to you.
I have heard that the former kings established and promoted those of illustrious virtue,
bestowing upon them lands,
dividing among them the people,
elevating them with honors and insignia,
and preparing for them ritual vessels,
all to protect and guard the royal house,
and to assist it throughout the ages.
In the time of King Chéng of Zhōu,
Guǎn and Cài did not remain peaceful,
so, reflecting on the difficulty and mindful of merit,
he sent Duke Shào Kāng to confer upon Tài Gōng of Qí his domain,
extending east to the sea,
west to the Hé River,
south to Mùlíng,
north to Wúdì,
so that the five ranks of nobles and the nine provincial chiefs,
he could indeed levy and command.
For generations they were enfeoffed as Grand Preceptor,
to represent the Eastern Sea.
Then came King Xiāng,
and again there were the people of Chǔ,
who did not fulfill their royal duties.
He also commanded Duke Wén of Jìn,
elevating him to be the leader of the marquises,
bestowing upon him two grand chariots,
tiger-warriors, axes of authority,
black millet wine, bows and arrows,
greatly opening up Nányáng,
and for generations he served as the leader of the alliance.
Thus, the Zhōu house did not crumble,
relying on these two states.
Now you, my lord, display great and illustrious virtue,
clearly protecting my person,
responding to the Mandate of Heaven,
guiding and promoting grand achievements,
pacifying and loving the nine regions,
with none who do not follow and obey,
your merit is higher than Yī and Zhōu,
yet your reward is lower than Qí and Jìn,
I am deeply ashamed.
I, with my insignificant person,
placed above the myriad people,
constantly think of these difficulties,
as if treading on deep water,
were it not for you to aid me,
I would be incapable.
Now, with the ten commanderies of Jìzhōu: Hédōng, Hénèi, Wèijùn, Zhàoguó, Zhōngshān, Jùlù, Chángshān, Ānpíng, Gānlíng, and Píngyuán,
I enfeoff you as Duke of Wèi,
