and send the Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, the Imperial Secretary Lǜ,
to confer upon you the seal and ribbon, the patent of enfeoffment,
the golden tiger tallies numbers one through five,
the bamboo envoy tallies numbers one through ten,
and bestow upon you the dark earth,
wrapped with white thatch,
to divine with your turtle shell,
for establishing your ancestral altar.
In former times in the Zhōu house,
Dukes Bì and Máo,
served within as ministers and assistants,
while Zhōu and Shào served as preceptors and guardians,
and went out as the two leaders,
the duties both internal and external,
you, my lord, are indeed fit for them.
You shall continue to serve as Chancellor and Governor of Jìzhōu as before.
Now I further bestow the seal of transmission,
solemnly carrying out my command,
to bring harmony to Huáxià,
and you shall return the former seal of Marquis of Wǔpíng.
Now I also confer upon you the Nine Bestowals,
respectfully heed the subsequent command.
Because you have organized the rites and laws,
serving as the model for the people.
Causing them to be secure in their occupations,
without any change of purpose,
therefore I bestow upon you one grand chariot and one war chariot,
and two teams of four black stallions.
Because you encourage division of labor and focus on fundamentals,
diligently guiding the people in their work,
so that grain and silk accumulate without stagnation,
and the great enterprise flourishes,
therefore I bestow upon you the ceremonial robe and crown,
with red ceremonial shoes to match.
Because you uphold and esteem humility and deference,
causing the people to emulate virtuous conduct,
so that young and old are courteous,
and high and low are all harmonious,
therefore I bestow upon you the music of the suspended chimes,
and the dance of six rows.
Because you assist in spreading moral transformation,
reaching out to the four directions,
so that distant peoples turn their faces [towards us],
and Huáxià is filled and substantial,
therefore I bestow upon you a vermilion gate for your residence.
Because you delve into wisdom and clarity,
pondering what even emperors find difficult,
appointing talent and employing the worthy,
so that all good men are certainly raised up,
therefore I bestow upon you a special staircase for your ascent.
Because you hold the balance of the state,
maintaining a stern countenance in the center,
so that even the slightest evil,
is not suppressed and driven away,
therefore I bestow upon you three hundred tiger-warriors.
Because you diligently enforce Heaven's punishments,
making clear those who are guilty,
so that those who violate laws and transgress norms,
are all executed without exception,
therefore I bestow upon you one axe of authority.
Because you soar like a dragon and gaze like a tiger,
surveying the eight directions,
suppressing and punishing rebellious factions,
and repelling enemies across the four seas,
therefore I bestow upon you one vermilion bow,
one hundred vermilion arrows,
ten black bows,
and one thousand black arrows.
Because you take warmth and respect as your foundation,
and filial piety and friendship as your virtue,
being bright, trustworthy, sincere, and earnest,
moving my thoughts,
therefore I bestow upon you one jar of black millet wine,
with a jade ladle to match.
The state of Wèi shall establish a Chancellor and all the various ministers and officials below him,
all according to the system of the various kings in the early Hàn.
Go forth, my lord, and be reverent!
Respectfully obey my command.
Select and care for your multitude,
constantly illuminating all achievements,
to complete your illustrious virtue,
and respond to and extol the glorious mandate of our High Ancestor.
The Empress Xuāndé respectfully inquires of the one in his position:
Merit that lies beyond reward,
thus the ceremonies for ordinary achievements are lacking,
deeds that match the Creator,
then the paths for expressing gratitude are already few.
Yet we must reluctantly create titles for them,
so that the ruler's intent has something to rely upon.
You, Duke, are truly endowed by Heaven with virtue,
sagely, vast, and profound.
Without changing the stars of Shēn and Chén, the nine stars look up to you;
without altering the sun and moon, the two luminaries observe you steadfastly.
In the past, whether in darkness or light,
you concealed your scales and folded your wings.
Widely versed in all texts,
yet yielding precedence to a teacher of a single scroll;
your sword's aura reached the clouds, yet you bent your traces beneath ten thousand men.
You could debate and analyze with heavenly eloquence,
yet seemed as if unable to speak;
your writing excelled at carving dragons,
yet you would always destroy the draft.
In your youth,
you first responded to the summons of bow and banner.
Traveling as a guest in the Liáng court,
your reputation and brilliance were greatly celebrated;
recommended by name to the ministerial office,
your praise and fame rose even higher.
In the late years of Lóngchāng,
your service to the king began to be prominent;
at the renewal of Jiànwǔ,
the establishment of the structure was due to you.
Your merit was lofty, your reward meager,
fine achievements had no equal.
With a field for but one horse,
the resolve of Jiè Shān grew even more stern;
with a salary of six hundred,
the title of the Great Tree remained.
When you held the command and governed the region,
the horses of Dài dared not graze southward;
when you pushed the chariot at Fán and Dèng,
the dust of the Hú rarely rose at dusk.
But that cunning youth,
utterly wicked and extremely cruel,
caused the caps and robes to be utterly destroyed,
and rites and music to collapse and perish.
Then he rallied the troops and swore an oath to the multitude,
speaking of plans to serve the royal house.
With a single wave of the white-feathered command flag,
the Yellow Bird was pacified.
Armor fell like scales,
and chariots shattered like tiles.
He brought down Heaven’s punishment,
bowing in salute to the assembled lords.
His abundant achievements and profound benefits
were such that no virtue could match them.
Thus auspicious light gathered and arrived,
and favorable energies filled the four directions;
the Five Elders roamed the river,
and shooting stars entered the constellation Mǎo.
Such were the greatness of his fundamental merit and the flourish of his accomplishments,
so magnificent as this.
Yet his territory was confined within four marches,
and his influence was humbler than that of the Nine Chiefs.
The Emperor felt ashamed of this,
and so the light carriages gathered here.
Now we dispatch such-and-such rank, so-and-so, and others,
leading these hundred officials,
each to express his sincerity.
It is hoped that the intention of “not on a mat”
will return from no great distance.
Administrative Order:
Now, a flourishing virtue does not perish;
righteousness is preserved in sacrificial rites.
The sigh, “But for Guǎn,”
grows deeper as we reflect on the matter.
Master Zhāng Liáng’s Way was second only to the yellow center;
his brilliance approached that of the near-perfect sage.
Wind and clouds mysteriously responded,
and he flourished as the Emperor’s teacher.
He pacified Xiàng Yǔ and secured Hàn,
greatly rescuing an era of chaos.
Truly he already matched the tracks of Yī and Wàng,
and stood foremost in virtue, akin to benevolence.
As for communing with spirits on the Yí Bridge,
and his Way aligning with Shāng and Luò,
in the realms of the manifest and the hidden,
it is profound and difficult to fathom.
The source and flow are vast and boundless,
impossible to measure their origin.
Passing by old Peì,
we halted our carriage at Liúchéng.
The spirit temple lay in ruins and disrepair,
the remaining images aged and dim.
Reflecting on the past and cherishing the man,
our long sigh is indeed deep.
Those who pass through Dàliáng
may pause in thought at the Yí Gate;
those who wander at Jiǔjīng
also linger in memory of Suí Huì.
Comparing him to such men,
this is indeed fitting to say.
The hall’s beams and framework may be rebuilt,
and the reds and blues restored.
With duckweed, wormwood, and roadside water,
offerings shall be made in due season.
To express the feelings of cherishing antiquity,
and preserve his unalterable heroic deeds.
Let those in charge carry this out.
Administrative Order:
Now, praising the worthy and honoring virtue
grows brighter over a thousand years;
revering the root and honoring the beginning
is a principle exalted from afar.
King Chǔ Yuán accumulated benevolence and founded virtue,
opening this frontier domain;
his pure customs and moral achievements
set a model for later generations.
The blessings of the main and branch lines
indeed flourished in our humble clan;
his lingering fragrance and remaining heroism
inspire through a hundred ages.
Yet his mound is overgrown and obscured,
and the grave site is not tended.
Moved by the distant and mindful of the past,
we sigh with lasting remembrance.
Now, loving the people and cherishing the tree,
even the gāntáng is left untrimmed;
honoring and distinguishing ruins and tombs,
even Xìnlíng may not be forgotten.
How much more for the rise of the melon vines,
whose opening source comes from the root!
Exempt five households near the tomb from service,
to provide perpetual sweeping and cleaning.
This may be carried out.
Question to the Xiùcai, those of high rank and clear understanding of the classics:
We have heard that rulers of divine intelligence and literary thought,
sovereigns of keen wisdom and sagely virtue,
embody the Way yet do not dwell in it,
and upon seeing goodness act as if they cannot catch up.
Thus, at Kōngtóng there was the request to follow the wind,
and at Huáfēng came the bow as if mounting clouds;
some raised banners to seek scholars,
others set up stone gates to await worthies.
Thus they could spread transformation for an age,
leaving heroic deeds for a thousand autumns.
We reverently receive the Mandate of Heaven,
respectfully contemplate the enduring plan,
listen carefully from on high,
and harbor constant reverence and fear.
Although affairs of speech must be recorded by historians,
yet the symbolic tower lacks admonitions;
awake or asleep, we think of excellent counsels,
and stand waiting for loyal and honest men.
You, gentlemen, selected by name and elevated through learning,
employ your talents to serve the king as guests.
Diligently set forth the essentials of the Three Paths,
to glorify the foremost of the Four Disciplines.
The harmony of salt and plum—
our hopes rest upon you.
Further question:
In the past, when King Xuān of Zhōu neglected the ritual of the thousand acres,
Duke Guó offered admonition;
when Emperor Wén of Hàn fell short in the ceremony of three pushes,
Master Jiǎ presented his words.
Truly, because food is the people’s heaven,
and agriculture is the foundation of governance.
Metal walls and boiling water cannot be held without grain;
flood and drought are awaited without shifting.
We illuminate the former classics as a model,
and treasure this sowing and reaping.
When the omens are correct, the blue banners solemnly attend to affairs;
when the soil is rich, the red cords warn according to the canons.
We shall ensure that apricot blossoms and calamus leaves,
plowing and harvesting do not err;
clear furrows and cool breezes,
following and adhering without neglect.
Yet discarding the plow and wearing the ox as ornament,
has been passed down without reversal.
Combining poverty and seizing wealth,
gradually becomes custom.
If we implement the well-field system,
we fear alarming the ignorant people;
if saline land can be made fertile,
we worry the times lack a Shǐ or Bó.
Methods for promoting and abolishing—
present fully your strategies.
Further question:
Deliberating on penalties and deferring executions—
the Great Change deeply prescribes this.
Revering laws and showing compassion in punishments—
the Yú Shū contains abundant canons.
Since customs have become decadent and lax,
laws and ordinances have proliferated.
The stone tablet records few who are not wronged;
the thorny woods hold many ghosts weeping at night.
This is why We stir with emotion at dawn,
and ponder anxiously while forgetting to eat.
Grieved by the dense net of autumn thistles,
pitying the severe authority of summer’s heat.
Ever mindful of the painted headdress,
and distantly recalling the laying aside of punishments.
Yet merely because a light penalty of a hundred huán
was reversed in the latter age;
and the heavy punishment of amputating four limbs
was indeed created in antiquity.
Seeking roaming birds over sheer ravines—
singing “the rooster crows” beneath the palace gate—
praised as benevolent in Hàn’s records.
If these two paths are clear,
then apply them in combination.
Speak forth on what brings peace—
We shall personally examine it.
Another question:
Gathering people requires wealth,
governing affairs relies on goods,
the flow of currency indicates no shortage,
trade and exchange circulate what is present or absent.
Since turtle shells and cowrie coins have long fallen into disuse,
and copper coins have become the sole currency,
generations have multiplied,
yet melting and loss have tripled.
The poor lack even a day’s livelihood,
the middle class lacks resources for successive years.
Only by caring for the afflicted and relieving the hidden,
can one avoid pity and sighing.
The Sovereign on High looks down universally,
bestowing upon me precious treasures,
commanding the valleys of Qióngxié,
to open and yield copper.
Moreover, there is a subsequent decree,
to undertake casting and molding,
filling the capital’s treasury with metal,
continuing the duties of the round mint.
But red-edged coins invite the trouble of clever imitation,
elm-pod coins make it difficult to balance weight and value.
What is appropriate to open or close,
devote your mind to answer.
Another question:
Regulating the calendar and clarifying the seasons,
continues the cycles of change and reform;
amending statutes and rectifying laws,
examines the origins of punishment and virtue.
Appointing officials was evident in the Tang era,
legal provisions shone in the theories of Zōu.
When the Yí region neglected its duties,
and the Mèi Valley deviated from its direction,
the Han dynasty relied on the omen of the plain spirit,
the Wei dynasty spoke of the verification of the yellow star.
Contentious disputes are futilely grieved,
doubtful debates find no resolution.
I have inherited the great foundation,
and wish to expand the supreme Way.
Hoping to make the sun and moon auspicious signs,
wind and rain harmonious as jade candles,
the intent of clarity is not far,
the principle of reverence returns again.
What say you, learned gentlemen?
As for the changing colors of the dark horse and white bird,
the differing establishments of yín and chǒu,
distinguish and write clearly.
Question to the xiùcai:
I hold the tally and rule by Heaven’s mandate,
grasp the pivot and oversee the utmost.
Yet the five time-periods are idly soothed,
the nine sequences remain unsung.
As for contemplating governance in the Bright Terrace,
seeking the Way in the Xuān Chamber,
the sorrow of falling is ever diligent,
the concern for the wounded is constant grief.
Thus I relieve poverty and lighten taxes,
reduce corvée and cautiously handle litigation.
Fortunately, the four borders are untroubled,
the three autumns yield abundant harvests.
Yet with much millet and much rice,
no song of double ears arises;
the sigh of the seventh month must be full.
Is it that governance is not yet excellent,
or that the weary people find it hard to thrive?
Raising you to the court,
is for grand counsel.
Do not fail to unite in heart,
to assist your ruler.
Another question:
The king establishes the state,
regulations appoint officials.
Above, they accord with celestial signs,
below, they match rivers and mountains.
Only when heavenly ranks are fully cultivated,
and human order is all attended to,
then according to talent assign duties,
assessing affairs divide responsibilities.
Thus the five rectifiers set by Zhū Xuān,
the common people do not err;
the nine artisans opened in the Yellow Academy,
all achievements are solidified.
The Zhōu offices numbered three hundred,
the Hàn positions doubled that,
since then onward,
idlers and loafers have indeed multiplied.
If the idle and redundant are all discarded,
then reckless criticism will not cease;
if official caps and tablets are not clarified,
then empty talk will only accumulate.
What then can be cultivated?
Carefully detail your response.
Another question:
In the past, worthy governors divided Shǎn,
good administrators governed together,
even small towns established their customs,
a single village could show achievement.
There were those who strummed the lute by morning,
set out fine wine by day,
cultured yet harmless,
strict yet not cruel.
Thus they could rescue people from perilous situations,
and elevate customs to lands of benevolence and longevity.
Therefore Jiǎ Yì said:
When there is evil in the world,
it is the fault of officials.
Recently, I deeply sifted jade tallies,
wisely selected bronze seals;
yet spring pheasants remain untamed,
autumn locusts do not disperse.
Before me, they gather with clever strategies;
out in the walled cities,
you remain silent and unheard.
Is it that the way of gathering firewood is not yet broad?
Or that the mesh of the net is still too coarse?
Express your thoughts and correct words,
without offending those in office.
Another question:
I have heard that superior wisdom benefits the people,
without adhering rigidly to ritual;
great worthies strengthen the state,
not clinging solely to old ways.
Is it not that relieving hunger does not await cauldron feasts,
saving the drowning does not require measured strokes?
Thus the Three Kings had different ways yet all flourished,
the Five Hegemons had distinct styles yet all stood prominent.
Now farming and warfare are not cultivated,
literary scholars compete instead,
abandoning the root for the trivial,
their ills are many.
In the past, a Sòng minister saw rites and music as harmful,
a Hàn ruler compared writings to Zhèng and Wèi tunes,
did they intend to defy sages and reject laws,
or to adapt the Way with flexibility?
Now I wish to devote men and women to farming and sericulture,
train villages in archery and horsemanship;
restore the five capitals and focus on schools,
enrich the four classes and return to literature.
How should this be done?
Do not merely agree to my face.
Another question:
Since the Jìn dynasty lost its guiding principles,
the passes and rivers were torn asunder,
the Sòng people lost control,
the Huái and Biàn regions collapsed and scattered.
I think of the former people,
and long speak of how to aid them.
Thus I select generals to open frontiers,
comfort and settle them;
moreover, by accepting surrender and fostering harmony,
spreading virtue and cultivating rites,
singing “Huáng Huá” and sending envoys,
composing “Gāo Yǔ” to cherish guests.
Therefore, Guān and Luò stir with longing gazes southward,
the Xūn-yí hasten with thoughts of returning north.
Withered leaves fear the wind,
startled birds easily fall,
without awaiting spears and shields,
merely using debate and persuasion,
a few words to seek the Three Adjuncts,
one discourse to settle the Five Provinces.
By what steps this path?
Who among men might achieve it?
Advance plans and recite your thoughts,
to nourish my heart.
Question to the scholars:
I have driven my forces far into Fán and Dèng,
directly pointing toward the outskirts of Shāng,
relying on the timely opportunity,
riding this turn of fate,
yet as I sit facing the screen in deep thought,
I still feel ashamed of my virtue.
Why is this?
The corruption of a hundred kings,
was most severe in the late Qí dynasty,
where the robes and caps, rites and music,
were swept away without a trace.
Carving away the ornate to restore simplicity,
I have managed affairs in a time of chaos.
Adopting the rites of the Three Kings,
the distinctions between cap and shoe are roughly set;
drawing from the music of the Six Dynasties,
the division of palace modes begins to be discerned.
Yet all regulations are newly established,
and the granaries are not yet full.
If fields remain untaxed to the end,
then state expenses will lack resources;
if the people do not have enough,
then compassion gives rise to deep concern.
Whenever the time comes for submitting hay and straw,
or the annual levy of field rents,
I feel pained and burdened at heart,
as if pitying an infant.
Now I wish to free myself from worries for the whole hall,
and have the people richly supplied for their households,
gradually reaching the积蓄 of nine years,
and step by step removing the taxes at passes and markets.
You, learned gentlemen, face these three issues,
and should serve the king with your usefulness—
from what principles should this proceed?
I await to hear your excellent counsel.
Question:
I originally came from among the scholars,
with aspirations from a young age,
shutting my door to refine myself,
opening books to gain insights alone.
The nine schools and seven summaries,
I have often perused;
the six arts and hundred schools,
I am hardly like one facing a wall.
Though daily affairs are myriad,
with early court and late adjournment,
in spare moments from hearing and reviewing,
I lose none of the three surplus times.
The transformation from above to below,
like grass bending to the wind,
yet in this emptiness and lack,
I am unable to move customs.
In the past, even the lowly purple garments,
changed the customs of Qí;
the crude preference for long tassels,
altered the ways of Zōu.
Though my virtue shames me before past worthies,
my achievements surpass former affairs.
Moreover, the way of the gentry is practiced
because of salaries and benefits.
I yearn for the bones of fine steeds,
not fearing the true dragon;
carriages and official robes,
are like picking up mustard from the ground.
Yet idlers who neglect their duties,
are nine out of ten households;
the singing birds are rarely heard,
and the blue-collared scholars do not arise.
The path of broad encouragement,
is thus already laid out,
yet it remains desolate—
there ought to be good plans.
Question:
I have set up the drum for remonstrance,
and erected the wood for criticism,
for three years now.
Though recently many gather at the palace gate,
most do not address key governance issues;
daily prostrating on the green rushes,
few can be straightforward and direct.
Is it that the late Qí had many taboos,
and that style has since passed away?
Or do they think I vainly admire antiquity,
and empty acceptance is not broad?
Yet since I came to rule over all lands,
standing above the people,
have I ever, for a single word missing the mark,
exiled anyone to the northern frontier,
or for a grudge or slight,
sentenced them to labor in the left camp,
thereby causing upright ministers to shut their mouths,
and the path of loyal counsel to be cut off?
I fear the way of broadening and extending
may have some inadequacy elsewhere.
Express your thoughts fully in stating them,
speak to the utmost without concealment.
Your subject has heard that when the floodwaters spread wildly,
the emperor thought of bringing order,
and sought widely in all directions,
to summon the worthy and outstanding.
In the past, when Shìzōng succeeded to the rule,
wishing to expand the ancestral enterprise,
he consulted on glorious deeds,
and a host of scholars responded and gathered.
Your Majesty, wise and sagely,
continue the foundation laid,
encountering times of hardship,
toiling humbly till the sun slants.
The sacred peaks send down spirits,
and extraordinary men emerge together.
I humbly observe the retired scholar Mí Héng of Píngyuán,
aged twenty-four,
styled Zhèngpíng,
of pure quality, steadfast and bright,
with outstanding talent, lofty and eminent.
First venturing into arts and letters,
he ascends the hall and sees the depths,
what his eyes see once,
he can recite by mouth,
what his ears hear briefly,
he does not forget in heart,
his nature in harmony with the Way,
his thoughts as if inspired by spirits.
The hidden calculations of Sāng Hóngyáng,
the silent memory of Zhāng Ānshì,
measured against Héng,
truly are not strange.
Loyal, resolute, upright, and honest,
his will holds frost and snow,
seeing good as if startled,
hating evil as if an enemy.
Rèn Zuò’s lofty conduct,
Shǐ Yú’s stern integrity,
are hardly surpassed by him.
A hundred birds of prey,
are not equal to one osprey.
If Héng were to stand at court,
there would surely be much to observe.
Soaring in debate, galloping with words,
his overflowing energy surges forth,
untying doubts, loosening knots,
facing opponents with ample skill.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì sought to be tested in a dependent state,
proposing to bind the Chányú by stratagem;
Zhōng Jūn wished with a long tether,
to pull and bring the strong Yuè.
In their youth, passionate and fervent,
praised by former generations.
Recently, Lù Cuì and Yán Xiàng,
were also promoted to court positions for their exceptional talents,
Héng should be compared with them.
If he could leap like a dragon in the heavenly thoroughfare,
spread wings in the Milky Way,
raise his voice in the Purple Tenuity,
shed light like the rainbow,
it would suffice to illuminate the many scholars in the nearby offices,
and enhance the solemn dignity at the four gates.
The vast music of the heavenly balance,
must have wondrous and beautiful sights;
the imperial house, the royal dwelling,
must store extraordinary treasures.
Such as Héng and his like are not easily found.
The stirring Chǔ tune, the Yáng’ē dance,
the most exquisite performances,
are what masters of skill crave;
the flying hare, the swift yǎoniǎo,
supreme in speed, galloping free,
are what fine judges urgently seek.
We, your subjects, in our insignificance,
dare not fail to report this.
Your Majesty is earnest and careful in selecting men,
and must test for effectiveness;
we beg that Héng be summoned in coarse cloth for an audience.
If there is nothing worthy of observation,
we shall bear the crime of deception to your face.
Your subject, Liàng, respectfully states:
The late Emperor founded his enterprise before it was half completed,
and yet midway on the road he passed away.
Now the realm is divided into three parts,
and Yìzhōu is exhausted and weakened.
This is truly a critical moment of survival or extinction.
However, the attending ministers within do not slacken,
and loyal, devoted officers outside sacrifice themselves,
because they remember the late Emperor's exceptional treatment,
and wish to repay it to Your Majesty.
It is truly fitting to open wide Your sagely hearing,
so as to glorify the late Emperor's remaining virtue,
and to expand the spirit of devoted officers.
You should not belittle yourself without reason,
nor use inappropriate analogies,
thereby blocking the path of loyal remonstrance.
The palace and the government offices
are all one body.
Promotions, punishments, praise, and blame
should not differ.
If there are those who commit wickedness or violate the law, or those who are loyal and good,
they should be handed over to the responsible officials,
to determine their punishment or reward,
in order to manifest Your Majesty's fair and enlightened governance.
You should not show partiality or favoritism,
causing the inner and outer courts to have different laws.
Attendant-in-Chief and Gentleman-in-Attendance Guō Yōuzhī, Fèi Yī, Dǒng Yǔn, and others—
these are all good and sincere men,
whose intentions and thoughts are loyal and pure.
Therefore, the late Emperor selected and promoted them to be left for Your Majesty.
I humbly believe that regarding matters in the palace,
no matter how great or small,
all should be consulted with them,
and then implemented.
This will certainly be able to remedy deficiencies and oversights,
and bring about broad benefits.
General Xiàng Chǒng,
is virtuous and fair in nature and conduct,
and thoroughly versed in military affairs.
Having been tested in former times,
the late Emperor praised him as capable.
Therefore, the assembly deliberated and recommended Chǒng as Supervisor.
I humbly believe that regarding matters in the camp,
all should be consulted with him.
This will certainly be able to make the ranks harmonious and orderly,
and ensure that the capable and less capable are appropriately placed.
Drawing close to worthy ministers,
and keeping petty men at a distance—
this is why the Former Hàn flourished and prospered.
Drawing close to petty men,
and keeping worthy scholars at a distance—
this is why the Later Hàn declined and fell.
When the late Emperor was alive,
each time he discussed this matter with me,
he never failed to sigh with regret and bitter resentment over Huán and Líng.
Attendant-in-Chief, Imperial Secretary, Chief Clerk, and Army Advisor—
these are all steadfast, loyal ministers who would die for their integrity.
I hope Your Majesty will draw close to and trust them.
Then the flourishing of the Hàn house
can be awaited by counting the days.
I was originally a commoner,
personally tilling the fields in Nányáng,
merely preserving my life in a chaotic age,
not seeking fame or advancement among the feudal lords.
The late Emperor did not consider me lowly and mean,
but lowered himself and condescended,
thrice visiting me in my thatched hut,
consulting me on the affairs of the time.
Because of this, I was deeply moved,
and thus pledged to the late Emperor to exert myself.
Later, encountering defeat,
I received my assignment at the moment of the army's collapse,
and undertook my mission in a time of crisis and difficulty.
From then until now, twenty-one years have passed.
The late Emperor knew I was cautious and careful,
therefore, on the verge of his passing, he entrusted me with the great task.
Since receiving this command,
I have been anxious and sighing day and night,
fearing that the trust placed in me would not be fulfilled,
and thus damaging the late Emperor's discernment.
Therefore, in the fifth month, I crossed the Lú River,
penetrating deep into the barren lands.
Now the south is already pacified,
and arms and armor are sufficient.
It is time to encourage and lead the three armies,
and pacify the central plains in the north.
I hope to exhaust my mediocre abilities,
to eradicate the wicked and vicious,
to revive and restore the Hàn house,
and return to the old capital.
This is how I repay the late Emperor and fulfill my duty of loyalty to Your Majesty.
As for deliberating on gains and losses,
and presenting all loyal advice,
that is the responsibility of Yōuzhī, Yī, and Yǔn.
I hope Your Majesty will entrust me with the task of punishing the rebels and reviving [the dynasty];
if I am not effective,
then punish my crime,
and report it to the spirit of the late Emperor.
Hold Yōuzhī, Yī, Yǔn, and others accountable for their faults,
to expose their negligence.
Your Majesty should also personally reflect,
to seek out good ways,
examine and accept upright words,
and deeply follow the late Emperor's final edict.
I cannot bear the depth of gratitude I feel!
Now, as I am about to go far away,
facing this memorial, tears fall,
and I know not what I have said.
Your subject, Zhí, respectfully states:
I have heard that a scholar living in the world,
at home serves his father,
and abroad serves his lord.
Serving one's father values bringing honor to the parents;
serving one's lord values revitalizing the state.
Therefore, a loving father cannot cherish a son who brings no benefit;
a benevolent lord cannot retain a minister who is of no use.
Now, to confer office based on virtue—
that is the lord who achieves success;
to receive rank based on measured ability—
that is the minister who fulfills his mission.
Thus, the lord does not confer emptily,
and the minister does not receive emptily.
Empty conferral is called erroneous promotion;
empty receipt is called enjoying emolument without merit.
The Odes' "eating the bread of idleness"
arises from this.
In the past, the two Guó did not decline the responsibility of two states—
their virtue was profound;
Dàn and Shì did not decline the enfeoffments of Yān and Lǔ—
their achievements were great.
Now I have received the state's heavy favor,
for three generations until today.
Right at the time of Your Majesty's peaceful and prosperous reign,
bathing in the sagely grace,
and being subtly moistened by virtuous teachings,
I can be said to be profoundly fortunate.
Yet I occupy a position in the eastern feudatory,
with rank among the highest,
my body clothed in light warmth,
my mouth sated with a hundred flavors,
my eyes beholding extreme splendor and extravagance,
my ears weary of string and bamboo music—
all this is due to the heaviness of my rank and the richness of my emolument.
Reflecting back, I consider those in ancient times who received rank and emolument:
they differed from this,
for all aided the state through meritorious service,
assisting the lord and benefiting the people.
Now I have no virtue to recount,
no achievement to record.
If I continue like this to the end of my years,
bringing no benefit to the state court,
I will incur the satirist's criticism of "that man."
Therefore, above I am ashamed before the dark crown,
and below I am ashamed before the red ribbon.
Now the realm is unified under one rule,
and the Nine Provinces are tranquil and peaceful.
Yet to the west there remains the defiant state of Shǔ,
and to the east, the disloyal kingdom of Wú.
That our borders have not yet been able to lay aside their armor,
and our strategists have not yet been able to rest easy on their pillows,
is truly because we desire to merge all within the four seas into one,
so as to achieve the Great Harmony.
Thus, when Qǐ destroyed the Yǒuhù, the achievements of the Xià became illustrious;
and when King Chéng overcame Shāngyǎn, the virtue of Zhōu became renowned.
Now Your Majesty, with sagely brilliance, rules the age,
and intends to complete the accomplishments of King Wén and King Wǔ,
continuing the prosperity of King Chéng and King Kāng.
Selecting the worthy and appointing the capable,
with ministers like Fāng Shū and Shào Hǔ,
to guard and secure the four frontiers,
serving as the claws and teeth of the state—
this can indeed be called fitting.
However, the reason high-flying birds have not yet been caught by light silk cords,
and deep-dwelling fish have not yet been hooked by bait,
is likely that the techniques of angling and shooting
have not yet been fully exhausted.
In the past, Gěng Yǎn did not wait for Emperor Guāngwǔ,
but urgently attacked Zhāng Bù,
saying he would not leave the bandits for his lord and father.
Thus, the chariot-right drew his sword at the sound of the axle,
and Yōngmén died by his own hand in the territory of Qí.
As for these two men,
did they despise life and esteem death?
Truly, they were angered by the disrespect shown to their lord and the insult to their sovereign.
For a lord's favored minister
seeks to eliminate harm and promote benefit;
a minister's service to his lord
must be to sacrifice his life to quell disorder,
and repay his lord with achievements.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì, while still a young man,
sought to be tested in a dependent state,
asking to bind the neck of the Chányú and control his fate.
Zhōng Jūn, in his splendid youth, was sent to Yuè,
wishing to obtain a long cord to bind their king
and bring him captive to the northern palace gate.
Did these two ministers delight in boasting to their lord and dazzling the common world?
Their aspirations were pent-up,
desiring to display their talents and abilities before an enlightened ruler.
In the past, when Emperor Hànwǔ built a mansion for Huò Qùbìng,
he declined, saying:
"The Xiōngnú are not yet destroyed;
I have no use for a home!"
Truly, to worry for the state and forget one's family,
to sacrifice one's life to aid in crisis—
this is the aspiration of a loyal minister.
Now, residing outside the court, my position is not without honor;
yet I cannot rest peacefully on my mat,
nor taste my food with leisure,
because I brood over the fact that the two regions have not yet been subdued.
I observe that among the military officers and veteran soldiers of the late Martial Emperor,
those who grew old and passed away are known;
though the worthy are not lacking in this age,
the seasoned generals and old troops
are still accustomed to warfare.
I venture, without considering my own limitations,
to aspire to devote my life,
hoping to establish even a hair's-breadth of merit,
to repay the grace I have received.
If Your Majesty were to issue an extraordinary decree,
employing my humble, awl-and-knife-like usefulness,
enabling me to be attached to the Great General in the west,
leading a single company of troops,
or attached to the Grand Marshal in the east,
commanding a flank division's responsibility,
I would surely tread peril and ascend danger,
drive boats and spur horses,
meet blades and touch spearpoints,
leading the way for the officers and men.
Though I may not capture Sūn Quán or behead Zhūgě Liàng,
I hope to capture their leading commanders,
annihilate their vile hordes,
and surely achieve a momentary victory
to extinguish the shame of a lifetime,
so that my name may be recorded in the historian's brush,
and my deeds arrayed among the court's honors.
Even if my body is divided in the territory of Shǔ,
or my head hung at the palace gate of Wú,
it would be as if I were still living.
If my slight talent goes untested,
and I pass from the world unknown,
merely glorifying my body and enriching my form,
alive contributing nothing to affairs,
dead subtracting nothing from the tally,
vainly occupying a high position and disgracing a heavy salary,
living like a bird or beast, gazing idly,
ending with white hair—
this is merely raising creatures in a pen or stable,
not what I aspire to.
Rumors have reached me that the eastern army was caught unprepared,
and the troops suffered a minor setback.
I ceased eating, cast aside my meal,
rolled up my sleeves and tugged my lapels,
grasped my sword and looked eastward,
my heart already racing to Wú and Kuàijī.
In the past, I followed the late Martial Emperor,
reaching south to the Red Bank,
approaching east to the Vast Sea,
gazing west toward the Jade Gate,
and marching north beyond the Dark Pass.
I observed the methods of marching and employing troops,
which could indeed be called divine and marvelous.
Thus, warfare cannot be spoken of in advance;
it is a matter of adapting to changes when facing difficulty.
I aspire to devote myself in this enlightened age,
to achieve merit in this sagely era.
Whenever I peruse historical records,
and observe the loyal ministers and righteous men of old
who gave their lives in a single morning,
sacrificing themselves for the crises of the state—
though their bodies were butchered and torn,
their merits were engraved upon the great bell,
and their names handed down on bamboo and silk—
I have never failed to beat my breast and sigh.
I have heard that an enlightened ruler employs his ministers
without discarding those who have committed offenses.
Thus, the general who fled defeat in battle was employed,
and Qín and Lǔ thereby achieved their merit;
the minister who broke a hat-tassel and stole a horse was pardoned,
and Chǔ and Zhào thereby overcame their crises.
I privately grieve that the late Emperor passed away early,
and King Wēi left this generation.
What manner of man am I alone,
to expect long life?
I often fear I will vanish like the morning dew,
filling the ditches and gullies,
before the grave-mound's earth is dry,
my body and name both perished.
I have heard that when the qíjì neighs long,
Bó Lè recognizes its ability;
when the Lú hound bays mournfully,
Hán Guó knows its talent.
Therefore, they test them on the roads of Qí and Chǔ,
to fulfill the task of a thousand lǐ;
they try them on the swiftness of the cunning hare,
to verify their usefulness in seizing and biting.
Now, I aspire to the slight merit of a dog or horse,
but privately considering and measuring myself,
in the end there is no recommendation from a Bó Lè or Hán Guó.
Thus, I am pained and privately grieve.
Those who stand on tiptoe watching a game of liubo,
or secretly clap upon hearing music—
perhaps there are those who appreciate the sound and understand the way.
In the past, Máo Suì,
a minor retainer of Zhào,
still borrowed the metaphor of the awl in the bag
to awaken his lord and achieve merit.
How much more, in the great court of Wèi with its multitude of scholars,
could there be no ministers fervently willing to die in crisis!
To boast of oneself or act as one's own matchmaker
is an ugly conduct for scholars and women;
to seek advancement by courting the times
is clearly taboo for Daoists.
Yet I dare to present this to Your Majesty
because I truly share form and breath with the state,
sharing its worries and troubles.
I hope that, with the slightness of dust and dew,
I may supplement the mountains and seas;
with the last gleam of firefly and candle,
I may add brightness to the sun and moon.
Therefore, I dare to risk ugliness and offer my loyalty,
fully aware that I will be laughed at by court officials.
A sage ruler does not discard words because of the person.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to lend a divine ear for a moment,
and I would be fortunate indeed.
Your subject Zhí states:
I have heard that Heaven is called lofty
because there is nothing it does not cover;
Earth is called vast
because there is nothing it does not bear;
the sun and moon are called bright
because there is nothing they do not illuminate;
rivers and seas are called great
because there is nothing they do not contain.
Therefore Confucius said:
How great was Yáo as a ruler!
Only Heaven is truly great,
and only Yáo modeled himself upon it.
Now the virtue of Heaven towards the myriad things
may indeed be called broad and vast.
As for Yáo's way of teaching,
he began with the close and then moved to the distant,
proceeding from the near to the far.
The Classic says:
He was able to make illustrious his eminent virtue,
thereby bringing affection to the nine clans.
When the nine clans had become harmonious,
he regulated and distinguished the hundred surnames.
As for King Wén of Zhōu,
he also honored this transformation.
The Ode says:
He set an example for his wife,
extended it to his brothers,
and thereby governed his family and state.
Thus, in harmony and reverence,
the poets sang of him.
In former times, the Duke of Zhōu lamented that Guǎn and Cài were not harmonious,
and broadly enfeoffed his close kin
to serve as a protective screen for the royal house.
The Commentary says:
In the covenant of the Zhōu ancestral temple,
those of different surnames came last.
Truly, the affection of bone and flesh
is clear and yet inseparable;
the principle of loving one's kin
lies indeed in strengthening and solidifying it.
There has never been one who upheld righteousness yet placed his ruler last,
or practiced benevolence yet abandoned his kin.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty inquires into the reverent and enlightened virtue of Emperor Yáo,
embodies the diligent benevolence of King Wén,
extends kindness to the inner chambers,
and makes your grace shine upon the nine grades of kinship.
The various lords and hundred officials
take turns resting and attending.
Governance is not neglected at the public court,
and the feelings of those below can be expressed in private quarters.
The path of familial relations is open,
and the sentiments of congratulations and condolences are expressed.
This may truly be called governing others by putting oneself in their place,
extending kindness and bestowing grace.
As for your subject,
the way of human relations is severed,
restricted and confined in this enlightened age.
I secretly grieve for myself.
I dare not even hope to associate with those of similar spirit,
cultivate human affairs,
or maintain human relationships.
Recently, even marriage connections are blocked,
brothers are forever cut off,
inquiries about good or ill fortune are obstructed,
and the rituals of congratulations and condolences are abandoned.
The violation of bonds of affection
is worse than with strangers;
the barrier of separation
is greater than between Hú and Yuè.
Now, due to the uniform regulations,
I have forever lost hope of attending court.
As for fixing my heart upon the imperial pole,
and binding my feelings to the purple palace gates,
the spirits are aware of it.
Yet if Heaven has truly ordained this,
what can be said!
Reflecting, I know the various kings often have hearts full of kinship sorrow.
I wish Your Majesty would graciously issue a decree,
allowing the various states to offer seasonal greetings,
and the four festivals to be observed,
so as to express the joy and affection of kinship,
and preserve the sincere bond of harmony.
For the families of consorts and concubines,
the gifts of oils and washes,
may be exchanged twice a year,
aligning their righteousness with the noble clans,
and equalizing grace with the hundred offices.
If so,
then what the ancients praised,
and what the Odes and Elegants extolled,
would be restored in this sage age.
I humbly ponder to myself,
could it be that I have not even the use of an awl or knife?
And observing those whom Your Majesty selects and appoints,
if I were of a different surname,
I secretly reckon
I would not be behind the court officials.
If I could relinquish the distant wanderer's cap,
don a military headdress,
remove the red cord,
and wear the blue绶,
serving as an attendant or charioteer,
hastily obtaining a single title,
settling in a residence in the capital,
holding the whip and tucking the brush behind the ear,
going out to follow the imperial canopy,
entering to attend the imperial carriage,
responding to the sage's questions,
picking up omissions for those around,
this would be the utmost desire of my sincere heart,
never leaving my dreams.
From afar, I admire the feast of lord and subject in "The Deer Cry";
in the middle, I recite the admonition of "The Tang Di" about being no stranger;
below, I reflect on the principle of friendship in "Felling the Tree";
and in the end, I harbor the boundless grief of "The Lù É".
Whenever the gatherings of the four festivals occur,
I am left desolate and alone,
with only servants on either side,
facing only my wife and children.
Lofty discourse finds none with whom to share it;
expressed principles find none to whom to unfold them.
Never do I hear music without beating my breast,
or face the wine cup without sighing.
I humbly believe that the sincerity of a dog or horse cannot move men,
just as the sincerity of men cannot move Heaven.
The collapse of walls and the falling of frost—
I once believed in such tales,
but comparing them to my own heart,
they are but empty words.
Like the sunflower's leaves turning,
though the sun does not turn its light back for it,
yet it ever turns towards it—
such is sincerity.
I secretly compare myself to the sunflower.
If there be a bestowal from Heaven and Earth,
a shining down of the light of the three luminaries,
it truly lies with Your Majesty.
I have heard Master Wén say:
Do not be the first to happiness,
nor the first to misfortune.
Now, in this state of obstruction and separation,
brothers share the same sorrow,
yet I alone raise my voice—
why is this?
I secretly cannot bear that in this sage age there should be those who receive no bestowal.
If there are those who receive no bestowal,
they will surely harbor bitter grief.
Thus, in "The Cypress Boat" there is the complaint against Heaven;
in "The Valley Wind" there is the lament of being cast aside.
Yī Yǐn was ashamed that his lord was not like Yáo and Shùn;
Mencius said:
He who does not serve his lord as Shùn served Yáo
does not revere his lord.
In my foolish ignorance,
I am certainly no Yú or Yī.
Yet as for wishing Your Majesty to enhance the beauty of widespread harmony,
and proclaim the virtue of increasing brightness and illustriousness,
this is the earnest sincerity of my humble heart,
which I secretly hold alone.
Truly harboring a heart that stands on tiptoe in crane-like anticipation,
I dare once more to state and make known,
hoping that Your Majesty might perhaps lend your heavenly ear and condescend to listen with divine attention.
Your subject, Hù, states:
Yesterday when I went out,
I humbly heard of the gracious edict,
promoting me to share the same office as the Three Excellencies.
Since I first entered official service,
barely over ten years have passed.
Though entrusted with duties both within and without the court,
and often placed in positions of the utmost prominence and importance,
I have always believed that one cannot forcefully advance by relying on intellect and ability alone,
nor can imperial favor be mistakenly enjoyed for long.
Day and night I have trembled with fear,
regarding honor as a source of anxiety.
I have heard the ancients say:
When one whose virtue is not yet acknowledged by the multitude
receives a high noble rank,
it causes talented ministers to not advance.
When one whose achievements are not yet recognized by the multitude
bears a generous salary,
it causes diligent ministers to lose encouragement.
Now, I myself am reliant on being an imperial relative by marriage,
and my affairs have encountered a fortunate turn of events.
The true danger lies in excessive favor,
not in being overlooked.
Yet, recklessly and abruptly, an edict issued from within the palace has descended,
bestowing upon me an honor beyond proper sequence.
What achievement do I possess that I can bear this?
With what mind can I be at peace with this?
To personally mislead Your Majesty,
dishonor a high position,
and ruin would soon follow thereafter.
To wish to return and guard my ancestors' humble cottage again—
how could that be possible now!
To disobey the command would truly offend the Celestial Majesty;
to reluctantly comply would lead again to such a state.
I have heard that the ancients were earnest in being known for their understanding,
and that the integrity of a great minister
is such that if something is not right, he should desist.
Although I am a man of little worth,
I dare, based on what I have received,
to keep this principle in mind.
Since the realm submitted to transformation under Your rule,
it has only been about eight years.
Although you have leaned from your seat seeking the worthy,
not neglecting the obscure and lowly,
we, your subjects, have been unable to promote those with virtue,
advance those with merit,
so that the Sage Hearing might know that those surpassing me are many,
and those who have not yet reached prominence are not few.
Suppose there were one with untapped virtue beneath the boards of a builder's hut,
or hidden talent among butchers and fishermen,
and yet the court's deliberations used me without considering it wrong,
and I occupied the position without feeling shame—
would not the loss be great indeed!
Moreover, although I have presumptuously held office for a long time,
it has not been like today, sharing the ultimate favor combining civil and military honors,
equal to the high position of a chief minister.
Although my view is narrow,
I note that the present Guanglù Dàfū Lǐ Xǐ,
upholds integrity with lofty purity,
and maintains rectitude at court.
The Guanglù Dàfū Lǔ Zhī,
keeps himself pure with few desires,
harmonious yet not conforming blindly.
The Guanglù Dàfū Lǐ Yìn,
administers affairs with broad simplicity,
and is just and solemn in public matters.
All have served until their hair turned grey,
maintaining ritual propriety from beginning to end.
Although they have experienced favor both within and without,
they are no different from cold and humble households.
Yet they have not yet received this selection,
while I surpass them further.
How can I appease the hopes of the realm,
or add even a little to the sun and moon's glory?
Therefore, I pledge my heart to guard my integrity,
without the ambition for improper advancement.
Now, the roads are not yet clear,
and the border regions face many troubles.
I beg to retain my former favor,
and allow me to quickly return to my garrison.
If not, lingering here,
will certainly lead to shortcomings in external defenses.
I am overwhelmed with worry and fear,
and reverently venture to present this memorial.
I only hope Your Majesty will understand that the will of a common man cannot be taken away.
Your subject, Mì, states:
I, because of misfortune and adversity,
early encountered grief and sorrow.
When I was an infant of six months,
my kind father passed away.
At the age of four,
my maternal uncle forced my mother to remarry.
My grandmother, Liú, took pity on me being orphaned and weak,
and personally nurtured and raised me.
I was often ill in my youth,
and at nine years old still could not walk.
Solitary and suffering,
I grew to adulthood.
I had neither uncles,
nor, in the end, brothers;
my family line declined and fortune was thin,
and I had children late.
Outside, I had no close relatives of the first or second mourning degree,
inside, no pageboy of five feet to answer the door;
alone and isolated,
my body and shadow comforted each other.
And Liú has long been afflicted by illness,
constantly confined to her bed;
I serve her medicine and broth,
and have never neglected or left her.
When I came to serve the Sage Dynasty,
I bathed in its pure influence.
First, the Grand Administrator, your subject Kuí, recommended me as Xiàolián,
later, the Inspector, your subject Róng, recommended me as Xiùcái.
Because I had no one to take care of my grandmother,
I declined and did not obey the summons.
An imperial edict was specially issued,
appointing me as a Lángzhōng,
and soon I received the state's grace,
appointing me as a Xiǎnmǎ.
Unworthily, with my lowly status,
I was to serve in the Eastern Palace—
this was not something I could repay even by dashing my head to the ground.
I fully reported this by memorial,
declining to assume the post.
The edict was stern and severe,
rebuking me for evasion and disrespect.
The commandery and county authorities pressured me,
urging me to set out on the road;
the provincial officials came to my door,
more pressing than sparks from a fire.
I wished to obey the edict and hasten,
but Liú's illness grew daily worse;
I wished to temporarily follow my private feelings,
but my pleas were not permitted.
My position, whether to advance or retreat,
was truly one of狼狈.
I humbly consider that the Sage Dynasty governs the realm with filial piety.
All among the aged,
still receive compassion and care,
how much more so I, solitary and suffering,
whose case is especially extreme.
Moreover, I served in my youth in the illegitimate court,
holding successive posts in the Langshu;
my original aim was official advancement,
not to cherish reputation and integrity.
Now I am a lowly captive from a destroyed state,
extremely insignificant and base.
I have received excessive promotion,
and gracious appointments of generous favor—
how dare I linger hesitantly,
harboring other hopes!
It is only that Liú's life is like the sun setting behind western mountains,
her breath is faint,
her life is precarious and shallow,
not considering the morning when evening comes.
Without my grandmother,
I would not have reached this day;
without me,
my grandmother would have no means to end her remaining years.
Grandmother and grandson, the two of us,
depend on each other for life.
Therefore, with my humble feelings, I cannot abandon her and go far away.
I, Mì, am now forty-four years old,
and my grandmother Liú is now ninety-six.
Thus, the days for me to devote my service to Your Majesty are long,
while the days to repay and care for Liú are short.
With the crow's private feeling of feeding in return,
I beg to be allowed to care for her to the end.
The bitterness and hardship I endure,
are not only clearly seen and known by the gentlemen of Shǔ and the two provincial governors,
but Heaven above and Earth below,
truly together bear witness.
I hope Your Majesty will pity my foolish sincerity,
and grant my humble wish,
so that Liú may, by fortune,
preserve and end her remaining years.
In life, I shall dash my head to the ground [in service],
in death, I shall knot grass [to repay].
I cannot bear the feelings of terror and fear, like a dog or horse,
and reverently present this memorial for your attention.
Your vassal, Lù Jī, states:
On the ninth day of this month,
the Administrator of Wèijùn Commandery dispatched the concurrent Assistant, Zhāng Hán,
bearing the wooden-slip edict, seal, and ribbons,
to provisionally appoint me as Néishǐ of Píngyuán.
I received the appointment with reverence and trepidation,
not knowing how to decide.
Your subject, Jī, kowtows and kowtows again,
guilty of a crime deserving death, guilty of a crime deserving death.
I, your subject, am originally a man of Wú,
hailing from an enemy state,
with no ancestral service of merit to the court,
and talent not distinguished as that of a recluse of integrity.
Yet the imperial grace has spread far and wide,
its beneficence reaching even the most distant,
and I was selected from among the multitude,
repeatedly honored with advancement.
For nine years I served at court,
holding six different offices,
ascended to the three pavilions,
and achieved rank in both palaces.
Clad in ceremonial robes and riding in carriages,
I associated with the noble and privileged;
rising in prominence and distinction,
I surpassed my peers.
The favors bestowed upon me were weighty as mountains,
and my duty should have been to repay them even unto death.
But when the state fell into turmoil,
I had no loyalty to record;
though granted boundless leniency,
how could I, alone, bear the shame?
Bowing my head and kneeling,
I am consumed by worry and remorse.
Yet I was unjustly implicated by the former Prince of Qí, Sīmǎ Jiǒng,
falsely accused of conspiring with others to draft an abdication edict,
imprisoned in the dungeons,
and marked for execution.
In my humble sincerity,
I have never betrayed heaven and earth.
In that moment of crisis,
fearing coercion,
I, along with my brother Lù Yún, the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Yuán Yú,
the Vice Director of the Central Secretariat Féng Xióng,
the Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat Cuī Jī,
the Commandant of Justice Gù Róng,
and the Governor of Rǔyīn Cáo Wǔ,
sought means to escape harm,
secretly maneuvering to avoid danger,
and painstakingly presenting our case.
Not a single word or phrase
connected me to the affair;
the events and handwriting
could all be examined and verified.
Yet in an instant, the situation reversed,
and it was again deemed a crime.
A life as insignificant as mine
is hardly worth sparing,
yet my humble intentions
are truly lamentable.
In fear of the imperial majesty’s pressure,
I accepted the charge with caution,
gagged and silenced,
unable to appeal to my sovereign.
This grave accusation
daily reached the sage ears,
yet the sincerity of my heart’s blood
was never once heard.
Thus, in facing adversity with fervor, I cannot but feel regret—
for this reason alone.
Now, graced again by Your Majesty’s compassionate pardon,
the frost recedes and lightning withdraws,
sparing me from ruin.
Once more, I can support the aged and guide the young,
emerging alive from the prison gates,
bearing gold and purple robes,
to retire among the common ranks.
Grateful yet remorseful,
my five emotions tremble with sorrow;
crouching under heaven and treading carefully on earth,
I feel as if there is no place for me.
I never imagined that the bright sun and moon
would deign to shine upon me,
or that the nurturing rain
would extend to this withered and ailing one.
Overlooking my feeble talent,
and that there is nothing commendable in my person,
pitying my desolation,
and considering that my crime may be examined.
If only the crimson record could be erased,
allowing me to return to commoner status,
then the dust would be washed from the heavenly waves,
and slander would cease from all mouths.
Such was my initial hope,
not daring to aspire further.
Yet I am undeservedly honored with a great mandate,
openly bestowed with tally and tiger seal,
causing withered spring branches
to once more share fragrance with autumn orchids;
and a sunken feather
to again soar with flying swans.
Though Ān Guó was spared from penal servitude
and rose to wear the blue绶带;
and Zhāng Chǎng, a fugitive,
was seated in a vermilion carriage—
compared to what I now bear,
their cases are not as grand.
How can one stained and shamed as I am presume to accept this?
Not even the destruction of my clan could repay such grace.
Joy and fear intermingle,
grief and shame choke my voice.
Bound by constant statutes,
I must take office along the way,
unable to hasten in person,
to kowtow at the palace gates.
Gazing toward the imperial road,
my heart races to the royal carriage,
overwhelmed with trepidation and longing.
Respectfully, I submit this memorial for Your Majesty’s attention.
On the eighteenth day Xīnchǒu, the first day of the third month being Guǐwèi, in the fifth year of the Jiànxīng era [317 AD],
the Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in the three provinces of Héběi, Bìng, and Yōu,
Concurrent Protector General, Commandant of the Xiōngnú,
Minister of Works,
Governor of Bìng Province,
Marquis of Guǎngwǔ, your subject Lǐu Kūn;
the Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Palace Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Jì Province,
General Who Pacifies the Army,
Governor of Jì Province,
Left Worthy Prince,
Duke of Bóhǎi, your subject Duàn Píngdī,
kowtow in mortal fear to present this memorial.
Your subjects Lǐu Kūn and Duàn Píngdī kowtow repeatedly,
in mortal fear, mortal fear.
We your subjects have heard that heaven gives birth to the multitudes
and establishes a ruler over them,
so that he may respond to heaven and earth
and shepherd the common people.
The sage emperors and enlightened kings, recognizing this,
knew that heaven and earth must not lack sacrifices,
thus humbling themselves to serve them;
knowing the people cannot be without a lord,
they reluctantly assumed governance.
When the altars of state face crisis,
the loyal kinsmen stabilize the toppling;
when the ancestral temples are neglected,
the wise among the lineage restore the sacrifices.
Thus, the distant traditions are broadly upheld,
securing the ten thousand generations.
Since the times of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
none have deviated from this path.
Your servants Kūn and Dī kowtow and kowtow again,
deserving death, deserving death.
We humbly consider that the High Ancestor, Emperor Xuān, initiated the foundation in response to the Mandate,
and the World Ancestor, Emperor Wǔ, subsequently established the realm of Xià.
Three generations shone with double brilliance,
four sages continued the tracks.
Their benevolent grace equaled that of Yǒuyú,
and their divined years surpassed those of the Zhōu house.
Since the Yuánkāng era,
calamities and disasters have frequently arisen.
During the Yǒngjiā period,
the baleful atmosphere grew ever darker.
The imperial throne lost its control,
and the emperor passed away among the vile tribes.
The peril of the state
was like dangling tassels.
Relying on the virtue of the former emperors
and the spirits of the ancestral temple,
the emperor succeeded and was established,
and the old heritage was able to be distinguished.
He was endowed with reverence and wisdom,
embraced intelligence and sagacity.
His jade-like quality was evident from childhood,
his golden sound resonated early.
The chief minister managed the guiding principles,
and the hundred officials assisted in governance.
All within the four seas longed for the beauty of restoration,
and the multitude cherished the hope of revival.
Unexpectedly, Heaven did not repent of the calamity,
and great disasters repeatedly arrived.
Before the state could forget its difficulties,
enemy harms soon arose again.
The rebellious Hú Liú Yào,
ran rampant in the western capital,
daring to unleash his dog-and-sheep-like forces,
to insult and oppress the heavenly city.
We, your servants, having presented memorials and returned from missions,
still relied on the western court.
But in the eleventh month of last year, it could not be defended,
our sovereign was seized and held captive,
sinking once more into the captors' court.
The sacred vessels were scattered and lost,
again disgraced by the wild rebels.
Whenever we, your servants, peruse historical records
and observe past accounts,
such extremity of adversity,
from ancient times to the present, has never existed.
Even those who partake of the land's produce,
all breathing creatures,
none do not beat their breasts in despair,
wailing in the streets and crying in the lanes.
How much more so we, your servants, who have received favor for three generations,
holding positions among the highest offices,
upon hearing the news, trembled with shock,
our spirits flew away,
both grieving and lamenting,
our five emotions without anchor,
raising lamentations in the northern borders,
from high to low, weeping tears of blood.
Your servants Kūn and Dī kowtow and kowtow again,
deserving death, deserving death.
We, your servants, have heard that obscurity and brightness alternate in use,
adversity and prosperity mutually aid each other.
The Mandate of Heaven has not changed,
the succession of epochs has its proper return.
Sometimes many difficulties serve to solidify the state,
sometimes deep worries give rise to sagely wisdom.
Qí had the disaster of Wúzhī,
yet Xiǎo Bái became the chief of the Five Hegemons;
Jìn had the calamity of Lí Jī,
yet Chóng'ěr presided over the alliance of the feudal lords.
When the altars of soil and grain are not at peace,
there must be someone to support them in their peril;
when the black-haired people are nearly extinguished,
there must be someone to continue their lineage.
We humbly consider that Your Majesty's profound virtue connects with the divine spirits,
and Your sage bearing aligns with the dual forces of heaven and earth.
You respond to the time of a generation's renewal,
inheriting the fortune of a thousand years.
The signs of auspicious tokens,
the correspondence between Heaven and man, are evident.
The omens of restoration,
are recorded in charts and prophecies.
Since the capital fell and was lost,
the nine regions collapsed and scattered,
the world was in clamorous chaos with nowhere to turn,
even compared to Xià encountering Yí Yì,
or the royal Jī clan facing the Quǎnróng,
it could not surpass this.
Your Majesty pacified and settled Jiāngzuǒ,
encompassing the ancient Wú territory.
You gently subdue with virtue,
punish rebellion with penalties,
uphold bright authority to overawe the unruly,
wield great accord to bring order to the world.
Once pure transformation is spread,
then all within the realm will settle their hearts;
once the righteous wind flows freely,
then distant regions will stand on tiptoe in anticipation.
All affairs are timely arranged above,
and the four gates are reverent below.
In the past, the prosperity of Shào Kāng,
the Xià teachings considered a beautiful tale;
the rise of King Xuān,
the Zhōu odes celebrated as fine songs.
How much more so Your Majesty's abundant merits reaching to August Heaven,
and clear radiance shining upon the four seas,
the common people gaze expectantly,
none not rejoicing and supporting.
Wherever Your voice and teachings reach,
they wish to become Your subjects and servants!
Moreover, of the descendants of Emperor Xuān,
only Your Majesty remains,
to whom the millions turn,
truly without a second.
Heaven's blessing upon Great Jìn,
must have a lord,
and the one to preside over Jìn's sacrifices,
if not Your Majesty, then who?
Therefore, near there are no dissenting words,
far there are no divergent hopes.
Those who sing praises all chant of Your splendid plans,
those involved in lawsuits all think of Your sage virtue.
The junction between Heaven and Earth is already connected,
the sentiments of Huá and Yì peoples are truly harmonious.
The unicorn beast,
the interlocking trees,
taken as auspicious signs,
number nearly a hundred;
the cap-and-gentry class,
the masses of distant borders,
without consultation speak in unison,
their numbers reaching tens of thousands.
Therefore, we, your servants, dare to examine the heart of Heaven and Earth,
follow the inclination of all Xià,
and risk death to present the honorable title.
We hope Your Majesty will preserve the utterly impartial sentiment of Shùn and Yǔ,
narrow the stubborn integrity of Cháo Fú and Xǔ Yóu,
take the altars of soil and grain as Your task,
not prioritizing minor conduct,
be concerned for the black-haired people,
not making refusal Your affair.
Above, to console the caring heart of the ancestral temple,
below, to relieve the hopes of all under heaven who look up with bowed heads.
Then it may be said: generating luxuriant blossoms from withered sprouts,
nurturing plump flesh from decayed bones,
spirits and men will gain peace,

Your subjects Kūn and Dī kowtow and kowtow again,

We have heard that the exalted throne cannot remain vacant for long,

If left vacant for a single day,
then the exalted throne will be endangered;
if left unattended for twelve days,
then the myriad affairs will fall into chaos.
Now is the end of a hundred kings’ reigns,
a time of calamitous convergence,
with cunning enemies watching and scheming,
awaiting flaws and gaps in the state,
and the people of Qí restless and turbulent,
with nothing to anchor their hearts.
How can we then neglect and not attend to this!
Even if Your Majesty wishes to hesitate and delay,
what will become of the ancestral temples,
what will become of the common people!
In the past, when Duke Huì was captured by Qín,
the state of Jìn was shaken with terror.
Through the plans of Lǚ and Xì,
they sought to establish Zǐ Yǔ.
Externally, to cut off the enemy’s ambitions,
and internally, to stabilize the sentiments of the entire realm.
Thus it is said, “When a ruler is lost, there is another ruler.”
The ministers were harmonious and respectful,

Not forgetting the affairs of the past
is the great model for later generations.
Your Majesty’s brilliance equals the sun and moon,

Unable to contain our canine and equine anxiety for the state,

We, your subjects, each undeservedly hold regional responsibilities,

We have heard that Chéng Tāng overthrew Xià yet enfeoffed Qǐ,

We humbly consider that the great Jìn responds to Heaven and accords with the people,

We have heard that spring rain moistens trees,

Thus Heaven is called the boundless grace,
and sages have the thoughtful and thorough beneficence.
Recalling the martial and fierce emperor of the false Wú,

King Huán, talented and martial,

Although his great merit was not completed,

The family accumulated the foundation of righteousness and courage,

Thus, citing their labors, their strength was given to former times;

If placed among the numbers of former worthies,
receiving the grace of the decree,
judiciously adding distinguished recognition,
to honor the departed spirits,

who would not say it is fitting?
The two lords’ private slaves
were mostly beside the tombs;
now they are commoners.
We beg to assign five people,
exempt them from corvée labor,
so they may repair the collapses and ruins throughout the seasons,

Your subject Liàng states:
Your subject is ordinary, stubborn, and shallow,
with little restraint or conduct in youth.
In the past, due to many troubles in the central provinces,

I followed and attended my late father,

I did not realize the fortune of encountering the times,

The late emperor rose like a dragon,

In youth, I rinsed my cap strings,
bathed in the profound teachings,
frequently attended the palace gates,

Over ten-plus years,
my rank surpassed earlier achievers;
without merit, I received such treatment—
none compares to your subject.
A petty person with meager salary,

the portion of knowing when to stop,

Yet I stole glory, blindly advanced,

I first wished to report myself,

Your Majesty has ascended the throne,

The ministers and advisors are wise and enlightened,

The song of prosperity

I, to Your Majesty,

The suspicion arising from marital ties

Although the utmost impartiality of the sovereign

Throughout the vast realm,

Thus, in both the Former and Later Hàn dynasties,

If the seven clans of the Western Capital

Their complete ruin
was precisely due to marital intimacy.
I have observed that commoners in the world,
without factions at court
or support in their time,
have shallow and weak roots;
they are light and thin.
If they have no major flaws,
they may still be tolerated.
But as for the imperial relatives by marriage,
they rely on the support of heaven and earth,
their influence connects with the four seasons,
their roots and branches are widespread,
they are weighty and great.
Yet, occupying positions of power and favor,
they are viewed with suspicion by all under heaven.
If their actions are not just,
their crimes cannot be pardoned even by death.
Not only do they bring calamity upon themselves,
but the state also suffers harm because of them.
What is the reason for this?
Simply because the private nature of marital ties
is something human sentiments cannot avoid,
so the suspicions they arouse are projected onto the state.
Thus, those who are distant are trusted,
while those advanced through marriage are doubted.
When doubt accumulates in the hearts of the people,
disaster brews within the palace walls.
These are all clear lessons from past dynasties,

In matters where the principles of all things do not align,
the sages and worthies do not force them.
To risk suspicion for the sake of employing a single talent

Now, with my limited ability

to invite disaster in this way

As for wealth, honor, and favor,

Now, obeying the command brings more suffering,

Although I am not enlightened,

Truly, I look up to the lessons of the past,

My own life is not worth cherishing,

Thus, with utmost sincerity, I have repeatedly stated my heartfelt feelings,

Anxious and fearful, I am at a loss,

I have heard that when the Great Simplicity is lost,

I humbly consider that the Great Jìn,
responding to the mandate and ruling the world,

Your Majesty, with your sage virtue, has risen to continue the line,

In the past, I served on a mission

Fate repeatedly summoned him with misfortune,

I have heard that when great waves shake the valleys,

brushing off my robes and withdrawing in lofty refusal.

Both name and righteousness were thereby lost,

I deserve the severest punishment,

The General Who Guards the Army, your subject Yù,

At that time, the imperial carriage was obstructed,

Now that the imperial pivot has returned to correctness,

Your subject humbly reflects:
since the founding of the Yìxī reign,
hardships and perils have not ceased;
external worries were already pressing,

I, with my meager and inferior abilities,

whether on campaign abroad or assisting within,
fortunately, he did not disgrace his mission.
Without this man's support and assistance,

He trod the path of humility and dwelt in scantiness,

I deem it fitting to add a posthumous grant of a full ministerial office,

Your subject, through shared hardships in both peril and peace,
looking back over the beginning and end,
the bond of metal and orchid,

What is presented above,

The earnest sincerity of Jùpíng will surely stand firm,

If it is said to be easily clear,
I dare hold to what is difficult to seize.
Therefore, one can broaden discussion to satisfy the multitude,
and measure oneself against others.
Unable to bear the sincerity of my fearful trepidation,

Your subject [personal name withheld] is truly awed and apprehensive.
