with mud on my head still upon my face,
and the carriage for my coffin not yet destroyed—
to have participated in founding the state in its rudimentary beginnings,
dare I claim Heaven's achievement?
Legal cases, lawsuits, songs and praises—
show the people shared purpose.
Yet noble vessels and great fame
are gathered upon me in a single morning.
Looking at myself and turning inward,
how have I reached this?
It would be proper only to connect with the White Waters,
and arrange dwellings in old Fēng,
forgetting the fault of abandoning lectures,
preserving the expenses of the various lords,
stooping to pick up the blue and purple ribbons—
must one wait to understand the classics?
Your subject Yún bows his head repeatedly,
worthy of death, worthy of death.
Now, the importance of assessing and balancing
concerns the rise and fall of the state.
Looking distantly to the principle of discerning the wise,
even for an emperor it is difficult.
Since Hàn and Wèi onward,
men of penetrating insight have followed the tracks,
but those to whom the refined and the vulgar turned,
were only called Xǔ and Guō.
Selecting ten to obtain five,
was still said to be shoulder to shoulder.
As for the rest, their successes and failures are unheard of;
occasionally observing children and youths,
whose natural wit momentarily shines forth—
looking back, none are worth counting.
In Wèi, there was Máo Jiè, just and principled;
in Jìn, there was Shān Tāo, with discerning judgment.
Comparing your subject to them,
how vastly inferior I am!
In the declining years of Qí,
official norms were confused and disordered.
The Hóngdū Academy lacked discipline,
the Western Garden became a market.
There was talk of golden seals filling bamboo boxes,
and deep sighs of insufficiency over sable-tail hats.
Now in the initial stage of creation,
the principle lies in reform and action.
You, reverent, face south as ruler,
and the responsibility for accomplishment rests here.
How can one recklessly bestow private favor,
to the detriment of the king's affairs?
The adornment of cicada pins
would merely become empty marks of favor.
Seeking it from both public and private perspectives,
both giving and receiving are mistaken.
In recent times, those who have been enfeoffed as marquises
have achieved merits of varying degrees:
some ensured ample provisions in Guānzhōng,
some formed armies in Hénèi,
some secured victory from within the command tent,
some drew their disciples closer through kinship,
some rose and fell with the times,
some stood firm as formidable as an enemy state,
some devised strategies within the palace,
some accomplished feats in open battle,
some possessed abundant virtue like Zhuó Mào,
some upheld the teacher's way like Huán Róng,
some, from the four surnames, attended the sacrifices,
but these are no longer worth recording.
As for the five marquises who were imperial relatives by marriage,
they did not follow the old statutes.
Yet the reason for my own enfeoffment
lies solely in imperial favor.
Since this differs in principle from rewarding merit,
it truly brings honor unbecoming of a Confucian scholar.
Although a petty man may covet such fortune,
how could I alone be without a conscience?
I originally came from among the scholars,
my family upholding a plain vocation.
Our gate knew no wealth or nobility;
I merely shifted from farming to official service.
My late grandfather Xuánpíng
possessed a Daoist demeanor that stood out in his generation.
During the Restoration era,
he served as a model for many gentlemen,
yet his rank only reached that of Yuán and Kǎi,
and his post was merely that of a regional governor.
My great-grandfather Shǎolián
early on embraced lofty ideals;
what he possessed in abundance was righteousness,
what he lacked was opportunity.
He held a minor post in the eastern court,
then resigned due to illness in a humble county.
Not forgetting these ancestral aspirations,
I, your foolish servant, strive to follow them.
Moreover, last winter,
I was merely an old erudite of the National Academy.
Now, at the beginning of this summer,
I am to become second only to the high ministers.
Even if Qiānqiū was promoted nine times in a single day,
or Xún Shuǎng reached high office from afar within a hundred days,
compared to your humble servant,
my advancement is not considered rapid.
Though I lack discernment,
I do consider gain and loss.
As for damaging my reputation and compromising integrity,
whether for the state or for myself,
knowing it cannot be done,
I dare not recklessly presume.
Your Majesty does not discard coarse grasses,
but cherishes them like silk and hemp.
If the words I have spoken in my lifetime
still reach Your Majesty's ears and consideration,
and my long-held heart and simple aspirations
allow no room for a second reply,
then, taking pity on my plea,
specially retract this gracious command,
so that the constant statutes may remain solemn,
and this insignificant person may know reprieve.
I am currently on leave,
and cannot come to the ministry in person.
Overwhelmed by fear and trepidation,
I respectfully present this memorial for Your Majesty's attention.
Your servant Yún, with sincere trepidation and so forth.
Your servant states:
I have heard that seeking the worthy entails temporary toil,
but leaning on one's staff brings eternal ease;
likening it to dredging soil,
it resembles channeling rivers.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty's Dao is concealed behind the imperial beads and tassels,
yet trust fills the seals and tallies.
The six steeds tread the same dust,
and five declines elevate the age.
White colts are in empty valleys,
egrets with flapping wings are in the court;
yet still there is fear that hidden scales may be among diviners,
and concealed vessels among butchers and keepers.
Seeking talents at the palace gate,
entrusting robes by the river,
is not to take a rule from a single fox,
but truly to seek flavor through gathering widely.
When the five notes weary of their sounds,
the nine artisans are consulted;
deliberations rest in the ancestral temple hall,
yet listening extends to the carriage drivers and servants.
My position and duties are weighty,
encompassing duty to both family and state.
I truly wish to see that name and reality do not diverge,
and the path of opportunism is cut off.
For powerful families and upper ranks,
they should still be measured by pure discourse;
for the talented among lower officials,
they must not be limited by rank or appearance.
I have privately observed the Secretariat Assistant Lángyà, your servant Wáng Jiǎn,
aged twenty-one,
courtesy name Sīhuì.
Seven generations have shone with successive glory,
making him a leader among the cap-and-gown elite of the realm.
His spirit is clear, his vitality abundant,
truly embodying the harmonious mean.
With Shūbǎo's discourse on principle and detachment,
and Yǎnfǔ's joy in reputation and teaching,
he thus illuminates the paths of former worthies,
and leads those who come after.
His dwelling is free of worldly clutter,
his home possesses bestowed books.
His rhapsodies and poems are fresh and pure,
his words touch upon the profound and distant.
His chamber is near, yet the man is expansive;
objects are distant, but the Dao is intimate.
Nourishing simplicity in garden hills,
while the steps of the court stand empty.
In the schools and the public court,
ten thousand men turn their gaze in hope.
How could it be merely that one might think of the worthy Xún,
or that Lord Lǐ is not forgotten!
Formerly, the Magistrate of Hòuguān in Jìn'ān Commandery, Dōnghǎi's Wáng Sēngrú,
aged thirty-five,
courtesy name Sēngrú,
his principles tend toward seclusion and simplicity,
his thoughts achieve tranquility and acuity.
He plowed with his brush to support himself,
and also served as a copyist to complete his studies.
He even gathered fireflies and reflected snowlight,
wove palm leaves and bound willow strips.
The words and deeds of the ancients,
the characters and customs of people,
the remaining rituals of Gānquán,
the old affairs of the Southern Palace,
he could draw them on the ground to form a map,
or clap his hands and narrate them.
How could it be merely that he had the ready debate of the flying squirrel,
or that the bamboo texts contained no error of missing strips?
Jiǎn sits and stabilizes the refined and the common,
his broad benefits are already many;
Sēngrú inquires and responds without cease,
his questioning and doubts lie herein.
Both are secret treasures of the Eastern Hall,
splendid vessels like ritual goblets.
Truly, words may be discarded because of the person,
but talent is truly the resource of the age.
Facing this memorial, I tremble with fear,
still apprehensive it may not meet approval.
I cannot bear my humble feelings, and so forth.
Your servant Zhēn states:
Yesterday I received a command from the Minister over the Masses,
upholding and citing an imperial decree,
granting the request of my elder brother Bēn,
that I should inherit the enfeoffment as Duke of Nánkāng Commandery.
My family's register derives from meritorious inheritance,
gloriously bestowed with land and domain.
My brother Bēn, generation after generation upholding the family,
truly embodies enduring virtue.
Yet with deep insight into knowing when to stop,
he cast off the sandals of a ruler of a thousand chariots.
Thus, from afar he mistakenly extended favor,
drawing near to gather upon my mediocrity and shallowness.
To be able to yield the state,
shows great righteousness has a home.
A common man's will is hard to change,
he holds to it without wavering.
In the past, Wǔshǐ was compelled by his steward's plan,
Língyáng was moved by Bào Shēng's words.
Zhāng made a sincere request,
Dīng was overcome by reason.
Moreover, my late father, because the main lineage was cut off,
commanded me to leave and continue the collateral line.
I received this charge in the past,
a principle severed as if by heaven's end.
Forever pondering these circumstances,
my eyes meet them and my heart collapses.
If Bēn were to exalt the style of Yánlíng,
and I were to forget the integrity of Zǐzāng,
this would be to abandon virtuous conduct;
could it be called worthy?
May Your Majesty examine my sincere heart,
and specially grant a halt and cessation.
If not,
I shall cast myself into the wilds and marshes,
merely to follow my foolish sincerity.
Unable to bear the utmost sincerity of my crimson heart,
I respectfully approach the palace gate to present this memorial for Your Majesty's attention.
Your servant, with sincere trepidation and fear, and so forth.
Your subject Yún states:
It is fundamental that to preserve one's exemplary conduct,
and to manifest illustrious achievements after death,
since the accounts of the elders will cease,
one must rely on enduring writings.
Yet if stored in famed mountains,
then hills and valleys may shift and change;
if kept in palace archives,
then bamboo slips may scatter and be lost.
Thus, the traces matching Heaven
are preserved above the Sìshuǐ River;
the Way of the Uncrowned King
is recorded beside the Yíchuān River.
Hence, the principle of honoring teachers
is modeled on Xīhé;
the sentiment of revering the sovereign
is extended to Yáo and Yǔ.
Therefore, when a humble academy is presumptuously established,
it must exhaust the splendor of carving inscriptions;
when a ruler governs a single city,
he also fulfills the beauty of engraving records.
How much more so for those who molded Zhōu and Shào,
and nurtured Yī and Yán?
Thus, the Grand Steward, Prince Wénxuān of Jìnglíng, your subject so-and-so,
in life and death,
embodied righteousness as the guardian of the altars of soil and grain;
in solemnly matching Heaven and pairing with the Emperor,
he was a man like the Duke of Zhōu.
In governing the state and rectifying the court,
serving abroad as a feudal lord and at home as a guardian,
in advancement he contemplated the way of always reporting,
in retreat he avoided the selfishness of seeking personal gain,
the five teachings were ordered,
and all affairs were timely arranged.
As for his every word and deed,
the aura of great virtue;
his mastery of zither, calligraphy, and arts,
the abundance of his writings and compositions—
if the Way did not extend to universal benefit,
and his deeds were merely for the joy of goodness,
still, there would be nothing inadequate to praise.
Now that he is gone,
suddenly the seasons have shifted;
the owls have flown east,
and pines and catalpas stand in rows.
The officials of the six ministries,
the men and women of the three fiefs,
each holding oiled silk,
each household treasuring writing brushes,
gaze at that lofty mountain,
only to yearn in vain.
In the past, when the Jìn dynasty first prohibited the erection of steles,
upon the death of Wèi Shū,
it was still permitted according to rank.
And though Ruǎn Lüè had already passed,
his family risked severe punishment by taking the lead,
yet those who acted were ultimately spared punishment,
and those who initiated it instead received praise.
As for one whose virtue reached such benevolence,
whose achievements matched the subtlety of Guǎnzhòng,
he truly deserved to be beyond ordinary measures.
Thus, for Grand Steward Yuān
and Chancellor Yì,
who were both close kin and worthies,
it became an established precedent.
I beg to follow the previous examples of these two lords,
and request permission to engrave and erect a stele.
How can we allow long yearning for the Nine Plains,
while gatherers of firewood remain unaware of the prohibition;
or halting the carriage at Chánglíng,
with envoys' carriages not knowing where to proceed?
Your subject, lowly and insignificant from the village lanes,
with no talent worth selecting,
encountered the broad net of the Qí dynasty,
which relaxed the restrictions on guests,
and having enrolled my name and offered my service,
suddenly two decades have passed.
Fearing I may die before the dogs and horses,
I cannot repay such deep grace.
And though my worn curtains and ruined canopies
are not yet bedding for ants;
pearl-sewn robes and jade caskets
already adorn the dark springs.
Your Majesty greatly encourages reputation and teachings,
not excluding even the humblest things,
allowing your subject to rush to the southern shore,
and wail long at the northern mound.
Having already received your previous generosity,
I truly hope for further kindness.
If Dù Yù's words on the mountaintop are verified,
perhaps the sentiment of Mǎ Jùn's inevitable bowing may be preserved.
Facing this memorial with grief and fear,
words cannot fully express it.
Your subject, in sincere trepidation and below.
Your subject has heard of the officials' proposal to expel guests,
and privately considers it mistaken.
In the past, Duke Mù sought men of talent,
taking Yóu Yú from the west among the Róng,
obtaining Bǎilǐ Xī in the east from Wǎn,
welcoming Jiǎn Shū from Sòng,
and attracting Pí Bào and Gōngsūn Zhī from Jìn.
These five men,
were not born in Qín,
yet Duke Mù employed them,
annexed thirty states,
and thus dominated the western Róng.
Duke Xiào employed the laws of Shāng Yāng,
transforming customs and practices,
so the people became prosperous,
and the state grew rich and strong,
the common people gladly served,
the feudal lords submitted closely,
captured the armies of Chǔ and Wèi,
seized a thousand lǐ of territory,
and remains well-governed and strong to this day.
King Huì employed the strategies of Zhāng Yí,
seized the lands of Sānchuān,
annexed Bā and Shǔ in the west,
took Shàngjùn in the north,
captured Hànzhōng in the south,
enveloped the nine Yí tribes,
controlled Yānyǐng,
occupied the strategic Chénggāo in the east,
carved out fertile lands,
thus dissolving the alliance of the six states,
making them serve Qín facing west,
and his achievements extend to the present.
King Zhāo obtained Fàn Jū,
dismissed the Marquis of Ráng,
expelled Huáyáng,
strengthened the royal house,
blocked private factions,
gradually encroached upon the feudal lords,
and enabled Qín to achieve imperial enterprise.
These four rulers,
all succeeded through the efforts of guests.
From this perspective,
how have guests failed Qín!
Had these four rulers rejected guests and refused to admit them,
distanced scholars and not employed them,
the state would lack the reality of wealth and benefit,
and Qín would not have the name of greatness and strength.
Now Your Majesty acquires jade from Kūnlún Mountain,
possesses the treasures of Héshì and Suíhóu,
hangs bright moon pearls,
wears the Tài'ē sword,
rides the Xiānlí horses,
raises banners of kingfisher feathers,
and sets up drums made of divine crocodile skin.
Among these several treasures,
not a single one is produced in Qín,
yet Your Majesty delights in them.
Why is this?
If only what is produced in Qín is acceptable,
then night-shining jade disks would not adorn the court,
rhinoceros and ivory objects would not serve as curios,
women from Zhào and Wèi would not fill the rear chambers,
fine steeds like Juétí would not stock the outer stables,
gold and tin from Jiāngnán would not be used,
and cinnabar and azurite from Xīshǔ would not supply pigments.
What adorns the rear chambers,
fills the lower ranks,
pleases the heart and mind,
and delights the eyes and ears—
if it must come from Qín to be acceptable,
then hairpins with Wǎn pearls,
earrings with attached beads,
robes of Ā-gauze,
ornaments of brocade and embroidery,
would not be presented before you;
and those elegant and refined with the times,
beautiful and graceful,
women of Zhào would not stand by your side.
Now, striking earthen jars and beating clay pots,
plucking the zhēng and slapping thighs,
while singing and shouting "wūwū" to please the ear—
this is truly the music of Qín;
the melodies of Zhèng and Wèi, the songs of Sāngjiān,
the Sháoyú and Wǔxiàng—
these are the music of other states.
Yet now, abandoning the beating of pots and jars for Zhèng and Wèi,
setting aside the zhēng for Sháoyú—
why is this so?
Simply because it brings pleasure in the moment,
and is suitable for enjoyment.
But in selecting people, it is not so:
without asking whether suitable or not,
without discussing right or wrong,
those not from Qín are dismissed,
and guests are expelled.
Thus, what is valued lies in beauty, music, pearls, and jade,
while what is slighted lies in the people.
This is not the way to span the seas and control the feudal lords.
It is said:
"Some remain strangers though their hair has turned white;
others become friends though they have just met on the road."
Why is this?
It is because of understanding or lack of understanding.
Thus, Fán Wūqī fled from Qín to Yān,
and lent his head to Jīng Kē to assist the cause of Prince Dān;
Wáng Shē left Qí for Wèi,
and cut his own throat upon the city wall to repel Qí and save Wèi.
Wáng Shē and Fán Wūqī were not new acquaintances of Yān and Wèi nor old friends of Qí and Qín,
yet they left their two states
and died for the two rulers
because their actions matched their aspirations,
and their admiration for righteousness was boundless.
Therefore, though Sū Qín was distrusted by all under heaven,
he became a loyal man like Wěi Shēng for Yān;
though Bái Guī lost six cities in battle,
he captured Zhōngshān for Wèi.
Why was this?
Because there was genuine mutual understanding.
When Sū Qín served as chancellor of Yān,
someone slandered him to the King of Yān,
but the king angrily grasped his sword
and fed him swift steeds;
when Bái Guī achieved fame in Zhōngshān,
someone slandered him to Marquis Wén of Wèi,
yet the marquis bestowed upon him a luminous night-shining jade.
Why was this?
Because the two rulers and two ministers
opened their hearts and livers in mutual trust—
how could they be swayed by empty words!
Thus, whether a woman is beautiful or ugly,
once she enters the palace, she incurs jealousy;
whether a scholar is worthy or unworthy,
once he enters the court, he incurs envy.
In the past, Sīmǎ Xǐ had his feet amputated in Sòng,
yet he eventually became chancellor of Zhōngshān;
Fàn Jū had his ribs broken and teeth knocked out in Wèi,
yet he eventually became Marquis of Yìng.
These two men
both held firm to their unwavering plans,
abandoned selfish cliques,
and maintained solitary friendships,
so they could not avoid envious and jealous people.
Thus, Shēntú Dí threw himself into the Yōng River,
Xú Yǎn carried a stone and drowned himself in the sea—
finding no place for themselves in the world,
they would not unrighteously seek to form cliques at court
to sway the ruler's mind.
Thus, Bǎilǐ Xī begged for food on the road,
yet Duke Mù entrusted him with governance;
Nìng Qì fed oxen beneath a cart,
yet Duke Huán entrusted him with the state.
Did these two men previously serve as officials at court
or borrow praise from those around them
before the two rulers employed them?
They moved the rulers' hearts,
matched their intentions,
bonded as firmly as glue and lacquer—
even brothers could not separate them.
How could they be confused by the words of the crowd?
Thus, listening only to one side gives rise to treachery,
and relying solely on one leads to chaos.
In the past, Lǔ listened to Jìsūn's words and expelled Confucius;
Sòng believed Zǐrǎn's scheme and imprisoned Mò Dí.
With the eloquence of Confucius and Mòzǐ,
they could not avoid slander and flattery,
and the two states were endangered.
Why?
Because many mouths can melt metal,
and accumulated slander can destroy bones.
Thus, Qín employed the Róng man Yóuyú and became hegemon of the Central States;
Qí employed the Yuè man Zǐzāng and strengthened the reigns of Duke Wēi and Duke Xuān.
Were these two states constrained by customs,
bound by the times,
or tied to biased and one-sided words?
They listened broadly and observed comprehensively,
establishing bright examples for their time.
Thus, when intentions align, even Hú and Yuè become brothers—
Yóuyú and Zǐzāng are examples;
when they do not align, even flesh and blood become enemies—
Zhū, Xiàng, Guǎn, and Cài are examples.
If a ruler today could truly employ the clarity of Qí and Qín
and avoid the narrow hearing of Sòng and Lǔ,
then the achievements of the Five Hegemons would be insufficient to match,
and the Three Sovereigns would be easy to equal.
Thus, when a sage king awakens,
he abandons the heart of a Zǐzhī,
and does not delight in the worthiness of a Tián Cháng;
he enfeoffs the descendants of Bǐgān,
and restores the graves of pregnant women—
thus his achievements cover all under heaven.
Why?
Because his desire for goodness is insatiable.
Duke Wén of Jìn befriended his enemy and became hegemon of the feudal lords;
Duke Huán of Qí employed his foe and unified and corrected all under heaven.
Why?
Because of compassionate benevolence and earnest sincerity,
truly admirable in the heart—
this cannot be borrowed with empty words.
As for Qín employing the laws of Shāng Yāng,
weakening Hán and Wèi in the east,
and establishing strength under heaven,
yet in the end had him torn apart by chariots;
Yuè employing the strategies of Minister Wén Zhǒng,
capturing strong Wú and becoming hegemon of the Central States,
yet eventually executed him.
Thus, Sūnshū Áo thrice left the chancellorship without regret;
Yúlíng Zǐzhòng declined the position of one of the Three Dukes
to water gardens for others.
If a ruler today could truly discard arrogant and haughty thoughts,
harbor intentions that can be repaid,
lay open his heart and belly,
reveal true feelings,
expose liver and gall,
bestow generous virtue,
share hardship and success to the end,
and be unstinting toward scholars,
then even Jié's dog could be made to bark at Yáo,
and Zhí's follower could be made to assassinate Yóu—
how much more so when relying on the authority of a myriad chariots,
and borrowing the resources of a sage king!
If so, then Jīng Kē's drowning of seven clans
and Yāolí's burning of wife and children—
are these even worth mentioning to Your Majesty!
I have heard that if one throws a bright moon pearl
or a night-shining jade
at someone on a dark road,
all will grasp their swords and glare askance.
Why?
Twisted roots of trees,
gnarled and bizarre,
yet become vessels for a myriad-chariot state.
Why?
Because those around have first adorned them.
Thus, when something arrives without cause,
even if it is the pearl of the Suí Marquis
or a night-shining jade,
it only invites resentment and gains no gratitude;
but if someone first speaks for it,
then even dry wood and rotten stumps
can achieve merit and not be forgotten.
Now, commoners and scholars living in poverty under heaven,
though in humble and lowly circumstances,
even if endowed with the methods of Yáo and Shùn,
holding the eloquence of Yī Yǐn and Guǎn Zhòng,
cherishing the intentions of Lóng Péng and Bǐgān,
and wishing to devote loyalty to the ruler of the time,
yet having no one to adorn them in advance,
even if they exhaust their spirit and energy,
wishing to demonstrate loyalty and trustworthiness,
and assist the ruler in governance,
the ruler will surely follow the precedent of grasping his sword and glaring askance.
This prevents commoner scholars
from gaining the advantage of dry wood and rotten stumps.
Thus, a sage king governs the world and guides customs,
shaping alone upon the potter's wheel,
unfettered by humble words,
unswayed by many mouths.
Thus, the Qín emperor trusted the words of the Palace Attendant Méng Jiā,
believed Jīng Kē's story,
and the dagger was secretly drawn;
King Wén of Zhōu hunted in Jīng and Wèi,
carried Lǚ Shàng back with him,
and became king over all under heaven.
Qín trusted those around and perished;
Zhōu employed a chance gathering and became king.
Why?
Because he could transcend constrained and rigid speech,
gallop beyond the bounds of conventional righteousness,
and gaze alone upon the bright and vast Way.
Now, if a ruler is sunk in flattering words,
fettered by the restraints of curtains and walls,
causing unfettered scholars to share the stable with oxen and steeds,
this is why Bào Jiāo resented the world and would not linger for the joys of wealth and honor.
I have heard that those who enter court in full regalia
do not defile righteousness with private interests;
those who sharpen their reputation
do not harm their conduct for profit.
Thus, when a village was named "Shèngmǔ" (Victorious Mother),
Zēngzǐ would not enter;
when a city was called "Zhāogē" (Morning Song),
Mòzǐ turned his carriage around.
Now, if you wish to cause broad-minded scholars under heaven
to be tempted by the authority of power and gravity,
intimidated by the prestige of position and influence,
to turn their faces and defile their conduct,
to serve flattering people,
and seek closeness to those around,
then scholars would rather lie dead in caves and dens among cliffs and marshes—
how could there be any who devote loyalty and trustworthiness and hasten to your palace gates!
I have heard that among things of the same kind, there are those with exceptional abilities.
Thus, for strength, we speak of Wū Huò;
for swiftness, we speak of Qìng Jì;
for courage, we look to Bēn Yù.
In my foolish ignorance,
I privately believe that if this is true for humans,
it should also be so for beasts.
Now Your Majesty enjoys scaling perilous heights
and hunting fierce beasts.
If suddenly you encounter a beast of extraordinary talent,
startled in a place where survival is uncertain,
and it assails the pure dust of your carriage train,
with the carriage unable to turn its shafts around in time,
and people having no chance to exert their skill,
even if you had the abilities of Wū Huò or Péng Méng,
their strength would be of no use,
and even withered trees and rotten stumps
would all become hazards.
This would be like having the Hú and Yuè rise beneath your chariot wheels,
and the Qiāng and Yí pressing close to your carriage.
Is that not perilous indeed?
Even if all were perfectly safe and without harm,
it is still not something the Son of Heaven should approach.
Moreover, even when the road is cleared before proceeding
and one gallops along the middle of the path,
there are still occasional accidents of bit or yoke breaking.
How much more so when traversing thick grass
and racing over hills and ruins,
with the pleasure of pursuing game ahead,
but without any thought for unexpected changes within,
the potential for harm
is not also difficult to foresee!
To treat lightly the weight of ten thousand chariots and not consider it safe,
yet take pleasure in venturing onto a path with one chance in ten thousand of danger for amusement—
I privately believe this is not something Your Majesty should choose.
I have heard that the clear-sighted foresee things before they sprout,
and the wise avoid danger before it takes form.
Disasters often lie hidden in subtlety
and erupt from what people overlook.
Thus, a common saying goes:
"With a household accumulating a thousand in gold,
one does not sit under the eaves."
Though these words are small,
they can illustrate greater truths.
I hope Your Majesty will pay heed and graciously consider this!
I have heard that those who attain completeness prosper,
while those who lose completeness perish.
Shùn had not even land enough to stand an awl,
yet he came to possess the world;
Yǔ had not a gathering of ten households,
yet he became king over the feudal lords.
The territories of Tāng and Wǔ did not exceed a hundred lǐ,
yet above, they did not cut off the light of the three luminaries;
below, they did not harm the hearts of the common people.
This was because they possessed the art of kingship.
Thus, the way between father and son
is innate nature.
If loyal ministers do not avoid severe punishment to offer straightforward remonstrance,
then affairs will lack misguided strategies,
and achievements will flow down for ten thousand generations.
I, Chéng, wish to lay bare my innermost thoughts and offer my foolish loyalty.
I only hope that Your Highness will show a little compassionate consideration for my words.
Take a single thread's burden,
bearing a weight of a thousand jūn,
suspended above to immeasurable heights,
hanging down into unfathomable depths.
Even a very foolish person would still grieve knowing it is about to snap.
A horse is already startled,
yet you beat a drum to frighten it further;
the cord is about to break,
yet you add more weight to it.
Once the cord snaps in the sky,
it cannot be reknotted;
once it falls into a deep abyss,
it is difficult to retrieve.
Whether it emerges or not
allows not a hair's breadth of margin.
If you can listen to the words of loyal ministers,
all actions will surely escape peril.
If you insist on pursuing what you desire,
it will be as precarious as piling eggs,
as difficult as ascending to heaven.
But if you change what you desire to do,
it will be as easy as turning over your hand,
as secure as Mount Tài.
Now, if you wish to exhaust the heavenly mandate of long life,
enjoy endless extreme pleasures,
and explore the power of ten thousand chariots,
it does not go beyond the ease of turning over your hand,
dwelling in the security of Mount Tài.
Yet you desire to ride the danger of piled eggs,
and tread the difficulty of ascending to heaven.
This is what greatly perplexes this foolish minister.
It is human nature to fear one's shadow and dislike one's footprints,
so one turns one's back and runs away.
But the footprints only increase,
and the shadow grows swifter.
It is better to go into the shade and stop,
where the shadow vanishes and footprints cease.
If you wish people not to hear,
better not to speak.
If you wish people not to know,
better not to act.
If you wish boiling soup to cool,
with one person heating it
and a hundred people fanning it,
it is of no benefit.
Better to remove the firewood and stop the fire.
If you do not cut it off at that point,
but try to save it here,
it is like carrying firewood to put out a fire.
Yǎng Yóujī
was an excellent archer of Chǔ.
At a hundred paces from a poplar leaf,
he could hit it a hundred times out of a hundred.
With a poplar leaf so small,
adding a hundred hits to it,
he could indeed be called an expert archer.
Yet the range of his skill
was only within a hundred paces.
Compared to your minister Chéng,
he would not know how to hold a bow and arrow.
Good fortune arises from a foundation;
disaster arises from an embryo.
Accept its foundation,
cut off its embryo,
and from where would disaster come?
The dripping from Mount Tài wears through stone;
a single rope from a well pulley can sever a trunk.
Water is not a drill for stone,
nor is a rope a saw for wood,
but gradual erosion makes it so.
If you weigh things grain by grain,
by the time you reach a shí, there is sure to be error;
if you measure things inch by inch,
by the time you reach a zhàng, there is sure to be excess.
Weighing by the shí and measuring by the zhàng,
you proceed directly and rarely err.
A tree ten arm-spans around
begins as a sprout.
It can be snapped off with a foot's scratch,
or plucked out by hand.
Seize it before it is born;
anticipate it before it takes form.
Grinding and whetting,
you do not see the damage,
but in time it is worn away.
Planting trees and raising animals,
you do not see the gain,
but in time they become large.
Accumulating virtue and building conduct,
you do not know its goodness,
but in time it finds use.
Abandoning righteousness and turning your back on principle,
you do not know its evil,
but in time it brings ruin.
I hope Your Highness will deeply consider this and personally practice it.
This is the unchanging way for a hundred generations.
In the past, Qín raised difficulties in the west against the Hú and Róng,
guarded the passes of Yúzhōng in the north,
blocked the barriers of the Qiāng and Zuó in the south,
and faced the alliance of the six states in the east.
The six states, relying on Xìnlíng's prestige,
clarifying Sū Qín's covenant,
and sharpening Jīng Kē's might,
united their strength and hearts to prepare against Qín.
Yet Qín eventually captured the six states,
destroyed their altars of soil and grain,
and annexed the world.
Why was this?
It was because the advantages of terrain differed,
and the people's weight was not equal.
Now Hàn holds all the land of Qín,
combines the masses of the six states,
cultivates the righteousness of the Róng and Dí,
and faces the Qiāng and Zuó to the south.
Compared to Qín,
its land is ten times greater and its people a hundred times more.
This is what Your Highness clearly knows.
Now, those slanderous and flattering ministers who make plans for Your Highness
do not consider the duty between flesh and bone,
the weight of the people,
or the size of the state,
but regard Wú as a calamity.
This is why I am anxious for Your Highness.
To raise the troops of Wú to contend against Hàn,
is like flies and gnats attaching themselves to a herd of oxen,
or rotten flesh meeting a sharp sword—
upon contact with the blade, they will surely come to nothing.
The world hears that Wú leads the disenfranchised feudal lords,
wishing to demand the fulfillment of the late emperor’s bequeathed covenant.
Now Hàn has personally executed its three highest ministers
to atone for past wrongs—
this is Your Majesty’s prestige extending over the world,
and achievements surpassing those of Tāng and Wǔ.
Wú holds the position of a feudal lord,
yet its wealth surpasses that of the Son of Heaven;
it bears the name of a hidden recluse,
yet its faults exceed those of the Central States.
Hàn combines twenty-four commanderies
and seventeen feudal lords;
supplies are transported in crisscrossing streams,
armies march for thousands of lǐ without cease in the suburbs,
yet its rare treasures do not compare to the treasuries east of the mountains.
Transporting grain westward,
overland routes never cease,
waterways fill the rivers,
yet it does not compare to the granaries of Hǎilíng.
Cultivating the Shànglín Park,
mingled with detached palaces,
accumulating collections of curios and delights,
enclosing and keeping birds and beasts,
does not compare to the gardens of Chángzhōu.
Strolling on winding terraces,
overlooking the high roads,
does not compare to the pools of Zhāoxī.
Deep walls and high ramparts,
supplemented by fortified passes,
do not compare to the perils of the Jiāng and Huái.
This is why I rejoice for Your Majesty.
Now if Your Majesty withdraws the troops and swiftly returns,
you may still retain half or more.
Otherwise,
when Hàn realizes Wú harbors the ambition to swallow the world,
it will blaze with wrath,
dispatch the Yǔlín and Huángtóu troops to follow the river downstream,
and attack Your Majesty’s capital;
Lǔ and Dōnghǎi will cut off Wú’s supply routes;
the King of Liáng will array chariots and cavalry,
feather arrows for battle,
stockpile grain and fortify defenses,
to press against Yíngyáng,
awaiting Wú’s famine.
Even if Your Majesty wishes to return to the capital,
it will be impossible.
The plans of the three Huáinán kings did not betray their covenant,
the King of Qí took his own life to erase his traces,
the four states could not dispatch troops from their commanderies,
Zhào was imprisoned in Hándān—
this cannot be concealed,
and is already clear.
Now Your Majesty has left a state of a thousand lǐ,
and is confined within ten lǐ.
Zhāng and Hán command the northern lands,
Gōnggāo is stationed to the left and right,
troops cannot descend from their walls,
the army cannot catch its breath—
I privately grieve for this.
I beg Your Majesty to consider this carefully!
In the past, a humble subject beat his breast,
and flying frost struck the land of Yān;
a common woman cried out to heaven,
and a raging wind assailed the terrace of Qí.
Whenever I, your humble servant, read these accounts,
I have never been able to finish without shedding tears.
Why?
Because a man has fixed principles,
a woman has unchangeable conduct;
to be faithful yet suspected,
chaste yet slain—
this is why stalwart men and righteous scholars
face death without looking back.
I, your humble servant, have heard that benevolence cannot be relied upon,
goodness cannot be depended on;
I thought these were empty words,
but now I know their truth.
I implore Your Majesty to pause a moment,
and grant me a little compassion and consideration.
I, your humble servant, am a man of humble origins,
a scholar in coarse cloth and leather girdle;
in retirement, I do not adorn myself with poetry and books to startle the ignorant;
in advancement, I do not buy fame and reputation in the world.
Recently,
I was mistakenly allowed to ascend and descend at the Chéngmíng Gate,
to enter and exit the Jīnhuá Palace;
how could I not constantly tread cautiously,
and keep to the side within the forbidden gates?
Privately admiring Your Majesty’s righteousness,
I again became a guest at your gate,
equipped with the remnants of trivial skills like crow-calling and petty theft,
placed at the end of lowly arts like the Three and Five.
Your Majesty bestowed grace and favor,
regarded me with kindness,
truly granting me the golden gifts of Jīng Qīng,
and I privately felt the distinction of Yù Ràng as a state scholar.
I have often wished to tie my cap-strings and fall upon my sword,
to repay even a ten-thousandth part,
to cut open my heart and grind my heels,
to repay my sovereign.
I never imagined that a petty man’s obstinate ignorance
would lead to slander and accusation,
my traces falling under clear laws,
my body bound in dark prison,
treading my shadow and grieving in my heart,
nose sour and bones aching!
I, your humble servant, have heard that to damage one’s name is a disgrace,
and to damage one’s body is next;
thus, whenever a thought comes,
it feels as if something is lost.
Moreover, as the months pass,
approaching late autumn,
the sky darkens and overcasts,
left and right are colorless.
I am not wood or stone,
yet I keep company with jailers.
This is why Shàoqīng looked up to heaven and beat his breast,
weeping until tears were exhausted and followed by blood.
Though I, your humble servant, lack reputation in my village,
I have heard of the conduct of noble men.
The highest among them hide among market stalls,
or lie beneath cliffs and rocks;
the next tie their ribbons in the courts of Jīnmǎ,
and deliberate loftily upon Yúntái;
retiring, they capture the lords of Nányuè,
and bind the necks of the Chányú.
All open vermilion records,
and are depicted in green history.
How could they contend over trifling inches,
or vie for the profit of awl and knife?
I, your humble servant, have heard that accumulated slander melts metal,
accumulated calumny grinds bones;
in ancient times, Zhí Shēng was suspected of stealing gold,
in recent times, Bóyú was named for unrighteousness.
Those two men,
were still treated thus,
how much more I, your humble servant,
how can I avoid it?
In the past, the shame of a supreme general—
Jiàng Hóu imprisoned;
the disgrace of a famed minister—
Sīmǎ Qiān cast into prison;
as for I, your humble servant,
what words can I say!
The wisdom of Lǔ Lián—
he declined salary and did not return;
the worthiness of Jiēyú—
he sang as he walked and forgot to return.
Zǐlíng closed his gate in Dōngyuè,
Zhòngwèi barred his door in Xīqín.
This too is well known.
If my affairs are not false,
and my crimes are true,
I should still gag my mouth and swallow my tongue,
fall upon a dagger to end my life—
how could I face the men of extraordinary integrity from Qí and Lǔ,
or the sorrowful singers of Yān and Zhào?
Now the sacred calendar is revered and bright,
the world enjoys its labors,
azure clouds float over Luò,
glorious light fills the river,
west reaching Líntáo and Dídào,
north extending to Fēihú and Yángyuán—
all are bathed in benevolence and righteousness,
illuminated by splendor and drinking sweet wine.
Yet I, your humble servant, embrace pain at the round gate,
harbor resentment in the prison door;
a trivial being,
yet with enough to grieve over.
I beg Your Majesty to bestow a little clarity,
then the soul at Wúqiū
will not be ashamed of its sunken head,
the ghost at Hú Tíng
will bear no resentment for its ashen bones.
Unable to bear the urgency of my innermost feelings,
I respectfully convey them through your attendants.
Your servant Fǎng respectfully states:
I have received the imperial command and the bestowed demonstration of the five-rhyme poem for the Double Seventh Festival.
I humbly consider that the traces of emperors are manifold,
and their condescension to similarity is not uniform;
entrusting emotions to the Airs of the States,
they are rarely matched in any age.
Although the Han had its four reigns,
and the Wei boasted its three ancestors,
how could they suffice to continue the thought of the "Southern Winds,"
and harmonize with the "Dew Tunes"?
Nature and the Way of Heaven,
are matters beyond description,
how could it be due to my great fortune,
to personally encounter the dawn and dusk?
Your servant early served during the dragon's submersion,
entering the inner chamber alongside Jiǎ and Mǎ;
later, belonging to the soaring heavens,
I compared to Yán and Xú while awaiting the imperial summons.
Only the ruler knows his servant,
as seen in the intent of reticent speech;
seeking without fault,
manifest in the play of eloquent talent.
I have hastily and clumsily led the vulgar and shallow,
to respond to Heaven's reward,
though clumsy and swift may have been effective,
the foolish and base have already been revealed.
As I present this, I am ashamed and embarrassed, not knowing where to place myself.
Respectfully stated.
Your servant Bīn states:
I have humbly seen the imperial edict and the proclamation of the decree by Zhèng Yìtài,
that I should be granted the repair of the tomb mound of my late great-grandfather, the Jin Dynasty's former General of Agile Cavalry, the Loyal and Devoted Duke of Jiànxīng, Hú.
My family line is not prosperous,
obscured by the Way of Heaven,
loyalty encountered personal danger,
filial piety accumulated family misfortune,
the teachings of reputation are equally sorrowful,
and reclusion brings melancholy.
Yet years and generations pass and change,
the solitary descendants are submerged and blocked.
Thus causing the stele inscriptions to become overgrown and vanish,
the mound trees to become desolate and ruined,
foxes and hares make their dens,
children and herdsmen sing mournful songs.
Moved by emotion, I grieve for myself,
as the sun and moon press urgently.
Your Majesty broadly proclaims the teachings of righteousness,
not seeking effectiveness only in the present;
Hú's remaining deeds are not extinguished,
and he surely exerted his strength in a different age.
But the grace of added ranks,
was recently lacking in the Jin codes;
the penalty of gathering firewood,
flows distantly to the imperial age.
What kind of person am I,
to dare decline such fortune?
I cannot bear the utmost of sorrowful gratitude!
Respectfully, I present this statement to be heard.
Respectfully stated.
Fǎng states:
Recently, I presented my plea to return and appeal,
hoping for understanding of my desperate sincerity,
but upon receiving the returned directive,
no compassionate consideration was bestowed,
grieving at heart, I lost my plan,
weeping blood as I awaited dawn.
You, towards the multitude of officials,
show equal molding and creation,
seeking salary and praying for glory,
I further strive to elevate myself.
Damaging teachings and abandoning rites,
how could it concern sight and hearing?
What I cannot bear to speak,
I fully set forth in this statement.
Fǎng, in the past, followed a minor official post,
salary not replacing farming.
Hunger and cold without the means for sweet delicacies,
limited by duties, abandoning half of morning and evening.
The joy of having parents at my knee,
has already passed like a crack;
the longing for the mat and table,
how much can be relied upon?
Moreover, not personally offering libations,
how can the presence be entrusted?
Mornings and evenings lonely and silent,
quiet as if without a master.
What I uphold has no alternative principle,
how can my choked sobs reach many metaphors?
Illustrious Duke, your achievements reach throughout the realm,
and your empathetic understanding has a path,
if generously you would descend,
bestowing the cessation of strict commands.
Then it would be known that the reach of filial governance,
extends even to the无心;
the conferral of categories reaches,
not merely the teachings of righteousness.
Unable to bear the feelings of collapse and urgency,
I respectfully present this statement for your attention.
Respectfully stated.
The Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, your servant Rén Fǎng, kowtows and says:
Your servant has heard that when a general dies in retreat,
not a step is taken backward;
looking around to avoid the enemy,
there is punishment for hesitation and cowardice.
Even to the extent that Zhào's mother, with deep insight,
begged not to be implicated;
the Wèi ruler established a law,
yet the punishment meted was light.
Thus it is known that the general of a defeated army,
faces death and family execution,
since ancient times,
clear punishment resides herein.
Your servant Fǎng kowtows and kowtows again,
worthy of death, worthy of death.
I humbly consider that the Xūnxiǎn invaded and raided,
temporarily disturbing the borderlands,
the royal army launched a modest campaign,
and wherever they went, the enemy crumbled.
Thus Huáixú presented victories,
and Héyǎn returned in triumph.
At the eastern pass, not a single battle's toil,
on the road, rarely a thousand in gold expenses.
Yet the Sī region hangs isolated,
slantingly facing the enemy territory,
thus allowing the cunning foe to encroach,
lingering for years and months.
The former Inspector of Sī Province, Cài Dàogōng,
led and roused the righteous and brave,
striving without regard for his life,
defending the city to the death,
from winter through autumn,
still turning to battle without end,
repeatedly crushing the vile foe.
Comparing him to Jūyán,
then Líng surrendered while Gōng held firm;
comparing him to Shūlè,
then Gěng survived while Cài perished.
If the rescue troops from the Yǐng region,
had slightly connected with support,
then the head of the Chányú,
would long have hung at the northern gate,
how could it merely be that a surrender could be built,
and Shè'ān open territory, that is all!
It truly stemmed from the Inspector of Yǐng Province, your servant Jǐngzōng,
who received orders to conduct the campaign,
yet did not advance in a timely manner,
thus allowing the enemy to gather like hedgehogs and ants,
relying on water and grass;
furthermore, he halted his armor and lingered,
delaying rescue and aiding the enemy,
thereby causing the isolated city to desperately hold out,
until its strength was exhausted by the fierce might.
Even so,
he should still have firmly held the three passes,
and further planned to advance and seize,
yet he withdrew his troops and extended his neck,
bringing defeat upon himself,
the borderlands invaded and alarmed,
this is precisely the reason.
Without strict punishment,
how can reward and penalty be placed?
Jǐngzōng is the principal.
Your servant respectfully submits that the Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs of the Two Provinces of Yǐng and Sī,
General of the Left,
Inspector of Yǐng Province,
Marquis of the Founding of Xiāngxī County, your servant Jǐngzōng,
promoted from among the ranks,
encountered this great fortune,
pointing the way was not his design,
how diligent was he in capturing prey?
Rewarded richly as a marquis,
honored highly among the generals,
the burden just relaxed,
the bells and tripods hastily arranged,
making peace with the barbarians without effect,
the two eights already arrayed.
From head to toe,
achievements belong to creation,
moistening grass and covering plains,
how could he claim it for himself?
Moreover, Dàogōng passed away,
yet the city was defended for dozens of days;
Jǐngzōng, while alive,
in one morning abandoned his armor.
Living Cáo, dead Cài,
superior and inferior like this,
only this man,
has the face to show.
In the past, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn appointed generals,
and while seated knew affairs a thousand miles away;
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi established laws,
and handled matters accordingly.
Thus, they could act in accordance with regulations,
without the slightest error.
I humbly consider Your Sagely and Martial Majesty to be outstanding and heroic,
with strategies unparalleled in this world,
assessing the enemy and adapting to changes,
making no mistakes even across ten thousand miles.
To uphold and implement this,
truly magnifies the court’s calculations.
Yet, this mediocre and stubborn one,
by principle, is beyond words of admonition.
Since the rebellious Hú ran rampant,
they have long plagued the various Xià.
The Sagely Court, looking upon this,
sought to unify chariots and writings.
Pitying those officials and commoners,
who suffered humiliation where they should not.
In early court, I sighed deeply,
filled with compassion and pity.
Having caused such loss and damage,
how can I escape blame?
It is proper to correct the penal code,
and strictly clarify the statutes and regulations.
I, your subject, respectfully present this impeachment,
requesting that based on the current matter, Jǐngzōng be removed from his official position,
that the Tàicháng strip him of his noble rank and fief,
and that he be handed over to the Tíngwèi for investigation and punishment according to law.
As for the military aides, staff officers,
subordinate generals and commanders, and all others who should be implicated and held accountable,
let the Acting Secretary of the Censorate separately investigate and submit further memorials according to their offenses.
I, your subject, respectfully present this white tablet to inform Your Majesty, and so forth.
The Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, your subject Rèn Fǎng, bows his head and says:
I have heard that Mǎ Yuán served his sister-in-law,
and would not enter without wearing his cap;
Fàn Yù raised orphans,
and his home had no permanent sons.
Therefore, righteous scholars and men of integrity,
hearing of this, established themselves,
a beautiful tale for a thousand years,
this is praised as foremost.
I, your subject Fǎng, kowtow and kowtow,
deserving death, deserving death.
Respectfully investigating: Fàn, wife of the late Xīyáng Neishǐ Liú Yín of Qí,
came to the tribunal to lodge a complaint stating:
She married into the Liú family,
for about twenty years.
After Liú’s death,
she raised the orphaned and weak.
The younger brother-in-law, Zhěng,
constantly sought to harm, encroach, and seize.
The previously divided slaves, Jiàozǐ
and Dāngbó,
had both been incorporated into the collective property.
Also, using money, the slave sisters and younger brother Wēn,
he still kept the slave for his own use;
Bó also seized the slave Lǜcǎo belonging to Yín’s son Qūn,
privately sold her for money,
and did not share with Qūn.
Yín’s second concubine-born son Shīlì,
last year in the tenth month went to Zhěng’s fields,
staying for twelve days,
Zhěng then demanded six dǒu of rice from Fàn for food.
Before the rice could be delivered,
he suddenly arrived in front of the door,
隔着 the curtain, clenched his fist and shouted abuses,
rushed into the room,
took the carriage curtain from behind the screen as collateral for the rice and left.
On the night of the second month, ninth day,
the slave girl Cǎiyīn stole the carriage rail, clamping rod, and dragon traces,
Fàn questioned about the missing items,
Zhěng then beat her son Qūn.
Zhěng and his mother along with slaves and others, six people in total, came to Fàn’s room,
shouting loudly and abusing,
the slave girl Cǎiyīn raised her hand and scratched Fàn’s arm.
Requesting investigation and examination,
as stated in the complaint.
Thereupon, we summoned Hǎigé, the old slave of Zhěng’s deceased father, to the tribunal for questioning,
who stated:
Zhěng’s deceased father Xīngdào,
previously served in Línglíng Commandery,
and obtained four slaves.
When dividing the property,
he gave the slave Jiàozǐ to his eldest son Yín.
After Yín’s death,
the second younger brother Zhěng still seized Jiàozǐ,
saying he should be incorporated into the collective property,
Zhěng then kept him for his own use.
The slave sisters and younger brother were each valued at five thousand cash,
and not shared with Qūn.
The slave Dāngbó,
was originally a collective slave.
Before the Zhěng brothers divided the property,
Zhěng’s elder brother Yín used Dāngbó as collateral for seven thousand cash,
for collective field work.
When Yín left his post in Xīyáng Commandery and returned,
although they had not yet separated their hearths for cooking,
Yín used his private money of seven thousand to redeem Dāngbó,
and still sent him to Guǎngzhōu.
Later, when Yín died,
the Zhěng brothers later divided the slaves,
only the slave girl Lǜcǎo remained to be incorporated into the collective property.
Zhěng again said that Yín had not divided the property to redeem Dāngbó,
so he should also belong to the collective.
Zhěng’s intention was to greedily obtain Dāngbó,
so he pushed Lǜcǎo onto Qūn.
Zhěng planned for Dāngbó’s return,
intending to take him for himself.
Dāngbó then did not return for seven years.
Zhěng suspected he had died and would not return,
so he seized the slave girl Lǜcǎo again,
sold her for seven thousand cash.
Zhěng and his brothers and sister together divided this money,
and again did not share with Qūn.
Yín’s wife Fàn said,
Dāngbó was privately redeemed by her deceased husband,
and should belong to her son Qūn.
Dāngbó returned from Guǎngzhōu in the sixth month of the second year of Tiānjiān,
Zhěng seized him again,
saying he should serve the collective,
offsetting the hire for four years of labor service to Guǎngzhōu,
and now is employed at Zhěng’s place.
Proceeding to interrogate Zhěng’s slave girl Cǎiyīn,
Liú Zhěng’s elder brother Yín’s second son Shīlì,
on the twelfth day of the tenth month last year, suddenly went to stay at Zhěng’s villa for twelve days,
Zhěng then went to his elder brother’s wife Fàn to demand six dǒu of rice for food.
Before Fàn could return it,
Zhěng became angry,
and proceeded to enter Fàn’s residence himself,
taking the carriage curtain from behind the screen as collateral.
Fàn delivered six dǒu of rice,
and Zhěng immediately accepted it.
On the night of the second month, ninth day this year,
Fàn lost the carriage rail, clamping rod, dragon traces, and other items,
Fàn and her son Qūn said it was Cǎiyīn who stole them.
Zhěng heard the noise,
and then beat Qūn.
Fàn called out and asked, “Why are you beating my son?”
Zhěng and his mother then together came out into the central courtyard,
隔着 the curtain and exchanged abuses with Fàn.

surpassing even flesh and blood.
Although Líng is not clever,
how could I not be deeply moved!
From the time I first surrendered,
until this very day,
my person in dire straits,
sitting alone in sorrow and bitterness,
all day seeing nothing,
only encountering alien kinds.
Leather sleeves and felt tents
to ward off wind and rain.
Rank meat and fermented milk
to satisfy hunger and thirst.
Lifting my eyes to speak and laugh,
with whom can I share joy?
In the Hú lands, dark ice,
the border soil cruelly cracked,
only hearing the mournful sound of desolate winds.
In the cool autumn ninth month,
beyond the frontier, grass withers.
At night unable to sleep,
inclining my ear to listen afar,
Hú jiā pipes call back and forth,
herding horses whinny mournfully,
neighing and whinnying in herds,
border sounds arise on all sides.
Sitting at dawn to listen,
tears fall unawares.
Alas, Zǐqīng!
What heart does Líng alone possess,
that he can not feel sorrow!
After parting from you,
increasingly without solace.
Above, I think of my aged mother,
in her later years slain;
wife and children innocent,
all became whales and sharks.
My person bears the nation’s grace,
pitied by the world.
You return to receive honor,
I remain to receive disgrace,
such is fate, what can be done!
Born from a land of ritual and righteousness,
yet entered into ignorant customs,
forsaking the grace of sovereign and kin,
long dwelling in barbarian regions,
how grievous!
That the heir of my late father
should become a tribe of Róng and Dí,
adds to my own sorrow!
Great in achievement, small in crime,
yet not granted clear discernment,
betraying Líng’s heart,
this sincere intent of mine,
each time the thought arrives,
suddenly I forget life.
Líng would not find it hard to pierce his heart to prove himself,
cut his throat to show his resolve,
but the state, to me, is already finished.
To kill myself would bring no benefit,
only adding shame,
thus each time I brace myself and endure disgrace,
again continue to cling to life.
Those around me,
seeing Líng thus,
thinking to offer unwelcome pleasures,
come to urge and encourage.
The joys of an alien land,
only bring sorrow,
increasing anguish.
Alas, Zǐqīng!
In mutual understanding between people,
what is valued is understanding the heart.
The previous letter was hastily written,
failing to fully convey my thoughts,
therefore I briefly state again:
In the past, the late Emperor bestowed upon me, Lǐ Líng, five thousand infantry troops,
and dispatched us on an expedition to a remote frontier.
Five generals lost their way,
and I alone encountered battle.
Carrying provisions for a journey of ten thousand *lǐ*,
leading an army on foot,
we ventured beyond the bounds of Tiānhàn,
and entered the territory of the powerful Hú.
With a force of five thousand men,
we faced an army of one hundred thousand.
Commanding weary and exhausted soldiers,
we confronted freshly bridled steeds.
Yet still we beheaded enemy commanders and captured their flags,
pursued the fleeing and chased the defeated northward,
wiping out their traces and sweeping away the dust,
and slew their fierce commander.
We caused the soldiers of the three armies
to look upon death as a homecoming.
I, Líng, though lacking in talent,
hoped to shoulder great responsibilities.
I believed that at that time,
my achievements would be difficult to surpass.
After the Xiōngnú were defeated,
the entire nation raised an army,
training even more elite troops,
their strength exceeding one hundred thousand.
The Chányú personally came to the battlefield,
and personally directed the encirclement.
The relative positions of guest and host
were already unequal;
the disparity between infantry and cavalry
was even more extreme.
Our weary troops fought again,
each man holding off a thousand,
yet still, supporting their wounds and bearing their pain,
they staked their lives to strive to be first,
until the dead and wounded piled up across the plain,
and fewer than a hundred remained,
all of them debilitated by illness,
unable to bear arms.
Yet when I, Líng, raised my arm and gave a shout,
the wounded and sick all arose,
raised their blades and pointed them at the enemy,
causing the Hú horses to flee;
when our weapons were exhausted and our arrows spent,
with not an inch of iron left among the men,
still, bareheaded, they shouted with fervor,
vying to be the first to ascend.
At that time,
heaven and earth were stirred to rage for my sake,
and the warriors drank blood for my sake.
The Chányú believed he could not capture me again,
and wished to withdraw his forces.
But a treacherous minister advised him,
and so they resumed the battle.
Thus, I, Líng, could not avoid capture.
In the past, Emperor Gāo, with a host of three hundred thousand,
was trapped at Píngchéng.
At that time,
fierce generals were as numerous as clouds,
strategic advisors as plentiful as rain,
yet still they went seven days without food,
and only then managed to escape.
How much more so for someone like me, Líng—
could it have been easy to exert such strength?
Yet those in charge say such things,
merely resenting me for not dying.
However, my not dying
is a crime;
but Zǐqīng, look upon me—
am I one who would cling to life,
or a person who fears death?
How could there be one who would turn his back on sovereign and parents,
abandon wife and children,
and yet act for personal gain?
Yet my not dying
was for a purpose.
Therefore, I wished, as stated in my previous letter,
to repay kindness to the ruler of the state.
Truly, I believed that to die in vain is not as good as establishing one's integrity,
and to have one's name extinguished is not as good as repaying virtue.
In the past, Fàn Lǐ did not die to atone for the shame of Kuàijī,
and Cáo Mèi did not die to escape the disgrace of three defeats;
in the end, they avenged Gōu Jiàn's enemy,
and repaid the disgrace of the state of Lǔ.
My humble heart
sincerely admired this.
How could I have foreseen that before my ambition was achieved, resentment had already formed,
and before my plans could be followed, my flesh and blood were subjected to punishment?
This is why I, Líng, look up to heaven, beat my breast, and weep tears of blood!
You also say:
"The Hàn dynasty treats its meritorious officials not ungenerously."
You are a minister of Hàn—
how could you not say such things?
In the past, Xiāo Hé and Fán Kuài were imprisoned and bound;
Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè were minced and pickled;
Cháo Cuò was executed;
Zhōu Bó and Wèi Qí were found guilty.
As for the other men who assisted the mandate and achieved merit,
such as Jiǎ Yì and Zhōu Yǎfū,
all were truly talents for the ages,
possessing the capacity of generals and ministers,
yet they suffered the slander of petty men,
and all endured the disgrace of calamity and ruin,
finally causing those with talent to bear slander,
and their abilities unable to be displayed.
The distant removal of those two gentlemen—
who does not feel heartache over it!
My late general,
whose achievements and strategies covered heaven and earth,
whose righteousness and courage were foremost among the three armies,
merely lost the favor of the esteemed ministers,
and met his end by the sword at the distant frontier.
This is why meritorious officials and righteous men lean on their halberds and heave long sighs!
How can this be called "not ungenerous"?
Moreover, in the past, you, with a single chariot as an envoy,
went to meet the ruler of ten thousand chariots among the enemy,
encountered an unpropitious time,
to the point of falling upon your sword without a second thought,
wandering in hardship and toil,
nearly dying in the wilds of the northern frontier.
You undertook your mission in the prime of life,
and returned with hoary head.
Your aged mother passed away in the hall,
your living wife left the curtains of your home.
This is rarely heard of in all the world,
unprecedented in ancient and modern times.
Even the people of the Mán and Mò tribes
still praised your integrity—
how much more should the ruler of all under heaven?
I, Líng, believed you should enjoy the recommendation for a fief of thatch and earth,
and receive a reward of a thousand chariots.
Yet I heard that upon your return,
the gifts bestowed did not exceed two million cash,
your position did not surpass Diǎn Shǔ Guó,
without an inch of land enfeoffed to you,
in addition to your toils.
While ministers who obstruct merit and harm the capable
all become marquises of ten thousand households,
and the kindred of greedy and flattering sorts
all become chief ministers in the court.
If even you are treated thus,
what hope is there left for me, Líng?
Moreover, Hàn severely punishes me for not dying,
and meagerly rewards you for maintaining integrity,
wishing to make distant, listening ministers
rush to obey upon hearing the news—
this is truly difficult.
This is why each time I look back, I do not regret.
Although I, Líng, have failed in gratitude,
Hàn has also been lacking in virtue.
People of old have said:
"Though loyal, one may not be fierce;
yet one looks upon death as a homecoming."
If I, Líng, can truly be at peace,
then how could the ruler again show concern?
A man lives, and if he fails to achieve fame,
then let him die and be buried among the barbarians.
Who could again bend his body and knock his head on the ground,
returning to face the northern palace gate,
to let the clerks of the brush and knife toy with their writings?
I hope you will no longer look to me, Líng!
Alas, Zǐqīng!
What more is there to say!
We are separated by ten thousand *lǐ*,
cut off from each other, our paths divergent.
In life, we are people of different worlds;
in death, we will be ghosts of separate lands.
Long must I bid you farewell, in life and death!
I am fortunate to convey regards to old friends—
strive to serve the sagely ruler.
Your son is well,
do not be concerned about him.
Strive to take care of yourself.
When the opportunity arises with the north wind,
favor me again with your virtuous words.
Lǐ Líng bows his head.
Your servant, the Grand Historian's ox and horse, Sīmǎ Qiān, bows twice and addresses you:
Venerable Shàoqīng,
Previously, you deigned to send me a letter,
instructing me to be compliant in dealing with people,
and to make it my duty to recommend the worthy and advance scholars.
Your spirit was earnest and sincere,
as if reproaching me for not following your advice,
and instead adopting the words of vulgar men.
I dare not be like this.
Though I am worn-out and feeble,
I have also occasionally heard from the side the enduring legacy of elders.
But I consider myself physically mutilated and dwelling in filth,
moving only to be blamed,
wishing to benefit but instead causing harm,
therefore I am alone in my melancholy and have no one to speak with.
As the saying goes:
"For whom should one act?
Who will listen?"
For when Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá never played the qin again for the rest of his life.
Why is this?
A gentleman acts for one who understands him,
a woman adorns herself for one who delights in her.
As for me, my great substance is already deficient and flawed,
even if my talents held the jewels of Suí and Hé,
and my conduct were like that of Yóu and Yí,
in the end it could not be considered honorable,
but would only suffice to invite ridicule and disgrace myself.
Your letter deserved a reply,
but I happened to be traveling east with the Emperor,
and was also pressed by humble duties,
our meetings were brief,
and in haste I had not a moment of leisure
to fully express my deepest thoughts.
Now you, Shàoqīng, bear an unpredictable crime,
passing through the months,
approaching the end of winter;
I am also soon to accompany the Emperor to Yōng,
and fear that suddenly the unspeakable may occur.
If I were to never have the chance to vent my indignation and make it known to you,
then the soul of the departed would harbor endless private regrets.
Allow me to briefly state my humble views;
long have I delayed in replying,
I hope you will not take offense.
I have heard:
Cultivating one's person
is the emblem of wisdom;
loving and giving
is the beginning of benevolence;
taking and giving
is the manifestation of righteousness;
knowing shame and disgrace
is the test of courage;
establishing a name
is the ultimate of conduct.
A gentleman who possesses these five
can then be entrusted to the world,
and stand among the ranks of noble men.
Therefore, no calamity is more grievous than coveting profit,
no sorrow more painful than a wounded heart,
no conduct more vile than disgracing one's ancestors,
no shame greater than castration.
A man mutilated by punishment
has no place for comparison or reckoning,
not just in one age,
but from times long past.
In the past, when Duke Líng of Wèi shared his carriage with Yōng Qú,
Confucius went to Chén;
when Shāng Yāng gained audience through Jǐng Jiān,
Zhào Liáng was chilled to the heart;
when the eunuch shared the imperial carriage,
Yuán Sī changed countenance.
Since ancient times, this has been considered shameful.
Even for a man of mediocre talent,
matters involving eunuchs
invariably dampen the spirit,
how much more so for a man of high aspirations!
Now though the court may lack men,
how could one who survives the knife and saw
recommend the heroes and talents of the world?
I have relied on my forefathers' legacy,
and managed to serve in disgrace beneath the imperial carriage,
for over twenty years.
Reflecting on myself,
first, I have been unable to offer loyalty and prove faithful,
to gain a reputation for extraordinary strategies and talents,
and thereby win the favor of an enlightened sovereign;
next, I have also been unable to gather omissions and repair deficiencies,
to summon the worthy and advance the capable,
and bring to light the recluses of the hills and caves;
externally, I have been unable to join the ranks of the army,
to attack cities and fight in the field,
and achieve the merit of capturing enemy generals and seizing their flags;
lastly, I have been unable to accumulate days and pile up labors,
to obtain high office and generous salary,
and thereby bring glory and favor to my clan and friends.
In these four, I have achieved not one,
merely conforming to gain acceptance,
with no effect of any distinction,
as can be seen here.
In the past,
I was once ranked among the lower grand masters,
participating in peripheral discussions at the outer court.
I did not take that opportunity to uphold the guiding principles,
and exhaust my thoughts and considerations.
Now, with my mutilated form as a menial sweeper,
among the lowly and worthless,
to wish to lift my head and raise my eyebrows,
and discourse on right and wrong—
would that not be to belittle the court and shame the gentlemen of the present age?
Alas!
Alas!
What more can I, such as I am, say?
What more can I say?
Moreover, the beginning and end of the matter are not easily understood.
In my youth, I bore unbridled conduct,
in adulthood, I lacked reputation in my hometown,
but the Emperor, fortunately due to my father's sake,
allowed me to offer my meager skills,
and come and go within the guarded precincts.
I thought, how can one look at the sky while carrying a pot on one's head?
Therefore, I cut off acquaintance with guests and friends,
neglected the affairs of my household,
day and night thinking to exhaust my unworthy talents and strength,
striving single-mindedly to attend to my duties,
in order to seek intimacy and favor with the Emperor.
Yet matters turned out to be greatly mistaken and not so.
I and Lǐ Líng both served at the palace gates,
and we were never particularly close.
Our paths and choices differed,
and we never shared a cup of wine
or exchanged warm, heartfelt joys.
Yet I observed his character:
he was a man of extraordinary integrity,
filial in serving his parents,
trustworthy with his comrades,
honest in matters of wealth,
and principled in giving and taking.
He was deferential in distinguishing rank,
humble and frugal, treating inferiors with respect,
and he always thought of striving without regard for his own life
to answer the urgent needs of the state.
Such were the qualities he had long cultivated,
and I believed he possessed the bearing of a true servant of the state.
Now, when a subject ventures forth on a plan that risks ten thousand deaths without a thought for his own life,
and rushes to meet the perils of the public cause,
this is already extraordinary.
Yet now, because one undertaking did not succeed,
those ministers who care only for preserving their own bodies and protecting their wives and children
immediately seize upon his shortcomings and magnify them.
Truly, in my heart, I ache for him.
Moreover, Lǐ Líng led foot soldiers numbering less than five thousand,
penetrated deep into the land of warhorses,
trod upon the royal court of the enemy,
dangled bait before the tiger's mouth,
and boldly provoked the mighty Hú.
Facing an army of countless thousands,
he fought the Chányú for more than ten days in succession.
The enemies he killed exceeded half their number.
The enemy could not even tend to their dead and wounded,
and the chieftains clad in felt and furs were all shaken with terror.
Then they summoned all their Left and Right Wise Kings,
mobilized every man who could draw a bow,
and the entire nation joined in attacking and surrounding him.
He fought his way for a thousand lǐ,
until his arrows were exhausted and his path was blocked,
and no relief troops arrived.
His soldiers lay dead and wounded in heaps.
Yet with one shout of encouragement from Lǐ Líng,
every soldier rose up,
tears streaming down their faces,
blood on their cheeks, swallowing their sobs,
drawing empty bows once more,
braving naked blades,
and facing north to contend in dying against the enemy.
Before Lǐ Líng was lost,
when messengers came with reports,
the Han dukes, ministers, princes, and marquises
all raised their cups in toast to the emperor's longevity.
A few days later,
when the news of Lǐ Líng's defeat arrived,
the sovereign found his food tasteless
and was unhappy during court audiences.
The great ministers were worried and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
I, in my lowliness, did not consider my own humble station,
but seeing the sovereign's grief and distress,
I sincerely wished to offer my simple, foolish loyalty.
I believed that Lǐ Líng had always shared the sweet and divided the little with his officers,
and thus could win men's desperate efforts.
Even the famous generals of antiquity
could not surpass him.
Though he himself had fallen into defeat,
from what I could see of his intentions,
he still wished to find an opportunity to repay the Han.
The matter had already reached a point beyond help,
but the destruction he had wrought
was achievement enough to be displayed to the world.
I wished to present these thoughts,
but had no way to do so.
Then, it happened that I was summoned for questioning,
and so I took this occasion to elaborate on Lǐ Líng's merits,
hoping to broaden the sovereign's understanding
and block the words of petty resentment.
I did not succeed in making everything clear,
and the enlightened sovereign did not comprehend.
He thought I was slandering Èrshī [General Lǐ Guǎnglì]
and speaking in advocacy for Lǐ Líng.
Thereupon I was handed over to the law officials.
My sincere loyalty
could not, in the end, be presented in my own defense.
Thus I was accused of deceiving the sovereign,
and the verdict of the officials was finally carried out.
My family was poor,
and the wealth for bribes was insufficient to ransom myself;
my friends and associates offered no rescue;
those close to the sovereign
did not speak a single word on my behalf.
My body is not made of wood or stone,
yet alone I was placed among the law officials,
deeply confined within prison walls.
To whom could I tell my sorrow?
This is something you, Shàoqīng, personally witnessed.
Is what I have related not true?
Lǐ Líng, having surrendered alive,
brought ruin to his family's reputation;
and I, in turn, was placed in the silkworm chamber,
becoming doubly an object of ridicule for the world.
How tragic!
How tragic!
These matters are not easily explained, one by one, to ordinary people.
My ancestors
had no merit of splitting tallies or receiving red-lettered patents,
and my work with documents, history, astronomy, and calendars
is akin to that of diviners and invocators,
truly something for the ruler to toy with,
kept like entertainers and jesters,
and despised by common custom.
If I were to submit to the law and accept execution,
it would be like losing one hair from nine oxen—
how would I differ from ants or mole crickets?
Moreover, the world would not count me among those who died for integrity;
instead, they would think I had exhausted my wisdom and reached the extremity of crime,
unable to escape by myself,
and thus ended up dying.
Why is this?
It is because of what I have established for myself that makes it so.
All men must die once,
but some deaths are weightier than Tài Shān,
while others are lighter than a goose feather—
it is the purpose for which one dies that differs.
The highest is not to bring disgrace upon one’s ancestors;
next is not to disgrace one’s own person;
next is not to disgrace one’s dignity and countenance;
next is not to disgrace one’s words;
next is to suffer disgrace by bending the body;
next is to suffer disgrace by changing into prisoner’s garb;
next is to suffer disgrace by being bound with wooden fetters and beaten with rods;
next is to suffer disgrace by having the hair shaved and wearing an iron collar;
next is to suffer disgrace by mutilating the skin and flesh or amputating limbs;
the lowest is castration—
the extreme!
The Record says:
“Punishments do not extend up to the great officers.”
This means that the integrity of a gentleman must be encouraged.
When a fierce tiger is in the deep mountains,
all beasts tremble with fear;
but when it is in a cage or pit,
it wags its tail begging for food—
this is the gradual effect of accumulated intimidation and constraint.
Therefore, even if one draws a circle on the ground as a prison,
its force is such that one must not enter;
if one carves a wooden figure as a jailer,
this is to decide on a course while still fresh.
Now, with hands and feet bound,
subjected to wooden fetters,
exposing bare skin,
enduring flogging and beating,
confined within circular walls—
at such a time,
upon seeing a jailer, one knocks one’s head on the ground;
at the sight of prison guards, one is filled with fear and holds one’s breath.
Why?
It is the accumulated force of intimidation and constraint.
And when it has come to this,
to say one is not disgraced
is merely what is called putting on a brave face—
how can it be considered honorable!
Moreover, Xī Bó
was a lord,
yet he was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ;
Lǐ Sī
was a chancellor,
yet he suffered the Five Punishments;
Huáiyīn
was a king,
yet he was shackled in Chén;
Péng Yuè and Zhāng Áo,
facing south and calling themselves “the solitary ones,”
were imprisoned and held accountable for crimes;
Jiàng Hóu executed the various Lǚs,
his power overshadowing the Five Hegemons,
yet he was imprisoned in the Petition Chamber;
Wèi Qí
was a great general,
yet he wore convict’s red garments,
and was bound with the three wooden restraints;
Jì Bù became Qián’s slave to the Zhū family;
