Guàn Fū suffered disgrace in the Residence.
These men all reached the status of kings, marquises, generals, or chancellors,
their fame heard in neighboring states,
yet when accusations fell upon them and the net was cast,
they could not take their own lives by decisive action,
but remained in the dust and dirt.
Ancient and modern are one in this—
how can it be said they were not disgraced?
From this perspective,
courage and cowardice
are a matter of circumstance;
strength and weakness
are a matter of form.
This is clear!
What is there to wonder at?
If a man cannot end his own life early, outside the bounds of the law,
and instead gradually declines,
until he is under the whip and rod,
and only then wishes to uphold his integrity—
is that not too late?
The reason the ancients valued sparing punishment for great officers
is probably due to this.
Now, by human nature, all men cherish life and hate death,
think of their parents,
and care for their wives and children;
only when stirred by righteousness and principle do they act otherwise,
for there are things they cannot help.
Now, I am unfortunate,
having lost my parents early,
with no close brothers,
alone and isolated—
Shàoqīng, how do you think I regard my wife and children?
Moreover, the brave do not necessarily die for integrity;
a coward who admires righteousness
can find encouragement anywhere!
Though I am timid and wish to cling to life,
I also understand well the distinction between advancing and withdrawing.
Why would I sink myself into the disgrace of bonds and fetters?
Even male and female slaves
can take decisive action;
how much more should I, who have no alternative?
The reason I endure in secret and cling to life,
buried in filth without protest,
is that I regret my private aspirations remain unfulfilled,
and I despise the thought of passing away obscurely
with my literary brilliance unknown to later generations.
In ancient times, many who were wealthy and noble saw their names wiped away,
too many to record,
only the exceptionally outstanding and extraordinary are remembered.
Thus, King Wén was confined and expanded the Zhōu Yì;
Zhòng Ní was in distress and composed the Chūnqiū;
Qū Yuán was exiled,
and then wrote the Lí Sāo;
Zuǒ Qiū lost his sight,
and thereupon produced the Guóyǔ;
Sūnzǐ had his feet amputated,
and his Art of War was set forth;
Bù Wéi was banished to Shǔ,
and the world received the Lǚ Lǎn;
Hán Fēi was imprisoned in Qín,
and there are “Shuì Nán” and “Gū Fèn”;
the three hundred poems of the Shī
are mostly the works of sages and worthies giving vent to their indignation.
All these men had pent-up feelings in their hearts,
unable to put their Way into practice,
so they recounted past events,
thinking of those to come.
Just as Zuǒ Qiū had no eyes,
and Sūnzǐ had his feet cut off,
and in the end could not be employed,
they withdrew to discuss books and strategies,
to give vent to their indignation,
hoping to leave behind empty writings to make themselves known.
I have presumptuously,
in recent times, entrusted myself to inadequate words,
gathering the lost old accounts of the world,
examining their deeds in outline,
synthesizing their beginnings and ends,
investigating the patterns of success and failure, rise and decline,
from above reckoning from Xuānyuán,
down to the present,
making ten tables,
twelve basic annals,
eight treatises,
thirty hereditary houses,
seventy biographies,
in all one hundred and thirty chapters.
I also wished to explore the boundary between Heaven and man,
comprehend the changes from ancient to modern times,
and complete the words of one school.
The draft was not yet finished
when I met with this disaster.
Regretting it might not be completed,
I submitted to the extreme punishment without a resentful expression.
If I truly can complete this book and store it in a famous mountain,
passing it on to the right person,
spreading it in great cities and metropolises,
then I will have repaid the debt of my former disgrace,
and even if I were executed ten thousand times,
would I have any regrets?
Yet this can be spoken to the wise,
but is difficult to explain to ordinary people.
Moreover, it is not easy to live under the burden of disgrace,
for those in lowly positions are often slandered and criticized.
I encountered this calamity because of my words,
and have been greatly ridiculed by my fellow villagers,
thus defiling and shaming my ancestors.
How could I have the face to visit my parents' graves again?
Even after a hundred generations,
the stain will only grow deeper!
Therefore, my heart churns nine times a day,
and at home, I feel as if I have lost something,
while outside, I do not know where to go.
Whenever I think of this shame,
sweat inevitably soaks my back and clothes.
Being merely a servant within the palace gates,
how could I withdraw and hide in deep caves and cliffs?
Thus, I drift along with the customs,
conforming to the times,
to express my madness and confusion.
Now, Shàoqīng, you advise me to recommend the worthy and advance scholars—
is this not contrary to my private thoughts?
Even if I now wish to polish myself,
and adorn myself with elegant words,
it would be of no benefit,
unbelievable to the common people,
and would only bring further disgrace.
Only after death,
will right and wrong be determined.
This letter cannot fully convey my thoughts,
but I have briefly stated my stubborn ignorance.
Respectfully, I bow again.
I, Yùn, am of rotten talent and tainted conduct,
with neither literary refinement nor substance to rely on.
Fortunately, I inherited the legacy of my ancestors,
and was able to serve as a palace guard.
Encountering a change in circumstances,
I obtained a noble rank,
but it was ultimately beyond my capacity,
and I eventually met with disaster.
You, sir, pity my foolish ignorance,
and bestowed a letter instructing and admonishing me on my shortcomings,
with profound kindness.
However, I regret that you did not deeply consider the whole story,
but rashly followed the slander and praise of the common crowd.
To speak of my humble and foolish thoughts
might seem to oppose your intent and gloss over my faults,
but to remain silent and keep to myself
would likely violate Confucius' principle of each speaking his own aspirations.
Thus, I dare to briefly state my foolish thoughts,
hoping that a gentleman will examine them!
When my family was at its peak of prosperity,
ten rode in vermilion carriages,
holding positions among the high ministers,
with noble ranks as marquises,
leading the retinue of officials,
and participating in government affairs.
Yet I was unable to achieve any notable accomplishments at that time
to propagate virtue and transformation.
Nor could I join forces with my colleagues
to assist the court in rectifying oversights,
so I have long borne the blame of occupying a position without merit.
Clinging to salary and coveting power,
I could not withdraw of my own accord,
and thus encountered a sudden change,
unjustly slandered by words,
imprisoned in the northern palace gates,
with my wife and children filling the prison.
At that time,
I believed that even my complete destruction would not suffice to atone for my faults—
how could I have preserved my head
and returned to tend my ancestors' graves?
I humbly reflect on the grace of the sagely ruler,
which is immeasurable.
A gentleman pursues the Way,
finding joy and forgetting sorrow;
a petty man preserves his body,
finding pleasure and forgetting his crimes.
I secretly reflect that my faults are already great,
my conduct already deficient,
and I shall remain a farmer until the end of my days.
Therefore, I lead my wife and children,
exerting ourselves in farming and sericulture,
tending gardens and managing property,
to provide for the public needs.
I did not expect to be criticized and ridiculed for this as well.
What human emotions cannot restrain,
even sages do not forbid.
Thus, even for the most revered sovereign and parent,
the mourning at their passing
has its time and end.
As for my offense,
it has already been three years.
Farming is arduous labor,
but during the seasonal festivals of Fú and Là,
we roast lamb and cook young goat,
and toast with a jug of wine to reward ourselves.
My family is originally from Qín,
so I can sing Qín tunes.
My wife is a woman from Zhào,
skilled in playing the zither.
Several of our servants can sing,
and after drinking, with ears warmed,
we look up to the sky, beat on earthen jars, and sing "wūwū."
The song goes:
"Cultivate the southern hills,
overgrown and untended;
plant a hundred acres of beans,
only to have them fall and become stalks."
In life, one must seek pleasure—
why wait for wealth and honor?
On such days,
I brush my sleeves in joy,
wave them high and low,
stomp my feet and dance,
truly indulging without restraint,
unaware that it is improper.
Fortunately, I have some surplus wealth,
buying low and selling high,
pursuing a ten-percent profit.
This is the business of merchants,
a disgraceful occupation,
yet I personally engage in it.
A person of low standing
becomes the target of public slander,
shivering without being cold.
Even those who once knew me well
now bend with the wind,
so how could there be any praise for me?
Did not Master Dǒng say:
"Those who earnestly seek benevolence and righteousness,
constantly fearing they cannot transform the people—
this is the intent of ministers and officials;
those who earnestly seek wealth and profit,
constantly fearing poverty and want—
this is the concern of common people."
Thus, those whose ways differ do not consult one another.
How can you now hold me to the standards of ministers and officials?
The region of Xīhé was part of the state of Wèi,
flourishing under Lord Wén,
with the lingering legacy of Duàngān Mù and Tián Zǐfāng,
all of noble character and integrity,
knowing the distinction between advancing and withdrawing.
Recently, you left your homeland
and came to Āndìng.
Āndìng lies among mountains and valleys,
the old territory of the Kūnyí tribes,
where the people are greedy and vulgar.
Could it be that customs truly change a person?
Now I finally see your true aspirations.
In this era of Hàn's great prosperity,
I hope you strive diligently,
with no need for further words.
Time does not stand still,
the seasons flow like a stream.
The age of fifty
has suddenly arrived—
for you, it has just been reached,
while for me, it is already two years past.
Friends and acquaintances across the land
have nearly all passed away,
only Shèng Xiàozhāng of Kuàijī remains.
He is trapped by the Sūn clan,
his wife and children lost,
left alone and isolated,
in peril, sorrow, and hardship.
If worry could harm a person,
this man would not live long!
The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
"When feudal lords face destruction,
if Duke Huán cannot save them,
then Duke Huán is shamed."
Now, Xiàozhāng is truly a hero among men;
scholars across the land
rely on him to spread their fame,
yet he himself cannot avoid imprisonment,
with his life hanging by a thread.
My ancestor should not have to again discuss friends who bring harm or benefit,
which is why Zhū Mù wrote on severing ties.
If you could dispatch a single envoy,
bearing a brief letter,
then Xiàozhāng could be rescued,
and the way of friendship could be upheld.
The youth of today,
delight in slandering their elders,
and some may even mock and criticize Xiàozhāng.
Yet Xiàozhāng is truly a man of great renown under heaven,
praised and admired
by people from all nine regions.
The lord of Yān purchased the bones of a fine steed,
not because he wished to gallop along the roads,
but rather to attract truly exceptional horses.
You, sir, are restoring the Hàn dynasty;
the ancestral temples were on the verge of collapse,
and you have been able to set them right again.
The method of setting things right
truly requires obtaining worthy men.
Pearls and jade come without legs,
because people desire them;
how much more so for worthy men, who have feet?
King Zhāo built a terrace to honor Guō Kuí;
although Kuí was a man of minor talent, he encountered great fortune,
and was ultimately able to inspire the sincere heart of an enlightened ruler.
Thus, Yuè Yì came from Wèi,
Jù Xīn came from Zhào,
and Zōu Yǎn came from Qí.
If Guō Kuí had been hanging upside down and the king did not release him,
or if he faced danger and the king did not save him,
then the scholars would have soared high and fled far away,
with none turning their heads toward the road to Yān.
All that I have cited and referenced
is already known to you, sir,
but I reiterate it
because I wish you to uphold and cherish this principle.
I have thus expressed myself, though not exhaustively.
I have heard that the wise plan according to the times,
while fools act contrary to reason.
I have often privately grieved for Jīngchéng Tàishū, who, due to his insatiability and lack of worthy assistants,
ultimately brought ruin upon himself in Zhèng.
Bótōng, with his reputation, governs a commandery,
having contributed to the founding of the dynasty;
overseeing the people and personally attending to his duties,
he cherishes the granaries and storehouses.
As for Fú, who bears the responsibility of military campaigns,
he seeks to adapt to the times and address emergencies;
both are acting for the sake of the state.
If you suspect Fú of slandering you,
why not go to the court and present your case yourself,
rather than resorting to a plan that will exterminate your clan?
The court's treatment of Bótōng
has also been generous;
entrusting him with a large commandery,
investing him with military authority,
assigning him responsibilities as a pillar of the state,
and treating him with the affection due to one's own descendants.
Even a common man or a humble serving woman can sacrifice their life for a single meal;
how could one who wears three official seals,
governing a great region,
disregard grace and righteousness,
and harbor thoughts of rebellion?
When Bótōng speaks with officials and the people,
what face can he show?
When walking, bowing, or rising,
what countenance can he present?
When sitting or lying down, pondering this,
what can he feel in his heart?
Holding up a mirror to look at his reflection,
how can he bear to face himself?
In his actions and achievements,
what kind of man is he?
Alas!
To abandon an excellent and fine reputation,
and instead devise treacherous schemes like an owl,
to cast away the blessings of a hereditary legacy,
and invite the heavy disaster of ruin and defeat,
to discourse loftily on the ways of Yáo and Shùn,
yet be unable to restrain the nature of Jié and Zhòu,
to be laughed at by the world while alive,
and become a foolish ghost after death—
is this not pitiable!
Bótōng and Gěng Xiáyóu both rose to assist in founding the dynasty,
and both received the state's grace.
Xiáyóu was humble and yielding,
often expressing modest and self-deprecating words,
while Bótōng boasted of himself,
believing his achievements surpassed all under heaven.
In the past, there was a pig in Liáodōng
that gave birth to a white-headed piglet.
Thinking it extraordinary, they presented it as tribute.
On the way to Hédōng,
they saw that all the pigs there were white,
and returned in shame.
If you, sir, consider your achievements superior and speak of them at court,
you are like the pig of Liáodōng.
Now, in your folly and arrogance,
you compare yourself to the Six States.
In the time of the Six States,
each was powerful in its own right,
expanding territories for thousands of *lǐ*,
with armies approaching a million strong.
Thus, they could each hold their states and contend with one another,
for many years.
Now, how many *lǐ* does the empire span?
How many cities are there in the various commanderies?
How can you, with the insignificant region of Yúyáng, provoke the enmity of the Son of Heaven?
This is like the people by the riverbank
trying to block the Mèngjīn ford with handfuls of earth—
it only shows their lack of self-awareness!
Now, the empire has just been stabilized,
and all within the seas desire peace.
Scholars, whether worthy or not,
all delight in establishing their names in the world.
Yet Bótōng alone raves like a madman,
casting himself away in this prosperous age,
listening internally to the misguided counsel of a jealous woman,
and trusting externally the flattering words of slanderous villains.
He will long serve as a negative example for the feudal lords,
and forever be a warning to meritorious ministers.
Is this not a grave error!
Those who stabilize the empire hold no personal grudges.
Do not let past events cause you doubt.
I hope you will consider your elderly mother and younger brother.
In all actions, do not cause pain to those close to you,
while bringing joy to your enemies.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month,
Hóng states:
Previously, after the initial defeat of the rebels,
my spirits were high and my ambitions extravagant,
so my accounts of events were somewhat exaggerated.
Having received your letter dated the twentieth day of the ninth month,
I read it with delight and laughter,
fondling it without tiring.
I also intended to have Chén Lín draft a reply.
But Lín has been occupied with many matters lately,
and could not do it.
Thinking to bring you joy from afar,
I have therefore exerted this old man's thoughts.
The words are many and cannot be listed one by one;
I have roughly outlined the main points,
to serve as conversation and amusement.
The terrain of Hànzhōng
is truly rugged and secure;
the Four Peaks and Three Paths
are not comparable to it.
They have tens of thousands of elite armored troops,
holding the heights and guarding the strategic points.
With one man brandishing a halberd,
ten thousand cannot advance.
Yet when our army passed through,
it was like a startled whale bursting through a fine net,
or a charging rhinoceros tearing through Lǔ gauze—
these are insufficient to describe the ease.
Although it is said that the army of a true king
marches without engaging in battle,
being strong without righteousness
has often been seen among the ancients.
Thus, even in the age of Táng and Yú,
the barbarians troubled Xià;
and in the prosperity of King Xuān of Zhōu,
there were also conflicts with great states.
The *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents* lament and record
the difficulty of such matters.
These all relied on rugged terrain and remote locations,
which made it so.
Therefore, considering this terrain,
I would say that even a man of average talent defending it
would be difficult to overcome hastily.
Your letter recounts their heinous and deluded crimes,
and describes the vast and generous virtue of the royal army—
how could it not be believed!
This is why Xià and Yīn perished,
and why Miáo and Hù were defeated;
why we were victorious,
and why they were defeated.
Otherwise,
how could Shāng and Zhōu have been unmatched?
In the past, Guǐfāng was deaf and benighted,
Chónghǔ was slanderous and vicious,
and Yīn Xīn was tyrannical and cruel—
all three were of the lowest category.
Yet Gāozōng campaigned for three years,
King Wén had an army that retreated to cultivate virtue,
and there were repeated campaigns at Méngjīn,
before they could defeat the enemy and overcome Yīn,
achieving these military accomplishments.
How could there have been anything like stars streaming and light gathering,
like a whirlwind seizing and thunder striking,
sweeping across mountains and rivers,
achieving victory from morning till dusk,
as there is today!
From this perspective,
if they are indeed not inferior to the most foolish,
then the defense of a person of average talent,
would not be otherwise, as is clear.
For one of average talent, it is said not to be so,
yet your letter suggests that their wickedness is so ripe,
even with Sūn, Tián, Mò, or Lí,
there would be no salvation,
which I privately doubt.
Why?
In ancient warfare,
even if an enemy state was in chaos,
if there were still virtuous men,
they would not be attacked.
Thus, before the three benevolent men departed,
King Wǔ of Zhōu withdrew his army;
while Gōng Zhī was in Yú,
Jìn did not raise arms;
while Jì Liáng remained,
mighty Chǔ’s schemes were thwarted.
Only when the multitude of worthies fled or were expelled,
did the three states become ruins.
This shows that if there are still people despite the ruler’s lack of virtue,
the situation can still be remedied.
Moreover, Mòzǐ’s defense,
using cords as walls,
was so high it could not be scaled;
breaking chopsticks as weapons,
so firm they could not be breached.
As for holding Yángpíng,
occupying Shímén,
deploying the Eight Formations,
and employing the strategy of the galloping oxen,
how could they crumble like earth or rot like fish!
If we suppose that defenses, whether clever or clumsy,
could all be scaled,
then Gōngshū would have already overrun Sòng’s walls,
and Yuè Yì would have already taken Jímò.
Why then is Mò Dí’s art praised?
Why is Tián Dān’s wisdom esteemed?
I, though not clever,
have never heard of such before.
I have heard that those passing through Gāotáng,
imitate Wáng Bào’s songs;
those wandering Suīhuàn,
learn the colorful patterns of embroidery.
Since entering Yì Province,
I have admired the legacy of Sīmǎ, Yáng, and Wáng,
and have developed a desire for literary excellence,
hence I have vigorously applied myself to writing,
different from before.
It is strange that you belittle my humble origins,
calling me a hired pen,
what kind of talk is this?
The green steed hangs its ears in the forest wilds.
The swan and sparrow fold their wings in muddy ponds,
those who demean them naturally regard them as ordinary birds of the garden,
inferior steeds of the outer stable.
But when they adjust their sinews,
spread their strong wings,
soar through the clear skies,
and gaze over a thousand miles,
how can one say they borrowed feathers from the morning wind,
or borrowed feet from the six-hued steed!
I fear you still do not believe my words,
and will surely laugh heartily.
Hóng respectfully states.
Since our separation,
it has now been three years,
not a day passes without remembering our former friendship.
It is like the bond of marriage,
where affection runs deep;
the regret of parting,
though recent, is still shallow.
I hold this feeling in my heart,
how could you not share it!
Whenever I observe the reasons for changes in ancient and modern times,
due to encroachments and insults,
or arising from flaws and rifts,
hearts grow resentful and minds unsettled,
leading to great upheavals.
Like Hán Xìn’s heartache at losing Chǔ,
Péng Chǒng’s accumulated resentment at receiving no special treatment,
Lú Wǎn’s suspicion and fear over existing rifts,
Yīng Bù’s anxiety and pressure from leaked secrets,
these are the causes of such events.
My relationship with you, General, is as close as flesh and bone,
I ceded the region south of the Yangtze to you,
not keeping it under my own province,
unlike the regret of Huáiyīn abandoning his old ties.
I restrained Liú Fù,
and our mutual affection grew even stronger,
far from allowing Zhū Fú’s open memorial to stand.
I did not conceal Zhāng Shèng’s loan incident,
nor was there any secret plot or report like Fèi Hè’s,
certainly there was no rift like that of the King of Yān or Huáinán.
Yet you cruelly severed the royal command,
openly abandoned a profound friendship,
truly manipulated by sycophants.
Words that seem plausible,
never fail to move listeners,
shaping images according to circumstances,
easily altering perspectives.
Showing the prospect of calamity,
stirring with shame and disgrace,
the ambitious heart of a great man,
cannot but be roused to fury.
In the past, Sū Qín persuaded Hán,
shaming it as the tail of an ox,
the King of Hán grasped his sword, changed countenance, and raged,
even though troops were defeated and land ceded,
he did not regret it,
such is human nature.
You, benevolent lord, are young and vigorous,
trusting those you favor,
both fearing calamity’s approach,
and harboring resentment,
unable to consider my intentions from afar,
or assess the immediate situation,
thus hastily deciding based on perceived slights,
adopting a sudden and firm resolution.
Added to this, Liú Bèi fanned the flames,
entangling matters and linking conflicts,
pushing them forward.
I believe your true heart,
did not wish for this.
My virtue is meager,
my position high and responsibilities heavy,
fortunate to encounter the state’s rising fortunes,
pacifying the realm,
embracing and gathering diverse peoples,
joyful in achieving complete success,
long enjoying its blessings.
Yet marital ties are broken,
strong support gives way to rift,
I often fear the world largely blames me,
thinking this old man harbors treacherous intentions,
secretly scheming like Zhèng Wǔ taking the Hú,
causing you, benevolent lord, to suddenly cut ties.
Therefore, I am filled with indignation,
ashamed and restless,
constantly thinking to set aside minor matters,
renew our former friendship,
bringing glory to both our clans,
blessing future generations,
to demonstrate the sincerity of our pure intentions.
Holding this thought for years,
I have not been able to express it.
In the past, during the battle of Chìbì,
we encountered a plague,
burned our ships and withdrew,
to avoid that cursed land,
it was not due to suppression by Zhōu Yú’s navy.
As for defending Jiānglíng,
supplies exhausted, grain depleted,
with nothing left to hold,
we moved the people and withdrew our troops,
again not something Yú could defeat.
The land of Jīng was not originally mine to begin with,
I gave it all to you,
hoping to take the remainder,
not to encroach on your flesh,
or cause any loss.
Considering this change,
it does no harm to me,
why would I willingly persist in this,
without turning back?
Emperor Gāo established a noble title to summon Tián Héng,
Emperor Guāngwǔ pointed to the river and swore to Zhū Wěi,
your burdens and troubles,
how could they compare to those two?
Thus, with utmost sincerity,
I wish to hear your gracious reply.
In previous years at Qiáo,
I newly built ships and boats,
taking just enough to carry myself,
and went as far as Jiǔjiāng,
wishing only to observe the shape of the lakes and marshes,
and to pacify the people along the riverbanks—
it was not a plan for deep penetration or aggressive warfare.
I fear that those who discuss matters greatly glorify themselves,
thinking their strategies successful,
believing the western troubles will be forever gone;
precisely for this reason,
they are unwilling to reconsider.
Yet the wise man’s considerations
consider what has not yet taken form;
the perceptive man’s plans
plan for what has not yet shown signs.
Thus, Zǐxū knew that Gūsū would become a haunt for deer;
Fǔ Guǒ recognized that Zhì Bó would be captured by Zhào.
Mù Shēng pleaded illness
to avoid the troubles of Chǔ;
Zōu Yáng traveled north,
and did not share in Wú’s calamity.
These four gentlemen—
were they sages?
Merely through understanding change and thinking deeply,
they discerned the significant from the subtle.
With your intelligence,
observe my methods and calculations;
measure the territory you hold,
compare and reckon the lands—
is it truly that your position is weak and strength lacking,
unable to advance far,
so you merely cling to the region south of the Yangtze,
seeking only ease and comfort?
Surely this is not so!
If you rely on naval warfare,
guarding the river and blocking strategic points,
hoping to prevent the royal army from ever crossing,
that may not necessarily succeed either.
For naval warfare over a thousand *lǐ*,
the tactics and ruses are myriad.
When Yuè divided into three armies,
Wú could not withstand them;
when Hàn secretly crossed at Xiàyáng,
Wèi Bào was caught unprepared.
Though rivers are broad,
their length is hard to defend.
In all matters, there is what is appropriate;
I cannot say everything,
but I wish to restore old friendship while displaying strength,
and not further threaten and pressure the enemy.
Yet I have fears—
fear that this letter may be of no use.
Why?
In the past, when the army pressed close, you withdrew on your own;
today, while I am far away, you offer appeasement and acceptance—
your words are humble but your intent narrow,
thinking my strength exhausted,
which only adds to your arrogance.
It is not enough to move you;
I merely clarify by citing the past,
and you should plan for yourself.
Formerly, Huáinán trusted Zuǒ Wú’s strategy;
Hàn’s Wěi Xiāo accepted Wáng Yuán’s words;
Péng Chǒng followed his close subordinate’s plan—
these three men did not awaken,
and ended as laughingstocks for the world.
King Liáng did not accept Guǐ Shèng’s advice;
Dòu Róng expelled Zhāng Xuán—
these two worthies, once awakened,
had fortune follow them.
I hope you will give this some thought.
If you can internally remove Zǐbù,
and externally strike Liú Bèi,
to demonstrate sincere loyalty,
and restore our former friendship,
then the responsibility for the region south of the Yangtze,
I will long entrust to you;
high position and weighty rank
will be plainly visible.
Above, it will spare the imperial court the toil of eastern concerns;
below, it will let the common people preserve the blessing of safety—
you will enjoy the glory,
I will receive the benefit—
is that not delightful!
If you neglect utmost sincerity and dwell on侥幸,
sparing those two men,
unable to bear imposing punishment,
this is so-called petty kindness,
the thief of great benevolence—
a man of great refinement
would not do such a thing.
If you pity Zǐbù,
wishing his words to be preserved together,
and can also wholeheartedly cast aside resentment,
acceding to your feelings,
I will again work with you,
taking the later good.
But capturing Liú Bèi alone
would also suffice as proof.
I present these two options;
carefully choose one.
I have heard from various generals of Jīng and Yáng,
and also from those who surrendered,
all saying that Jiāozhōu has been seized by you,
that Yùzhāng resists orders,
not accepting your authority,
that plague and drought occur together,
men and soldiers are reduced and weakened,
and each seeks to advance the army—
such are their words.
Hearing this,
I am not pleased.
Yet the roads are distant,
and those who surrender are hard to trust;
rejoicing in others’ calamities
is not what a gentleman does.
Moreover, the people belong to the state;
with sincere concern,
I delight in promoting harmony,
hoping for bright virtue,
that you may come to show clear support,
achieving stability without toil—
this would be more precious to me.
Therefore, I hold the troops in place,
and send this letter to convey my intent.
In ancient times, when armies clashed,
envoys moved between them;
I hope that you, benevolent sir, and I may open our hearts and reconsider,
responding to the poet’s sigh of mending the robe,
and heed the *Zhōuyì*’s meaning of “pulled back to return.”
Wash your scales in the clear stream,
spread your wings on the heavenly road—
the good time is here;
only encouragement is needed.
The eighteenth day of the fifth month,
Pī writes:
Jìchóng, I hope you are well.
Though the road is short,
and official duties confine,
the longing to speak with you
is truly hard to bear.
The place you govern is remote and out of the way;
letters and inquiries are few,
which only adds to my longing.
Whenever I recall our past wanderings in Nánpí,
they are truly unforgettable.
We pondered the profundities of the Six Classics,
and roamed freely among the Hundred Schools;
we set up chess for leisure,
and ended with games of liùbó;
lofty conversations delighted our hearts,
plaintive zithers pleased our ears.
We galloped on the northern grounds,
and feasted in the southern lodge;
floating sweet melons in clear springs,
sinking crimson plums in cold water.
When the white sun had hidden,
followed by the bright moon,
we rode together in the same carriage,
to wander in the rear garden;
the carriage wheels turned slowly,
attendants silent;
clear winds rose at night,
sad reed-pipes softly hummed;
joy departed, sorrow came,
and desolation wounded the heart.
I looked back and said,
“This happiness is hard to keep”;
you and your companions
all agreed.
Now indeed we are separated,
each in a different place.
Yuányú has long passed away,
transformed into a different substance;
whenever this thought comes,
when can we speak of it!
Now, as Ruíbīn marks the season,
the jǐng wind fans all things,
the weather mild and warm,
and all fruits abundant.
I sometimes ride out to wander,
northward along the river bend;
attendants sound reed-pipes to clear the way,
literary men ride in the following carriage.
The season is the same, the times different;
things remain, people are gone—
how weary I am!
Now I send a rider to Yè,
so he may make a detour to visit you.
Go forth, and take care of yourself.
Pī writes.
On the third day of the second month,
Pī writes:
Time passes easily,
and it has already been nearly four years since we parted.
Not seeing each other for three years,
even the Dōngshān would lament its distance,
how much more so when it exceeds that?
How can one bear the longing!
Although letters have been exchanged back and forth,
they are insufficient to dispel the weariness and sorrow.
In the past year, due to the plague,
many relatives and old friends suffered from the disaster.
Xú Gàn, Chén Lín, Yìng Chàng, and Liú Zhēn—
all passed away within a short time.
How painful it is to speak of it!
In the past, when we traveled and spent time together,
we rode in carriages side by side,
and when we stopped, our mats were joined.
Never were we apart even for a moment.
Whenever cups of wine circulated,
and string and wind instruments played together,
with wine warming our ears and hearts,
we would look up and compose poems.
At such times,
we hardly realized how joyful we were.
We thought it was our lot to live a hundred years,
and that we could long preserve our companionship.
Who would have thought that within a few years,
they would nearly all be gone?
Speaking of it breaks my heart!
Recently, I compiled their remaining writings,
gathering them into a single collection.
Looking at their names,
they are already recorded among the ghosts.
Recalling our past travels,
they still linger in my mind and heart,
yet these friends
have turned to dust and soil.
What more can be said!
Observing scholars throughout history,
most do not guard their minor conduct,
and few are able to establish themselves with reputation and integrity.
Yet Wěicháng alone possessed both literary talent and substance,
serene and with few desires,
holding the aspiration of retiring to Jīshān.
He can truly be called a refined gentleman.
He wrote more than twenty chapters of the Zhōng Lùn,
forming a unique school of thought.
His language and ideas are elegant and classical,
worthy of being passed down to later generations.
This man has achieved immortality.
Déliǎn often had a brilliant desire to write and create,
and his talent and learning were sufficient to produce books.
Yet his fine aspirations were not fulfilled—
truly a great pity.
Recently, as I perused the writings of these friends,
I wiped away tears while facing them,
grieving for the departed,
and reflecting on myself as well.
Kǒngzhāng’s memorials and petitions were exceptionally vigorous,
though slightly verbose and ornate.
Gōnggàn had an untrammeled spirit,
but it lacked intensity;
however, the best of his five-character poems
surpassed his contemporaries in excellence.
Yuányú’s letters and documents were graceful and elegant,
truly delightful.
Zhòngxuān continued to excel in poetic prose,
though it is a pity his style was weak,
unable to fully elevate his writing.
Yet in what he excelled at,
even the ancients could not far surpass him.
In the past, Bóyá broke his strings after Zhōngqī’s death,
and Zhòngní overturned the meat sauce upon Zǐlù’s demise—
grieving the difficulty of encountering a true friend,
and lamenting that disciples could not match their master.
Although these friends may not have equaled the ancients,
they were the outstanding talents of their time.
Those who remain today
are already not their equals.
The younger generation is to be regarded with awe,
and future talents should not be underestimated,
yet I fear neither you nor I will live to see them.
My years have already grown long,
and my thoughts are endless.
At times, worries arise,
keeping me awake all night.
When will my spirit ever be like it was in the past?
I have already become an old man,
though my hair is not yet white.
Emperor Guāngwǔ said that after turning thirty,
he spent ten years in the army,
experiencing countless changes.
Though my virtue cannot compare to his,
my age is now the same.
With the substance of a dog or sheep,
yet clad in the stripes of a tiger or leopard;
lacking the brightness of the many stars,
I merely borrow the light of the sun and moon.
Every move is watched and observed—
when will this ever change?
I fear I will never again experience the joys of our past travels.
In youth, one must truly strive,
for once the years have passed,
how can they be retrieved!
The ancients longed to hold a torch and wander at night—
indeed, they had good reason.
How have you been amusing yourself lately?
Have you been engaged in any writing or creation?
Gazing eastward with sorrow,
I write this letter to express my heart.
Pī writes.
Pī writes:
Fine jade is compared to the virtue of a gentleman;
guī and zhāng jades are praised by poets.
The Chuíjí of Jìn,
the Yúfán of Lǔ,
the Jiélǜ of Sòng,
the Hépú of Chǔ—
their worth surpassed ten thousand gold,
valued throughout the capital cities,
praised in the past,
and their fame flows into the future.
Thus, when the Chuíjí left Jìn,
both Yú and Guó were captured;
when the Héshì Bì entered Qín,
Lìn Xiàngrú stood firm in his integrity.
I have privately read jade texts praising beautiful jade,
white as sliced fat,
black like pure lacquer,
red resembling a rooster’s comb,
yellow matching steamed chestnuts.
I have heard such descriptions,
but never witnessed such forms.
Though my virtue is not that of a gentleman,
nor my righteousness that of a poet,
I privately admire
the high mountains and great paths.
Yet these four treasures are now distant and remote,
and since Qín and Hàn, none have been heard to compare.
For years I sought them,
but never encountered their true form.
My private wish remained unfulfilled,
and my thirst was not quenched.
Recently, Zōng Huìshū of Nányáng mentioned that you, my lord, once possessed a beautiful jué jade.
Hearing this, I was startled and delighted,
laughter and joy mingling.
I intended to write to you myself,
but feared the rumor might be inaccurate,
so I had my younger brother Zǐjiàn, through Xún Zhòngmào,
convey my humble intention at an opportune moment.
You did not neglect or disregard it,
but generously offered high praise.
When the messenger from Yè arrived,
and the precious jué first came,
I held the casket and knelt to open it.
My innermost being trembled with awe.
As the cords were undone and the casket opened,
a dazzling brilliance filled my eyes.
With my ignorant and humble nature,
I was able to behold a treasure rare in the world.
Without troubling a single envoy,
nor diminishing its worth of connected cities,
I experienced the sight of Zhāoxiāng of Qín at Zhāngtái,
yet without the deceit and seizure of Lìn Xiàngrú.
Your generous gift is even more abundant,
how dare I not reverently accept it?
I respectfully offer a piece of poetic prose,
to praise its beautiful essence.
Pī writes.
Zhí writes:
Several days without seeing you,
I miss you so much it pains me,
and I imagine you feel the same.
Since childhood, I have loved writing,
and up to now,
it has been twenty-five years.
As for the writers of our time,
I can briefly discuss them.
In the past, Zhòngxuān stood alone in Hànnán,
Kǒngzhāng soared like an eagle in Héshuò,
Wěicháng gained fame in Qīngtǔ,
Gōnggàn displayed literary brilliance in Hǎiyú,
Déliǎn rose to prominence here in Wèi,
and you, my friend, looked down from the capital with lofty vision.
At that time,
everyone claimed to hold the pearl of the divine serpent,
each household boasted of possessing the jade of Jīngshān.
Our prince then set a heavenly net to encompass them all,
gathered the eight directions to cover them,
and now they are all assembled in this state.
Yet these few men,
still cannot soar to the highest heights,
nor travel a thousand miles in a single leap.
With Kǒngzhāng’s talent,
he is not skilled in poetic composition,
yet often claims to match Sīmǎ Xiàngrú in style—
like trying to paint a tiger but ending up with a dog.
I previously wrote mocking him,
but he instead wrote an essay praising my admiration for his writing.
Zhōng Zǐqī never misjudged music,
and is still praised today.
I too cannot forget to sigh,
fearing later generations will laugh at me.
People’s writings
cannot be without flaws.
I often welcome others to criticize my compositions,
and when there are shortcomings,
I revise them promptly.
In the past, Dīng Jìnglǐ often wrote short pieces
and asked me to polish them.
I thought my talent was no greater than his,
so I declined to do so.
Jìnglǐ said to me:
“Why do you hesitate?
Whether the writing is good or bad,
I will know it myself.
In later ages, who will know it was you who finalized my work?”
I have often admired this insightful remark,
considering it a fine saying.
In the past, even Confucius’s writings
were circulated among others for discussion,
but when it came to compiling the Spring and Autumn Annals,
even disciples like Zǐyóu and Zǐxià could not alter a single word.
Beyond this, I have never seen
anyone whose words are without flaw.
Only one with the beauty of Nánwēi
can discuss the loveliness of others.
Only one with the sharpness of Lóngquán
can comment on the cutting of blades.
Liú Jìxù’s talent does not match that of true writers,
yet he delights in disparaging their works,
picking out their strengths and weaknesses.
In the past, Tián Bā slandered the Five Emperors,
condemned the Three Sovereigns,
and criticized the Five Hegemons at Jìxià—
in one day, he convinced a thousand people.
Yet with one discourse, Lǔ Lián
made him shut his mouth for life.
Liú’s arguments
are not as formidable as Tián’s,
and today’s Zhònglián
is not hard to find—
can such criticism not cease?
Everyone has their own preferences:
the fragrance of lán, chǎi, sūn, and huì
is loved by the masses,
yet by the seaside there are those who chase after foul odors;
the music of Xiánchí and Liùjīng
brings joy to all,
yet Mò Dí had arguments against it—
how can tastes be the same?
Now I send you a copy of the poetic compositions I wrote in my youth.
Even street talk and alley gossip
must contain something worth gathering;
the songs of cart-drivers
may resonate with the Odes and Elegantiae.
The thoughts of a common man
should not be lightly dismissed.
Poetic composition is a minor art,
indeed insufficient to extol great principles
or illuminate them for future generations.
In the past, Yáng Zǐyún was merely a halberd-bearing official of the former dynasty,
yet he said a true man would not engage in it.
Though my virtue is shallow,
and my position is that of a feudal lord,
I still hope to exert myself for the state,
spread kindness to the common people,
establish enduring achievements,
and leave a legacy as lasting as metal and stone.
How could I merely take writing as my merit,
or poetic composition as the mark of a gentleman?
If my aspirations are not realized,
and my way does not prevail,
then I shall gather the true records of various officials,
discern the gains and losses of current customs,
determine the essence of benevolence and righteousness,
and establish a school of thought of my own.
Though I may not be able to hide it in a famous mountain,
I will pass it on to those who share my interests.
If not for entrusting it until white-haired old age,
why would I speak of this today?
That I speak without shame
relies on your understanding, like Huìzǐ knowing me.
I will meet you early tomorrow morning;
this letter cannot fully express my feelings.
Zhí writes.
Zhí writes:
Jìzhòng, my friend.
The other day, though due to routine duties,
we were able to sit closely together,
and though we feasted all day long,
given the rarity of our meetings and the distance of our partings,
it still did not fully relieve the weariness of longing.
As for the wine cups floating on waves before us,
and the flutes and reed pipes sounding behind,
you, my friend, soared like an eagle in posture,
gazed like a phoenix and glared like a tiger,
saying even Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shēn were not your match,
Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbīng not your equals.
Looking left and right,
you acted as if no one else was there—
is this not the bold ambition of a man like you?
Passing by a butcher’s shop and chewing heartily,
though one gets no meat,
it is precious for the momentary satisfaction.
At such a time,
I wish to lift Tàishān as meat,
pour the Eastern Sea as wine,
cut bamboo from Yúnmèng to make flutes,
and fell catalpa from the banks of the Sì River to make zithers.
To eat as if filling a giant ravine,
to drink as if pouring into a leaky cup—
such joy is truly immeasurable.
Is this not the joy of a great man?
Yet time does not wait for us;
the sun hurries on its course.
Before us, the fleeing shadows speed away;
between us, the separation is as vast as Shēn and Shāng.
I long to rein in the heads of the six dragons,
halt Xīhé’s reins,
pluck the blossoms of the Ruòmù tree,
and close the valley of Méngsì.
But the heavenly road is high and distant,
with no chance for a long while.
With yearning and restlessness,
what can be done, what can be done!
I received the letter you sent,
its literary grace intricate and winding,
radiant as spring blossoms,
clear as a fresh breeze.
Reading it over and over,
it felt as if we were face to face again.
As for the writings by the various worthies,
I imagine upon returning to your post,
you will read them again.
You might have an eager minor clerk recite them aloud.
The difficulty of writing
is not unique to our time.
Even the gentlemen of old
also struggled with it.
If every home had a thousand-mile steed,
then even a fine horse would not be prized;
if everyone held a foot-long jade,
then even Héshì’s jade would not be valued.
For a gentleman to understand music
is, according to ancient profound discourse,
called being broad yet obscured.
Mò Dí did not favor music,
so why did he turn his carriage upon reaching Zhāogē?
You, my friend, delight in music,
yet find yourself in the county where Mò Dí turned his carriage—
I hope you will help me see more clearly.
I have also heard that you, sir, are there,
and have established excellent governance.
There are those who seek but do not obtain,
but there has never been one who obtained without seeking.
Moreover, to change course and alter one’s actions
is not the driving of a good charioteer;
to change the people and govern them
is not the governance of Chǔ and Zhèng.
I only hope that you, sir, will strive in this.
Just now, facing esteemed guests,
I dictated this and could not express everything.
Let us correspond frequently to hear from each other.
Cáo Zhí states.
Zhì states:
Your letter has arrived,
and I have received your gracious gift.
Opening the envelope and unrolling the paper,
how magnificent is its literary brilliance,
and how profound its comforting words!
Only by ascending the Eastern Peak
does one then realize the winding paths of the lesser mountains;
only by serving the Most Honored
does one then understand the lowliness of a hundred lǐ.
Since my return,
I have pondered for five or six days,
up to ten days,
my spirit scattered, my thoughts wandering,
as if lost in confusion.
I dare not envy the glory of favor and radiance,
nor covet the wealth of Yīdùn.
Truly, with my humble status like that of dogs and horses,
and virtue lighter than a goose feather,
to have passed through the Dark Gate,
pushed open the Golden Gate,
ascended the Jade Hall,
prostrated before the empty railing of the front hall,
and feasted by the winding pool—
my dignified bearing was lacking,
my words were flawed and inadequate.
Though I relied on your nurturing of scholars, as noble as the Lord of Píngyuán,
I am ashamed to lack the talent of Máo Suì, who shone like an awl’s tip.
Deeply honored by the courtesy of Lord Xuē, who lowered himself,
yet I lack the effectiveness of Féng Xuān, who prepared three retreats.
Repeatedly receiving the virtue of Lord Xìnlíng, who left the left seat vacant,
yet I lack the admirable qualities of Hóu Shēng to recount.
All these points
are why I am filled with pent-up frustration in my breast,
and feel melancholy and distressed with longing.
If we were to recall the previous banquet,
and say it was not fully enjoyed,
pouring the sea as wine,
heaping mountains as delicacies,
cutting bamboo in Yúnmèng,
felling catalpa by the Sì River’s banks,
only then could we exhaust refined sentiments,
and fully express joyous feelings.
Truly, such grandeur befits a noble son,
and is not something a humble person like me could hope for.
As for my own aspirations,
they truly lie in what is ordained by Heaven.
I long to cast aside my seal and official insignia,
to attend you morning and evening, seated by your side,
studying the teachings left by Zhòngfǔ,
perusing the essential words of Lǎozǐ,
facing clear wine without drinking,
restraining myself from enjoying fine delicacies,
letting Xīshī emerge from behind the curtain,
while Mómǔ attends at my side—
this is the path of great virtue,
and what the wise and discerning uphold.
As for the recent spectacle,
it truly stirred my humble heart.
Qín zithers sounded their notes,
sixteen dancers performed in succession.
Xūn and xiáo flutes resonated within splendid halls,
spirit drums stirred beside the seats.
My ears were so overwhelmed they seemed to hear nothing,
my spirit leapt as if on a galloping horse.
I thought it could awe the Sùshèn in the north,
making them offer their arrowwood arrows;
shake the Bǎiyuè in the south,
making them present their white pheasants;
how much more so Sūn Quán and Liú Bèi—
what are they worth looking at!
Upon returning to my duties, I pondered and appreciated your writings,
observing and reflecting on their excellence,
truly they are the model of odes and eulogies,
the teacher of writers.
The works composed by the many worthies
also each have their own aspirations.
In the past, when Zhào Wǔ passed through Zhèng,
the seven sons composed poems,
the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded and listed them,
considering it a beautiful tale.
I am but a petty man,
unable to fulfill your command.
Moreover, my reply to your gift,
its words crude and meaning shallow,
even after repeated revisions,
makes me break into a sweat of shame.
The people of this region
are well-versed in poetic prose,
the three high ministers
all recite and chant them—
how could it be only minor officials!
You have bestowed repeated kindness and earnest words,
instructing me on governance and affairs,
your compassionate grace
manifest in writing.
Mòzǐ turned his carriage back,
and I have been here for four years;
though I have no virtue toward the people,
they sing and dance in praise.
The differences between Confucianism and Mohism
have indeed been long-standing.
Yet a force of one brigade
is insufficient to spread one’s fame;
within a few steps
one cannot gallop far.
If we do not change course and alter our driving,
how can we exert our strength effectively!
Now, to seek great achievements while remaining here
is like hobbling the feet of a fine steed
and demanding it bear the task of a thousand lǐ;
caging a monkey
and expecting it to display nimble agility.
I am overwhelmed by your concern,
and respectfully append this reply,
not daring to be verbose.
Wú Zhì states.
Qú states:
Yesterday, you did not neglect me,
but graciously came to visit.
Even in the past, when Hóu Shēng received regard at the Yí Gate,
and Máo Gōng was favored at the inn,
it could not surpass this.
Outwardly, I praise your humble and respectful virtue, young master;
inwardly, I rejoice that my stubborn talent has found a sincere friend.
Joyful and elated,
my feelings are boundless.
Therefore, I dispatched servants in haste,
spreading orders to seek far and wide,
like Yáng Shū persuading Zhān Hé,
or Yáng Qiàn advising Fàn Wǔ.
Thus, fresh fish emerged from hidden depths,
fragrant delicacies came from secluded lanes,
elaborate dishes exquisitely arranged,
feathered goblets flying about,
Yá and Kuàng’s lofty melodies,
Yìqú’s mournful strains.
At that moment,
Zhòngrú did not decline the attire of his sibling,
Mènggōng disregarded the appointment with the Secretary.
Only regretting that as the banquet’s joy reached its peak,
the sun set in the west,
the black horses were harnessed to the carriage,
and our sentiments could not be fully expressed.
Recalling your uprightness,
I remained awake until dawn.
I was about to send a letter,
when I received your message,
learning that you gentlemen are having another gathering at the Zhāng Canal.
West of the Zhāng Canal lies Bóyáng’s lodge,
north stretches the view of the open wilderness,
tall trees shaded by morning clouds,
colorful birds sheltering by green waters,
the sandy grounds level and broad,
the clear breeze solemn and serene—
this is the pleasure of Jīngtái;
could it be that you will linger and not return?
I happen to have matters to attend to,
which require my personal management,
so I cannot join you at the gathering.
This truly increases my melancholy.
Thus, I state this without full detail.
Qú states.
Qú states:
Since you, sir, departed,
I have missed you greatly.
Shū Tián sang of having no one,
Yīndū thought of one who was not present—
the works of the poets of old,
were they in vain!
Wáng Sù, with his long-standing virtue, was prominently appointed;
Hé Zēng, as a later arrival, was selected and promoted;
both soared like eagles and gazed like tigers,
with aspirations spanning ten thousand miles.
Those lacking support and assistance,
unable to ascend to such lofty heights,
fold their wings and return to their old branches,
solitary and isolated,
harboring a desire to withdraw from the crowd.
Jí Àn delighted in his position at the Langshǔ;
Hé Wǔ felt ashamed to serve as prime minister;
considering this over a thousand years,
we know there are reasons for it.
My virtue is not like Chén Píng’s,
my gate bears no traces of carriages in rows;
my learning is not like Yáng Xióng’s,
my hall lacks guests drawn by scholarly pursuits;
my talent is inferior to Zhòngshū’s,
I lack the diligence to study behind lowered curtains;
my family is as poor as Mèng Gōng’s,
I have no means to host feasts and revelry.
A mournful wind rises within the women’s quarters,
red dust covers the tables and couches.
Fortunately, there is Master Yuán,
who occasionally graces me with his presence,
gathering firewood but not cooking,
merely engaging in refined conversation,
resembling Zhōu Dǎng’s visit to Mǐnzǐ.
When the skin decays, the fur falls;
when the river dries up, the fish depart;
what blooms in spring flourishes,
what thrives in autumn withers and fades;
such is the natural order,
how can there be regret?
I merely share my bitter thoughts with you, my dear younger brother.
I trust we shall meet again soon,
so I will not elaborate further.
Yīng Qú writes.
Yīng Qú writes:
Recently, the scorching drought
has grown increasingly severe day by day;
sand and gravel melt under the heat,
grass and trees wither and curl;
even in cool pavilions, one feels stifled and restless,
bathing in cold water brings the misery of scalding burns.
Though the universe is vast,
there is no shade to find respite.
How could the poem “Yún Hàn”
surpass this description?
The earthen dragon raises its head at the Xuán Temple,
the clay figure stands like a crane at Quèlǐ,
yet after ten days of rituals,
there is no sign of efficacy in the stillness;
these methods of exhortation and teaching
are not the means to bring forth rain.
I know you care for the people below,
exposing yourself to the elements,
bowing and rising at the sacred altar—
your diligence is indeed utmost.
In ancient times, when Xià Yǔ prayed to resolve the drought in Yángxū,
and Yīn Tāng offered prayers at Sānglín,
before their words were fully spoken, water began to flow,
before their pleas concluded, abundant rain poured down.
Now, clouds gather thickly only to disperse again,
rain begins to fall only to be held back;
could it be that the worthiness of sages differs in grade,
their excellence and inferiority distinct in form,
so that cutting hair should reach the skin,
and trimming nails should pierce the flesh?
When Zhōu campaigned against Yīn, the year was abundant;
when Wèi attacked Xíng, rain was brought forth;
the response to good and ill
is swifter than shadow and echo—
this cannot be dismissed as untrue.
Thinking your elegant thoughts may not have reached this,
I respectfully write to inspire reflection.
Yīng Qú writes.
Yīng Qú replies:
Recently, I traveled north,
and my joy was boundless.
Ascending Máng Mountain and crossing the Hé River,
the vastness felt like a veil lifted from my eyes.
The Wind Lord swept the path,
the Rain Master sprinkled the way;
holding the reins on a clear road,
gazing all around at mountains and fields—
once I arrived,
I drank that spring wine.
Treading upon thatched roofs,
the coolness surpassed grand halls;
with a modest spread of delicacies,
the flavor exceeded a feast of abundance.
Wandering freely above the pond banks,
chanting poems beneath lush willows,
gathering spring blossoms to adorn my sash,
plucking radiant flowers to shade the sun,
shooting down birds from high clouds,
baiting fish from deep abysses—
Pú Qiě would praise such skill,
Pián Xuān would call it marvelous;
how exceedingly joyful it was!
Even Confucius forgetting the taste of meat while hearing the Sháo music of Yú,
or the Chǔ people lingering at Jīngtái,
could not surpass this.
Bān Sì’s writings
truly do not exaggerate.
Upon returning to the capital,
I am solitary and isolated once more.
My dwelling by the Luò River
is plagued by noise and dust;
my thoughts wander to the Wèn River’s banks,
arising even in dreams.
In ancient times, Yī Yǐn left his plowing,
Zhì Yùn cast aside his fishing rod,
yearning to bring their lord to the age of Yǒuyú,
and rescue the people from dire suffering.
Yet here I am, wishing to grasp plow and hoe in Shānyáng,
and sink hook and line into the Dān River—
I know I fall far short of the ancients.
Still, Shānfù did not covet the joys of heaven and earth,
Zēng Shēn did not envy the wealth of Jìn and Chǔ—
such is their resolve.
Earlier, our townsfolk thought of you incessantly,
hoping the provincial authorities would honor you with rites,
and officials would grant you a fief—
truly a kind intention.
But looking back and forth through history,
those who entered military offices,
even until their hair turned white,
often never found opportunity,
only toiling in hunger, cold, and frantic haste.
Waiting for the Hé River to run clear—
how long does a human life last?
Moreover, I lack the backing of the Jīn and Zhāng families in officialdom,
and in social circles, I lack the resources of a Zǐ Mèng;
to seek the glory of wealth and honor,
or hope for exceptional favor,
is like traveling to Lǒngxī
or shooting arrows as a Yuè person might.
Fortunately, relying on my late father’s spirit,
I am spared the burden of toil;
following in the footsteps of the elders,
raising chickens and planting millet,
immersing myself in ancient texts,
establishing myself and spreading my name—
this is what I can achieve.
Do not heed idle gossip,
lest it add to your distress.
As for the fields in the suburban pastures,
please give them due thought;
broaden the land and dwellings,
for there I shall grow old.
Messieurs Liú and Dù,
I trust you visit them often.
The season of Zhūmíng
has arrived once more;
since we shall meet soon,
I will not write further.
Take care in summer and cherish yourself.
Yīng Qú writes.
Jī Kāng writes:
You once praised me to Yǐngchuān,
and I often considered your words perceptive.
Yet I have long wondered about this sentiment—
how could you, not yet deeply familiar with me,
have come to such an understanding?
The year before last, upon returning from Hédōng,
Xiǎnzōng and Ādū told me you proposed I take your place;
though the matter did not proceed,
it showed you truly did not know me.
You are versatile and adaptable,
tolerant of much and critical of little;
I am straightforward, narrow-minded,
and find many things intolerable—
it was merely chance that we became acquainted.
Hearing recently of your promotion,
I felt uneasy and displeased,
fearing you might be ashamed of the butcher working alone,
and drag the sacrificial priest to assist,
handing him the ceremonial knife,
soiling him with the stench of blood—
thus I have laid out for you what is feasible and what is not.
In the past, when I read books,
I encountered descriptions of individuals who could be both reclusive and engaged in society.
Some said such people did not exist,
but now I truly believe they do.
There are aspects of one’s nature that cannot be endured,
and truly, they cannot be forced.
Now, it is empty talk to claim that everyone knows of enlightened individuals
who can endure anything,
who outwardly do not differ from the common customs,
yet inwardly do not lose their integrity,
who flow with the currents of the world,
yet harbor no regrets or resentments.
Lǎo Zǐ and Zhuāng Zhōu
are my teachers,
yet they personally held lowly positions;
Liǔ Xià Huì and Dōngfāng Shuò
were enlightened individuals,
yet they were content with humble stations.
How dare I belittle them!
Moreover, Zhòng Ní (Confucius) practiced universal love,
and was not ashamed to hold the whip;
Zǐ Wén had no desire for the positions of minister or chancellor,
yet three times ascended to the role of Lìng Yǐn.
This is the intention of a noble person to benefit the world.
As it is said, when successful, they broadly benefit others without wavering;
when in adversity, they find contentment within themselves without distress.
From this perspective,
the rulership of Yáo and Shùn,
the cliff-dwelling seclusion of Xǔ Yóu,
the assistance of Zǐ Fáng to the Hàn dynasty,
and the singing while walking of Jiē Yú—
their principles are one and the same.
Looking up to these several gentlemen,
they can be said to have fulfilled their aspirations.
Thus, the noble person’s hundred actions
follow different paths but arrive at the same end,
acting in accordance with their nature,
each finding their own place of peace.
Hence, there is the saying that some remain in the court without leaving,
while others enter the mountains and forests without returning.
Moreover, Yánlíng admired the style of Zǐ Zāng,
and Cháng Qīng admired the integrity of Xiàng Rú.
The aspirations and spirit they entrusted themselves to
could not be taken away.
Whenever I read the biographies of Shàng Zǐ Píng and Tái Xiào Wēi,
I am filled with admiration and longing,
imagining their character.
From a young age, I was orphaned and exposed,
and was indulged by my mother and elder brother,
so I did not engage in the study of the classics.
My nature is further lax and lazy,
with sluggish muscles and lax flesh.
My head and face often go unwashed for fifteen days a month;
unless greatly uncomfortable or itchy,
I do not bathe.
Often, when I need to urinate,
I endure it and do not rise,
waiting until my bladder is nearly bursting before getting up.
Moreover, I have long been unrestrained and indulgent,
with a proud and scattered disposition.
Simplicity conflicts with ritual,
and laziness pairs with arrogance,
yet I am tolerated by my peers,
who do not criticize my faults.
Furthermore, reading Zhuāng Zǐ and Lǎo Zǐ
has only increased my unrestrained nature.
Thus, my desire for advancement and glory daily declines,
while my inclination to follow my true nature grows stronger.
This is like a wild deer: if tamed from a young age,
it will submit to training and control;
but if restrained only when grown,
it will wildly look around, struggle against the reins,
and even rush into boiling water or fire.
Even if adorned with a golden bridle
and fed with fine delicacies,
it will long even more for the deep forests,
its heart set on lush grasslands.
Ruǎn Sì Zōng never spoke of others’ faults,
and I always take him as my teacher,
though I have not yet reached his level.
His innate nature surpassed others,
and he harmed no one,
except for occasionally drinking to excess.
Yet he was bound by the ritualists,
who hated him like an enemy,
and he was fortunate to rely on the Grand General for protection.
I am not as virtuous as Sì Zōng,
and have the flaw of being lax and negligent;
moreover, I do not understand human feelings,
and am ignorant of proper timing;
I lack the caution of Wàn Shí,
and am burdened by a tendency to speak too frankly.
If I were long engaged in affairs,
faults and conflicts would daily arise,
and even if I wished to avoid trouble,
how could it be possible?
Moreover, human relations have their rituals,
and the court has its laws.
Having deeply reflected on this,
there are seven things I absolutely cannot endure,
and two that are especially unacceptable:
I enjoy sleeping late,
but the gatekeeper would call me incessantly—
this is the first thing I cannot endure.
Carrying a qín, walking and chanting,
hunting and fishing in the wilds,
but with officials and soldiers guarding me,
unable to act freely—
this is the second thing I cannot endure.
Sitting upright for hours,
numb and unable to move,
with a nature prone to lice,
scratching endlessly,
yet having to wear formal robes,
and bowing to superiors—
this is the third thing I cannot endure.
I have never been skilled at writing,
nor do I enjoy writing letters,
yet in the human world, affairs are many,
piling up on the desk and filling the table.
If I do not respond,
I violate teachings and harm righteousness;
if I force myself,
I cannot persist for long—
this is the fourth thing I cannot endure.
I do not enjoy attending funerals,
yet human society regards this as important.
I would be resented by those who do not forgive me,
even to the point of being slandered.
Though I might startle and blame myself,
my nature cannot be changed.
If I try to humble myself and conform to custom,
it would be hypocritical and insincere.
Even so, I would ultimately not escape blame or gain praise—
this is the fifth thing I cannot endure.
I do not like vulgar people,
yet would have to work alongside them.
Sometimes guests fill the seats,
their clamoring voices grating on the ears,
amidst the noise, dust, and foul places,
with a hundred tricks and changes
constantly before one’s eyes—
this is the sixth thing I cannot endure.
My heart is impatient,
yet official duties are overwhelming,
administrative affairs entangle my mind,
and worldly matters burden my thoughts—
this is the seventh thing I cannot endure.
Moreover, I often criticize Tāng and Wǔ and belittle Zhōu Gōng and Confucius,
and this will not cease in the human world.
This matter will surely become apparent and be intolerable to the world’s teachings—
this is the first especially unacceptable thing.
My straightforward nature hates evil,
and I am prone to speak bluntly and recklessly,
acting out when encountering issues—
this is the second especially unacceptable thing.
With a narrow and cautious nature,
coupled with these nine afflictions,
even without external troubles,
there would surely be internal illness.
How could I long remain in the human world!
Moreover, I have heard the words passed down by Daoist masters
that taking herbs like zhú and huángjīng
can prolong life,
and I deeply believe this;
roaming mountains and marshes,
observing fish and birds,
brings great joy to my heart.
Once I take up an official post,
these things would be abandoned.
How could I give up what I love
to follow what I fear!
In the mutual understanding between people,
what is valued is recognizing each other's innate nature,
and thereby assisting them.
Yǔ did not force Bóchéng Zǐgāo,
in order to preserve his integrity;
Zhòngní did not borrow an umbrella from Zǐxià,
to protect his shortcoming;
more recently, Zhūgě Kǒngmíng did not force Yuánzhí to enter Shǔ;
Huá Zǐyú did not compel Yòu'ān to serve as a minister.
This can be said to be the ability to maintain relationships from beginning to end,
truly understanding one another.
You see that straight wood cannot be made into wheels,
and crooked wood cannot be used as rafters,
for one does not wish to distort their innate talent,
but to let them find their proper place.
Thus, the four classes of people each have their occupations,
and each finds joy in fulfilling their aspirations,
only the enlightened can comprehend this,
and this is within your understanding.
One should not, upon seeing a fine ceremonial cap,
force the Yuè people to wear ornate headgear;
nor, because one relishes rotten meat,
feed dead rats to the yuānchú.
I have recently been studying the art of nurturing life,
rejecting external glory and splendor,
abandoning rich flavors,
letting my mind wander in solitude,
valuing non-action above all.
Even without the nine troubles,
I would still not care for what you favor,
and moreover, I suffer from a heart ailment,
which has recently grown increasingly severe.
In my private thoughts, I have tested myself,
and I cannot endure what I do not enjoy.
Having examined myself thoroughly,
if my path ends and the road runs out, so be it.
There is no need for you to wrong me unjustly,
causing me to be cast into the ditches.
I have recently lost the joy of my mother and elder brother,
and my heart is often filled with sorrow.
My daughter is thirteen years old,
my son is eight,
not yet grown,
and moreover, they are often ill.
Reflecting on this fills me with anguish,
how can I put it into words!
Now I only wish to dwell in my humble lane,
teaching and nurturing my children and grandchildren,
occasionally meeting with relatives and old friends to recount our partings,
and talk about our lives,
with a cup of coarse wine,
and a tune played on the qin,
my aspirations would be fully satisfied.
If you persist in harassing me without cease,
it is merely because you wish to recruit someone for office,
to benefit the needs of the times.
You have long known that I am disheveled and careless,
unfit for practical affairs,
and I myself think that I am not as worthy and capable as the men of today.
If it is because ordinary people all delight in glory and splendor,
and I alone can detach myself from it,
finding joy in this,
this is closest to the truth,
and can be spoken of.
However, if one possesses great talent and broad vision,
excelling in all things,
and yet does not seek advancement,
then that is truly praiseworthy.
But as for me, afflicted by many illnesses and hardships,
wishing to withdraw from affairs to preserve myself,
and protect my remaining years,
this is truly due to my shortcomings,
how can one see a eunuch and praise his chastity!
If you are eager for us to ascend the path of kings together,
hoping to bring me to that point,
expecting mutual joy and benefit,
and suddenly press me,
it will surely provoke my madness,
and unless you bear a deep grudge against me,
you would not go to such lengths.
There was a rustic who found joy in warming his back in the sun and thought celery delicious,
and wished to offer these to the sovereign.
Although he had sincere intentions,
they were rather misguided.
I hope you will not resemble him.
My thoughts are thus,
both to explain myself to you,
and to bid farewell.
Jī Kāng respectfully states.
Bāo states:
I have heard that acting upon recognizing opportunity,
is valued in the Zhōu Yì;
while the small not serving the great,
is condemned in the Chūnqiū.
These are the beginnings of fortune and misfortune,
the origins of honor and disgrace.
Thus, Xǔ and Zhèng preserved their states by offering jade discs,
while Cáo and Tán were destroyed due to their lack of propriety.
Historical records have documented their successes and failures,
and ancient and modern times have revealed their folly and wisdom.
I will not further extend analogies and examples,
nor embellish with empty rhetoric,
merely to boast and gain fame,
thereby losing the substance of sincere advice.
Now I shall briefly discuss the situation,
to bring mutual awareness.
In the past, the fiery essence grew dim,
the mandate was nearing its end,
Huán and Líng lost their virtue,
disasters and conflicts arose together,
wolves and jackals bared their poisonous claws,
and the people suffered the hardships of extreme distress.
Thus, the nine provinces lost their order,
the imperial rule unraveled,
the four seas fell into desolation,
and they were no longer under Hàn's possession.
Tàizǔ received the mandate,
with divine martial prowess answering the times,
he campaigned against violence and chaos,
bringing peace to the central region;
cooperating to establish auspicious signs,
the heavenly mandate was gathered upon him,
and he expanded the great foundation,
encompassing the domain of Wèi.
The land is the central peak of the divine continent,
the vessel is the Nine Tripods still preserved,
generations have carried forth virtue and beauty,
with glorious reigns succeeding one another,
firmly knowing that the four corners are united,
a magnificent spectacle under heaven.
Gōngsūn Yuān relied on his father and brother's legacy,
dwelling for generations in the eastern borderlands,
controlling Yān and the Hú regions,
relying on perilous and remote terrain,
he drilled troops and lingered,
not fulfilling tribute duties,
inwardly arrogant toward the imperial command,
outwardly communicating with the southern state,
sailing rafts upon the dark currents,
exchanging goods and bribes,
Géyuè cloth spread to the northern lands,
sable and horses reached Wú and Kuàijī;
he believed himself to command a hundred thousand archers,
with enough to mobilize,
truly capable of bending Yān and Qí to the right,
shaking Fúsāng to the left,
trampling over the desert,
and proclaiming himself king facing south.
Xuānwáng launched a swift campaign,
fiercely and sharply driving deep.
The army reached Liáoyáng,
and the city walls could not hold;
with one beat of the drum,
the chief villain was beheaded.
Thereafter, the distant borders were pacified,
commanderies were established in the great wilderness,
the scattered and dispersed were gathered,
all settled in their dwellings,
the common people were pleased and submitted,
and foreign customs sincerely attached themselves.
From then on, prosperity rose,
the nine regions were clear and peaceful,
the eastern barbarians offered their musical instruments,
Sùshèn presented their hù arrows,
unruly for generations,
they responded to transformation and came,
lofty and vast,
I believe you have heard all of this.
The founding ruler of Wú,
rising from Jīngzhōu,
encountered a time of turmoil and unrest,
and fled to the region south of the Yangtze;
Liú Bèi, alarmed and fearful,
also fled to Bāmín.
Thus relying on the natural defenses of hills and piled stones,
with the three rivers and five lakes,
vast and boundless,
they sustained themselves like wandering spirits,
lasting for four decades.
These two states formed an alliance,
echoing each other from east to west,
mutually inciting and supporting,
resisting the Central Plains.
They believed their tripartite balance of power,
like a tripod, could endure as long as Mount Tài.
The Chancellor, Prince of Jìn,
assisting the imperial house,
with martial and civil prowess,
his will as stern as autumn frost,
his strategic calculations in the ancestral temple,
adapting to changes without limit,
his unique foresight,
transcending ordinary concerns.
Our sovereign, wise and reverent,
entrusted him with all affairs of state,
holding the long reins to guide from afar,
subtle strategies secretly imparted,
allied forces united in purpose,
high and low exerting their strength,
displaying awe and launching attacks,
penetrating deep into their strongholds,
concentrating force against a single direction,
seizing their courage and spirit.
After a minor battle by the river,
Chéngdū itself collapsed;
displaying troops at Jiàngé,
and Jiāng Wéi surrendered bound.
Five thousand lǐ of land were opened,
thirty commanderies established.
The campaign did not exceed the season,
Liáng and Yì were pacified,
causing the usurping heroes,
to bow in submission at the crimson gates,
with precious jades and rich brocades,
filling the treasuries.
The fall of Guó and the demise of Yú,
the annexation of Hán and the relocation of Wèi,
these are all proofs from past mirrors,
lessons for future affairs.
Moreover, Lǚ Xīng in Nánzhōng,
deeply perceiving Heaven’s Mandate,
shed his old shell and turned inward,
wishing to become a subject.
Externally losing the support of mutual dependence,
internally facing the gradual shedding of feathers,
yet lingering in a perilous state,
hoping to prolong their days,
this is like Marquis Wǔ of Wèi pointing to the rivers and mountains to claim strength,
not realizing that all things have their rise and fall,
so what he praised was not truly secure.
Now all officials are gathered in multitude,
talented men fill the court,
fierce ministers and martial generals,
can repel enemies from ten thousand lǐ,
the state is wealthy, the army strong,
the six armies are well-trained.
Thinking to soar once more,
and water our horses in the Southern Sea.
Recently the state,
has repaired and organized its equipment,
built and prepared ships,
trained and drilled in naval warfare.
Felling trees from the northern mountains,
until the Tàiháng range is depleted,
dredging and opening the Hé and Luò rivers,
so all streams flow freely.
Towered warships by the tens of thousands,
stretch for a thousand lǐ.
Since the hollowing of wood to make boats,
the use of ships and chariots,
has never been as grand as today.
A million brave warriors,
store their strength and await the moment,
the campaign need not be launched twice,
this is what is meant today.
Yet our sovereign, with deep concern,
has not swiftly advanced like lightning,
believing that loving the people and governing the state,
is esteemed by the Daoist school,
lowering oneself before lofty walls,
as King Wén retreated his encampment,
thus first demonstrating great sincerity,
explaining survival and destruction,
the earnest intent,
is to be understood by the envoy sent.
If you can clearly recognize safety and danger,
and seek abundant blessings for yourselves,
suddenly changing your demeanor,
respectfully accepting the past admonition,
emulating Nányuè,
where Yīng Qí entered to serve,
facing north and declaring yourselves subjects,
humbly listening to the proclamation,
then your lineage will endure south of the river,
forever as a protective vassal,
with generous rewards and illustrious honors,
more splendid than today.
If you insult and defy the royal command,
then plans and forces will converge like clouds,
directed as the wind follows,
from Yōng and Yì provinces,
flowing eastward down the current;
from Qīng and Xú, warriors
line the river advancing west;
from Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù,
racing to the eight thoroughfares;
the eastern expedition armored troops,
will stride like tigers through Wúlíng.
Then the imperial carriage will set forth in order,
the six armies advance steadily,
feathered dispatches bright as the sun,
banners and flags like shooting stars,
roaming dragons illuminating the road,
songs and music filling the ears,
soldiers rushing forth,
gathering like a forest,
dust and smoke rising together,
shaking heaven and startling earth,
warriors thirsting for reward,
will contend to be first in battle,
and suddenly one day heads and bodies will be severed,
ancestral sacrifices slaughtered and overturned,
a warning for ten thousand generations,
stretching your necks gazing south,
truly chilling to the heart.
