To cure a disease in the vitals, bitter medicine must be administered;
to resolve doubts, words that grate on the ears must be told.
If you remain deluded and mistaken,
not knowing where to turn,
I fear even Yú Fū would see you already in distress,
and Biǎn Què would know his efforts futile.
Strive to consider this good plan,
and decide your course of action.
Shí Bāo respectfully states.
Ān states:
In the past, the old man Lǐ entered Qín,
and sighed upon reaching the pass;
Liáng Shēng went to Yuè,
and chanted a long song upon ascending the peak.
Even in the act of noble seclusion,
there is still lingering regret,
how much more for those who have no choice!
Since our parting,
I have wandered alone, apart from the group,
turning away from glorious feasts,
leaving behind dear friends,
traversing winding roads,
crossing deserts.
At the cock’s crow heralding dawn,
I swiftly set out at morning;
as the sun declines in the west,
my horse’s head finds no rest.
Navigating twisted obstacles,
then deep thoughts become tangled knots,
climbing high to gaze afar,
mountains and rivers stretch distantly apart.
Sometimes whirlwinds rage fiercely,
the daylight dims,
rugged paths crisscross,
hills and marshes in view.
Wandering within the nine marshes,
sighing with emotion atop layered peaks,
advancing with nothing to rely on,
retreating with no place to stand,
crossing marshes seeking paths,
parting brambles to find the way,
whistling and chanting by ditches and canals,
truly hard to measure,
such are the hardships of the journey,
yet these are not what my heart fears.
As for the orchid and zhǐ grass being uprooted and fallen,
the cassia trees transplanted,
their roots not yet firmly established,
their tender sprouts and taut strings,
I often fear that hidden winds and waves may strike,
and crises may erupt in secret.
This is why I am apprehensive on the long road,
holding the reins and sighing.
Moreover, the nature of the northern land
makes it difficult to take root.
Offering a luminous pearl at night,
few would not grasp their swords in suspicion.
Now, to plant oranges and pomelos in the dark north,
or lotus flowers on high ridges,
to display dragon patterns in a land of nakedness,
or perform the Sháo dance among the deaf—
it is truly difficult to gain honor.
If things do not value me,
then none will stand with me;
if none stand with me,
then those who harm me will arrive.
A wanderer drifting far away,
finding shelter in a desolate land,
holding the reins on a distant road,
faces the hardships foretold;
hanging the saddle in a humble dwelling,
he is warned of future worries.
When morning clouds herald the dawn,
his body is weary from hasty travel;
when the sun hides its light,
his spirit is exhausted by evening vigilance.
Gazing across the flat marshes,
he sees only vast emptiness;
listening intently on the long plains,
he hears only profound silence.
Alas, how sorrowful!
How heartbroken and distressed!
Only then does he realize that the man of measured steps
is not worthy of honor.
If, then, he looks back at the Central Plains,
his indignation surges like clouds,
grieving for things and mourning the world,
his passions stirred like fierce winds.
Like a dragon gazing over the great wilderness,
or a tiger roaring across the six directions,
his fierce spirit in tumult,
his ambition spreading in all directions,
he longs to tread the cloud ladder,
to sweep across the eight extremes,
to clear away hardships and filth,
to calm the seas and level the mountains,
to kick Kūnlún and make it fall westward,
to stomp on Tàishān and topple it eastward,
to cleanse and purify the nine regions,
to restore order to the universe—
this too is my humble wish.
But time does not favor me,
so with folded wings I depart far away.
My sharp edge unused,
my wings broken and bent,
if not for knowing fate,
who could avoid feeling resentment?
You, sir, have planted your roots in fragrant gardens,
rising splendidly from clear streams,
spreading leaves on flowery cliffs,
your writings soaring like clouds in the marketplace.
Bending over the abyss where dragons hide,
looking up to the shade of forests where phoenixes perch,
glory and splendor dazzle before you,
beauty and allure entice behind you,
good companions gather to your left,
fame and reputation race to your right.
Soaring among peers and factions,
posing gracefully within curtained chambers,
leisurely looking around,
with ample ease and comfort,
bowing and raising your head, chanting and whistling,
you consider yourself to have achieved your ambitions.
How could you share the joys and sorrows of a great man like me?
Farewell, Jī Shēng,
forever separated!
Alone and drifting,
I face the desert!
Vast and distant, three thousand lǐ,
a road hard to traverse!
The day we join hands again,
is far off and uncertain!
My longing heart grows more entangled,
who can say it will be released?
Do not let your words be like gold and jade,
yet keep a distant heart.
Though our bodies are like Hú and Yuè apart,
our intentions remain as firm as cut metal.
Each of you, respect your demeanor,
diligently tread the path of simplicity and depth.
The fleeting glamour and dissipation,
the noble man does not admire.
Facing this letter, filled with sorrow,
what more can I say?
Chí bows his head.
To General Chén, at your feet:
I hope you are well,
most fortunate, most fortunate!
Your courage is unmatched in the three armies,
your talent is rare in this world.
Abandoning the petty ambitions of sparrows,
you aspired to soar high like the swan.
In the past, seizing opportunity and adapting to change,
you encountered an enlightened lord,
achieved merit and accomplished deeds,
founded a state and claimed nobility.
Riding in vermilion carriages with ornate hubs,
bearing the commander’s banner across ten thousand lǐ—
how magnificent that was!
How is it that now, suddenly, you are a fugitive captive,
trembling at the sound of whistling arrows,
kneeling before felt tents?
How base this is!
Examining the circumstances of your departure,
there was no other reason
but that you failed to reflect inwardly on yourself,
and were swayed by external rumors,
becoming confused and reckless,
leading to this state.
The sagely court pardons offenses and demands merit,
overlooks flaws and employs talent,
extends a sincere heart to all under heaven,
and reassures the wavering among all things.
This, General, you know well,
and need not be elaborated by me.
Zhū Wěi stained his hands with the blood of his own kin,
Zhāng Xiù stabbed his beloved son with a blade,
yet the Hàn ruler did not doubt him,
and the Wèi sovereign treated him as before.
How much more so for you, General, who bear no such past crimes,
and whose achievements are weighty in this age.
To realize one’s error and turn back,
is praised by the wise of old;
to return before going far astray,
is esteemed by ancient classics.
Our sovereign tempers the law with grace,
letting even the fish that could swallow a boat slip through the net.
Your ancestral pines and cypresses remain uncut,
your relatives live in peace,
your high towers still stand,
your beloved concubines are yet present.
Ponder deeply in your heart—
what more is there to say?
Now, the meritorious officials and famed generals
are arrayed in orderly ranks like geese,
wearing purple ribbons and holding gold seals,
planning strategies within the command tent,
riding light carriages and bearing tall insignia,
entrusted with duties at the borders.
Together they have sworn oaths over a sacrificial horse,
to be passed down to their descendants.
Yet you alone, General, shamelessly cling to borrowed life,
serving the felt-clad chieftain,
is this not pitiable?
Consider the strength of Mùróng Chāo—
he was executed in the eastern market;
the prosperity of Yáo Hóng—
he was bound and presented in the western capital.
Thus we know that where frost and dew fall evenly,
alien breeds are not nurtured;
the ancient lands of the Jī and Hàn dynasties,
do not accept mixed species.
The northern barbarians usurp and plunder the Central Plains,
for many years now,
their evils accumulated, disasters overflowing,
their doom is surely at hand.
Moreover, their false rulers are dim and crafty,
slaughtering each other;
tribes are divided and estranged,
chieftains suspicious and disloyal.
Soon they will be bound at the barbarian lodge,
their heads hung on Gǎojiē Street.
Yet you, General, are like a fish swimming in a boiling cauldron,
or a swallow nesting on a fluttering curtain—
is this not delusion?
In late spring, the third month,
south of the river, grass grows long,
mixed flowers bloom on trees,
flocks of orioles fly in disarray.
Seeing the banners and drums of your homeland,
recalling the days of your past life,
strumming the lute atop the battlements—how can it not bring sorrow?
Thus, Lián Pō longed to lead Zhào’s armies again,
Wū Qǐ wept by the Western River—
such is human feeling.
Do you alone, General, lack such feeling?
To the Governor of Bāshǔ Commandery:
The barbarians have acted on their own authority,
and have long gone without chastisement.
From time to time they invade and encroach upon the border regions,
causing toil for the officers and gentlemen.
Since His Majesty ascended the throne,
he has preserved and comforted the world,
settling and pacifying the Central States.
Thereafter he raised armies and dispatched troops,
campaigning northward against the Xiōngnú.
The Chányú was terrified,
crossed his arms and submitted to service,
bent his knee and begged for peace.
Kāngjú and the Western Regions,
through repeated translation, presented tribute,
knocking their foreheads to the ground to come and offer allegiance.
Shifting the army eastward to point toward them,
Mǐnyuè attacked one another.
To the right, condolences were sent to Pānyú,
and the crown prince entered the court.
The lords of the southern barbarians,
the chiefs of the western Bó,
constantly perform their tribute duties,
not daring to be negligent or remiss.
Craning their necks and rising on tiptoe, eagerly,
all turn toward the wind and admire righteousness,
desiring to become subjects and servants.
But the roads are distant and far,
mountains and rivers obstruct and run deep,
so they cannot come of their own accord.
Those who were disobedient have already been punished,
yet those who do good have not been rewarded.
Therefore, we have dispatched a Commandant of the Palace Gentlemen to treat them as guests,
mobilizing five hundred men each from the gentlemen of Bā and Shǔ,
to present silks and fabrics,
and to guard the envoy against unforeseen events—
there is no affair of weapons and armor,
no calamity of battle and combat.
Now we hear that they have instead initiated military mobilization and regulations,
frightening the young men,
and worrying the elders.
Moreover, the commandery has presumptuously undertaken the transfer of grain and transport,
all of which is not His Majesty’s intention.
Those who ought to go either flee or kill themselves,
which is also not the duty of a subject.
The gentlemen of the border commanderies,
hearing the beacon fires raised and the signal fires lit,
all grasp their bows and gallop,
shoulder their weapons and run,
sweat flowing in succession,
fearing only to be left behind.
They meet white blades,
brave flying arrows,
with no thought of looking back,
no plan of turning on their heels.
Each man harbors an angry heart,
as if avenging a private grudge.
Do they perhaps delight in death and hate life,
are they not people registered in the rolls,
and do they differ from Bā and Shǔ in having a different ruler?
They plan deeply and consider far,
urgently address the difficulties of the state,
and delight in fulfilling the way of a subject.
Therefore, there are those who receive the splitting of tallies as enfeoffment,
the dividing of jade tablets for rank,
whose position is that of a full marquis,
who dwell in the eastern mansions.
In the end, they leave a glorious name for later generations,
transmit land to their sons and grandsons.
Their conduct is most loyal and reverent,
their station is most peaceful and comfortable.
Their fame spreads without end,
their achievements are illustrious and do not perish.
Thus, worthy men and gentlemen,
spill liver and brains across the central plains,
moisten the wild grasses with fat and blood, and do not refuse.
Now, when presenting silks and performing service for the southern barbarians,
they instead kill themselves,
or flee and incur punishment,
dying with no name,
posthumously deemed most foolish,
shame reaching their parents,
laughed at by the world.
How people’s measures differ—
is it not far indeed!
Yet this is not solely the fault of those who go.
The teaching of fathers and elder brothers did not come first,
the example set for young men was not careful.
Lacking in integrity and shame,
the customs are not long on honesty.
That they suffer punishment and execution,
is it not fitting!
His Majesty is distressed that the envoys and officials are like that,
and grieves that the unworthy and foolish people are like this.
Therefore, he dispatches a trustworthy envoy
to clearly instruct the common people about the matter of mobilizing troops,
and thereby enumerate the crimes of disloyalty leading to death,
reproaching the village elders and exemplars of filial piety and fraternal duty for the fault of failing to teach and instruct.
At present, it is the farming season;
to heavily trouble the common people,
we have already personally visited the nearby counties.
Fearing that the people of distant streams, valleys, mountains, and marshes may not hear comprehensively,
when this proclamation arrives,
promptly circulate it to the counties and circuits,
so that all may understand His Majesty’s intention.
Do not neglect this.
The General of the Left, concurrently Governor of Yùzhōu, to the Chancellors of Commanderies and States.
It is heard that an enlightened ruler plans for danger to control change,
and a loyal minister considers difficulties to establish authority.
Therefore, there must be extraordinary people,
and then there are extraordinary affairs;
there are extraordinary affairs,
and then extraordinary achievements are established.
The extraordinary,
is precisely what ordinary people cannot imitate.
In former times, the powerful Qín had a weak ruler;
Zhào Gāo held the handle of power,
monopolized court authority,
dispensing favor and punishment as he pleased.
People of the time were coerced and intimidated,
none dared to speak uprightly.
In the end, there was the defeat at Wàngyí,
the ancestral temples burned and destroyed,
defilement and shame lasting to this day,
a perpetual mirror for the world.
When it came to the latter years of Empress Lǚ,
Lǚ Chǎn and Lǚ Lù monopolized governance,
within combining the two armies,
without commanding Liáng and Zhào,
presumptuously deciding myriad matters,
settling affairs within the palace precincts,
those below encroached, those above declined,
the whole realm chilled at heart.
Thereupon, the Marquis of Jiàng and Zhūxū raised troops in righteous anger,
punished and exterminated the rebellious and violent,
honored and established Tàizōng.
Thus, the kingly way could flourish and prosper,
bright and illustrious, radiant and glorious.
This is the clear example of ministers establishing authority.
The Minister of Works Cáo Cāo’s grandfather was the Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary Cáo Téng,
who, together with Zuǒ Guàn and Xú Huáng, practiced monstrous deeds,
acting with insatiable greed and unrestrained tyranny,
injuring moral transformation and oppressing the people.
His father, Cáo Sōng,
was a beggar and foster child,
who obtained office through bribery,
transporting gold and jade,
delivering goods to the powerful,
stealing the position of the Minister of Works,
and overturning the weighty vessel of state.
Cáo Cāo is the leftover disgrace of eunuchs,
originally lacking in virtuous conduct,
frivolous, cunning, and sharp-tongued,
fond of chaos and delighting in calamity.
The General’s Headquarters, commanding with martial prowess,
swept away the wicked rebels,
and later encountered Dǒng Zhuó,
who encroached upon offices and ravaged the state.
Thereupon, raising swords and beating drums,
issuing commands in the eastern region,
gathering heroes,
overlooking flaws and employing them,
thus we consulted and plotted together with Cáo Cāo,
granting him the rank of deputy commander,
considering him to have the talent of a hawk or hound,
capable of serving as claws and fangs.
Yet he was foolish and rash, lacking in strategy,
advancing lightly and retreating easily,
suffering injuries and defeats,
repeatedly losing troops.
The General’s Headquarters repeatedly divided troops and dispatched elites,
repairing and replenishing,
recommending him for the post of Administrator of Dōngjùn,
appointing him as Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
clothing him in tiger stripes,
encouraging and empowering him,
hoping to obtain the reward of a single victory like that of the Qín army.
Yet Cáo Cāo, relying on these resources, became arrogant and domineering,
indulging in wickedness and treachery,
exploiting the common people,
harming the worthy and injuring the good.
Thus, the former Administrator of Jiǔjiāng, Biān Ràng,
a man of outstanding talent and greatness,
known throughout the realm,
frank and upright in speech,
whose discussions did not flatter,
was executed and his head displayed,
his wife and children suffering the calamity of annihilation.
From then on, the scholars were filled with indignation and pain,
the people’s resentment grew ever heavier,
one man raised his arm,
and the entire province echoed in response.
Thus, he was personally defeated in Xúfāng,
his territory seized by Lǚ Bù,
wandering in the eastern borderlands,
with no place to stand.
The General’s Headquarters, upholding the principle of strengthening the trunk and weakening the branches,
and moreover not joining the faction of rebels,
thus again raised banners and donned armor,
rolling out like a mat and launching an expedition,
with the sound of gongs and drums shaking the earth,
Lǚ Bù’s forces fled and collapsed,
saving him from the peril of death,
and restoring him to his position as a regional lord.
Thus, the General’s Headquarters has no virtue toward the people of Yǎnzhōu,
but has greatly favored Cáo Cāo.
Later, when the imperial carriage turned back,
hordes of enemies attacked.
At that time, Jìzhōu was facing alarms from the northern borders,
and there was no leisure to leave our posts,
so we sent the Attendant Officer Xú Xūn to dispatch Cáo Cāo,
ordering him to repair the suburban temples,
and protect the young sovereign.
Cáo Cāo then indulged his ambitions and acted arbitrarily,
forcing the relocation of the imperial court to the forbidden palace,
demeaning and insulting the royal house,
corrupting laws and disrupting order,
presiding over the Three Terraces,
monopolizing court governance,
granting titles and rewards according to his whims,
meting out punishments and executions with his words,
those he loved brought glory to five generations,
those he hated exterminated to three clans,
those who spoke openly suffered public execution,
those who harbored private criticisms met secret deaths,
all officials silenced,
people on the roads communicating only with their eyes,
the Imperial Secretariat merely recorded court assemblies,
and the high ministers served as mere figureheads.
Thus, the former Grand Commandant Yáng Biāo,
who had served in two ministries,
and enjoyed the highest position in the state,
was, due to a petty grudge by Cáo Cāo,
accused of false crimes,
subjected to flogging and torture,
with all five poisons applied,
acting on personal feelings and allowing treachery,
disregarding the legal net.
Also, the Court Counselor Zhào Chǎn,
loyal and outspoken in remonstrance,
whose righteous words were worthy of acceptance,
was thus listened to by the sagely court,
which changed expression and showed respect.
Cáo Cāo, wishing to confuse and seize the clarity of the times,
blocked the path of speech,
arbitrarily arrested and immediately killed him,
without awaiting report or hearing.
Moreover, Liáng Xiàowáng was the maternal brother of a former emperor,
his tomb majestic and illustrious,
the mulberry and catalpa, pine and cypress,
should still be treated with reverence.
Yet Cáo Cāo led officers and soldiers,
personally overseeing the excavation,
breaking open coffins and exposing corpses,
plundering gold and treasures,
causing the sagely court to shed tears,
and scholars and commoners to grieve.
Cáo Cāo also specially established the Tomb-Raiding General and the Gold-Touching Colonel,
wherever they passed, they rampaged,
leaving no skeleton unexposed.
Occupying the position of one of the Three Dukes,
yet behaving like a savage bandit,
defiling the state and oppressing the people,
poisoning both men and ghosts.
Added to this, his petty governance is harsh and cruel,
with regulations and defenses set everywhere,
nets and snares filling the paths,
pits and traps blocking the roads,
raising a hand entangles one in the net,
taking a step triggers a hidden trap,
thus in Yǎnzhōu and Yùzhōu there are people with no means of livelihood,
and in the imperial capital there are sighs of grievance.
Surveying the historical records,
among ministers without virtue,
greedy, cruel, and fierce,
Cáo Cāo is the worst.
The General’s Headquarters was just interrogating external traitors,
and had not yet had time to rectify and instruct,
but added tolerance and forbearance,
hoping he might mend his ways.
Yet Cáo Cāo, with the wild ambition of a wolf,
secretly harbored treacherous plots,
wishing to break the pillars and beams,
weaken and isolate the Hàn house,
eliminate the loyal and upright,
and become a ruthless overlord.
Previously, when we beat drums and marched north to attack Gōngsūn Zàn,
a powerful and rebellious enemy,
who resisted siege for a year,
Cáo Cāo, taking advantage of his not yet being defeated,
secretly exchanged letters and orders,
outwardly aiding the royal army,
while inwardly planning a surprise attack,
thus leading troops to the river,
and preparing boats to cross north.
It happened that his envoy was exposed,
and Gōngsūn Zàn was also destroyed,
so his sharp edge was blunted and withdrawn,
and his plot did not succeed.
Then our great army swept through the western hills,
the Túgè and Zuǒxiào tribes,
all bound their hands and offered hostages,
vying to be the first to ascend,
the remaining rabble of dogs and sheep,
vanished into the valleys.
Thereupon, Cáo Cāo’s army was terrified,
fleeing day and night,
encamping and occupying Áocāng,
relying on the river for defense,
wishing to use the axe of a mantis
to block the path of a great cart.
The General’s Headquarters, upholding the majestic might of Hàn,
wields power throughout the universe,
with a million long halberds,
and a thousand troops of Hú cavalry,
rousing warriors like Zhōnghuáng, Yù, and Huò,
employing the force of strong bows and crossbows,
Bīngzhōu crossing the Tàiháng Mountains,
Qīngzhōu fording the Jì and Tà rivers,
the great army crossing the Huáng Hé to confront them from the front,
Jīngzhōu descending from Wǎn and Yè to strike from behind.
With the force of thunder and the stride of tigers,
converging on the enemy’s court,
like raising a blazing fire to burn flying tumbleweed,
or overturning the blue sea to douse flaming charcoal,
what could possibly not be destroyed!
Moreover, among Cáo Cāo's officers and soldiers,
those capable of fighting originally came from Yōuzhōu and Jìzhōu,
or were former troops under his command.
All are resentful of long separation and yearn to return home,
shedding tears as they gaze northward.
The remaining people from Yǎnzhōu and Yùzhōu,
along with the remnants of Lǚ Bù and Zhāng Yáng's forces,
were coerced after their defeat and destruction,
complying temporarily out of desperation.
Each has suffered wounds,
and every man regards him as an enemy.
If our banners turn and advance,
ascending the high ridges to beat drums and blow horns,
raising white flags to open the path of surrender,
they will surely crumble and disintegrate,
without awaiting the clash of blades.
Now the Hàn house is in decline,
its laws and bonds slackened and severed.
The sacred court lacks even a single minor supporter;
its limbs and aides possess no power to repel the foe.
Within the imperial domain,
the seasoned and trained ministers
all hang their heads and droop their wings,
with nothing to rely upon.
Though there are loyal and righteous assistants,
coerced by violent and cruel ministers,
how can they display their integrity?
Furthermore, Cáo Cāo holds seven hundred elite troops from his own command,
surrounding and guarding the palace gates.
Outwardly he claims they are the palace guard,
but in reality, he uses them to enforce confinement,
fearing that the sprout of usurpation and rebellion
might arise because of this.
This is the time for loyal ministers to spill their liver and brains upon the ground,
the moment for determined men to achieve merit.
Can we not strive?
Cáo Cāo also falsely issues commands in the Emperor's name,
dispatching envoys to mobilize troops,
fearing that the distant commanderies and provinces,
misled by his words, might supply him,
thus strengthening the bandit and weakening the sovereign,
acting against the multitude and joining rebellion,
bringing upon themselves loss of reputation,
and becoming the laughingstock of the world—
a course the wise would not take.
On this very day, the four provinces of Yōu, Bìng, Qīng, and Jì are advancing together.
When this document reaches Jīngzhōu,
immediately marshal the troops at hand,
and join forces with General Jiànzhōng to coordinate momentum.
Let each commandery and province prepare its warhorses,
deploy along the borders,
raise armies and display might,
and together uphold the altars of state.
Then extraordinary achievements
will thereby be made manifest.
Whoever obtains Cáo Cāo's head
shall be enfeoffed as a marquis with five thousand households,
and rewarded with fifty million cash.
Officers, commanders, and officials of all ranks under his command who surrender
shall not be questioned.
Widely proclaim grace and good faith,
promulgate tallies and rewards,
announce to all under heaven,
so that all may know the sacred court faces the hardship of coercion.
According to the statutes and ordinances.
On the first day of the month, in such-and-such year,
I, the Imperial Secretary Xún Yù,
proclaim to all the officers, commanders, troops, and to the Sun Quán clan and kin, both within and without, in Jiāngdōng:
It is heard that fortune and calamity have no gate;
they are summoned only by men themselves.
To perceive opportunity and act,
not dwelling in peril and danger,
is the wisdom of the highest sage;
to confront affairs, control change, and find passage through difficulty—
this is the deliberation of the wise;
to sink gradually into dissipation and delusion,
going forward without return,
is the blindness of the lowest fool.
Therefore, the noble gentleman of great refinement,
in safety thinks of danger,
to avoid future blame and regret;
the petty man, facing calamity, harbors indulgence,
awaiting death.
Are not the measures of these two
vastly different indeed!
Sun Quán, this petty fellow,
cannot yet distinguish beans from wheat.
His neck is insufficient to grease the axe of execution;
his name is unworthy to soil the bamboo slips and ink.
He is like a fledgling bird or unhatched egg,
just beginning to grow flight feathers,
yet already acts recklessly and arrogantly,
turning to bark at his master.
He believes his boats and oars suffice to resist the imperial might,
that rivers and lakes can let him escape divine punishment,
not knowing the net of heaven is spread,
its meshes already set,
like a fish in a boiling cauldron,
destined only to dissolve and rot.
If water could be relied upon,
then Dòngtíng would not hold the ruins of the Sān Miáo,
Zǐyáng would not have met defeat at Jīngmén,
the fortifications of Cháoxiǎn would not have been razed,
and the banners of Nányuè would not have been torn down.
Of old, Fūchāi, following the distant footsteps of Hélǘ,
employed Shēn Xū's trained troops,
and drove Yuè to perch at Kuàijī—
this could be called strength.
Yet when he contended with the Central States,
vying for supremacy with Jìn,
his capital was slaughtered by Gōu Jiàn,
his warriors scattered at Huángchí,
ending in utter destruction,
his own life taken by the Yuè army.
And when the King of Wú, Liú Bì, grew arrogant, willful, and obstinate,
recklessly beginning rebellion,
he believed himself strong in arms and rich in state,
his power overshadowing the capital.
Yet as soon as the Grand Commandant led his army,
and had just descended upon Xíngyáng,
the armies of the Seven States
dissolved like ice breaking apart.
Bì's curses had not yet left his lips
when the blade at Dāntú pierced his chest.
Why was this?
Because the awe of heaven cannot be withstood,
and the crime of rebellion is grave.
Moreover, the multitudes of the rivers and lakes
are not to be relied upon.
Since Dǒng Zhuó stirred up rebellion,
up to the present day,
nearly thirty years have passed.
During this time, heroes and strongmen have roamed freely,
like bears and tigers holding their ground,
as powerful as the two Yuáns,
as brave as Lǚ Bù,
spanning provinces and connecting commanderies,
wielding authority and fame,
more than ten such figures.
The rest, who rose up fiercely,
with the gaze of hawks and the watchfulness of wolves,
vying to become overlords,
are too numerous to count.
Yet all have fallen under the axe and halberd,
their heads and bodies separated,
scattered like clouds and burned like plains,
leaving not a single survivor.
Recently, the various generals in Guānzhōng,
once again gathered together,
continuing their rebellion,
blocking the two Huà mountains,
occupying the Hé and Wèi rivers,
driving and leading the Qiāng and Hú tribes,
aligning their forces eastward,
with high spirits and lofty ambitions,
as if invincible.
The Prime Minister, wielding his halberd like a soaring eagle,
like a wildfire driven by the wind,
with the great army setting forth,
broke them before the drums even sounded,
leaving corpses strewn by the thousands,
blood flowing enough to float shields,
all of which is known throughout the realm.
After this, the reason the great army approached the river but did not cross
was because Hán Yuē and Mǎ Chāo fled and escaped,
running back to Liángzhōu,
intending to bark once more.
The rebel Sòng Jiàn,
arrogated a title at Héshǒu,
aiding each other in wickedness,
standing together like lips and teeth.
Also, General Who Guards the South Zhāng Lǔ,
relied on his stronghold and showed no respect.
All were first to receive the punishment of our king.
Therefore, we temporarily displayed our troops and turned our banners,
reorganized the six armies,
marched westward in a long campaign,
to carry out the punishment of the realm.
When our side generals crossed Lǒng,
Jiàn and Yuē were exterminated,
their heads displayed across ten thousand lǐ;
when the army entered Sànguān,
the various Dī tribes submitted,
kings, marquises, and brave leaders,
rushed forward to lead the way.
Advancing to Hànzhōng,
then Yángpíng could not hold,
an army of a hundred thousand,
collapsed like earth and rotted like fish,
Zhāng Lǔ fled in haste,
running into Bāzhōng,
feeling gratitude and repenting his faults,
he surrendered and pledged allegiance;
the Bā tribal king Púo Hú and the Cóngyì marquis Dù Hù,
each leading their tribes,
together raised Bā commandery,
to serve the king's duties.
With one beat of the drums,
both regions were pacified,
benefits extending to the Western Sea,
our blades not dulled.
Such events as these,
are all due to the awe-inspiring might of Heaven,
the divine martial power of the state,
not merely the strength of men that could achieve.
The sagely court, broad and benevolent, covers and supports all,
truly trustworthy and truly cultured,
greatly bestowing ranks and commands,
to show the four directions.
Lǔ and Hú Hù both enjoyed enfeoffments of ten thousand households,
Lǔ's five sons,
each received estates of a thousand households,
Hú Hù's sons, brothers, troops, officers, and generals, over a thousand people, were made marquises, generals, and below.
The common people lived in peace,
the four classes returned to their occupations.
But Jiàn, Yuē, and their kind,
all became whales and sharks [slaughtered];
Chāo's wife and children,
had their heads burned in Jīnchéng,
parents and infants,
lay dead in Xǔ market.
It is not that the state brought disaster upon them,
and bestowed blessings upon these others,
but the distinction between rebellion and loyalty,
must inevitably be so.
The fierce bird strikes from on high first,
such is the momentum of seizing prey;
the awe of Mùyě,
the retreat at Méngjīn.
Now, thorns and brambles have been cleared away,
both Róng and Xià are purified,
ten thousand lǐ are orderly and united,
the six armies have no tasks.
Therefore, we raise the heavenly army of a million troops,
together with the Southern Chányú of the Xiōngnú Hūwánchú, and the six commanderies' Wūhuán, Dīnglíng, Túgè tribes,
the Qiāng and Bó tribes of Huángzhōng,
like thunder and a rolling mat,
from Shòuchūn southward.
Also, we have sent General Who Conquers the West Xiàhóu Yuān and others,
leading fifty thousand elite armored troops,
and the Dī and Qiāng of Wǔdū,
the sharp troops of Bā and Hàn,
south to the Wèn River,
seizing and holding Yōng and Shǔ.
The various armies of Jiāngxià and Xiāngyáng,
cutting across the Xiāng and Yuán rivers,
to approach Yùzhāng,
the tower ships and cross-sea forces,
directly pointing to Wú and Kuàijī.
Across ten thousand lǐ, setting the date,
five routes advancing together,
Sūn Quán's allotted time,
has now arrived.
The Prime Minister, bearing the authority of the state,
works to eliminate harm for the people.
The chief villains and great criminals
are certain to be beheaded and eradicated.
As for those who are merely attached like branches and leaves,
they are not specifically targeted for capture by the imperial edict.
Therefore, whenever a powerful enemy is defeated,
we have always prioritized accepting surrenders before executing,
selecting generals and recruiting talents,
each to be utilized to their fullest potential.
Thus, those who seek to achieve merit
all eagerly crane their necks and stand on tiptoe,
responding to the wind and following the call.
In the past, when Yuán Shù usurped and rebelled,
and the royal punishment was about to be imposed,
Liú Xūn, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, was the first to surrender his commandery
and return to the state.
When Lǚ Bù created chaos,
and our army approached Xiàpī,
Zhāng Liáo and Hóu Chéng
led their troops out to surrender.
When we later campaigned against Suī Gù,
Xuē Hóng and Jiū Shàng
opened the city gates and submitted.
During the Guāndù campaign,
Zhāng Hé and Gāo Lǎn rose up and achieved merit.
Later, when we campaigned against Yuán Shàng,
the Military Governor General Mǎ Yán,
the former Inspector of Yùzhōu, Yīn Kuí,
and the Commandant of Archers, Guō Zhào, surrendered on the battlefield.
When we besieged and guarded Yèchéng,
General Sū Yóu turned to serve as an inside agent,
and Shěn Pèi's nephew opened the gates to admit our troops.
After Yuán Tán was executed,
the great general of Yōuzhōu, Jiāo Chù, attacked and expelled Yuán Xī,
rising up to submit.
All these individuals, numbering in the hundreds,
were loyal, brave, resolute, and fierce,
possessing both wisdom and benevolence.
They all participated with the Prime Minister in planning strategies,
overcoming obstacles and resolving difficulties,
cutting down enemies and capturing flags,
bringing peace and stability to the land.
How could these actions be taken lightly?
Truly, Heaven opened their hearts,
their plans were deep and their considerations far-reaching.
They discerned the path between evil and righteousness,
clarified the distinction between what is permissible and what is not.
Their courage was not wasted in vain death,
their integrity was not established recklessly.
They bent and stretched, adapted and changed,
guided solely by the Way.
Thus, they established merits as weighty as mountains,
enjoyed immeasurable emoluments.
In the morning, they were enemies and captives;
by evening, they became senior generals.
This is what is called knowing to adapt when facing difficulties,
turning calamity into fortune.
As for those who are seduced by sweet words,
cling to petty favors as treasures,
remain mired in complacency,
sinking without awareness,
drifting with the waves,
perishing together with the flames—
they are also exceedingly numerous.
Their fortunes and misfortunes, gains and losses—
is it not lamentable?
In past years, when our army was in Hànzhōng,
separated by a great distance east and west,
the defense left at Héféi
numbered less than five thousand.
Sūn Quán personally led tens of thousands of troops,
yet was defeated and fled.
Now, to think of withstanding thunderous force—
it is difficult to have hope.
For Heaven's Way assists the compliant,
and human virtue aids the trustworthy.
Serving one's superior is called righteousness;
cherishing one's kin is called benevolence.
Shèng Xiàozhāng
was your lord,
yet Sūn Quán executed him.
Sūn Fǔ
was your elder brother,
yet Sūn Quán killed him.
To violate righteousness and destroy benevolence—
nothing is more extreme than this.
This is a crime that even the spirits flee from,
and the common people jointly detest.
One who bears such guilt and enmity
is called a vicious bandit.
Therefore, Yī Zhǐ left Xià,
and it was not considered damaging to virtue;
Fēi Lián died for Zhòu,
and cannot be called worthy.
Why?
Because the principles of leaving and staying
each have their appropriateness.
The Prime Minister deeply reflects that the former virtuous and renowned ministers of Jiāngdōng
are mostly recorded in the annals.
Recently, Wèi Shūyīng stood out loftily,
famous throughout the land;
Yú Wénxiù honed a pure integrity,
devoted to learning and antiquity;
Zhōu Tàimíng was an outstanding talent of his time,
with cultivated and illustrious virtue.
All should have received abundant blessings,
protecting and nurturing their descendants.
Yet the Zhōu and Shèng households were innocently slaughtered,
their remnants scattered and displaced,
lost in the wilds.
Speaking of it brings sorrow;
we hear that Wèi Zhōuróng and Yú Zhòngxiáng each continue their family lines,
able to bear the burden of splitting firewood.
As for the various old clans and elders of Wú, such as the Gù and Lù families,
who for generations have held high positions,
they should repay the Hàn dynasty's virtue,
glorifying their ancestors and making their names known.
And as for the various generals, officers, and relatives by marriage of Sūn Quán,
all are fine treasures and sharp tools of our state.
Yet they are all driven and oppressed,
cut off from heaven like rain severed,
having an axe but no handle—
how can they save themselves?
To follow along toppling into ruin—
is it not lamentable?
For the phoenix sings from the high ridge,
keeping far from nets and snares—
this is the virtue of the wise and sage.
The wren-like bird
nests among the reed flowers;
when the reed breaks, its young perish—
this is the delusion of the lowest fool.
Now the land of Jiāngdōng
is no different from reed flowers.
The various worthies residing there—
truly, they are also in danger.
The sagely court opens wide with magnanimity,
deeply cherishing the people's lives.
Punishment is for one man alone;
the masses have nothing to fear.
Therefore, extraordinary rewards are established
to await extraordinary achievements.
This is the excellent time for heroes and determined men to exert themselves—
can you not strive?
If you can turn around and rise up greatly,
establishing primary merit,
to correspond with illustrious emoluments—
this is the highest fortune.
If you cannot do this,
then weigh the greater and lesser,
exchanging survival for destruction—
this is the next best.
For if a snare traps the foot,
even the fierce tiger will sever its paw;
if a viper is in the hand,
the strong man will cut off his finger.
Why?
Because what he preserves is weighty,
and what he discards is light.
If, however, you delight in calamity and cling to false peace,
confused and forgetting to turn back,
oblivious to what the great and elegant preserve,
turning your back on the wise men's choices of leaving and staying,
neglecting the safety of the morning sun,
content with the fragile tip of the reed,
forgetting day by day,
until complete ruin—
once the great army is unleashed,
jade and stone will be shattered together.
Even if you wish to save yourselves,
it will be too late.
Therefore, we issue this to purchase and recruit with ranks and rewards;
the regulations are as listed below.
When this proclamation arrives,
carefully consider these utmost words.
Act in accordance with the edict and statutes.
In the past, the fortunes of Hàn declined,
the entire land was divided and collapsed,
the lives of the people
were nearly extinguished.
Our Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wǔ,
divinely martial and sagely wise,
rectified chaos and restored order,
saving what was about to fall,
and establishing our domain of Xià.
Emperor Wén, the High Ancestor, responded to Heaven and complied with the people,
receiving the mandate and ascending the throne.
Emperor Míng, the Illustrious Ancestor, continued the glorious legacy through generations,
expanding and consolidating the great enterprise.
However, beyond the rivers and mountains,
there were different administrations and customs,
and the common people across the land
had not yet received the kingly transformation.
This is why the Three Ancestors cherished their unfulfilled aspirations.
Now, our sovereign is sagely virtuous, reverent, and enlightened,
carrying on and glorifying the former legacy.
The chief ministers are loyal, respectful, enlightened, and trustworthy,
toiling diligently for the royal house.
They spread governance and bestow kindness, harmonizing all states;
they extend virtue to the hundred barbarians, and Sùshèn presents tribute.
We grieve for those in Bā-Shǔ,
who alone are treated as not being our people,
and pity these common folk,
whose labor and service have not ceased.
Therefore, we have commanded the six armies,
to reverently execute Heaven’s punishment.
The armies of the West, Yōngzhōu, and the Western Garrison
advance together along five routes.
In ancient times, the conduct of armies
was based on benevolence
and governed by righteousness.
The armies of a true king
engage in expeditions but not in battles.
Thus, Yú Shùn danced with shield and axe, and the Yǒumiáo submitted;
King Wǔ of Zhōu had the righteousness of distributing wealth, opening granaries, and honoring the virtuous.
Now, the Western Garrison, upholding the command and bearing the mandate,
leads the war chariots,
hoping to broadly propagate the instruction of civil proclamation,
to save the lives of the common people,
not wishing to exhaust military force or engage in extreme warfare
to satisfy a momentary ambition.
Therefore, we briefly state the essentials of safety and danger:
listen respectfully to these words.
The former ruler of Yìzhōu, with his talent of a generation,
raised troops at Xīnyě,
was trapped and stumbled in the outskirts of Jì and Xú,
controlled by the hands of Shào and Bù.
Our Grand Ancestor saved and aided him,
and his fortunes greatly flourished.
Later, he turned his back and violated
abandoning the like and aligning with the different.
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng repeatedly planned for Qínchuān,
Jiāng Bóyuē frequently marched out to Lǒngyòu,
harassing our borders,
invading and disturbing our Dí and Qiāng.
At that time, the state faced many troubles,
and there was no leisure to undertake the nine punitive expeditions.
Now, the borders are pacified and clear,
and within the realm, there is no trouble.
We have accumulated strength and await the time,
concentrating our troops in one direction.
Yet, with the forces of a single province like Bā-Shǔ,
divided and stretched in defense,
it is difficult to withstand the armies of the realm.
The defeated morale at Duàngǔ and Hóuhé
is hard-pressed to oppose our majestic formations.
In recent years,
there has hardly been a year of peace.
The conscripted men are weary and exhausted,
unable to match the people who come willingly.
All of this you, esteemed gentlemen, have personally witnessed.
The Marquis of Shǔ was captured by Qín;
Gōngsūn Shù surrendered his head to Hàn.
The strategic terrain of the nine provinces
does not belong to a single clan.
All of this you, gentlemen, have fully heard.
The clear-sighted perceive danger before it takes form;
the wise plan for fortune before it sprouts.
Thus, Wēizǐ left Shāng
and long remained a guest of Zhōu;
Chén Píng turned his back on Xiàng
and achieved merit in Hàn.
How could one indulge in comfort like poisoned wine,
clinging to salary without change?
Now, the state dynasty bestows the grace of Heaven’s cover,
and the chief ministers extend the virtue of leniency and forgiveness,
first bestowing kindness, then executing punishment,
cherishing life and abhorring killing.
In the past, the Wú general Sūn Yī
led his followers to submit internally,
and was appointed to high office,
receiving exceptional favor and rank.
Wén Qīn and Táng Zī,
who were great harms to the state,
rebelled against their lord and became enemies,
yet returned as leaders of armies.
Zī, trapped and forced, was captured;
Qīn’s two sons returned and surrendered.
Both were enfeoffed as marquises,
and Zī participated in state affairs.
Yī and others, in desperate straits, submitted to the mandate,
and still received added favor.
How much more so for the wise and discerning of Bā-Shǔ who act upon recognizing the opportunity!
If you can deeply reflect on success and failure,
and loftily withdraw,
following in the footsteps of Wēizǐ,
placing yourselves on the path of Chén Píng,
then your fortune will equal that of the ancients,
and blessings will flow to your descendants.
The common people and gentry
will dwell in peace and enjoy their livelihoods,
farmers will not need to change their fields,
markets will not need to shift their stalls,
removing the danger of piled eggs,
and adopting the plan of eternal peace—
is this not excellent!
If you steal comfort for a morning and evening,
confused and not turning back,
once the great army is unleashed,
jade and stone will both be shattered.
Even if you wish to regret it,
it will be too late.
Each of you, make this known,
so that all may be informed.
Since the rise of Hàn, seventy-eight years have passed,
and its virtue has flourished through six reigns.
Martial might is abundant,
and profound grace is vast and deep,
moistening all living beings,
overflowing beyond the borders.
Thus, we were commanded to campaign westward,
pushing back along the currents,
wherever the wind reaches,
none do not submit.
We thereby made Rǎn and Máng submit,
pacified Zuó and preserved Qióng,
conquered Sīyú,
raised Bāopú,
turned our chariots around,
heading east to report,
arriving at the capital of Shǔ.
Twenty-seven elders, great officers, and gentlemen of the girdle,
solemnly came to visit.
After their address,
they advanced and said:
"We have heard that the Son of Heaven’s governance of the barbarians
means only to bridle and not sever ties.
Now, exhausting the soldiers of three commanderies,
opening the road to Yèláng,
for three years now,
the task remains uncompleted.
The soldiers are weary and tired,
and the myriad people are not provided for.
Now, further connecting with the western barbarians,
the people’s strength is exhausted,
fearing they cannot finish the task.
This is also a burden for the envoy.
We privately worry for you.
Moreover, Qióng and Zuó, the western barbarians, have coexisted with the Middle Kingdom
for many years,
too many to record.
The benevolent do not attract them with virtue,
the strong do not annex them by force.
We suspect it may be impossible!
Now, dividing the common people to attach to the barbarians,
exhausting what we rely on to serve the useless—
we, humble folk, are ignorant and narrow-minded,
and do not understand what is meant."
The envoy said:
"How can you say this?
If it were as you say,
then Shǔ would not change its clothing and Bā would not transform its customs.
I have always disliked hearing such talk.
However, this matter is of great importance,
and certainly not something observers can fully grasp.
My journey is urgent,
and the details cannot be fully heard.
Allow me to roughly outline it for you, gentlemen:
"For in the world there must be extraordinary men,
and only then can there be extraordinary deeds;
with extraordinary deeds,
only then can there be extraordinary achievements.
The extraordinary,
are indeed what ordinary people find strange.
Therefore it is said:
At the origin of the extraordinary,
the common people are fearful;
but when it reaches its completion,
the world is at peace.
In ancient times, when the floodwaters boiled forth,
overflowing and spreading everywhere,
the people moved up and down, shifting and migrating,
struggling and unsettled.
The Xiàhòu clan grieved over this,
and so blocked the flood and sealed its source,
channeled the rivers and dredged the waterways,
dispersed the silt and calmed the disaster,
directing it eastward to the sea,
and the world was forever peaceful.
In the toil of that time,
was it only the people?
His mind was troubled with worries,
and his body personally undertook the labor;
his hands and feet were calloused and without fine hair,
his skin grew no down.
Thus his glorious legacy shines forth boundlessly,
and his reputation spreads to this day.
"Moreover, when a worthy ruler ascends the throne,
does he merely cling to trivialities and pettiness,
constrained by texts and bound by customs,
reciting and practicing traditions,
seeking only to please the present age?
He must elevate grand discourse and profound deliberation,
founding enterprises and establishing a lasting legacy,
setting a model for ten thousand generations.
Therefore, he ranges far and wide, embracing all,
and diligently contemplates matching heaven and doubling earth.
And does the Book of Songs not say?
'Under the vast sky,
there is no land that is not the king's;
to the shores of all lands,
there is no one who is not the king's subject.'
Thus within the six directions,
beyond the eight borders,
spreading and overflowing,
if any living thing is not moistened by his grace,
the worthy ruler considers it a disgrace.
Now within the borders,
among the cap-and-girdle class,
all have received excellent blessings,
with none omitted or left behind.
But in the states of the Yí and Dí with their different customs,
in distant, isolated, and alien regions,
where boats and carts do not reach,
and human footprints rarely tread,
where governance and teachings have not yet been applied,
and the influence of culture remains faint.
Internally, they occasionally violate righteousness and encroach upon propriety at the borders;
externally, they engage in wicked deeds and lawless acts,
overthrowing and killing their superiors.
Ruler and minister exchange positions,
the noble and humble lose their proper order,
the elderly suffer injustice,
the young and orphaned become slaves and captives,
bound and weeping,
turning inward with resentment,
saying:
'We have heard that in the Central Kingdom there is the utmost benevolence,
where virtue flows abundantly and grace is universal,
and nothing fails to find its proper place.
Why now are we alone left out?'
They rise on tiptoe in longing,
like a parched drought yearning for rain.'
Even a cruel man would shed tears for this,
how much more a supreme sage,
how could he remain unmoved?
Therefore, he sends armies north to chastise the strong Hú,
and dispatches envoys south to reproach the vigorous Yuè.
His virtue spreads in all directions,
and the rulers of these two regions,
gathering like scales and looking up to the flow,
wish to receive his commands by the hundreds of millions.
Thus he opens the Mòruò Pass,
patrols the Zāngkē region,
carves through the Língshān mountains,
and bridges the Sūnyuán plains.
He creates the path of virtue,
establishes the tradition of benevolence and righteousness,
intending to broaden his grace and extend his beneficence,
pacifying from afar and driving long,
so that the distant are not shut out,
and the dim and obscure
may shine in the light,
thus laying aside arms here,
and ceasing campaigns there.
Far and near become one body,
within and without enjoy peace and happiness,
is this not prosperity?
To rescue the people from drowning,
to uphold the supreme virtue of the sovereign,
to reverse the decline of an age of decay,
to continue the severed enterprise of the Zhōu house,
this is the urgent task of the Son of Heaven.
Though the people may toil,
how can it be halted?
"Moreover, a true king certainly never begins without worry and toil,
and ends in ease and pleasure.
Yet the sign of receiving the mandate,
lies precisely in this.
He will soon increase the fēng sacrifice at Tàishān,
add the shì ceremony at Liángfù,
ring the harmonious bells,
raise the music and hymns,
ascend to surpass the Five Emperors,
and rise to join the Three Sovereigns.
Observers have not yet glimpsed his intent,
listeners have not yet heard his sound,
yet like the jiāomíng bird already soaring in the vast heavens,
while the net-casters still gaze into the
At this, the various grand masters were bewildered, losing what they had intended to say,
forgetting their reasons for advancing,
and sighed in unison, saying:
'Truly, the virtue of Hàn,
this is what we humble men wish to hear.
Though the people may toil,
we ask to lead them by our own example.'
They were at a loss and shifted uneasily,
delaying and excusing themselves.
King Xiāng of Chǔ asked Sòng Yù:
'Sir, do you have some failing in conduct?
Why do the scholars and common people speak so ill of you?'
Sòng Yù replied:
'Yes,
indeed, there is.
I beg Your Majesty to pardon my offense,
and allow me to finish my words.
There was a guest singing in Yǐngzhōng,
who began with "Xiàlǐ Bārén,"
and several thousand in the state joined in harmony;
when he sang "Yáng'ē Xièlù,"
several hundred in the state joined in harmony;
when he sang "Yángchūn Báixuě,"
only several tens in the state joined in harmony;
when he drew the shāng note and carved the yǔ note,
mingled with the flowing zhǐ note,
only a few in the state joined in harmony.
Thus, the higher the song,
the fewer join in harmony.
Therefore, among birds there is the fèng, and among fish there is the kūn.
The fènghuáng strikes upward for nine thousand lǐ,
piercing the clouds and rainbows,
bearing the azure sky,
soaring in the heights of the vast and obscure.
Can the quail in the hedge
possibly measure with it the height of heaven and earth?
The kūn fish sets out at dawn from the Kūnlún ranges,
bares its fins at Jiéshí,
and rests at evening in Mèngzhū.
Can the ní in a foot-deep pond
possibly measure with it the vastness of rivers and seas?
Thus it is not only among birds and fish that there are fèng and kūn,
among scholars there are also such.
The sage, with his magnificent thoughts and noble conduct,
stands aloof and dwells alone;
how could the common people of the world understand what your servant does!'
A guest challenged Dōngfāng Shuò, saying:
'Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí, once they met the lords of ten thousand chariots,
immediately attained the positions of ministers and chancellors,
and their favor extended to later generations.
Now you, Sir, cultivate the arts of the former kings,
admire the righteousness of the sages,
recite and chant the words of the classics, histories, and the hundred schools,
too many to record,
writing them on bamboo and silk,
until your lips rot and teeth fall out,
holding them in your heart without release,
the effect of loving learning and delighting in the Way,
is exceedingly clear.
You consider yourself peerless in wisdom and ability within the seas,
and may indeed be called broad in knowledge and eloquent in wisdom.
Yet you exhaust your strength and devote your loyalty,
serving a sage emperor,
spending long days and enduring over time,
accumulating several decades,
yet your office does not exceed that of a shìláng,
your rank does not exceed that of a halberd-bearer.
Could it be that you still have some failing in conduct?
Even among your own brothers,
there is no place to accommodate you.
What is the reason for this?'
Master Dōngfāng sighed deeply,
looked up, and replied:
"This is not something you can fully understand.
That was one era,
this is another.
How can they be the same?
In the time of Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
the Zhōu court was in great disarray,
the feudal lords did not pay homage,
they contended for power through force,
capturing each other with armies,
merging into twelve states,
with none yet dominant.
Those who gained talented men became strong,
those who lost them perished.
Therefore, persuasive arguments could be put into practice.
One could attain a position of honor,
treasures filling one's household,
granaries abundant outside,
benefits extending to later generations,
with descendants enjoying them long.
Now it is not so.
The sage emperor's virtue flows,
all under heaven tremble in awe,
the feudal lords submit as guests,
connecting lands beyond the four seas like a belt,
as stable as an overturned bowl,
all under heaven is balanced and equal,
united as one family.
When actions are taken and affairs initiated,
it is as easy as moving something in the palm.
How can the worthy and the unworthy be distinguished?
Following the Way of Heaven,
complying with the principles of Earth,
nothing fails to find its proper place.
Thus, pacify them and they are at peace;
stir them and they suffer.
Honor them and they become generals;
demean them and they become captives.
Raise them up and they are above the azure clouds;
suppress them and they are beneath the deep abyss.
Employ them and they are tigers;
do not employ them and they are mice.
Even if one wishes to exhaust one's loyalty and offer one's sincerity,
how can one know what is before or behind?
In the vastness of Heaven and Earth,
among the multitudes of scholars and commoners,
those who exhaust their energy racing to persuade,
advancing together like spokes converging on a hub,
are too numerous to count.
They strive with all their might to be admired,
yet are distressed by food and clothing,
and some lose their family standing.
If Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí were born together with me in this present age,
they would not even attain the post of a petty clerk,
how would they dare aspire to be a gentleman attendant?
The tradition says:
'When the world is without harm,
even if there are sages,
they have no way to apply their talents.
When superiors and inferiors are harmonious and united,
even if there are worthies, they have no way to achieve merit.'
Therefore it is said: times differ, affairs differ.
"Nevertheless,
how can one not devote oneself to cultivating one's character?
The Odes say:
'When bells are beaten in the palace,
their sound is heard outside.'
'The crane cries in the nine marshes,
its sound is heard in Heaven.'
If one can cultivate one's character,
why worry about not attaining glory?
Tàigōng personally practiced benevolence and righteousness,
until he was seventy-two,
and only then was he employed by King Wén and King Wǔ,
gaining trust in his doctrines,
enfeoffed in Qí,
for seven hundred years without interruption.
This is why scholars day and night diligently,
cultivate learning and act diligently, not daring to be idle.
They are like the wagtail,
flying and crying out.
The tradition says:
'Heaven does not cease its winter because men dislike the cold;
Earth does not cease its vastness because men dislike its perils;
the gentleman does not change his conduct because of the clamor of petty men.'
'Heaven has constant measures,
Earth has constant forms,
the gentleman has constant conduct;
the gentleman follows his constancy,
the petty man calculates his gain.'
The Odes say:
'If there is no transgression of ritual and righteousness,
why worry about what others say?'
'Water that is too clear has no fish;
a man who is too discerning has no followers.
The tassels hanging before the crown
are to obscure sight;
the yellow silk plugs filling the ears
are to block hearing.'
Thus, sight sometimes does not see,
hearing sometimes does not hear.
Praise great virtue,
pardon minor faults—
this is the principle of not demanding perfection from any one person.
Bend what is crooked to make it straight,
but let it find its own way;
be generous and gentle with it,
letting it seek for itself;
measure and assess it,
letting it search on its own.
Such is the teaching and transformation of the sage:
he desires that they attain it themselves.
When they attain it themselves,
then they are diligent and broad.
"As for the recluses of the present age,
though the times do not employ them,
solitary and without followers,
expansive and dwelling alone,
looking up they observe Xǔ Yóu,
looking down they examine Jiē Yú,
their plans match those of Fàn Lǐ,
their loyalty aligns with Zǐxū.
In an age of peace and harmony under heaven,
upholding righteousness,
having few companions and followers—
this is indeed fitting.
Why then do you doubt me?
As for Yān employing Yuè Yì,
Qín appointing Lǐ Sī,
Lì Yìjī persuading Qí to submit,
their persuasions flowing like water,
compliance following like a ring,
obtaining whatever they desired,
achievements like mountains,
the realm settled,
the state secure—
this was because they encountered their time.
Why then do you find this strange?
The saying goes:
'To view the sky through a tube,
to measure the sea with a ladle,
to strike a bell with a reed'—
how can one comprehend its systematic connections,
examine its patterns and principles,
or elicit its sounds?
From this perspective,
it is like a shrew attacking a dog,
or a lone piglet biting a tiger:
they arrive only to be crushed—
what achievement can there be?
Now, for one of the lowest folly to criticize the recluse,
even if he wishes not to be confounded,
it is truly impossible.
This merely serves to show that he does not understand adapting to circumstances,
and remains ultimately confused about the great Way."
During the reign of Emperor Āi,
Dīng, Fù, and Dǒng Xián held power.
Those who attached themselves to them
rose from their households to positions of two thousand shi.
At that time, Yáng Xióng was just drafting the Tàixuán,
having means to maintain himself,
and was content.
Someone mocked Yáng Xióng, saying his Mysterious was still white,
and Yáng Xióng explained himself,
calling it "Explanation of Ridicule."
His words said:
A guest mocked Yáng Zǐ, saying:
"I have heard that the gentlemen of antiquity,
the models and exemplars of humanity,
if they were not born, it was all right;
but if born, they would certainly honor the sovereign above
and bring glory to their parents below,
splitting the jade tokens of others,
shouldering the ranks of others,
holding the tallies of others,
sharing the emoluments of others,
draped in dark green and trailing purple,
with vermilion lacquering their carriage wheels.
Now you, sir, are fortunate to encounter a bright and prosperous age,
to dwell in a court without taboos,
to walk in the same ranks as a host of worthies,
to have passed through the Golden Gate,
and ascended the Jade Hall for some time now.
Yet you have never been able to devise a single stratagem,
propose a single policy,
persuade the ruler above,
or converse with the high ministers below.
With eyes like shining stars,
a tongue like lightning's flash,
arguing now this way, now that,
so that no debater could withstand you—
instead, you silently composed the *Tàixuán* in five thousand words,
with branches and leaves spreading luxuriantly,
expounding alone over a hundred thousand words.
Its depths plunge into the Yellow Springs,
its heights soar beyond the azure sky;
its breadth encompasses the primal ether,
its fineness enters the space between things.
Yet your position does not exceed that of a Gentleman Attendant,
and your promotion only reached Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
Does it mean that the *Xuán* is perhaps still white?
Why is your official career so desolate?"
Yáng Zǐ laughed and replied to him:
"You, sir, only see the vermilion lacquer on my carriage wheels,
not knowing that one misstep will redden my entire clan with blood.
In the past, when the net of Zhōu loosened its knots,
the herd of deer struggled to escape,
dividing into twelve states,
coalescing into six or seven,
split four and five ways,
all becoming Warring States.
Scholars had no constant lord,
states had no settled ministers;
he who gained scholars prospered,
he who lost them grew poor.
They could spread their wings and sharpen their pinions,
going wherever they pleased.
Thus, some scholars carried their belongings in sacks to seek employment,
others chiseled through walls to flee.
Therefore, Zōu Yǎn, by soaring aloft, gained the resources of the age;
Mèng Kē, though repeatedly frustrated,
still became teacher to a ruler of ten thousand chariots.
"Now the great Hàn: to the left lies the Eastern Sea,
to the right, Qúsōu;
in front, Pānyú;
behind, Jiāotú.
In the southeast, a single commandant;
in the northwest, a single lookout post.
Restrained by the black cord of law,
controlled by the axe of punishment,
dispersed by rites and music,
influenced by the *Odes* and *Documents*,
given ample time over the years,
bound by the mourning hut.
The scholars of the world,
like thunder moving and clouds gathering,
like overlapping fish scales,
all strive within the eight regions.
Every family considers itself to have a Jì or Xiè,
every person considers himself a Gāo Yáo.
Those wearing silk caps and dangling tassels
all compare themselves to Ā Héng in conversation;
even a child of five feet
is ashamed to be likened to Yàn Yīng or Yí Wú.
Those on the path rise to the azure clouds;
those who lose the way are cast into the ditches.
Grasp power in the morning, and you are a minister or chancellor;
lose influence by evening, and you are a common man.
It is like the shores of rivers and lakes,
the islands of the vast sea:
a flock of wild geese alighting does not make it seem more numerous,
a pair of ducks flying away does not make it seem less.
In the past, when the three benevolent men left, Yīn became ruins;
when the two elders returned, Zhōu grew strong;
when Wǔ Zǐxū died, Wú perished;
while Wén Zhǒng and Fàn Lǐ survived, Yuè became hegemon;
when the five rams' skins entered, Qín rejoiced;
when Yuè Yì departed, Yān feared;
Fàn Jū, by being broken and bent, endangered the Marquis of Ráng;
Cài Zé, by keeping silent and groaning, laughed at Táng Jǔ.
Thus, when there are affairs of state,
without Xiāo Hé, Cáo Shēn, Zhāng Liáng, Chén Píng, Zhōu Bó, Fán Kuài, or Huò Guāng, there can be no peace;
when there are no affairs of state,
the pedants of textual exegesis sit together and guard it,
and there is still no cause for worry.
Therefore, when the age is chaotic, even sages and philosophers gallop about and it is not enough;
when the age is well-ordered, even mediocrities can rest on high pillows and have plenty.
"As for the gentlemen of antiquity,
some were released from bonds and became ministers,
some cast off their coarse garments and became tutors;
some leaned against the Yí Gate and laughed,
some fished across the river pools;
some presented their doctrines seventy times yet met no opportunity;
some were enfeoffed as marquises after a single conversation;
some had a thousand chariots humbly visit a mean alley,
some swept the path with brooms to lead the way.
Thus, scholars could quite freely trust their tongues and wield their brushes,
plugging gaps and treading on flaws without being thwarted.
Nowadays, the district magistrates do not invite scholars,
the commandery governors do not welcome teachers,
the various high ministers do not bow to guests,
the generals and chancellors do not lower their brows;
those who speak cleverly are viewed with suspicion,
those whose conduct is unusual meet with punishment.
Thus, those who wish to speak curl their tongues to echo the same sounds,
those who wish to walk measure their steps to follow in the same tracks.
Suppose the gentlemen of antiquity
were placed in the present age:
if their policy essays were not top grade,
their conduct not that of Filial and Incorrupt,
their recommendation not as Upright and Straightforward,
they could only submit memorials of protest,
occasionally speaking of right and wrong,
at best obtaining an appointment as Attendant,
at worst being dismissed after an audience,
so how could they attain the dark green and purple?
"Moreover, I have heard:
that which blazes fiercely is extinguished,
that which rumbles loudly is cut off;
observe thunder and fire—
they seem full and substantial;
Heaven takes back their sound,
Earth stores away their heat.
For families of high eminence,
ghosts peer into their chambers.
Those who snatch and seize perish,
those who are silent and still survive;
those at the pinnacle of position are in high danger,
those who guard themselves preserve their persons.
Therefore, to know the dark and know silence
is the ultimate in guarding the Way;
to cherish clarity and cherish stillness
is the courtyard for wandering spirits;
only in solitude and emptiness
lies the abode for preserving virtue.
Ages differ, affairs change,
yet the way of humanity is not different;
if they and we exchanged times,
who knows how it would be?
Now you, sir, take an owl to laugh at the phoenix,
grasp a lizard to mock the tortoise and dragon—
is this not sick indeed!
You laugh at my *Xuán* for being still white,
I also laugh at your grave sickness,
unmet by Yú Fū or Biǎn Què—
how lamentable!"
The guest said:
"Then, without the *Xuán*, one can achieve no fame?
From Fàn Jū and Cài Zé onward,
why must there be the *Xuán*?"
Yáng Zǐ said:
"Fàn Jū,
a fugitive from Wèi,
with broken ribs and crushed hipbone,
escaped from ropes and bonds,
hunched his shoulders and trod on his back,
crawled into a sack,
yet stirred the lord of ten thousand chariots to anger,
stood between Jīngyáng,
and pressed against Rǎnghóu to replace him—
this was due to opportunity.
Cài Zé,
a common man from east of the mountains,
with a sunken chin and broken nose,
drooling tears and spittle,
bowed westward to the powerful minister of Qín,
seized his throat and stifled his breath,
pressed his back and wrested away his position—
this was due to timing.
When the world was already settled,
and weapons of war were already laid aside,
with the capital at Luòyáng,
Lóu Jìng abandoned his cart and unhitched the traces,
wagged his three-inch tongue,
proposed an unshakable strategy,
and moved the central realm to settle in Cháng'ān—
this was due to suitability.
The Five Emperors handed down canons,
the Three Kings transmitted rituals,
unchanged for a hundred generations;
Shūsūn Tōng arose from amidst the war drums,
laid aside armor and cast aside spears,
and then established the ceremonies between ruler and minister—
this was due to attainment.
The laws of Lǚ grew corrupt and decayed,
the laws of Qín were cruel and severe,
the sage Hàn dynasty established temporary regulations,
and Xiāo Hé created the statutes—
this was due to appropriateness.
Thus, had Xiāo Hé's laws been created in the age of Táng and Yú,
they would have been mistaken.
Had Shūsūn Tōng's ceremonies been made in the times of Xià and Yīn,
they would have been deluded;
had Lóu Jìng's strategy been proposed in the era of Chéngzhōu,
it would have been perverse;
had the theories of Fàn and Cài been discussed among the likes of Jīn, Zhāng, Xǔ, and Shǐ,
they would have been deemed mad.
As for Xiāo's regulations followed by Cáo,
Liúhóu's strategic plans,
Chén Píng's extraordinary schemes,
their achievements like Mount Tài,
their echoes like crumbling cliffs,
though due to the courage and wisdom of these men,
it was also because they met with a time that allowed such deeds.
Therefore, to do what can be done in a time when it can be done,
brings success;
to do what cannot be done in a time when it cannot be done,
brings disaster.
As for Lìn Xiàngrú achieving merit at Zhāngtái,
the Four Haos gathering glory at Nánshān,
Gōngsūn Hóng founding his career at Jīnmǎ,
Piàoqí Fā making his mark at Qílián,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú stealing wealth from the Zhuō family,
Dōngfāng Shuò dividing roast meat for his wife—
I truly cannot compare with these several gentlemen,
therefore I silently and alone guard my 'Tàixuán'."
During the Yǒngpíng reign, he served as a court gentleman,
overseeing the collation of secret archives,
wholly devoted to Confucian studies,
taking writing as his occupation.
Some ridiculed him for having no achievement,
and he, moved by the self-analogies of Dōngfāng Shuò and Yáng Xióng,
because he did not encounter the times of Sū, Zhāng, Fàn, and Cài,
had never refuted them with the correct path,
nor clarified what the gentleman holds to,
therefore he casually responded once more.
His words said:
The guest playfully addressed the host:
"I have heard that the sage has fixed principles,
the determined scholar has unchanging duties,
and it is also said to be a matter of reputation.
Therefore, the highest is to establish virtue,
the next is to achieve merit.
Virtue cannot be especially abundant if it does not follow one's person,
merit cannot be uniquely illustrious if it goes against the times.
Thus, in the governance of sages and wise men,
they were restless and hurried,
Kǒngzǐ's mat was never warm,
Mòzǐ's chimney never blackened.
From this perspective,
choosing and rejecting were the foremost tasks of the ancients,
while writing was but a leftover matter for those ahead.
Now, you, sir, are fortunate to wander in an emperor's age,
personally wearing the robes and crown of office,
floating in splendor,
steeped in the Way and virtue,
gazing upon the patterns of dragon and tiger,
for a long time.
Yet you ultimately cannot stretch head and tail,
beat wings and scales,
rise from the mire,
leap and soar upon wind and clouds,
to make those who see you startle like shadows,
those who hear you tremble like echoes.
You merely delight in pillowing on classics and stacking books,
bending your body within a humble gate,
above having no stem,
below having no root.
Alone, you express your thoughts beyond the cosmos,
focus your mind within the tiniest details,
immerse your spirit in silent memory,
bound by the passing years.
Yet your vessel is not valued in your own time,
your usefulness does not show in this generation;
though you debate as swiftly as surging waves,
adorn with phrases like spring blossoms,
it still avails nothing for ranking highest or lowest.
It seems to me,
you should rather devise strategies for morning and evening,
settle plans for meetings and assemblies,
so that while alive you have a glorious title,
and when dead, a fine posthumous name—
would that not be better?"
The host smiled leisurely and said:
"What you, the guest, have said
is what is called seeing the splendor of worldly gain,
while being blind to the substance of the Way and virtue;
guarding the flickering candlelight in a dark corner,
without ever looking up at the heavenly court to behold the bright sun.
In the past, the royal way was overgrown and foul;
the Zhōu lost its control,
the feudal lords and earls drove their chariots side by side,
the Warring States ran rampant,
and thus the seven mighty powers roared and clashed,
splitting apart the various Xià states,
dragons fought and tigers contended.
The wandering persuaders,
swift as wind and sudden as lightning,
all arose to save the age,
and the rest, like whirlwinds flying and shadows attaching,
dazzling and brilliant among them,
were too many to record.
At that time,
even wielding decayed wood and rubbing blunt edges,
leaden knives could all make a single cut;
thus, Lǔ Lián flew a single arrow and overturned a thousand pieces of gold;
Yú Qīng, with a mere glance, cast aside his ministerial seal.
As for chirping and tossing out tunes,
sounds that please the ear,
if matched to musical scales,
become excessive and cacophonous, unfit for listening—
they are not the music of Sháo and Xià.
Adapting to circumstances and conforming to change,
meeting the appearance of the times,
shifting winds and altering customs,
if perverse and contradictory, impossible to harmonize—
that is not the method of the gentleman.
And when it came to those who followed others to unite them,
or used horizontal alliances to scatter them,
men without allegiance drifting in persuasion,
travelers lodging abroad who displayed their rhetoric,
Shāng Yāng, grasping three strategies, drilled into Duke Xiào;
Lǐ Sī, striving with timely affairs, sought to win over the First Emperor.
They all trod upon the gathering of wind and dust,
trod the situation of upheaval and distress,
seized upon petty advantages and rode upon wickedness,
to seek a single day's wealth and honor.
In the morning they were glorious and splendid,
by evening they were haggard and worn.
Their fortune did not fill the space between the eyelids,
yet calamity overflowed into the world.
Even wicked men would thereby regret it themselves,
how much less should auspicious scholars rely on such ways?
Moreover, achievement cannot be founded on emptiness,
fame cannot be established through falsity.
Hán Fēi set up arguments to provoke his lord;
Lǚ Bùwéi practiced deceit to purchase a state.
Once 'The Difficulties of Persuasion' was completed,
his own person was imprisoned;
once the Qín goods became expensive,
his clan also fell.
Therefore, Zhòngní upheld the will of floating clouds,
Mèng Kē nurtured the vast and flowing breath;
did they delight in being impractical and broad?
The Way cannot be divided.
Now the great Hàn has washed away all foulness,
leveled dangers and cleared wilderness,
expanded the imperial net,
restored the royal guiding principles,
its foundation loftier than Fúxī and Shénnóng,
its scope broader than Huángdì and Táng Yáo.
Its ruler over the world
shines upon it like the sun,
awes it like a spirit,
contains it like the sea,
nurtures it like spring.
Therefore, within the six directions,
none do not share the same source and flow together,
bathed in the profound virtue,
receiving and looking up to the great harmony.
Branches attach and leaves cling,
just as plants and trees are planted in mountain forests,
birds and fish are nurtured in rivers and marshes:
those that obtain the vital breath flourish and multiply,
those that miss their season wither and fall.
Aligning with heaven and earth to spread transformation,
how can one speak of the thickness or thinness of human affairs?
Now you, my friend, dwell in a glorious age yet discuss the Warring States,
dazzled by what you have heard and doubting what you see,
wishing to follow a mound's height to measure the loftiness of Tài Shān,
or, holding a trickling stream, to sound the depths of the abyssal chasm—
you have not yet arrived. "
The guest said:
"As for the likes of Yāng and Sī,
wicked men of the declining Zhōu,
I have already received your instruction.
May I venture to ask about the scholars of high antiquity,
who established themselves and practiced the Way,
assisted their age and achieved fame,
whose deeds can be related to later generations—
were they silent and that is all?"
The host said:
"How could it be so!
In the past, Gāo Yáo counseled Yú,
Jīzǐ was consulted by Zhōu,
their words connected with emperors and kings,
their plans matched with the divine and sage.
The Yīn dream-speaker arose from Fùyán,
the Zhōu hope stirred by the Wèi riverbank;
Qí's Níng Jī raised his voice at the broad road,
Hàn's Liáng received the book at Pīyín.
