All awaited fate and communed with spirits,
not relying on mere words and speech.
Therefore they could establish strategies of certainty,
and unfold achievements without end.
In more recent times, Master Lù wandered at ease,
and the 'New Discourses' arose;
Master Dǒng lowered his curtains,
and his literary brilliance shone among the Confucian grove;
Liú Xiàng oversaw the classics,
distinguishing and clarifying old knowledge;
Yáng Xióng pondered deeply,
producing the 'Model Sayings' and 'Great Mystery'.
All timely entered the gates of their rulers,
exhaustively explored the inner chambers of the former sages,
roamed leisurely in the fields of arts and techniques,
rested in the parks of texts and records,
thereby preserving their substance and expressing their refinement,
employing it to be received into sagely virtue,
their shining deeds brilliant to later men.
Are these not second to none?
As for Bóyí upholding his conduct at Shǒuyáng,
Liǔ Xiàhuì lowering his will to accept a demeaning post,
Yán Yuān finding joy in a single bamboo dish and gourd dipper,
Kǒngzǐ completing his writings with the western hunt,
their sound fills heaven and abyss,
truly they are the models and teachers for us, their followers.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
One yīn, one yáng,
that is the method of heaven and earth;
now refinement, now substance,
that is the guiding principle of the kingly way;
sometimes the same, sometimes different,
that is the constant of sages and wise men.
Therefore it is said:
Carefully cultivate your will,
guard your heavenly tally,
entrust fate and devote yourself,
savor the richness of the Way.
If the spirits hear this,
how could they abandon your name?
Have you, guest, not also heard of Héshì's jade,
concealed within the stone of Jīng,
or Suíhóu's pearl,
hidden within the clam shell?
For generations none saw it,
not knowing it would contain shining light,
emit exquisite essence,
and after a thousand years of obscurity, still radiate flowing brilliance.
The Yìnglóng lies hidden in a stagnant puddle,
fish and turtles treat it with familiarity,
not seeing its ability to rouse its numinous virtue,
join with wind and clouds,
transcend the vast wilderness and tread upon the azure heavens.
Therefore, to wallow in mud yet soar in the sky—
that is the spirit of the Yìnglóng.
To be lowly first and noble later—
that is the treasure of Héshì and Suíhóu.
To be obscure for a time yet illustrious long after—
that is the genuineness of the gentleman.
As for Yá and Kuàng purifying the ear with pipes and strings,
Lílóu straining his eyes to the finest hair's breadth;
Péng Méng possessing peerless skill with bow and arrow,
Bānshū displaying ingenuity with axe and adze;
Liáng and Yuè surpassing in ability at judging and driving horses,
Wū Huò exerting strength against a thousand jun;
Hé and Què expressing essence with needle and stone,
Yán and Sāng calculating in their minds without limit.
I, too, am unfit to place my skill among that company,
therefore I dwell closely, amusing myself with this culture. "
The Emperor traveled to Hédōng,
sacrificed to the Earth Spirit,
looked back toward the imperial capital with joy,
and in mid-stream feasted and drank with his assembled ministers.
The Emperor was exceedingly merry,
and thereupon personally composed a "Song of the Autumn Wind," saying:
The autumn wind rises, oh! while white clouds fly,
Grass and trees yellow and fall, oh! while wild geese southward return.
Orchids have their elegance, oh! chrysanthemums their fragrance;
Taking lovely ladies along, oh! I cannot forget.
Floating in a storied boat, oh! we cross the Fén River;
Mid-stream we sweep across, oh! raising white waves.
Flutes and drums sound, oh! the rowers' songs arise;
Joy and pleasure reach their peak, oh! but sorrowful feelings abound.
How long does youth and vigor last, oh! what can one do about old age!
Preface:
My family is poor,
and my heart dreads distant service.
Péngzé County is a hundred lǐ from home,
so I sought that post.
After a few days,
I felt a longing to return,
and resigned from my position.
Following events and complying with my heart,
I named this piece “Guīqùlái.”
Ah, to go home!
My fields and gardens will be overgrown—why not return?
Since I have let my heart be enslaved by my body,
why be sorrowful and grieve alone?
I realize the past cannot be mended,
but know the future can yet be pursued.
Truly, I have not strayed far from the path,
and feel that today I am right, yesterday wrong.
My boat sways lightly as it drifts afar,
the wind flutters, blowing my robes.
I ask a traveler about the road ahead,
resent the dimness of the dawn light.
Then I glimpse my humble house,
and joyfully I run.
Servants welcome me,
young children wait at the gate.
The three paths are nearly overgrown,
but pines and chrysanthemums remain.
Leading the little ones indoors,
I find wine filling the jar.
Lifting the pot and cup, I pour for myself,
gazing at the courtyard trees, my face brightens.
Leaning by the south window, I indulge my pride,
content that a cramped space brings ease.
Daily strolls in the garden become a delight,
the gate, though set, is often closed.
Leaning on a staff, I wander and rest,
sometimes raising my head to gaze afar.
Clouds drift idly from the peaks,
birds, weary of flight, know to return.
Sunlight dims as dusk approaches,
stroking the lone pine, I linger.
Ah, to go home!
Let me end friendships and cease wanderings.
The world and I have parted ways,
what more should I seek by driving forth?
I delight in kinsfolk’s heartfelt talk,
find joy in lute and books to dispel cares.
Farmers tell me spring has come,
there will be work in the western fields.
Sometimes I order a covered cart,
sometimes I pole a solitary boat.
Exploring deep ravines through winding paths,
crossing rugged hills over uneven ways.
Trees flourish with vibrant growth,
springs trickle as they begin to flow.
I admire how all things thrive in season,
and sigh that my life approaches its end!
Enough now!
How long shall this form dwell within the cosmos?
Why not let the heart follow its own course, accepting departure or stay?
Why rush about—where would I go?
Wealth and rank are not my desire,
the realm of immortals cannot be hoped for.
Cherishing fine days, I go out alone,
or, planting my staff, I weed and hoe.
Climbing the eastern ridge, I whistle long,
facing the clear stream, I compose poems.
Let me follow nature’s course to my end,
rejoicing in Heaven’s decree—what doubt remains?
“Guānjū” expresses the virtue of the queen consort,
it is the beginning of the “Airs,”
used to influence all under heaven and rectify husband-wife relations.
Thus it is applied among the common people,
and applied in the states and domains.
“Fēng” means “to influence,”
it means “to teach.”
Influence moves them,
teaching transforms them.
Poetry is where the will goes.
In the heart it is will;
expressed in words it is poetry.
Emotion stirred within takes form in words;
if words are insufficient,
then sighing follows;
if sighing is insufficient,
then prolonged singing follows;
if prolonged singing is insufficient,
unconsciously the hands dance it,
the feet tap it.
Emotion issues in sound;
sound patterned is called music.
The music of a well-ordered age is peaceful and joyful—
its governance is harmonious.
The music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry—
its governance is perverse.
The music of a perishing state is sorrowful and pensive—
its people are distressed.
Thus, to rectify gains and losses,
move heaven and earth,
and stir ghosts and spirits,
nothing comes closer than poetry.
The former kings used it to regulate husband-wife relations,
perfect filial piety and respect,
strengthen human bonds,
beautify education and transformation,
and alter customs.
Thus, poetry has six principles:
first, called “Airs”;
second, called “Exposition”;
third, called “Comparison”;
fourth, called “Evocation”;
fifth, called “Odes”;
sixth, called “Hymns.”
Those above use the Airs to transform those below;
those below use the Airs to criticize those above.
They employ refined language and indirect remonstrance,
so the speaker is without fault,
and the listener is sufficiently warned.
Hence they are called “Airs.”
When the kingly way declines,
ritual and righteousness are abandoned,
governance and teaching fail,
states have different policies,
families have different customs,
then the “Changed Airs” and “Changed Odes” arise.
The state historians, understanding the traces of success and failure,
grieving over the neglect of human bonds,
lamenting the harshness of punishments and governance,
chant and express their feelings and nature,
to influence their rulers,
comprehend the changes of events,
and cherish the old customs.
Thus, the “Changed Airs” arise from emotion,
but stop within ritual and righteousness.
Arising from emotion is human nature;
stopping within ritual and righteousness is the legacy of the former kings.
Therefore, affairs of one state,
linked to the foundation of one person,
are called “Airs.”
Speaking of affairs of all under heaven,
shaping the customs of the four quarters,
are called “Odes.”
“Odes” means “correct”;
they speak of how kingly governance declines and rises.
Governance has minor and major aspects,
hence there are the “Minor Odes”
and the “Major Odes.”
“Hymns” are descriptions praising abundant virtue,
announcing their achievements to the spirits and deities.
These are called the “Four Beginnings,”
the aim of the Poetry.
Thus, the transformation of “Guānjū” and “Línzhǐ,”
the Airs of the king,
are therefore linked to the Duke of Zhōu.
“South” means the transformation spread from north to south.
The virtue of “Quècháo” and “Zōuyú,”
the Airs of the feudal lords,
is what the former kings used for teaching,
therefore linked to the Duke of Shào.
“Zhōunán” and “Shàonán”
are the way of correct beginnings,
the foundation of kingly transformation.
Thus, “Guānjū” rejoices in obtaining a virtuous maiden to match the noble man,
concerned with advancing the worthy,
not excessive in her beauty,
lamenting the fair and graceful,
thinking of talented worthies,
and without a heart that harms goodness—
this is the meaning of “Guānjū.”
In ancient times, when Fúxī Shì ruled the world,
he first drew the Eight Trigrams,
created written records,
to replace the governance by knotted cords,
and from this, literature and records arose.
The writings of Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Huángdì
are called the Three Mounds,
which speak of the great Way.
The writings of Shàohào, Zhuānxū, Gāoxīn, Táng, and Yú
are called the Five Canons,
which speak of the constant Way.
As for the writings of the Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu dynasties,
although their teachings differ,
their elegant proclamations and profound meanings
all converge to the same principle.
Therefore, successive generations treasured them,
regarding them as great instructions.
The explanations of the Eight Trigrams
are called the Eight Cords,
seeking their meanings.
The records of the Nine Provinces
are called the Nine Mounds.
A mound means to gather.
It speaks of all that the Nine Provinces possess,
what the land produces,
and what the climate suits,
all gathered in this book.
The Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals says:
“The left historian Yǐ Xiàng of Chǔ
could read the Three Mounds, Five Canons, Eight Cords, and Nine Mounds.”
This refers to the surviving writings of the ancient emperors and kings.
Our ancestor Confucius,
born at the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
observed the verbose and complex nature of historical records,
and feared that readers would not grasp them uniformly.
Thus, he established rites and music,
clarified the old regulations,
edited the Book of Songs into three hundred poems,
condensed the historical records and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals,
praised the Way of the Changes and dismissed the Eight Cords,
and described the duties of the regions to eliminate the Nine Mounds.
He discussed the Mounds and Canons,
cutting off from after Táng and Yú down to the Zhōu,
removing the verbose and chaotic,
trimming the superfluous words,
lifting up the grand outline,
extracting the essential points,
sufficient to hand down to the world and establish teachings.
The writings of canons, counsels, instructions, announcements, oaths, and charges,
altogether one hundred chapters,
were meant to expand the ultimate Way,
and show rulers the model.
The system of the emperors and kings
was clear and plain,
capable of being implemented.
The three thousand disciples
all received its meaning.
When Qín Shǐhuáng destroyed the ancient classics,
burned the books and buried the scholars alive,
the scholars of the world
fled and scattered in distress.
My ancestor then hid his family’s books in the walls of his house.
When the Hàn dynasty rose like a dragon,
it established schools,
widely sought refined scholars,
to elucidate the great plan.
Fú Shēng of Jǐnán,
over ninety years old,
had lost the original classics,
and transmitted them orally,
only about twenty-some chapters.
Because they were ancient writings,
they were called the Shàngshū.
The meaning of the hundred chapters
was not heard of in the world.
When Lǔ Gòngwáng liked to build palaces,
he tore down Confucius’s old residence
to expand his dwelling,
and from the walls obtained the ancient writings of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu that our ancestor had hidden,
along with the commentaries on the Analects and the Classic of Filial Piety,
all in tadpole script.
The king also ascended the hall of Confucius,
hearing the sounds of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo,
and thus did not destroy the residence,
returning all the books to the Kǒng family.
Tadpole script had long been abandoned,
and people of the time could not understand it.
Using what was heard from Fú Shēng’s book,
they examined and discussed the meaning,
determining what could be known,
and fixed it in ancient clerical script;
then copied it onto bamboo slips,
adding twenty-five chapters more than Fú Shēng’s.
Fú Shēng also combined the Shùn Diǎn with the Yáo Diǎn,
the Yì Jì with the Gāoyáo Mó,
the three Pán Gēng chapters into one,
and the Kāngwáng Zhī Gào with the Gù Mìng.
Reissuing these chapters along with the preface,
altogether fifty-nine chapters,
made forty-six volumes.
The rest were disordered and worn away,
impossible to know again,
all sent up to the officials,
stored in the library,
awaiting those capable.
I received the decree to write commentaries on the fifty-nine chapters,
and so I delved deeply and pondered thoroughly,
extensively consulted the classics and records,
gathered the words of the rulers,
to establish instructional commentaries,
condensing the text and expanding the meaning,
elaborating and clarifying its intent,
hoping it may be of some benefit to the future.
The preface to the Shū
explains the author’s intention,
clearly revealing the meaning;
it is fitting to attach it nearby,
so I have quoted it to head each chapter.
After finishing the fifty-eight chapters,
the state encountered the affair of witchcraft,
and the way of the classics ceased,
so it was no longer presented to the court,
but passed down to descendants,
to bequeath to later generations.
If there are gentlemen who love antiquity and are broad and refined,
sharing my aspirations,
I will not hide it from them either.
The Spring and Autumn Annals
is the name of the historical records of Lǔ.
The recorder of events
attaches events to days,
attaches days to months,
attaches months to seasons,
attaches seasons to years,
in order to record distances in time,
and distinguish similarities and differences.
Therefore, what the historian records
must mark the year to begin the events;
the year has four seasons,
so they are alternately used to name the records.
The Zhōu Rites had historians
in charge of affairs of the state and the four regions,
conveying the aspirations of the four regions.
The feudal lords also each had their own state histories,
major events written on bamboo tablets,
minor events on slips and tablets only.
Mèngzǐ said:
“In Chǔ it is called Táowù,
in Jìn it is called Shèng,
and in Lǔ it is called Spring and Autumn,
but in reality, they are the same.”
When Hán Xuānzǐ went to Lǔ,
he saw the Images of the Changes and the Spring and Autumn of Lǔ,
and said:
“The Zhōu Rites are all in Lǔ.
Now I know the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu,
and why Zhōu became king.”
What Hánzǐ saw
were likely the old classics and ritual texts of Zhōu.
When the virtue of the Zhōu dynasty had declined,
officials lost their proper duties,
and those in high positions could not make the Spring and Autumn Annals clear and bright.
Reports, announcements, and official records,
along with various recorded annotations,
often violated the old statutes.
Confucius, based on the historical records and official documents of Lǔ, formed the text,
examined their authenticity and falsehood,
and recorded their rituals and ceremonies,
in order to uphold the remaining institutions of the Duke of Zhōu above,
and to clarify the laws for the future below.
Where the teachings were preserved,
and the text was harmful,
he revised and corrected it,
to demonstrate encouragement and warning.
The rest he simply used the old historical records as they were,
for histories have their ornate and plain styles,
and wording has its detailed and concise forms,
so there was no need to change them.
Therefore, the commentary says:
"He was good at recording."
It also says:
"Who but a sage could have compiled it?"
Thus, the intention of the Duke of Zhōu
was further clarified by Confucius.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng received the classics from Confucius,
believing that the classics were unalterable texts.
Therefore, the commentary sometimes precedes the classic to begin a matter,
sometimes follows the classic to conclude its meaning,
sometimes relies on the classic to distinguish principles,
or interweaves with the classic to harmonize differences,
following the meaning to highlight the important aspects of its examples.
The old historical records and remaining texts
are not exhaustively cited,
because they are not essential to what the sage compiled.
As the state historian himself,
personally examining the recorded texts,
he must broadly record and fully discuss them.
Its style is gentle,
its meaning far-reaching,
intending to make scholars trace origins and grasp ends,
explore its branches and leaves,
investigate its limits,
soothing and easing them,
letting them seek for themselves;
satisfying and nourishing them,
letting them advance on their own.
Like the soaking of rivers and seas,
the moistening of rich rain,
melting away like ice,
pleasantly and logically ordered,
only then is it achieved.
Its establishment of general principles to speak of examples
are all constant institutions for governing the state,
the enduring laws of the Duke of Zhōu,
the old statutes of historical texts,
which Confucius followed and refined,
to form the unified structure of a classic.
Its subtle revelation and clarification of the obscure,
and shaping of righteous categories,
all rely on old examples to express meaning,
pointing to actions to correct praise and blame.
Various references such as "recorded,"
"not recorded,"
"recorded first,"
"therefore recorded,"
"not mentioned,"
"not referred to,"
"recorded as saying," and the like,
are all used to distinguish old and new,
elucidate great meanings,
and are called variable examples.
However, there are also cases where what the history did not record
is taken as having meaning,
which is the new intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Therefore, the commentary does not speak of general principles,
but elaborates subtly and thoroughly.
Where the classic lacks explicit examples,
it speaks based on actions,
so the commentary simply states its main point,
and it is not an example.
Thus, the forms of commentary exposition are three,
and the nature of examples is five.
The first is subtle yet clear:
the text appears here, but the meaning arises there,
such as referring to the clan to honor the ruler's command,
omitting the clan to honor the lady,
the fall of Liáng,
and the fortification of Yuánlíng.
The second is recording yet obscure:
using concise words to show rules,
inferring to know examples,
such as meetings not at a fixed place,
and "participating in planning" called "and."
The third is tactful yet well-composed:
subtly following righteous instruction,
to show great propriety,
such as various avoidances and taboos,
and the jade disc borrowed from Xǔtián.
The fourth is exhaustive yet not excessive:
directly recording the events,
fully presenting the text to show meaning,
such as red pillars,
carved rafters,
the Heavenly King requesting chariots,
and the Marquis of Qí presenting spoils.
The fifth is punishing evil and encouraging good:
seeking fame but losing it,
wanting to conceal but becoming exposed,
such as recording Qí Bào as a thief,
and naming the three rebels.
Extending these five forms to explore the classic
and commentary, expanding by analogy,
attached to the events of 242 years,
the correctness of the kingly way,
and the principles of human relations are fully prepared.
Some say:
The Spring and Autumn Annals uses varied wording to reveal meaning.
If as discussed,
then the classic should have cases of identical events with different wording but no meaning.
What earlier scholars transmitted
all does not agree with this.
The reply is:
Although the Spring and Autumn Annals uses a single character for praise or blame,
all require several sentences to form meaning,
unlike the hexagrams of the Eight Trigrams,
which can be interwoven into sixty-four.
Thus, one must rely on the commentary for judgment.
Throughout history, many have spoken about Zuǒ's Spring and Autumn Annals.
Now, the remaining texts that can be seen number over ten schools,
generally inheriting and expounding each other,
yet failing to interweave the classic text to exhaust its variations,
and failing to adhere to Zuǒ Qiūmíng's commentary.
Regarding Zuǒ Qiūmíng's commentary,
where they did not understand,
they omitted and did not explain,
instead superficially citing the Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng commentaries,
only confusing themselves.
What I, Dù Yù, now do differently
is to exclusively study Zuǒ Qiūmíng's commentary to explain the classic.
The structure of the classic
must derive from the commentary.
The meaning and examples of the commentary
are all summarized in its general principles.
Extending variable examples to correct praise and blame,
simplifying the two other commentaries and removing heterodox views—
this is the intention of Zuǒ Qiūmíng.
Where there are doubts or errors,
I discuss them fully and leave them open,
awaiting later worthies.
However, Liú Zǐjùn pioneered and elucidated the great meanings,
Jiǎ Jǐngbó and his son,
Xǔ Huìqīng,
are all excellent among earlier scholars.
Later, there was Yǐng Zǐyán,
who, though shallow, also became a renowned master.
Therefore, I specifically note the differences of Liú, Jiǎ, Xǔ, and Yǐng,
to show similarities and differences.
I align the years of the classic with those of the commentary,
compare their meanings and categories,
and explain each accordingly,
naming it Collected Explanations of the Classic and Commentary.
Additionally, I separately compile various examples,
along with place names,
genealogical records,
and chronological calculations,
grouping them into sections,
totaling forty sections,
fifteen volumes,
all highlighting their similarities and differences,
and explaining them accordingly,
naming it Explanations of Examples,
intending to let scholars observe the gathered differing views,
which Explanations of Examples details.
Some say:
The composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
is not explicitly recorded in the Zuǒ Zhuàn and Gǔliáng Zhuàn,
commentators believe that after Confucius returned to Lǔ from Wèi,
he revised the Spring and Autumn Annals,
establishing himself as an uncrowned king,
with Qiūmíng as his uncrowned minister.
Those who follow the Gōngyáng tradition also claim that he demoted the Zhōu dynasty and elevated Lǔ to kingship,
acting cautiously and speaking humbly,
to avoid the dangers of his time,
thus making his text subtle,
and concealing its meaning.
The Gōngyáng version ends with the capture of the qílín,
while the Zuǒshì version concludes with the death of Confucius.
May I ask which is correct?
The reply is:
This differs from what I have heard.
Confucius said:
"King Wén is gone;
does not the culture reside here?"
This was the original intent of his work.
He sighed:
"The phoenix does not come;
the river gives forth no chart.
It is all over with me!"
This was his lament for the governance of the kings of his time.
The qílín, phoenix, and the five auspicious creatures
are the auspicious signs of a true king.
Now, the qílín appeared at an inopportune time,
its omen empty and its purpose lost,
this is why the sage was moved.
Ending his writing with the sentence about the capture of the qílín
was inspired by this feeling,
and thus naturally served as the conclusion.
It is asked:
Then why does the Spring and Autumn Annals begin with Duke Yǐn of Lǔ?
The reply is:
King Píng of Zhōu
was the first king of Eastern Zhōu;
Duke Yǐn
was a virtuous ruler who yielded the state.
Examining their times, they are connected;
considering their positions, they were among the feudal states;
tracing their origins, they were descendants of the Duke of Zhōu.
If King Píng could have prayed to Heaven for lasting mandate,
reviving the mid-dynasty resurgence,
and Duke Yǐn could have broadly promoted the ancestral enterprise,
brilliantly restoring the royal house,
then the beauty of Western Zhōu could have been recovered,
and the traces of King Wén and King Wǔ would not have been lost.
Therefore, based on their chronological order,
attaching their deeds,
adopting the old practices of Zhōu,
to assemble and complete the kingly righteousness,
he established a model for the future.
The king referred to in the text
is King Píng;
the calendar used
is the Zhōu calendar;
the duke mentioned
is Duke Yǐn of Lǔ.
How can this be called demoting Zhōu and elevating Lǔ to kingship?
The Master said:
"If anyone were to employ me,
would I not create an Eastern Zhōu?"
This is its meaning.
As for the literary composition,
it is meant to illuminate the past and examine the future,
with emotions revealed in the words,
lofty language conveying profound intent,
concise expressions containing subtle meanings.
This is the constant principle,
not concealment.
For the sage to take precautions for his own safety
and only after composing the work
conceal and obscure to avoid harm—
this is not what I have heard.
When Zǐlù had disciples serve as ministers,
Confucius considered it a deception of Heaven.
To speak of Confucius as an uncrowned king
and Qiūmíng as an uncrowned minister
is also not a sound argument.
Earlier scholars believed he spent three years composing the work,
and its completion brought forth the qílín,
which is already superstitious and absurd.
Moreover, citing the text to extend to Confucius's death
is also close to falsehood.
Based on the Gōngyáng version ending with the capture of the qílín,
and the Zuǒshì version
"Xiǎo Zhū Shè"
not being counted among the three rebels,
I therefore believe it was inspired by the qílín,
beginning with its capture,
and the text ends where it began,
which captures the truth.
As for wiping his face with his sleeve
and saying
"my way is exhausted,"
this is also not to be adopted.
Xuānyàn Xiānshēng said:
The ancients said that not singing but reciting is called fù.
Thus, fù
is a form that uses objects as a starting point,
expands and elaborates on principles,
making it impossible for others to surpass.
Extending and elaborating on it,
the language must be supremely beautiful;
expanding through association,
the diction must be fully ornate.
Thus, ornate and beautiful writing
is the essence of fù.
Writers of the past
did not merely value rhetoric,
but aimed to connect it with kingly teachings,
rooted in exhortation and admonition.
Before the Xià and Yīn dynasties,
their writings are lost,
and details cannot be known.
Zhōu drew lessons from the two preceding dynasties,
and the styles of refinement and substance
can be known for a hundred generations.
Thus, Confucius collected the customs of myriad states,
corrected the names of the Yǎ and Sòng,
and compiled them into what is called the Shī.
The works of the poets
included elements of the fù style.
Zǐxià, in his preface to the Shī, said:
first is fēng,
second is fù.
Thus, it is known that fù
is a branch of ancient poetry.
By the time of the Warring States period,
the kingly way declined,
and the fēng and yǎ traditions waned.
Then, worthy men lost their purpose,
and cí and fù arose.
Thus, figures like Xúnqīng and Qū Yuán
left brilliant writings,
with admirable language and meaning.
Preserving their sentiments,
all possessed the spirit of ancient poetry,
using literature to convey their hearts,
and principles to complete their forms—
these are the origins of fù.
By the time of Sòng Yù and others,
excessive and unrestrained writing flourished,
words surpassing reality,
giving rise to competition in hyperbole,
gradually losing the proper form,
and the standards of fēng and yǎ
were thus violated.
When it came to Jiǎ Yì of Hàn,
he somewhat restrained it with ritual.
From then on,
literary writers
did not follow classical norms,
but all pursued expansion,
their writings broad, exaggerated, and empty.
The grand ones covered the expanse of heaven and earth,
the minute ones entered the finest details.
Even with carts and teams of four horses,
they could not be carried;
with vast halls and connected rafters,
they could not be housed.
Among the best of these,
such as Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Shànglín Fù,"
Yáng Xióng's "Gānquán Fù,"
Bān Gù's "Liǎng Dū Fù,"
Zhāng Héng's "Èr Jīng Fù,"
Mǎ Róng's "Guǎngchéng Fù,"
and Wáng Shēng's "Língguāng Fù,"
begin with extremely lavish language,
and end with concise restraint,
brilliantly literary,
richly gathered like fish scales—
all are great works of recent cí and fù.
As for lands having constant produce,
and customs having old traditions,
things gather by kind,
and objects divide by group.
But writers like Chángqīng
introduced inappropriate things from afar,
placing them in the central realm,
exaggerating the exotic,
and attributing existence to the nonexistent.
Imitators
echoed and followed like shadows,
wandering and forgetting to return—
this was not just a temporary trend.
In the past, the Han dynasty crumbled from within,
and the realm was torn asunder.
The Sun and Liu clans
seized control of Jiāozhōu and Yìzhōu;
while Emperor Wǔ of Wèi brought order to chaos,
and held sway over the central plains.
Thus, the author first created two guests from Wú and Shǔ,
who lavishly praised the rugged and magnificent terrain of their native lands,
arguing they could maintain independent rule,
but then had the host from Wèi describe his capital region,
vast, open, rich, and splendid,
embodying the idea of encompassing all of Huáxià.
Speaking of Wú and Shǔ, he compared their capture and destruction to fallen states,
while likening Wèi’s peaceful abdication to the eras of Táng and Yú.
Having thus clarified rebellion and loyalty,
he also intended it as a warning.
For Shǔ encompassed the resources of Liángzhōu and Mínzhōu,
Wú carved off the wealth of southern Jīngzhōu,
and Wèi spanned the fertile central region.
Examining the distribution of celestial divisions,
calculating the abundance of produce,
comparing the purity or turbidity of customs,
and assessing the quality of scholars—
these cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
The scholars of the two states,
each immersed in what they had heard,
each family considered their own land delightful,
each person believed their own people good—
all were not comprehensive or impartial views.
The author, through the dialogue of guest and host,
corrected them with the reality of Wèi’s capital,
and refuted them with the principles of the Kingly Way.
The products and resources of their lands
can be checked against maps.
The structure of the state and its institutions
can be verified according to records—
how could this be false!
In my youth, I had great ambitions,
transcending the common customs of the time.
I entered court service at the age of twenty,
and held office for twenty-five years,
leaving officialdom at fifty due to certain matters.
In my later years, I grew fond of unrestrained freedom,
deeply loving forests and marshes;
thus, I retreated in comfort to my estate in Héyáng.
Its layout:
in the rear, it is sheltered by a long dike,
in front, it faces a clear canal,
with nearly ten thousand trees of all kinds,
and flowing water encircling the dwelling.
There are viewing towers, pavilions, ponds, and pools,
where many fish and birds are kept.
My family has long been skilled in music,
quite adept at the melodies of Qín and Zhào.
Outdoors, I occupy myself with sightseeing, hunting, and fishing;
indoors, I enjoy the pleasures of the qin and books.
I also take pleasure in consuming elixirs and practicing breath control,
aspiring to immortality,
aloof, with the bearing of one soaring above the clouds.
Yet suddenly I find myself bound again,
lingering among the nine ranks of high officials;
troubled by the vexations and impurities of the human world,
I often think of returning home and sigh deeply.
Searching through musical compositions,
I found the "Melody of Longing for Return."
Perhaps the sentiments of the ancients
were the same as mine today,
so I composed this tune.
This tune had strings but no lyrics;
now I write the song lyrics
to express my feelings.
I regret that there is no one who understands music in this time,
to create new melodies and play them on string and bamboo instruments.
The foundation for establishing virtue is constant,
but the paths to achieving merit are not uniform.
Why is this?
Following one’s heart as the measure lies within oneself;
relying on external things to accomplish tasks depends on others.
What lies within oneself—
its rise and fall are confined to its own sphere;
what depends on external things—
their abundance or scarcity is solely a matter of circumstance.
A falling leaf awaits a gentle breeze to descend,
yet the power of the wind is slight;
Mèng Cháng wept upon hearing Yōngmén’s playing,
yet the qin’s influence is but a minor cause.
Why?
A leaf about to fall
needs no fierce wind;
tears about to be shed
require no mournful sound to evoke them.
Therefore, if the time is opened by Heaven,
and principle is fulfilled among the people,
even a mediocre person can achieve the merits of a sage,
and a petty vessel can establish the deeds of a heroic martyr.
Thus it is said: talent not half that of the ancients,
yet merit already doubled—
this is gained through the advantage of time and situation.
Looking throughout history,
there are those who achieved momentary merit
and occupied positions like Yī Yǐn and the Duke of Zhōu.
As for the self asserting itself,
even wise men are burdened by it;
as for things perceiving each other,
even insects share this sentiment.
Now, with the capacity of the self,
and wielding extraordinary achievements,
the imperial authority shines upon one’s gaze,
and all things follow one’s every move.
The heart becomes accustomed to the comfort of routine,
the ears are sated with flattering words—
how could one recognize that merit lies beyond the self,
and responsibility exceeds one’s talent!
Moreover, loving honor and hating disgrace
is the great aspiration of all living beings;
resenting fullness and harming superiors—
even ghosts and spirits cannot avoid this.
The ruler holds the constant handle of power,
and the realm submits to his great integrity.
Thus it is said: can Heaven be opposed?
Yet there are times when men in splendid attire, bearing halberds,
stand beneath the temple gates,
raising banners and vowing to the multitude,
rousing themselves in the fields.
How much more so for those who act on behalf of the ruler to issue commands,
and distribute wealth from below!
Widely bestowing favors cannot suffice to counter resentment;
diligently promoting benefits cannot suffice to repair harm.
Therefore it is said: he who chops wood in place of the master carpenter
will surely injure his own hand.
Moreover, when governance lies with the Nìng clan,
loyal ministers are filled with righteous indignation;
when sacrifices are performed by the ruler alone,
the sovereign cannot long endure it.
Thus, Jūnshì was discontented,
unhappy with the Duke of Zhōu’s actions;
Gāopíng’s officials,
looked askance at Bólù’s power.
Yet King Chéng harbored no suspicion or resentment in his heart,
while Emperor Xuān felt as if bearing thorns on his back—
is this not so?
Alas!
Radiating light to the four quarters,
no virtue could be richer;
the king said, "My uncle,"
no kinship could be closer.
Ascending to the imperial throne,
no achievement could be greater;
maintaining integrity until the end of one’s days,
no loyalty could be more complete.
Yet they were toppled and cast down,
barely preserving themselves.
Thus, Yī Yǐn, holding bright sincerity, met with execution;
Wénzǐ, cherishing loyalty and reverence, faced the sword—
this was indeed their lot.
From this perspective,
with such sincere sageliness and harmonious kinship,
possessing such excellence,
with such great virtue and utmost loyalty,
displaying such magnificence,
they still could not gain trust in the ruler’s heart,
nor stop slander from the mouths of the multitude.
Beyond this,
how can one see what is possible!
The principle of safety and danger
can surely be discerned.
How much more so for those who covet great fame and violate the taboos of the Dàoist way,
employing shallow talent to attempt what even sages and philosophers found difficult!
Personal danger arises from excessive power,
yet one does not know to relinquish power to seek safety;
calamity accumulates from excessive favor,
yet one does not know to decline favor to attract fortune.
Seeing the common people plotting against oneself,
one then reinforces palace guards and alerts defenses,
to heighten a majesty that cannot be preserved;
fearing the multitude’s disobedience,
one then imposes harsh punishments and severe laws,
to purchase the resentment of wounded hearts.
Thereafter, authority is exhausted in shaking the sovereign,
and resentment spreads above and below.
The hearts of the people daily crumble,
a crisis is about to erupt,
yet one still reclines at ease, gazing arrogantly,
believing it sufficient to boast to the world,
laughing at the ancients’ lack of skill,
forgetting one’s own affairs are already clumsy,
knowing only to boast of past merits,
oblivious to the convergence of success and failure.
Thus, when affairs reach their limit and fortune is exhausted,
one is bound to fall headlong;
when the wind rises and dust gathers,
the disaster that arrives is often cruel.
Sages fear excessive merit and fame for themselves,
and detest favor and emolument beyond measure—
it is precisely for this reason.
The great ends of desire and aversion,
are shared by the wise and foolish alike;
the wanderer sacrifices himself for high rank in life,
the man of purpose thinks of leaving a name after death.
The allotment of life
is nothing but this.
Now, achievements that overshadow the age,
no fame is greater than that;
a power that shakes the ruler,
no position is more exalted than that;
following one's will without opposition,
no desire is more gratified than that.
If such a man could broadly observe the Way of Heaven,
knowing that exhaustion cannot be increased,
that fullness is hard to maintain long,
and withdraw himself transcendentally,
retiring with a lofty bow,
then his towering magnificence
would look up and surpass former worthies,
his vast and flowing style
would look down and crown future records,
and his great desires would not be lacking in his person,
his utmost joy would not differ from the past,
his integrity more effective and his virtue more extensive,
his person more at ease and his name more illustrious.
Not doing this,
but persisting in that delusion,
then the traces of rivers and seas are blocked into dried-up streams,
the faults of a single basket accumulate into mountains,
his name is listed among the vicious and stubborn,
his body suffers the pain of poison and torment,
is this not absurd!
Therefore, I casually compose this rhapsody,
hoping to make a few in a hundred generations awaken.
Now, since the records are already set down,
the traces of emperors and kings have differed;
since bells and stones are fully arrayed,
the sentiments of dance and song are not uniform.
Though the deep streams have passed by,
and details differ in what is heard,
yet in residing in the heart of Heaven,
and establishing the people's ultimate standard,
none did not revere their Way,
and make divine their position,
expanding the age and bequeathing the tradition,
firmly measuring it for ten thousand generations.
The Sòng embraces all Xià,
the imperial plan is vast and far-reaching.
Gāozǔ with holy martiality settled the tripods,
his planning was like that of the Creator;
the present Emperor with profound culture received the calendar,
his brilliance belongs to the imperial residence.
The divination of prosperous Zhōu being already eternal,
the omen of ancestral Hàn lies therein.
The rightful heir nurtures virtue in Shàoyáng,
the royal minister proclaims wisdom as chief assistant.
Sun and stars clearly respond,
mountains and rivers manifest numinous power.
The five regions mingle in confusion,
from the four remote corners they come.
Selecting the worthy and establishing relatives,
then places them according to splendid statutes;
issuing commands and giving orders,
must be measured by ancient precedents.
The Grand Music Master harmonizes music,
the Upper School spreads teaching.
Regulations are clear and detailed,
standards and models are comprehensive and complete.
State ceremonies move according to orders,
military administration is equipped like symbolic objects.
Officials who admonish faults and record words,
who collate texts and discuss arts,
gather remnants within;
light carriages and red canopied carts,
envoys who pacify the wild and stir the distant,
discuss virtue abroad.
Red stems and white down,
joint branches and shared ears as auspicious signs,
the historians never cease recording;
building roads over mountains and sailing the seas,
tribute crossing sands and traversing deserts,
the storehouses have no empty month.
Beacon fires for a thousand cities,
post stations connecting for ten thousand lǐ.
Lords of dome-shaped dwellings,
within first receive the calendar;
chiefs in plant-fiber clothing,
turn their faces to accept officials.
Therefore, extraordinary men admire and yearn,
outstanding people appear in intervals;
guards clear and pacify,
inside and outside are joyful and harmonious.
About to move the capital to the central region,
set up music at the Tài mountain's outskirts.
Increase the palaces for emulating the divine,
adorn the halls for ritual to the spirits,
road songs and town recitations,
have long looked to the dust of the imperial carriage train.
The sun passes through Wèi and its bonds,
the moon's orbit in the green land.
The time when the imperial spirits begin generation,
the hour when kings spread harmony,
thinking to respond to the heart of the high spirits,
to bestow favor on the wishes of the common sprouts.
Moreover, with the two princes setting forth,
going out to farewell feasts with warnings and admonitions,
there is an edict to the archivists,
and so commands the calendar officers,
to present the rituals of the Luòyǐn feast,
and prepare the ceremonies of the Shangsi festival.
To the south clear the imperial path,
to the north cleanse the forbidden grove,
left open the rocky steps,
right bridge the tidal source.
Pass by the waterside pavilions,
stride across the mushroom fields,
encompass the Tàiyè pond,
embrace the layered mountains.
Pines and stones steep and towering,
verdant and emerald, shaded by mist,
where swimmers gather and cluster,
where fliers and gallopers come and go.
Then the detached palaces set up guards,
separate halls surrounded by patrols,
banner gates stand open,
extended curtains connect to railings,
encircling water surrounds the steps,
channeled pools divide the mats.
Spring officials join in affairs,
the blue spirit offers the way.
Then ascend the secret carriage,
continue with the crimson riders,
shake the jade bells,
set forth flowing winds,
heaven moves and spirits shift,
deep whirls and clouds cover,
to descend at the traveling lodge,
such is the ritual.
Soon the imperial radiance approaches the tent,
all officials take their fixed positions,
the phoenix canopy suddenly halts,
the rainbow flags hang down their pennants.
Meats and vegetables fragrantly spread,
cups and wine float and brim.
The appearance of exquisite songs and wonderful dances,
the instruments with hanging ribbons and set feathers.
Tunes of three performances and four presentations,
melodies of six stems and nine completions.
Competing energies and numerous sounds,
combining changes and contending rhythms.
Dragon patterns adorn the reins,
blue-scribbled boats wait for驾驭.
Chinese and foreign abundantly arrive,
sights and hearings eagerly gather.
Raising sleeves like a windy mountain,
lifting sleeves like a shady marsh.
Adorned beauties embellish the fields,
gorgeous attire enriches the rivers.
Thus they abundantly spread to outer regions,
and brilliantly extend within the capital.
Above receiving ten thousand longevities,
below securing a hundred blessings.
All mats receive harmony,
the whole hall relies on virtue.
Emotions linger as the scene hastens,
joy harmonizes as the sun slants.
The golden carriage gathers the teams,
the holy presence prepares to pause.
Regretting not yet approaching the钧台,
lamenting the酆宫 not being displayed.
About to push open the phoenix tower for lofty wandering,
open the爵园 for broad feasting.
Together command those in position,
to unfold poems and express intentions.
Then will not the recitation of beauty have its chapters,
and the presentation of sincerity be without shame?
Your servant hears that when appearing in leisure forms the image,
the music of钧天 is displayed;
when riding the time takes position,
the carriage驾驭气 soars.
Therefore, attaining the One to serve the celestial,
roaming free in the realm of Xiāngchéng;
embodying the primal to emulate greatness,
gazing wistfully at the slopes of Gūyè.
Yet dark, distant, silent, and deserted,
it is only suitable for oneself.
As for Xiàhòu's two dragons,
carrying him driving on the Xuántái之上;
Mùmǎn's eight steeds,
dancing like on the north of Yáoshuǐ;
they also feasted,
but certainly did not share with the myriad people.
Our Great Qí, grasping the cosmic pivot and establishing the calendar,
receiving the Mandate and founding the dynasty,
continued the rituals of the two ancestral temples,
and examined achievements in the Grand Chamber.
The realms of darkness and light presented their offerings in due season,
thunder and wind conveyed the sacrificial feasts.
The treasure of Zhāohuá was already transferred,
the jade of Yánxǐ found its rightful place.
Replacing Sòng and receiving Heaven's Mandate,
it preserved life for the myriad states.
It settled the capital, quieting the sighs of Lùqiū;
it moved the sacred cauldron, ending the shame of Dàjiōng.
It continued the pure harmony in the emperor's plans,
linking illustrious virtue to the royal standard.
Swiftly it initiated its far-reaching auspicious signs,
securely it established its grand enterprise.
The Emperor, embodying the highest sagehood,
his fortune marking a successor to martial virtue,
crowned with the finest essence of the Five Phases,
surpassed the heroic spirit of the Three Dynasties.
His brilliance illuminated the Milky Way,
his splendor rivaled the sun and moon.
He encompassed heaven and earth,
overpowered mountains and rivers.
He established divine principles to transform customs,
spread culture to pacify distant lands.
His grace was universal and without partiality,
his laws were broad and avoided harshness.
Yet still, with clear understanding, he neglected sleep,
and forgot meals while measuring the shadows.
Mindful of bearing heavy responsibility as if on spring ice,
controlling the galloping team like the autumn charioteer.
Truly, lofty and peerless,
vast and beyond naming.
Holding the divine chart, he was not arrogant;
crossing Mèngmén, how could it be perilous?
The Crown Prince, with wisdom inherent in his person,
and exquisite goodness as his innate quality,
accumulated harmony and obedience within,
and radiated brilliance and splendor without.
He adorned the highest virtue,
polished the excellent model.
His words shone like cinnabar and azure,
his Way enriched gold and jade.
Emerging from the Dragon Tower to inquire of the attendants,
entering the Tiger Gate to take his place among the heirs.
Love and reverence were fully given to the One Man,
his radiance reached to the Four Seas.
As for the clan flourishing like the lin's toes,
the ancestral house firm as a磐石,
surpassing and overshadowing the prosperous Jī,
eclipsing and outshining the fiery Hàn.
The chief ministers stood shoulder to shoulder with Shàngfù,
the central pillars succeeded those of Zhōunán.
The division at Shǎn flowed with the joy of "Do not cut down";
those coming to serve truly earned the praise of "able to implement."
None were not like ritual jades,
possessing fine reputation and noble bearing.
Vermilion insignia, thus resplendent—
these are the rulers of households and states.
The flourishing of root and branch being such,
the governance based on antiquity being thus,
thus they were able to rescue the multitude from boiling water and fire,
and bring the hundred families into peace and harmony.
The common people delighted in their occupations,
the guardians of the borders fulfilled their duties.
Holding up a mirror, all had clear vision;
facing the pool, none needed to wash their ears.
The resentment of the submerged and obscure was already absent,
the distress of poverty and hardship had already vanished.
Promoting the incorruptible and recommending the filial—
seasonally at the outer bureaus;
recording conduct and deliberating on age—
daily within the central suburbs.
The offices of harmonizing pitch and managing ceremonies
strengthened human relations and corrected customs.
The posts of venerating literature and perfecting equanimity
guided virtue and aligned with ritual.
The clepsydra keepers and night proclaimers
distinguished the solar terms and new moons at the Spirit Terrace.
The scribes with tablets and red-tasseled pens
recorded words and affairs in the Immortal Chamber.
Officials who lifted curtains and cut their robes,
wore tall caps and empty sandals;
warriors swift and fierce as fluttering banners,
men who could lift cauldrons and raise flags.
Diligently they cared for the people's hidden sufferings,
exposed and removed the ruler's faults.
They shot down hawks upon high walls,
brought down the great wind in the long tunnel.
The unhumane were kept far away,
only the Way was put into practice.
Slander and weeds were unheard of,
strife and contention were suppressed and stilled.
Rarely did the alarm drum sound on the level road,
luxuriant grass filled the round prison gates.
The elderly lacked the wanderings of the marketplace,
the young had their fill of the pleasures of carriages and horses.
The palace precincts were brightly peaceful,
the distant borders were clear and pacified.
Those who ate with their hands came to acknowledge sovereignty,
speakers of strange tongues entered to serve.
Rulers with bodies parted or heels reversed,
chieftains with hair tied up or chests pierced,
bent their knees and knocked their heads,
begging to receive the reins and halters.
Tribute of patterned axes and green arrow-stones,
tributes of rare trunks and Shànfāng birds,
curiosities like silken oxen and dew dogs,
steeds like Chénghuáng and Zībái,
overflowed the storehouses,
filled the suburban preserves.
Memorial boxes and documents followed in succession,
interpreters and translators had no leisure.
A single commandant sufficed for east and west,
carriages and scripts were unified across north and south.
Smooth axles buried the rumbling wheel-tracks,
peaceful banners furled their dangling pennants.
No region offered resistance,
no martial tribe kept its distance.
Leather armor was laid aside, chariots dismissed;
metal was melted down, blades retired.
Heavenly auspices descended,
earthly tokens arose.
Blessed horses came,
divine vehicles emerged.
Purple tuó plants flowered,
vermilion yīng plants flourished.
The flatterer's branch was planted,
the calendar grass multiplied.
Clouds were moist, stars shone bright;
winds wafted, the moon arrived.
Rivers and seas presented their images,
turtles and dragons bore their patterns.
About to grasp the river and sink the jade,
seal the mountains and inscribe the stones,
surpassing the Three and Five and leaving them behind,
treading the distant traces of the Eight and Nine.
The achievement is already complete,
the age is already upright.
Surely one can now be leisurely and at ease,
creating music to exalt virtue, can one not?
At this time, the azure birds preside over the opening of spring,
the gentle winds usher in the new year.
It is now the third month,
the late days of spring.
Harmonious rhythms prevail,
and plants and trees rejoice on their own.
The day for the purification feast is here,
and the spirit of dancing in the wind stirs all hearts;
departing from solemnity aligns with the seasonal teachings,
while festive activities move in accord with heavenly favor.
I think of the level gardens,
and gaze upon the fragrant groves.
The Fragrant Grove Garden is
a convergence of blessed lands and profound regions,
an ancient site like Dānlíng and Ruòshuǐ.
Its lushness equals the marshes of Yáo,
and its fertility rivals the plains of Zhōu.
Narrower than the yet-unexpanded Fēngyì,
and humbler than the still-cramped Qiáo residence.
Seeking balance and harmony in its layout,
measuring the sun and stars to lay its foundations.
Soaring towers move as if divinely,
empty eaves are constructed like clouds.
Separate chambers are newly arranged,
layered pavilions rise intermittently,
facing the morning sun with elevated halls,
spanning the spiritual pond with floating splendor.
Rainbow patterns are mirrored in ornate lattice windows,
and orchid springs soak the jade steps.
Dense and serene thickets,
orderly riverbanks,
winding paths twist and turn,
gurgling streams meander and return.
Fresh duckweed floats on islets,
blossoming paulownias emerge from peaks,
vibrant colors mingle among tender shoots,
and chirping sounds interweave with feathered flocks.
The imperial carriage awaits the royal visit,
and the clear palace prepares for the feast.
Orange curtains are set overnight,
and canopies are hung by evening.
Then, as the lingering clouds clear and the rosy dawn fades,
the rising light reveals the colors of day,
guards clear the way with spears in hand,
carriages are readied and horses harnessed,
bells ring in measured rhythm,
bright chimes resonate with clear sounds.
Seven elite troops ride side by side,
nine banners align in unison,
flags raised brush against the rainbows,
reeds shaken stir the trees.
Fish-scale armor gathers like mist,
shell helmets scatter like stars.
Adorned with layered plumes and curved ornaments,
mounted on steeds surpassing shadows and outracing the wind.
Brilliantly arrayed in divisions,
mighty and splendid in formation,
like tigers watching and dragons leaping,
like thunder startling and lightning flashing,
rumbling and resonating,
swarming and bustling,
truly beyond description.
Then the carriage turns and halts,
as stable as mountains and as still as deep pools,
the sovereign’s dignified countenance serene,
and the guests’ rituals orderly arranged.
Mats are spread and tables set,
following the flow of water to determine seating;
fragrant dishes and fine wines,
move along with the rushing streams.
Dancers line the steps,
golden gourds grace the mats,
martial dances are performed with vigor,
flutes play the ballads of Bīn.
Summoning the singing birds from Yǎnzhōu,
recalling Líng Lún in the Xiègǔ Valley;
evoking the melodies of Prince Jìn,
transmitting the exquisite tunes of Dìjiāng.
As the formal songs conclude,
winged cups pass without count.
Above, blessings and favors are bestowed,
below, longevity like the Southern Mountains is offered;
truly, a joyous feast among the water plants,
knowing harmony and joy in feasting on duckweed.
The shade of mulberry and elm does not linger,
the dew on grass is still fresh.
An edict was issued:
"Today’s splendid gathering
all may compose poems."
In total, forty-five people,
their words are as follows.
The Duke, named Jiǎn,
styled Zhòngbǎo,
was from Línyí in Lángyá.
His ancestors, from the Qín to the Sòng dynasties,
are detailed in state histories and family records.
Since the revival of Jìn,
for six generations, renowned virtue
has crowned the family within the realm.
An ancient saying goes:
"The benefits of the benevolent
follow the way of heaven’s movement."
Thus, Lǚ Qián returned his girdle knife,
and Guō Pú pledged by the Huái River.
As for the cessation of killing by Lí and Jiǎn,
and the sincere感动 of Jí Jùn,
they were aided by this.
At the Duke’s birth,
he was endowed with a destiny to lead the age,
embodying the excellence of the three talents,
and grasping the opportunity of attaining the twofold.
Truly, the constellation Mǎo shone its light,
and virtuous essence descended with blessings.
With even one of these,
he would flourish as an imperial mentor.
Moreover, his profound forehead bore extraordinary signs,
and his lofty brow displayed unique features;
gazing at the road, few could discern his methods,
viewing the sea, none could reach the breadth of his waves.
He broadly examined historical records,
and extensively engaged with talents and righteousness.
As for the texts on golden plates and jade caskets,
and the teachings of famed mountains beyond the seas;
profound and elegant thoughts,
discourses that distinguish the solid and unite the disparate—
all were mastered with clear understanding,
and successively became the pinnacle of his mind.
These indeed encompass what the comprehensive man embraces,
not merely the ultimate realm of empty clarity.
What cannot be exhausted
is perhaps only the divine application?
Yet, reflecting on what he embodied,
he exemplified human relations,
like a cloud-piercing structure built by heaven—
what need for a craftsman?
Since the fall of Xián and Luò,
institutions and regulations were interrupted.
Master Hè, the patriarch of ritual understanding,
and Master Cài, second only in the Confucian forest,
left incomplete classics,
now fully restored on this day.
As for the elderly with precarious teeth and silvery hair,
and students immersed in classics and savoring the Way,
all turned north to honor him as their master,
regarding him with the same reverence.
His nature inclined toward tranquility and detachment,
and from youth, he shunned worldly clutter.
Unless it could promote elegance and refinement,
or enhance outstanding virtues,
he never paid it heed.
He was orphaned at the age of one.
His uncle, the Sikōng, Duke Jiǎnmù,
had recognized his exceptional talent from an early age.
When he first began his studies at fifteen,
the family's rituals and teachings
were all guided by his judgment.
His nature of filial piety and fraternal love,
how could it be compared to the bridge and catalpa?
His dignified and elegant demeanor,
required no admonition from leather or bowstring.
Rǔ Yù's profound innocence in childhood,
Huáng Wǎn's early display of intelligence and insight—
how could they be considered superior?
At the age of six,
he inherited the title of Marquis of Yùníng.
On the day of his investiture,
his family, considering him still young,
had not informed him beforehand.
After receiving the jade tablet and official insignia,
he responded to the royal command,
and was overcome with emotion,
as if unable to bear it.
Earlier, when Emperor Míng of Sòng was still a prince,
he had long been at odds with the Duke's mother, Princess Wǔkāng.
After ascending the throne,
he issued an edict to destroy the old family graves,
and discard the coffins.
The Duke pleaded firmly at the risk of death,
vowing not to comply,
his memorials filled with bitter sorrow,
their righteousness moving both gods and men.
Emperor Tàizōng heard of this and was moved to pity,
and thus could not force the issue.
He was first appointed as a Secretary Gentleman,
then promoted to Gentleman of the Heir Apparent's Household.
Selected to marry a princess,
he was appointed Commandant of Imperial Escorts.
In the early Yuánhuī era,
he was promoted to Secretary of the Palace Library.
Thereupon, he adopted Zhèng Mò's "Zhōngjīng",
and revised Lǐ Chōng's "Four Categories";
following Liú Xīn's "Seven Summaries",
he recompiled the "Seven Records".
He once composed a poem that said:
"Jì and Qì supported Yú and Xià,
Yī and Lǚ assisted Shāng and Zhōu."
From then on, he began to leave traces of practical governance,
and the people placed their hopes in him!
At that time, the Minister of Education Yuán Càn,
possessed a lofty, transcendent demeanor,
detached from worldly customs.
Seeing the Duke in his youth,
he immediately admired and deferred to him from afar,
sighing:
"The refinement of the elite and the rites and music reside here!"
At the time, Càn's position was second only to the highest ministers,
while the Duke was just twenty years old.
Despite the disparity in age and status,
the Duke treated him as an equal.
He then presented a poem to Càn,
urging him to set a time for retirement,
and admonishing him with the principle of knowing when to stop.
Càn replied with a poem:
"What else does this old man have to rely on?
This gentleman illuminates my pure heart."
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Right Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education.
He went out to serve as Governor of Yìxīng,
where the excellence of his moral influence
earned him the highest evaluation in performance reports.
Upon returning, he was appointed Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates.
Within ten days,
he was promoted to Director of the Ministry of Personnel, participating in official selections.
In the past, Máo Jiè was known for his impartiality and integrity,
Lǐ Zhòng for his discernment and insight;
the Duke combined both.
Soon he was promoted to Palace Attendant,
but citing the lifelong service of the late Marquis Mǐn,
he firmly declined the appointment.
He was instead appointed Right Chief Clerk to the Grand Commandant.
At that time, the Sacred Warrior was establishing his enterprise,
laying the foundation for royal mandate,
dreaming of gathering clouds and winds,
truly relying on men of outstanding talent.
Thus, the imperial abode corresponded to the array of stars,
and charts and prophecies revealed signs of a king's assistant.
Soon he was promoted to Left Chief Clerk.
When the Qí court was first established,
he was appointed Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
overseeing the Ministry of Personnel,
at the age of twenty-eight.
In the troubled final years of Sòng,
a decadent end for a hundred kings.
Rites were disordered from their ancient origins,
music deviated from its constant norms.
From court regulations and state laws,
to canonical vessels and ritual objects,
memorials, edicts, and tallies,
literary compositions, petitions, and records—
whatever had not been previously conceived,
or never implemented in ancient times—
were all decided in an instant,
with divine efficiency and no delays.
When Emperor Tàizǔ received the mandate,
for his merit in assisting the founding,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Nánchāng County,
with a fief of two thousand households.
In the second year of Jiànyuán,
he was promoted to Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
continuing to oversee selections as before.
Since Yíng Shì divided responsibilities,
and Lú Qīn held concurrent posts,
the reputation and prestige that gathered around them
were truly concentrated on this day.
Soon he petitioned to be relieved of selection duties,
and an edict added the title of Palace Attendant.
He was also appointed Supervisor of the Heir Apparent's Household,
while retaining his positions as Palace Attendant and Vice Director.
He firmly declined the Palace Attendant post,
and was instead appointed Regular Attendant of the Imperial Secretariat,
with other positions unchanged.
When Emperor Tàizǔ passed away,
his final edict appointed the Duke as Palace Attendant, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and General Who Guards the State.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
his title was advanced to General of the Guards.
In the second year,
he was appointed, in his official capacity, Governor of Dānyáng Commandery.
The six commanderies had different customs,
the five regions distinct practices.
Without deliberate instruction or preaching,
he transformed sentiments in both Chǔ and Xià.
Thus, he could make enemies lay down their swords and bow in reconciliation,
and people return to their fields, ceasing litigation.
Former governors Wēn Tàizhēn and Liú Zhēncháng,
one with achievements inscribed on tripods and vessels,
the other with virtue marking pure aspirations—
their shared spirit and connection through wind and clouds
remained undiminished for a thousand years.
He personally offered condolences and sacrifices,
petitioning to recommend their orphaned descendants,
harmonizing with divine expectations from afar,
thus manifesting the sacrifices of generations.
When Duke Jiǎnmù passed away,
due to the grace of his upbringing,
he felt a particularly deep and constant grief,
and petitioned to resign from his post.
An edict did not permit it.
When the Imperial Academy was first established,
both Chinese and foreigners admired its righteousness.
As a master of the classics and a model for others,
he truly relied on prestige and substance.
He was again appointed, in his official capacity, Chancellor of the Imperial Academy.
In the third year,
he was relieved of the governorship of Dānyáng,
and appointed Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
with other positions unchanged.
Hanging up official robes and donating horses—
former worthies took this as a model;
lying before carriages and abandoning sons—
later generations all lamented.
The Crown Prince did not pride himself on his heavenly gifts,
but humbly followed human examples.
The righteousness between teacher and friend
was harmonious like gold and orchids.
He was also appointed Grand Impartial and Just for his home province,
but soon resigned from the post.
In the fourth year,
he was granted the honor of establishing a ministry with the same ceremonial status as the Three Excellencies, under his current title,
with other positions unchanged.
His humble virtue grew even more distant,
yet the great ceremony was not yet fulfilled.
In the sixth year,
the previous appointment was reaffirmed.
In the seventh year,
he firmly declined the selection appointment.
The Emperor, reluctant to oppose him,
issued an edict adding the title of Director of the Central Secretariat,
while he still participated in selection affairs.
Cháng Yú regretted the monopoly of the carriage,
while Gōng Zēng accepted the loss of the Phoenix Pond.
The path of contention and striving
has existed since ancient times.
With a nature difficult to know,
coupled with emotions easily lost,
to ensure there are no disputes,
one must deeply engage in broad guidance.
You, sir, upheld fairness and integrity,
for a full cycle of twelve years,
selecting the extraordinary and embracing the unique,
reviving the declining and continuing the severed.
You looked to the side steps to accommodate the worthy,
awaiting the auspicious winds to model the classics.
At the age of thirty-eight,
on the third day of the fifth month in the seventh year,
you passed away in the official residence in Jiànkāng.
The imperial court was deeply grieved,
the crown prince and high officials were sorrowful.
Those with understanding bore silent grief,
and passersby wept openly.
How could it be merely that the pounders ceased their work,
and the weaving women left their looms?
Thus, the pain deeply affected the gentry,
and sorrow entangled the teachings of righteousness.
Was it not because your efforts were as profound as grinding a whetstone,
and your way surpassed that of boats and ships?
Leaving behind love for the world,
you were a beneficial friend of ancient virtue.
Posthumously, you were granted the title of Grand Marshal,
with the positions of Palace Attendant and Director of the Secretariat remaining as before.
You were bestowed with a ceremonial staff,
granted feather canopies and military music,
and had sixty additional ceremonial swordsmen added to your retinue.
The posthumous title Wénxiàn was conferred,
in accordance with ritual.
You, sir, were generous to others,
yet frugal in your own life.
You abstained from indulging in pleasures for the eyes and ears,
and simplicity was evident even in haste.
Your household had no concubines or beauties,
but your gate was frequented by many elders.
Your words were always elegant,
never boasting of your strengths;
your discussions were calm and composed,
never speaking of others' shortcomings.
You promoted refinement and grace,
and associated with those of similar character;
even those from humble backgrounds or younger generations,
you would kindly guide;
encouraging them with the value of the crimson sky,
and broadening their horizons with the promise of the azure heavens.
You evaluated human relationships,
ensuring each was utilized to their fullest,
so those in abundance did not boast of their wealth,
and those in scarcity did not resent their lack.
Reaching the limits, they would return;
filled to capacity, they knew their place.
The imperial court, with order established, set rituals,
and with achievements accomplished, composed music,
thinking of the people's praise,
to glorify the imperial plans.
Even if Zhāng and Cáo debated in the Hàn court,
or Xún and Zhì vied for excellence in the Jìn dynasty,
none could fathom the depth of your wisdom,
or serve as a model for future generations.
Whenever distant regions sought to atone for their crimes,
or remote barbarians admired righteousness,
you demonstrated authority and gave instructions,
truly entrusting grand strategies.
When principles accumulated, the spirit faced no opposition;
when matters stirred emotions, joy naturally arose.
Without a self-centered mind,
matters were free from flattery;
rarely swayed by love or hatred,
principles were beyond praise or blame.
In reasoning, you often seemed approachable,
yet in handling affairs, you were unyielding;
you restrained yourself without being harsh to others,
and showed magnanimity without tolerating wrongdoing.
You confronted heterodox views,
guiding them back to righteousness.
Born into an illustrious family,
you were detached from worldly affairs,
yet when it came to grand strategies for the military and state,
or major codes of punishment and governance,
as your way lay in the court,
your principles naturally led the people.
As for being well-versed in various affairs,
discerning the essence of governance,
it came to you as naturally as if bestowed by heaven,
without premeditation.
Searching through historical records,
no writings had documented it;
inquiring of the elderly,
their eyes and ears had never encountered it.
As for documents circulating in cycles,
with hundreds in charge,
all were officials skilled in intricate laws,
with ingrained habits leading to deceit,
harboring the severity of the brush and knife,
and intentions of light or heavy judgment.
You, sir, acted with reason and illuminated matters,
every move carefully considered.
Contemporaries sighed in admiration,
as if guided by divine will.
Were you not a rare talent of the age,
a grand vessel like a ritual jade?
I, Fǎng, have no exceptional conduct,
nor any extraordinary talent,
yet I have had the honor of upholding your reputation and integrity,
for nearly a full cycle.
A single word of praise from you,
made Dōnglíng equal to Xīshān;
a moment of honor bestowed,
made the Zhèng jade surpass the Zhōu treasure.
A scholar feels the gratitude of a true friend,
how can I express the depth of this feeling!
Entering and leaving the ceremonial gates,
morning and evening in the old residence,
gazing at the beams and rafters, I am moved with admiration,
reflecting on your personal fame, I mourn your kindness.
From youth to adulthood,
you never tired of writing and composing.
Truly, your works exhaustively explored principles of speech and action,
and encompassed matters of military and state,
how could they be merely ornate phrases and elaborate embellishments?
As for the overall structure being invariably excellent,
with no place left for additional praise,
even the multitude of talents from Chǔ and Zhào,
or the numerous works of Hàn and Wèi,
how could they compare!
How could they compare!
I, Fǎng, was once recognized for my writing,
and I wish to repay your virtue with my humble skills,
thus I compile your remaining works,
to be a lasting model for the world.
They are arranged in several volumes,
totaling several scrolls.
The compiled records of ancient and modern works, now titled *Seven Records*,
stand as a school of thought on their own,
and are not included in this collection.
The collection is recorded as follows.
Those clad in felt and fur
cannot be spoken to of the fine beauty of pure silk;
those who eat wild herbs and dry grain
are unfit to discuss the flavors of the grand sacrifice.
Now, I reside in remote Xīshǔ,
born in a humble alley,
raised under thatched roofs,
lacking the knowledge gained from extensive travel and observation,
burdened instead with extreme foolishness and ignorance,
insufficient to meet high expectations,
or respond to your enlightened decree.
Nevertheless,
how dare I not briefly express my foolish thoughts,
and pour out my sincere feelings!
It is recorded:
Respectfully, the essential principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals regarding the five beginnings lies in
examining oneself and rectifying the orthodox succession.
Now, the worthy are
the instruments of the state.
When the appointed are worthy,
then decisions are simplified and achievements are widespread;
when the instruments are sharp,
then effort is minimal and accomplishments are numerous.
Thus, when a craftsman uses blunt tools,
he strains his sinews and toils his bones,
toiling all day long.
But when a skilled smith forges the raw material of Gānjiàng,
quenches its edge in clear water,
and sharpens its blade on Yuè whetstones,
it cuts through water-dragons in the water,
and slices rhinoceros hide on land,
as easily as sweeping dust or drawing lines in mud.
In this way, even if Lílóu oversees the plumb line
and Gōngshū carves with the ink-line,
though the tower rises five stories high,
stretching a hundred zhàng without confusion,
it is because the craftsman and his tools are well-matched.
When an ordinary man drives a worn-out horse,
he also suffers from chafed lips and a broken whip, unable to advance,
with heaving chest and sweating skin,
exhausting both man and horse.
But when he harnesses a knee-biting steed,
with swift charioteers at dawn,
Wáng Liáng holding the reins,
and Hán'āi assisting the carriage,
galloping and racing freely,
swift as a fleeting shadow,
passing through cities and crossing states,
as if leaping over clods of earth;
chasing the fleeing lightning,
pursuing the vanishing wind,
circling the eight extremes,
covering ten thousand lǐ in a single breath.
How vast it is!
It is because man and horse are well-matched.
Thus, those clad in cool linen
do not suffer the stifling heat of midsummer;
those wrapped in warm fox and raccoon furs
do not worry about the bitter cold of deep winter.
Why is this?
Those who possess the means find preparation easy.
Worthy men and gentlemen
are likewise the means by which sage kings govern the realm with ease.
Therefore, with gentle acceptance,
they open broad and generous paths
to attract the talented and heroic of the world.
Those who exhaust their wisdom to attach themselves to the worthy
will surely establish benevolent policies;
those who seek out and recruit men of talent
will surely achieve outstanding deeds.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu personally endured the toil of spitting out food and grasping hair,
thus achieving the prosperity of empty prisons;
Duke Huán of Qí established the ritual of courtyard torches,
thus accomplishing the feat of rectification and unification.
From this, it can be seen that
rulers should diligently seek the worthy and find ease in obtaining them.
Ministers are likewise.
In the past, before worthy men encountered opportunity,
when they planned affairs and devised strategies,
the ruler would not employ their counsel;
when they presented their views with sincere loyalty,
the sovereign would not trust their honesty.
Advancing in office, they could not implement their effectiveness;
being dismissed and exiled, it was not due to their faults.
Thus, Yīyǐn toiled at the cauldron and cutting board,
Tàigōng was trapped wielding a butcher’s knife,
Bǎilǐ sold himself,
Nìng Qì fed oxen,
all suffering such hardships.
But when they encountered enlightened rulers
and met sage sovereigns,
their planning aligned with the ruler’s intentions,
their remonstrances were heeded,
their advances and retreats allowed them to express their loyalty,
their positions enabled them to practice their methods,
they rose from lowly and humiliating obscurity to ascend the imperial court,
left behind coarse vegetables and straw sandals to enjoy rich delicacies,
received tallies and enfeoffed lands,
bringing glory to their ancestors,
transmitting to their sons and grandsons,
to serve as material for storytellers.
Thus, the world must first have wise and sagely rulers,
before there can be worthy and enlightened ministers.
When the tiger roars, the valley wind grows fierce;
when the dragon rises, it brings forth clouds;
crickets await autumn to chirp,
mayflies emerge in the shade.
The Yìjīng says:
"The flying dragon is in the heavens,
it is beneficial to see the great man."
The Shījīng says:
"How splendid are the many officers,
born in this royal kingdom."
Thus, when the age is peaceful and the ruler sagely,
the talented and virtuous will come of their own accord.
Like the rulers Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ,
who obtained ministers like Jì, Qì, Gāoyáo, Yīyǐn, and Lǚ Wàng,
brilliantly present at court,
solemnly arrayed in rows,
concentrating their spirits and uniting their minds,
mutually enhancing and illuminating each other.
Even if Bóyá played the qìng and bell,
and Péngménzǐ bent the Wūháo bow,
it would still be insufficient to convey their meaning.
Thus, a sage ruler must await worthy ministers to expand his achievements,
and talented scholars also await enlightened rulers to display their virtue.
When both superior and subordinate desire this,
joyfully delighting in each other,
a meeting once in a thousand years,
discussing without doubt.
Soaring like a goose feather meeting a favorable wind,
swiftly like a giant fish released into a vast ravine.
When they achieve such satisfaction,
then what prohibition cannot be upheld,
what order cannot be carried out?
Transformation overflows to the four borders,
spreading boundlessly without end,
distant barbarians bringing tribute,
all auspicious signs surely arriving.
Thus, the sage ruler does not need to look around extensively to see clearly,
nor strain his ears to listen attentively.
Grace rides on auspicious winds,
virtue wanders with harmonious energy,
the responsibility for peace is fulfilled,
