the hope for ease and leisure is attained.
Following the natural course of wandering,
in the realm of tranquility and non-action.
Auspicious omens arrive of themselves,
longevity without limit,
dignified and composed, with hands folded,
enduring for ten thousand years.
Why must one bend and stretch like Péngzǔ,
breathe and exhale like Qiáosōng,
aloofly cutting off from the world and leaving society?
The Shījīng says:
"Numerous are the officers,
King Wén thereby found peace."
Truly, it is credible that he thereby found peace!
The enlightened spirit is only Xuān,
the Róng have the Xiānlián.
The Xiānlián run rampant,
invading the western borders of Hàn.
Hàn commands tiger-like ministers,
only the Rear General.
He marshals our six armies,
to chastise and awe them.
Having reached their territory,
he instructs them with might and virtue.
Some defenders boast of their merit,
saying they cannot be overcome.
He requests to rally his troops,
against the Qiāng of Hǎn.
The Son of Heaven commands me,
to follow him to Xiānyáng.
Yíngpíng maintains his integrity,
repeatedly submitting memorials.
Assessing the enemy and securing victory,
his威严 and strategies unmatched.
Thus he conquered the Western Róng,
and returned the army to the capital.
The Guǐfāng submitted as guests,
none failing to attend court.
In the past, during the Xuān period of Zhōu,
there were Fāng and Hǔ.
Poets sang of their merits,
and they were recorded in the Yǎ.
In the restoration of Hàn,
Chōngguó performed martial deeds.
Valiant and majestic,
he also continued their legacy.
Vast and boundless is the high heaven,
which bestowed its blessing upon the Hàn.
Laying the foundation and opening the enterprise,
both men and spirits gave their aid.
The five planets shone in the night sky,
the white spirit sighed in the dark.
The imperial destiny came to be received,
and myriad treasures increased in splendor.
Through twelve cycles of reign,
the Mandate of Heaven shifted in its course.
The Xīlíng rebelled in the west,
the Dōngyí transgressed in the east.
Then the supreme general was commanded,
and entrusted with the mighty halberd.
Majestic was the supreme general,
truly opened by heaven itself.
Accomplished in both letters and arms,
he illuminated the odes and delighted in ritual.
He modeled regulations for all officers,
becoming a pattern for the age.
In ancient times at Mèngjīn,
there was the Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ.
With a wave of his plain banner,
he unified all within the realm.
The black-haired people made a fresh start,
as the northern wind transformed Chǔ.
He campaigned against the Xiǎnyǔn,
advancing as far as Tàiyuán.
The poets sang of him,
yet still sighed at the hardship.
How much more so for our general,
at the farthest city on the extreme frontier!
The drums knew no cease in their sound,
the banners knew no moment of furling.
His grace moistened the distant wilds,
his merit was inscribed on the tripod’s lugs.
I dispatched my army,
to that western border.
The Son of Heaven feasted me,
with road-carriages and team of yellow steeds.
Speaking of my uncle,
his grace ran deep as the Wèi’s northern bank.
The jade tablet of investiture already granted,
lands were apportioned to reward his service.
Now our general,
opens territory in Shàngjùn.
To be passed to sons and grandsons,
illustrious and renowned forever.
There was a Great Man, a Master,
who considered heaven and earth as a single morning,
and ten thousand ages as an instant.
The sun and moon were his windows and doors,
the eight directions his courtyard and thoroughfare.
He traveled leaving no track or trace,
dwelled having no house or hut.
With heaven as his tent and earth as his mat,
he followed wherever his fancy led.
When stopping, he grasped the zhī and held the gū;
when moving, he carried the kē and lifted the pot.
His sole concern was wine,
what knew he of the rest?
There were noble young lords,
gentry and retired scholars.
Hearing of my reputation,
they debated its reason.
Then they flung back their sleeves, bared their collars,
glared with angry eyes and gnashed their teeth.
They expounded on ritual and law,
right and wrong rose sharp as blades.
The Master at this time was just holding a jar beneath the spout,
sipping from the cup and rinsing with the dregs.
Stroking his beard, he sat with legs sprawled,
pillowed on the yeast and cushioned on the lees.
Without thought, without care,
his joy was boundless and serene.
Blankly he became drunk,
suddenly he awoke.
Listening quietly, he did not hear the thunder’s roar;
gazing intently, he did not see Mount Tài’s shape.
He felt not the cold and heat that pierce the skin,
nor the stirring of desires for gain.
Looking down upon the myriad things,
bustling and confused like duckweed borne on the Jiāng and Hàn.
The two worthies attended at his side—
what were they to him but the guǒluǒ wasp to the mínglíng caterpillar?
Chancellor, Marquis Wénzhōng of Cuó, Xiāo Hé of Pèi;
Chancellor, Marquis Yì of Píngyáng, Cáo Shēn of Pèi;
Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent, Marquis Wénchéng of Liú, Zhāng Liáng of Hán;
Chancellor, Marquis Xiàn of Qūnì, Chén Píng of Yángwǔ;
King of Chǔ, Hán Xìn of Huáiyīn;
King of Liáng, Péng Yuè of Chāngyì;
King of Huáinán, Qíng Bù of Lù;
King Jǐng of Zhào, Zhāng Ěr of Dàliáng;
King of Hán, Hán Xìn;
King of Yān, Lú Wǎn of Fēng;
King Wén of Chángshā, Wú Ruì;
King of Jīng, Liú Jiǎ of Pèi;
Grand Tutor, Marquis Ānguó Yì, Wáng Líng;
Left Chancellor, Marquis Jiàng Wǔ, Zhōu Bó of Pèi;
Chancellor, Marquis Wǔyáng, Fán Kuài of Pèi;
Right Chancellor, Marquis Qūzhōu Jǐng, Lì Shāng of Gāoyáng;
Grand Coachman, Marquis Rǔyīn Wén, Xiàhóu Yīng of Pèi;
Chancellor, Marquis Yǐngyīn Yì, Guàn Yīng of Suīyáng;
Chancellor of Dài, Marquis Yánglíng Jǐng, Fù Kuān of Wèi;
General of Chariots and Cavalry, Marquis Xìnwǔ Sù, Jìn Xī;
Grand Herald, Lord Guǎngyě, Lì Yìjī of Gāoyáng;
Palace Attendant, Marquis Jiànxìn, Liú Jìng of Qí;
Grand Master of the Palace, Lù Jiǎ of Chǔ;
Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent, Lord Jìsì, Shūsūn Tōng of Xuē;
Wèi Wúzhī;
Commandant of the Central Army, Suí Hé;
Elder of Xīnchéng, Dǒng Gōng;
Yuán Shēng;
General Jì Xìn;
Imperial Counselor, Zhōu Kē of Pèi;
Lord Píngguó, Hóu Gōng;
The above thirty-one men
are those who helped stabilize the realm and secure the altars of state.
The Eulogy says:
Boundless is the cosmos,
above murky, below defiled.
Waves shook the four seas,
dust flew over the five peaks.
The nine domains wavered in uncertainty,
the three numina changed their divination.
Illustrious indeed was Gāozǔ,
who first received Heaven’s mandate.
Submerged in obscurity in Zhōngxiāng,
he soared to fame upon the imperial register.
Auspicious clouds responded with radiance,
the imperial steps received the wood’s virtue.
The dragon rose by the banks of the Sì,
the tiger roared in the valley of Fēng.
Crimson clouds gathered by day,
the white spirit wept at night.
The metal essence still declined,
the vermilion glow thereby flourished.
All states found their heart in him,
the outstanding people offered their service.
Stately and grand, Lord Xiāo,
upon him the kingly path relied.
Intimately bound to the sagely sovereign,
none could rival him among men.
Externally he aided the six armies,
internally he pacified the three Qín.
He promoted the exceptional and quelled disasters,
spreading virtue and uplifting the people.
He structured the state and handed down institutions,
above reverent, below intimate.
His name overshadowed all other lords,
he is called the pillar minister.
Píngyáng delighted in the Way,
adapting to change, he penetrated through.
Profound and silent,
thus he achieved these martial merits.
He drove far into Héshuò,
struck like lightning east of Rǎng.
He coordinated strategy with Huáiyīn,
his footsteps followed those of Lord Xiāo.
Wénchéng served as mentor,
penetrating the obscure and piercing the dark.
Ever matching his actions to fate,
following his heart, thus he was numinous.
He exhausted the spiritual and observed transformations,
gauged shadows and fathomed circumstances.
Ghosts had no hidden schemes,
things had no concealed forms.
The Wǔguān Pass was opened,
the Hóngmén banquet was pacified.
He followed in hardship at Xíngyáng,
then planned at Xiàyì.
He melted seals to forestall enfeoffment,
urged the attack on Qí and advised establishing kings.
He deployed strategy at Gùlíng,
settled plans for the eastern campaign.
The three kings followed like the wind,
the five marquises truly assembled.
The hegemon of Chǔ was thereby lost,
the imperial Hàn triumphantly entered.
With pleasant countenance he gazed afar,
furled his wings like the phoenix at rest.
He traced his path to Huáng-Lǎo,
left the world and abstained from grain.
Qūni was broad-minded and profound,
Fond of strategy and capable of deep thought.
His spirit roamed the vast and obscure,
Seeking traces of the divine.
The profound mysteries were not too deep for him,
Nor the ninefold earth too sunken.
He anticipated the signs before plotting,
Squeezing echoes from sound.
Six times he displayed wondrous strategies,
Four times he devised excellent plans.
He guided his lord with careful steps,
And separated Xiàng Yǔ from his heart.
When the discerning man declined,
The wings of Chǔ were truly crushed.
Hán Wáng was trapped and captured,
The Hú horses were thrown into disarray.
He welcomed Wén with strategy,
And mourned Gāo with sorrow.
Brilliant Huáiyīn,
His divine martial prowess crowned the age.
His strategies emerged without fixed patterns,
His thoughts entered divine realms.
Raising his arms, clouds arose,
Soaring like a tiger on the hunt.
Facing peril, he always smoothed it out,
Crushing the strong as if they were brittle.
He first devised plans by the Hàn River,
Then pacified the lands beyond the Wèi.
Jīng and Suǒ were firmly held,
Leading the army north to campaign.
Crossing the river, he subdued Wèi,
Climbing mountains, he destroyed Zhào.
His might blazed like fire,
His momentum swept like the wind.
Taking Dài was as easy as picking up something dropped,
Toppling Qí was like trampling grass.
Two provinces were pacified,
Four states all raised their banners.
Then he turned his gaze to Běiyān,
And displayed his might in the Eastern Sea.
He defeated and destroyed Lóng Jū,
And took his troops.
The fates of Liú and Xiàng hung in the balance,
Human strategy decided the outcome.
Reflecting on merit and virtue,
He declined enfeoffment and severed ties with Chǔ.
Péng Yuè observed the times,
Concealing his traces and hiding his light.
People gazed upon him,
Expecting him to soar like an eagle.
His might overawed the lands of Chǔ,
His allegiance was pledged to Hàn Wáng.
He pacified troubles by the Hé and Jì Rivers,
And was enfeoffed in the old territory of Liáng.
Fierce and formidable Qíng Bù,
With a piercing gaze.
His fame surpassed the mighty Chǔ,
His edge like a startling lightning bolt.
Seeing the opportunity, he shed his old skin,
Awakening to serve a new lord.
That fierce and rebellious wind,
Turned to fan our flames.
The Mandate of Heaven was settling,
The king was in the Eastern Xià.
Three heroic figures,
Gathered at Gāixià.
The great villain was vanquished,
Favor and emolument came to them.
To preserve the great and complete fortune,
Who but the virtuous could do so?
If plans are not good,
One forsakes blessings and invites disaster.
Zhāng Ěr, with his worthiness,
Had a reputation in Liáng and Wèi.
A man of no constant loyalty,
He brought shame upon himself.
Bowing, he thought of old kindness,
Looking up, he observed the five planets.
Escaping hardship,
He pushed through thorns to come.
Changing strategy to serve Western Qín,
He avenged his humiliation in Northern Jì.
Withered leaves regained their luster,
Dry branches sprouted anew.
Wáng Xìn, a descendant of Hán,
Established territory and expanded borders.
I consider your talent,
And move you to Jìnyáng.
Lú Wǎn, from humble origins,
Was gentle and devoted to our emperor.
Surpassing merit and exceeding virtue,
He was granted glorious honors.
When men covet disaster,
They bring chaos and ruin upon themselves.
Wú Ruì’s kingship,
Came from Méi Xuān.
With modest merit and weak influence,
His generations upheld loyalty and worthiness.
Solemn Jīng Wáng,
Commanded our three armies.
I plan for the four directions,
And greatly commend his achievements.
Relatives toiled diligently,
Dividing the old territory of Chǔ.
Going to fulfill his duties,
He greatly opened up the Huái region.
Ānguó turned against his kin,
My thoughts wander far.
The devoted and wise mother,
Was both enlightened and kind.
She took her own life with a sword,
Firmly upholding her principles forever.
A virtuous gentleman,
Is truly the foundation of the state.
Righteousness shows in his countenance,
Indignation bursts forth in his words.
When the lord perishes, he perishes with him,
Awaiting the final command.
Jiànghóu was simple and unadorned,
Full of strategies but sparing in words.
Truly loyal and brave,
He was praised by the emperor.
Clouds galloped over Língqiū,
Scenes flitted over Shànglán.
Pacifying Dài and capturing Xī,
He possessed Yān and Hán.
Quelling chaos with martial prowess,
Destroying the Lǚ clan with authority.
Cleansing the filth from the Purple Palace,
He summoned the emperor from Tàiyuán.
Truly, the Grand Commandant,
Brought peace to the Liú clan.
To hold merit and overawe the sovereign,
Has been difficult since ancient times.
His achievements shone in earlier generations,
Yet he ended his life in a subordinate fief.
Wǔyáng welcomed on the road,
Leading the emperor from the deep marshes.
Exerting strength for the royal house,
Not only through martial prowess.
Bearing a shield at Hóngmén,
Pushing open the palace gates.
Raising his countenance to rebuke Xiàng,
Wiping tears to awaken his lord.
Qūzhōu’s advancement,
Came from his wise elder brother.
Leading his followers,
He followed the king on campaigns.
Displaying might at Lóngtuì,
Unleashing force at Yōngchéng.
The six armies relied on him,
To overcome and capture Qíng.
Ah, Rǔyīn,
Ample and generous.
Beginning his traces in a military carriage,
Carrying strategies to join.
Horses weary, reins slack,
Yet not letting go of the guiding tree.
The crown prince was timely aided,
With strategies for Píngchéng.
Yǐngyīn was sharp and quick,
Often serving as the vanguard.
Wielding a spear at Dōngchéng,
Capturing Xiàng and securing merit.
Riding the wind, borrowing its echo,
Striding high along the Long River.
Subduing Wú and drawing from Huái,
Spreading light in the east.
Yánglíng’s achievements,
Were inherited by the marshal.
Xìnwǔ launched a campaign,
Raising banners at Jiānglíng.
Subduing kings and destroying states,
Making chaos a warning.
Vast and boundless wilderness,
Gave birth to a man of noble plan.
He advanced to offer wise counsel,
And retreated to guard a famed city.
To the east, he observed White Horse,
To the north, he held back Flying Fox.
He secured granaries and provisions,
Occupying the strategic Three Paths.
Light carriages trod eastward,
The customs of Hàn were carried forth.
He died in Qí,
Not due to any fault of persuasion.
Our emperor truly remembered him,
And bestowed grace upon his orphan.
Jiànxìn laid down his carriage,
Clad in coarse cloth, he offered treasure.
He pointed out the ways of Zhōu and Hàn,
Weighed the times and discoursed on principles.
He moved the emperor to Yīluò,
Established the capital at Fēnghào.
Pacifying the distant and steadying the near,
He truly revered what was examined.
Modest and restrained, Master Lù,
Knew the essence of speech.
He went to subdue mighty Yuè,
And came to visit the imperial Hàn.
Aligning with Píng and Bó,
He quelled the vicious and quashed chaos.
Such a man as this,
Is a luminary of the state.
The zenith of a hundred kings,
Old statutes no longer remained.
Though Hàn’s virtue was bright,
Court rituals were in disarray.
Jìsì established rites,
Bringing order below and reverence above.
Majestic were the imperial codes,
Brilliantly filling the gates.
Their style emulated the Three Dynasties,
Their laws flowed to later generations.
Wúzhī, wise and keen,
Alone revealed wondrous deeds.
His discernment matched Xiāo the Chancellor,
His gifts were like a teacher’s instruction.
Suí Hé, eloquent and perceptive,
Leveraged resources from the enemy.
Relieving Hàn and weakening Chǔ,
Was solely the achievement of this man.
White-haired Elder Dǒng,
Advised our peace at Píngyīn.
The three armies donned plain white,
And all under heaven turned their hearts.
Master Yuán, elegant and bright,
Deep-minded and skilled in insight.
Hàn’s banners shook the south,
Chǔ’s might was bent by itself.
His grand strategy profound and far-reaching,
His great deeds echoed and shone.
How distant, yet such a man,
So marvelous in understanding!
Jì Xìn deceived Xiàng,
Riding in a light carriage.
Adjusting his robes to meet the moment,
Who would punish such a death?
His body vanished like smoke,
His name rose with the wind.
Zhōu Kē, fervent and bold,
His heart as if holding ice.
His body could be tortured,
But his will could not be subdued.
His steadfast path perished with him,
Yet his shining deeds ascended doubly.
The emperor considered his service,
And his descendants inherited it.
Though heaven and earth were harmonious,
The king’s heart held regrets.
Longing for kin, gazing toward Chǔ,
Ever speaking, ever grieving.
Hóu Gōng leaned on his chariot rail,
The imperial dowager returned.
This was called pacifying the state,
His honored command shone brightly.
A sweeping wind passes over things,
Clear and turbid each produce their sound.
When great men rise,
Benefit lies in where they go.
Vast seas are formed by rivers,
Lofty mountains are made of soil.
Sháo and Hù music interweave,
Dragon robes compare to images.
Bright and clear, the many sages,
Together uphold heaven’s net.
Swords display their sharpness,
Mirrors offer their clarity.
Civil and martial virtues fully present,
Hàn’s fortune could expand.
Far-reaching, the distant customs,
For a thousand years are looked up to.
The grand master, his given name Shuò,
Courtesy name Mànqiàn,
Was a man of Yàncì in Píngyuán.
During the Jiàn’ān era of Wèi,
Yàncì was divided to form Lèlíng Commandery,
Thus he was also considered a man of that commandery.
He served Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
And the Hàn Shū fully records his deeds.
The master was extraordinary, broad, and penetrating,
His thoughts encompassing adaptation.
He believed that in a corrupt age, one cannot seek wealth and honor,
So he wandered lightly to attain position.
He held that acting rashly could not uphold the upright way,
So he soared and hovered, aloof from the world.
Aloofness could not serve as a lasting example,
So he remonstrated directly to clarify his integrity.
Clarifying integrity could not ensure long-term safety,
So he used humor to gain acceptance.
He purified his principles but obscured his traces,
Kept his essence clear but muddied his outward expression.
He relaxed and tightened without turning to evil,
Advanced and retreated without leaving the group.
As for his far-reaching mind and broad tolerance,
His abundant wisdom and great talent,
Unrestrained and knowledgeable in all things,
Touching upon categories, skilled in many abilities.
He combined changes to clarify calculations,
Profoundly aided to know the future.
From the Three Fén and Five Diǎn,
The Eight Suǒ and Nine Qiū,
The studies of Yīnyáng, charts, and weft texts,
The theories of the hundred schools and various streams,
Debates that were comprehensive and agile,
Techniques of fragmentation and reversal,
Arts of channels, vessels, medicines, and stones,
Skills of archery, charioteering, writing, and arithmetic—
He delved deeply to investigate their principles,
Mastering them without practice, exhausting their functions.
What passed before his eyes, he could recite,
What passed his ears, he kept in mind.
His clarity and openness,
Encompassed vastness and greatness.
He overawed ministers and chancellors,
Mocked and laughed at heroes and stalwarts.
Unmatched, he overshadowed all before him,
Trampled upon the noble and powerful.
In prominence, he did not revel in display,
In lowliness, he felt no sorrow.
He jested with the sovereign as with a colleague,
Regarded his peers as mere weeds.
His heroic integrity surpassed his kind,
His lofty spirit overshadowed the age.
Truly, he stood out from the crowd,
Roaming beyond the confines of the world.
Commentators also say the master breathed in harmony,
Exhaling the old, inhaling the new.
Like a cicada shedding its shell, a dragon transforming,
He cast off the mundane and ascended to immortality.
In spirit, he communed with creation,
In soul, he became a star.
These are again strange and elusive matters,
Not to be fully discussed.
The great man came to govern this state,
I, your servant, returned from the capital to pay respects.
Beholding the master’s county and town,
I imagined his lofty demeanor.
Pacing in the ceremonial hall,
I saw the master’s remaining portrait.
Wandering the city walls,
I viewed the master’s temple.
Filled with deep emotion,
I composed this eulogy.
The words are as follows:
Noble and lofty is the gentleman,
Who retreats in seclusion, preserving his integrity.
In retreat, he does not remain in perpetual adversity;
In advancement, he also shuns glory.
Facing the world, he washes his feet;
Aspiring to antiquity, he adjusts his cap strings.
Though stained, he remains untainted;
Though in turbidity, he can purify himself.
How is he untainted?
By being lofty and bright, yet capable of gentleness.
How can he purify himself?
By regarding filth as if it were floating foam.
He finds joy in what must be done,
And dwells in obscurity without worry.
Transcending his era, surpassing his time,
He roams afar in solitude.
Gazing upon past generations,
I think of distant traces.
Remote and profound is the gentleman,
His Way is like a dragon.
Though marked by courtly seclusion,
He harmonizes without conforming.
Lingering in humble positions,
He passes the time with ease.
I come from the east,
And journey to this town.
Reverently I inquire about the ruins and graves,
Standing expectantly on the plains and lowlands.
Only the tombs and ruins remain,
While the spirits rest forever.
The people remember his path,
And thus this shrine was erected.
Wandering through the temple chambers,
His likeness remains in paintings.
Circling the shrine,
The courtyard and halls lie desolate.
Beams and pillars tilt and crumble,
Weeds and grasses remain uncleared.
Solemn and dignified, O gentleman,
How can this be your dwelling?
This dwelling lacks form,
Yet my feelings linger longingly.
In ancient times, those with virtue
Never lacked lingering spirits.
Heaven’s order includes rites,
And divine oversight is most clear.
Vaguely, like windblown dust,
I offer these words of praise.
Since the common people cannot govern themselves,
A ruler is established to govern them.
An enlightened ruler cannot govern alone,
So ministers are appointed to assist him.
Thus, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors rose in succession,
Each generation inheriting the foundation.
Whether through abdication or armed conflict,
Civil virtue or military achievement,
All relied on master craftsmen shaping talents and the multitude shining brightly,
With the sovereign planning strategies and his ministers exerting their strength.
Circumstances differed,
And their deeds varied in excellence.
Yet, in substance, they were firmly rooted,
And their Way remained unwavering.
The influence of their admirable conduct,
And their teachings reformed the ages,
All followed the same principle.
Thus, with the rise of the Eight Worthies, the Táng dynasty flourished;
With Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng employed, Tāng and Wǔ achieved peace;
With three worthies advancing, Xiǎo Bái prospered;
With five ministers distinguished, Chóng’ěr became hegemon.
In the middle ages, decline set in,
And this Way fell into disuse.
Those in high positions no longer governed with utmost impartiality,
While subordinates sought glory through private means.
Those ruling with flexibility no longer led with sincerity and trust,
While those adhering to rigidity displayed themselves through schemes and power.
Thus, ruler and minister grew estranged, and the teachings of names grew shallow,
The world fell into chaos, and the times lacked order.
Hence, Qú Yuán and Níng Wǔ withdrew or advanced accordingly;
Liǔ Xià Huì was thrice dismissed;
Jiē Yú sang as he walked;
Lǔ Lián threw himself into the sea.
In an age of decline,
They preserved their reputation and integrity,
And the relationship between ruler and minister,
Was as if matching tally tokens.
Thus, Yān Zhāo and Yuè Yì
Are examples from antiquity.
If Bó Lè is not encountered,
Then for a thousand years, not a single steed appears.
When the time meets a dragon’s countenance,
Then in that era, three heroes are harnessed.
Hàn’s acquisition of talent
Was most precious in this regard.
Though Gāozǔ did not govern with the Way prevailing,
His subordinates could exhaust their loyalty;
Though Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shěn did not serve their lord as in the Three Dynasties,
The common people did not lose their livelihoods.
Quelling chaos and protecting the people
May also be considered secondary.
When the times are turbulent and unstable,
Then prominence is不如 seclusion;
When all things yearn for order,
Then silence is不如 speech.
Therefore, the noble person of antiquity
Did not worry about the difficulty of broadening the Way;
He worried about encountering the right time.
Encountering the right time is not difficult;
Encountering a worthy ruler is difficult.
Thus, having the Way but not the time
Is why Mèngzǐ sighed deeply;
Having the time but no ruler
Is why Jiǎ Shēng shed tears.
Once in ten thousand years,
Is the common path for all living beings;
Once in a thousand years,
Is the auspicious meeting of the wise and talented.
Encountering it, one cannot but rejoice;
Losing it, how can one not lament?
The words of the ancients
Truly carry deep feeling!
In my leisure days,
I often peruse the Records of the States,
Examining its rulers and ministers,
Comparing their actions.
Though their Way falls short of earlier generations,
They are still of the same era in a different age.
Wén Ruò possessed the insight of unique vision,
And had a heart to save the world.
Assessing the times, the people were in dire distress;
Considering ability, none surpassed Wèi Wǔ.
Thus, he turned his face to the hegemon’s court,
And participated in deliberations on worldly affairs.
Recommending talent without seeking recognition,
He only became prominent after a long time;
Planning strategies without striving for merit,
Matters were settled only when they arose.
Though he perished to clarify his loyalty,
His insight was also lofty!
During Dǒng Zhuó’s rebellion,
The imperial authority was displaced and coerced.
Gōng Dá was filled with emotion,
His will set on sacrificing his life.
Speaking from this perspective,
He thus preserved his reputation and integrity in a grand manner.
As for being a subject of Hàn in person,
Yet leaving traces in Wèi’s tent,
In origins and choices,
This is also said of Wén Ruò.
Therefore, the circumstances of survival and perish differ,
And beginnings and ends are not the same.
Could it be that since Wén Ruò was already enlightened,
The teachings of names found a place in him?
Benevolence and righteousness must be clarified,
So the era’s exemplars uphold their essence;
The principle of life must be fully preserved,
So the profoundly insightful grasp its core.
Together, broadening the Way—
Is this not far-reaching!
Cuī Shēng was lofty and bright,
Bending but not breaking.
The reason he recorded his name under Wèi Wǔ
And held the tablet at the hegemon’s court
Was because the Hàn sovereign faced the sun,
While the Wèi ruler faced north!
If one day the imperial seal were presented,
And ruler and minister exchanged positions,
This is what Cuī Zǐ would not accept,
And what Wèi Wǔ would not tolerate.
The rivers and lakes that carry boats
Can also overturn them;
Benevolence and righteousness that preserve the self
Can also lead to its demise.
Yet, earlier worthies shattered like jade before,
And later wise men roll up their sleeves after,
Is it not because heavenly feelings arise from within,
And the teachings of names restrain external things?
Kǒngmíng lingered in seclusion,
awaiting the opportune moment to act,
his thoughts reaching back to Guǎn Zhòng and Yuè Yì,
his distant brilliance manifesting an elegant demeanor.
He governed the state with ritual propriety,
and among the people there were no voices of complaint;
punishments were not excessive,
and there were no lingering tears of grief.
Even the cherished legacies of antiquity—
how could they surpass this!
When it came to the final entrustment on his deathbed,
receiving the bequest to serve as chancellor,
Liú Hòu conferred it without suspicion,
and Wǔhóu accepted it without a trace of fear.
The successor accepted him without duplicity,
and the common people trusted him without dissent.
Between ruler and minister—
truly something to be celebrated!
Gōngjǐn was outstanding,
his lofty aspirations setting him apart from the crowd.
In youth, he assessed his lord,
forming a pure bond with Bófú;
in his later years, he revealed his brilliance,
achieving a tripartite division at Chìbì.
It is lamentable that his life was cut short—
his potential was immeasurable.
Zǐbù assisted Cè,
contributing to the beauty of spreading his reputation;
he ceased weeping and restrained his grief,
performing the meritorious service of supporting and upholding.
Where his spirit and emotions were involved,
was it merely stubborn frankness?
Yet he closed his doors and was not employed,
and when he ascended the altar, he faced ridicule.
Now, for a single person,
the illumination they receive does not differ,
yet between being employed and cast aside,
there can be sudden variation.
How much more so for those submerged in the ditches and gullies,
whether encountered or not encountered?
The composition of odes and hymns
has existed since ancient times.
Some use them to chant and express their nature and emotions,
others to recount virtue and display merit.
Although their main intent converges,
what they entrust to them may diverge.
As for those whose conduct and retirement follow the Way,
whose reputation and substance are not stagnant,
whose exemplary conduct and virtuous words
serve as models for the age—
these cannot be discarded.
Therefore, I again compose a preface to express my thoughts,
using it to create these eulogies.
Nine persons from the Wèi Records,
four from the Shǔ Records,
seven from the Wú Records.
Xún Yù, styled Wénruò;
Zhūgě Liàng, styled Kǒngmíng;
Zhōu Yú, styled Gōngjǐn;
Xún Yōu, styled Gōngdá;
Páng Tǒng, styled Shìyuán;
Zhāng Zhāo, styled Zǐbù;
Yuán Huàn, styled Yàoqīng;
Jiǎng Wǎn, styled Gōngyǎn;
Lǔ Sù, styled Zǐjìng;
Cuī Yǎn, styled Jìguī;
Huáng Quán, styled Gōnghéng;
Zhūgě Jǐn, styled Zǐyú;
Xú Miǎo, styled Jǐngshān;
Lù Xùn, styled Bóyán;
Chén Qún, styled Chángwén;
Gù Yōng, styled Yuántàn;
Xiàhóu Xuán, styled Tàichū;
Yú Fān, styled Zhòngxiáng;
Wáng Jīng, styled Chéngzōng;
Chén Tài, styled Xuánbó.
The Fire Virtue having already declined,
fate was entangled with great excess.
A great tempest fanned the sea,
and both oceans raised their waves.
Though the horned dragon and tiger were startled,
wind and clouds were not yet harmonious.
Hidden fish chose the depths,
lofty birds awaited the branches.
Illustrious were the three heroes,
all turning the axis of heaven.
They vied to gather the finest timber,
struggled to pluck the pine and bamboo.
The phoenix found no time to roost,
the dragon no leisure to lie hidden.
In the valleys, no secluded orchids;
on the ridges, no steadfast chrysanthemums.
Brilliant Wénruò,
with spiritual insight penetrating and illuminating.
Responding to change, he understood subtleties;
probing the profound, he grasped essentials.
Sun and moon resided in his person,
concealed yet ever more radiant.
Civilized brilliance reflected in his heart,
the deeper one delved, the more wondrous it became.
When the azure sea overflowed its banks,
jade and stone were shattered alike.
The enlightened man benefits all,
setting aside himself to preserve what he cherishes.
His plans resolved the troubles of the time,
his achievements aided all within the realm.
First, he saved the living people;
ultimately, he clarified his noble demeanor.
Gōngdá, profound and clear,
his thoughts akin to the divining stalks and tortoise shell.
His application was without fixed method,
his actions capturing the essence of the assembly.
From the beginning of his rise,
he encountered this turmoil and distress.
His spirit serene and steadfast,
he faced it with ever greater composure.
Quietly within the tent,
no calculation was left unconsidered.
Earnestly, in harmonious rhythm,
his traces never paused.
Though he cherished a foot-long jade,
he looked upon a chain of cities with a smile.
His wisdom could save things;
his seeming folly sufficed to preserve his life.
The Gentleman of the Interior was gentle and refined,
his capacity and understanding pure and simple.
Upright yet not rigidly scrupulous,
penetrating yet able to be firm.
Sincere and respectful was his virtuous heart,
vast and deep his measure of conduct.
His will formed in early youth,
his Way spread in his later years.
The benevolent are necessarily courageous,
and virtue also has its words.
Though he encountered treading on a tiger,
his spirit and energy remained tranquil.
His conduct was not adorned,
yet his name and deeds were without fault.
His actions were not vehement,
his simple style ever more vivid.
Distant indeed, Master Cuī,
upright in form and straight in heart.
His natural frame open and clear,
his walls and eaves lofty and steep.
Loyalty resided in his tracks,
righteousness took form in his demeanor.
He thought to plant fragrant orchids,
and cut away thorns and brambles.
Men detest those above them,
the times do not tolerate the wise.
Resplendent Master,
elegantly wielding fame and integrity.
Though he encountered dust and fog,
he still shook off frost and snow.
When fortune reached its limit and the Way dissolved,
this bright moon was shattered.
Jǐngshān, expansive and unconventional,
his resonance in harmony with the Way.
Form and vessel did not persist,
yet within a square inch, the sea was contained.
Harmonious yet not identical,
penetrating yet not mixed.
When drunk, he forgot his words;
when sober, he left behind his replies.
Chángwén, penetrating and refined,
his righteousness consistent from start to finish.
Thinking to support the sovereign,
he aspired to share Yī Yǐn's sense of shame.
If the people did not yet know virtue,
he felt as if the fear were his own.
Excellent plans flourished at court,
forthright words filled the ears.
Though jade, when born, is beautiful,
its light does not exceed a handful.
Though accumulated virtue may be slight,
its Way illuminates all under heaven.
Profound indeed is Tàichū,
his measure and capacity lofty and refined.
His natural vessel and model,
his standard without pretense.
To preserve oneself through integrity,
traces of filth must be false.
Facing death is not difficult,
where principle exists, it is easy.
The myriad things surge and toss,
who can bear their burden?
The six directions are vast in vain,
nowhere to lodge one's body.
The ruler and parents are natural,
not from fame and teaching.
Respectful deference being the same,
both affection and propriety are fulfilled.
Fierce and ardent, Wáng Shēng,
knowing death, he did not yield.
Seeking benevolence is not far,
his aim lay in loyalty and filial piety.
Xuánbó, firm and simple,
greatly preserved name and substance.
His ambition was for lofty structures,
adding halls and ascending steps.
Upright in the tiger gate,
his correct words increasingly revealed.
Facing peril, he gave his life,
exhausting his heart's propriety.
Majestic and dignified, Kǒngmíng,
his foundation vast and far-reaching.
His vessel like that of all people,
yet alone endowed with foreknowledge.
Setting the standard for grace and talent,
far illuminating Guǎn and Yuè.
At first, the dragon coiled,
his noble resolve grew ever firmer.
As the hundred and sixth path was lost,
shields and spears were used in turn.
If not one fated for the age,
who could sweep away the gloom?
The imperial scion longed for peace,
with few words, he loosened control.
Casting off common robes in the central grove,
he flourished as the pillar of his time.
Shìyuán, broad and far-reaching,
his refined nature inwardly harmonious.
Honoring goodness and cherishing beings,
observing beginnings, he knew the ends.
Loss and chaos were complete,
the path to victory not yet ascended.
The master marked it out,
raising a clear wind.
Intimately bound to the wise lord,
without error, only timely.
From dawn to dusk, never slackening,
his duty lay in making bright.
The three strategies already laid out,
the foundation for hegemony was set.
Gōngyǎn planted his roots,
never forgetting centrality and correctness.
How could it be called imitation?
It truly lay in his refined nature.
Once also bridled and reined,
he bore the mandate of the times.
Pushing forth the worthy and reverencing himself,
over time, he became worthy of respect.
Gōnghéng Zhòngdá,
his heart deep and sincere.
Cherishing this one man,
facing difficulty, he was not confused.
In former days, not achieving,
he borrowed wings from a neighboring state.
Advancing, he could produce fine notes,
retreating, he did not lose virtue.
The six directions in chaos,
the people's hearts about to change.
Birds choose tall phoenix trees,
ministers must look to their lord.
Gōngjǐn, outstanding and perceptive,
his clear mind uniquely discerning.
Pushing through the grass to seek a lord,
he established friendship at first meeting.
Mighty and martial, Wèi Wǔ,
outwardly relying on hegemonic traces.
His ambition to overshadow Héng and Huò,
relying on war, he forgot the enemy.
Lofty and exceptional, such a man,
shone with marvel at Chìbì.
The three lights divided into three,
the cosmos temporarily separated.
Zǐbù, renowned for his fame,
encountered an age of turmoil.
Nurturing his wings in his homeland,
he rested his shoulders south of the river.
The royal strategy imperiled,
Wú and Wèi both treasured him.
Thus he presented grand plans,
rectifying this hegemonic way.
Upon Huánwáng's death,
the great enterprise not yet pure.
Taking arms, entrusting the orphan,
only to the worthy and kin.
Ceasing weeping, halting grief,
facing difficulty, forgetting self.
Achieving this southern-facing throne,
truly due to the old minister.
Talent emerges for the age,
the age also needs talent.
Obtaining and being able to employ it,
the value lies in having no doubts.
Proud and lofty, Zǐjìng,
rising from the wild grasses.
Shouldering burdens, uttering marvels,
then constructing the cloud terrace.
Zǐyú, dignified and elder,
his substance and nature pure and excellent.
Remonstrating without offense,
correct without severity.
Bearing commands in the public court,
retiring, he forgot private position.
Was there not the jílíng bird?
He firmly guarded name and vessel.
Bóyán, steadfast and loyal,
aiding the age with the Way.
In service, he could diligently achieve merit,
at court, he could offer replacements.
Planning to pacify the altars of soil and grain,
resolving disputes and blunting sharpness.
Uprightness thus inviting suspicion,
loyalty thus incurring fault.
Yuántàn, solemn and far-reaching,
spirit harmonious, form restrained.
Like that white jade scepter,
its substance without dust or flaw.
Establishing superiors with constancy,
correcting superiors with gradualness.
Purity not increasing cleanness,
turbidity not adding stain.
Zhòngxiáng, lofty and bright,
his nature not harmonizing with things.
Fond of this, he stood apart from the crowd,
broken but not bent.
Repeatedly striking the reverse scales,
the straight way met with dismissal.
Sighing past Sūnyáng,
exiled like Jiǎ and Qū.
Numerous and gathered, these many worthies,
a single encounter in a thousand years.
Adjusting reins on the high road,
lifting heads toward the heavenly path.
Looking up, drawing from the dark current,
looking down, broadening contemporary affairs.
Fame and integrity, different paths,
refined tastes, the same direction.
Sun and moon adorn the sky,
gazing upon them, they do not fall.
Benevolence and righteousness in one's person,
using them, they are not exhausted.
Still longing for their double brilliance,
drawing it, savoring it.
Later generations beat the rhythm,
cowards gain courage.
Ah, in the beginning of high antiquity,
from the vast heavens, the people were born.
Reviewing the array of past rulers,
down to the Qín.
Those near followed in their steps,
those far heard their fame and influence.
Profuse and luxuriant,
those obliterated and unmentioned,
cannot be fully counted.
Succeeding Sháo and Xià,
honoring titles and posthumous names,
briefly worth mentioning are seventy-two lords.
None who were good did not flourish,
who, opposing and erring, could survive?
Before the time of Xuānyuán,
it is far and remote,
and the details cannot be heard.
The transmissions of the Five Classics and Six Canons,
only their customs can be observed.
The Book of Documents says:
"How enlightened is the sovereign!
How excellent are the ministers!"
Based on this, it can be said,
no ruler was greater than Táng Yáo,
no minister was more worthy than Hòu Jì.
Hòu Jì founded his enterprise under Táng Yáo,
Gōng Liú rose to prominence among the Western Róng,
King Wén reformed the institutions,
and thus the Zhōu reached its zenith,
the great undertaking was accomplished,
and later it declined and waned,
silent for a thousand years,
was it not a good beginning and a good end?
Yet there is no different path,
careful about the origins in the past,
and cautious about the teachings left for the future.
Thus the tracks are level and easy,
easy to follow;
the deep grace is vast and great,
easy to enrich;
the laws and regulations are clear and evident,
easy to emulate;
the transmitted system is orderly and reasonable,
easy to inherit.
Therefore, the enterprise flourished in infancy and was exalted above the two later rulers.
Considering its origins,
and examining its end,
there is no extraordinary achievement or unparalleled deed that can be verified today.
Yet still they trod upon Liángfù,
ascended Tài Shān,
established illustrious titles,
and bestowed honorable names.
The virtue of the great Hàn,
gushes forth like a spring from its source,
overflowing and spreading widely,
extending to the four borders,
like clouds spreading and mist dispersing,
reaching up to the nine heavens,
and down to the eight extremities.
All living beings,
are moistened and soaked,
harmonious energy flows everywhere,
martial spirit swiftly passes,
those nearby wander at the source,
those far away swim in the foam,
the chief villains are submerged and vanish,
the obscure becomes clear and bright,
insects and creatures rejoice in the marsh,
turning their heads to face inward.
Then they enclose precious herds of zōuyú,
intercept strange beasts like the mí lù,
guide the single-stemmed six-ear grain to the kitchen,
sacrifice the beast with double antlers sharing a single base,
capture the remaining treasure of Zhōu and release the turtle at Qí,
summon the cuìhuáng and ride the dragon in the pond.
Ghosts and spirits connect with Líng Yǔ,
and are hosted in the leisure halls.
Strange things are deceitful and诡异,
extraordinary and endlessly changing.
How admirable,
that auspicious signs have reached this point,
yet still they consider their virtue shallow,
and dare not speak of the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
It is said that in Zhōu, fish leaped and boats sank,
and they offered sacrifices with burning.
If not for such signs as these,
to ascend the great mound,
would it not be shameful?
The way of advancing and yielding,
how different it is!
Then the Grand Minister of War came forward and said:
"Your Majesty benevolently nurtures all living beings,
righteously campaigns against the unruly,
the various Xià joyfully offer tribute,
the hundred Mán present gifts,
your virtue matches that of the ancients,
your achievements are unparalleled,
glorious deeds are widespread,
auspicious signs and numerous changes,
the expected responses follow one after another,
not merely occasional appearances.
It is thought that Tài Shān and Liángfǔ have set up altars hoping for your visit,
to bestow titles and compare glory,
but Your Majesty humbly declines and does not proceed.
This forfeits the joy of the three spirits,
lacks the rituals of the kingly way,
and the ministers are ashamed.
Some say that heaven is inherently obscure,
and showing precious signs should not be refused;
if you refuse them,
then Tài Shān will have no record and Liángfǔ no hope.
Each age also had its glory,
all fulfilled their era and then declined,
what then would later commentators praise,
and speak of the seventy-two rulers?
Cultivating virtue to receive signs,
receiving the mandate to carry out affairs,
is not overstepping.
Thus the sage kings did not neglect,
but practiced rituals for the earth spirits,
paid homage to the heavenly gods,
inscribed achievements on the central peak,
to glorify the supreme,
display great virtue,
issue honorable titles,
receive abundant blessings,
to benefit the common people.
How magnificent is this grand spectacle of the world,
the ultimate achievement of a king,
which should not be belittled.
I hope Your Majesty will complete it.
Then, incorporating the strategies of the gentry scholars,
let them receive the last rays of the sun and moon,
to display their talents and handle affairs.
Still, we should also correct and arrange their principles,
purify and adorn their writings,
to create one art of the Spring and Autumn.
We will follow the old six to make seven,
spreading it endlessly,
so that for ten thousand generations they may stir the clear stream,
raise gentle waves,
spread illustrious fame,
and elevate abundant achievements.
This is how the former sages eternally preserved their great names and were always praised.
It is appropriate to order the archivists to fully present the rituals for review."
Then the Son of Heaven, with a changed expression,
said:
"Yes indeed,
I shall try it!"
Then he reconsidered and reflected,
gathered the discussions of the ministers,
inquired about the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
sang of the vastness of the great marsh,
and broadened the richness of the auspicious signs.
Then he composed a eulogy, saying:
From our heaven's cover,
clouds drift richly.
Sweet dew and timely rain,
this land can be roamed.
Nourishing moisture seeps and drips,
what life does not thrive!
Fine grain with six ears,
how can our harvest not be stored?
Not only does it rain,
but also moistens and enriches.
Not only does it reach me everywhere,
but spreads and protects all.
All things are joyful,
cherishing and longing.
Famous mountains and illustrious positions,
await the ruler's arrival.
O ruler, O ruler,
why do you not come forth!
The gentle beast,
delights in our ruler's garden.
White body with black patterns,
its appearance is admirable.
Gentle and respectful,
the demeanor of a nobleman.
We have heard of its sound,
now we see its arrival.
Its path cannot be followed.
A sign of heaven's auspiciousness.
This also happened with Shùn,
the Yú clan thus rose.
The gleaming qílín,
roams that spiritual altar.
In the early winter tenth month,
the ruler goes to the suburban sacrifice.
Galloping our ruler's carriage,
the emperor enjoys blessings.
Before the three dynasties,
such a thing had never occurred.
The coiling yellow dragon,
rises with virtue and ascends.
Its colors dazzling and shining,
brilliant and radiant.
The true yang clearly appears,
awakening the common people.
In the records it is written,
saying it is the vehicle of the received mandate.
That it has its patterns,
need not be repeatedly explained.
Relying on categories and寄托寓意,
it metaphorically speaks of the Fēng sacrifice on the mound.
Having examined the arts and observed them,
the connection between Heaven and humanity has already been established,
and the interactions between high and low are harmonious and responsive.
The virtue of the sage kings
was cautious and reverent.
Thus it is said: when rising, one must consider decline;
when at peace, one must think of danger.
Therefore, even at the height of their dignity and solemnity, Tāng and Wǔ
did not lose their reverence and piety.
When Shùn was in possession of the great statutes,
he reflected and examined what was lacking or omitted.
This is what is meant.
To the various officials:
Your servant, the Grand Master of Palace Leisure, Yáng Xióng,
bows his head and kowtows twice to present this memorial to Your Majesty, the Emperor:
Your servant Xióng is shallow in classical learning and technique,
with no exceptional conduct or ability.
Yet I have repeatedly received abundant grace,
been promoted beyond my peers,
and placed among the group of worthies.
I am ashamed to have nothing with which to fulfill my duties.
Your servant humbly considers that Your Majesty, with your supremely sagely virtue,
has ascended like a dragon rising to assume the throne.
Reverently brilliant and esteeming antiquity,
you act as father and mother to the people,
and are the sovereign of all under Heaven.
Holding the purest and clearest Way,
you illuminate the four seas as with a mirror,
listen to and heed local customs,
observe broadly and encompass widely,
participate with Heaven and assist Earth,
combining divine intelligence,
matching the Five Emperors,
surpassing the Three Kings—
since the opening of Heaven and Earth,
such has never been heard of.
Your servant sincerely delights in making your new virtue shine forth,
to illuminate it boundlessly.
In former times, Sīmǎ Xiàngrú composed a piece on the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices
to manifest the excellence of the Hàn house.
Your servant has long suffered from dizzy spells,
and fear that one day, before the dogs and horses
fill the ditches,
what is in my heart will not be made clear,
leaving eternal regret in the Yellow Springs.
I dare to exhaust my innermost feelings,
pour out my heart,
and compose a piece titled "Denouncing the Qín and Praising the Xīn."
Although it does not capture even one ten-thousandth part,
it represents the utmost of your servant's thoughts.
Your servant Xióng bows his head and kowtows twice to present this for your attention,
saying:
At the beginning, when Heaven and Earth had not yet parted,
all was vast and indistinct.
Some things were dark and sprouting,
some were yellow and budding.
When the dark and yellow separated and divided,
high and low mutually nurtured.
Then, at the dawn of humanity,
emperors and kings first existed.
In that chaotic and boundless era,
things were faint, obscure, and not clearly perceived;
the world could not yet speak of them.
When there were those who did speak,
none were more illustrious than Fúxī and Huángdì in high antiquity;
none more flourishing than Táng Yáo and Yú Shùn in the middle ages;
and none more eminent than Chéng Zhōu in recent times.
When Zhòngní (Confucius) did not meet with employment,
the Spring and Autumn Annals arose from this difficulty.
Speaking of what the spirits bless
and what the myriad people rely upon,
none fail to speak of virtue, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom.
Only Qín arose abruptly from the Western Róng,
in the borders of Bīn, Huāng, Qí, and Yōng.
Following the overstepping traces of Xiāng, Wén, Xuān, and Líng,
it laid its foundation under Duke Xiào,
flourished under Huìwén,
strove under Zhāo and Zhuāng,
until under Zhèng (the First Emperor) it destroyed the vertical and horizontal alliances,
annexed the six states,
and then proclaimed itself under Shǐ Huáng.
It promoted the wicked governance of Yāng, Yí, Wéi, and Sī;
galloped with the military campaigns of Qǐ, Jiǎn, Tián, and Bēn;
eradicated ancient writings,
scraped away speech and burned books,
relaxed rites and collapsed music,
blinding and deafening the people.
Then it wished to wash away Táng and float off Yú,
cleanse Yīn and sweep away Zhōu,
burn and eliminate the texts of Zhòngní,
engrave its own achievements,
alter institutions, regulations, and measures,
all recorded in the Qín annals.
Therefore, aged Confucian scholars and great elders
clasped their books and fled far away;
ritual officials and erudites
rolled their tongues and did not speak.
The birds that came in auspicious display,
the beasts with fleshy horns,
became fierce and unapproachable and did not arrive.
Sweet dew and fine wine,
the auspicious signs of radiant light soaking deep, lay hidden;
while great comets streaked and fell,
huge barbarians, ghostly omens, and monstrous portents arose.
Spirits rested and divine threads snapped,
the seas boiled and flew in masses.
It perished in the second generation—
how extreme it was!
The Way of emperors and kings
is something one must be ever cautious of and cannot depart from.
Those who can be upright and enlightened exhaust auspicious signs;
those who turn away and are benighted reach the extreme of monstrous calamities.
Looking up to antiquity and the past,
there were those who relied on responses and yet still had deficiencies.
How could one who ruins and overturns be able to preserve all?
Thus, those who emulate antiquity praise Yáo and Shùn,
while those who intimidate and insult fall into the ways of Jié and Zhòu.
How much more so for one who completely sweeps away the achievements of former sages over thousands of years
and relies solely on his own private desires—could he enjoy blessing and protection?
Then Hàn's founder, Gāozǔ, rose like a dragon in Fēng and Pèi,
leaped swiftly in Wǎn and Yè,
from Wǔguān joined forces with Xiàng Yǔ at Xiányáng,
founded his enterprise in Shǔ and Hàn,
made his mark in the Three Qín,
defeated Xiàng east of the mountains,
and became emperor over all under Heaven.
He removed the especially harsh and excessive aspects of Qín's governance,
abolishing them in accordance with the times.
As for the use of Confucian scholars,
penal laws,
calendrical records,
and charts and classics, these were gradually increased.
The remaining institutions of Qín,
and the noble titles of the Xiàng house,
though contrary to antiquity, were still inherited.
Therefore, the imperial statutes were lacking and not repaired,
the royal bonds were slackened and not tightened,
the Way reached its limit and the numbers were exhausted,
falling into obscurity and not returning.
When it came to the Great Xin receiving the Mandate,
the Supreme Deity bestowed favor,
the Earth Spirit looked upon with care,
mystical tallies and spiritual covenants,
auspicious omens surged forth,
gushing and swirling,
rivers flowed and seas calmed,
clouds moved and winds stilled,
mists gathered and rains dispersed,
spreading across the eight regions,
ascending to be displayed in the celestial court,
shaking sounds and daily radiance,
fiery light and flying echoes,
filling the space between heaven and the abyss,
there must be that which cannot be declined or refused, so it is said.
Thereupon, they reverently complied with the Mandate of Heaven,
exhausting honors and reaching the utmost reverence,
dividing the divine tallies with Heaven,
uniting with the spiritual covenants of Earth,
creating for the multitudes,
planning for ten thousand generations,
extraordinary, magnificent, unrestrained, and mysterious,
sacrificing to Heaven and serving Earth.
As for the strange objects and peculiar wonders,
they reside with the Five Majestic Generals,
and those promulgated throughout the world
amount to forty-eight chapters.
Ascending to the vast heavens,
spreading across the lower earth,
who but the Xin house could partake in this?
Splendid and glorious,
truly the emblem of the Son of Heaven.
As for the white dove and crimson crow,
the white fish and severed snake,
these are insignificant in comparison.
Receiving the Mandate was very easy,
but upholding it required great diligence.
In the past, emperors succeeded sovereigns,
kings succeeded emperors,
following the footsteps of antiquity,
some ruled through non-action,
some perished through additions or subtractions.
How could they know that the Xin court devoted its heart and accumulated its intentions,
storing thoughts and attending to affairs,
acting with solemn reverence on all sides,
bright and vigilant without sleep,
diligent and earnest—
was this not the way of Qín?
If not diligent,
then the predecessors would not have been proper;
if not earnest,
then the awakened virtue would not be joyful.
Therefore, they opened the secret archives,
perused the forest of books,
gathered distantly in the garden of elegance,
soared in the arena of rites and music,
inherited the lost legacy of Yīn and Zhōu,
continued the severed customs of Táng and Yú,
excellent laws and fine measures,
golden rules and jade ordinances,
divine hexagrams and spiritual omens,
ancient texts all brought forth,
brilliant and shining,
nothing was not fully achieved.
They displayed chariots, canopies, and banners to show them,
raised harmonious bells and played the "Sìxià" to regulate them,
adorned with embroidered robes and ceremonial caps to make them illustrious,
rectified marriages, funerals, and burials to honor them,
and drew close to the nine clans and virtuous worthies to harmonize them.
As for reforming and fixing the spirits and deities,
this is the highest ritual.
Reverently cultivating the hundred sacrifices,
all are in proper order.
The Bright Hall and the Yōng Terrace,
these are magnificent sights.
The nine temples and long life,
this is the ultimate filial piety.
Establishing the six classics,
this is a grand achievement.
Pacifying the north and embracing the Chányú,
this is broadening virtue.
As for restoring the five ranks of nobility,
regulating the three grades of land,
organizing the well-field system,
exempting people from corvée,
modeling on the "Fǔxíng,"
rectifying the horse laws,
restoring and honoring the customs of reverence, diligence, brilliance, virtue, and harmony,
broadening the paths for officials to lecture, study, advise, admonish, and recite,
the sound of egrets filling the court,
the ranks of swans and phoenixes gradually ascending the steps.
Causing the legacy of the former sages
to spread and flow without being concealed or stored away,
how lush and brilliant!
The affairs of Heaven and humanity flourished,
the expectations of spirits and ghosts were truly fulfilled.
All the lords and former worthies,
none failed to display proper decorum;
traitors, rebels, bandits, and thieves,
none failed to be awed by authority.
Continuing the lineage of Shǎodiǎn,
manifesting the descendants of Huángdì and Yú.
What was missing from the imperial codes has been supplemented,
what was slack in the royal governance has been tightened,
brilliant and glorious,
is this not excellent!
Those who were bathed in this transforming influence:
the capital deeply immersed,
the inner regions thoroughly permeated,
the outer marches diligently striving,
the remote borders cleansed and refreshed,
and following the ancient statutes,
inspecting the four classes of people,
reaching the four sacred mountains,
increasing the feng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
performing the shàn sacrifice at Liángfù,
this is the canonical work of those who receive the Mandate.
For those who receive the Mandate, the days are insufficient,
and even those who do not receive the Mandate
still have affairs to attend to.
How much more for the majestic and grand Xin,
rightly at its time,
the spirits of lofty mountains, still seas, and connecting rivers,
all set up altars and grounds,
hoping for the arrival of the Mandate.
Beyond the seas and distant lands,
sincerely crane their necks and stand on tiptoe;
turning their faces inward,
yearning eagerly.
Even if the emperor is diligent,
how can he cease?
It is fitting to command the wise and profound to compose one chapter of the Imperial Code,
combining the old three into one set,
to show to future people,
spreading it without end.
Let ten thousand generations always bear the lofty,
tread with trepidation,
smell the fragrance,
savor the sweet fruit,
mirror the purest essence,
hear the clear and harmonious proper sounds,
then all tasks will be accomplished,
and all achievements will be joyful.
Bearing the heavenly path,
holding the earthly order,
this is the highest rule of the world,
indeed, it may be tried!
Your subject Bān Gù states:
In the seventeenth year of the Yǒngpíng era,
your subject, along with Jiǎ Kuí, Fù Yì, Dù Jǔ, Zhǎn Lóng, Xī Méng, and others,
was summoned to the Yúnlóng Gate.
The junior eunuch Zhào Xuān, holding the Basic Annals of the First Emperor of Qín, asked us:
"In the concluding remarks by Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān,
is there perhaps something erroneous?"
Your subject replied:
"This conclusion quotes Jiǎ Yì's 'Guò Qín' essay, stating:
'If only Zǐ Yīng had possessed the talent of an average ruler,
and merely obtained moderate assistance,
the altars of state of Qín would not have been doomed to extinction.'
This statement is incorrect."
Thereupon, I was summoned to enter,
and was asked:
"Did you originally hear this argument as erroneous?
Or did you come to understand the meaning upon being questioned?"
Your subject fully replied, explaining the circumstances of what I had long known and heard.
The imperial edict then stated:
"Sīmǎ Qiān, in writing his work, established a school of thought of his own,
and spread his fame to later generations.
However, due to the circumstance of personally suffering corporal punishment,
he instead subtly used his writing to satirize and criticize,
belittling and disparaging his own era—
he was not a righteous scholar.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's conduct was defiled and without restraint;
he merely possessed ornate and superficial language,
not suited for practical use.
Yet, when approaching death due to illness, he left behind a loyal testament.
The sovereign sought and obtained his writings,
and ultimately they served to eulogize and recount virtuous achievements,
speaking of the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices—
this is the act of a loyal minister.
In this regard, he was far more worthy than Sīmǎ Qiān."
Your subject Bān Gù has often prostrated myself, engraving and reciting this sagely discourse.
It clarifies likes and dislikes,
not overlooking even the subtlest details,
judging righteousness based on events,
with every action having its rules and standards.
Even Confucius, who conveyed meaning through history,
could not surpass this.
Your subject Bān Gù, having received instruction for the longest time,
and having been favored with deep grace,
sincerely wishes to exhaust my strength and utmost feeling—
how boundless is the great Heaven!
Your subject Bān Gù kowtows repeatedly.
I humbly consider that Xiàngrú's piece on the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
though elaborate, lacks classical substance;
Yáng Xióng's 'Eulogy on the New Dynasty',
though classical in form, lacks truthfulness.
Yet both have been promoted and circulated among later generations,
handed down as established models.
Your subject Bān Gù's talent is decayed and inferior to that of former men.
Indeed, for those who chant the 'Yúnmén' melody, it is difficult to produce sound;
for those who view the Suí Hé jewels, it is difficult to perceive their preciousness.
Unable to bear my insignificance,
I have presumptuously composed a piece titled 'Diǎnyǐn'.
Although it is insufficient to convey even one ten-thousandth of the majestic brilliance,
it may yet stir and vent pent-up feelings,
enlighten the ignorant youth,
glorify and exalt the great Hàn,
surpass the reputation of former dynasties.
Thereafter, I may retreat into the ditches and gullies,
and die without decay.
Your subject Bān Gù is foolish and blunt,
kowtowing repeatedly,
and says:
In the origin of the Supreme Ultimate,
the Two Forms first separated.
Misty and vaporous,
some sank and became profound,
some floated and became clear.
Sinking and floating intermingled,
and the myriad categories were formed in chaos.
Then began the mandate for the people's ruler,
the Five Virtues commenced their cycles.
It was akin to the dawn of creation,
within the dark and undifferentiated chaos.
Transcending cords and passing beyond tallies,
silent and desolate, without edicts—
no lineage can be connected to it.
Only when clans and appellations existed,
continuing Heaven's work and elucidating its principles,
did none not commence their origin from the beginning of Tàihào's imperial era.
How lofty and distant it is!
Yet their records can still be compiled.
The generations following this,
though their transformations were spiritual and divine,
contained radiance that had not yet shone forth.
As for those who examined the patterns of Heaven above,
and received the mandate descending like a dragon's wings,
illuminating them in the canons and counsels,
to crown virtue as peerless and supreme—
none were more exalted than Yáo of Táng.
Yáo of Táng passed over his own descendants and abdicated to Shùn of Yú;
Shùn of Yú also charged the Hóu of Xià.
Jì and Xiè gloriously carried on the work,
down to Chéng Tāng and King Wǔ.
When the supporting ministers were complete,
Heaven then attributed the merit to the sovereign head,
and prepared to bestow it upon Liú of Hàn.
Causing him to inherit the desolate end of the three declining dynasties,
encountering the calamity of the dragon at its zenith,
when celestial signs were dim and constant patterns awry,
the constant principles ruined and the old statutes deficient.
Therefore, He first commanded the Mysterious Sage,
causing him to continue learning and establish institutions,
to amplify and make resplendent the great enterprise,
to manifest the likeness of the ancestors,
to praise and extol the enlightened wisdom,
so complete and splendid,
truly the model of divine intelligence.
Even the diligent assistance of Gāo, Kuí, Héng, and Dàn
was narrow compared to this.
Therefore, the two sagely emperors Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ
dwelt in their proper realms.
When the time arrived and the force moved,
then the dragon appeared from the deep and leaped.
Flapping its wings before soaring,
its majestic spirit was manifold.
Within the seas, clouds billowed,
thunder moved and lightning flashed.
The Hú hanged themselves and the Mǎng were divided,
yet they did not live to receive their punishment.
Thereafter, reverently complying with Heaven and Earth,
respectfully receiving the multitude of lords,
correctly positioning and measuring the ancestral temple,
there was the yielding due to virtue not matching the profound reverence,
without the display of summoning armies or brandishing weapons in urgent struggle.
It was because they received the legitimate succession ordained by Heaven,
accepted the destiny of yielding that returned to them,
accumulated the blazing essence of flame rising upward,
and contained the grand array of Confucius's support.
Vast and magnificent, such virtue—
the highest ceremony of emperors,
unreachable by proclamations and oaths.
Surveying the grand and minute measures of the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
their profundity can be fathomed.
Both commenced their traces from a single basket of earth,
both received the service of Hóu and Diǎn domains,
generation after generation diligently caring for the people,
ruling as overlords and shepherds.
Relying on the authority granted by the mandate—the vermilion bow and yellow axe—
they used them to chastise Wéi, Gù, Lí, and Chóng for their disrespect.
As for intermingling with the Huáxià,
moving the capital to Hào and Bó,
then turning to face north as subjects,
their armies like tigers and hornless dragons,
they overthrew and extinguished the heavenly capital.
Therefore, righteous scholars were ornate but not sincere,
military achievements were not fully proclaimed,
and the Protector had cause for shame in his virtue—
is this not so?
It is also like the solemn 'Wū Mù' and graceful 'Yī Nuó',
harmonious, pure, bright, and continuous,
used to honor and revere the ancestors.
The Yīn honored them by matching them with the Lord,
issuing auspiciousness and flowing down blessings,
facing and responding to Heaven and Earth—
resplendent for a thousand years.
How could they not be capable of divine intelligence themselves!
Great strategies have constancy,
examining words and deeds in the records,
their brilliant luster bright and unchanging.
How much more for the illustrious, majestic, and sagely Hàn,
with its lofty Táng-dynasty foundation!
Tracing and measuring its source,
it first nurtured Yú and reared Xià,
molded Yīn and formed Zhōu,
and then displayed the double brilliance of the two founders,
inheriting the accumulating brightness of the four honored ancestors.
Divine spirits shine like the sun,
illuminating the six directions of darkness.
Benevolent winds soar beyond the seas,
majestic spirits move in the regions of ghosts.
Nothing hidden turns away without being extinguished,
nothing subtle or trivial is not nurtured.
Therefore, the achievement of clearly establishing the Three Powers and gloriously ascending—
without Yáo, it would not have arisen;
the instruction of spreading the heard, bequeathed plans below—
without Hàn, its Way would not have been expanded.
As for weaving the warp and woof of Heaven and Earth,
entering and exiting with the Three Lights,
externally operating the Primal Chaos,
internally moistening the finest tip,
natures and categories following principle,
all beings and things attaining smoothness—
this has been so for a long time.
The historian remarks:
In the past, the Xuan Emperor of the Gaozu, with his great talent and profound capacity,
rose to office in response to the times.
At the beginning of the founding of the Wei dynasty by Emperor Taizu,
he planned military and state affairs,
and his excellent strategies were often successful.
Thus, he served in the imperial carriage,
serving diligently through three reigns.
His nature was deep and guarded, like a walled city,
yet he could be broad and tolerant,
acting with calculation to manage affairs,
and knowing how to recognize and select talent.
Therefore, both the wise and the foolish cherished him,
and all, great and small, exerted their strength.
Thus, he selected Dèng Ài from the farming off-season,
and promoted Zhōu Tài from military service,
entrusting them with civil and military duties,
each excelling in their tasks.
Hence, he was able to capture Mèng Dá in the west,
subdue Gōngsūn Yuān in the east,
pacify Cáo Shuǎng internally,
and attack Wáng Líng externally.
With divine strategy and independent decision-making,
he triumphed in all his campaigns.
He governed the various lords,
holding great power in his own hands.
He repeatedly repelled the disciplined troops of Zhūgě Liàng,
and weakened the mutual support of the Wu people in the east.
Shìzōng inherited the foundation,
and Tàizǔ continued the enterprise.
Though military campaigns were frequent,
the borders remained intact.
Thus, the people supported the capable,
and the great structure began to take shape.
When Xuán and Fēng caused internal disorder,
and Qīn and Dàn raided externally,
though their secret plots were well-concealed,
their schemes were inevitably revealed.
Though the Huáipǔ region was disturbed again,
Xǔ and Luò remained unshaken.
All aberrant plans were suppressed,
and the achievements of the predecessors were consolidated.
Then, they promoted Zhōng and Dèng,
and advanced swiftly into Yōng and Shǔ.
The three passes were swept through like lightning,
and Liú Shàn submitted as a subject.
Thus, the mandate of heaven and human affairs were in harmony.
This was indeed credible.
At first, he received extraordinary honors,
and in the end, he was granted complete ceremonial regalia.
His fame and authority surpassed those of the Duke of Zhōu,
and his control was stricter than that of Yī Yǐn.
As for Shìzǔ,
he eventually ascended to the imperial throne.
He assumed the correct position and embodied the proper form,
valuing words and being cautious with laws,
benevolent in treating his subjects,
and frugal to ensure sufficiency.
Harmonious yet not lax,
broad-minded yet decisive.
Thus, the people sang of renewal,
and all within the four seas rejoiced and were encouraged.
He cultivated the aspirations of his ancestors,
and sought to alleviate the sufferings of the warring states.
Though his close advisors differed,
and the ministers held divergent opinions,
he alone adopted Yáng Hù’s strategy,
following the good for the sake of the multitude.
Thus, by the end of the Xiánníng era,
he overruled the various opinions and relied on the decisions of Wáng and Dù.
Boats sailed through the Three Gorges,
and armored horses reached Guìyáng.
The campaign did not last long,
and Jiāng and Xiāng submitted.
The fortifications of Wú and Shǔ were leveled,
and the perilous passes of both regions were opened.
He restored the ancient domains of Táng and Yú,
and spread the calendar to the eight wildernesses.
In the Tàikāng era,
the world shared the same script,
and the same gauge for carts.
Oxen and horses covered the fields,
surplus grain lay in the paddies,
travelers lodged in grass huts,
and outer gates were left unbolted.
When people met, they treated each other as kin.
Those in need
could obtain provisions along the roads.
Thus, at that time, there was a saying that under heaven, no one was impoverished.
Though perfect peace was not yet fully achieved,
it was enough to show that officials upheld the laws,
and the people enjoyed their lives.
It was an era unmatched for a hundred generations.
After Emperor Wǔ had passed away,
before his tomb had even dried,
Yáng Jùn was executed,
the empress dowager was deposed,
and dozens of clans of court officials and old ministers were exterminated.
Soon, due to the upheaval involving the two dukes and the Prince of Chǔ,
the imperial clan lacked the support of a fortified city,
and the feud between Èbó and Shíchén was rekindled year after year;
the high ministers lacked the dignity of being looked up to,
and the disasters of downfall, slaughter, and humiliation occurred daily.
They even changed the Son of Heaven’s title to “Grand Emperor,”
yet there were rumors of his dismissal from office.
The people saw no virtue,
hearing only of chaos.
In the morning, they were praised as Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng,
by evening, they were reviled as Jié and Zhí.
Good and evil were judged by success or failure,
praise and blame were coerced by power and profit.
Thus, frivolous and unscrupulous men,
employing cunning and deceit to advance themselves,
rushed forward like moths to a flame.
Internal and external affairs became confused,
officials lost their competence,
names and realities were reversed and disordered,
and the great net of heaven came undone.
State governance repeatedly fell into the hands of troublemakers,
the imperial guards were scattered abroad to the four directions,
regional commanders lacked the strength of a thousand catties to maintain order,
and the passes and gates lacked even the flimsy defense of knotted grass.
Lǐ Chén and Shí Bīng
overturned Jīng and Yáng provinces;
Liú Yuān and Wáng Mí
disrupted Qīng and Jì provinces.
In little more than twenty years, the Hé and Luò regions became ruins.
The Róng and Jié tribes usurped imperial authority,
the two emperors lost their dignity,
and their tombs were left unattended.
Why was this?
Because authority was misplaced in its establishment,
entrusted to those without talent,
the four cardinal principles were not upheld,
and makeshift governance was rampant.
To establish laws amidst order,
their flaws may still lead to chaos;
to establish laws amidst chaos,
who can save it?
Thus, at that time, the empire was not temporarily weak,
nor were the armies unprepared.
That Liú Yuān
was merely a commandant of soldiers in Líshí;
Wáng Mí
was an insignificant clerk in Qīngzhōu.
They were but men skilled in archery and horsemanship,
drivers and runners,
men of ordinary talent,
without the abilities of the former ruler of Wú or Zhūgě Kǒngmíng.
They were newly risen bandits,
a motley crowd,
no match for the forces of Wú or Shǔ.
They cast aside plows to take up arms,
tore their garments to make banners,
yet lacked the instruments of warring states.
Rising from below to oppose those above,
they lacked the advantage of neighboring states.
Yet success and failure produced different results:
they threw the empire into turmoil as if driving a flock of sheep,
and seized the two capitals as easily as picking up lost items.
Generals, ministers, marquises, and kings
were beheaded in succession,
pleading to become slaves yet still not obtaining mercy.
Empresses, concubines, consorts, and princesses
were captured and humiliated by barbarian soldiers—
is this not lamentable!
The empire
is a great vessel;
the multitude of living beings
are a precious herd.
Love and hatred clash against each other,
benefit and harm contend with one another—
this is the constant tendency.
It is like accumulating water behind a dam,
or setting a prairie ablaze—
never truly at rest.
A great vessel cannot be governed by petty ways,
a dynamic situation cannot be disturbed by contention.
The wise kings of antiquity,
knowing this to be so,
thus warded off great calamities without claiming credit for themselves,
and resisted great disasters without appropriating the benefits.
The common people all knew that the ruler’s virtue gave them life,
yet did not say he drained them to sustain himself.
Therefore, they were moved and responded to him,
delighted and turned to him,
like morning breezes gathering in the northern woods,
or dragons and fish hastening to deep pools and marshes.
Complying with Heaven, they enjoyed its fortune;
responding to the people, they harmonized with their righteousness.
Only then did they establish rituals and culture to govern them,
enact punishments to awe them,
carefully distinguish between good and evil to show them,
clarify fortune and misfortune to enlighten them,
seek the clear-sighted to appoint as officials,
and deepen kindness and love to secure them.
Thus, the masses knew the proper direction,
all rejoiced in life and mourned death,
delighted in the teachings and were content with their customs.
The noble-minded diligently observed rites,
the common people exerted their strength,
integrity and shame were deeply rooted in households and alleys,
and wickedness and depravity vanished from hearts and minds.
Therefore, the people would face danger and sacrifice their lives,
rather than seek survival at the cost of righteousness.
How much less would they raise their arms and shout,
gathering to commit transgressions and stir rebellion?
A broad foundation is hard to topple,
deep roots are hard to uproot,
orderly principles prevent chaos,
and firm cohesion prevents dissolution.
This is why those of old who possessed the empire
endured for so long.
Were there no wayward rulers among them?
They relied on virtue, principles, and laws to maintain it.
Thus, Jìzǐ of Yánlíng could discern the fate of the feudal lords and the length of their reigns by listening to music,
for the sentiments of the people and the influence of customs
are the foundation of a state’s safety or peril.
In the rise of the Zhōu dynasty,
Hòujì was born of Jiāngyuán,
and the Mandate of Heaven shone brightly.
The achievements of King Wén and King Wǔ
originated from Hòujì.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"How wise was Hòujì,
able to match Heaven's will."
And also:
"He established our multitudes,
none but by your utmost virtue."
And also:
"Full-headed and plump-grained,
he settled in Tái with his household."
When Gōngliú encountered the turmoil of the Dí people,
he left Tái for Bīn,
personally enduring the toil.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"Then he packed dry provisions,
into bags and sacks."
"He ascended the ridges,
descended again to the plains,
to settle his people."
When Tàiwáng was pressured by the Róng and Dí,
