unable to bear the suffering of the common people,
he took his staff and departed.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"At dawn he galloped his horses,
leading along the western riverbank,
until he reached below Qí."
The people of Zhōu followed and thought of him,
saying:
"A benevolent man must not be lost,"
so they followed him as to a market.
After one year of settlement, a town formed;
after two years, a capital;
after three years, it grew fivefold from its start.
He constantly comforted and settled them.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"Then they were comforted, then they settled,
some to the left, some to the right,
they demarcated boundaries, they organized lands,
they opened channels, they plowed fields."
When it came to Wángjì,
he was able to spread his virtuous influence.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"Able to illuminate, able to classify,
able to lead, able to rule,
thus bestowing glory upon him."
When it came to King Wén,
he fully cultivated the ancient virtues,
and renewed the Mandate.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"This King Wén,
cautious and reverent,
brightly served the Lord on High,
thus securing abundant blessings."
From this we see
that the Zhōu house accumulated loyalty and kindness over generations,
their benevolence extended even to plants and trees,
internally harmonizing the nine clans,
externally revering and serving the elderly,
nurturing the aged and seeking their counsel,
thus achieving their fortune and prosperity.
Moreover, their consorts personally practiced the four teachings,
respected their instructors,
wore plain, washed garments,
attended to tedious and humble tasks,
transforming the world with wifely virtue.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"Setting an example for his wife,
extending to his brothers,
thus governing the family and state."
Thus, women by the Hàn River
maintained pure and chaste resolve;
scholars in the deep forests
possessed sincere and unified virtue.
Therefore it is said:
"From 'Tiānbǎo' onward, King Wén and King Wǔ governed internally;
from 'Cǎiwēi' onward, they governed externally,
beginning with diligence and concern,
ending in ease and joy."
When two-thirds of the world was under their sway,
they still served the Yīn dynasty,
eight hundred lords gathered without summons,
yet they still said the Mandate of Heaven had not arrived.
With the wisdom of three sages,
they attacked the tyrant Zhòu,
yet they justified it with proper teachings, saying:
"Taken by rebellion, held by righteousness,
preserving greatness, securing achievements,
pacifying the people, harmonizing the masses."
They still described the grandeur of the 'Great Martial' dance as
"not yet perfectly good."
When the Duke of Zhōu encountered turmoil,
he recounted the customs and transformations from Hòujì and the earlier lords,
and the hardships of establishing the royal enterprise,
all of which were matters of clothing and food for farmers and women workers.
Thus, from Hòujì's initial foundation of settling the people,
fifteen kings passed until King Wén began to pacify them,
sixteen kings until King Wǔ began to reside among them,
eighteen kings until King Kāng was able to secure peace.
Therefore, their accumulated foundation and rooted establishment,
weaving rituals and customs,
regulating human sentiments,
showing compassion for the people's hardships—
were so deeply intertwined.
Looking back to ancient times,
though refinement and substance differed with the era,
and achievements varied,
in their pacifying the people and establishing governance,
the principle was one and the same.
Now, the rise of the Jin dynasty,
its achievements surpassing those of a hundred kings,
its affairs more swiftly accomplished than in the Three Dynasties,
was indeed brought about by deliberate action.
Emperor Xuān and Emperor Jǐng encountered times of great turmoil,
devoting themselves to subduing heroes,
executing the many arrogant to facilitate their tasks,
without time to cultivate the benevolence of Gōngliú or Tàiwáng.
Receiving the legacy and assisting in governance,
they repeatedly faced depositions and appointments,
so that Prince Qí, lacking clarity,
did not gain the chance to contemplate governance in Bó;
the young Gāoguì,
could not restore the enlightened rule of the son;
the two ancestors were pressed by the timing of abdication and succession,
with no leisure to await the gathering of the eight hundred lords in threefold division.
Thus, their founding of the base and establishment of the foundation
differed from those of previous dynasties.
Moreover, the court lacked men of pure virtue,
and the countryside was wanting in elders of unwavering loyalty.
Customs were depraved and perverse,
shame and honor misplaced;
scholars took Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ as their masters,
while demoting the Six Classics;
debaters prized empty and shallow arguments as eloquence,
and disdained reputation and frugality;
those conducting themselves considered unrestrained dissipation as sophistication,
and belittled integrity and trustworthiness;
those seeking office regarded opportunistic gain as noble,
and despised upright conduct;
officials in power esteemed empty formalism as lofty,
and mocked diligence and conscientiousness.
Therefore, the Three Dukes were labeled with the epithet of “withered stumps,”
and high-level discussions were branded with the name of empty talk.
Liú Sòng repeatedly spoke on the way of governance,
Fù Xián constantly rectified the crooked and upright,
yet all were called vulgar officials.
Those who relied on empty vagueness,
and conformed without principle,
were all renowned throughout the land.
As for King Wén, who toiled from dawn to dusk with no time to eat,
or Zhòngshān Fǔ, who labored day and night without respite,
they were generally mocked and dismissed as dust,
and mutually scorned and criticized.
Thus, praise and blame became confused with the reality of good and evil,
and passions and vices raced along the path of material desires.
Selectors chose officials for personal favor,
and officials sought profit for themselves.
Those holding the reins of power and occupying pivotal positions
held multiple concurrent offices, numbering in the tens.
The highest positions were filled with the most esteemed,
while the lower ranks recorded the essentials,
yet failures in critical affairs
occurred eight or nine times out of ten.
The sons and younger brothers of powerful clans and noble relatives
advanced by leaps and bounds,
unrestrained by seniority or order.
In the swirling dust of the world,
all were men of striving and competition;
though officials numbered in the hundreds and thousands,
there was no practice of yielding to the worthy.
Zǐzhēn wrote “Chóng Ràng” (Exalting Yielding), yet none heeded it;
Zǐyǎ established the Nine Ranks system, but it was not implemented;
Chángyú repeatedly recorded truthfully, yet could not rectify matters.
As for the women, their hairdressing, weaving, and sewing
were all done by maids and servants;
they knew nothing of women’s work like silk and hemp spinning,
or the affairs of preparing wine and food in the household.
They married before the proper age,
and acted according to their whims,
so none felt shame for the faults of licentiousness and excess,
nor were restrained by the evils of jealousy and envy.
Some were disobedient to their parents-in-law,
some reversed the roles of firmness and gentleness,
some killed or harmed concubines,
some brought disorder to the hierarchy of superiors and inferiors,
yet fathers and brothers did not punish them,
and the world did not condemn them.
How much less could they be expected to heed the ancient four teachings,
or cultivate chastity and obedience in the present,
to assist their husbands!
Ritual, law, punishment, and governance
were thus greatly corrupted,
like a house built but with its joints removed,
like water accumulated but with its dikes breached,
like fire stored but with its fuel scattered.
When a state is about to perish,
its foundation must first crumble—
is this not what is meant here?
Thus, observing Ruǎn Jí’s conduct,
one realizes the reasons for the collapse of ritual and teaching;
examining the affairs of Yǔ Chún and Jiǎ Chōng,
one sees the many deviations of the high ministers.
Reviewing the achievement of pacifying Wú,
one knows the lack of deference among generals;
reflecting on Guō Qīn’s strategy,
one understands the vulnerabilities of the Róng and Dí.
Reading the words of Fù Xuán and Liú Yì,
one discerns the corruption of the hundred officials;
scrutinizing Fù Xián’s memorials
and the “Discourse on the God of Money,”
one witnesses the blatancy of favoritism and bribery.
With the people’s customs and the state’s situation as such,
even if governed by a ruler of moderate talent
who upheld established laws,
Xīn Yǒu would surely have foreseen it in the sacrifices,
Jì Zhá would have discerned it in the music,
Fàn Xiè would have pleaded to die for it,
and Jiǎ Yì would have wept bitterly over it.
How much more so when our Emperor Huì, with his lax virtue, presided over it!
Thus, Empress Jiǎ rampaged through the six palaces,
and Hán Wǔ abetted disorder within and without;
the origins of this were gradual,
how could it be attributed solely to the evil of one woman?
Emperor Huái inherited the throne after the turmoil,
but was constrained by powerful ministers.
Emperor Mǐn, after fleeing and wandering,
merely held the empty title.
The governance of the world
had already been lost,
and none but a hero of the age
could reclaim it.
Yet, in the early years of Emperor Huái’s reign,
auspicious grain grew in Nánchāng.
Those observing the ethers also said that Yùzhāng had the aura of a Son of Heaven.
When the state faced many difficulties,
and the imperial clan rose repeatedly,
despite the legitimacy of Mǐnhuái,
the strength of Huáinán,
the achievements of Chéngdū,
and the authority of Chángshā,
all ultimately ended in collapse.
Yet Emperor Huái, as Prince of Yùzhāng, ascended to the heavenly throne.
Liú Xiàng’s prophecy stated
that after the destruction,
one with a name resembling “water” would gain it,
the initiator would occupy Qínchuān,
and the southwest would find its ally.
Consider Emperor Mǐn—
he was the son of the Prince of Qín,
and gained the throne in Cháng’ān.
Cháng’ān
was indeed the land of Qín.
To the west, he appointed the Prince of Nányáng as Right Chancellor,
and to the east, the Prince of Lángyá as Left Chancellor.
The emperor’s personal name was Yè,
so Yè was changed to Línzhāng.
Zhāng is the name of a river.
From this, we may deduce
that there were also signs and portents,
yet the imperial standard was not upheld,
and calamity and disgrace reached his person.
Was it that the Lord on High looked upon us but wavered in His heart,
or that it is humans who can broaden the Way,
not the Way that broadens humans?
The blazing glory of virtue had not yet faded,
so the great mandate gathered again upon Emperor Yuán, the Middle Ancestor.
Regarding the systems of empresses and consorts above the Xia and Yin dynasties,
the records are sparse.
According to the Rites of Zhou,
the king establishes an empress,
three consorts (fūrén),
nine concubines (pín),
twenty-seven ladies of the household (shìfù),
and eighty-one female attendants (nǚyù),
to fulfill the inner palace duties.
The empress holds the correct position within the palace,
sharing status with the heavenly king.
The consorts sit and discuss women's rites,
the nine concubines oversee the teaching of the four virtues,
the ladies of the household primarily manage mourning,
sacrifices, and guests,
and the female attendants are arranged in the king's private resting quarters.
Offices were distributed and duties divided,
each with its own regulations and responsibilities.
Female historians with red-tube brushes recorded merits and wrote down faults.
In residence, there were the instructions of the governesses;
in movement, there was the sound of jade pendants.
They recommended worthy and talented individuals to assist the gentleman,
and pitied the graceful and modest without indulging in their beauty.
This is how they were able to propagate the hidden transformations,
cultivate and complete the inner rules,
so that the women's quarters were solemn and harmonious,
and improper requests did not occur.
Therefore, when King Kāng held court late,
the "Guān Jū" was composed as a remonstrance;
when Empress Xuǎn rose late,
Lady Jiāng requested to bear the fault.
By the time the Zhou house moved east,
the order of rites had decayed and become deficient.
The feudal lords overstepped and acted wantonly,
and regulations and systems lacked proper order.
Duke Huán of Qí had six women like consorts,
and Duke Xiàn of Jìn elevated a Rong woman to be his principal consort,
ultimately leading to the rebellion of the five sons
and calamity for the heir.
Reaching the Warring States period,
moral standards grew ever thinner,
following passions and indulging desires,
turning clothes upside down,
resulting in the destruction of states and loss of lives,
too many to count.
This was indeed due to轻视ing rites and relaxing defenses,
putting beauty before virtue.
When Qín unified the world,
it was mostly arrogant and grandiose,
its offices equipped from the seven states,
its ranks arranged in eight grades.
When Hàn arose,
it followed these titles,
yet the system for women was not set in order.
Emperor Gāozǔ did not maintain proper separation of curtains,
Emperor Wén made no distinction on the mat.
However, the selection and接纳 were still simple,
and adornments and luxuries were few.
From the time of Emperor Wǔ and Yuán onward,
each generation increased wasteful expenditures,
to the extent that the rear palaces had three thousand women,
with ranks increased to fourteen levels.
The signs of bewitching favorites ruining governance,
the traces of external relatives throwing the state into disorder—
previous histories have recorded these in detail.
By the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ's restoration,
carving was cut to return to simplicity.
Among the titles of the six palaces,
only the empress and the noble consort (guìrén) had gold seals with purple ribbons,
and their salaries did not exceed several tens of hu of grain.
Furthermore, three grades were established: beauties (měirén), palace women (gōngrén), and selected women (cǎinǚ),
none of whom held noble rank or salary,
receiving only seasonal gifts and provisions.
According to Hàn law, during the eighth month when the population was counted,
a grand master of the palace and a deputy of the rear palaces along with physiognomists
would inspect good-family maidens in the villages of Luòyáng,
those aged thirteen and above,
twenty and below,
of graceful appearance and upright beauty,
who matched the legal physiognomy,
were transported to the rear palace,
examined for suitability,
and then presented for the imperial favor.
This was to demonstrate care in betrothal and接纳,
and to seek out virtuous and wise women in detail.
Emperor Míng diligently followed the former intent,
and palace instruction was considerably cultivated.
When establishing concubines and empresses,
he always prioritized virtuous character.
Within, there were no words that went beyond the women's quarters;
in authority, there were no grants based on private favoritism.
This can be said to have corrected the abuses.
If, building on this, prohibitions concerning external relatives had been established,
compiled and recorded in the primary ordinances,
and the system of empresses and consorts reformed,
bequeathing it to future generations,
would it not have been excellent!
Although he governed himself with measure,
the precautions and restrictions were not steadfast,
so from Emperor Zhāng onward,
gradually beauty was used for granting favors,
affection flourished in fond union,
and thus the hidden corruption was forgotten.
Since ancient times, even when the ruler was young and times difficult,
and the royal house faced many troubles,
authority was entrusted to the chief minister,
seeking loyalty and steadfastness through selection,
never was there exclusive reliance on women
to decide and cut the vital vessels of state.
Only the Dowager Empress of Qín, Mǐ, began to administer government affairs,
so the Marquis of Ráng held greater power than King Zhāo,
and his family grew richer than the Yíng state.
Hàn perpetuated this error,
aware of the trouble but not reforming it.
In the Eastern Capital, the imperial line was repeatedly broken,
and authority fell to female rulers.
Four emperors were established from outside the line,
and six empresses administered court affairs.
None failed to determine policies within the curtains,
entrusting affairs to their fathers and brothers,
coveting child rulers to prolong their rule,
suppressing the wise and worthy to monopolize their authority.
The burden was heavy and the road long;
the profit deep and disaster swift.
Their persons encountered dew and mist upon the Cloud Terrace,
their families were bound by fetters within prison walls below.
Destruction followed closely one upon another,
overturned carriages continued along the road.
Yet they rushed forward without cease,
until scorched and ruined became their end,
finally leading to the decline of the great fortune,
and the fall and loss of the divine treasure.
What the Book of Songs and Documents lament
is roughly of the same principle.
Therefore, examining and arraying their deeds and traces,
I have made the Basic Annals of Empresses.
Although their successes and failures differ,
those who shared the correct title in their time
are all arrayed together in this chapter.
Those who were posthumously honored due to personal favor,
not those revered in their own time,
are then attached and mentioned along with other events.
Matters concerning their relatives separately
each follow their biographies.
For the rest who are not seen elsewhere,
they are connected to this basic annals,
to continue the "Accounts of the External Relatives" of the Western Capital.
Discussion says:
The twenty-eight generals of the restoration,
previous generations considered them to correspond above to the twenty-eight constellations,
but the details of this are unknown.
Yet they all were able to sense and meet the winds and clouds,
exerting their wisdom and courage,
called assistants to the Mandate,
and each was also a man of will and ability.
From the reign of Emperor Ming onward,
up to the Yánpíng era,
the employment of eunuchs gradually expanded,
and their authority steadily increased.
The number of Zhōngchángshì reached ten,
and Xiǎohuángmén also numbered twenty.
Their headgear was changed to gold dang ornaments with right-side sable tails,
and they concurrently held offices of the various ministries.
When Empress Dèng governed as a female ruler,
state affairs were numerous and far-reaching.
Court ministers deliberated on policies,
but had no means to participate in decision-making within the inner chambers;
issuing decrees and commands
did not extend beyond the confines of the palace apartments.
Thus, she had no choice but to rely on castrated men,
entrusting them with the fate of the state.
They held royal titles in their hands,
and imperial decrees issued from their mouths.
They were no longer confined to duties within the palace courtyards and long lanes,
nor to responsibilities of the inner chambers and women's quarters.
Later, Sūn Chéng secured the achievement of establishing Emperor Shùn,
and Cáo Téng participated in the strategy of establishing Emperor Huán.
Subsequently, the Five Marquises conspired together,
and Liáng Jì received the battle-axe of command.
Their actions were based on public justice,
and their favor was firmly rooted in the ruler's heart.
Therefore, both inside and outside the court, people submitted,
and high and low held their breath in fear.
Some were praised for merits like Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng,
not inferior to those of past records;
some were said to possess the strategies of Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng,
revived in the present age.
Although there were occasionally loyal and public-spirited officials,
they were invariably rejected and excluded.
Their every move could shift mountains and seas,
their every breath could change frost and dew.
Those who flattered their wishes and sought favor through crooked means
saw glory bestowed upon their three clans;
those who were upright and offended their intentions
faced the extermination of their five lineages.
The laws and order of the Hàn dynasty were thrown into great chaos.
As for those wearing tall hats and long swords,
draped in vermilion and bearing gold seals,
they filled the palace gates;
those enfeoffed with lands and granted tiger tallies,
facing south as rulers over subjects,
numbered in the tens.
Their mansions, offices, and residences
lined the foundations of both the capital and the countryside;
their sons, brothers, and attached followers
exceeded half the population of the provinces and states.
Accumulations of southern gold,
Héshì jade,
ice-like silk gauze,
and mist-like crepe
overflowed their treasuries;
the amusements of beautiful concubines,
maidservants,
singing boys,
and dancing girls
filled their ornate chambers.
Dogs and horses were adorned with carved patterns,
buildings and earthworks were covered with embroidered silk.
All these were carved from the flesh of the common people,
as they vied to indulge their extravagant desires.
They framed and harmed wise and virtuous men,
exclusively fostering their own factions.
Those who sought mutual support and recommendation,
hoping to attach themselves to the powerful,
all castrated themselves or had their sons castrated,
in order to boast and advance themselves.
Sharing the same corruption, they aided one another,
so their followers multiplied.
The affairs of ruining the state and corroding governance
cannot be fully recorded.
Therefore, throughout the land, people sighed in bitterness,
and men of purpose dwelt in impoverished seclusion.
Bandits and rebels arose from the gaps,
shaking and throwing the central region into chaos.
Although loyal and good men harbored indignation,
and sometimes stirred with fervor,
as soon as they spoke, disaster followed,
and they were quickly executed along with their families.
Consequently, there were again great investigations of factions,
with accusations spreading and contaminating one another.
All who were called good scholars
could not avoid suffering calamity and poison.
Dòu Wǔ and Hé Jìn,
holding lofty positions as close relatives of the emperor,
riding on the seething resentment of the nine regions,
and aligning with the strength of the multitude of heroes,
yet hesitated and remained indecisive,
leading to their utter defeat.
Was this not the extreme of fortune?
Although Yuán Shào acted righteously,
and mowed them down without remnant,
yet replacing violence with disorder—
what can be said of that?
Ever since Cáo Téng persuaded Liáng Jì,
ultimately establishing a foolish and weak ruler,
Cáo Cāo followed this precedent,
and thus transferred the imperial cauldron.
As the saying goes,
"As one begins with this,
so must one end with this."
Truly, it is so!
The Yìjīng says,
"Great indeed is the meaning of the time of retreat."
It also says:
"They do not serve kings and marquises,
but hold their affairs in high esteem."
Therefore, Yáo was praised as modeling himself on Heaven,
yet he did not compel the recluses of Yǐngyáng to bend;
King Wǔ achieved perfect beauty,
but ultimately preserved the purity of the men of Gūzhú.
From that time onward,
such refined customs became ever more abundant.
The tracks of those who withdrew for good were not the same,
yet the reasons that moved them were not uniform.
Some lived in seclusion to fulfill their aspirations,
some withdrew to preserve their Way,
some calmed themselves to restrain their restlessness,
some left danger to seek safety,
some defied vulgar customs to stir their integrity,
some criticized worldly things to stimulate their purity.
Yet observing them content in the fields and paddies,
or haggard upon rivers and lakes—
was it necessarily that they delighted in fish, birds, forests, and grasses?
It was also simply due to their inherent nature.
Therefore, guests who endured disgrace
were repeatedly dismissed but did not leave their state;
the integrity of those who would leap into the sea
could not be moved by a thousand chariots.
If one were to forcibly change their choices of advance or withdrawal,
then they could not act for one another.
Although they may seem stubborn, akin to those who fish for fame,
yet they shed their mortal coils amidst the clamor and dust,
placing themselves beyond the bounds of the mundane world—
are they not different from those who adorn themselves with cunning wisdom to chase floating profits?
Xúnzǐ once said,
"When will and purpose are cultivated, one slights wealth and honor;
when the Way and righteousness are valued, one despises kings and lords."
When the Hàn house declined midway,
and Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
the righteous indignation stored up among the scholars was extreme.
At that time, those who tore their caps and destroyed their ceremonial crowns,
supporting each other as they departed,
were too numerous to count.
Yáng Xióng said:
"The wild goose flies into the vast darkness;
how can the archer snare it?"
This speaks of their distance from harm.
Emperor Guāngwǔ anxiously awaited recluses,
seeking them as if he could not catch up.
Those summoned with silken banners and moxa-cushioned carriages
were seen everywhere among the cliffs and caves.
For instance, Xuē Fāng and Péng Méng were invited but refused to come;
Yán Guāng, Zhōu Dǎng, and Wáng Bà came but could not be subjugated.
All quarters were thus satisfied,
and men of purpose cherished benevolence.
Was this not what is called: "Raise up the recluses, and the hearts of all under Heaven turn to you"?
Emperor Sùzōng also honored Zhèng Jūn and summoned Gāo Fèng,
thereby completing their integrity.
Afterward, the imperial virtue gradually declined,
and wicked villains held sway at court.
Men of integrity,
placed alongside ministers and chancellors,
often voiced their fierce indignation without regard,
and many failed to maintain the Mean in their conduct.
Therefore, recording those whose dust could not be overtaken,
and who share the purpose of the authors,
they are listed in this chapter.
The historian remarks:
The people receive the numinous essence of Heaven and Earth,
and contain the virtues of the Five Constants.
Hardness and softness are used alternately,
joy and anger differentiate emotions.
When intent stirs within,
then song and chant issue forth outwardly.
This is the basis of the Six Principles,
and what the Four Beginnings depend upon.
The rise and fall of odes and ballads,
the profusion of airs and hymns.
Although from before the times of Yú and Xià,
no surviving texts are seen,
the endowment of vital breath and harboring of numinous spirit—
in principle, there may be no difference.
Thus, the rise of song and chant
should indeed begin with the birth of the people.
After the Zhōu dynasty declined,
its literary influence grew even more prominent.
Qū Píng and Sòng Yù pioneered the pure source in earlier times,
while Jiǎ Yì and Xiàng Rú carried forward the fragrant legacy in later generations.
Their splendid words adorned metal and stone,
their lofty principles reached the clouds and heavens.
From this point onward,
the scope of emotion and intent expanded further.
Figures such as Wáng Bāo, Liú Xiàng, Yáng Xióng, Bān Gù, Cuī Yuán, and Cài Yōng,
though following different paths, raced forward together,
successively learning from and emulating their predecessors.
Although clear phrases and beautiful melodies
occasionally emerged in their writings,
yet redundant sounds and cumbersome energy
were indeed plentiful.
As for Zhāng Héng (Zǐ Píng), whose brilliance flourished,
his writing transformed according to emotion,
his supreme songs and lofty traces
long lacked successors.
By the time of the Jiàn'ān era,
the Cáo family laid the foundation of mandate,
the Three Ancestors and Prince Chén,
all amassed rich literary elegance,
then began to weave emotion into literature,
and adorn substance with literary form.
From the Hàn to the Wèi dynasty,
over four hundred years,
the poets and talented writers
underwent three transformations in literary style.
Xiàng Rú excelled at descriptive language,
the two Bāns were adept at discourses on reason and emotion,
Cáo Zhí (Zǐjiàn) and Wáng Càn (Zhòngxuān) took personal vitality as their substance,
each showcasing their abilities and mastering beauty,
shining uniquely in their time.
Thus, the scholars of an era
each admired and learned from one another,
tracing the origins of their trends and currents,
none did not take the *Fēng* and *Sāo* as their common ancestors.
Merely due to differing tastes and preferences,
their ideas and compositions diverged.
Descending to the Yuánkāng era,
Pān Yuè and Lù Jī were exceptionally outstanding,
their prosody differed from Bān Gù and Jiǎ Yì,
their style transformed from Cáo Zhí and Wáng Càn,
their ornate meanings dense as stars,
their elaborate texts intricately woven.
They continued the lingering echoes of the Píngtái,
gathered the lofty tones of Nánpí,
the remaining influence and enduring achievements
reached their peak in the region south of the Yangtze.
During the Eastern Jìn restoration,
the Mystical Learning (Xuánxué) wind blew uniquely strong,
scholarship was exhausted within the *Lǎozǐ* (under the pillar),
and broad knowledge stopped at the *Zhuāngzǐ* (seven chapters).
Galloping through literary expression,
meaning was exhausted therein.
From the Jiànwǔ era up to the Yìxī era,
nearly a hundred years passed,
although echoes were paired and phrases linked,
waves connected and clouds gathered,
none failed to lodge words in Supreme Virtue,
entrust meaning to the Mystical Pearl,
forceful and beautiful phrases
were unheard of.
Yīn Zhòngwén began to change the style of Sūn Chuò and Xǔ Xún,
Xiè Hùn (Shūyuán) greatly transformed the spirit of the Tàiyuán era.
Then reaching the Liú Sòng dynasty,
Yán Yánzhī and Xiè Língyùn soared in reputation,
Xiè Língyùn's inspired compositions rose high,
Yán Yánzhī's stylistic structure was clear and precise,
both ran parallel to the outstanding predecessors,
setting examples for later generations.
As for spreading the lapels and discussing thoughts,
deliberating on past literary works,
the principles of skill and clumsiness,
there may be something to say.
Now, the five colors enhance each other,
the eight tones harmonize smoothly,
through the mysteries of dark, yellow, and the pitch-pipes,
each suits its object appropriately.
One must make the *gōng* and *yǔ* notes alternate,
high and low vary in rhythm,
if there are floating sounds in front,
then behind must be solid echoes.
Within a single line,
the sounds and rhymes are entirely different;
between two lines,
the light and heavy are all distinct.
Only by profoundly understanding this principle
can one begin to speak of literature.
As for the fine compositions of earlier masters,
praised as lofty and long admired,
Cáo Zhí's work on Hánguān,
Wáng Càn's piece on the Bà riverbank,
Sūn Chǔ (Zǐjīng)'s chapter on drizzling rain,
Wáng Zàn (Zhèngcháng)'s line on the northern wind,
all directly expressed heartfelt emotions,
not relying on poetry or history,
precisely because their tonal patterns and rhymes were regulated,
they surpassed previous models.
Since Qū Yuán (Língjūn) onwards,
many ages have passed,
although literary style gradually refined,
this secret remained unseen.
As for lofty words and wonderful lines,
with sounds and rhymes naturally formed,
they all unknowingly conformed to principle,
not achieved through deliberate thought.
Zhāng Héng, Cài Yōng, Cáo Zhí, Wáng Càn,
never had prior awareness;
Pān Yuè, Lù Jī, Yán Yánzhī, Xiè Língyùn,
were even farther from it.
Those in the world who understand tones,
have a way to grasp it,
these words are not false.
If you say it is not so,
please await future sages.
Now, the terms gentleman and petty man
are general classifications for types of people.
Treading the Way makes one a gentleman,
deviating from it makes one a petty man.
Butchering and fishing
are lowly occupations;
plank-pounding and wall-building
are humble labors.
Yet Lǚ Shàng (Tàigōng) rose to become the teacher of Zhōu,
Fù Yuè left to become the minister of Yīn.
They were not discussed based on generations of dukes and marquises,
or qualifications for tripod feasts,
but whether obscure and lowly,
only talent was given.
Reaching the two Hàn dynasties,
this principle was not abandoned,
Hú Guǎng came from generations of farmers,
yet Bóshǐ attained the position of duke and minister;
Huáng Xiàn was the son of an ox doctor,
yet Shūdù's fame stirred the capital.
Moreover, scholars serving at court
all had their duties and responsibilities,
although seven generations wore sable-tail ornaments,
esteemed in the Western Hàn,
yet the Palace Attendant personally presented memorials,
and also separately managed imperial garments;
Dōngfāng Shuò served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
holding a halberd below the palace hall.
Commandery and county clerks
all came from powerful families;
bearing spears and guarding the palace
were all from influential clans—
unlike later generations where they were divided into two separate paths.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, chaos and collapse ensued.
Wèi Wǔ (Cáo Cāo) laid the foundation,
and amid the urgency of military affairs,
he provisionally established the Nine Ranks system,
intending to assess the merits and shortcomings of talents,
not to distinguish between noble and humble lineages.
Thus, it was passed down,
and eventually became an established law.
From Wèi to Jìn,
none could change it.
Provincial and commandery officials
evaluated people based on talent and rank,
yet throughout the realm,
there were few promotions or demotions of talent.
Merely relying on hereditary status,
they overpowered one another.
Common officials,
considering the exigencies of the times,
adjusted the number and categories of ranks,
adapting to circumstances.
As Liú Yì said, "There are no high-born among the lower ranks,
and no low-born among the upper ranks."
As time passed and errors accumulated,
this practice gradually intensified.
All those of official robes and caps
were invariably of the second rank,
while those below
became commoners.
The ways of Zhōu and Hàn
used the wise to govern the foolish,
with distinctions between officials and servants,
forming a hierarchy.
Since Wèi and Jìn,
the noble have governed the humble,
and the distinction between scholars and commoners
has become clearly defined.
The ruler faces south,
ensconced in the deep recesses of the ninefold gates,
attended morning and night
by those separated by duty from the high ministers.
The responsibilities at the steps and gates
should be managed by officials.
Yet, familiarity breeds favor,
and trust is solidified through favor.
Without an awe-inspiring demeanor,
they assume an easily approachable appearance.
From the Xiàojiàn to Tàishǐ eras,
imperial authority was exercised alone,
leaving the hundred offices empty,
with no delegation of power outward.
Yet, punishments and governance became entangled,
making it difficult to comprehensively manage.
Thus, the ruler's eyes and ears
were entrusted to close attendants.
The essence of rewards and punishments,
which constitutes state authority,
the issuance and reception of royal commands,
fell into their grasp.
Thus, paths converged,
and spokes gathered, rushing together.
The ruler thought them lowly and insignificant,
believing they could not wield heavy power.
He did not realize that rats rely on the altar for prestige,
and foxes borrow the tiger's might.
Outwardly, there was no suspicion of oppressing the ruler,
while inwardly, they monopolized influence.
Their power tilted the realm,
yet none came to realize it.
Forming cliques and fostering factions,
governance was achieved through bribery.
Executions and wounds
were orchestrated in the privacy of bedchambers,
while donning crowns and riding chariots
emerged from beneath words and laughter.
Southern gold and northern furs
arrived fully laden on ships,
plain silks and cinnabar gems
came in double loads.
The Xǔ and Shǐ of Western Capital
could hardly compare,
and the Wáng and Shí of the Jìn court
were perhaps unmatched.
By Tàizōng's late reign,
contemplating the vicissitudes of prosperity and decline,
those in power and favor
feared the imperial relatives,
wishing to isolate the young ruler
and permanently usurp state authority.
They fabricated divisions,
sowing discord and strife.
Imperial brothers and princes
were successively slaughtered.
The people forgot the virtue of Sòng,
though not for a single reason;
the early collapse of the precious throne
was truly due to this.
Alas!
The Hànshū contains a "Table of Enfeoffed by Grace"
and a "Biography of Sycophants."
Now, I gather their names
and compile them into the "Chapter on the Favored and Fortunate."
Great indeed was Hàn's founder,
continuing Yáo's legacy.
Truly heaven-endowed with virtue,
wise, divine, and martial.
The Qín people lacked order,
their net letting Chǔ slip through.
From this, he rose to prominence,
slaying the serpent and rallying troops.
A divine mother foretold the sign,
and the vermilion banner was raised.
He marched into Qín's suburbs,
and Yīng came bowing in submission.
Revolutionizing and establishing institutions,
the Three Articles were the guidelines.
Answering heaven and顺应 the people,
the five stars aligned in the same orbit.
Xiàng rebelled and turned traitorous,
expelling us to Bā and Hàn.
The western lands found solace in him,
and warriors seethed with resentment.
Seizing the opportunity, he advanced,
sweeping through the Three Qín.
Dividing and holding rivers and mountains,
he protected and cherished the people.
His right-hand men, Xiāo and Cáo,
managed the state's affairs.
His claws and teeth, Xìn and Bù,
and his trusted advisors, Liáng and Píng,
carried out heaven's punishment,
majestic and brilliant.
Xiàochéng, resplendent and grand,
presided over court with radiance.
The splendor of his dignified bearing
was like jade tablets and scepters.
Yet, within the palace, Zhào held sway,
and court governance lay with Wáng.
A blazing wildfire,
its light unable to shine brightly.
Xìn was but a starving servant,
Bù indeed a tattooed convict.
Yuè was also a dog thief,
Ruì governed rivers and lakes.
Clouds arose and dragons soared,
transforming into marquises and kings.
They partitioned Qí and Chǔ,
and controlled Huái and Liáng.
Wǎn, from the same lane,
guarded our northern frontier.
Virtue thin, position lofty,
not fortune but calamity.
Wú upheld loyalty and trust,
thus his lineage endured long.
Eulogy says:
The flame of governance waned midway,
and great thieves shifted the state.
Nine regions whirled in turmoil,
three luminaries fogged and blocked.
The people wearied of excess and deceit,
and divine thought turned back to virtue.
Shìzǔ received the mandate,
divine favor self-revealed.
With profound strategy anticipating events,
deep plans woven with civility.
Xúnyì's million troops,
with panthers and tigers as their ranks.
Long chariots thundered across the plains,
high banners swept the clouds.
Once heroic might was stirred,
Xīndū burned itself.
Slaughtering Yōng and Dài,
chaos in Liáng and Zhào.
The Three Rivers not yet clear,
the Four Passes again disturbed.
The divine banner then turned,
progressively executing heaven's chastisement.
Metal walls and boiling moats lost their peril,
chariots and scripts shared the way.
Divine blessings now opened,
human plans all praised.
Brilliant were the temple's strategies,
valiant the heroic decisions.
Oh, glorious was the mandate,
linking to our imperial Hàn.
Duke Xiào of Qín, relying on the strategic strength of Xiáo and Hángu Passes,
held the territory of Yōngzhōu,
where ruler and ministers firmly guarded it,
gazing covetously upon the royal house of Zhōu,
with the intent to roll up the world like a mat,
to encompass all within the universe,
to gather the four seas into a bag,
and the heart to swallow up all the eight directions.
At that time,
Lord Shāng assisted him,
internally establishing laws and regulations,
devoting efforts to farming and weaving,
repairing instruments for defense and warfare,
and externally practicing the Horizontal Alliance to set the feudal lords against each other.
Thereupon, the people of Qín effortlessly took the lands west of the Hé River.
After Duke Xiáo passed away,
Dukes Huì, Wén, and Zhāo,
inheriting the former enterprise,
following the bequeathed strategies,
took Hànzhōng in the south,
seized Bā and Shǔ in the west,
cut off fertile lands in the east,
and acquired crucial commanderies.
The feudal lords grew fearful,
forming alliances and plotting to weaken Qín,
not sparing precious vessels, valuable treasures, or rich lands,
to attract the talents of the world,
forming the Vertical Alliance and establishing ties,
uniting as one.
At this time,
Qí had Mèngcháng,
Zhào had Píngyuán,
Chǔ had Chūnshēn,
and Wèi had Xìnlíng;
these four lords,
all wise, discerning, loyal, and trustworthy,
generous, kind, and caring for the people,
honoring the worthy and esteeming scholars,
joined the Vertical Alliance and disrupted the Horizontal,
uniting the masses of Hán, Wèi, Yān, Zhào, Sòng, Wèi, and Zhōngshān.
Thus, the scholars of the six states,
with the likes of Nìng Yuè, Xú Shàng, Sū Qín, and Dù Hè devising plans for them,
Qí Míng, Zhōu Zuì, Chén Zhěn, Shào Gǔ, Lóu Huǎn, Zhái Jǐng, Sū Lì, and Yuè Yì conveying their intentions,
and Wú Qǐ, Sūn Bìn, Dài Tuó, Ní Liáng, Wáng Liáo, Tián Jì, Lián Pō, and Zhào Shē commanding their troops,
once with ten times the territory,
a million-strong multitude,
knocked at the pass and attacked Qín.
The people of Qín opened the pass and lured the enemy in,
and the armies of the nine states fled, not daring to advance.
Qín expended not a single arrow or lost a single arrowhead,
yet the feudal lords of the world were already exhausted.
Thereupon, the Vertical Alliance disbanded and the covenants dissolved,
and they vied to cede lands to bribe Qín.
Qín, with strength to spare, exploited their weakness,
pursuing the fleeing and routing,
leaving a million corpses fallen,
blood flowing enough to float shields.
Seizing advantage and convenience,
they carved up the world,
split apart rivers and mountains,
so that strong states begged to submit,
and weak states came to court.
Extending to King Xiàowén and King Zhuāngxiāng,
their reigns were brief,
and the state saw no major events.
When it reached the First Emperor,
he stirred the accumulated might of six generations,
brandished a long whip to drive the universe,
swallowed the two Zhōu and extinguished the feudal lords,
ascended the supreme position and controlled the six directions,
wielding clubs and whips to lash the world,
his might shaking the four seas.
He took the lands of Bǎiyuè in the south,
establishing them as Guìlín and Xiàng commanderies.
The lords of Bǎiyuè,
bowed their heads and tied ropes around their necks,
entrusting their lives to lowly officials.
Then he sent Méng Tián north to build the Great Wall and guard the barriers,
repelling the Xiōngnú over seven hundred lǐ,
so that the Hú people dared not come south to pasture their horses,
and warriors dared not bend their bows to seek revenge.
Thereupon, he abolished the ways of the former kings,
burned the writings of the hundred schools,
to stupefy the black-headed people.
He destroyed famous cities,
killed the outstanding and heroic,
collected all the weapons of the world and gathered them in Xiányáng,
melted down the spearheads and arrowheads to cast twelve metal men,
to weaken the people of the world.
Then he trod Mount Huà as a wall,
used the Hé River as a moat,
relying on a wall ten thousand fathoms high,
facing unfathomable gorges as his stronghold;
with excellent generals and powerful crossbows,
guarding crucial points,
and trusted ministers and elite troops,
displaying sharp weapons to challenge any who approached?
The world already settled,
the First Emperor’s mind,
believed that the strength of Guānzhōng,
a thousand lǐ of metal walls,
would be an imperial enterprise for his sons and grandsons,
lasting ten thousand generations.
After the First Emperor passed away,
his remaining might still shook distant customs.
Yet Chén Shè,
a son of broken jars and rope-hinged doors,
a man of the peasantry and bondsmen,
and one of those conscripted for forced labor,
whose ability did not reach the average,
who lacked the worthiness of Zhòngní or Mò Dí,
or the wealth of Táo Zhū or Yī Dùn,
stepping among the ranks of soldiers,
rising from the fields and paths,
leading weary and scattered troops,
commanding a few hundred men,
turned to attack Qín,
cutting trees for weapons,
raising poles as banners,
the world gathering like clouds and responding like an echo,
carrying provisions and following like shadows,
the heroes east of the mountains,
then rose together and destroyed the Qín clan.
Moreover, the world was not small or weak,
the territory of Yōngzhōu,
the strength of Xiáo and Hángu remained as before.
Chén Shè’s position,
was not more exalted than the lords of Qí, Chǔ, Yān, Zhào, Hán, Wèi, Sòng, Wèi, and Zhōngshān;
his hoes, mallets, and thornwood spears,
were not sharper than hooked halberds or long lances;
the multitude of conscripted garrison troops,
were not a match for the armies of the nine states;
in deep plans and far-reaching schemes,
the ways of marching armies and employing troops,
he did not equal the scholars of former times.
Yet success and failure changed differently,
achievements and enterprises turned opposite.
If one were to try comparing the states east of the mountains with Chén Shè in length and size,
measuring authority and weighing strength,
then they could not be spoken of in the same breath.
Yet Qín, with its modest territory,
attained the authority of ten thousand chariots,
summoned the eight provinces and made its peers pay court,
for over a hundred years.
Xiáo and Hángu its palace,
one man raising trouble caused the seven ancestral temples to be destroyed,
he himself died at the hands of others,
becoming the laughingstock of the world—
why is this?
Because they did not practice benevolence and righteousness,
and the circumstances of attack and defense had changed.
Feiyǒu Xiānshēng served in the state of Wú,
yet in advancing, he could not cite antiquity to broaden his lord’s vision,
and in retreating, he could not extol his lord’s virtues to manifest his achievements.
For three years, he remained silent and spoke not a word.
The King of Wú, finding this strange, asked him:
“I have inherited the merits of my ancestors,
and am placed above the multitude of worthies.
Rising early and retiring late,
I have never dared to be negligent.
Now you, sir, came forth loftily,
traveling far to gather in the land of Wú,
intending to assist in governing me.
Truly, I privately admire this.
My body finds no rest upon the mat,
my food has no flavor,
my eyes do not gaze upon seductive beauty,
my ears do not listen to the sounds of bells and drums.
With an open mind and a settled will,
for three years now I have wished to hear your flowing counsel.
Yet now, in advancing, you do nothing to assist in governance;
in retreating, you do not extol your lord’s reputation.
I privately consider this unworthy of you, sir.
For to harbor ability and not reveal it—
this is disloyalty;
to reveal it and not act upon it—
this is the lord’s lack of clarity.
Is it perhaps that I am indeed lacking in clarity?”
Feiyǒu Xiānshēng bowed low and murmured assent.
The King of Wú said:
“You may speak now.
I shall compose my thoughts and listen.”
The master said:
“Alas!
Is it permissible?
Is it permissible?
How difficult it is to speak!
For speech may offend the eyes and grate upon the ears,
be contrary to the heart yet convenient for the body;
or it may please the eyes,
soothe the ears,
gladden the heart, yet ruin conduct.
If there is no enlightened king or sage ruler,
who can listen to it?”
The King of Wú said:
“Why should it be so?
‘Those of middling ability and above may be spoken to of higher things.’
Try speaking, sir,
and I shall consider it.”
The master replied:
“In the past, Guān Lóngpéng remonstrated deeply with Jié,
and Prince Bǐgān spoke directly to Zhòu.
These two ministers
both exhausted their thoughts and devoted their loyalty,
grieving that their lord’s grace did not flow downward,
and that the myriad people were in turmoil.
Therefore, they spoke directly of their faults
and admonished earnestly against their wickedness,
intending to bring honor to their lord
and remove calamity from their ruler.
But now it is not so.
Instead, it is considered slandering the lord’s conduct,
lacking the propriety of a minister.
Indeed, they were grievously wounded in body,
bore the name of the innocent,
their punishment extended to their ancestors,
and they became the laughingstock of the world.
Therefore, I say: How difficult it is to speak!
Thus, ministers of support and correction disintegrated,
and wicked, flattering men advanced together,
reaching even Fēilián
and Èláigé and others.
These three men were all deceitful and false,
skilled in speech and sharp of tongue,
using these to advance themselves.
Secretly, they served the lord’s fondness for carving and engraving,
to win his heart.
They strove to gratify the desires of eyes and ears,
taking temporary accommodation as their measure.
Thus they proceeded without caution,
met their end and were slain,
the ancestral temples collapsed and fell into ruin,
the state became a wasteland,
worthy ministers were slaughtered,
and slanderers were drawn close.
Does the Book of Songs not say?
‘Slanderers know no bounds,
they throw the four quarters into chaos.’
This refers to such cases.
Therefore, to humble one’s body and demean one’s form,
with pleasing countenance and subtle words,
smiling and coaxing—
in the end, it brings no benefit to the governance of the ruler above.
This is what men of purpose and benevolence cannot bear to do.
If one were to assume a stern and solemn demeanor,
speak profoundly and remonstrate directly,
above, to correct the ruler’s wickedness,
below, to reduce the harm to the common people,
then one would offend the heart of a wicked ruler
and encounter the laws of a declining age.
Therefore, men who cherish longevity are unwilling to advance.
They dwell in the depths of remote mountains,
piling earth to make chambers,
weaving reeds for doors,
playing the zither within,
singing of the ways of the ancient kings—
here, too, one may find joy and forget death.
Thus, Bóyí and Shūqí avoided Zhōu,
starving at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain.
Later generations praise their benevolence.
Thus,
the conduct of a wicked ruler is truly enough to inspire fear.
Therefore, I say: How difficult it is to speak!”
Thereupon, the King of Wú, startled, changed his expression,
cast aside his mat and removed his armrest,
and sat upright to listen.
The master said:
“Jiéyú avoided the world,
Jīzǐ let down his hair and feigned madness.
These two men
both avoided a turbid age to preserve their persons.
Had they encountered an enlightened king or sage ruler,
and been granted the leisure of pure feasts,
with an expression of leniency and harmony,
they would have exerted themselves with utmost sincerity,
planning for safety and peril,
measuring gain and loss,
above, to secure the ruler’s person,
below, to benefit the myriad people.
Then the way of the Five Emperors and Three Kings might nearly be seen.
Thus, Yīyǐn endured shame and disgrace,
carried cauldron and chopping block,
and harmonized the five flavors to seek out Tāng.
Tàigōng fished on the north bank of the Wèi River to meet King Wén.
Hearts united and wills in accord,
no plan failed to succeed,
no strategy went unheeded—
truly, they found their rightful lords.
With deep reflection and far-reaching consideration,
they drew upon righteousness to rectify themselves,
extended kindness to broaden their influence below,
rooted themselves in benevolence and took righteousness as ancestor,
honoring the virtuous,
enfeoffing the worthy and capable,
punishing the wicked and chaotic,
bringing order to distant regions,
unifying categories,
beautifying customs—
this is how emperors and kings flourish.
Above, not altering heavenly nature;
below, not disrupting human relations—
then heaven and earth are harmonious,
distant regions cherish them,
hence they are called sage kings.
When the duties of ministers and subjects are thus fulfilled,
then lands are divided and fiefs established,
titles of duke and marquis conferred,
passed on to sons and grandsons,
their names illustrious for later generations,
the people to this day praise them—
because they encountered Tāng and King Wén.
Tàigōng and Yīyǐn were thus,
while Guān Lóngpéng and Bǐgān were only so—
is this not lamentable!
Therefore, I say: How difficult it is to speak!”
Thereupon, King Wú fell silent,
bowed his head in deep contemplation,
then looked up, tears streaming down to his chin,
and said:
"Alas!
That my state has not perished,
hanging by a thread,
is perilous indeed,
that its line has not been severed!"
Thereupon, he rectified the court at the Bright Hall,
aligned the positions of ruler and ministers,
promoted the worthy and talented,
spread virtue and kindness,
practiced benevolence and righteousness,
and rewarded the meritorious;
he personally practiced frugality,
reduced the expenses of the rear palace,
and cut back on the use of carriages and horses;
he banished the music of Zhèng,
kept flatterers at a distance,
reduced the kitchen staff,
eliminated extravagance and waste,
humbled his palaces and lodges,
dismantled his parks and gardens,
filled in his ponds and moats,
and gave them to the poor who had no property;
he opened the inner treasury,
relieved poverty and distress,
cared for the elderly,
comforted the orphaned and solitary,
lightened taxes and levies,
and reduced punishments and penalties.
After practicing this for three years,
the land within the four seas was tranquil,
the world was in great harmony,
yīn and yáng were in balanced accord,
and all things attained their proper state;
the state was free from calamitous changes,
the people showed no signs of hunger or cold,
every household was well-supplied and every person content,
stores and savings were abundant,
and the prisons stood empty;
phoenixes came to gather,
qílín appeared in the suburbs,
sweet dew had already descended,
vermilion grass sprouted and budded,
and people from distant lands with different customs,
drawn by his influence and admiring his righteousness,
each fulfilling their duties, came to pay tribute and offer congratulations.
Thus, the way of order and chaos,
the beginning of survival and destruction,
are as easily seen as this,
yet those who rule over others are unwilling to act accordingly.
I, your humble servant, privately consider this a fault.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"The royal state can produce them,
they are the pillars of Zhōu.
With many officers gathered,
King Wén found peace."
This is what it means.
Since Wáng Bāo had composed the poems "Zhōnghé," "Lèzhí," and "Xuānbù" for Wáng Xiāng, the Governor of Yìzhōu,
he also wrote a commentary,
titled "Sìzǐ Jiǎngdé" (Four Masters Discussing Virtue),
to clarify their meaning.
Wēi Sī, the man of letters, asked Master Xūyí:
"I have heard that when the state possesses the Way,
to remain poor and lowly
is a disgrace.
Now, you, Master, have secluded yourself, leaping over barriers,
and have devoted yourself wholeheartedly to study for many days.
Fortunately encountering a sagely ruler in a time of peace,
yet long harboring your treasure,
this is like Bóyá leaving Zhōng Zǐqī,
or Shùn
and Yǔ fleeing from Emperor Yáo.
Thus, to wish to make your name illustrious
and achieve merit and enterprise,
is it not difficult?"
The Master said:
"Yes,
there is such a saying.
Mosquitoes and gadflies bustle all day,
yet cannot cross the courtyard steps;
clinging to a steed's tail, they traverse a thousand lǐ;
climbing a swan's wing, they soar across the four seas.
Though I am dull and obstinate,
I wish to follow you.
However,
by what means can I reach others?"
The man of letters said:
"Present your sincere earnestness before the court above,
and practice persuasive speech at the gates of the high ministers."
The Master said:
"Without the way of introduction,
how can one approach the high ministers?"
The man of letters said:
"Why must it be so?
In the past, Nìng Qì sang a merchant's song to gain access to Duke Huán of Qí;
Yuè Shí, carrying firewood, awakened Yàn Yīng;
they had no long-accumulated, longstanding friendship,
but all met by chance on the road,
and were treated as intimates.
Therefore, for Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī,
even skilled slanderers cannot obscure their beauty;
for Mómó and Wōguī,
even skilled praisers cannot conceal their ugliness.
If one possesses the supreme Way,
why is introduction necessary?"
The Master said:
"Ah,
to be truly understood without introduction
is a meeting once in a thousand years.
To summon the worthy and dwell in friendship
is the common path for the multitude of scholars.
Thus, an empty axe handle without a blade—
even Gōngshū could not carve with it;
a bowstring merely hung with a fine silk cord—
even Pú Jū could not shoot with it.
Therefore, to breast the waves and swim across waters
is not as easy as riding in a boat;
to charge through brambles and cross fields to reach a distant place
is not as swift as following the road.
Talent is obscured by lack of recognition,
conduct declines from lack of fellowship.
This is the affliction of past and present,
which only the man of letters considers."
The man of letters said:
"Yes, yes,
I respectfully heed your command."
Thereupon, they joined as companions,
joined hands and traveled together,
seeking the worthy and searching for friends,
journeying through Xīzhōu.
There were two men there,
riding in a carriage and singing.
Leaning against the carriage yoke, they listened:
the chanting and sighing were elegant,
the melodic turns were in harmony with the pitch-pipes,
broad, gentle, relaxed, and continuous,
the twists and turns never losing rhythm.
They asked who the singers were?
They were the so-called Master Fúyóu and Chén Qiūzǐ.
Thereupon, they befriended them with the ritual for scholars meeting.
After the ritual formalities were gathered,
the man of letters
and the Master descended from their mats and declared:
"We rustics are ignorant,
of scant sight and little hearing.
Just now, from the end of the road,
we looked and listened to your jade-like voices,
and were privately moved in heart.
May we dare ask what poems you were singing?
We beg to hear an explanation."
Master Fúyóu Chén Qiūzǐ said:
"They are the so-called poems 'Zhōnghé,' 'Lèzhí,' and 'Xuānbù,'
composed by the Governor of Yìzhōu.
The Governor, seeing the supreme sage's brilliance,
his ministers exerting their strength,
his virtue and grace vast and abundant,
the common people harmonious and amiable,
Heaven and humanity responding together,
and auspicious blessings repeatedly descending,
therefore composed these three poems to sing and chant of it."
The man of letters said:
"When a gentleman acts, there is a response;
composed and at ease, he attains measure.
Nánróng thrice repeated the 'White Scepter,'
and Confucius observed his cautious warning;
the Crown Prince Jī recited 'Morning Wind,'
and Marquis Wén understood his intended meaning.
Now, what do you, sir, find pleasing in these poems that you chant them?"
The Master said:
"Music moves people deeply and profoundly,
transforming customs and shifting mores.
The reason I sing and chant of it
is to praise the ruler's enlightened methods and the ministers' attainment of the Way.
The ruler is the heart,
the ministers are the outer limbs.
When the outer limbs act,
then one knows the heart's likes and dislikes;
when the ministers below move,
then one knows the ruler's rhythm and direction.
If likes and dislikes are not manifested,
then right and wrong are not distinguished;
if rhythm and direction are not established,
then merit and fame are not proclaimed.
Thus, fine jade is concealed within rough stone;
ordinary people look upon it and ignore it.
A skilled artisan polishes it,
and only then does one know it is a harmonious treasure.
Refined metal lies hidden in crude ore;
mediocre people look upon it and neglect it.
A clever smelter casts it,
and only then does one know its strength.
How much more so the lofty and vast sage virtue,
which the common people cannot even name!
Therefore, the Regional Inspector promotes and chants of it,
extolling the ruler's virtuous excellence,
so profound and expansive,
leaving nothing uncovered or unsupported,
filling heaven and earth in abundance,
pervading the silent cosmos.
The enlightened ruler's benevolence is made manifest,
the loyal minister's integrity is fully realized.
In the glorious age of the Táng,
what could surpass this!
Thus, whenever I sing of it,
I do not notice old age approaching."
The Scholar said:
"The Documents say:
'Guide the One Man so that he may employ the four quarters like divination.'
Now, loyal and worthy ministers
guide the ruler's will,
receive the ruler's favor,
spread his abundant virtue to effect great transformation,
bringing peace and tranquility to all under heaven,
so that every household is worthy of enfeoffment.
Why must one sing and chant odes and rhapsodies to extol the ruler!
I am privately perplexed by this."
Master Fúyóu's countenance flushed and his eyes widened,
saying:
"What kind of talk is this!
In ancient times, the Duke of Zhōu praised King Wén's virtue and composed the 'Qīng Miào,'
establishing it as the head of the Odes.
Jǐfǔ extolled King Xuān, serene as a clear breeze,
placing it among the Greater Odes.
When the age declines and the Way is obscure,
ministers who falsely claim merit
are perilous.
When the age is peaceful and the Way is bright,
ministers and sons who do not proclaim it
are base.
The burdens of baseness and peril
injure the Kingly Way.
Therefore, since the Regional Inspector's arrival,
he has proclaimed the imperial edicts,
laboring tirelessly to encourage and comfort,
ensuring all the common people fully understand the sage virtue,
and none fail to be moistened by it.
The elderly with thick eyebrows and hoary heads
all cherish each morning and evening,
wishing to be sustained a little longer,
to behold the pure flow of the great transformation.
Thus, the imperial grace has become abundant and overflowing,
the ruler's favor brims full,
the common people are joyful,
harmony stirs and inspires,
and therefore they compose songs and chant of it.
The Tradition says:
'The poet is moved, then reflects;
he reflects, then accumulates;
he accumulates, then becomes full;
he becomes full, then creates.
If words are insufficient,
then he sighs over it;
if sighing is insufficient,
then he chants and sings of it;
if chanting and singing are not enough,
he unconsciously dances with his hands and feet.'
This is the constant duty of ministers and sons toward their ruler and father,
the same in ancient times and today.
Now you cling to inches and feet, ignoring vast measures,
dwelling within your grasp yet rejecting the expansive,
and wish to discuss the pivotal mechanisms of great men,
to discourse on the successes and failures of feudal lords—
is this not far off the mark?"
Chén Qiūzǐ, seeing the Master's words were pointed,
fearing the two guests would be shamed,
advanced on his knees and said:
"Master, consider this carefully:
When puddles suddenly gather,
the rivers and seas do not consider it an increase;
when loaches and eels flee together,
the fine nets do not consider it a void.
Thus, Xǔ Yóu hid from Yáo and lived in deep seclusion,
yet the house of Táng did not decline because of it;
Bóyí and Shūqí were ashamed of Zhōu and starved far away,
yet King Wén and King Wǔ were not demeaned because of it.
Blue flies cannot defile the pendant jade of Chuíjí,
and perverse arguments cannot confuse Kǒngzǐ or Mòzǐ.
Now, the Regional Inspector, with his acute intelligence, spreads kindness,
extends transformation to spread his fame,
collects poems to manifest supreme virtue,
chants and sings to supervise their refinement.
He receives his mandate like a thread,
and makes it clear like a silk cord.
The breeze of the Gāntáng
can be leaned upon and awaited.
Even if these two guests block plans and hinder counsel,
what harm is there?"
He turned and said to the Scholar Master:
"The Master is slightly proud in discoursing on the Way,
and does not yield when benevolence is at stake,
but this is not a great fault either.
I hope you two gentlemen will set your minds at ease."
The Master said:
"No.
When thunderclaps must sound,
the depths below tremble and shake;
when war drums clang and crash,
armored soldiers rouse and stir.
Thus, things do not stir unless shaken,
and men are not brave unless roused.
Now, the Scholar's words
aim to deliberate on folly and stir the opponent,
to vent the Master's indignation.
I hope you two gentlemen also do not doubt it."
Thereupon, literary discourse gathered once more,
and they began to expound on virtue.
The Scholar Master said:
"In the ages of King Chéng and King Kāng of old,
was it due to the virtue of the noble men,
or the strength of the ministers?"
The Master said:
"Without a ruler of sage wisdom,
how could there be ministers of the Gāntáng?
Thus, when the tiger roars, the wind grows fierce and shrill;
when the dragon rises, it brings forth clouds and vapor.
The cricket awaits autumn to chirp,
the mayfly emerges in the shade.
The Yìjīng says:
'The flying dragon is in the heavens;
it is beneficial to see the great man.'
Call and response harmonize,
mates and companions follow each other.
People unite through shared intent,
things group together by kind.
Thus, the sage ruler does not peer and gaze everywhere, yet sees with clarity;
he does strain his ears to the utmost, yet hears with acuity.
Why is this?
Because good and noble men
draw many to approach them.
Therefore, a fur robe worth a thousand gold
is not from the armpit of a single fox;
the timber for a great mansion
is not from the trees of a single hill;
the achievement of great peace
is not from the strategy of a single man."
"For the sovereign is the head,
the ministers are the limbs;
understanding that they form one body,
they rely on each other to achieve success.
To have a sovereign but no ministers,
the Spring and Autumn Annals criticize such a case.
Before the Three Dynasties,
all had tutors and mentors;
after the Five Hegemons,
each sought their own friends.
Duke Huán of Qí had Guǎn Zhòng, Bào Shūyá, Xí Péng, and Nìng Qí,
who convened the feudal lords nine times,
and brought order to the whole realm.
Duke Wén of Jìn had Jiù Fàn and Zhào Cuī,
who established his prestige and secured his hegemony,
thereby honoring the Son of Heaven.
Duke Mù of Qín had Yóu Yú and the five rams' skins,
who repelled the Western Róng,
and began to lay the foundation for imperial rule.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had Shūsūn and Zǐ Fǎn,
who pacified both the Jiāng and Huái regions,
and awed all the states of Xià.
Gōu Jiàn had Wén Zhǒng, Fàn Lǐ, Zhè Yōng, and Yōng,
who overcame and destroyed powerful Wú,
avenging the shame of Kuàijī.
Duke Wén of Wèi had Duàngān, Tián Zǐfāng, and Dí,
causing the Qín people to cease warfare,
and resolving conflicts from ten thousand lǐ away.
King Zhāo of Yān had Guō Wěi and Yuè Yì,
who crushed mighty Qí,
and trapped King Mǐn in Jǔ.
Now, if feudal lords, as minor figures,
could achieve such merit and fame,
how much more should an emperor, chosen from across the four seas,
with the people as his wings!
"Thus, where there is a sage sovereign,
there must be wise and enlightened ministers.
If he wishes to accumulate virtue,
then the realm is not too vast to be pacified.
If he wishes to establish authority,
then all the barbarians are not too many to be repelled.
Now, our sagely lord wears the crown of morality,
treads the path of pure benevolence,
is robed in the Six Arts,
and adorned with ritual and literature.
He has repeatedly issued enlightened decrees,
promoting the worthy and good,
seeking men of skill,
summoning those of extraordinary talent,
and elevating the brilliant and outstanding.
Therefore, within the seas, all rejoice and admire,
rushing like wind and gathering like rain,
arriving in throngs,
filling the courtyards and overflowing the palace gates.
Songs extolling purity and virtue fill the ears,
rituals of ascent, descent, bowing, and yielding meet the eye everywhere.
Those advancing delight in the clear order,
while the weary wish to stop but cannot.
They rest and humble themselves at the gates of the Odes and Documents,
wander and observe within the realm of morality.
All purify themselves and cultivate their thoughts,
expressing their genuine feelings and laying bare their hearts,
each exerting their utmost energy to offer loyal service,
sincerely wishing to support our sovereign,
to spread customs and achieve great peace.
With such a multitude of talented men,
King Wén found tranquility.
"As for the beautiful governance implemented,
the vast kindness bestowed,
it cannot be fully recounted.
Promoting filial piety to encourage sincere conduct,
honoring ability to attract the worthy,
removing burdens and abolishing harshness to comfort the people,
increasing salaries and rewards to encourage integrity and honesty.
Reducing meals,
humbling palaces and towers,
curtailing agricultural officials,
decreasing parks and gardens,
lightening corvée labor,
relieving the destitute and distressed,
sympathizing with the people's calamities,
with no leisure for idle feasts.
Pitying the elderly who encounter guilt,
compassionating those in mourning garments who serve,
grieving for the decaying bodies of the dead,
sorrowing for sons and brothers imprisoned and hidden away.
Kindness extends to flying birds,
favor adds to running beasts,
eggs and embryos are able to develop and grow,
plants and trees achieve their flourishing and shedding.
The amiable and upright gentleman,
is the father and mother of the people—
is this not indeed so?
"Have you, sir, not heard of the time of Qín?
It turned away from the Three Kings,
背离了五帝,
destroyed the Odes and Documents,
ruined ritual and righteousness;
trusted petty men,
hated the benevolent and wise,
promoted the deceitful and false,
admitted the flattering and sycophantic.
The chancellor was harsh and severe,
the chief judge enforced draconian laws.
Those in positions of authority and governance
were all deficient in benevolence and righteousness,
but proficient in cruelty and oppression,
like wolves and tigers seizing prey,
harboring brutality and wielding violence.
Wherever they presided,
none did not tremble in fear and submit,
they nitpicked and found fault,
and simultaneously inflicted venomous stings.
The common people were anxious and alarmed,
with nowhere to place their hands and feet.
Wailing with sorrow and resentment,
they ultimately caused the Qín clan to perish.
Therefore, those who raise chickens do not keep cats,
those who herd animals do not rear jackals,
those who plant trees worry about borers,
those who protect the people eliminate the violent.
Thus, the governance of the great Hàn
esteems simplicity and ease,
honors leniency and gentleness,
advances purity and benevolence,
promotes the worthy and talented,
so that high and low bear no resentment,
and the people live in harmony.
"Now, within the seas, all delight in their occupations,
the court is virtuous and pure.
Heavenly signs are already manifest,
human auspices are also clear.
All things flourish,
mountains and rivers bestow their spirits.
Divine light shines brilliantly,
vast and penetrating, illuminating the sky.
The phoenix has come in ceremony,
dignified and harmonious.
Flocks of birds follow together,
dancing with virtue and displaying grace.
Divine sparrows repeatedly gather,
qílín arrive of their own accord.
Sweet dew moistens and nourishes,
auspicious grain stands dense like comb teeth.
The great transformation is profoundly harmonious,
men and women are orderly and content.
Homes are provided for, years are abundant,
all follow the three grades of soil.
Is this not magnificent!
In the past, King Wén responded to the nine-tailed fox, and the Eastern Yí submitted to Zhōu;
King Wǔ captured the white fish, and the feudal lords unanimously pledged allegiance;
the Duke of Zhōu received the black millet aromatic wine, and the Guǐfāng became subjects;
King Xuān obtained the white wolf, and the Yí-Dí paid tribute.
For when the name is correct, affairs settle themselves.
Now, Nánjùn has captured a white tiger,
which is also an omen of laying down arms and promoting culture.
The captor is Zhāng Wǔ,
'Wǔ' means martial, and fierceness is subdued.
Therefore, the Northern Dī submit peacefully,
the borders need not worry about invaders,
soldiers rest and banners lie down."
The learned master said:
"Heavenly signs we have heard commanded;
may we ask about human auspices?"
The Master said:
"The Xiōngnú are
the strongest among all barbarian tribes.
By nature they are arrogant and obstinate,
their customs are fierce and violent,
they despise the old and honor the strong,
and they compete in physical prowess.
Their occupation lies in attack and conquest,
their affairs in hunting and archery.
Children can ride sheep,
shoot arrows and hurl darts,
they follow water sources and move with their herds,
having no permanent settlements.
They gather like birds and scatter like beasts,
coming and going, galloping swiftly,
roaming across the vast wilderness,
to satisfy their desires.
Their plow and hoe are the bow, arrow, saddle, and horse;
their sowing is the drawing of the bowstring and gripping of the bow;
their autumn harvest is chasing foxes and hares;
their reaping is the toppling and slaying of prey.
Pursue them and they flee and hide,
release them and they become raiders.
Thus, the Three Sovereigns could not pacify them,
the Five Hegemons could not subdue them.
They startle the borders and harass the soldiers,
repeatedly violating the grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers.
The poets sang of them,
and since ancient times they have been a source of trouble.
Now, with the sage virtue flourishing and abundant,
and majestic power extending outward to cover all,
the Rìzhú have submitted their entire state and turned to virtue,
and the Chányú has declared himself a subject and come to offer tribute.
All lands opened by Heaven and Earth,
all regions where yīn and yáng meet,
those with knotted hair and tattooed faces,
blackened teeth and fierce eyes,
those who cut their hair, tattoo their heads,
adorn their bodies and go bare-chested—
none fail to hasten with tribute,
joyfully coming to submit,
dancing and singing,
clapping their sides and laughing.
In an age of great harmony,
what creature is not joyful?
Birds fold their wings in contentment,
fish in springs leap with vigor.
Thus, the Inspector, moved and inspired, voiced his feelings and sang of the ultimate virtue.
I, an ignorant and shallow man,
cannot fully comprehend it,
but respectfully following what I have heard,
I have not been able to exhaust it."
Thereupon, the two guests, intoxicated with benevolence and righteousness,
sated with abundant virtue,
looked up and sighed all day long,
pleased and delighted, submitting joyfully.
In ancient times, when Emperor Yáo abdicated, he said:
"Ah, you, Shùn,
the celestial mandate rests upon your person."
Shùn also charged Yǔ with these words.
As for Jì and Xiè,
they all assisted Táng and Yú,
spreading their light to aid all within the Four Seas,
and their virtue was carried through generations.
Reaching Tāng and Wǔ,
they possessed the world.
Although the times they encountered differed,
and the manner of abdication and succession varied,
in responding to Heaven and complying with the people,
their principle was one.
Therefore, the Liú clan received Yáo's legacy;
the generations of their clan
are recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Táng possessed the virtue of Fire,
and Hàn succeeded it.
Beginning its rise from the marshes of Pèi,
a divine mother cried out at night,
to manifest the omen of the Red Emperor.
Thus it is said,
the mandate of emperors and kings
must have the virtue of brilliant sageliness and illustrious excellence,
and the accumulated deeds of abundant merit and profound benefit,
only then can sincere essence communicate with the divine intelligence,
and flowing grace be bestowed upon the living people.
Thus they can be blessed and enjoyed by the spirits and gods,
and become that to which the world turns.
Never has it been seen that an era's fortune had no foundation,
or that merit and virtue were unrecorded,
yet one could forcefully rise to this position.
Common people see that Gāozǔ rose from common cloth,
and do not understand the reason,
thinking he merely encountered violent chaos,
managed to wield his sword,
and that traveling persuaders
even compared the world to chasing a deer,
and he was fortunate to capture it.
They do not know that the sacred vessel is ordained by fate,
and cannot be sought through intellect or strength.
Alas!
This is why there are so many rebellious ministers and villainous sons in the world.
If so,
are they merely ignorant of the Way of Heaven?
They also fail to observe it in human affairs!
Those starving refugees,
suffering hunger and cold on the roads,
think of having a short coarse garment to wear,
a store of a dàn of grain,
their wish no more than a single piece of gold,
yet they end up dying in ditches and gullies.
Why is this?
Poverty and destitution also have their fate.
How much more so the honor of the Son of Heaven,
the wealth of all within the Four Seas,
the mandate of the divine spirits—
can these be recklessly occupied?
Therefore, although some encounter times of crisis,
usurp authority and power,
brave as Xìn and Bù,
strong as Liáng and Jí,
successful as Wáng Mǎng,
yet they end up boiled in cauldrons or beheaded by the executioner's block,
dismembered or made into mincemeat,
how much more those petty and insignificant, not equal to these few men,
who wish to secretly covet the heavenly position.
Therefore, a nag of a horse
cannot gallop on a thousand-mile road;
swallows and sparrows,
cannot exert the use of six-feathered wings;
material fit only for brackets and short pillars cannot bear the load of beams and ridgepoles;
men of dǒu and sháo capacity
cannot uphold the weight of imperial majesty.
The Yì says:
"The cauldron's legs break,
overturning the duke's stew."
It is being unequal to the task.
At the end of the Qín,
the heroes jointly recommended Chén Yīng and made him king.
Yīng's mother stopped him, saying:
"Since I became a wife in your family,
we have been generationally poor and lowly.
Suddenly attaining wealth and honor
is inauspicious.
It would be better to entrust the troops to another.
If the affair succeeds,
you will receive some benefit.
If it does not succeed,
the calamity will have somewhere to return."
Yīng followed her words,
and the Chén clan thereby found peace.
Wáng Líng's mother
also saw that the Xiàng clan was certain to perish,
and the Liú clan was about to rise.
At that time,
Líng was a Hàn general,
and his mother was captured by Chǔ.
When a Hàn envoy came,
Líng's mother saw him
and said:
"I wish to tell my son
that the King of Hàn is a magnanimous man,
he will certainly obtain the world.
My son must serve him diligently,
without a divided heart."
Thereupon, before the Hàn envoy, she fell upon her sword and died,
to firmly encourage Líng.
Afterward,
it was indeed settled by Hàn.
Líng became prime minister,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
With the insight of an ordinary woman,
she could still deduce the ultimate principle of affairs,
