probe the mechanism of calamity and fortune,
preserve the ancestral sacrifices for endless generations,
and leave her record in the Spring and Autumn Annals—
how much more so the affairs of a great man!
Therefore, obscurity and success are determined by fate,
good and ill fortune depend on man.
Yīng's mother knew about decline,
Líng's mother knew about rise.
Examining these two cases,
the distinction for emperors and kings is decided.
As for Emperor Gāozǔ,
his rise to power can be attributed to five factors:
first, he was a descendant of Emperor Yáo;
second, his appearance was extraordinary and unusual;
third, his divine martial prowess was accompanied by auspicious signs;
fourth, he was broad-minded, clear-sighted, benevolent, and forgiving;
fifth, he knew people well and excelled at employing them.
Added to these were his trustworthiness, sincerity, and fondness for strategy,
his openness to listening and accepting advice,
his eagerness to pursue goodness as if he could never catch up,
his use of others as if they were extensions of himself,
his acceptance of remonstrance as smoothly as following a flowing stream,
and his responsiveness to the times as swiftly as an echo to a sound.
While eating, he spat out his food
to adopt Zhāng Liáng’s strategy;
while having his feet washed, he rose and dismissed the attendant
to heed Lì Shíqí’s counsel;
he was enlightened by the words of a garrison soldier
and severed his attachment to his homeland;
he esteemed the reputation of the Four White-haired Elders
and sacrificed his personal affection;
he promoted Hán Xìn from the ranks of the army,
and recruited Chén Píng from among the fugitives.
Heroes exerted their strength,
and all strategies were fully employed.
This was Gāozǔ’s grand plan,
by which he achieved imperial rule.
As for spiritual omens and auspicious responses,
they can also be briefly mentioned.
Initially, when Liú Āo was pregnant with Gāozǔ,
she dreamed of encountering a deity,
with thunder, lightning, and darkness,
and strange phenomena of dragons and serpents.
As he grew, he displayed many spiritual signs,
distinguishing him from the masses.
Thus, Wáng Wù was moved by a portent and tore up the contract,
and Lǚ Gōng, upon seeing his appearance, offered his daughter in marriage;
the Qín Emperor traveled east to suppress his aura,
and Empress Lǚ, by observing the clouds, knew his whereabouts;
when he first received the mandate, a white serpent was split,
and when he entered the pass to the west, the five planets converged.
Therefore, Huáiyīn and Liú Hóu said it was bestowed by Heaven,
not achieved by human effort.
Examining the successes and failures throughout history,
verifying the outcomes of actions,
investigating the fortunes of emperors and kings,
and considering the aforementioned five factors,
if one’s choices do not align with this position,
and auspicious signs do not correspond to this measure,
yet one blindly covets power and profit,
presumptuously seizes a position beyond one’s station,
externally failing to assess one’s strength,
internally unaware of one’s fate,
then one will surely lose the master who safeguards the family,
forfeit the lifespan destined by Heaven,
encounter the calamity of a broken leg,
and suffer execution by axe and halberd.
If heroes truly awaken to understanding,
fear such warnings of disaster,
rise above to see far and wide,
and possess profound and deep insight,
accept the clear distinction of Líng and Yīng,
cut off the ambitions of Xìn and Bù,
reject the blind talk of chasing the deer,
recognize that the sacred vessel is bestowed,
and understand that greed cannot be indulged,
then they will not be laughed at by the two mothers,
and their blessings will flow to their descendants,
with Heaven’s mandate enduring forever.
Literary men disparage each other,
a practice that has existed since ancient times.
Fù Yì and Bān Gù
were roughly equal in talent,
yet Bān Gù looked down on him,
writing to his younger brother Bān Chāo:
“Wǔzhòng, though skilled in writing and serving as a Lántái Commandant,
cannot stop himself once he starts writing.”
People are good at seeing their own strengths,
but literature is not of a single style,
and few can master all.
Thus, each uses their own strengths
to disparage others’ shortcomings.
A common saying goes:
“One’s own broken broom
is worth a thousand pieces of gold.”
This is the fault of lacking self-awareness.
Among contemporary literary men,
there are Kǒng Róng Wénjǔ of Lǔguó,
Chén Lín Kǒngzhāng of Guǎnglíng,
Wáng Càn Zhòngxuān of Shānyáng,
Xú Gàn Wěicháng of Běihǎi,
Ruǎn Yǔ Yuányú of Chénliú,
Yìng Yáng Déliǎn of Rǔnán,
and Liú Zhēn Gōnggàn of Dōngpíng:
These seven masters
left no field of learning untouched,
and their writings were entirely original,
each galloping like a thoroughbred for a thousand miles,
racing side by side with equal speed.
For them to admire one another
is truly difficult.
A gentleman examines himself to judge others,
thus avoiding such pitfalls,
and writes this discourse on literature.
Wáng Càn excelled in poetic prose;
Xú Gàn often had the leisurely style of Qí,
yet he was a match for Wáng Càn.
Works like Wáng Càn’s “Chūzhēng,” “Dēnglóu,” “Huáifù,” and “Zhēngsī,”
and Xú Gàn’s “Xuányuán,” “Lòuzhī,” “Yuánshàn,” and “Júfù,”
even Zhāng Héng and Cài Yōng could not surpass.
However, in other genres,
they did not achieve the same excellence.
Chén Lín and Ruǎn Yǔ’s memorials, petitions, and letters
are outstanding in their time.
Yìng Yáng’s style was harmonious but not vigorous.
Liú Zhēn’s style was vigorous but not refined.
Kǒng Róng’s literary spirit was sublime and exquisite,
surpassing others in some aspects,
yet he could not sustain arguments,
with reasoning inferior to rhetoric,
often mixing in mockery and jest.
However, in his strengths,
he was comparable to Yáng Xióng and Bān Gù.
Ordinary people value the distant and disdain the near,
follow reputation rather than substance,
and suffer from lack of self-awareness,
considering themselves superior.
Literature,
fundamentally similar, differs in its branches.
Memorials and proposals should be elegant,
letters and discourses should be logical,
inscriptions and eulogies should emphasize truth,
and poetry and poetic prose should be beautiful.
These four categories differ,
so masters excel in specific areas;
only versatile talents can master all styles.
Literature takes qì as its foundation;
qì has its forms of clarity and turbidity,
which cannot be forced or attained by effort.
Analogous to music,
though the melody may be the same,
and the rhythm follows the same measure;
yet the breath control varies,
and skill or clumsiness is innate,
so even among fathers and brothers,
it cannot be passed on to sons or younger brothers.
Literature is a great undertaking for governing the state,
an immortal and magnificent endeavor.
Lifespan has its end,
and glory and pleasure cease with one’s body.
Both inevitably reach their fixed limits,
unlike literature, which is boundless.
Therefore, ancient authors
devoted themselves to writing,
expressing their thoughts in books and records,
without relying on the words of good historians,
or the influence of swift advancement,
yet their fame naturally passed down to later generations.
Thus, King Wén of the West, while imprisoned, expanded the “Yìjīng,”
and the Duke of Zhōu, in prominence, established the rites,
neither neglecting their work due to hardship,
nor increasing their efforts due to comfort and pleasure.
For this reason,
the ancients valued a moment of time over a foot of jade,
fearing the passage of time.
Yet most people do not exert themselves,
fearing hunger and cold in poverty and lowliness,
or indulging in comfort and pleasure in wealth and honor,
thus busying themselves with immediate affairs,
and neglecting achievements for a thousand years.
As the sun and moon pass above,
and physical appearance declines below,
suddenly one transforms with all things,
which is the great sorrow of the determined scholar!
Kǒng Róng and others have passed away,
only Xú Gàn wrote discourses,
establishing a school of thought.
In ancient times, the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties lasted for dozens of generations,
while the Qin dynasty perished after only two.
Why was this?
The rulers of the Three Dynasties shared their people with the world,
so the world shared their worries;
the King of Qin alone controlled his people,
so when he faced collapse and danger, no one came to his rescue.
Those who share their joys with others
will find others sharing their sorrows;
those who share peace with others
will find others saving them from peril.
The ancient kings knew that ruling alone could not last long,
so they shared governance with others;
they knew that guarding alone could not be secure,
so they shared defense with others.
They employed both close and distant relatives,
and advanced those with both similarities and differences.
Thus, the light and heavy could balance each other,
the close and distant could protect each other,
the path to annexation was blocked,
and rebellious acts did not arise.
When the dynasty declined,
Dukes Huán and Wén upheld the rites;
when the tribute of bundled thatch was not paid,
the army of Qí attacked Chǔ;
when Sòng did not fortify Zhōu,
Jìn executed its minister.
The royal laws slackened but were restored,
the feudal lords grew arrogant but were subdued again.
After the two hegemons,
the decline gradually deepened.
Wú and Chǔ relied on the rivers,
and fortified themselves with the Fāngchéng mountains.
Although they coveted the Nine Tripods,
they feared the pressure from the royal Ji clan.
Their treacherous thoughts were kept in their hearts,
and their rebellious plans never left their lips.
Was this not because trust was placed in relatives,
and the worthy and capable were employed,
so that the branches and leaves flourished,
and the roots relied on them?
After this,
they turned to attacking each other.
Wú was annexed by Yuè,
Jìn was divided into three,
Lǔ was destroyed by Chǔ,
and Zhèng was absorbed by Hán.
By the time of the Warring States period,
the various Ji clans had declined,
and only Yān and Wèi remained.
However, they were all weak and small,
pressed from the west by the powerful Qín,
and fearing Qí
and Chǔ to the south, struggling to survive,
with no time to care for each other.
As for King Nǎn,
he was demoted to a commoner,
yet the branches and trunk still supported each other,
allowing him to retain an empty throne.
The realm was without a ruler
for over forty years.
Qín occupied a strategically advantageous position,
employed deceitful tactics,
conquered the lands east of the passes,
and nibbled away at the nine states.
By the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
he finally secured the heavenly throne.
So long as the time taken,
and so great as the effort expended—
was this not the way to deepen roots and strengthen foundations,
making them unshakable?
The Book of Changes says:
"It totters, it totters,
bound to the clump of mulberry trees."
The virtue of Zhōu can truly be said to match this.
Qín observed the flaws of Zhōu,
thinking that weakness led to its loss,
so it abolished the five ranks of nobility,
established commanderies and counties,
abandoned the teachings of rites and music,
and employed harsh governance.
The royal sons and brothers received not an inch of land,
the meritorious officials had not even a place to stand a needle,
internally there were no clan sons to assist,
externally there were no feudal lords to serve as a protective screen.
Benevolence was not extended to relatives,
kindness did not flow to the branches and leaves.
It was like cutting off one's own limbs,
relying solely on the torso;
floating a boat on rivers and seas,
yet discarding oars and rudders.
Onlookers felt chilled,
yet Qín Shǐhuáng remained complacent,
believing that the defenses of Guānzhōng were secure,
that the thousand-mile metal walls
would be an imperial enterprise for his descendants for ten thousand generations.
How deluded!
At that time,
Chúnyú Yuè remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that the kings of Yīn
and Zhōu
enfeoffed their sons, brothers, and meritorious officials,
lasting over a thousand years.
Now Your Majesty rules the realm,
yet your sons and brothers are mere commoners.
If suddenly there appear ministers like Tián Cháng or the six ministers of Jìn,
with no one to assist,
how can you be saved?
I have never heard of affairs not modeled on antiquity
yet able to last long."
Qín Shǐhuáng listened to Lǐ Sī's biased argument and rejected this reasoning.
By the time of his death,
there was no one to entrust,
he left the weight of the world in the hands of ordinary men,
and placed the fate of succession in the mouths of treacherous ministers.
This led to men like Zhào Gāo
exterminating the imperial clan.
Húhài learned harsh teachings from a young age,
and followed in his cruel father's footsteps as he grew,
unable to reform institutions or change laws,
to favor and employ his brothers.
Instead, he studied the strategies of Shēn and Shāng,
sought counsel from Zhào Gāo,
secluded himself deep in the palace,
entrusted governance to slanderous villains,
met his end at Wàngyí,
and wished to become a commoner—
how could that be possible?
Thus, commanderies and states became disloyal,
the masses rebelled and scattered.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng raised the call first,
Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ finished it later.
If only Qín Shǐhuáng had adopted Chúnyú's strategy,
and suppressed Lǐ Sī's argument,
divided the provinces and states,
enfeoffed sons and brothers,
granted lands to the descendants of the Three Dynasties,
rewarded the merits of功臣,
so that the land had constant rulers,
and the people had settled lords,
branches and leaves supporting each other,
head and tail working together—
even if later子孙 had wayward conduct,
and the people of the time lacked the virtue of Tāng and Wǔ,
before treacherous plots could unfold,
they would already be slaughtered.
How then could the insignificant Chén and Xiàng
have had a chance to move hand or foot?
Thus, Hàn Gāozǔ brandished his three-foot sword,
drove a crowd gathered like crows,
and within five years,
established an imperial enterprise.
Since the beginning of creation,
those who rose to achieve merit and accomplishment
have never done so as easily as Hàn Gāozǔ.
To cut down deep roots is difficult to achieve,
but to break dry rot is easy to accomplish—
such is the natural principle and trend.
When a spring dries up, its flow ceases;
when roots decay, the leaves wither.
Luxuriant branches provide shade for the roots;
when branches fall, the trunk stands alone.
Thus the saying goes:
"A centipede,
even in death, does not stiffen,
because it is supported by many legs."
Though these words are small,
they can illustrate a great truth.
Moreover, a city wall's foundation cannot be hastily completed,
and a reputation for authority cannot be established in a single day.
All things must develop gradually,
and be built upon a solid foundation.
Take planting a tree as an example:
over time, its roots grow deep and firm,
and its branches and leaves become lush.
But if it is recklessly moved from the mountain forest
and planted beneath the palace gates,
even if it is covered with fertile black soil
and warmed by the spring sun,
it still cannot be saved from withering—
how could it have time to flourish and multiply?
Just as a tree is like one's kin,
so the land is like the common people.
If institutions are not long established,
then inferiors will act lightly and superiors will be disrespected.
Even in times of peace, one fears their rebellion—
what then in times of crisis?
Thus, the sage king remains secure but not complacent,
for he considers danger;
he preserves the state but prepares defenses,
for he fears its downfall.
Therefore, when a sudden storm arrives,
there is no worry of destruction;
when upheaval occurs in the world,
there is no peril of collapse.
A noble man feels ashamed if, in his lifetime, he achieves no merit;
he grieves if, at his death, his name remains unknown.
Thus it is said:
"In learning, as if you could never catch up,
you still fear losing what you have gained."
For this reason, the aspiring men of antiquity
lamented the swift passage of time
and feared that their reputation would not be established.
They exerted their spirit and disciplined their conduct,
rising early and retiring late,
with no leisure for rest.
They measured their progress by years and months,
accumulating effort day by day.
Like the diligence of Nìng Yuè,
or the dedication of Master Dǒng,
they immersed themselves in the depths of virtue and righteousness,
and dwelled in the realm of the Way and arts.
Even with the sagacity of King Wén of Zhōu,
and the talent of the Duke of Zhōu,
they still labored late into the night awaiting dawn,
thus enabling the rise of the Zhōu Way,
and leaving their names for ten thousand generations.
How much more, then, for us, their subjects and commoners—
how can we cease our efforts?
Observing throughout history those who achieved merit and fame,
all had accumulated extraordinary deeds,
straining their spirits and exhausting their bodies,
enduring hardship with diligent thought,
never slacking in their duties even in peaceful times,
and not changing their principles even in poverty.
Thus, Bǔ Shì set his resolve in farming and herding,
and Huáng Bà received instruction while in prison,
yet ultimately they attained the blessings of honor and prominence,
and achieved immortal names.
Therefore, Shān Fǔ toiled from dawn till dusk,
and Wú Hàn never left the gates of public service—
how could there be idleness among them?
People of the present age,
mostly do not devote themselves to the study of the classics,
but instead delight in board games and gambling,
neglecting affairs and abandoning their duties,
forgetting sleep and food,
exhausting the daylight,
and continuing by candlelight.
When they sit before the board, locked in competition,
with victory undecided,
they focus intently,
their minds entranced and bodies weary.
Human affairs are neglected and left unattended;
guests and visitors are omitted and not received.
Even if there were the feast of the Great Sacrifice,
or the music of Sháo and Xià,
they would have no time to appreciate them.
Some even go so far as to gamble away their clothing and belongings,
moving pieces and changing strategies,
their sense of shame slackens,
and expressions of anger and malice appear.
Yet their ambition extends no further than the chessboard,
and their efforts are confined within the grid lines;
defeating an opponent brings no reward of noble titles,
and capturing territory yields no real expansion of land.
Its skill is not among the Six Arts,
and its use does not govern the state.
Those who establish themselves do not rely on such techniques,
and those selected for office do not follow this path.
If examined in terms of warfare,
it is not comparable to Sūn Wǔ or Wú Qǐ;
if evaluated in terms of the Way and arts,
it does not belong to the school of Confucius;
if focused on deception and cunning,
it is not the work of loyalty and trust;
if named for plunder and killing,
it is not the intention of the benevolent.
Yet it emptily wastes time and ruins one's duties,
ultimately offering no benefit.
How is this different from setting up a wooden target to strike,
or placing stones to throw at them?
Moreover, when a noble man is at home,
he labors diligently to provide support;
when at court,
he exhausts his life to offer loyalty;
facing affairs of state, he even eats late—
how then could he have leisure to indulge in board games?
Only thus
can the conduct of filial piety and fraternal duty be established,
and the name of integrity and purity be made illustrious.
Now, the great Wú has received the Mandate,
yet within the seas, peace is not yet achieved.
Our sagely court toils diligently,
striving to obtain worthy men.
Those with courage and strategy
are entrusted with the responsibilities of bears and tigers;
those of scholarly refinement
are placed in the offices of dragons and phoenixes.
All virtues are embraced,
civil and military pursuits advance together.
Excellent talents are broadly selected,
and the outstanding are honored and chosen.
Regulations for examinations are established,
and rewards of gold and rank are bestowed.
Truly, this is a splendid gathering of a thousand years,
a fine opportunity for a hundred generations.
The scholars of our time
should diligently contemplate the highest Way,
cherish merit and treasure effort,
to assist this enlightened age.
Let your names be recorded in the historical annals,
and your achievements stored in the covenant archives.
This is the foremost task for a noble man,
and the most urgent matter of the present.
A single wooden board—
how can it compare to the enfeoffment of a region?
Three hundred dried chess pieces—
how can they compare to commanding ten thousand troops?
The robes embroidered with dragons,
the music of metal and stone—
these are enough to surpass the chessboard and replace gambling.
If the scholars of our time
would shift the effort spent on board games to the study of poetry and books,
they would possess the resolve of Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn;
if applied to wisdom and strategy,
they would have the insight of Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng;
if applied to wealth and goods,
they would attain the riches of Yī Dùn;
if applied to archery and charioteering,
they would acquire the preparedness of generals and commanders.
In this way,
merit and fame would be established, and baseness and lowliness would be kept far away.
Some in the world say that immortality can be attained through study,
and that deathlessness can be achieved through effort;
others say the upper limit of longevity is one hundred twenty years,
which is the same in ancient and modern times,
and that beyond this,
all is but deceit and falsehood.
Both views miss the truth of the matter.
Allow me to attempt a brief discussion of this.
Though immortals have never been seen with one's own eyes,
yet according to the records in the texts,
and the accounts passed down through earlier histories,
when examined and discussed,
their existence is certain.
It seems they uniquely received an extraordinary essence,
endowed by nature itself,
not something achievable through accumulated learning.
As for guiding and nurturing life with proper principles,
to fully realize one's nature and lifespan,
the highest attainment could be over a thousand years,
the lower could be several hundred years—
this is possible.
But people in the world are not proficient in this,
therefore none can attain it.
How can this be explained?
Take taking medicine to induce sweating—
sometimes one may not succeed;
yet when feelings of shame gather,
sweat flows profusely.
Not having eaten all morning,
one feels famished and thinks of food;
yet Zēngzǐ, bearing grief,
went seven days without hunger.
Sitting late into the night,
one grows drowsy and thinks of sleep;
but harboring deep worry within,
one stays awake until dawn.
A stiff brush to groom the hair,
strong wine to bring color to the face—
these barely achieve their effect;
yet the anger of a strong man,
strikingly alters his appearance,
making his hair stand on end.
From this it can be said,
the spirit in relation to the body
is like a ruler to a state.
When the spirit is agitated within,
the form deteriorates without,
just as when the ruler is benighted above,
the state falls into chaos below.
To farm crops in the time of Tāng,
if one benefits from even a single irrigation,
though they will ultimately wither and burn,
those that received that one irrigation will wither later.
Thus, the benefit of one irrigation
certainly cannot be denied.
Yet people often say one bout of anger is not enough to harm one's nature,
one episode of grief not enough to injure the body,
and so they take them lightly and indulge freely.
This is like not recognizing the benefit of one irrigation,
yet expecting fine grain from drought-stricken sprouts.
Therefore, the noble person knows the body relies on the spirit to stand,
the spirit needs the body to exist,
understands how easily the principle of life can be lost,
and knows the harm a single transgression can do to life.
Thus, they cultivate their nature to preserve the spirit,
calm the mind to protect the whole body,
letting neither love nor hate dwell in their emotions,
neither worry nor joy linger in their thoughts,
remaining placid and unaffected,
so that the body's energy is harmonious and balanced.
Furthermore, through breathing exercises and exhalations,
taking nourishment to sustain the body,
they cause form and spirit to be intimate,
and inner and outer to support each other.
As for field-sown grain,
ten hú per mǔ
is called good land—
this is the common saying in the world.
People do not know that intensive planting can yield over a hundred hú.
The seed is the same,
but depending on the method of planting and nurturing,
the results achieved are vastly different.
To say merchants have no hope of tenfold profit,
or farmers no hope of a hundred hú yield,
is to cling to convention without change.
Moreover, beans make people heavy,
elm makes people drowsy,
héhuān dispels anger,
xuāncǎo makes one forget sorrow—
this is known to both foolish and wise.
Pungent vegetables harm the eyes,
pork and fish are not nourishing—
this is recognized in common experience.
Lice on the head turn black,
musk deer eating cypress become fragrant;
those living in mountainous regions get goiters,
teeth in Jìn turn yellow.
Extending this reasoning,
all the energies from what one consumes
steam and dye one's nature and body,
nothing fails to have a corresponding effect.
How could it be that steaming only makes things heavy and never light,
harming only makes things dim and never bright,
fumigating only makes things yellow and never firm,
perfuming only makes things fragrant and never enduring?
Therefore Shénnóng said,
"Superior medicines nurture life,
middling medicines nurture nature"—
truly understanding the principles of life and nature,
and thereby aiding and nurturing to achieve harmony.
Yet people of the world do not examine this,
seeing only the five grains,
indulging in music and beauty.
Eyes bewildered by dark and yellow,
ears devoted to lewd and clamorous sounds.
Rich flavors sear their organs,
strong liquors boil their intestines and stomach.
Fragrant aromas rot their marrow,
joy and anger pervert their upright energy.
Thoughts and worries consume their spirit,
sorrow and joy ruin their calm purity.
With such a tiny body,
assaulted from not just one direction,
an easily exhausted form,
attacked from without and within,
the body is not wood or stone—
how can it last long?
Those who are most self-indulgent:
they do not regulate eating and drinking,
thus giving rise to a hundred illnesses;
tire not in their lust,
thus leading to exhaustion and depletion;
harmed by wind and cold,
injured by a hundred poisons,
they die prematurely on the path amidst numerous calamities.
The world all knows to laugh and lament them,
saying they did not know how to care for life.
As for those who place themselves in violation of principle,
losing it in the subtle,
accumulating the subtle into damage,
accumulating damage into decline,
from decline comes greying,
from greying comes old age,
from old age comes death,
dimly as if without beginning.
Those of middling intelligence and below
call this natural.
Even if slightly awakened,
they all sigh with regret over the beginning of their encounter,
yet do not know to be cautious of all dangers before signs appear.
This is like Duke Huán harboring a fatal illness,
yet raging at Biǎn Què's foresight,
taking the day he felt pain
as the start of his sickness.
Harm completes in the subtle, yet rescue comes when it is obvious,
hence there is treatment that achieves nothing;
galloping in the realm of ordinary people,
hence there is only ordinary lifespan.
Looking up and observing down,
there is none for whom it is not so.
Using the multitude to prove themselves right,
using similarity to comfort themselves,
they say the principles of heaven and earth are exhausted here and no more.
Even if they hear of life-nurturing practices,
they judge based on what they have seen,
saying it is not so.
Next are those who are skeptical;
though they somewhat aspire,
they do not know the way.
Next,
they strive to take medicines themselves,
for half a year or a year,
labor without seeing effect,
their will thus wearied and declining,
they abandon it midway.
Some add a trickle of water,
yet let it drain through a vast outlet.
Wanting to sit and await obvious reward—
or they suppress emotions and restrain desires,
cut off and abandon glorious aspirations,
yet their cravings are constantly before their eyes and ears,
what they hope for lies decades later,
and they fear losing both,
harboring hesitation within,
the mind battling inside,
objects tempting outside,
immediate and distant pulling against each other—
thus they fail again.
The most profound things are subtle and mysterious,
They can be understood through reason,
But are difficult to recognize with the eyes.
Take, for example, the yùzhāng tree,
Which takes seven years to grow before it can be noticed.
Now, with a restless and competitive heart,
One treads the path of tranquility and stillness,
Wishing for speed while matters progress slowly,
Hoping for closeness while responses are distant,
Thus, none can see it through to the end.
Those who are indifferent do not seek because they see no effect,
While those who seek fail in their endeavors due to lack of focus,
Those who rely on one-sided methods achieve nothing because they lack comprehensiveness,
And those who pursue techniques drown themselves in trivial paths.
All such types
Are among the ten thousand who desire it, yet not one can succeed.
Those who are skilled in nurturing life are not like this.
They are clear, empty, tranquil, and peaceful,
With few selfish desires.
They understand that fame and status harm virtue,
So they disregard them and do not pursue them,
Not because they desire them but forcibly restrain themselves.
They recognize that rich flavors harm one’s nature,
So they abandon them without a second thought,
Not because they crave them but later suppress them.
External things that burden the mind are not retained,
The spirit and energy become pure and bright, standing out alone.
Open and carefree, without worries or troubles,
Serene and without anxious thoughts.
Moreover, they hold fast to unity,
And nurture it with harmony.
Harmony and principle daily assist each other,
Aligning with the great order of nature.
Then they steam themselves with língzhī mushrooms,
Moisten themselves with sweet springs,
Bask in the morning sun,
And soothe themselves with the five-stringed lute.
Acting without forced effort, they attain naturally,
Their bodies subtle, their minds profound.
Forgetting joy, they later find contentment,
Letting go of life, they later preserve their bodies.
If one continues like this,
Truly, one could compare in longevity to Xuànmén
And contend in years with Wáng Qiáo.
How could it be said that such a thing does not exist?
Order and chaos
Are matters of fate;
Adversity and success
Are matters of destiny;
Nobility and lowliness
Are matters of timing.
Thus, when fate is about to rise,
A sage and enlightened ruler is sure to be born.
A sage and enlightened ruler
Is sure to have loyal and worthy ministers.
The way they encounter each other
Is without seeking yet they naturally come together;
The way they become close
Is without introduction yet they naturally grow intimate.
When one sings, the other is sure to harmonize;
When one plans, the other is sure to follow.
Their virtue and principles mysteriously align,
Their twists and turns match like tallies.
Gains and losses cannot shake their resolve,
Slander and schemes cannot sever their bond.
Only then can they achieve success.
The reason they are able to do so—
Is it merely human effort?
It is Heaven that grants it,
Spirits that announce it,
And fate that accomplishes it.
When the Yellow River runs clear, a sage is born;
When the village altar resounds, a sage emerges;
When a group of dragons appears, a sage is employed.
Thus, Yī Yǐn,
Though a lowly retainer of the Yǒushēn clan,
Became the Āhéng of the Shāng dynasty.
Tàigōng,
Though an old and humble man by the Wèi River,
Became the Shàngfǔ of the Zhōu dynasty.
Bǎilǐ Xī was in Yú, and Yú perished;
He was in Qín, and Qín became hegemonic.
It was not that he lacked talent in Yú but had talent in Qín.
Zhāng Liáng received the tally from Huángshí,
Studied the teachings of the *Three Strategies*,
And traveled among the many warlords.
His words then
Were like throwing water on stone—
None accepted them.
But when he encountered Hàn Gāozǔ,
His words then
Were like throwing stone into water—
None opposed them.
It was not that Zhāng Liáng spoke clumsily to Chén Shè and Xiàng Yǔ
But skillfully to Péigōng.
Yet Zhāng Liáng’s words were the same.
Do we not understand the reason for their acceptance or rejection?
The reason for acceptance or rejection
Lies in the way of divine understanding.
Thus, those four worthies
Had their names recorded in prophetic charts,
And their deeds corresponded with Heaven and humanity.
How could they be measured by mere wisdom or folly?
Confucius said:
“When clarity and brightness reside in one’s person,
One’s energy and will are like spirits.
When desires are about to arise,
There must be an opening beforehand.
When Heaven sends timely rain,
Clouds emerge from the mountains and rivers.”
The *Book of Songs* says:
“The sacred mountain sends down spirits,
Giving birth to Fǔ and Shēn;
It is Shēn and Fǔ
Who are the pillars of Zhōu.”
This is what is meant by fate.
Is it only for rising rulers?
Those who bring chaos and ruin are also like this.
King Yōu’s infatuation with Bāo Sì
Began with the ominous signs in the Xià court.
Cáo Bóyáng’s encounter with Gōngsūn Qiáng
Was foretold by signs at the village altar.
Shūsūn Bào’s closeness to Shù Niú
Led to disaster arising from Gēngzōng.
Good fortune, misfortune, success, and failure
Each arrive according to their destined numbers.
All come together without seeking,
And grow close without introduction.
In ancient times,
the sages received the mandate at Héluò, saying:
Those who rise through civil virtue
decline after seven or nine generations;
those who flourish through martial prowess
plan after six or eight generations.
When King Chéng fixed the tripods at Jiárǔ,
it was divined that the dynasty would last for thirty reigns,
and seven hundred years—
such was the mandate of Heaven.
Thus, from the time between Yōu and Lì,
the Way of Zhōu greatly deteriorated;
after the two hegemons,
rites and music fell into decline.
The shallowness of culture,
began with Líng and Jǐng;
the deceit of sophistry and cunning,
culminated in the Seven States.
The extreme of cruelty,
accumulated in the doomed Qín;
the value of literary refinement,
was discarded by Hàn’s founder.
Even Confucius, the supreme sage,
and Yán Huí and Rǎn Gēng, great worthies,
bowing and yielding within the bounds of propriety,
earnestly discoursing along the Zhū and Sì rivers,
could not halt its beginnings;
Mèng Kē and Xún Qīng,
embodying duality and aspiring to sagehood,
composedly following the correct Way,
could not sustain its end,
and the world ultimately sank beyond rescue.
With Confucius’s talent,
his capacity was not fully employed in Lǔ or Wèi;
with Confucius’s eloquence,
his words were not heeded by Dìng or Āi;
with Confucius’s humility,
he was envied by Zǐxī;
with Confucius’s benevolence,
he incurred the hatred of Huán Tuí;
with Confucius’s wisdom,
he suffered hardship in Chén and Cài;
with Confucius’s conduct,
he attracted slander from Shūsūn.
His Way was sufficient to save the world,
yet he was not valued by men;
his words were sufficient to guide ten thousand generations,
yet they were not trusted in his time;
his actions were sufficient to respond to the spirits,
yet they could not encompass the customs of the age;
he offered his service to seventy states,
yet not once did he gain a true lord;
he hastened through the realms of barbarians and Huáxià,
suffering humiliation at the gates of dukes and ministers—
such was his lack of recognition.
As for his grandson Zǐsī,
he aspired to sagehood and possessed the form but did not attain it;
wrapping himself in self-regard and cultivating loftiness,
his influence moved the rulers.
The feudal lords he visited,
all came with teams of four horses to his gate;
yet even those who came were not all treated as guests.
His disciple Zǐxià,
ascended the hall but did not enter the inner chamber.
Retiring in old age to his home,
Lord Wén of Wèi took him as teacher;
the people of Xīhé reverently turned to his virtue,
comparing him to the Master, and none dared question his words.
Thus it is said:
Order and chaos,
are a matter of fortune;
adversity and success,
are a matter of fate;
nobility and baseness,
are a matter of timing.
Yet later gentlemen,
cling anxiously to a single lord,
sighing over a single court.
Qū Yuán thereby drowned himself in the Xiāng,
Jiǎ Yì thereby vented his indignation—
is this not excessive?
Yet the reason why sages are sages,
lies precisely in rejoicing in Heaven and knowing fate.
Thus they encounter without resentment,
dwell without doubt.
Their persons may be suppressed,
but their Way cannot be bent;
their positions may be pushed aside,
but their names cannot be taken.
They are like water:
channel it, and it becomes a river;
dam it, and it becomes a deep pool;
raise it to the clouds, and it falls as rain;
sink it into the earth, and it moistens the soil.
Its substance is clear, washing things,
untainted by turbidity;
it receives turbidity to aid things,
unharmed in its clarity.
Therefore, sages remain the same in adversity and success.
That loyalty and uprightness offend the ruler,
and independence bears the burden of convention,
is the natural course of principle and circumstance.
Thus, a tree that towers in the forest
is sure to be felled by the wind;
a mound that protrudes from the bank
is sure to be eroded by the current;
conduct that rises above others
is sure to be condemned by the multitude.
The mirror of the past is not far,
yet overturned carts follow the same tracks.
Nevertheless, men of purpose and benevolence
still tread this path without regret,
hold to it without losing it—
why?
It is to fulfill their purpose and achieve renown.
Seeking to fulfill their purpose,
they brave wind and waves on perilous roads;
seeking to achieve their name,
they endure slander and criticism in their time.
Their way of handling it
is surely calculated.
Zǐxià said:
“Life and death are a matter of fate,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven.”
Thus, when the Way is about to prevail,
and fate is about to bring honor,
then Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shǎng rise in Shāng and Zhōu,
Bǎilǐ Xī and Zhāng Liáng are employed in Qín and Hàn—
unsought, they are obtained;
unasked, they are encountered.
When the Way is about to be abandoned,
and fate is about to bring baseness,
is it only that gentlemen are ashamed and refrain from action?
They surely also know that action would be futile.
All those who seek worldly favor and compromise,
the fawning and sycophantic,
bowing to the faces of the noble,
meandering between power and profit,
their minds devoid of right and wrong,
praise flows like water;
their words without affirmation or denial,
response echoes like sound.
They take spying and watching as their spirit,
and shifting with the wind as their adaptability.
Where power gathers,
they flock like a market;
where power departs,
they cast it off like shedding a burden.
They say:
“Which is dearer, name or self?
Which is worthier, gain or loss?
Which is more precious, glory or disgrace?”
Thus they adorn their clothing,
show off their carriages and followers,
flaunt their wealth and bribes,
indulge in music and beauty,
smugly thinking themselves successful.
They see Lóng Péng and Bǐ Gàn losing their lives,
but do not consider Fēi Lián and È Lái exterminating their clans.
They know Wǔ Zǐxū receiving the sword Zhǔlòu in Wú,
but are not warned by Fèi Wújì’s execution and extermination in Chǔ.
They ridicule Jí Àn growing old in the office of Zhǔjué,
but are not chastened by Zhāng Tāng’s calamity of the ox-cart.
They laugh at Xiāo Wàngzhī stumbling and falling earlier,
but do not fear Shí Xiǎn’s strangulation later.
Thus, the calculations of the enlightened ones,
each also have their limits.
It is said: Why do ordinary people rush and strive for wealth and honor?
What is the purpose?
If establishing virtue must rely on high status,
then the reigns of Yōu and Lì as Sons of Heaven
are inferior to Confucius serving as a vassal minister.
If it must rely on power,
then Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Xián serving as the Three Dukes
are inferior to Yáng Xióng and Dǒng Zhòngshū with their quiet doors.
If it must rely on wealth,
then the thousand chariots of Duke Jǐng of Qí
are inferior to Yán Huí and Yuán Xiàn restraining themselves.
Is it for material goods?
Then one who scoops water from a river with a ladle
can drink no more than a full belly;
one who discards shelter and stands in the rain
can only get his body wet;
beyond this,
nothing more can be received.
Is it for fame?
Then good and evil are recorded in historical annals,
praise and blame flow through a thousand years;
rewards and punishments hang upon the Way of Heaven,
fortune and misfortune are illuminated by ghosts and spirits—
truly, these are fearsome.
Is it to please the ears and eyes,
to delight the heart and mind?
It is like commanding a carriage to tour the markets of the five capitals—
then all the goods under heaven are displayed.
Lifting one's robes to cross the hills of Wènyáng—
then the crops under heaven are like clouds.
With hair tied simply, guarding the granaries of Áo Yǔ and Hǎilíng—
then mountainous stores lie before one.
Tucking in one's lapels to ascend the peaks of Zhōngshān and Lántián—
then the treasures of night-lustrous pearls and fine jade can be seen.
Thus being so,
the things are many,
but what is for oneself is very little.
Not loving one's own body,
yet begrudging one's spirit.
Wind alarms, dust rises,
scattering without cease.
Six ailments await before them,
five punishments follow behind.
Gain and harm arise on their left,
attack and plunder emerge on their right—
yet they themselves believe they perceive the closeness or distance of body and fame,
distinguishing host and guest in glory and disgrace.
Heaven and Earth's great virtue is called life;
the sage's great treasure is called position.
How to maintain position is called benevolence;
how to rectify people is called righteousness.
Thus the kings of old
governed all under heaven by means of one person,
not using all under heaven to serve one person.
The officials of old
used their office to practice righteousness,
not using profit to risk their office.
The noble persons of old
were ashamed to gain something and not be able to govern it,
not ashamed to be able to govern and not gain it.
Examining the nature of Heaven and humanity,
scrutinizing the distinction between evil and upright,
weighing the gateway of calamity and fortune,
and concluding with the calculation of glory and disgrace—
this is clear indeed.
Thus the noble person rejects that and chooses this.
As for advancing or withdrawing without violating the times,
remaining silent or speaking without missing the right person—
though Heaven moves and stars revolve, the celestial pole remains in its place;
though the jade sphere rotates and wheels turn,
the central axis still holds its position—
being both enlightened and wise,
to preserve one's person,
leaving plans for descendants,
to protect and assist sons—
my former friend of old
once engaged in such conduct.
In the past, when the Hàn dynasty lost control,
treacherous ministers stole the mandate,
calamity was rooted in the capital region,
poison spread throughout the realm.
The imperial order slackened and fell into chaos,
the royal house thus declined.
Then heroes swarmed like bees, rising in alarm,
righteous troops assembled from all sides.
The Martial and Fierce Emperor of Wú, impassioned from his lower state,
struck like lightning from southern Jīng,
his strategies and tactics numerous and varied,
his loyalty and bravery unmatched in his generation.
His awe-inspiring might shook even the barbarian Yí;
in battle, the ugly foes offered their severed ears.
Thus he swept clean the ancestral temples,
and offered sacrifice to the imperial ancestors.
At that time, generals rose like clouds, commanding provinces;
armies surged like whirlwinds, spanning cities.
Roaring hordes were driven like the wind;
hosts of bears and panthers gathered like mist.
Though troops united for righteousness,
allies joined forces,
yet all harbored treacherous hearts,
relying on arms and cherishing chaos.
Some leaders lacked strategic discipline,
losing prestige and emboldening enemies.
In loyal planning and martial integrity,
none were as illustrious as he.
After the Martial and Fierce Emperor passed away,
the Chángshā Huan King, with extraordinary talent renowned in his age,
showed brilliance while still young.
He gathered surviving elders,
and with them continued the enterprise.
Divine troops drove eastward,
the few daringly attacking the many.
In attack, no general defended an impregnable city;
in battle, no foe engaged him in combat.
Punishing rebels and pacifying the submissive,
he stabilized the region beyond the river;
reforming laws and training troops,
his awe and virtue became resplendent.
Honoring worthy men with guest rites,
Zhāng Zhāo became the foremost among them;
associating with and employing heroes,
Zhōu Yú became the outstanding one.
Those two noble persons,
both broad-minded, keen, and full of marvels,
elegant, penetrating, intelligent, and wise.
Thus those of like direction attached by category;
those of equal bond gathered by shared spirit,
and Jiāngdōng indeed had many talented men.
He planned to campaign north against the various Huá states,
to eradicate those who violated the law.
To turn the imperial carriage back onto the level path,
and restore the imperial seat to the purple palace.
Holding the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords,
clearing Heaven's steps and returning to the old heritage.
War chariots already arrayed,
all villains watched with sidelong glances.
But the great enterprise not yet achieved,
he fell in mid-life.
Thus arose our Great Emperor.
With extraordinary traces following the path of the exceptional,
a sagely mind continuing the excellent plans.
In governance, he consulted old precedents;
in spreading laws, he examined inherited customs.
And to this he added deep steadfastness,
extending it with frugality.
Seeking out the talented and outstanding,
he was fond of planning and skilled in decision.
Silk bundles were presented in the hills and gardens;
banners of summons crisscrossed the streets and lanes.
Thus heroic men, hearing his reputation, responded and gathered;
aspiring scholars, hoping for his light, raced like shadows.
Extraordinary people converged like spokes;
fierce warriors stood like a forest.
Then Zhāng Zhāo served as mentor and tutor;
Zhōu Yú, Lord Lù, Lǚ Sù, Lǚ Méng, and their peers
entered as trusted advisors,
went out as pillars of support.
Gān Níng, Líng Tǒng, Chéng Pǔ, Hè Qí, Zhū Huán, Zhū Rán, and their like exerted their might;
Hán Dāng, Pān Zhāng, Huáng Gài, Jiǎng Qīn, Zhōu Tài, and their associates displayed their strength.
In refinement and elegance, Zhūgé Jǐn, Zhāng Chéng, Bù Zhì
brought glory to the state with their reputations;
in administration, Gù Yōng, Pān Jùn, Lǚ Fàn, Lǚ Dài
handled duties with their abilities and appointments;
in extraordinary greatness, Yú Fān, Lù Jī, Zhāng Wēn, Zhāng Dūn
offered remonstrance and discussion to correct affairs;
in diplomatic missions, Zhào Zī, Shěn Héng
won extended praise with their keen discernment;
in mystical arts, Wú Fàn, Zhào Dá
harmonized virtue with omens and portents.
Dǒng Xí, Chén Wǔ
gave their lives to protect their lord;
Luò Tǒng, Liú Jī
strongly remonstrated to correct faults.
No plan overlooked hidden schemes,
no action missed the proper strategy.
Thus they came to control mountains and rivers,
dominating Jīng and Wú,
and vied for supremacy with all under heaven.
The Wei clan once leveraged the prestige of military victories,
leading a million-strong army,
sailing the boats of Dèngsài,
descending with the masses of Hànyīn,
with countless feathered oars,
dragons leaping along the current,
a thousand brigades of sharp cavalry,
tigers striding across plains and marshes,
strategists filling the chambers,
generals forming alliances,
sighing with ambition to swallow the riverbanks,
unifying the spirit of the universe.
Yet Zhōu Yú drove our flank forces,
repelling them at Chìbì,
losing banners and scattering tracks,
barely escaping with their lives,
gathering traces and fleeing far away.
The King of Hàn also relied on the title of emperor,
commanding the people of Bā and Hàn,
seizing danger to enact change,
building fortifications over a thousand miles,
determined to avenge Guān Yǔ's defeat,
plotting to reclaim the lands west of Xiāng.
Yet Lord Lù also thwarted them at Xīlíng,
overturning their army and causing defeat,
struggling before finding relief,
meeting their end at Yǒng'ān.
Following with the incursion at Rúxū,
facing the river, their edge was shattered;
the battle at Pénglóng,
not a single wheel returned.
Thus, the generals of these two states,
lost morale and blunted their锋芒,
their momentum broken and resources depleted,
while Wú sat serenely, exploiting their weakness.
Therefore, the people of Wei sought peace,
the Hàn clan begged for alliance,
and thus ascended to heavenly titles,
standing like tripods in opposition.
To the west, they slaughtered in the outskirts of Yōng and Yì,
to the north, they split the banks of Huái and Hàn,
to the east, they encompassed the lands of Bǎiyuè,
to the south, they included the regions of the many Mán tribes.
Then they deliberated on the rites of eight dynasties,
searched for the music of three kings.
They reported to the Supreme Deity,
bowed to the assembled lords,
with fierce ministers and resolute soldiers,
guarding along the river,
long spears and strong halberds,
rising like whirlwinds in anticipation.
All officials offered their counsel above,
the four classes of people pursued their livelihoods below.
Culture harmonized with distant tribes,
customs spread to far borders.
Then they sent a single envoy,
to pacify and inspect foreign domains.
Giant elephants and swift steeds,
were tamed in outer stables;
bright pearls and precious gems,
shone in the inner treasury.
Rare treasures arrived repeatedly,
exotic curiosities responded to the call.
Light carriages galloped in the southern wilderness,
war chariots rested in the northern plains.
The common people were spared the calamity of war,
the army horses had no fear of morning harness.
And the imperial enterprise was secured.
After the Great Emperor passed away,
a young ruler ascended the court.
Treacherous officials ran rampant,
but Emperor Jǐng rose in response,
reverently upholding the inherited laws,
with governance free of major faults,
a good ruler who preserved the written ways.
Descending to the beginning of Guīmìng's reign,
the statutes and punishments had not yet perished,
the old veterans still remained.
The Grand Marshal Lù Gōng brought civil and military prosperity to the court,
the Left Chancellor Lù Kǎi offered forthright admonitions with full dedication,
while Shī Jì and Fàn Shèn were renowned for their威严,
Dīng Fèng and Lí Fěi were praised for their martial resolve,
figures like Mèng Zōng and Dīng Gù served as high ministers,
Lóu Xuán and Hè Shào oversaw confidential affairs,
though the head was ailing,
the limbs and bones still remained.
But as it reached the final age,
after all these lords had perished,
then the common people harbored thoughts of disintegration,
the royal house faced the fissure of collapse.
The ordained mandate responded to change and waned,
the royal army followed fortune and advanced.
Soldiers scattered on the battlefield,
people fled to the towns;
city walls lacked the solidity of fences,
mountains and rivers held no strategic advantage of trenches and mounds.
There were no artificer's cloud-ladder devices,
no calamities like Zhì Bó's flooding assaults,
no sieges like the Chǔ master's encirclement,
no armies like the Yān people's crossing west,
yet before a fortnight had passed,
the altars of state were leveled.
Though loyal ministers harbored solitary indignation,
and staunch men died for principle,
what could they have saved?
Now, the generals of Cáo and Liú,
were not selected in a single generation;
the armies of that time,
were no less numerous than in former days.
The principles of warfare and defense,
moreover had precedents to follow;
the advantages of terrain and obstacles,
remained unchanged in a short while.
Yet success and failure exchanged their logic,
ancient and modern diverged strangely in tendency,
why was this?
Because the transformations on each side differed,
and the talents entrusted with responsibility varied.
In the past, when the three kingdoms ruled,
the Wei people held the central plains,
the Hàn clan possessed Mín and Yì,
Wú controlled Jīng and Yáng and encompassed Jiāo and Guǎng.
Though the Cáo clan achieved merits benefiting all Huá,
their cruelty was also profound,
and their people resented them.
Lord Liú used peril to adorn his wisdom,
his achievements were already meager,
and his customs were crude.
As for Wú,
King Huán laid its foundation through martial prowess,
the Grand Ancestor completed it through virtue,
wise and profoundly discerning,
with noble measures far-reaching.
They sought worthy men as if fearing to miss them,
cared for the people as if for infants.
Receiving scholars with the utmost virtuous demeanor,
亲近 the benevolent with the full love of a sincere heart.
They elevated Lǚ Méng from the ranks of soldiers,
recognized Pān Jùn among captives.
Extending sincere trust to gentlemen,
not worrying about others deceiving them;
measuring ability to confer office,
not fearing authority pressing upon them.
Holding the whip and bowing respectfully,
to enhance the prestige of Lord Lù;
fully entrusting military defense,
to support Zhōu Yú's army.
Humble palaces and plain fare,
to enrich the rewards for meritorious officials;
opening their hearts and emptying themselves,
to accept the strategies of advisers.
Thus Lǔ Sù entrusted himself after a single meeting,
Shì Xiè braved danger to dedicate his life.
They exalted the virtue of Lord Zhāng,
and reduced the pleasures of excursions and hunts;
valued the words of Zhūgě,
and cut off the joys of personal desires.
Moved by the admonitions of Lord Lù,
they simplified the complexities of penal law;
marveling at Liú Jī's proposals,
they made the oath of three cups.
Holding their breath and treading carefully,
to attend to Zǐmíng's illness;
sharing provisions and reducing sweetness,
to nurture Líng Tǒng's orphan.
Ascending the altar with fervor,
they attributed the merit to Lǔ Zǐ;
discarding and rejecting slanderous words,
they trusted Zǐyú's integrity.
Therefore, loyal ministers vied to exhaust their strategies,
and men of purpose all could exert their strength.
Grand plans and far-reaching strategies,
certainly were not satisfied with petty concerns.
Thus, the hundred officials merely complied,
and myriad affairs were left unattended.
When the capital was first established at Jiànyè,
the ministers requested the establishment of proper ceremonial ranks,
but the Son of Heaven declined and did not permit it,
saying:
"What would the world think of me?"
Thus, the palaces, carriages, and ceremonial attire remained modest.
By the middle period,
the division between Heaven and humanity was already settled,
and the deficiencies in the various regulations were roughly repaired.
Although the profound transformation and excellent governance
did not match that of earlier generations,
still, the means for administering the state and managing the realm
were sufficient for governance.
The territory spanned nearly ten thousand *lǐ*,
with armored troops approaching a million,
its fields fertile,
its soldiers well-trained,
its weapons sharp,
and its wealth abundant.
To the east, it leaned upon the vast sea;
to the west, it was blocked by perilous passes;
the Long River defined its boundaries,
and towering mountains girded its frontiers.
The advantages of the state
had never been greater than this.
If a ruler of average talent could guard it with the Way,
or a virtuous person govern it with skill,
diligently following the inherited statutes,
attending to the people and governing prudently,
adhering to established policies,
and guarding the constant dangers,
then it could have endured for generations,
with no peril of downfall.
Some say:
Wú and Shǔ were interdependent states,
so when Shǔ perished, Wú would fall—
in principle, this is so.
Yet Shǔ
was but a supporting ally,
not the determinant of Wú's survival.
Why?
Their borders met
amidst layered mountains and accumulated perils,
with no broad paths for chariots on land;
the rivers were narrow and swift,
and the waters held the hardship of raging waves.
Even with a million crack troops,
those advancing could not exceed a thousand men;
even with a thousand *lǐ* of ships,
the vanguard could not surpass a hundred vessels.
Thus, when the Liú clan attacked,
Lord Lù compared it to a long serpent—
such was the natural disposition.
When Shǔ first fell,
court ministers had differing plans:
some wanted to pile stones to block the river's flow,
others wished to use mechanical devices to counter changes.
The Son of Heaven gathered all opinions and consulted the Grand Marshal Lord Lù Jī,
who said that the four great rivers are how Heaven and Earth regulate and diffuse their *qì*,
and thus cannot be forcibly obstructed;
while mechanical devices are shared by both sides.
If they abandoned their long-range skills for their shortcomings,
and contended with us in Jīng and Yáng over the use of boats,
then Heaven would be aiding us.
We should carefully guard the gorge entrance,
and await their capture.
When Bù Chǎn's rebellion arose,
he relied on fortified cities to harbor strong enemies,
and used great wealth to lure the various barbarians.
At that time, the masses of the great state
descended like clouds and lightning,
hanging banners along the riverbanks,
building fortresses following the islets,
grasping the vital points,
to halt the Wú people's westward advance.
Meanwhile, the Bā-Hàn naval forces sailed east down the river.
Lord Lù, with a detachment of thirty thousand troops,
held the eastern ridge to the north,
digging deep trenches and raising high ramparts,
resting his armor and nurturing his might.
The rebel, trapped and awaiting execution,
dared not look north for a path to life;
the powerful enemy, defeated, fled under cover of night,
losing more than half their army.
He then dispatched five thousand elite troops
to the west to counter the water forces,
achieving victory on both fronts,
with tens of thousands of captives taken.
Truly,
the plans of a worthy man—
how could they deceive us!
From then on, beacon fires rarely gave alarm,
and the borders saw little trouble.
But after Lord Lù's death, hidden schemes arose,
and as Wú's internal strife deepened, the six armies were thrown into panic.
In the Tàikāng campaign,
the enemy forces were not larger than in former days;
in the Guǎngzhōu rebellion,
the calamity was no greater than past difficulties.
Yet the state was overthrown,
and the ancestral temples became ruins.
Alas!
"When men are lost,
the state is stricken"—
is this not so?
The *Yìjīng* says:
"The revolutions of Tāng and Wǔ
were in accord with Heaven."
Xuán states:
"If disorder does not reach its extreme, order does not take form."
This speaks of emperors and kings following Heaven's timing.
The ancients said:
"Heaven's timing is not as good as Earth's advantages."
The *Yìjīng* says:
"Kings and marquises establish perils
to guard their states."
This speaks of relying on strategic advantages for the state.
It is also said:
"Earth's advantages are not as good as human harmony,"
and "It lies in virtue, not in perils."
This speaks of human factors in guarding strategic advantages.
When Wú rose,
it combined all three factors,
as Xúnzǐ called "uniting the three."
When it fell,
it relied only on strategic advantages,
again as Xúnzǐ called "abandoning the three."
The people of the four provinces were not few,
the talents south of the Great River were not lacking,
the mountains and rivers were easily defensible,
the sharp weapons were easily wielded,
and the policies of former rulers were easily followed.
Why then did achievements not arise, and calamity instead be encountered?
Why?
Because those who employed these means were at fault.
Therefore, the former sages understood the enduring principles of statecraft,
and discerned the ultimate patterns of survival and downfall;
they humbled themselves to pacify the common people,
and practiced kindness to achieve human harmony;
they were broad and open to attract the counsel of the talented,
and kind and gentle to win the affection of scholars and people.
Thus, when at peace,
the masses rejoiced with them;
and when in peril,
the multitude shared hardship with them.
When peace is shared in celebration with the masses,
then peril cannot befall;
when hardship is shared with the people,
then difficulty is not to be feared.
In this way,
they could preserve their altars of soil and grain,
and secure their territory,
so that "the wheat sprouts" brought no sorrow for Yīn,
and "the millet grows" evoked no lament for Zhōu.
Administering the state and organizing the land
was something the former kings treated with care;
establishing institutions and laying foundations
aimed to prosper later generations.
Yet methods of governance differed,
and techniques for enduring varied.
The system of five ranks
began with Huángdì and Táng.
The administration of commanderies and counties
was created by Qín and Hàn.
Successes, failures, gains, and losses
are all recorded in the classics,
so their details
can be discussed.
The former kings knew that the imperial enterprise was of utmost importance,
and the realm was of utmost vastness.
Vastness cannot be governed through partial control,
and importance cannot be borne alone;
bearing great responsibility must rely on borrowed strength,
and governing vastness ultimately depends on others.
Therefore, they established offices and divided duties,
to lighten their burden;
and appointed five chiefs,
to expand their governance.
Thus, they established the statutes for territorial boundaries,
determined the appropriate degrees of kinship,
so that the myriad states supported one another,
forming a solid foundation like a massive rock;
with the royal clan and commoners living intermingled,
they secured the enterprise of maintaining the city walls.
Moreover, they understood the long-term governance of pacifying the world,
and recognized the fundamental principles of human nature;
knowing that benefiting others is not as good as enriching oneself,
and that aiding others is not as good as planning for oneself;
the stability of the ruler lies in pleasing the people,
and self-interest lies in benefiting others.
Therefore, the *Yìjīng* says:
"If you make the people happy,
they will forget their toil."
Xúnzǐ said:
"To benefit others without benefiting oneself
is not as good as benefiting oneself and then benefiting others."
Thus, they shared the wealth of the world to bring great joy,
while they themselves shared in its worries;
they allowed the world to enjoy abundant benefits,
while they themselves shared in its harms.
When benefits are widespread, kindness becomes deep;
when joy is far-reaching, worries become profound.
Therefore, the feudal lords enjoyed the reality of ruling their lands,
and the myriad states received the blessings of hereditary succession.
In this way,
the rulers facing south,
each focused on their governance;
the people within the nine regions,
knew they had a settled lord.
Thus, the ruler's affection was born,
and the people's trust was solidified.
In times of good governance, it was sufficient to uphold customs;
in times of declining principles, it was sufficient to resist tyranny.
Thus, strong and resolute states
could not monopolize power for a time;
heroic and outstanding individuals
had no place to harbor ambitions of hegemony.
Then, the stability of the state relied on the myriad states' desire for order,
and the ruler's dignity depended on the feudal lords' planning for themselves.
It is like many eyes watching in all directions,
so the net of heaven naturally becomes clear;
the four limbs avoid difficulties,
and the heart and spine are preserved.
This is why the Three Dynasties followed the right path,
and the Four Kings established lasting achievements.
The rise and fall, prosperity and decline,
are inherently governed by principle;
the abandonment and revival of teachings
depend on the people.
Hopes for laws may end in disappointment,
and bright principles may sometimes become obscure.
Thus, the system of hereditary succession
became corrupted by powerful oppression;
the statutes of enriching the lower ranks
leaked away due to minor fractures.
The transgression of encroaching on the weak
began in the three declining ages;
the disaster of gradual decline
culminated in the Seven Hegemons.
In the past, Chéng Tāng personally observed the mirror of the Xià dynasty,
and Zhōu Gōng Dàn witnessed the warnings of the Shāng people;
refinement and substance complemented each other,
and adjustments and benefits were made accordingly.
Therefore, the rituals of the five ranks
were not abolished in their time,
and the system of territorial boundaries
was elevated accordingly.
How could they have ignored the disasters of the two kings
and been blind to the calculations of governing the world?
They certainly knew that a hundred generations could not be governed by rigid rules,
and that even good systems could not be without flaws.
Yet the disgrace of encroaching on the weak
is worse than the extinction of sacrifices,
and the distress of collapse
is more painful than gradual decline.
Therefore, they began by weighing the greater blessings,
and considered the end by taking the lesser calamities.
This does not mean that feudal lords and earls had no potential for chaos,
or that commanderies and counties were not tools for achieving order.
Thus, the state's worries relied on them to relinquish their positions,
and the ruler's weakness depended on them for support.
When they inherited decline and accumulated flaws,
the royal house became humble,
yet they still preserved their names and positions,
passing down blessings to later generations.
The imperial lineage, though obscured, did not cease,
and the sacred vessel, though blocked, necessarily endured.
Was this not due to the establishment of power making it so?
Descending to the fallen Qín,
they abandoned the Way and relied on tactics,
punishing the failures of Zhōu,
and boasting of their own achievements.
They sought axes from those they sheltered,
and governed the state ignorantly by weakening the lower ranks.
The state's celebrations were enjoyed alone,
and the ruler's worries were not shared with others.
Though they hastened their downfall and rushed into chaos,
it was not necessarily due to one principle alone;
the calamity of collapse
truly arose from isolation.
This was because they considered the minor grievances of the five ranks,
and forgot the great virtue of the myriad states;
they knew the worry of gradual decline,
but were blind to the pain of collapse.
The decline of Zhōu
had its origins.
The state lacked good rulers
for more than ten generations,
yet with a single word to serve the king,
the feudal lords would surely respond;
with one moment of arrogance,
distant states would rebel first.
Thus, the powerful Jìn restrained its ambition to request the tunnel burial,
and the violent Chǔ halted its desire to inspect the tripods.
How could Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ have dared to breach the passes,
or Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng have dared to raise their banners in the marshes?
If the Qín people had followed the Zhōu system,
even if they were without the Way,
they would have had others to share their flaws,
and the disaster of overthrow
would not have occurred as it did in the past!
Hàn corrected Qín's errors,
greatly establishing feudal kings.
Their territories overflowed,
not following the old statutes.
Therefore, Jiǎ Yì worried about their danger,
and Cháo Cuò lamented their chaos.
Thus, the feudal lords relied on the wealth of their states,
and the strength of their people.
Those with sufficient power rebelled quickly,
while those with narrow lands resisted slowly.
Six ministers violated the weak net,
and seven sons exploited the leaky web.
The imperial ancestor was humiliated by tattooed convicts,
and the Western Capital suffered from the Eastern Emperor.
This was the disaster of excessive correction,
not the burden of establishing feudal lords.
Yet during the crisis of the Lǚ clan,
the court officials looked outward;
Sòng Chāng, in planning for Hàn,
always praised the feudal lords.
By the middle period,
fearing their loss of integrity,
they cut down and weakened the imperial clansmen,
leaving them with names but no substance.
The world became vast and empty,
again following the path of fallen Qín.
Thus, the five marquises wielded power,
disregarding the myriad states;
Xīndū usurped Hàn,
as easily as picking up something dropped.
Guāngwǔ revived the dynasty,
continuing the imperial lineage,
yet still followed the tracks of the overturned cart,
nurturing the chronic illness of a ruined family.
In just a few generations,
traitors and villains filled the land.
Finally, when powerful ministers monopolized the court,
the world followed like the wind;
when one man acted recklessly,
the city walls crumbled on their own.
How could this not be dangerous!
In the decline of Zhōu,
difficulties arose for the royal house.
Seven ministers abandoned their duties,
and three sons usurped positions.
The succeeding king abandoned the nine tripods,
and wicked clans seized the heavenly capital.
War drums shook within the palace gates,
and arrows flew into the crimson towers.
Yet the disaster stopped at the capital region,
and the harm did not spread far.
The world remained peaceful,
awaiting order amidst chaos.
Thus, King Xuān arose during the Gònghé period,
and King Xiāng and King Huì were supported by Jìn and Zhèng.
How could this compare to the two Hàn dynasties,
where disturbances at the palace steps
caused the four seas to boil,
and when treacherous ministers entered the court in the morning,
the nine regions were thrown into chaos by evening!
Looking back at the distant usurpation and rebellion of Wáng Mǎng,
and observing the recent era of Dǒng Zhuó’s arrogation of power,
hundreds of millions mourned in their hearts,
and both the foolish and the wise shared the same grief.
Yet the Zhōu dynasty survived through such events,
while the Hàn perished because of them.
What is the reason for this?
Was it that the age lacked ministers like those of old,
or that scholars no longer possessed the ambition to restore and unite the realm?
It is rather that distant achievements were thwarted by changed times,
