In recent times, there were Liú Huán of the Pei State,
and his younger brother Liú Jìn,
both outstanding scholars of their era.
Huán was known as the Confucius west of the Pass,
well-versed in the Six Classics,
patient and adept at guiding others,
devoted to Confucian conduct.
Jìn possessed a will as stern as autumn frost,
a heart as pure as Kūnlún jade,
tall and upright,
untainted by worldly dust.
Both cultivated virtue in humble gates,
and their fame spread across heaven and earth.
Yet their official posts were merely minor court attendants,
their ranks never reaching that of halberd-bearers;
they passed away one after another,
with no descendants to offer sacrifices.
Using these two worthies to speak of antiquity,
then those of jade-like quality and gold-like appearance,
the brilliant and outstanding talents,
were all rejected in their own time,
their rare abilities concealed and unused,
withering along with plants and trees,
dying together with deer in the wild,
their fat smearing the plains,
their bones filling rivers and valleys,
buried and forgotten without a trace—
how could such cases be fully recounted!
This shows that between chief ministers and petty clerks,
between Róng and Péng and children who die young,
between Yī Dùn and Qián Lóu,
between Yáng Wén and Dūn Qià—
all attain their lot by nature,
not by reliance on talent or wisdom.
Hence it is said:
"Life and death are decreed by fate,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
This is what it means.
Yet the substance of fate circulates everywhere,
its transformations are not uniform:
some first weep and later laugh,
some begin auspiciously and end in misfortune,
some come without being summoned,
some succeed through the aid of others.
Intertwined and entangled,
turning and shifting,
it cannot be verified by a single principle,
nor tested by a single path.
Its way is subtle and obscure,
silent and elusive,
with no form to be seen,
no sound to be heard.
It must manifest its efficacy through events,
and also rely on people to take shape;
like the emperor's crown with its pendants,
entrusting duties to the hundred officials.
Yet some, seeing Tāng and Wǔ's dragon-like rise,
claim quelling chaos lies in divine power;
hearing of Confucius and Mozi's outstanding birth,
say exceptional wisdom alone produces extraordinary fame;
observing Péng Yuè and Hán Xìn's leopard-like transformation,
assert fierce prowess leads to noble rank;
seeing Zhāng Tāng and Huán Róng's vermilion insignia,
declare mastering classics yields high office.
Do they not know that a powerful force moves them onward?
Thus, to speak without acknowledging fate
entails six delusions.
Allow me to outline them.
Now, smooth skin and fine texture,
or gaping mouth and furrowed brow—
these are differences in form.
Morning blooms that die by evening,
tortoises and cranes living a thousand years—
these are disparities in lifespan.
Hearing words and responding like an echo,
or being confused even about beans and wheat—
these are distinctions in intelligence.
Knowing that these three are determined by the Creator's realm of glory and disgrace,
yet insisting they depend solely on man—
this is to know two and five but not recognize ten.
This is the first delusion.
Dragon-like brow and sun-like forehead—
these are marks of an emperor;
river-like eyes and tortoise-shell patterns—
these are signs of a duke or marquis.
Gazing in a mirror foretells impending punishment;
pressing a knob reveals one's destined reign.
Starry rainbows and pivotal lightning—
these illuminate tokens of sage virtue;
nocturnal weeping and gathering clouds—
these amass omens for a rising king.
All portents emerge in advance,
and fulfillment comes in later ages.
If one claims to drive fierce warriors,
wield a short sword,
enter the Purple Palace,
and ascend the imperial way—
then one fails to grasp the profound mysteries,
and cannot fathom the divine calculations.
This is the second delusion.
The village of Kōngsāng
turned into a great river;
the capital of Lìyáng
transformed into a realm of fish and turtles.
When Chǔ troops slaughtered Hàn soldiers,
the Suī River clogged with their bodies;
when Qín men buried Zhào troops alive,
the seething sound was like thunder.
When fire engulfed Kūnlún,
common stones and fine jade burned together;
when harsh frost fell at night,
weeds and orchids perished alike.
Even with the talent of Zǐyóu and Zǐxià,
or the near-perfection of Yī Yǐn and Yán Huí,
who could withstand such forces?
This is the third delusion.
Some say the bright moon pearl
cannot be without flaws;
the jade of Emperor Yǔ
cannot be without cracks.
Thus, Tíng Bó died as a county magistrate,
and Xiàngrú passed away as a park superintendent.
Their talents were not unremarkable,
their rulers were not unenlightened,
yet the great splendor of Jiélǜ jade was shattered,
the night-glowing beauty of Xuánlí jade was damaged—
was it because the ruler's measure was too short?
If so,
when Zhǔfǔ Yǎn and Gōngsūn Hóng failed in their examinations,
wandered preaching without gaining entry,
herded pigs in Zīyuán,
and were rejected by their districts—
had they then suddenly vanished like a gap,
perishing swiftly from frost and dew,
would their shame and disgrace
not rival that of Cuī Yuān and Mǎ Sī?
Yet later, opening the eastern gate,
arraying the five tripods,
like lightning flashing and wind blowing,
their fame spreading across the seas—
were they foolish before and wise after?
Wrong at first and right in the end?
Or do glory and decline have fixed numbers,
does Heaven's decree have ultimate limits,
while beauty and ugliness arise erroneously?
This is the fourth delusion.
When the tiger roars, the wind races;
when the dragon rises, clouds gather.
Thus, when Chónghuá ascended, the Yuán and Kǎi were promoted;
when Shòu of Xīn was born, Fēi Lián advanced.
Yet in the world, good men are few,
evil men are many;
benighted rulers abound,
enlightened monarchs are rare.
Fragrant herbs and foul weeds do not share the same vessel;
owls and phoenixes do not wing together.
Thus, Hùndūn and Táowù tread upon the Cloud Terrace,
while Zhòng Róng and Tíng Jiān plow beneath rocky cliffs.
To claim arbitrarily that rise and fall lie with man,
unconnected to Heaven—
this is the fifth delusion.
Those barbarians of the west and north—
human-faced but beast-hearted,
indulging in poison as if at feast,
taking slaughter as morality,
incest as benevolence and righteousness—
even if the Great Wind stood at Qīngqiū,
or Zǎochǐ raged in Huá's wilds,
compared to their wolfish ferocity,
how could these suffice as metaphors?
Since the Metal Virtue declined,
heaven and earth fell into chaos;
those with boiling lips on the left,
seizing the moment, flashed like lightning,
overwhelmed Luòyáng and Chánshuǐ,
toppled the five capitals,
dwelt in the mulberry and catalpa lands of former kings,
usurped titles in the central counties,
vied with the Three Sovereigns for their people,
contended with the Five Emperors for their domains,
their tribes flourishing densely,
filling the Divine Land.
Alas!
"Bless the good and curse the wicked"—
mere empty words!
Is it not that adversity and prosperity displace each other,
fullness and waning alternate in cycle,
yet man muddles this process?
This is the sixth delusion.
Now, what is referred to as destiny encompasses
life and death,
nobility and baseness,
wealth and poverty,
order and chaos,
fortune and misfortune.
These ten things
are bestowed by Heaven.
Foolishness and wisdom, goodness and evil,
these four things
are enacted by humans.
Now, if one’s spirit is not like Shùn or Yǔ,
and one’s heart differs from Zhū and Jūn,
yet one’s talent is tethered to mediocrity,
it lies in what one practices.
Therefore, plain silk has no constancy;
dark and yellow hues arise in turn.
Salted fish and fragrant orchids,
once entered, change of themselves.
Thus, Jìlù studied under Zhòngní,
and tempered a character that endured wind and frost;
Chǔ Mù conspired with Pān Chóng,
and brought about the calamity of regicide.
Yet the wickedness of Shāngchén
made his grand enterprise shine upon his descendants;
the goodness of Zhòngyóu
could not halt the tying of his cap-strings.
This shows that depravity and rectitude depend on man,
while fortune and misfortune reside in destiny.
Some say ghosts and spirits harm the full,
and August Heaven assists the virtuous.
Thus, with one word from the Duke of Sòng,
the law-star shifted thrice;
the Emperor of Yīn cut himself,
and clouds came from a thousand lǐ.
If good and evil brought no evidence,
this principle would not be understood.
Moreover, Yú Gōng built a high gate awaiting enfeoffment;
Yán’s mother swept the grave awaiting mourning;
this is how the gentleman strives without cease.
If benevolence brought no recompense,
why would one cultivate goodness and establish a name?
This is an extreme statement.
Now, the words of the sage are clear yet obscure,
subtle yet tactful,
profound and distant, hard to hear,
vast as the Milky Way and unfathomable.
Sometimes he establishes teachings to advance the mediocre and lazy,
sometimes speaks of destiny to exhaust the nature and spirit.
"Accumulate goodness, and there will be surplus blessings" —
this is establishing teachings;
"The phoenix does not come" —
this is speaking of destiny.
Now, to discern their essential purport from a fragment of their words —
how is this different from a creature that dies at dusk discoursing on the changes of spring and autumn?
Moreover, Jīng Zhāo had virtuous words,
yet crimson clouds did not roll back;
Zhōu Xuān prayed for rain,
and the jade tablets were exhausted;
Old Man Yú planted virtue,
yet did not reach the heights of Xūn and Huá;
Yánnián was cruel and fierce,
yet not as severe as Dōnglíng’s cruelty.
Doing good is one,
doing evil is the same,
yet fortune and misfortune differ in their course,
decline and prosperity vary in their traces.
Vast and majestic is the Lord on High —
could He be like this?
The Odes say:
"The wind and rain are dark as night,
the cocks crow without cease."
Therefore, the good man does good.
How could he ever cease?
Now, to eat fine grains,
to present fodder and livestock,
to wear fox and badger furs,
to don ice-silk garments,
to watch the wondrous dances of the graceful,
to listen to the lutes and zithers of Yúnhé —
these are what living men urgently desire,
not done for any specific aim.
To cultivate the Way and virtue,
to practice benevolence and righteousness,
to honor filial and fraternal duty,
to establish loyalty and steadfastness,
to gradually imbibe the richness of ritual and music,
to tread the glorious norms of the former kings —
these are what the gentleman urgently pursues,
not done for any specific aim.
Thus, the gentleman abides in rectitude and embodies the Way,
rejoices in Heaven and knows destiny,
understands what cannot be helped,
recognizes what does not depend on intellect or strength.
When things depart, he does not summon them;
when they come, he does not reject them.
He does not rejoice in life,
nor grieve at death.
Jade towers and summer houses
cannot please his spirit;
earthen rooms and thatched huts
are not enough to trouble his thoughts.
He is not elated by wealth and honor,
nor anxious about his desires.
How could there be writings like those of Sīmǎ Qiān or Dǒng Zhòngshū about not meeting one’s time?
A guest asked his host:
"Zhū Gōngshū’s 'Discourse on Severing Friendships' —
is it right?
Or is it wrong?"
The host said:
"Why does the guest ask this?"
The guest said:
"When grass insects chirp, the mound locusts leap;
when the striped tiger roars, the clear wind arises.
Thus, through subtle interaction they stir each other,
mists surge and clouds steam;
through calling and answering they summon each other,
stars flow and lightning flashes.
Therefore, when Wáng Yáng rose, Gǒng Gōng rejoiced;
when Hǎn Shēng passed away, Guó Zǐ grieved.
Moreover, when hearts harmonize like lute and zither,
words are fragrant as orchids and angelica;
when the Way joins like glue and lacquer,
aims are lovely as ocarina and flute.
Sages and worthies thus engraved metal plates and inscribed bowls,
wrote on jade tablets and carved bells and tripods.
If even the craftsman ceased his wondrous skill of catching the wind,
and Bóyǎ ended his elegant strains of flowing waves,
Fàn and Zhāng were sincere at Xiàquán,
Yǐn and Bān were joyful through the long night.
Continuous and crisscrossing,
like mist scattering and rain dispersing,
even the cleverest reckoner cannot know it,
the most calculating mind cannot fathom it.
Yet Zhū of Yìzhōu muddied the constant order,
violated the canons and instructions,
attacked straightforward honesty,
and severed friendships.
He compared the black-haired people to hawks and sparrowhawks,
and matched human intelligence to wolves and tigers.
I have doubts about this,
and beg to resolve my confusion."
The host listened and said with a smile:
"What the guest calls plucking strings for fine music
fails to grasp how dryness and dampness change the sound;
setting nets in a marsh
does not see the wild geese flying through clouds.
For the sage holds the golden mirror,
elucidates the ethos of the age.
The dragon soars, the inchworm bends,
following the Way’s rise and fall.
Sun and moon joined as paired jades
praise the grand achievement of diligence;
clouds fly and lightning approaches
reveal the subtle intent of the flowering cherry.
Like the variations of the five notes,
they complete the wondrous melody of the ninefold music.
This is Zhū obtaining the dark pearl at Chìshuǐ,
planning with divine wisdom to speak.
As for weaving together benevolence and righteousness,
polishing and carving the Way and virtue,
sharing in their joys and pleasures,
sympathizing in their decline and fall,
entrusting connection beneath the spiritual tower,
leaving traces upon the rivers and lakes,
not ceasing their sound though wind and rain are fierce,
not changing their color though frost and snow fall,
this is the pure friendship of the worthy and enlightened,
encountered once in ten thousand ages.
But when it comes to the decadent age, with people corrupted,
cunning and deceit surge like a gale,
ravines and valleys cannot exceed their peril,
ghosts and spirits cannot fathom their changes.
They compete for the lightness of fur and feather,
rush after the tip of an awl or knife.
Then pure friendship ends,
and profit-based friendship arises.
All under heaven is in tumult,
birds startle and thunder terrifies.
Now, though profit-based friendship shares a single source,
its branches and streams differ.
To roughly state its outline,
there are five methods:
"If one's favor matches that of Dǒng Xián and Shí Xiǎn,
and power surpasses that of Liáng Jì and Dòu Xiàn,
carving and shaping all artisans,
forging and hammering myriad things.
Exhaling and inhaling stirs clouds and rain,
breathing in and out brings down frost and dew.
The nine domains tremble at his wind and dust,
the four seas are layered with his scorching heat.
None fail to race like stars at the sight of his shadow,
rushing like rivers at the sound of his echo.
When the rooster-caller first sings,
carriage canopies form a shade;
as the lofty gates open at dawn,
flowing carriages link like a stream.
All are willing to grind their heads to their heels,
shatter their gallbladders and spill their intestines,
pledging like Yào Lí to burn wife and children,
vowing to follow Jīng Kē in drowning seven clans.
This is called 'friendship of influence,'
its first current.
"Wealth rivaling Táo Zhūgōng and Bái Guī,
assets surpassing Chéng Zhèng and Luó Shì,
mountains monopolizing copper mines,
homes hiding gold-filled caves,
riding out on the plains with linked steeds,
residing in village lanes with bells chiming.
Then there are guests from poor alleys,
scholars with rope-hinged doors,
hoping for the last gleam of a night candle,
seeking a tiny favor from a richly adorned house;
like fish in a row or ducks leaping,
swarming and gathering like scales,
sharing the rice and grain of geese and ducks,
moistened by the leftover dregs of jade cups.
Grateful for the encounter,
offering sincere devotion,
pointing to green pines to show their hearts,
swearing by clear waters to pledge their faith.
This is called 'friendship of bribery,'
its second current.
"Minister Lù Jiǎ feasted joyfully in the western capital,
Guō Tà assessed human relations in the eastern state,
nobles and ministers valued their great reputations,
officials envied their ascension to immortality.
Moreover, with wrinkled brows and furrowed noses,
spitting and drooling foam,
galloping through intense debates like yellow horses,
unleashing heroic arguments like green roosters,
describing warmth so that cold valleys turn balmy,
discussing harshness so that spring clusters shed leaves,
rise and fall depend on their glance and gesture,
honor and disgrace are fixed by their single word.
Thus there are young scions of nobility,
dandy princes in silks,
whose ways are not noted by the learned,
whose fame has not reached the cloud-pavilions,
cling to their scales and wings,
beg for their leftover discourse,
attaching to the mane-tips of swift steeds,
surpassing returning geese at Jiéshí.
This is called 'friendship of talk,'
its third current.
"Sunny ease and gloomy distress,
are the great sentiments of living people;
sorrowful unions and joyful separations,
are the constant nature of all things.
Thus fish blow bubbles when springs dry up,
birds cry mournfully when near death.
Those with the same ailment pity each other,
composing sad songs by the river;
fear lodged in the heart,
illuminates the grand canon of the valley wind.
This is how unbreakable bonds arise from narrow huts,
and sworn friendship springs from thatched roofs.
Thus Wǔ Yuán was watered by Zǎi Pǐ,
and Zhāng Ěr found shelter under Chén Yú's wing.
This is called 'friendship of adversity,'
its fourth current.
"The customs of chasing fame,
the shallow-minded kind,
all wield scales,
hold fine floss.
The scale is to weigh their lightness or heaviness,
the floss is to test their breath.
If the scale cannot lift them,
the floss does not flutter,
even if they are like Yán Huí and Rǎn Qiú—phoenix chicks of dragons,
or Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú—orchid-fragrant and snow-white,
Shū Kuàng and Xiàng Sì—gold and jade in deep seas,
Qīng Yún and Fǔfú—embroidery in the Milky Way,
they are seen as drifting dust,
encountered as clay figurines,
none willing to spare half a bean,
rarely shedding a single hair.
If the scale tips by a hair's weight,
the floss flutters slightly,
even if they are like Gònggōng in hidden wickedness,
Huāndōu in covering righteousness,
the overbearing of southern Jīng,
the great villain of Dōnglíng,
all will crawl and wriggle,
break branches and lick hemorrhoids,
offering gold paste and kingfisher feathers to convey their intent,
using greasy flattery to guide their sincerity.
Thus where carriage wheels and canopies roam,
are surely not the homes of Bó Yí or Liǔ Xiàhuì;
where bribes enter,
are truly the houses of Zhāng Tāng and Huò Guāng.
Plan before acting,
with not a hair's breadth of error.
This is called 'friendship of measurement,'
its fifth current.
"All these five friendships,
are akin to buying and selling,
thus Huán Tán likened them to marketplaces,
Lín Huí compared them to sweet wine.
Now cold and heat alternate in progression,
prosperity and decline succeed each other,
some flourish first then wither later,
some start rich but end poor,
some exist at first but perish in the end,
some were frugal in ancient times but lavish now,
cycling and turning over,
swift as waves.
This shows that the sentiment of chasing profit never differs,
but the ways of change are not uniform.
From this perspective,
we can understand why Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú met a violent end,
and why Xiāo Wàngzhī and Zhū Bó ended in rift.
Clearly discernible.
Yet Duke Zhái meticulously carved admonitions for guests on his gate—
how belated was his realization!
"Because of these five friendships,
three conflicts arise:
ruining virtue and extinguishing righteousness,
resembling beasts and birds,
is the first conflict.
Hard to solidify, easy to split,
gathering enmity and disputes,
is the second conflict.
Names sinking into greed,
shamed by the upright and principled,
is the third conflict.
The ancients knew these three conflicts as obstructions,
feared the five friendships for hastening blame.
Thus Wáng Dān disciplined his son with catalpa rods,
Zhū Mù spoke boldly to show severance—
profound indeed!
Profound indeed!"
"In recent times, there was Rèn Fǎng of Lè'ān,
a distinguished talent within the realm,
who early on wore the silver and yellow seals of office,
and whose reputation among the people was long established.
His vigorous writings and beautiful phrases
rivaled those of Cáo Zhí and Wáng Càn;
his outstanding character and brilliant spirit
paralleled those of Xǔ Shào and Guō Tài.
Like Tián Wén, he loved to host guests;
like Zhèng Zhuāng, he delighted in worthy men.
Upon seeing a single good deed, he would widen his gaze and clench his wrist in admiration;
encountering a single talent, he would raise his eyebrows and clap his hands in praise.
Praise and criticism flowed from his lips,
and judgments of high and low proceeded from his monthly assessments.
Thus, officials and nobles converged like spokes to a hub,
their robes gathering like clouds,
their carriages and chariots jostling wheel to wheel,
and his seats were constantly filled with guests.
To tread upon his threshold
was like ascending to the hall of the Quèlǐ;
to enter his inner chambers
was said to be like climbing the slope of the Dragon Gate.
As for those he looked upon, their value doubled;
those he groomed and encouraged found their voices to neigh long.
Those who donned official silks and ascended the Yúntái rubbed shoulders;
those who hastened to the crimson-painted palace steps left overlapping footprints.
None failed to form bonds of deep affection,
to weave close ties of intimacy,
aspiring to the pure dust of Huì Shī and Zhuāng Zhōu,
hoping to emulate the noble deeds of Yáng Juéāi and Zuǒ Bó Táo.
But when he closed his eyes in the eastern lands of Yuè,
and his bones returned to the banks of the Luò River,
while the mourning curtain still hung,
his gate rarely saw scholars who came to sprinkle libations;
before grass had grown over his grave,
the countryside was devoid of guests whose carriages would stir.
His pitiful orphans,
uncertain from morning to evening,
drifted to the southern shores of the great sea,
entrusting their lives to a land of miasmal pestilence.
Yet those who were once arm-in-arm companions,
friends sworn like metal and orchid,
showed not a trace of the compassion that moved Yáng Shé to weep,
let alone aspiring to the virtue of Hòu Chéng, who divided his house.
"Alas!
The ways of the world are treacherous,
to such an extent!
Even the Tàiháng and Mèngmén mountains
could hardly be called precipitous in comparison.
Therefore, men of integrity,
disgusted by such a state,
tear their garments to wrap their feet,
and abandon it to flee far away.
They stand alone atop high mountain peaks,
happy to herd with deer and elk,
shining brightly, severed from the foul mist,
truly ashamed of it,
truly in awe of it."
Your servant has heard that as the sun declines and stars revolve,
the vault of heaven thereby orders all things;
as mountains fill and rivers flow,
the earth thereby disseminates its vital breath.
The Five Agents interact and thus achieve utility;
the Four Seasons alternate and thus complete the year.
Therefore, all officials diligently attend to their posts,
to contribute to the harmony of the eight tones;
the enlightened ruler holds the tally,
to achieve the convergence of perfect accord.
Your servant has heard that when responsibility exceeds strength,
talent is exhausted and hardship follows;
when use overextends the vessel,
responding too broadly brings misfortune.
Therefore, if the object outweighs the weight, the scale is endangered;
if the form exceeds the mirror, its reflection is exhausted.
Thus, an enlightened sovereign measures talent to verify achievement,
and loyal ministers exert their strength while declining excessive rewards.
Your servant has heard that men of eminent talent
are rare and scarce in the world;
the excellence hidden in hills and gardens
emerges according to the times.
Therefore, when a great man lays the foundation of his mandate,
he does not pluck talent from the earth;
when an enlightened ruler arises,
he does not have assistants sent down from the azure heavens.
Your servant has heard that what the world discards
is not necessarily worthless;
what the ruler treasures
is not always suited for governance.
Therefore, in the haunts of the worthy and able,
few receive the summons of the raised-chariot;
from the crags of gold and jade,
one is sure to disgrace the envoy of the phoenix's ascent.
Your servant has heard that emoluments bestowed through favoritism
are not the act of a family seeking greatness;
offices granted privately to kin
are not the selection for a state seeking prosperity.
Therefore, when the three ministerial families became hereditary,
the eastern state suffered many policies of decline and weakness;
when the five marquises ran abreast,
the western capital experienced a fate of decline and decay.
Your servant has heard that the numinous radiance appearing at dawn
shines upon things according to their nature;
the seasonal wind sprinkling at dusk
measures forms and bestows sounds.
Therefore, when the perfect Way prevails,
all creatures find sufficiency in the world;
when the great transformation is fully achieved,
the common people lack nothing in their hearts.
Your servant has heard that lowering a net into the abyss
cannot summon a dragon;
shaking a net amid the clouds
need not summon a phoenix.
Therefore, the old man of Cháo and Jī
did not care for the gifts from hills and gardens;
the people who washed in the Wèi
did not dream of Fù Yán.
Your servant has heard that a mirror's substance has no thickness,
yet its reflection can penetrate the depths of layered abysses;
the eye's perception has its limits,
yet its vision can encompass the bounds of heaven and earth.
Why is this?
Because it responds to things with essence, not form;
it creates things with spirit, not vessel.
Therefore, when all states rejoice in harmony,
it is not from delight in the entertainment of bells and drums;
when all under heaven return to benevolence,
it is not moved by the favor of jade and silk.
Your servant has heard that accumulated substance, though slight,
must stir external things;
exalted emptiness, though vast,
cannot move the heart.
Therefore, the beauties of the capital, adorning themselves,
do not delight in the shadow of Xī Shī;
horses circling in file
do not halt in the shade of Mount Tài.
Your servant has heard that responding to things with proper method
makes dwelling in difficulty easy;
concealing talent within oneself,
what is lacking is the opportune time.
Therefore, the fragrance filling the hall
is not difficult for the secluded orchid;
the sound that lingers around the beams
is truly what the entwined strings long for.
Your servant has heard that wisdom comprehends both obstruction and passage,
and is not constrained by the times;
talent withstands both peril and safety,
and is not bent by the world.
Therefore, feathers that brave the storm
do not seek a contrary wind;
eyes that shine in the night
do not long for a reversed sun.
Your servant has heard that loyal ministers follow their will,
not scheming for reward;
steadfast gentlemen vent their indignation,
hoping to make worthies known.
Therefore, when Liǔ Zhuāng halted the funeral,
it was not from greed for the reward of Guāyǎn;
when Qín Xī smashed his head,
could it have been to claim the fields of Xiānmáo!
Your servant has heard that sharp eyes facing the clouds
cannot cast their light downward;
bright jade covered in grime
cannot emit its radiance.
Therefore, even the wisest of rulers
sometimes suffer the burden of being obscured and blocked;
the most talented of ministers
often harbor the sorrow of being too late.
Your servant has heard that intense, fragrant aromas
emerge from extinguished ashes;
rich, harmonious music
is born from severed strings.
Therefore, chaste women seek fame after death,
and ardent men devote themselves to integrity in their prime.
Your servant has heard that a good minister planning for the court
need not borrow authority;
a loyal minister defending his lord
needs only to cultivate his own person.
Therefore, the strength of the Three Jìn
yielded to the sacrificial stand in the hall of Qí;
the might of a thousand chariots
was weakened by the weeping at the Yáng Gate.
I have heard that in music that follows the melody,
both loud and soft tones enter into harmony;
in postures that follow the rhythm,
both lowering and raising conform to the chant.
Thus, if words are suited to the matter,
the refined and the coarse can be applied;
if a scholar is suited to the Way,
the long and the short can be determined.
I have heard that when moisture is sprinkled because of the clouds,
then fragrance easily flows;
when sound is carried by riding the wind,
then its resonance naturally reaches far.
Thus, virtuous teaching relies on things to achieve its effect,
and glorious reputation depends on the times to become manifest.
I have heard that observing a shadow to match the substance
cannot resolve solitude;
pointing at tracks while admiring the distant
does not save from delay.
Thus, those who follow empty vessels
are not equipped to respond to things;
those who toy with empty words
are not the means to achieve order.
I have heard that drilling wood to produce fire
continues the sunlight of Tānggǔ;
waving wings to generate wind
succeeds the achievements of Fēilián.
Thus, things may be subtle yet contribute to prominence,
and affairs may be trivial yet assist greatness.
I have heard that the spring breeze warms in the morning,
and both mugwort and artemisia receive its warmth;
the autumn frost falls at night,
and both orchids and angelica are covered by its chill.
Therefore, authority is stern when it treats all things equally,
and virtue is vast when it universally benefits.
I have heard that skill is exhausted in the tool,
and practice makes perfect through repetition;
the Way is connected to the spirit,
and when a person perishes, it vanishes.
Thus, a wheelwright who uses his eyes
does not lack the ingenuity of Xī Zhòng;
a blind elder who sharpens his hearing
does not possess the discernment of Líng Lún.
I have heard that in what nature aspires to,
the noble and the lowly are of equal measure;
in what principle reaches its extreme,
the humble and the lofty become one.
Thus, drawing water by the moonlight
cannot increase its coolness;
kindling fire by the sunlight
need not enhance its brilliance.
I have heard that the highest songs with broken rhythms
are not mourned by ordinary ears;
righteous teachings and fragrant messages
are not appreciated by common listeners.
Thus, in Nánjīng there are songs with few to harmonize,
and in Dōngyě there are debates that are not relinquished.
I have heard that seeking fragrance from smoke,
the scent lingers even after the incense burns out;
recording the resonance of a subtle note,
it ends when the playing stops.
Why is this?
What is passed down to the world can be continued,
but what stops with the body is difficult to sustain.
Thus, the style of Xuán Yàn endures forever,
while the transformative power that moves the spirit has already vanished.
I have heard that hiding one's form in darkness
is not a clever secret;
relying on wisdom to conceal feelings
is insufficient to hide oneself.
Thus, when bright light emits its splendor,
it seeks the void and captures shadows;
when the great person observes with correctness,
he probes the heart and reveals errors.
I have heard that parting the clouds to look at the sky,
then the patterns of heaven are clear;
calming the wind to observe the water,
then the river flows smoothly.
Thus, when the four clans were exiled, Táng became illustrious;
when the two ministers were executed, Chǔ became peaceful.
I have heard that sound is beautiful when it pleases the ear,
and color is joyful when it delights the eye.
Thus, what captivates the multitude's hearing
does not rely on the skill of Bó Yá;
what enchants ten thousand men
does not await the beauty of Xīzǐ.
Therefore, the sage selects assistants according to the times,
and the enlightened ruler appoints officials in accordance with the era.
I have heard that what emerges from oneself
is not exalted by borrowing external things;
what is constrained by the times
is not encouraged by self-restraint.
Thus, even if one benefits all things,
one cannot enlighten the heart of a foolish child;
even if one's virtue serves as a model for the people,
one cannot save from the disgrace of distress and turmoil.
I have heard that acting according to fixed standards,
heaven can be observed;
responding without constant rules,
the self may be difficult to illuminate.
Thus, observing shadows to measure the sun,
the full cycle can be anticipated;
but pressing the chest to discuss the heart,
sometimes leads to error.
I have heard that straining the ear to seek sound,
the vision is superior but the hearing suffers;
purifying the mind to follow things,
the body is at ease but the spirit is weary.
Thus, when heaven differs in its principles,
even those of the same method cannot share their sorrow;
when principle blocks its passage,
then even shared substance cannot partake in its joy.
I have heard that those who withdraw from the world
do not possess the nature of a bitter gourd;
the maiden who lives in seclusion
is not without the feelings of longing for spring.
Thus, when reputation overcomes desire,
the integrity of matching one's shadow becomes proud;
when poverty surpasses success,
the integrity of reaching the clouds becomes stern.
I have heard that when hearing is satisfied with sound,
one does not yearn for the music of the heavenly court;
when the body is content with shade,
one does not need the clouds that hang from the sky.
Thus, the people of Pú and Mì
forget the era of universal harmony;
the scholars of Fēng and Pèi
forget the ruler of great achievement.
I have heard that when the flying reins halt in the west,
then Lí Zhū and the blind lose their sight;
when the suspended brilliance shines in the east,
then night-bright pearls and warrior stones hide their glow.
Thus, when talent changes with the times, all are in difficulty;
when achievement coincides with the era, all become illustrious.
I have heard that showing response in the near,
the far can be observed;
entrusting verification in the manifest,
the subtle may be encompassed.
Thus, with a short pipe pointing downward,
heaven and earth cannot deceive with their energy;
with a short gnomon standing upright,
the sun and moon cannot escape with their forms.
I have heard that the string has a constant sound,
so when the tune ends, it changes;
the mirror does not store reflections,
so when it encounters a form, it reflects.
Thus, emptying oneself to respond to things,
one will surely investigate the appearance of a thousand changes;
clinging to emotions to suit affairs,
one will not observe the wonder of ten thousand differences.
I have heard that the wooden percussion instruments have sparse sounds,
to harmonize with the metal and stone instruments;
the drums are struck intermittently,
to regulate the agreement of numerous strings.
Thus, in governing, one must promote its thoroughfare;
in planning things, one must always examine their convergence.
I have heard that the eyes do not have the ability to examine sound,
and the ears do not have the spirit to illuminate sights.
Therefore, what lies within me,
I do not blame in myself;
what exists in things,
I do not demand perfection from others.
I have heard that living freely,
the body at ease brings peace;
eating without restraint,
satisfaction brings fullness.
Thus, when the royal sturgeon is placed on the sacrificial stand,
it does not rely on fish that swallow waves;
when orchid-scented oil is stored in the room,
one does not think of the dragon that holds a candle in its mouth.
I have heard that when the waves are calm and the current is tranquil,
even a dragon boat cannot be swept away;
when a violent wind suddenly arises,
even a great house may sometimes collapse.
Why is this?
When tethered to movement, stillness congeals;
when bound to stillness, movement remains steadfast.
Thus, when wanton customs prevail,
virtuous women regret adorning themselves;
when pure teachings flow abundantly,
even a robber like Dào Zhí may harbor the sentiments of Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú.
I have heard that what the prosperous wear,
though precious, may sometimes be discarded;
what the destitute encounter,
though humble, will surely be sought.
Thus, the lord of Jiāng and Hàn
grieved over his lost sandal;
the woman of Shàoyuán
wept for her missing hairpin.
I have heard that if one touches something not of its kind,
though swift, it will not respond;
if moved in its proper manner,
though subtle, it will comply.
Thus, an autumn gale may sweep over mountains,
yet not stir clouds an inch thick;
a valley breeze brushing the branches,
will surely bring a rain that soaks the sky.
Therefore, those ignorant of governance
sing loudly but find few to join;
those who understand the nature of things
exert little effort yet achieve great results.
I have heard that smoke arises from fire,
yet is not the harmony of fire;
emotions arise from nature,
yet are not the fulfillment of nature.
Thus, when fire is strong, smoke is faint;
when nature is full, emotions are restrained.
Therefore, the ruins of Yīn evoke sorrow for things lost;
the capital of Zhōu leaves no trace of lingering grief.
I have heard that skills suited to things
vary in use with every movement;
tools fit for tasks
differ in function according to obstruction or ease.
Thus, birds roosting in clouds are struck by flying arrows;
fish hiding in deep waters are caught by sinking nets.
A tightly wrapped drum contains its sound;
a thinly pierced flute emits its notes.
I have heard that what principle upholds,
force often seizes;
what the Way closes,
expediency must open.
Thus, life is weightier than profit,
so one holding a map feels no pain in casting aside a sword;
righteousness is more precious than the self,
so facing a river, one may grieve to leave footprints behind.
I have heard that those who comprehend change
use little yet benefit greatly;
those who grasp the essentials
employ simple tools yet achieve profound responses.
Thus, the profundity of heaven and earth
is encompassed in the six positions;
the myriad variations of melody
are exhausted within the five strings.
I have heard that drawing a shape from its shadow
cannot capture all its delicate beauty;
observing fire through its ashes
does not reveal its blazing fury.
Thus, to inquire about the Way depends on the person;
to observe things, one must reach their essence.
I have heard that when emotions appear through objects,
though distant, they remain estranged;
when spirit is hidden within form,
though near, it remains intimate.
Thus, measuring the sky by the sundial’s shadow,
length and shortness can be gauged;
standing by a deep pool to fathom the water,
its shallowness or depth is hard to discern.
I have heard that the scorching heat of summer, filling the sky,
does not diminish the cold of solid ice;
the freezing yin congealing the earth
does not hinder the heat of a hilltop fire.
Thus, the might of one who swallows kingdoms
cannot reverse the resolve to tread the sea;
the awe of one who floats shields on blood
cannot bend the integrity of the Western Hills.
I have heard that what principle opens,
force often reaches;
what fate blocks,
power must eventually exhaust.
Thus, a blazing fire that melts metal
cannot burn a shadow;
a deep cold that freezes the sea
cannot congeal the wind.
I have heard that those content in their nature
cannot be penetrated by heaven’s harm;
those steadfast in their season
cannot be swayed by temporal burdens.
Thus, in violent storms and torrential rains,
the morning bird’s observation is not mistaken;
in harsh cold and withering seasons,
the heart of the winter tree does not decay.
Vast and boundless is creation,
the two principles now divided.
Scattered qi flows into forms,
molded and shaped.
In the time of Emperor Fúxī,
he first established the principles linking heaven and man.
Thus began husband and wife,
and then ruler and subject.
The way of the family was set right,
the kingly path gained order.
A woman’s virtue esteems gentleness,
embodying grace, steadfast and auspicious.
Gracious, gentle, virtuous, and cautious,
she maintains her proper place within the home.
Bestowing girdles and tying sashes,
she reverently attends to household duties.
Solemn and careful in her demeanor,
she gazes upon pure virtue.
Fán Jī moved Duke Zhuāng,
refusing to eat fresh game.
The woman of Wèi admonished Duke Huán,
turning her ear from harmonious music.
Their wills stern, their righteousness lofty,
and the hearts of two lords were changed.
A black bear climbed the railing,
Féng Yuán rushed forward.
Was she without fear?
Knowing death, she did not begrudge it!
Consort Bān had her words,
cutting off favor, refusing the same carriage.
Did she not cherish it?
She guarded against the subtle, considering the distant!
No way is exalted without decline,
no thing flourishes without decay.
The sun at its zenith must wane,
the full moon must diminish.
Glory is like dust accumulating,
downfall like a triggered trap.
All know to adorn their appearance,
but few know to adorn their nature.
If nature is not adorned,
it may transgress ritual and correctness.
Carve and polish it,
and with concentrated thought, become a sage.
If one’s words are good,
a thousand li will respond.
If this principle is violated,
even sharing a quilt will breed suspicion.
Words may be subtle,
yet honor and disgrace arise from them.
Do not say they are obscure and dark,
for the spiritual watch has no form.
Do not say they are silent and still,
for divine hearing has no sound.
Do not pride yourself on your glory,
for the Way of Heaven detests excess.
Do not rely on your nobility,
for the lofty are bound to fall.
Take warning from the small stars,
and guard against such recklessness.
Compare your heart to the katydids,
and your kind will multiply.
Joy must not be profaned,
favor must not be monopolized.
Monopoly breeds arrogance,
love at its extreme shifts away.
Fullness inevitably leads to loss,
a principle firmly established.
The beautiful deem themselves beautiful,
yet lightly bring blame upon themselves.
Adorning oneself to seek favor
is what the nobleman despises.
When bonds of grace are severed,
this is often the cause.
Thus it is said:
Cautious and reverent,
thus fortune arises.
Quietly respectful, reflecting on oneself,
thus glory and prominence are anticipated.
The female historian in charge of admonitions
dares to advise all consorts.
In the autumn, seventh month, of the first year of the Yongyuán era,
the Han Dynasty's chief maternal uncle, the Chariot and Horse General Dòu Xiàn,
reverently enlightened the sage emperor,
assisted and supported the royal house,
was entrusted with great responsibilities,
and maintained purity and brightness.
He then, together with the Commandant of the Capital Guards Gěng Bǐng,
carried out his duties by patrolling and defending,
and trained troops in Shuòfāng.
The eagle-like commanders,
the dragon-tiger warriors,
thus comprised the six armies,
along with the multitudes of chieftains and kings of the Southern Chányú, Eastern Hú, Wūhuán, Western Róng, Dī, and Qiāng tribes,
forming a force of one hundred thousand fierce cavalry.
The main army, light and swift,
with long chariots arrayed in four divisions,
their thunderous supply wagons covering the roads,
numbered over thirteen thousand vehicles.
Deployed in the eight formations,
presiding with awe-inspiring might,
their black armor gleaming under the sun,
their vermilion banners dyeing the sky red.
They then scaled the high passes,
descended upon Jīlù,
traversed the saline deserts,
crossed the great wilderness,
beheaded Wēnyú to smear the drums with blood,
and stained their blades with the blood of Shīzhú.
Thereafter, the four columns swept across,
like shooting stars and sweeping comets,
leaving desolation for ten thousand lǐ,
with no enemy left in the wilds.
Thus, the region was annihilated and the area cleared,
and they turned their banners to return,
consulting records and verifying maps,
exhaustively surveying the mountains and rivers.
They then crossed Zhuōxié,
spanned Ānhóu,
ascended Yānrán,
trod upon the territories of Mòdú,
and burned the dragon court of Lǎoshàng.
Above, to vent the long-held grievances of Gāozǔ and Wéndì,
and glorify the profound spirits of the ancestors;
below, to secure and stabilize future generations,
expand and open up the borders,
and uplift the heavenly voice of the great Hàn.
This may be said to achieve lasting ease through one effort,
and eternal peace through temporary expense.
Thus, they sealed the mountain and engraved the stone,
to manifestly inscribe their great virtue.
The inscription reads:
Brilliant are the royal armies, marching to distant lands,
exterminating the cruel and fierce, cutting through beyond the seas,
vast and far-reaching, spanning the bounds of the earth,
sealing the divine mound, erecting lofty monuments,
glorifying the emperor's deeds, resonating for ten thousand generations.
Do not speak of others' shortcomings,
do not boast of your own strengths.
When bestowing favors, be careful not to dwell on them;
when receiving favors, be careful not to forget them.
Worldly praise is not worth admiring,
only benevolence is the guiding principle.
Reflect in your heart before acting,
how can slanderous talk harm you then?
Do not let reputation exceed reality,
embracing simplicity is praised by the sages.
In darkness, value remaining unstained,
dimly glowing with inner light.
Gentleness and softness are companions of life,
Lǎozi warns against rigidity and strength.
The rash and hasty are the aims of petty men,
the calm and profound are hard to measure.
Be cautious in speech and moderate in eating and drinking,
knowing contentment overcomes misfortune.
If you practice these with constancy,
in time, you will naturally become fragrant.
Towering is Liáng Mountain,
its piled stones lofty and steep.
Far, it connects to Jīng and Héng,
near, it links to Mín and Bō.
To the south, it reaches Qióng and Bó,
to the north, it extends to Bāo and Xié.
Narrower than Péng and Jié,
higher than Sōng and Huà.
It is the gateway to Shǔ,
serving as a stronghold and bulwark.
This is called Jiàn'gé,
with cliffs standing a thousand rèn high.
It exhausts the perils of the land,
reaches the extremity of rugged paths.
When the world is corrupt, it becomes an obstacle;
when the way is clear, it allows passage.
Closed during the Hàn dynasty,
opened again in the Jìn.
Qín, possessing a hundred and two,
annexed the various feudal lords.
Qí, possessing twelve,
Tián Shēng offered his strategies.
How much more this narrow defile,
a remote region of the land.
One man holding a halberd,
ten thousand men hesitate to advance.
A strategically vital place,
should not be entrusted to those not of kin.
In the past, Marquis Wǔ,
rejoiced midstream.
The security of mountains and rivers,
was refuted by Wú Qǐ.
Prosperity truly lies in virtue,
danger is also hard to rely on.
Dòngtíng and Mèngmén,
two states lost their sacrifices.
From ancient times to the present,
heaven's mandate is not easily gained.
Relying on obstacles to act foolishly,
rarely ends without defeat.
Since Gōngsūn was destroyed,
the Liú clan offered jade.
The tracks of an overturned cart,
should not be followed again.
Inscribe this on the mountain's side,
dare to admonish Liáng and Yì.
In the past, Shùn went to the ancestral temple,
Yǔ reached the divine ancestor;
Zhōu changed the customs of Shāng,
Tāng abolished the governance of Xià.
Although revolution differs from inheritance,
and yielding differs from armed conflict,
yet the shadows and stars darkly align,
heaven and humanity open the way,
to illuminate outstanding virtue,
and greatly protect the living people,
the principle is one.
In the late Qí period,
a dark and cruel ruler reigned,
defying the five elements,
neglecting the three correct principles,
punishments cruel as burning charcoal,
tyranny worse than the grease pillar,
the people resentful, the gods angry,
the masses rebellious, kin estranged,
treading the ground with no place to return,
gazing at crows with no perch to trust.
Then our emperor saved them,
grasping the Dipper's pivot,
holding the Hooked Array,
assisted by a hundred spirits,
bestowing ten thousand blessings.
The dragon soared from the Black Water,
the tiger strode through the Western River,
like thunder moving, wind driving,
heaven proceeding, earth halting.
Calling the troops brought a response like gathering clouds,
ascending the altar had the auspice of descending fire,
tortoise and milfoil divinations in harmony,
humans and spirits echoing in support.
The brave with bared chests and uncovered heads,
the chieftains sitting cross-legged with topknots,
all seized banners, asking to strive,
grasping weapons, vying to be first.
Xiàshǒu relied on its strongholds,
Yōng and Mín depended on their barriers,
uniting those with divided hearts,
resisting those of shared virtue.
The emperor blazed with anger,
training horses and drilling troops,
before the stern drums fully sounded,
the chief culprits bowed their heads in mud.
Great vessels linked axle to axle,
huge masts connected prow to stern,
iron cavalry in a thousand groups,
vermilion banners across ten thousand lǐ.
With a simple note, they captured Lú Jiǔ,
with a circulated proclamation, they took Xiāng and Luó.
Blades not stained with blood,
soldiers not losing an arrow,
yet Fán and Dèng were awed and won over,
Bā and Qián were pacified and settled.
Thus, the factions that boiled water and grasped coals,
in defense were like mere fences,
in battle akin to withered decay.
War chariots drew near,
army camps spread across the Shang and Mù regions.
Men and women, both Huá and Yí,
their caps and canopies visible from afar,
supporting the elderly and leading the young,
gathered like clouds in a single day.
Jugs of broth filled the fields,
baskets of food overflowed the roads.
It was as if the people of Xià had turned to Chéng Tāng,
or the scholars of Yīn had looked toward Zhōu Wǔ.
The elderly were comforted, the young cherished;
crimes were punished, the people consoled.
Farmers did not abandon their work,
markets saw no change in trade.
From all directions, reports were submitted;
from the four corners, maps were presented.
Feather dispatches raced back and forth,
military documents arrived in rapid succession.
Day after day,
affairs numbered not merely ten thousand.
Yet, his dignified demeanor
remained unchanged amidst the troops;
his profound and silent composure
was unaltered on the battlefield.
His strategies flowed like water,
his thoughts turned like a compass.
Plans were settled within the tent,
schemes completed upon the desk.
In less than twelve days,
the tyrant was beheaded.
Then, he burned the ornate mats,
discarded the precious robes,
returned the pearls of Xuántái,
and gave back the jade of the feudal lords.
With a wave of his hand, the four seas were at peace;
upon descending from his carriage, all under heaven was settled.
He rescued them from this turmoil,
saved them from this chaos.
His merit equaled heaven and earth,
his brilliance matched the sun and moon.
Thus, in accordance with the three spirits above
and yielding to the millions below,
he received the jade of Zhāohuá,
and accepted the chart of the dragon tally.
He honored the ancestors and revered the gods,
and gloriously possessed the sacred vessel.
He ascended to offer sacrifices to all the deities,
and with sleeves gathered, received the homage of all Xià.
He disseminated teachings in the capital region,
and promulgated governance beyond the borders.
His plans aligned with the highest strategies,
his punishments followed the middle statutes.
The distant southerners with drooping ears,
the westerners with twisted tongues,
the nations under felt tents,
and the people sharing caves by the same river—
all knelt and crossed their arms,
knocking their heads and bowing to the ground.
He opened paths for ten thousand lǐ,
seized lands of a thousand cities.
The barriers south of the desert were removed,
and west of the river, no alarms were raised.
Thus, with order established and achievements completed,
near and far were pacified and subdued.
The panic of deer was forgotten,
the wary glances of wolves ceased.
He then rectified the six forms of music,
regulated the five rites,
revised the statutes and regulations,
and created laws and ordinances.
He established the office of Erudites,
and the students who registered were like clouds.
He opened the Hall of Collected Elegance,
and those seeking learning crowded like a market.
He founded schools and academies,
and inaugurated suburban altars.
Every talent, however small, was recorded;
every rite, even unwritten, was properly ordered.
Thus, scholars across the land
turned to him as the wind bends grass.
People understood integrity,
families knew ritual and deference.
Education reached the sons of attendants,
transformation touched the guards at the gates.
The realm was peaceful and orderly,
all regions were calm and quiet.
Labor was light, duties simple;
the years were abundant, the people harmonious.
The plans of past dynasties,
the precedents of former kings—
all were pruned and trimmed,
held with perfect balance.
He believed that the system of symbolic towers
had a long history.
The Spring and Autumn Annals established teachings of old regulations,
the Classic of Rites transmitted texts on proclaiming laws,
the Records of the Dai showed words on inspection tours,
and the History of Zhōu recorded dreams of erecting towers.
The bright moon of the northern wilderness,
the flowing essence of the western extremes;
the gold of mountains and seas,
the purple shells of the river courts;
the designs of azure dragons and dark warriors,
the craftsmanship of bronze sparrows and iron phoenixes—
some were for hearing grievances and redressing wrongs,
some for proclaiming teachings and displaying laws,
some for marking the correctness of the royal abode,
some for glorifying the imperial capital.
The Jìn dynasty gradually weakened,
the Sòng era declined and faltered.
The old classics of rites,
were silent and unrecorded;
the grand regulations and splendid achievements,
were buried and rarely praised.
They borrowed the heavenly tower from Niútóu,
entrusted distant plans to Bówàng,
deceiving the eyes and ears,
with no benefit to the statutes.
Thus, he ordered officials skilled in measurement,
selected scholars clear in judgment,
set up the gnomon and placed the marker,
observed the stars and measured the earth,
restored the marking gates,
and began constructing the splendid towers.
Thus, in the year corresponding to Tiānjì,
in the month aligned with Tàicù,
it was the seventh year of the emperor’s reign over all under heaven.
He established these grand principles,
raised this lofty magnificence.
Moreover, they hastened to show reverence,
observed and understood the laws.
All beheld the appearance of the twin steles,
people recognized the codes of a hundred layers.
Creating models and bequeathing teachings—
how majestic, how grand!
Then he commanded his humble servant
to inscribe these words on solid stone.
The inscription reads:
The emperor establishes the state,
corrects positions and distinguishes directions.
Zhōu built at the banks of Luò,
Hàn opened at Qí and Liáng.
Dwelling prospers through achievements,
culture shines through transformation.
Thus, there are symbolic towers,
which are the old regulations.
The blue canopy moves southward,
the yellow banner points east.
The display of laws went unheard,
the storage of books left unrecorded.
The great man creates things,
the dragon’s virtue ends adversity.
He raised these hundred constants,
built these twin structures.
How grand their towering height,
how magnificent their lofty form!
Beside them, layers reflect;
above, they touch the emerald haze.
The proclamation of teachings now shines,
the sun’s light first spreads.
Suspended writings find their place,
entrusted boxes know their home.
Majestic peaks with layered eaves,
arched roofs and upturned corners.
Their forms soar with flying beams,
their might surpasses floating pillars.
Colors follow the circle above,
designs model the square below.
Gazing all around at plains and marshes,
looking down upon mist and rain.
Before, welcoming from four directions;
behind, backed by nine chambers.
Northward, connecting two tracks;
southward, converging five regions.
Heat comes, cold goes;
earth endures, heaven lasts.
Divine, these splendid towers!
Forever matching the boundless.
When observing celestial phenomena from the heavens,
the moments of dusk and dawn remain undifferentiated;

the measures of surplus and deficit lack precision.
The establishment of the clepsydra and the naming of its masters,

Lù Jī’s rhapsody,

The legacy of Hóng Dù,

Like those spring blossoms,

Moreover, the official clepsydras of today,

The year’s path in Yānmào,
the moon’s station in Gūxǐ.

Rivers and seas are calm and peaceful,
