Holding court early and retiring late,
rising at dawn each morning,
attending to the sounds of the water clock’s transmission,
listening to the calls of the rooster men.
Deeming the stellar fire erroneous in its marking,
and the metal and water misapplied,
the timing deviating from openings and closings,
the arrows differing by minute measures.
Thus commanding the calendar officials,
to draft and create a new instrument.
Thereupon, observing below and gathering broadly,
ascending towers and mounting storehouses.
Aligning with the four of earth,
and referencing the one of heaven.
The遗留 flaws of Jiànwǔ,
the residual errors of Xiánhé,
the square and round designs of golden tubes,
the patterns of flowing and intake,
altering pitch pipes and changing classics,
all were corrected and reformed.
In the sixth year of Tiānjiān,
the cyclical year Dīnghài,
the first day of the tenth month, Dīnghài,
the sixteenth day, Rényín,
the clepsydra was completed and presented to the court.
To examine the hours and correct the gnomon’s shadow,
measure the gauge and observe the shade,
without error by a guī or a cuō,
not deviating by a shǔ or a lěi.
It can also verify the convergence of calculations,
distinguish the deviation and correctness of celestial divisions,
observe the fullness and emptiness of the four seasons,
and assess the precision of the six calendars.
A rule bequeathed for eternity,
transmitted endlessly.
Resplendent and brilliant,
beyond description.
In the past, even fine objects like measuring vessels,
small utensils like plates and bowls,
still had their virtues recorded and merits inscribed,
preserved in inscriptions and classics.
How much more for a creation of human and divine craft,
in harmony with the transformations of creation;
the capability to complete things,
matching the covenant of the earth’s origin;
merits doubling those of pillars and mats,
achievements a hundredfold those of towels and tables.
How could it be allowed to pale in comparison to Zēngshuǐ,
or be deemed inferior to Kūnwú,
with golden characters unpassed down,
and silver writings unengraved?
Thus, the emperor commanded his humble servant to compose an inscription, saying:
One heat, one cold,
there is brightness, there is darkness.
The ways of the spirits leave no trace,
the work of heaven is rarely substituted.
So the clepsydra is established,
this indeed glorifies the age.
The breath balanced as with weights and measures,
the shadow corrected as with scales and standards.
The ways of the world are lost together,
the arts of rites dissolve and perish.
Hastily shifting water and fire,
scrambling to颠倒 garments.
Striking knives in erroneous sequence,
gathering wood in improper manner.
Delving into study and measurement,
this is the time of our emperor.
Square vessels arranged externally,
circular flows contained within.
Great and small differing in grade,
high and low distinct in level.
Divine dragons receive the flow,
hidden creatures exhale and inhale.
Swiftly coming and suddenly going,
emerging like ghosts, entering like spirits.
Subtle as drawing silk from a cocoon,
fleeting as a lightning flash.
The ear never ceases hearing sound,
the eye retains no lingering sight.
Bronze historians oversee the markings,
golden attendants hold the arrows.
Treading on thin ice, not in fear,
facing the depths, without trembling.
Giving and receiving without error,
ascending and descending without discrepancy.
Exclusively refined and unified,
worthy of emulation and example.
The moon does not conceal its coming,
the sun does not hide its going.
Division in accord with tallies and tokens,
arrival as immediate as shadow and echo.
The合昏 tree furls at dusk,
the míngjiá plant sprouts at dawn.
Still discerning heaven’s intent,
yet measuring earth’s disposition.
How much more our divine creation,
penetrating the obscure and piercing the spiritual.
Matching the emperor, equaling the ultimate,
establishing standards for the ages.
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, Wùshēn, in the twenty-second year of Jiàn’ān,
the late Wèi Attendant-in-Ordinary and Marquis Within the Passes, Wáng Jūn, passed away.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
The august heavens observe with divine clarity,
relying on the wise man.
How is it, O divine spirits,
that you extinguish our auspicious scholar?
Who says he was not accomplished?
Early in life, he entered darkness.
Who says there is no grief?
Blossoms abundant, yet falling mid-growth.
Existence and demise flow apart,
premature death and fulfillment share the same time.
Hearing in the morning, gone by evening,
as the ancients pondered.
How to extol his virtue?
Display it on plain banners.
How to honor his end?
With sorrow, send him forth.
Thus, composing a eulogy, it says:
Ah, the Palace Attendant,
Your distant ancestors were ever fragrant.
Gōnggāo established the enterprise,
Assisting King Wǔ in conquering Shāng.
His fief was equal to Qí and Lǔ,
Yet his state’s sacrifices were cut off and lost.
His descendant Bì Wàn,
His merit and achievements alone shone brightly.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn granted him a fief,
In the lands of Wèi.
Heaven opened this blessing,
And his later descendants claimed kingship.
From his surname came this clan,
Branching and spreading like leaves.
Through generations, their fragrant glory grew,
Their fame resounded in Qín and Hàn.
Then came the calamity of yángjiǔ,
The fiery light of Hàn was dimmed.
Emperor Shìzǔ brought order from chaos,
And in his time established harmony.
The Three Dukes took their positions,
And the Way was concentrated in them.
The bestowal of noble ranks,
Was not out of favor but reverence.
From your two ancestors,
They were the light, they were the dragons.
All said, “How excellent!
They should assist the Hàn state.”
One commanded as Grand Commandant,
Another presided as Minister of Works.
All affairs were well-ordered,
The Five Teachings were followed.
Heaven was tranquil, people harmonious,
The imperial teachings spread far and wide.
Your illustrious father,
Generation after generation aided the times.
Inside, he managed secrets and plans,
And court governance was well-ordered.
Outside, he oversaw Shuò and Dài,
And all achievements flourished.
You, with your virtuous beauty,
Inherited this great foundation.
Possessing noble virtue,
Your talents and skills were widely displayed.
Strong memory, broad knowledge,
Profound insight into subtle words.
Your writing like spring blossoms,
Your thoughts like gushing springs.
Your spoken words could be sung,
Your brush produced finished compositions.
What principle did you not master?
What art were you not skilled in?
In board games, you displayed cleverness,
In gambling, you were peerless.
The royal house fell into misfortune,
The capital crumbled and fell.
The chief minister seized power,
And the emperor moved west.
You became a traveler,
Parted from this, facing hardship.
Swiftly, like a phoenix rising,
You fled far to Jīngmán.
Though destitute, your will was lofty,
Dwelling humbly, your conduct was pure.
Shaking your cap on Southern Peak,
Washing your tassels in clear streams.
Living hidden in a thatched hut,
Not seeking power or influence.
Our lord raised his battle-axe,
Displaying might in Southern Chǔ.
Some in Jīng rebelled,
Arraying troops for war.
You then rose with righteousness,
Planning strategies for our army.
Exalting the achievements of hegemony,
You devoted yourself to the imperial domain.
These words once spoken,
The strategists agreed.
What was their agreement?
They responded to our bright virtue.
Laying down arms at Biānruò,
Bowing in submission north of the Hàn River.
Our lord truly praised you,
Honoring you in the capital.
Golden tortoise seal, purple sash,
To display your meritorious deeds.
What were these deeds?
Toiling humbly without cease.
Concerned for the age, forgetting home,
With extraordinary strategies, standing tall.
Then you were appointed Libationer,
To accompany our lord in actions.
In planning, no strategy was overlooked,
In plotting, no principle was missed.
Our king established the state,
All offices filled with talented men.
You were prominently elevated,
Holding authority in the palace offices.
Wearing cicada hats, ear pendants of sable,
Crimson robes, white belts.
Entering to attend the imperial chambers,
Exiting under ornate canopies.
Glorious in your time,
Your fragrant influence widespread.
Alas, those eastern barbarians,
Relying on rivers and lakes,
Harassed the borders,
Wearying our troops.
Glorious were the military roads,
Like thunder startling, like wind sweeping.
You attended in ornate carriages,
Shining on the king’s path.
Thinking of glory, embracing submission,
Hoping they would come in awe.
How could it not succeed?
But fate reached its limit, life declined.
Lying ill, lingering long,
Good fortune departed, misfortune returned.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The lonely heir, fluttering in grief,
Wailed and crumbled in anguish.
Setting out from northern Wèi,
Traveling far to southern Huái.
Passing through mountains and rivers,
Tears fell like collapsing walls.
Mournful winds stirred emotions,
Wandering clouds lingered.
Swimming fish lost their waves,
Returning birds forgot their perches.
Alas, how sorrowful!
I and you, Master,
Our bond was etched in red and blue.
Harmonious as qín and sè,
Closer than ordinary friends.
We hoped for long years,
To journey hand in hand.
How could it be so sudden,
That you abandon me, left alone?
Recalling past feasts,
Our aspirations each lofty and fierce.
I jested with you, Master,
That metal and stone are hard to break.
Human life is not constant,
Good fortune and misfortune differ in measure.
Among this joyful company,
Who would be the first to fall?
Who would have thought, Master,
That you would indeed depart first!
We also discussed life and death,
The numbers of existence and demise.
You still had doubts,
Seeking clear evidence.
If your spirit alone remains,
Wandering in the primal essence,
I shall borrow wings,
Soaring high and floating far.
Ascending beyond the radiant clouds,
To meet you on the heavenly path.
The funeral bier has arrived,
Soon to return to Wèi’s capital.
The spirit carriage turns its wheels,
White horses neigh in sorrow.
Empty and vast, nothing to see,
Hidden light, concealed form.
Who says, Zhòngxuān,
That we do not hear your voice?
Stretching my neck, sighing deeply,
Tears like rain, necks entwined.
Alas, Master!
Rest peacefully in the dark underworld.
Who among men does not die?
The enlightened sacrifice for fame.
Honored in life, mourned in death,
This too is great glory.
Alas, how sorrowful!
In the first year of the Xiánníng era,
on the yǐchǒu day of the fourth month in summer,
the late General of the Breaking Charge, Governor of Jīngzhōu, Dōngwǔ Marquis Dài of Yíngyáng, Lord Yáng, passed away.
Alas, how sorrowful!
When the Son of Heaven establishes a state,
the feudal lords establish their households.
Selecting the worthy and employing the capable,
governance is thereby harmonious.
The Zhōu relied on Shàngfù,
the Yīn depended on Tài'ē.
The valiant Marquis Yáng,
was the claws and teeth of Jìn.
Loyal and steadfast, clearly manifest,
his abundant achievements were truly commendable.
He was to expand the royal strategy,
and pacify the distant wilderness.
But his allotted years were not long,
his dark hair not yet gray.
Bearing regret to the end of his days,
such is fate—what can be done?
Alas, how sorrowful!
Since ancient times, in ages past,
all who live must die.
The body perishes, but fame endures—
this is what the sages of old deemed right.
Conduct is made illustrious through praise,
virtue is made beautiful through narration.
Daring to entrust to the banner’s streamers,
I therefore compose this elegy.
Its words are as follows:
Far, far distant ancestors,
their lineage traces back to the Zhōu.
Generations flourished and multiplied,
branches and offshoots spread and diverged.
The clan began with Bóqiáo,
the surname issued from Marquis Yáng.
For generations illustrious and grand,
truly following the great way.
Heaven grew weary of the Hàn’s virtue,
dragons battled, undivided.
Then your grandfather and father,
amidst those urgent affairs.
As birds choose their trees,
so ministers select their lord.
They turned their hearts to the Wèi court,
pledged their names and gave their bodies.
Leaping vigorously from the abyss’s path,
soaring aloft through wind and cloud.
One commanded the Valiant Cavalry,
another held the post of Leader of the Army.
Sincerely born was Marquis Dài,
abundant virtue succeeding his time.
Inheriting the grand legacy,
able to construct the hall’s foundation.
In youth, he savored the Way,
without contention, only timely.
Filial piety truly steaming upward,
fraternal love also harmonious and joyful.
Multitalented and richly skilled,
strong in memory, broad in knowledge.
His eyes discerned the tip of a hair,
his mind calculated without bounds.
Grass and clerical script both mastered,
every letter surely treasured.
Feet never ceasing to walk,
hands never releasing texts.
Brush moving as if flying,
paper falling like clouds.
When studies excelled, he entered service,
thus joining the king’s governance.
Unpolished jade emitting radiance,
he served as magistrate of Línzhǐ.
Transformation spread through town and village,
kindness reached the common people.
Then ascending to a director’s post,
he solemnized our court’s commands.
This Chief Judge,
the state’s statutes and regulations.
When the lord assumed this duty,
he regarded the people as if wounded.
All cases clearly and carefully handled,
punishments just and detailed.
In hearings, he matched Gāo and Lǚ,
in reputation, equaled Yú and Zhāng.
Transferred to agricultural administration,
there in Yěwáng.
Granaries full, storehouses abundant,
the state grew rich, the army strong.
The glorious Empress Wén,
gradually advanced the Jìn house.
The lord, with dual qualifications,
joined the military as an aide.
Thus granted land and domain,
receiving this illustrious rank.
Green altar, white thatch,
also vermilion his ribbon.
The Wèi house obeyed Heaven,
the sage emperor received the mandate.
Fierce and ardent Marquis Yáng,
truly commanded the palace guard.
In charge of the palace gates,
he purified our imperial palace.
Harsh evils did not arise,
serene as a gentle breeze.
To reward his meritorious labor,
his appointed rank grew ever more honored.
Vast are the seas and Tàishān,
dark transformations not yet complete.
Torrential are the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
battlefields divided and flowing.
Wielding both civil and martial arts,
at that time, it was Marquis Yáng.
First guarding Dōngguǎn,
then governing Jīngzhōu.
Breaking the charge across ten thousand lǐ,
responding to and extolling the king’s grace.
Hearing of goodness as if startled,
hating evil as an enemy.
Displaying awe, displaying virtue,
with attack, with gentleness.
The cruel and arrogant Wú barbarians,
their false armies feared the pressure.
Intending to exploit enmity and conflict,
to sweep across the southern extremes.
Supplies exhausted, provisions spent,
his divine strategy never erred.
A gentleman’s fault,
he took the crooked upon himself, ascribed the straight to others.
Like the sun and moon,
sometimes they are eclipsed.
He bore the blame himself,
yielded the credit for achievements to others’ strength.
Already having turned back the banners,
he suffered dismissal for the sake of law.
Retiring to guard the ancestral mounds,
he closed his gate and did not emerge.
Letting his gaze roam over ancient texts,
giving free rein to his heart in Confucian arts.
Gradually, the gentry and officials,
ascended his hall and entered his chamber.
No affair they did not consult,
no doubt they did not inquire.
Position贬谪, but the Way advanced,
body impoverished, but will at ease.
Without worry, without scheming,
then he lay down, then fell ill.
The great Heaven showed no pity,
his bright mandate reached its end.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Zǐnáng assisted Chǔ,
left words to fortify Yǐng.
Shǐ Yú remonstrated with Wèi,
used his corpse to manifest governance.
When this lord faced his end,
he did not forget loyalty and reverence.
Lying prostrate on his bed mat,
his thoughts were on the court and government.
In the morning, his words reached them,
by evening, his life was gone.
The sage king sighed in grief,
graciously bestowed shrouds and burial clothes.
Eulogizing virtue, recording merit,
examining his end, determining his posthumous title.
All officials mourned with aching hearts,
the state and clan wiped away tears.
The orphaned heir in distress,
colleagues and subordinates bearing sorrow.
Those who attended shared the grief,
passersby added their sighs.
Alas, how sorrowful!
I, in my stubborn obscurity,
covered by heavy shade of dew.
Looking up, I recall my late father,
and the heart of a close friend.
Looking down, I feel the knowing friend,
the depth of his perceptive understanding.
Receiving the sad news, anguished and pained,
tears and snivel soaked my lapels.
How could I forget to rush there?
But worry and illness weighed me down.
During his illness, I did not visit,
at his death, I was not present.
Raising my voice adds to the sorrow,
grief has lingering echoes.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Yáng Suǐ,
styled Zhòngwǔ,
was from Wǎnlíng in Xíngyáng.
He was the great-grandson of Sù Hóu, the Central Army Commander,
grandson of Dài Hóu, the Governor of Jīng Province,
and son of Kāng Hóu of Dōngwǔ.
He lost his father at the age of eight.
His mother, née Zhèng,
was the eldest daughter of Chéng Hóu of Mìlíng, the Minister of the Imperial Household,
and possessed a highly virtuous character.
She cared for and raised the young orphan,
preserving and protecting her husband’s household
and sparing it from many hardships.
Dài Hóu and Kāng Hóu produced numerous writings and discourses,
and were also skilled in the art of cursive and clerical script.
Their son, with his outstanding talent in his youthful years,
was naturally able to comprehensively grasp their principles and ideas,
and follow their models and examples.
Although his maternal uncles were prosperous and influential,
he remained in orphaned poverty, adhering to frugality,
content in humble circumstances,
and clad in simple garments.
I found him most remarkable.
As for his pure talent and outstanding brilliance,
and his abundant virtue that renewed itself daily,
I witnessed his progress,
but never saw him cease.
Having relied on the kindness of three generations of family ties,
and his aunt
being my own spouse,
he passed away last year in Dé Gōng Lǐ.
We shared the mourning garments and the same place of mourning,
bound together for many months.
If humans must possess sincerity,
this was the utmost expression of heartfelt devotion.
Unfortunately, his life was cut short,
at the age of twenty-nine.
He died on the jǐhài day of the fifth month in summer, in the ninth year of Yuánkāng.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus, I composed this elegy:
Ah, your ancestors,
for generations flourished gloriously.
Both grandfather and great-grandfather
carried forth their splendid legacy.
Your illustrious father, Kāng Hóu,
met an untimely end without official emolument.
Though his reputation and rank shone brightly,
his achievements and merits were not fully realized.
You were born with earnest promise,
endowed with graceful beauty.
Wise and discerning from youth,
you understood both the manifest and the subtle.
Delving deep into mysteries,
you savored the Way and studied its workings.
Not merely an ordinary man,
you were the glory of the state and family.
The adversity you encountered
came before you lost your baby teeth.
Like a precarious root
facing a raging blaze.
Virtue, bright and excellent,
no obscurity it did not rise above.
In your youth, your fragrance spread,
your noble reputation clear and distinguished.
Your uncles were honored,
your own clan in decline.
From childhood you upheld exceptional conduct,
turning from abundance to embrace want.
Compiling and recording ancestral teachings,
you ensured they would not be lost.
Ancient texts and new arts,
none you did not study.
The harmony between Pān and Yáng
has existed for long.
How much more so today,
careful to the end as at the start.
Your joys and sorrows,
were as if they were my own.
You regarded me as a father,
I could not treat you as merely a nephew.
Respect was already profound,
affection already deep.
Though our years differed,
our hearts were truly one.
The sun sets in the west,
I looked to you as the morning shade.
How could you be cut short,
leaving the world, submerged and silent?
Alas, how sorrowful!
Lying ill, lingering near death,
you upheld filial piety and fraternal love.
Facing the end, forgetting yourself,
you longed for your kind mother.
Sorrowful, kind mother,
heartache and headache.
Wailing, your siblings,
grieving, your uncles.
Spring orchids sprout stems,
just as their blossoms flourish.
A Jīng treasure reveals uncut jade,
soon to be carved by Hé.
Bearing fragrance, bestowed with radiance,
shattered jade, broken boughs.
Alas, Zhòngwǔ,
how painful, what can be done!
The hardship in Dé Gōng,
we shared the outer mourning chamber.
Only you and I,
facing mats, sharing pillows.
From that time till now,
not yet a full year.
Aunt and nephew perished in succession,
how profound this pain.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Opening books, scattering scrolls,
repeatedly I see your留下的 writings.
Some composed, some copied,
some in draft, some in final form.
Holding and pondering, over and over,
I imagine seeing the person.
Paper wearied in hand,
tears soaked the kerchief.
Turtle and yarrow divination done,
the tomb passage opened.
Painful, oh Yángzǐ!
Forever parted from the world.
Morning, crossing the Luò River,
evening, resting by mountain curves.
Returning birds fly up and down,
passing clouds linger.
Facing the grave, eternal farewell,
stroking the coffin, pouring out grief.
Your form left behind, none to continue,
increasing sorrow in my heart.
Soul, gone now,
the beam of the house truly broken.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Xiàhóu Zhàn,
styled Xiàoruò,
was from Qiáo.
He became known in his youth,
and at the age of twenty was recruited into the Grand Commandant’s office,
summoned as Worthy and Upright,
then served as Gentleman of the Heir Apparent,
Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
Magistrate of Yěwáng,
Secretary in the Central Secretariat,
and Chancellor of Nányáng.
Due to family hardship, he requested to return.
Shortly after,
he was selected as Steward of the Heir Apparent,
but before assuming the post, Emperor Shìzǔ passed away.
The Son of Heaven appointed him as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
to follow the ranks of officials.
He was forty-nine years old
when, on the rénchén day of the fifth month in summer, in the first year of Yuánkāng,
he fell ill,
and died at his residence in Yánxǐ Lǐ.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus, I composed this elegy:
Yǔ received the dark jade tablet,
Truly named Wén Mìng.
Able to be wise, able to be sage,
He gloriously opened the Xià dynasty’s rule.
As for the Hàn period,
The outstanding merit belonged to Yīng.
He sought to expand the Confucian enterprise,
With both minor and major names.
The illustrious ancestor displayed virtue,
Governing Yǎn and Jīng provinces.
His father guarded Huái and Dài,
His administration also gained renown.
Brilliant, brilliant master,
Shining, shining in his excellence.
Soaring in debate, weaving literary splendor,
Blossoms abundant, jade-like resonance.
Like those Suí pearls and Hé shì jade,
Emitting radiance, flowing with luster.
Like those brocade embroideries,
Arrayed on plain silk, dotted with brilliance.
People see his surface,
None fathom his depths.
They merely say of my life,
“When refinement prevails, it becomes ornate.”
Heart illuminating, spirit connecting,
Only you and I.
Moreover, through youth and maturity,
I have observed from start to end.
In your serving of parents,
Filial piety matched Mǐn Zǐqiān and Zēng Shēn.
In your fraternal friendship,
Harmony like that of lutes and zithers.
Serving the ruler with upright principles,
With friends, sincere in heart.
Though truly singing high notes,
I still appreciate your voice.
At capping age, striving with wings,
Feathers and demeanor first ascending.
The duke’s bow already summoned,
The imperial carriage then summoned you.
Within, assisting two palaces,
Without, governing the common people.
Loyalty and integrity truly manifest,
Pure virtue thus arose.
Vast that joyful capital,
Favored by the king alone.
Establishing offices and appointing aides,
Exquisitely selecting the finest of the state.
Employed as the mouthpiece,
Assisting you, Nányáng.
Benevolent instruction tireless,
Regarding the people as if wounded.
Then turning northward with care,
Declining emolument at Yánxǐ.
I too rested in leisure,
Without duties in enlightened times.
Our past wanderings,
Two cycles have passed thus.
Gray-haired, hand in hand,
What joy could compare!
Stay, let me tell you,
The multitude truly overcomes the few.
People detest outstanding talent,
The vulgar fault elegance.
The weary Yáng as halberd-bearer,
Jiǎ exiled to Chángshā.
Do not claim your loftiness,
Shame to dwell beneath others.
You then became cleansed,
Changing countenance, altering appearance.
Sighing with emotion, said:
“The Way indeed differs.
Practicing benevolence depends on oneself,
Not I seeking the ignorant.
Who slanders? Who praises?
What to abandon? What to follow?
Nothing dyed but turns black,
Nothing polished but wears thin.
I alone maintain upright countenance,
Dwelling in obscurity, yet will expressed.
Though not used by you,
Still I dedicate myself.
Offering remonstrance, fulfilling admonition,
To please this one person.
Frank words and loyal counsel,
Shìzǔ praised them.
Appointed to attend the crown prince,
Holding the reins at Chénghuá.
The former court’s final command,
The sage rank clearly bestowed.
Entering to serve the imperial chambers,
Going forth to glorify his family.
I hear that accumulating goodness,
The spirits bestow auspiciousness.
Should enjoy long life,
Long preserving heaven’s ordained rank.
How is it this man,
Has such illness?
Not yet knowing fate,
In midlife fallen and deceased.
Alas, sorrowful!
Only your existence,
Without rank yet noble.
Sweet food, fine clothing,
Valuing treasures and varied flavors.
At life’s end, leaving a vow,
Forever bestowing upon your kind.
Shrouded in seasonal garments,
Encoffined without sparing vessels.
Who can rise above custom,
In life fully providing support?
Who, while nurturing life,
Would slight his burial?
Profound indeed, such a man!
Following his heart, smooth and free.
Outstanding conduct, clear and perceptive,
In hardship, even brighter.
The hearse having departed,
The countenance and body long returned.
Separation between existence and demise eternal,
The departed cannot be pursued.
Gazing at your old carriage,
Viewing your left-behind garments.
Choked with sorrow, losing voice,
Tears bursting forth, mingling.
Not for you alone my grief,
For whom then is my grief?
Alas, sorrowful!
Days go, months come,
Heat retreats, cold assails.
Dewdrops moisten and congeal,
Fierce winds bleak and urgent.
Miserable, how it wounds,
Thinking of my good companion.
Visiting your plain dwelling,
Comforting the orphan, weeping together.
Former thoughts not yet stilled,
Later feelings still gather.
Accumulated sorrow fills the heart,
Gone, how can it be reached!
Alas, sorrowful!
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month in autumn, in the seventh year of Yuánkāng,
the late Marquis of Guānzhōng, the Commandant of Fúfēng, Mǎ Jūn, passed away.
Alas, how grievous!
Initially, within the Yōng region,
the Qiāng rebellion had not yet been quelled,
and the registered Dí tribesmen again ran rampant in revolt.
Although the royal army launched a punitive campaign,
eventually achieving their annihilation,
yet wasps and scorpions carry venom,
and we repeatedly suffered minor losses,
causing the common people to flee into exile,
facing the brink of utter devastation.
The General Who Establishes Might lost his head at Hǎozhì,
and the Regional Governor fled overnight to Dàxī.
As for the deputy commanders and supporting generals who perished and saw their armies destroyed,
they numbered in the tens;
those who held tallies and governed cities,
officials adorned with blue and black ribbons,
who fled in haste, abandoning their posts,
could be seen everywhere across the territory.
Among the rebels of Qín and Lǒng,
Gǒng Gēng was the chief instigator,
who, having already attacked Qiān, made the county his base.
You, with your humble person,
stood isolated within the heavy siege;
leading a meager and weak force,
you held a city of only ten ramparts.
Hordes of Dí rose like bristling porcupine quills,
raining arrows upon the city from all sides.
Within the city, people dug caves to dwell in,
carrying doors on their backs to fetch water.
Timber and stones were nearly exhausted,
firewood and fodder were depleted,
and provisions of grass and fuel were utterly spent.
Thereupon, beams and pillars were dismantled for use,
fitted with iron chains and mechanisms,
and after releasing rolling stones, they were hoisted up again.
They cooked parched wheat for meals,
and used pine from rafters and eaves as fuel.
Thus able to ensure that firewood and fodder did not run out,
providing for both people and livestock,
blue smoke rose alongside,
and tethered horses neighed long.
The vile rebels, alarmed and suspicious,
then dug tunnels to attack.
You ordered counter-tunnels to be dug and moats deepened,
placing jars, cauldrons, and urns to detect them.
As they were about to break through,
a sound was heard,
and inside, torches were lit to smoke them out,
annihilating the Dí lurking within.
After a long time,
relief forces from Ānxī arrived,
finally sparing you from the peril of the tiger’s jaws,
preserving stores amounting to millions of dàn,
with documents recorded at the headquarters.
The sagely court deliberated and consulted,
advancing you to a distinguished rank,
and bestowing upon you the insignia of banners and canopies.
Yet the officials of the province,
on account of a few private servants,
and ten hú of grain,
interrogated officers and soldiers,
using confessions extracted under torture to implicate you.
The Grand General repeatedly protested in memorials,
saying:
"Dūn firmly defended an isolated city,
standing alone against hordes of bandits,
resisting many with few,
enduring the passing of cold and heat,
rising to the occasion in the face of danger,
preserving the grain and saving the city.
Yet the Yōngzhōu Attendant Officer,
envious of Dūn’s achievements,
exaggerated minor flaws to the extreme,
which is no way to commend great merit.
Dūn’s impeachment should be lifted and his appointment restored."
The imperial edict hastily approved,
but you had already been imprisoned and, in indignation, passed away.
The court, hearing of this, grieved for you,
and issued a decree stating:
"The Emperor commends the late Commandant, Marquis of Guānzhōng, Mǎ Dūn,
for his loyalty, bravery, decisiveness, and resolve,
for leading and inspiring with skill,
for firmly defending an isolated city,
and for being rescued from dire peril.
Honors and rank had not yet been conferred,
when, unfortunately, he met his demise.
We are deeply saddened by this.
Now, we posthumously bestow upon him the seal and ribbon of General of the Tooth-Gate,
and offer sacrifices with a shàoláo."
If your soul has awareness,
may you delight in this honor and glory.
Yet when a pure scholar hears of such defilement,
how can he not be moved to reflection?
As for the petty officials who freely inflicted harm through slander,
they are all envious individuals.
Alas!
The envy that deceives the good—
is it not also a vendetta seeking the other’s head?
There is a saying:
"Some warn their sons,
'Be careful not to do good.'"
That words could go so far—
how sorrowful!
In the past, at the Battle of Chéngqiū,
Xiàn Bēnfù drove the chariot for Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ.
The horses bolted, and they suffered a defeat.
Bēnfù said:
"On other days, we never suffered defeat,
yet today we are defeated—
this shows I lack courage."
Thereupon, he died in battle.
When the groom was bathing the horses,
he found a stray arrow embedded in their flesh.
The Duke said:
"This was not his fault."
And so he composed a eulogy for him.
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
there was one Sīmǎ Shūchí,
who, in broad daylight at the marketplace, slew his father’s enemy with his own sword,
facing death as if returning home.
He too commanded the historian Bān Gù to compose a eulogy for him.
Thus, for those of loyalty, filial piety, righteousness, and martyrdom,
who die heroically and untimely,
writers who craft compositions
have never neglected them.
Since the Son of Heaven has already decreed and bestowed honors upon you,
how dare I, a humble servant, relying on the end of the old histories,
omit such writing?
Therefore, I compose this eulogy, saying:
To know a person is not easy,
nor is a person easily known.
Alas, this Mǎ Jūn,
of lowly station and humble name.
When the Western Róng disturbed Xià,
he then displayed his extraordinary prowess.
He defended this city of Qiān,
rescuing our border from peril.
What peril did that border face?
The city was small, but its grain stores were abundant.
You, with your humble person,
determined its defense.
No additional guards were added to the troops,
nor were the walls heightened or fortified.
The greedy hordes of Dí,
like jackals and tigers, vied in pursuit.
Gǒng Gēng acted with reckless abandon,
covertly occupying the government offices.
Qí Wàn roared fiercely,
shocking the imperial ministries.
The tumult of their声势 reached a boiling point,
and their tribes blazed with fervor.
Banners unfurled like lightning,
spears and halberds stood like a forest.
Red pearls streaked like stars,
and flying arrows fell like rain.
Trembling men and women,
wept and cried out to Heaven.
They cooked parched wheat for meals,
and carried doors on their backs to fetch water.
In peril as precarious as piled eggs,
in urgency as dire as being hung upside down.
Mǎ Shēng's valor shone forth,
brighter still in peril.
His spirit rivaled the sun,
fierce as autumn frost.
His awe-inspiring might could rouse,
making cowards brave.
Bestowing grace, he soothed and cared,
warming poor scholars with cotton-wool.
The rabble of dogs and sheep,
relying on numbers, bullied the few.
They tunneled in secret to attack,
from deep beneath the earth.
The desperate, isolated city,
its breath seemed to falter.
Once fate hung by Heaven's thread,
now it rested solely on Mǎ.
This Mǎ Shēng alone,
broad in talent, rich in wisdom.
He used jars and pots to listen,
arrayed long trenches.
Before spades showed their edge,
fire had already burst into flame.
Corpses filled the tunnels, smoked,
caves were sealed with clubs.
Timber and stones ran out,
chaff and stalks were exhausted.
Yet calmly, Mǎ Shēng,
appeared as if he had plenty.
He made beams into rolling stones,
used pine shavings as fodder.
In defense, he lacked no weapons,
through the ordeal, there were neighing steeds.
Alas, the General of Established Might,
his body fell beneath the axe.
The distant, fierce commanders,
lost their armies, their weapons gone.
The enemy released our men,
openly executed our commander.
To exchange life for death,
who could be unwavering?
The sacred court looked west,
Guānxī trembled in alarm.
They divided our Qiānyǔ stores,
turning them into rebel grain.
Truly, we relied on you, sir,
your plans and strategies far-reaching.
You made all have courage,
willing to die, knowing the way.
Though I am of shallow learning,
I have heard from ancient texts:
For ten generations, pardon the able,
mark graves, honor the good.
Thinking of the man, loving the tree,
the sweet pear-tree remains uncut.
How much more for you, sir,
your merit deep, suspicion shallow.
The two parties' cases not complete,
witnesses and proof were few.
Who with such merit and service,
would not be spared?
Treacherous were the officials,
their hearts fickle and deceitful.
They harmed the good, injured the able,
hated the upright, loathed the honest.
The shepherds meandered,
from public duties retired to dine.
Hearing filth, the falcon soared,
yet did not fold its wings.
Forgetting your great toils,
suspecting your small gains.
If hearts are not opened,
to what depths will they not sink?
Resolute was Mǎ Shēng,
his noble spirit shone bright.
Indignant in prison,
in death his gaze still clear.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
Ānpíng used surprise,
defeated Qí, kept Wán intact.
Zhāng Mèng wielded strategy,
saved endangered Zhào to safety.
The people of Qiān relied on you,
like those on Tándān relied.
How could petty envy,
wag its tip of the brush?
The full granary could be rewarded,
how much more private grain?
Captive slaves could be bestowed,
how much more household servants?
They stripped your twin tortoise-seals,
pierced you with the three woods.
Your merit preserved Qiān city,
your body died in Qiān prison.
All your fellow besieged,
hearts torn with grief.
Supporting the old, leading the young,
streets wailed, alleys wept.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
The brilliant Son of Heaven,
honored with special grace.
Glorious, generous posthumous gifts,
and carved his gate with honors.
The Minister of Awards conferred rank,
also blessing later generations.
If the dead have spirits,
may this comfort the wronged soul.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
In the third year of Yǒngchū, eleventh month, eleventh day,
the former Sīmǎ of Níngyuǎn,
Tàishǒu of Púyáng, Péngchéng's Yáng Jūn, passed away.
Alas, sorrowful indeed!
Zàn, from youth, upheld will and integrity,
his nature loyal and resolute,
serving superiors with sincerity,
leading subordinates with method.
The court praised his ability,
thus entrusted him with border affairs.
At the end of Yǒngchū,
he assisted in defending Huátái.
Meeting the state's repeated disasters,
the royal strategy faltered midway.
The Xūn barbarians seized the rift,
ravaged Sī and Yǎn;
cavalry and crossbows from Yōu and Bìng,
encamped and pressed Gǒng and Luò.
Fortified camps lined the borders,
each fell to slaughter and collapse.
Zàn exerted his fierce sharpness,
his will undaunted by hardship,
standing among officers and soldiers,
to gather the multitude of Huá and Yì.
Exhausted, they protected each other,
held firm for forty days,
strength above and below spent,
they fell to the fierce enemy.
Officers fled in chaos,
abandoning the army, scrambling to escape.
But Zàn vowed to sink with the city,
offered his body to flying arrows,
weapons exhausted, supplies spent,
he fell beneath the banner.
Had it not been for his steadfast, stout spirit,
his brave and fierce resolve,
how could he have faced the enemy, upheld righteousness,
and died for his integrity!
In the first year of Jǐngpíng,
the court heard and grieved for him,
issuing an edict:
"The former Sīmǎ of Níngyuǎn,
Tàishǒu of Púyáng, Yáng Zàn,
during the crisis at Huátái,
with stern loyalty held firm in defense,
devoted his life to integrity,
in peril, unwavering.
Among ancient martyrs,
none surpassed him.
He may be posthumously appointed Jǐshìzhōng,
aid and comfort his orphaned children,
to console the living and the dead."
Posthumous honors thus made clear,
people knew to admire integrity;
between the Hé and Biàn rivers,
righteous winds arose.
When Yuánjiā expanded the reign,
the sage emperor recorded deeds,
illuminating glorious legacies,
honoring and recording past merits.
If there is one who embodies loyalty and filial piety,
truly his deeds move the benevolent and wise.
Your humble servant, ignorant and stubborn,
has heard the highest teachings,
dared to consult ancient texts,
and composed this elegy.
The words are as follows:
Virtue does not always receive aid,
yet righteousness is sure to be distinguished.
Chǔfù served his lord diligently,
yet resentment arose from promoting the worthy.
Shànyí achieved resolute deeds,
and Tízi served in the ranks.
The fervor of loyalty and valor
should begin with you first.
Though old merits were discarded,
the fief and clan name were passed down.
Only the fief and the clan name,
from Wēn to Yáng.
Húxù having declined,
the Jìn clan did not flourish.
This man’s birth,
established achievements for the Sòng emperor.
Fierce and resolute, deep and steadfast,
gentle, keen, solemn, and good.
Like that bamboo grove,
bearing snow and embracing frost.
Like those paired steeds,
matched in harness and yoke.
Border troops lost discipline,
the royal strategy not yet restored.
Hán and Shǎn blocked and obstructed,
Chán and Luò overgrown with weeds.
Northern horses galloped east,
barbarian winds brought southern dust.
Roads held no returning chariots,
fields were strewn with abandoned bones.
The emperor’s plan faced such hardship,
he selected troops and entrusted talent.
Truly he commanded Yángzǐ,
to aid the army at Wēitái.
That perilous Wēitái,
in the outskirts of Huá.
Zhōu and Wèi clashed there,
Zhèng and Zhái fought over it.
Once a splendid state,
now a border outpost.
Relying on cliffs to set passes,
backed by the river, winding walls.
Bronze clappers struck at night,
city gates closed by day.
Assessing the enemy, overcoming hardship,
at that time, it was Yángshēng.
Cold winter, fierce air,
beyond the frontier, grass withered.
Distant Xūn barbarians,
crossing barriers to violate might.
Neighing steeds swept across,
frost-tipped arrows soared high.
Overrunning our Hé county,
capturing our Luò outskirts.
Spearpoints gathered like a forest,
saddles thrown down to form a siege.
Dim and desolate, the desperate fort,
wailing and wailing, the mournful crowd.
Troops aged, morale changed,
isolated position, aid far away.
Soldiers had not half a bean,
horses indeed gnawed on bits.
Defenses not yet burned by rams,
attackers already soaked their felt.
Fierce Yángzǐ,
in hardship even more resolute.
Encouraging and comforting the wounded,
patrolling and tending the hungry and thirsty.
Strength could be exhausted,
but spirit could not be taken.
Righteousness stood on the border,
his life ended by spear and arrow.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Bìnfǔ died upholding integrity,
the people of Lǔ recorded it.
Qiāndū proved his loyalty,
the records of Jìn preserve it.
The emperor praised and mourned,
thinking to bestow honor posthumously.
With what to reward him?
He was promoted to Jǐshì.
Enfeoffment to record merit,
caring for orphans to show heirs.
Alas, you righteous man,
in death there is lasting honor.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Though xuán jade is supremely beautiful,
it is not a treasure for moats and ponds;
though cassia and pepper are truly fragrant,
they are not fruits of garden groves.
Is it because they are deep and love remoteness?
It is merely their nature being different.
Thus, what arrives without feet
is borrowed by things;
what stands following heels
is belittled by men.
As for the lofty conduct of Cháo and Gāo,
the stern integrity of Yí and Hào,
they already regarded Yáo and Yǔ as mere elders,
and Zhōu and Hàn as trifles,
yet as generations passed distantly,
their radiant spirit did not continue,
until their essence was hidden and lost,
their fragrant legacy cut off and ceased—
is it not regrettable!
Though among present writers,
each has his own measure,
many who start on the same dusty road
halt midway and take different paths.
How can this illuminate the last rays
and extend the remaining waves?
Jìn dynasty recluse Táo Yuānmíng of Xúnyáng,
was a recluse in the southern peaks.
In youth, he disliked frivolity;
in maturity, he truly had a simple heart.
His learning did not claim to be a teacher’s;
his writing aimed only at clarity.
Among the crowd, he did not lose his solitude;
in speech, his silence became more evident.
Young and beset by poverty and illness,
he lived without servants or concubines.
Well and mortar tasks he could not manage;
wild greens and beans did not suffice.
His mother old, his children young,
providing for them was laborious and lacking.
Deeply considering Tiánshēng’s counsel on caring for parents,
he later understood Máozǐ’s feelings upon receiving the summons.
At first, he declined three appointments from the provincial government;
later, he became magistrate of Péngzé.
His principles did not align with the world;
he abandoned office to follow his inclinations.
Thus, he freed himself from worldly turmoil,
focused his will beyond the mundane sphere,
settled his traces in deep seclusion,
thereby distancing himself far away.
Watering gardens and selling vegetables,
to supply fish and bean offerings;
weaving sandals and plaiting rushes,
to cover the cost of grain.
His heart loved unusual books;
his nature delighted in the virtue of wine.
He simplified and discarded haste and urgency,
achieving brevity and spaciousness.
Was he not what is called “one who rejects noble rank for the state,
whose family forgets poverty”?
An edict summoned him to be a court historian,
but he pleaded illness and did not go.
At the age of so many springs and autumns,
in the fourth year of Yuánjiā, on a certain month and day,
he passed away in a certain village of Xúnyáng County.
Close acquaintances grieved and mourned;
distant scholars felt sorrow.
Silent and dark, blessings respond—
alas, virtuous and upright!
Substance is adorned by eulogy’s flourish;
reputation is elevated by the posthumous title.
If it truly matches virtue and righteousness,
what does high or low status matter?
As for his beauty of broad cheerfulness and a good end,
his conduct of loving integrity and self-restraint,
it accords with the canon of posthumous titles,
not violating former intentions.
Therefore, consulting his friends,
he should be posthumously titled “Recluse of Tranquil Integrity.”
The verse says:
Objects may stand alone in existence,
And humans are inherently independent in character.
How could this be due to encountering the right time?
How can it be said to be inherited from the world?
Alas, such a gentleman!
Gazing upon antiquity, he distantly gathers its essence.
He conceals his illustrious lineage,
Disdaining those ranks and titles.
His conduct in cherishing kinship
Arose not from forced diligence.
His trustworthiness in keeping promises
Was weightier than the pledges of common folk.
Pure and profound, simple and unsullied,
Upright and gentle, refined and warm.
Harmonious yet capable of sternness,
Broad-minded yet not verbose.
To conform to the world is to seek uniformity,
To oppose the times is to be different.
To possess either of these traits
Would not allow for silent indifference to both.
How could it be like our Master,
Who followed his heart and transcended worldly affairs?
He revered honor yet loved antiquity,
Valuing little for himself but holding lofty aspirations.
The powerful of the world offered him empty courtesy,
The regions praised his influence.
Filial piety was expressed through righteous support,
His way inevitably embraced concern for the state.
In human nature’s endowment,
He was neither narrow-minded nor overly deferential.
His rank was equal to a lowly scholar,
His emolument matched that of a superior farmer.
His measure was difficult to gauge,
Yet his advances and withdrawals had their limits.
Zhǎngqīng abandoned office,
Zhìbīn resigned of his own accord.
You understood this,
How discerning was your understanding!
Composing poetry, you returned home,
Soaring high in solitude and self-cultivation.
Already transcending and broad-minded,
There was nowhere your heart did not find contentment.
Drawing water from old streams,
Repairing your dwelling amidst family woods.
Morning mists and evening hazes,
Spring warmth and autumn shade.
Laying aside books and scrolls,
Setting out wine and playing the qín.
In daily life, diligent and frugal,
Personally enduring poverty and illness.
Others lamented such worries,
Yet you accepted your fate with equanimity.
Living in seclusion, embracing leisure,
Delaying and declining offers of appointment.
Not merely for straightforward clarity,
But because it was your inherent nature.
Entangled and swirling currents,
Dark and obscure are the ways of retribution.
Who says it favors the benevolent?
Truly, I doubt the wisdom of this.
They say Heaven is lofty,
Why does it err in this principle?
Where is the reliance on keeping faith?
How is thinking of obedience placed?
In the middle years of life,
Afflicted by recurring illness.
Facing death as returning home,
Confronting misfortune as if it were auspicious.
Not tasting medicinal brews,
Nor caring for prayers and sacrifices.
Quietly heading toward the幽暗, announcing the end,
Embracing harmony, long departed.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Respectfully recounting his tranquil integrity,
Following his遗言 with reverence.
In life, he desired no abundance,
In death, he sought no lavishness.
Sparing obituaries and declining funeral gifts,
Light mourning and simple burial.
Choosing a plot of land to dig,
Swiftly interred and laid to rest.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Deep in heart, recalling the past,
Distant emotions following transformation.
Since you lived in seclusion,
And I had much leisure.
Our mutual fondness and harmony,
Connected through neighboring dwellings.
Nightly conversations and daytime rests,
Without need for boat or carriage.
Remembering past private feasts,
Raising cups to offer admonitions.
“The solely upright face danger,
The extremely square encounter obstacles.
The wise retract or extend,
As recorded in former texts.
The mirror for reflection is not far,
My admonitions you should wear.”
You indeed looked solemn,
Speaking from the heart:
“Opposing the multitude hastens blame,
Going against the wind, one stumbles first.
Physical talent is not substantial,
Glory and reputation will fade.”
Your wise words are forever stilled,
Who will admonish my shortcomings?
Alas, how sorrowful!
The benevolent thus end,
The wise thus perish.
Qiánlóu has already passed,
Zhǎnqín has also departed.
As for our先生,
He joins the dust of bygone ages.
Honoring this tranquil integrity,
Adding to that peace and kindness.
Alas, how sorrowful!
In the sixth year of Dàmíng, summer, fourth month, on the day Rénzǐ,
The Xuānguìfēi passed away.
The valley of music ceased its warmth,
The land of dragons halted its dawn.
The radiant carriage left Wèi,
The connected cities bid farewell to Zhào.
The emperor grieved that the palace chambers had fallen silent,
Mourned that the path to the springs had become a palace.
Strolling along the covered walkways, approaching the orchid path,
Gathering at the lofty heights, gazing toward the pepper-scented breeze.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Heaven’s favor was just bestowed,
The royal princess descended in marriage.
Solemn and harmonious, measuring the shadows,
Ascending the slopes, she arrived.
The state was wounded by the loss of virtue,
The family凝结 in sorrow over the fallen shelter.
Daring to inscribe virtue upon the banners,
Hoping to depict her fragrance in bells and chimes.
The words say:
The dark mound shrouded in mist,
The jade terrace descending with fragrance.
Gāotáng’s lingering rain,
Wūshān’s gathering clouds.
Born with orchid-like grace,
Shining with jade-like bearing.
Gazing at the moon, like the moon goddess,
Looking upon the stars, akin to the constellation Nǚ.
Nurturing virtue in plain abodes,
Dwelling in splendor within imperial halls.
At home, adorned in fine and coarse hemp,
Outwardly, excelling in water plants and artemisia.
Cultivating poetry, embellishing the Way,
Praising illustrations, illuminating words.
Assisting instruction in the consort’s chamber,

Intimately connected to the historical archives,
At ease within the classics’ chambers.
Displaying elegance in composing odes,
Approaching the hexagrams, discerning subtleties.
Roaming the arts, exhausting numbers,
Handling pitch pipes, probing mysteries.
Hesitating in winter’s affection,
Melancholy in autumn’s sunlight.
Such blooming splendor,
Truly the state’s fair lady.
Reverently diligent in Xiǎnyáng,
Solemnly respectful in Chóngxiàn.
Upholding honor with restraint,
Receiving kindness with humility.
Extending harmony to those below,
Facing friends, avoiding resentment.
Fortune gathered blessings,
Auspiciousness welcomed felicity.
The imperial heir, a jade model,
The emperor’s daughter, golden in appearance.
Connected calyxes, aligned tips,

As feudal lords, as shepherds,

Observing the朔 for signs,

The detached palace, heaven’s remoteness,

The breath of seasons shifts, the silken gauze transforms,

Bound by love and affection,

Passing through Jiànchūn, turning right,

The morning hearse parts from the phoenix,
