The divine form dissolves into the soil’s end,
The ethereal soul disperses to the sky’s edge.
Echoes ride the breath, orchids drive the wind,
Virtue reaches far, its sound endless.
Alas, how sorrowful!
At dusk, the night awakens,
Grief cuts off the lineage, none to inherit.
Suddenly, the dragon hearse at the gate’s side,
Lamenting the awaited hour of ascent.
Sisters-in-law and nieces in distress,
The kind mother-in-law shows pity.
Hearing the rooster crow, warning of dawn,
All cry out in shock, beating their breasts.
Days gone are long, years of life short,
Sorrows many, joys few.
Those distant thoughts, living apart,
Sighing at the wide river, Sòng so far.
Now, what to do? In one departure,
Far into eternity, never to return!
Exhausting my grief at the ancestral dawn,
Raising bright torches, pulling the spirit hearse.
Removing room curtains, spreading courtyard mats,
Lifting the libation cup, announcing eternal departure.
Bitter and mournful, sighs increase,
Bowing and looking up, tears are shed.
Thinking of the lonely soul longing for the old abode,
Gazing fleetingly, as if in a blur.
Only a blur remains in thought,
No sight or sound, not even one encounter.
Halting the carriage, lingering,
Pacing back and forth at the old place.
Searching all around, what is gained?
Turning away, it is time to depart.
Leaving the splendid carriage, first steps taken,
Horses turn their heads, banners swirl.
Wind, cold and clear, enters the curtains,
Clouds, thick and dense, bear the canopy.
Birds lower their wings, forgetting the woods,
Fish gaze upward at foam, losing the rapids.
Melancholy, slow and heavy,
Following the auspicious road to a mournful return.
Thinking of that person, already gone,
Looking at remaining traces, not yet faded.
Once walking the same path, now in different worlds,
Recalling old joys adds new sorrows.
Speaking of plains and marshes, no bounds,
Speaking of rivers and streams, no banks.
Gazing at mountains, vast and empty,
Facing waters, broad and boundless.
Looking at sky and sun, pale and dim,
Viewing villages and hamlets, desolate and scattered.
Not that external things have changed,
But surely joy and sorrow shift with feeling.
Alas, the hidden tunnel now open,
Soon to send the form on its long journey.
Leaving the orchid chamber, its splendor,
Enshrouded in the poor springs, decaying soil.
Inward longing cries out, beating the breast,
This child descends to the burial ground.
Caressing the spirit coffin, bidding farewell to the dark chamber,
The coffin in deep darkness, the tomb passage secluded.
The door closes, the lamp extinguishes,
When will night turn to dawn again?
Returning to wail at the funeral hall,
Sounds may cease, but grief has no end.
Is it real or not? How bewildering!
Hoping for one encounter before my eyes.
Once before my eyes, no sign remains,
Even in waking or sleep, no dream appears.
Having looked back at the family’s way,
Longing lingers in my heart for you.
Again it is said:
It is over!
This is but the nature of fresh grief.
How long will this sorrow last?
May I be without shame before Zhuāngzǐ.
In the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā, on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month,
The Great Departed Empress passed away in the Xiǎnyáng Hall.
On the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month,
She was to be moved to her resting place at Chángníng Tomb,
In accordance with ritual.
The dragon bier draped with cords,
The ceremonial carriage yoked with steeds.
The imperial road brightly arrayed,
The sacred path solemn and deep.
The emperor personally attended the ancestral farewell,
Witnessing the nocturnal departure.
Adorning the departing ceremony with tasseled banners,
Letting the fading sounds sink into jade pendants.
Mourning the shifting feast of the embroidered mat,
Grieving the renewed darkness of the pheasant robe.
Descending the carriage to the guest’s place,
Clearing offerings from the funeral steps.
Then commanding the historian,
To recount virtue and express sorrow.
The words say:
Orderly and paired, they ascend,
With substance and support.
The round essence first refined,
The square divinity begins to congeal.
Illustrious indeed, the noble lineage,
Auspicious signs arise, blessings received.
Secret rites of glorious descent,
Radiant as the jade rope constellation.
Glorious light in the shadows,
Gentle brightness about to advance.
Following ritual, treading in harmony,
Citing poetry, accepting compliance.
Since awaiting maturity,
Her golden reputation early resounded.
Once she journeyed forth,
Plain elegance gained added splendor.
Adorned with the ceremonial robe,
her demeanor was observed as the model.
She enabled our royal customs
to first establish the virtues of a consort.
Her gracious reputation flowed like rivers,
her fine plans deep and profound.
As the Jiāng and Hàn rivers swelled,
songs spread throughout the southern kingdom.
Alas, in times past, misfortune struck,
and the grand transformation declined midway.
Thus, the precious mandate was gathered,
and she ascended to grasp the heavenly opportunity.
Leaving her position for the ducal palace,
she rose to shine in the purple chambers.
Reverently following the imperial mother-in-law,
she truly upheld the former virtues.
Filial piety reached to comfort her parents,
and reverence was shown in ancestral sacrifices.
Advancing, she considered talents and virtues,
while broadly mastering charts and histories.
Her utterances became songs,
her every gesture formed a rule.
Domestic governance was harmonious and proclaimed,
chamber music was Sháo-like and well-ordered.
The principle of Kūn was followed and accomplished,
the starry canopy adorned with grace.
Where virtue reached,
no depth was left unmeasured.
Below, restraint calmed tremors,
above, purity rectified deviations.
All who came were harmonized,
no thought lacked its utmost expression.
It is said the Way assists benevolence,
yet the steward of transformation remains unseen.
Just as auspicious signs approached,
ominous portents announced disorder.
When the Great Harmony had fully merged,
she laid down her splendor and left the world.
The orchid hall grows shadowed,
the pepper path loses its guard.
Alas, how sorrowful!
As coolness warns during the encoffining,
the late autumn brings the burial.
Frosty nights carry flowing chants,
the dawn moon rises, its soul ascends.
Eight deities alertly lead the way,
five carriages shift their traces.
The bright crown prince,
the grieving assembled nobles.
Tears sprinkle the jade steps,
rain falls on the crimson side courts.
Comforting the living, mourning the departed,
feeling the present, remembering the past.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Southward, turning from the capital gate,
northward, heading toward the mountain garden.
Servants regulate the pace,
horses gaze at the carriage yoke.
From afar, sorrow pierces the purple canopy,
faint weeping in the plain carriage.
Colors vanish in the pure capital,
her body rests in the longevity plain.
City and wilds sink into gloom,
armies and Xia people mourn with lament.
Fragrance that came can be recounted,
the departed carriage cannot be pulled back.
Alas, how sorrowful!
In the first year of Yǒngtài.
On the first day of the ninth month in autumn,
the coffin of the Reverent Empress was moved from the former tomb,
to be attached to a certain mausoleum.
On that day,
His Majesty personally offered sacrifices to a certain emperor,
then ordered the concurrent Grand Commandant someone to set up the ancestral ceremony at the traveling palace,
as ritual dictates.
Green canopies spread over mounds,
the dark hall opens its doors.
The sacrificial stand cleared after three offerings,
the mat rolled up with the six garments.
The mourning son, the succeeding emperor,
clutching the serpent guard, stretches his neck,
longing for the phoenix carriage, presses his heart.
Grieving that the pepper path is now desolate first,
sorrowing that Chángxìn Palace sees her no more.
His body separated, attending to both,
time allows no double display.
Soon he decreed the left historian
to gloriously spread her sage goodness.
The words say:
Distant descendant of Emperor Táng,
remote lineage of Yùlóng.
In Qín, they became Liú,
in Hàn, they opened Chǔ.
Then began the virtuous saint,
capable of gentleness, capable of goodness.
The clear Milky Way displayed her spirit,
the layered sands received blessings.
Thus her auspicious sign was fixed,
her virtuous fame truly solemn.
Radiant splendor in pond islets,
glorious brightness in the central valley.
Reverence began with the crown strings,
teaching started with early and late grains.
Her wise reputation flowed like rivers,
her divine heart orchid-fragrant and lush.
Earlier virtues concealed their light,
the way of rulership was just spreading.
In seeking worthies for assistance,
in audience, there was no bias.
Consulting histories to broaden models,
presenting poems to display righteousness.
Enriching the lower is called benevolence,
preserving the past shows wisdom.
The ten able ministers thus awaited,
the four teachings never erred.
Delighting the various aunts,
she bequeathed to me the consort’s rules.
Transformation spread from the ducal palace,
far-reaching to the southern kingdom.
The carriage canopy cherished her light,
the plain carriage awaited her virtue.
Pity me, not blessed,
the kind instruction early lost.
Just young in years, tender and small,
no lap or sleeve to rely on.
The family reached the treasure enterprise,
I myself succeeded the flourishing brightness.
The longevity palace, silent and distant,
the pure temple, empty upon return.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The emperor shifted the bright mandate,
people and spirits all rejoiced.
The dry signs shone from without,
the yin presence lacked within.
Vainly grieving the old sword,
only sighing at the gold vault.
How to offer the jade libation cup?
The ceremonial robes nowhere set.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The astrologer announced the ominous sign,
the imperial abode long departed.
She left behind far-reaching plans,
the final command is encouragement.
Cherishing the intimacy of Fēng and Pèi,
yet turning from the grand expanse of the divine capital.
Disdaining Cāngwú’s lack of followership,
following Fùyú to share the same soil.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Arranging symbolic settings in the garden tomb,
reflecting carriage ornaments among pines and catalpas.
Gazing toward Chéngmíng but not entering,
crossing the clear Luò to travel south.
Continuing the pond ropes on the thorough track,
connecting dragon curtains on the constructed boat.
The winding pond silent as dusk falls,
the eastern river calm and unmoving.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Recording the distant achievements of the secluded palace,
hearing the remote blessings of the continuing woman.
First harmonizing virtue with duckweed and artemisia,
finally matching the deity and displaying the mandate.
Longing just entangled by bestowed robes,
sorrow daily deepened by the mirror’s touch.
Thinking of the cold spring without limit,
entrusting to the red tube these remaining chants.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The gentleman's given name was Tài,
his courtesy name was Línzōng,
and he was from Jièxiū in Tàiyuán.
His ancestors descended from the revered lineage of King Jì of the Zhou dynasty.
There was one named Guó Shū,
who indeed possessed virtuous excellence,
and King Wén consulted him.
When the state was established and the clan name conferred,
some called it Guō,
and he was their descendant.
The gentleman was born in response to Heaven's intent,
intelligent and wise,
filial, fraternal, gentle, and respectful,
benevolent, sincere, kind, and gracious.
His capacity and depth were vast and profound,
his demeanor and bearing broad and great,
expansive and boundless,
deep and vast,
so profound as to be unfathomable.
As for tempering his integrity and cultivating his conduct,
upholding the straight path and righteous words,
his steadfastness was sufficient to manage affairs,
and his ability to correct and adjust was enough to rectify the times.
Thus he studied and examined the Six Classics,
exploring and synthesizing charts and apocrypha.
He traveled throughout Huáxià,
gathering at the imperial academy.
He gathered what was about to be lost from King Wén and King Wǔ,
and rescued subtle teachings that had not yet perished.
At that time, those of official rank,
gentlemen with sashes and pendants,
looked to his visible example and followed like shadows,
listened to his fine reputation and echoed in response,
just as all rivers return to the great sea,
or as scaled and shelled creatures revere the turtle and dragon.
Thereupon he lived in seclusion behind a humble gate,
gathering friends and diligently instructing,
so that the young and ignorant relied on him,
using this to dispel their obscurity.
The provincial and commandery authorities, hearing of his virtue,
humbled themselves and prepared rituals,
yet none could secure his service.
The assembled lords admired him,
and thus he was recruited as an assistant in the Ministry of Education,
and also recommended as a man of outstanding virtue,
but he declined all on grounds of illness.
He intended to tread the distant traces of Hóng Yá,
and continue the severed path of Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu,
soaring beyond the region to spread his wings,
transcending the heavenly thoroughfare to stand aloft.
But his allotted life was not long,
enjoying only forty-two years of age,
and he passed away on the yǐhài day of the first month in the second year of the Jiànníng era.
All we, his friends from the four directions,
eternally cherish sorrow and mourning,
with nowhere to place our thoughts.
Thus we joined together to consider the gentleman's virtue,
planning for an enduring legacy.
We all believed that when the ancients had passed away,
yet their virtuous words still remained,
it was also due to being recorded in writing.
How could we now neglect this rite!
Therefore we erected a stele to mark the tomb,
clearly inscribing his shining conduct,
so that his fragrant achievements would flourish for a hundred generations,
and his fine reputation be displayed for eternity.
The inscription reads:
Ah, excellent gentleman,
with bright virtue penetrating the profound.
Pure, virtuous, kind, and spiritual,
bestowed upon him by Heaven.
Lofty, robust, deep, and serene,
like a mountain, like an abyss.
He delighted in ritual and music,
and esteemed the Odes and Documents.
Not merely plucking the blossoms,
but seeking their very roots.
The palace walls were many ren high,
yet he truly found the gate.
How virtuous his purity,
how firm his conduct.
The numerous officials,
spoke of observing his loftiness.
Dwelling leisurely on the hillock,
skilled at guiding and able to teach.
The illustrious Three Dukes,
nearly succeeded in summoning him.
He declined the summons and recommendation,
preserving this pure excellence.
His allotted years were not long,
and the people thus mourn him.
Therefore we engraved this inscription,
to spread his radiance.
Oh, you future generations,
take this as your model and emulate it.
The gentleman's given name was Shí,
his courtesy name was Zhònggōng,
and he was from Xǔ in Yǐngchuān.
He embodied the harmony of primordial essence,
responding to the numbers of the destined cycle.
He combined the resources of the nine virtues,
and cultivated all hundred conducts.
Among the village community, he was respectful and deferential,
cultured and refined,
skilled at guiding and instructing,
benevolent and loving others,
so that both young and old felt secure and cherished by him.
His way was such that
he was employed when needed and withdrew when not,
his advancement and retreat could be measured,
he did not flatter or expose faults to court the times,
nor did he shift blame or show duplicity when overseeing subordinates.
Four times he served as a commandery merit officer,
five times recruited by Yùzhōu,
six times recruited by the Three Offices,
twice recruited by the Grand General,
he administered Wénxǐ for half a year,
and Tàiqiū for one year.
His virtue aimed at the mean,
his teaching emphasized earnestness without severity.
Governance was accomplished through ritual,
transformation proceeded with tranquility.
Then he encountered the Partisan Prohibitions affair,
confined for twenty years,
yet he delighted in Heaven and knew his fate,
serenely at ease.
In interactions, he did not flatter superiors,
in affection, he did not befriend inferiors improperly.
He acted upon recognizing opportunity,
without waiting all day.
When the documents of pardon arrived,
he was already seventy years old,
so he withdrew to the hills,
retired his carriage and declared old age,
with the four gates observing proper rites,
he lived in leisure and quietude.
Grand General Lord Hé,
Minister of Education Lord Yuán,
successively summoned and recruited him,
sending messengers to explain,
saying they wished specially to recommend him,
so that he could enter and serve as a regular court official,
be promoted exceptionally to the Three Dukes,
wear the gold and purple insignia,
bringing glory to the state and leaving meritorious deeds.
The gentleman said:
"I have long abandoned hope,
and merely await my time adorned with a simple headcloth."
Thus he did not go to any.
Lord Yáng from Hóngnóng,
and Lord Chén from Dōnghǎi, whenever they held high ministerial positions,
and the assembled officials congratulated them,
they would raise their hands and say:
"Lord Chén of Yǐngchuān,
peerless and surpassing his generation,
has not yet ascended to high office,
making us ashamed of occupying positions like Zāng Wénzǐ who usurped his post."
Therefore people of the time esteemed his virtue,
and valued the positions of duke and minister because of him.
At the age of eighty-three,
on the bǐngwǔ day of the eighth month in the third year of the Zhōngpíng era,
he fell ill and passed away.
On his deathbed, he gave his final instructions:
to be buried where he died,
in plain clothes and a simple coffin,
with an outer coffin just large enough to encase the inner one,
the funeral arrangements to be frugal,
and expenses kept to a minimum.
All the lords and officials
could not help but sigh in lament;
even the recluses in the mountains and marshes who knew his name
wept until they lost their voices.
The Grand General offered condolences and sacrifices,
bestowing upon him an honorable posthumous title,
saying:
"The Recluse Gentleman Chén,
endowed with the essence of the mountains and rivers,
embodied the purity of the spiritual radiance.
Heaven, sparing the aged,
let him shield our king.
Now the pillar has collapsed, the sage has withered,
and the times lack a model.
The gentry and Confucian scholars,
discussing his virtue and tracing his deeds,
grant him the posthumous title of Wénfàn Xiānshēng."
The Classic says:
"How rich and splendid is its culture!"
The Book says:
"The Great Plan with its nine divisions
sets forth the constant principles of order."
Wén (culture) is the manifestation of virtue,
fàn (model) is the standard for scholars.
To be instructed by him in life and honored by this title in death—
is this not fitting indeed!
The Three Dukes dispatched their clerks to offer sacrifices with a middle-grade offering.
The Regional Inspector reverently mourned.
The Grand Administrator of Nányáng, Prefect Cáo, ordered an official to compose a eulogy, saying:
"Illustrious was Gentleman Chén,
born to command his age.
Embodied radiance and pure virtue,
setting the standard for scholars.
His foundation was upright from the start,
and he maintained integrity to the end.
He upheld ritual until his death—
how splendid, his pure reputation!"
He dispatched his subordinate officials and clerks
to attend the funeral in succession,
and had a stone inscribed with an epitaph.
The Assistant Prefect and neighboring counties gathered for the burial.
Xún Címíng, Hán Yuáncháng, and over five hundred others
donned mourning garments of sīmá and set up positions,
mourning as they sent him off.
Those who gathered from near and far for the burial
numbered over a thousand.
The Governor of Hénán, Prefect Chóng, overseeing the commandery,
reflected with admiration on his virtuous deeds,
recorded his lofty conduct,
believing that few near or far could match him,
and repeatedly ordered his senior clerks
to complete the epitaph in due time.
This may be called honored in life and mourned in death,
one who perishes but does not decay.
Thus the epitaph was composed, saying:
Lofty, towering sacred peak,
issuing tallies, sending down spirits;
O glorious Xiānshēng,
embracing treasures, holding jewels.
How could Heaven above
deprive us of this culture?
Subtle words cut off and lost—
what shall later generations hear?
Fluttering yellow birds,
gather upon the thornbush.
Fate cannot be redeemed—
how boundless is our grief!
Now, the highest achievement is to establish virtue,
the next is to establish merit;
this is called immortality.
Thus, when Zǐchǎn passed away,
Xuānní wept for the love he left behind;
when Suíwǔ was gone,
Zhàowén cherished his lingering influence.
In Wénjiǎn Gōng we see this.
His given name was Yuān,
courtesy name Yànhuí,
a man of Yángdí in Hénán.
Wēizǐ, with utmost benevolence, founded the house;
Sòng Duàn, for his lofty merit, established the clan name.
Down through the two Hàn dynasties,
refined scholars succeeded one another;
from Wèi and Jìn onward,
generations shone with renown.
His ancestor, the Grand Tutor Yuánmù Gōng,
matched his virtue to the times,
and his conduct was a model for the region.
Deeply discerning good and ill,
he did not let praise or blame shape his words;
serving the royal house with bright talent,
he always cherished the way of humility and emptiness.
He may be said to have been subtle yet accomplished in writing,
reserved yet profound in intent.
From that time onward,
none departed from the former standards;
offices were filled only with the worthy,
and high rank passed down in succession.
Gōng, endowed with the numinous radiance of rivers and mountains,
contained the splendor of jade tablets, shining forth;
gentleness and harmony congealed within,
brilliance and flower blossomed without.
His spirit flourished in early learning,
his achievements rose high by the age of twenty.
Thus, with benevolence as warp and righteousness as weft,
he fostered harmony within the household;
like the chime of metal and the resonance of jade,
his fame rang clear throughout the realm.
Filial piety and reverence, deep and pure,
were his constant guides;
bringing joy to his parents morning and evening,
none could find fault in his words.
He wandered freely in the garden of culture and refinement,
soared in the arena of ritual and music.
His demeanor was as clear as the autumn moon,
his grace as moistening as spring clouds.
His bearing was vast and deep—
joy and anger never showed on his face;
his mind was bright and penetrating—
in employing others' words, he always followed his own judgment.
Vast like the waters,
boundless like the ocean,
he may be said to have been so clear that stirring could not muddy him,
so pure that disturbance could not sully him.
Yuán Yángyuán, with his lofty and extraordinary talent,
comprehensive in examination and precise in judgment;
Emperor Wén of Sòng, upright and enlightened on the throne,
discerning and never mistaken in appreciation.
Yuán praised his reputation far and wide,
and the Emperor also arranged a marriage with the royal family.
He was chosen to marry Princess Yúyáo,
and appointed Commandant-escort.
Compared to Hàn's union with Shūgāo,
or Jìn's marriage to Wǔzǐ,
this was nothing less.
He began his career as Assistant Editor of the Imperial Library,
then transferred to Gentleman of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
Purifying his cap-strings, he ascended to court,
crowning his generation with honor;
serving in both palaces, rising and falling,
he was truly the treasure of his time.
The model for all to look up to was already established,
and the expectation for ministerial responsibility gathered upon him.
He went out to serve as Army Advisor to the Grand Steward,
entered as Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
and soon was promoted to Assistant Director of the Palace Library.
Admired in the court of the locust tree,
overseeing literature in the celestial pavilion;
his brilliance shone upon the feudal lords,
his elegance and reputation were exceedingly great.
He left office due to mourning for his father,
his grief in mourning exceeding propriety,
nearly destroying himself.
Those who understood were moved to linger,
and passersby were wounded with sorrow.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed as Vice Director of the Secretariat.
The king's words are like fine silk,
yet their issuance is like a thick cord.
He diligently fulfilled his official duties,
his wisdom and efficacy were harmonious.
At that time, Prince Xīn'ān was the most favored among the feudal lords,
and he extensively promoted the state's teachings.
For the selection of his assistants,
the finest talents of the nation were sought.
He was appointed as Senior Clerk of the Right of the Minister of Education,
and later transferred to the post of Director of the Bureau of Appointments in the Department of State Affairs.
He conducted evaluations with fairness,
and managed complexities with simplicity.
The clarity and insight of Péi Kǎi,
and the conciseness and precision of Wáng Róng,
were once again embodied in him.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era,
he entered the court as Palace Attendant.
Within less than a month,
he was promoted to Minister of Personnel.
At that time, the imperial path was just beginning to be pacified,
and the royal road was still obstructed.
The grand army had set out,
but the officials were not yet in order.
Internally, he assisted in planning and strategizing;
externally, he rectified the ranks of officials.
The strategies for victory were far-reaching,
and distinctions became clear as the Jīng and Wèi rivers.
Rewards were given without neglecting merit,
and recommendations were made without overlooking virtue.
His achievements were recorded in the emperor's heart,
and his reputation spread far and wide.
When affairs were settled,
he was appointed as Commander of the Right Guard of the Crown Prince,
but he firmly declined the post.
Soon after, he was appointed as General of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry.
For his contributions in planning and strategy,
he received a fitting rank of honor.
He was enfeoffed as the Earl of Yúdū County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
He upheld the principle of declining the Liang estate,
and cherished the ambition of the Qǐnqiū land.
The fields and towns he received
did not exceed a hundred wells.
After a long time,
he was again appointed as Palace Attendant,
and concurrently as General of the Right Guard.
He exhaustively offered advice and recommendations,
matching the merits of Shān Fǔ;
he brought order to the royal troops,
combining the prestige of Fāng Shū.
Dānyáng, as the capital's auxiliary region,
set an example for both near and far;
Wúxīng, as a strategic area,
was truly a vital support.
He served repeatedly as the governor of these two regions,
and was additionally granted the cicada-embroidered cap.
Governance was achieved through ritual,
and the people thereby found rest.
When Emperor Míng fell ill,
and the crown prince was young and immature,
the responsibility of entrusting the legacy
rightly fell upon the esteemed figures of the time.
He was summoned to serve as Minister of Personnel,
concurrently as Commandant of the Guards,
but he firmly declined the post.
He was instead appointed as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
Upright and balanced in conduct,
outwardly lenient yet inwardly principled.
He expanded upon the lofty strategies of the sixteen ministers,
and propagated the teachings of the "Yóu Gēng" ode.
When Emperor Tàizōng passed away,
his will appointed the Duke as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
Director of the Secretariat,
and General Who Guards the Army.
He served the deceased and attended to the living,
with unwavering loyalty and integrity.
Holding the balance of the state,
he stabilized all four directions.
The hundred officials acted in accordance with their roles,
and military affairs were prepared without need for orders.
The Duke's ascent to high office and governance of the realm
was regarded by gentlemen as a praiseworthy tale,
much like Mèng Kē's admiration for Yuèzhèng,
or Yáng Zhí's appreciation for Shì Bó.
He observed mourning for his birth mother,
and resigned from his post.
The severity of his grief and illness
stemmed from the depths of his heart.
The court deliberated that acting for a greater cause,
as exemplified by the Marquis of Lǔ, was appropriate;
prioritizing public duty over personal feelings,
as demonstrated by Fāng Jìn, set a clear standard.
An imperial edict was thus issued,
urging him to resume his duties.
He persistently requested leave for a year,
with memorials and petitions submitted continuously.
As circumstances did not permit his wish,
he humbled himself to promote transformation.
At a time when the three crises were at hand,
and rebellious feudal lords internally defied authority;
Guìyáng, having lost his way,
coveted the imperial throne.
The oars stirred, causing the waves to surge;
banners raised, obscuring the sun and moon.
He emerged from the river's course like the wind soaring,
and entered the capital with the force of thunder.
Bows were drawn within the ancestral temples,
and arrows flew toward the palace gates.
Although valiant commanders led the troops,
and the chief rebel was timely eliminated;
the remaining factions were numerous,
posing a threat to the palace and temples.
The Duke then gathered warriors as fierce as bears and brown bears,
and ministers of unwavering loyalty,
exerting their strength and devising strategies,
to quell the turmoil.
He stabilized the precarious state fortune,
and restored the royal order from the brink of collapse.
This was truly due to the awe-inspiring might of Tàizǔ,
but also aided by the Duke's benevolent assistance.
It can be said that virtue and punishment were balanced,
ritual, righteousness, and trustworthiness upheld—
these are the instruments of war.
For his merit in quelling the rebellion,
he was advanced to the rank of Marquis,
and concurrently appointed as Director of the Department of State Affairs,
General of the Central Army,
and granted an honor guard of twenty men with decorated swords.
He did not claim credit for the achievement,
but firmly maintained humility and deference.
He was instead appointed as Palace Attendant,
Supervisor of the Secretariat,
while retaining his position as General Who Guards the Army.
He again left office to observe mourning for his mother.
Although the matter was driven by duty,
his emotions were akin to those of a natural bond.
The propriety of Yán Dīng,
and the exemplary mourning of Èr Lián—
how could they surpass this!
Heaven grew weary of the virtue of Sòng,
and the water phase announced its decline.
The succeeding king neglected his heavenly mandate,
while powerful ministers encroached from Jīng and Chǔ.
The merit of deposing the incompetent and continuing the lineage,
and the virtue of quelling chaos and pacifying the people—
the Duke indeed assisted in the grand design,
and participated in the divine strategy.
Though he did not have the merit of receiving the sacrificial meat and leading the chariots,
he achieved the feat of resting peacefully while holding the feather banner.
He was then made Minister of Works,
bringing order to the mountains and rivers;
concurrently appointed as General of the Guards,
harmonizing military governance.
Thereafter, the virtue of Qí arose in glory,
and the Shùn Emperor abdicated the throne in lofty manner.
Deeply comprehending the workings of prior heaven,
he supported and assisted the enterprise of upholding the times.
Harmonious and truly upright,
his splendid plans were vast and far-reaching.
He established customs and reputation,
and set forth words of instruction.
This is like how Jì and Xiè served Yú and Xià,
or how Xún and Péi served Wèi and Jìn.
If not for his open-hearted utmost impartiality,
and eternal vigilance over rise and decline,
who could have gloriously assisted five sovereigns,
and reverently illuminated two dynasties?
Greatly opening up Nánkāng,
he thus ascended to the central tripod;
though the time called for territorial enfeoffment,
he firmly declined the governance of the state.
The present-day Shàngshū Lìng,
the ancient Zhǒngzǎi,
though his rank was lighter than that of the Gǔn officials,
his responsibilities were weightier than all the nobles.
Temporarily following his modest wish,
he was transferred to the head of the court.
Nearby, there were no dissenting voices;
afar, there were no divergent hopes.
The Emperor praised his great achievements,
and reiterated the previous edict of appointment.
Upholding the five rites to rectify the people,
he simplified the eight punishments and rarely used them.
Thus he could display his achievements on the broad road,
extending kindness to the wise sovereign.
Righteousness lay in supporting with reverence,
affection was like that among commoners;
accompanying the imperial carriage when out,
attending within the curtained palace when in.
Raising his voice to sing the lofty odes of the southern breeze,
he savored the secret treasures of the eastern wilderness.
Elegant discussions during mornings of governance hearings,
unfolding writings during evenings of private feasts.
Seasoned with the virtue of wine,
leisurely with the heart of the qin.
Warm with lingering sunlight,
far-reaching and leaving lasting thoughts.
The lord bestowed the warmth of winter sun,
the minister exhausted the caution of autumn frost.
Solemn and dignified,
reverent and harmonious.
Herein was seen the unity of lord and kin,
knowing the oneness of the three respects.
When Tàizǔ ascended afar,
entrustments were meticulously arranged.
As Shìzhōng,
Sītú, and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Receiving the final instructions by the jade table,
performing the rites of the funeral garments.
Selecting the admirable statutes of Imperial Qí,
bringing sound transformation to harmonious prosperity.
Peace within and accomplishment without,
truly illuminating his former duties.
Increasing his ceremonial guard by thirty men with bānjiàn,
things had their proper appearance,
insignias and honors were thus fitting.
His position was exalted yet his rituals humble,
dwelling on high yet his thoughts descended.
From summer to autumn,
he pleaded retirement due to illness.
The court, respecting his wish to decline glory,
thereby expressed esteem for transcending worldly norms,
changing his appointment to Sīkōng,
concurrently Piàoqí Dàjiāngjūn,
Shìzhōng and Lù Shàngshū Shì as before.
His destined mandate did not last long,
his great decline prolonged at the end.
On the twenty-first day of the eighth month of the fourth year of the Jiànyuán era, he passed away in his private residence,
at the age of forty-eight.
In the past, when Liǔ Zhuāng was critically ill,
the Lord of Wèi halted the sacrificial rites;
after Yàn Yīng had departed,
the Lord of Qí hastened his carriage and wept as he went.
Now that the Duke has perished,
the sacred court above is shaken with grief,
the multitude of lords below are agitated with sorrow.
How could mourning be confined to one state alone,
or pain be deep only for one sovereign?
He was posthumously honored as Tàizǎi,
Shìzhōng and Lù Shàngshū Shì as before,
granted ceremonial insignia, yǔbǎo, drummers and flutists, and a guard of sixty men with bānjiàn.
He was given the posthumous title Wénjiǎn,
as ritual dictated.
One who abides by virtue,
the myriad things cannot harm his integrity;
one who empties oneself to wander,
the contemporary world cannot disturb his measure.
Equalizing noble and base in the gentle breeze,
forgetting glory and disgrace between others and self.
Only then can one benefit all under heaven,
and thus pass the years.
Planning the beginning and considering the end,
so as to avoid regretful reverence.
Who can claim perfect attainment?
Yet the Duke truly possessed it.
Thus his righteousness bound gentlemen,
his kindness moistened the multitude.
Beyond what words and images can shape,
beyond what narration and song can exhaust.
Therefore, his former subordinates such as Mǒu Jiǎ and others,
feeling the ceaseless flow of the passing river,
grieving the distant silence of his clear light.
Hearing the carriage songs in the villages,
gazing upon the elegant odes in the capital.
Thinking of the inscribed texts on Wèi tripods,
recalling the遗留 rules of Jìn bells.
Facing the high mountain and looking up with reverence,
they engrave dark stone to manifest his virtue.
The inscription says:
The essence of the stars sensed the times,
the spirit of Áng gave forth auspicious signs.
The sovereign head alone was bright,
the minister limbs alone were good.
Heaven observed the jade-like brilliance,
treading in the steps of former kings.
Reverently compliant, the chief minister,
embodying subtlety, knowing clarity.
Eternal words spoke of filial piety,
from the heart arose brotherly love.
Benevolence reached all, aiding widely,
love profound, skillfully guiding.
Viewing the sea, equal in measure,
ascending the peak, even in thickness.
The five ministers here become six,
the eight worthies here become nine.
Planning within the tented command,
shining without upon the ministerial steps.
Far, none not awed;
near, none not cherished.
Like grass bending to the wind,
like music in harmony.
Glorifying our imperial statutes,
ordering well the common people.
Following ritual, treading with humility,
truly the stem of his person.
His traces bent the vermilion carriage,
his will exalted the balanced lodge.
Profound and distant, the mysterious source,
luxuriant and rich, the literary brush.
Righteousness flowed like rivers,
writings scattered like mist.
The lofty structure crumbled like clouds,
the beam's shade now bears a gap.
Virtuous plans have no successor,
demeanor and form long passed.
Melancholy, the lingering emblems,
resounding, the遗留 splendor.
Older, yet more fresh;
used, yet not exhausted.
I have heard that one who scoops from the pool of morning and evening
cannot fathom its shallows or depths;
one who gazes at the azure hue above
cannot know its distance or nearness.
How much more for what lies beyond sight and hearing,
seeming to exist, seeming to vanish;
beyond the surface of mind and action,
neither born nor perishing!
Therefore, the silent one of Mójié
opened the ford of ceasing words;
the one who closed his mouth at Píxié
cleared the path of attaining meaning.
Yet those who speak of constant principles
must seek their source in the nine categories;
those who discuss yīn and yáng
also probe their subtleties in the six positions.
Thus, once the three realms are distinguished,
one recognizes the work of wondrous things;
once the myriad phenomena are arrayed,
one comprehends the ultimate of the supreme pivot.
That speech cannot be ceased—
is it not here?
Yet what the hexagram lines seek to capture
is exhausted within this domain;
then what designations cut off
takes form on the other shore.
The other shore: drawn into existence,
it transcends the four streams;
pushed into non-existence,
it broadly encompasses the six pāramitās.
Names and words cannot grasp its nature and marks,
approach and departure do not see its end or beginning.
It cannot be known through the stage of learning,
nor reached through the mind of thought.
This is the essence of Nirvāṇa.
The secluded valley, impartial and selfless,
echoes every sound that reaches it;
the great bell, empty and receptive,
responds to every strike that comes.
How much more so the Dharmakāya, perfectly responsive,
with its rules silently established;
with a single sound naming all things,
the musical notes operate unseen.
Thus the Tathāgata, for the benefit of all, appeared in Kapilavastu,
taking birth in a royal household.
Relying on the chariot of the Five Vehicles,
he saved those drowning in the river of time;
opening the gate of the Eightfold Path,
he greatly sheltered a world in mutual decline.
Thus, the profound barrier, the hidden bolt,
moved by feeling, became passable;
the distant source, the deep waves,
could be drawn from without exhaustion.
Practicing the dāna of non-abandonment,
his charity reached all beings;
proclaiming compassion without condition,
his grace encompassed the myriad things;
expounding the illumination that does not shine,
his discernment penetrated the sandy realms;
guiding with the skillful means of no contrivance,
his merit aided through the dust-like kalpas.
Profound indeed is the meaning of the times!
The great task was completed!
Then he brushed his robe at the twin śāla trees,
and cast off his sandals by the golden sands.
Vague and indistinct,
neither bright nor dark,
not bound by coming or going,
he returned again to non-being.
Speaking in this way,
then, though dwelling restlessly in the great chiliocosm,
the quiescence of non-action is undisturbed;
though the firm forest is burned,
the inexhaustible spirit does not cease.
How great it is!
After the True Dharma had declined,
the teaching through images fell into decay.
Those who drilled into heterodox views
considered deviation from the norm as attaining the One;
those who followed error and argued falsely
compared subtle words to superficial talk.
Then Aśvaghoṣa offered profound praise,
Nāgārjuna sought the emptiness,
and together they shook the slackened net,
and restored the severed cords.
Shading with the Dharma-cloud in the realm of truth,
then the burning house grew cool at dawn;
shining the sun of wisdom on the broad road,
then the deepest darkness grew bright at night.
Thus they enabled the Thirty-seven Aids to Enlightenment to have a master for the ritual vessels;
and the Ninety-six Heretical Schools to have no firmness in their fences.
Thereafter, the Vaipulya sūtras spread eastward,
and the teachings flourished as they moved south.
The two Zhuāngs of Zhōu and Lǔ,
personally witnessed the mirror of the night scene;
the two Míngs of Hàn and Jìn,
both recorded the adornments in red and blue.
Afterward, surviving texts appeared intermittently,
monasteries stood in rows facing each other,
with Dào'ān and Kumārajīva leaving tracks west of the mountains,
and Huìyuǎn following closely south of the river.
The Tóutuó Temple
was established by the śramaṇa Shì Huìzōng.
To the south lies a vast, mighty river,
where clouds and mists billow and surge.
To the north stand layered peaks, sheer as if carved,
where the sun and moon wheel and press close.
Gazing west toward the city walls,
one sees the hundred battlements winding and lingering.
Looking east over the level marshes,
a thousand *lǐ* stretch vast and distant.
Truly it is a scenic spot of the Chǔ capital.
Dharma Master Zōng, whose conduct was pure as jade discs,
came traveling, holding his monk's staff.
Considering that embodied life depends on conditions,
when karma is empty, conditions cease;
that attachment to the body is delusion,
when principle prevails, delusion perishes.
He thus wished to relinquish a full lifespan in his middle years,
to sacrifice his flesh to fierce birds,
and for a long time sat on spread grass under the shade of pines.
In the fifth year of the Dàmíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
he first built a square hut of thatch,
to shelter scriptures and images.
The Later Army Senior Administrator and Internal Historian of Jiāngxià of Kuàijī, Lord Kǒng, named Jì,
cleared the weeds and opened the woods for him,
and built a hall for walking meditation.
General Ānxī, Regional Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, and Earl of Jiāng'ān of Jìyáng, Lord Cài, named Xīngzōng,
further raised the foundation and erected the temple pole,
and built a hall for meditation and recitation.
As the Dharma Master's conduct mirrored that of Mahākāśyapa,
it was named "Tóutuó" at the outset.
Later there was Dharma Master Sēngqín,
of steadfast virtue and earnest resolve,
who sought benevolence and nurtured his will,
continuing the construction of the halls and buildings,
but passed away before completion.
His lofty path was hard to follow,
the hidden boat easily drifts far.
The monastic community fell silent and empty,
the rafters decayed with none to rebuild.
Truly, one can only heave a long sigh!
The Qí dynasty alone inherited the great name of the Five Emperors,
and continued the severed enterprise of the Three Kings.
The virtue of ancestral martial and civil rule,
shone brightly in solemn sacrifices;
the merit of reaching Heaven and illuminating all,
broadly initiated the revival of rites and robes.
Thus it renewed the old ways,
bringing peace and aid through many troubles;
its steps matched the odes of the *Yǎ* and *Sòng*,
its strides joined the music of Sháo and Hù;
in the fiery regions, interpreters of nine tongues,
at the sandy frontiers, a single beacon of peace.
This was during the Jiànwǔ era.
Then an edict commanded the General of the Western Central Guard and Regional Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, Prince of Jiāngxià, to oversee governance in the frontier regions,
and establish customs along the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
selecting the excellent statutes of Fāngchéng,
considering the old precedents of Guīméng.
Governance strict, punishments clear,
thus it was achieved.
General Níngyuǎn, Senior Administrator and Acting Internal Historian of Jiāngxià of Péngchéng, Lord Liú, named Xuān,
wherever his wisdom's blade reached,
the old was daily renewed;
the tone of one who triumphs through the Way,
went forth empty and returned full.
Seeing this temple's work abandoned just as peace was achieved,
its merit on the verge of establishment yet fallen,
he sighed deeply over the overturned basket of earth,
and grieved as over a discarded well.
Taking advantage of the people's surplus,
and the leisure of a world without strife,
he assembled workers and chose the day,
with each having his assigned duty.
Then the people came joyfully,
the craftsmen vied with heart and mind.
Across mounds and covering hills,
they built high and reached far.
Tiered verandas stretched long and wide,
rising up to pierce the clouds and rainbows.
Flying galleries wound their way,
hanging over emptiness below.
Evening dew became pearl nets,
morning mist became cinnabar hues.
Grasses along the nine paths numbered in the thousands,
flowers shining on all sides in ten thousand varieties.
Cliffs and valleys shared the clarity,
wind and springs refreshed each other.
Golden resources and precious forms,
forever rely on tranquil peace;
with minds at rest and meaning understood,
they finally gather here to wander.
Dharma Master Shì Tánzhēn, pure in practice and cultivation,
profound and far-reaching in understanding,
is now appointed to oversee the temple's duties,
to forever serve the divine abode.
When the people labor and achieve merit,
it is engraved in writing on bells and tripods;
when speaking of the times and recounting deeds,
stelae are also erected at the ancestral temple.
As ages accumulate, merit is proclaimed;
as the person recedes further, his name grows brighter.
I dare to lodge words in carved seal script,
hoping to approximate the myriad wonders.
The inscription says:
Matter distinguishes the dark and the yellow,
qi divides the clear and the turbid.
Vessels number a thousand names,
beings of spirit ten thousand clans.
Pure sources flow from above,
shallow customs defile below.
Love's currents become a sea,
passion's dust forms a mountain.
Great indeed is the Able and Benevolent One,
who, in due time, was destined for the world.
He then turned His gaze to the Central Land,
and came to Jiāwèi.
He encompassed the great chiliocosm,
and thus ruled the three realms.
He deeply contemplated the four gates,
and secludedly sought for six years.
Having perfected His virtue,
He wondrously exhausted non-action.
The Emperor offered a square stone,
Heaven opened a clear pool.
The auspicious river ceased its flow,
the jeweled trees lowered their branches.
The broad road wound nine times,
He walked safely on the three perils.
Rivers stilled, waves cleared,
dragons soared, clouds rose.
Qíshān's influence spread wide,
Jǐyuán gathered many scholars.
Jīnsù came in proper form,
Wénshū arrived and settled.
Responding to Heaven's movement and stillness,
complying with the people's end and beginning.
The Dharma was originally not so,
now it is without extinction.
Though the image of the orthodox may fade,
the subtle and imperceptible is not lacking.
Oh, illustrious is the Qí dynasty,
which promotes this grand achievement.
The net of Dharma is re-strung,
the dark ford's oar is grasped anew.
Only this famed region,
is where meditation and wisdom find their trust.
Leaning against lofty cliffs,
overlooking connecting ravines.
Moats and pools like the Xiāng and Hàn rivers,
mounds and hills like the Héng and Huò mountains.
Lush are the level marshes,
deep and serene the woods and thickets.
Charming is this lord of the land,
who draws from the flow of Dharma.
His qi flourishes with the three clarities,
his spirit transcends the six senses.
With care he regards this spiritual abode,
bearing in mind its restoration.
Vermilion carvings soar like pheasants in flight,
tiered pavilions stand apart in splendor.
Since the image-shrine was opened,
the venerable countenance has been set in peace.
Deep laurels bring warmth in winter,
sparse pines bring coolness in summer.
The divine feet roam and rest,
the spiritual mind comes and goes.
The banner of victory waves to the west,
the steadfast stone is inscribed to the south.
The Duke, whose taboo name was Miǎn,
courtesy name Jǐngyè,
was a man of Nánlánlíng.
Jì and Qì personally assisted Táng and Yú,
achieving great merit for Heaven and Earth.
Shāng Wǔ and Jī Wén,
thus received the charts and tallies.
Xiāo and Cáo supported and aided Hàn's founder,
destroying Qín and Xiàng to quell chaos.
The Wèi clan seized the opportunity before,
the Imperial Qí grasped the tally after.
Their spiritual source vies in flow with Jīshí;
their divine foundation rivals the heavens in height.
His grandfather, Emperor Xuān,
with heroic talent and grand achievements,
his fame overshadowed his time.
His father, Emperor Jǐng,
embraced the Way and dwelled in steadfastness,
withdrawing from the affairs of the former age.
The Duke contained the fine virtue of the celestial bodies,
embodied the superior spirit of rivers and mountains,
his qi amassed wind and clouds,
his person bore the sun and moon.
His conduct established a model,
his words set a standard.
Brilliance shone forth outwardly,
clarity and brightness shone inwardly.
The virtue of Heaven's constant principles and Earth's righteousness,
he exhaustively fulfilled from his heart;
the methods of simplicity, endurance, far-reaching vision, and greatness,
he invariably achieved through this.
Those who draw from his source swim in depths unfathomable,
those who cherish his Way use it daily yet unknowingly.
Luminous, like the three luminaries adorning the heavens,
vast and flowing, like the four waterways ordering the earth.
The six directions were truly harmonized,
his single virtue was without flaw.
All things looked up to him and found him ever loftier,
a thousand li responded without his speaking.
As for the day he donned his cap and took office,
the year he was employed and assumed duties,
the sequence of military commands and ceremonial robes,
the numbers of supervised regions and departments,
these are indeed detailed in the state histories,
and may now be briefly passed over.
The virtue of Water was just declining,
the Mandate of Heaven had not yet changed.
Tàizǔ, like a dragon leaping, awaited his time,
and governed from Huáisì.
His mind, like that of a benevolent man vigilant at dusk,
turned over nine times at midnight;
his intent to quell the age and save it from chaos,
he alone held in his bosom.
Deep plans and secret deliberations,
none among the multitude could fathom.
The Duke attended him morning and evening,
moving calmly by his side,
akin to Prince Zǐ's years by the Luò riverbank,
truly the age of Pìjiāng in inner service.
He inspired our sagely lord's thoughts,
his words hit the mark of the imperial will.
Beginning with literary pursuits, he traveled to Liáng,
and soon entered to oversee imperial edicts.
Orchids and cassia have fragrance,
their pure radiance naturally reaches far.
The Emperor arose from Zhèn,
the sun's robe was of azure light.
Sharing the path of the Máo altar fief,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānlù;
receiving the auspicious token and divided jade tally,
he thus ruled over Yúnyě.
To oversee the heir's instruction,
the Emperor found it hard to choose the right man,
but the Duke, as a paragon of the imperial clan,
was truly fit for this excellent selection.
He harmonized and elevated the three excellences,
and broadly displayed the four virtues.
The Bówàng Garden thus shone with splendor,
the Dragon Tower's gate thereby stood lofty.
Advising before the screen and throne,
he truly held the office of the lips and throat.
He presented memorials written before dawn,
bearing edicts fine as silk threads.
Radiance before and light behind,
his reception was not merely constant.
The Duke, as a close relative and superior worthy,
soon undertook his duties,
his handling of affairs was always fitting,
adding luster to the swords and seals.
In ancient times, under Emperor Táng,
all nine ministers attended to affairs,
with bear and leopard skins at court,
the office of presenting remonstrances was established.
From then till now,
this duty has never been flawed.
Thus, from being a close attendant,
he came to assist in balancing the scales of power.
Yet the imperial mind remained deeply concerned,
pondering profoundly to seek out the people's afflictions.
Gūsū, a land of rich resources,
holds a crucial position in strategic passes and rivers,
a bustling metropolis with abundant wealth,
governing a vast territory of a million households.
Even the splendid attire of the entire Zhào state at Cóngtái
pales in comparison to this;
the crowds of Línzī, where sweat could be shaken into rain,
are hardly worth mentioning.
Thus, like a great swan soaring over the ancient Wú,
he was appointed as governor of the Eastern Chǔ.
He promoted righteousness and humility to encourage the noble-minded,
and fostered fairness and kindness to nurture the common people.
Governing with the highest virtue,
he pacified the region with moderate laws.
In doubtful legal cases, he uncovered the truth without pride;
in long-standing disputes, he encouraged mutual concessions, leading to reconciliation.
Even Chūnshēn’s vast expansion of territories
and Dèng Yōu’s diligent nurturing of the populace
could not surpass him.
Xiàshǒu, a key frontier region,
entrusted with heavy responsibilities,
guarded the central flow of the river,
a land abundant along the Jiāng and Hàn.
To the south, it connected to Héng and Wū,
with roads stretching a thousand *lǐ* through wind and clouds;
to the west, it linked to Yōu and Dèng,
with waterways and land routes spanning three-tenths of the distance.
This was a place of strategic advantage,
foremost beyond the capital’s gates.
Raising the banner as a regional governor,
his illustrious virtue resided here.
He shone with the autumn sun’s warmth,
and wielded authority like the summer sun’s intensity.
His benevolence reached everywhere,
leaving no ant or insect hole untouched;
his discernment penetrated all,
illuminating even the slightest glimmer of light.
From the near to the far,
from himself to all things,
his kindness soared with the eight winds,
and his virtue operated in harmony with the five elements.
Those afar were all drawn to him,
those nearby all treated with reverence.
In the towns, no barking dogs were heard at night;
among herders, no sheep drinking at dawn were seen.
His reputation exemplified the six virtues of governance,
his achievements stood supreme across ten thousand *lǐ*.
Returning to serve closely by the throne,
he also held military rank.
The marquis’s residence was entrusted with high honor,
the heir’s tutor bore a distinguished duty—
in both the Eastern and Western Jìn dynasties,
this selection was exceptionally difficult.
Yáng Xiù aspired to it but never attained it,
while Xiè Yǎn, with lofty achievements, arrived later.
Rising and serving in both palaces,
his fine accomplishments awaited here;
the imperial guards were dignified,
the heir’s position more secure.
Yǔxué, a divine and elevated land,
matched the importance of Fēnshǎn,
and since the establishment of Jiāngzuǒ,
this post had always been rotated.
To the east lay the vast sea,
to the south, one gazed toward Qínjī.
Deep pools and marshes gathered here,
reeds and rushes grew in abundance.
Among the merchants and traders,
houses worth a thousand gold stood side by side;
within the outer walls and suburbs,
cloud-like rooftops numbered ten thousand homes.
Laws and governance were complex and tangled,
long difficult to unify in detail.
The bandits of Nánshān
were not enough to be called numerous;
the tangled ropes of Bóhǎi
were easier to unravel than this.
Upon taking office, he spread his transformative influence,
like the wind moving and spirits acting,
sincerity and compassion already trusted,
no need for cunning methods.
Without relying on punitive authority,
he eradicated the chief villains;
without using neighborhood registers,
he punished all the wicked.
He treated others with compassionate pity,
winning trust through integrity and compliance.
The reed staff of Nányáng
could not compare to his benevolence;
the timely rain of Yǐngchuān
could not match the abundance of his grace.
Taking the reins and mounting his carriage,
he governed prefectures and commanded commanderies,
deeply connecting with the people and spirits,
not waiting for a full year.
The elderly found peace, the young felt cherished,
songs and chants filled the roads and villages,
all joyful as if among kin,
fragrant as pepper and orchid.
Each time his banner turned to depart,
the road wept with sorrow.
The attachment of clinging to his carriage or lying before its wheels,
made people forget the distance in their struggle;
the sentiment of longing for his memory, like borrowing something precious,
grew stronger and more enduring with time.
The Fangchéng fortress and Hàn River,
to the south, none are more important.
To the north, pointing to Xiáotóng,
the level roads do not exceed seven hundred li;
to the west, connecting to Yáowǔ,
the mountain passes and roads have never been full a thousand.

to reverently mourn the Master.
Meeting a world without justice,
he thus lost his life.
Alas, sorrowful!
Encountering an inauspicious time!
Phoenixes lie hidden,
while owls soar.
The base are exalted,
slanderers and flatterers succeed.
Sages are dragged backward,
the upright are upended.
The world calls Suí and Yí filthy,
and says Zhí and Jué are honest.
Mòyé is deemed blunt,
while lead knives are sharp.
Alas, silent and wordless,
born without cause!
Discarding the Zhōu tripod,
treasuring a broken jar.
Harnessing weary oxen,
yoking lame donkeys.
A steed droops its ears,
pulling a salt cart.
A ceremonial cap used as a shoe pad,
cannot last long.
Alas, suffering Master,
alone you met this calamity!
The inquiry says:
Enough!
The state does not know me,
to whom can I speak my solitary gloom?
The phoenix flutters high and departs,
naturally withdrawing far away.
Following the divine dragon of the nine abysses,
it hides deep, treasuring itself.
Turning from otters to dwell in seclusion,
how could it follow shrimp and worms?
What is valued is the sage's divine virtue,
withdrawing from a turbid world to hide.
If a qíjì could be tethered and bridled,
how would it differ from dogs and sheep?
So numerous are those who leave these troubles,
and this too is the Master's doing!
Traverse the nine provinces to serve a ruler,
why must you cling to this capital?
The phoenix soars a thousand rèn high,
descending only upon seeing virtuous radiance.
Seeing the perilous signs of petty virtue,
it soars high and strikes from afar.
Those common filthy ditches,
how could they hold giant fish that swallow boats?
The zhān whales spanning rivers and lakes,
would surely be controlled by ants.
In the eighth year of Yuánkāng,
Jī first left his post as a court郎 to serve as a compiler,
and while roaming the secret archives,
he saw Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's final decree,
sighed with deep emotion,
and grieved for a long time.
A guest said:
"Beginning and end
are the great return of all things;
life and death
are the realm of fate.
Thus, one grieves upon facing a funeral,
and ceases weeping at old graves.
Now you sorrow over a century past,
arousing grief in a heartless place.
Is it not that you know grief can exist,
but do not recognize that emotion can be absent?"
Jī replied:
Solar eclipses occur due to the intersection of celestial paths,
and mountain collapses arise from crumbling soil—
these too are but matters of natural law.
Yet why do the common people find them strange?
Is it not because they possess a lofty and brilliant nature,
yet cannot escape the burden of base impurity;
they dwell in a state of constant security,
yet ultimately face the calamity of collapse and separation?
With the power to reverse heaven and topple the sun,
yet unable to revive their own physical forms;
with the wisdom to save the age and quell disasters,
yet trapped beneath the palace gates.
Those who once reached the heights and depths
are now concealed within a mere coffin;
those whose light shone to the four corners
are now obscured by a handful of earth.
Lofty ambitions are crushed by frail emotions,
grand plans end in sorrowful resolve.
Long-term strategies yield to short days,
distant traces halt on a hurried path.
Alas!
Is this merely the astonishment of blind musicians and historians at eclipsed sunlight,
or the bewilderment of common folk at crumbling riverbanks?
Observe how he gave his final instructions to his heir,
leaving plans for his four sons:
his strategies for governing the state were far-reaching,
and his teachings for elevating the family were vast.
He also said:
"When I was in the army,
upholding the law was right.
As for minor anger
and major faults,
they should not be emulated."
How admirable are the honest words of a wise man!
Holding his young daughter and pointing to Jì Bào, he showed his four sons and said:
"I entrust them to your care!"
Then he shed tears.
How sorrowful!
Once he took the world as his responsibility,
now he entrusts his beloved children to others.
What is shared in death leaves nothing behind,
and what is gained in loss leaves nothing preserved.
Yet within the inner chambers, tender and affectionate,
attending diligently to family affairs—
how meticulous he was!
He also said:
"My concubines and entertainers
shall all reside at the Tóngquè Terrace.
Place an eight-foot bed in the hall of the terrace,
with a fine silk canopy,
and offer dried meat and provisions morning and evening.
On the fifteenth day of each month,
perform music facing the canopy.
From time to time, ascend the Tóngquè Terrace
and gaze upon my tomb at Xīlíng."
He also said:
"The remaining incense may be divided among the various ladies.
If there is nothing to do in the chambers,
learn to make silk ribbons and sell them.
The official seals I obtained throughout my career
shall all be stored in the treasury.
My remaining robes and furs
may be placed in a separate treasury.
If this cannot be done,
my brothers may divide them among themselves."
In the end, they were divided.
The deceased need not seek,
the living need not oppose—
would not both seeking and opposing cause mutual harm?
How lamentable!
There are great loves that must be lost,
and deep hatreds that must be gained;
wisdom cannot rid one of hatred,
nor power preserve love intact.
Thus, foresight pays no heed to such matters,
and sages rarely speak of them.
If one is bound by emotions and entangled in external things,
lingering with petty thoughts in the inner chambers,
should this not also be abandoned by the worthy and talented?
Thus, filled with indignation, I offer this lament.
Inheriting the last threads of the great Hàn,
encountering the many deviations on the royal path.
Lingering in deep waters to nurture scales,
caressing auspicious clouds to soar afar.
Employing divine ways to uphold virtue,
riding spiritual winds to fan authority.
Crushing the multitude of heroes like a lightning strike,
lifting formidable foes as if discarding refuse.
Pointing to the eight extremes with far-reaching strategy,
only after cutting down would there be peace.
Rectifying the deficient codes of the three realms,
opening the forbidden gates of heaven and earth.
Raising the broken threads of the grand web,
tying the loosened strings of the great music.
Sweeping away clouds and objects to achieve proper governance,
gathering myriad paths to return to unity.
Expanding great virtue to broadly cover all,
lifting the sun and moon to shine with equal brilliance.
Achieving supreme merit across the nine regions,
truly praised by the entire world.
Such great achievements in human affairs,
where could they not reach?
About to overturn baskets into deep valleys,
piling up mountains to the ninth heaven.
If principles are exhausted and nature spent,
how can long-term strategies be studied?
Realizing the sorrow of facing the river,
the great beam is bound to collapse.
In the thirty-eighth year of Jiàn'ān,
truly a time of great destiny's hardship.
Though shining brightly in past records,
he would rest his carriage in this year.
Only the descent of the spirit is distant and remote,
gazing afar over a thousand years.
Believing this martial virtue not yet lost,
receiving the divine mandate here and now.
Though the dragon soared from Wénchāng,
it was not the king's heart's delight.
Indignant at the western Xià, he marshaled troops,
heading toward Qínchuān, raising banners.
Passing Hàojīng without ease,
reaching the Wèi River's banks with doubts.
Hoping the next day would bring recovery,
yet over forty days, disaster formed.
Chanting of returning, turning banners back,
ascending Xiáomiǎn, then departing.
Stopping at Luòruì, his condition worsening,
pointing to the six armies, saying, "Remember this!"
Oh, the majesty of this sovereign king,
truly rare throughout the ages.
Authority surpassing heaven, overwhelming the world,
strength shaking seas and uprooting mountains.
What peril did he not overcome,
what strong enemy did he not crush?
Often turning calamity into blessing,
also treading danger to find safety.
Yet here, he is shrouded in darkness,
thoughts sealed, without beginning or end.
Entrusting body and life to await hardship,
grieving that after death, words remain eternal.
Comforting his four sons with deep thoughts,
stroking his own body, sighing in decline.
Before soul and spirit have parted,
borrowing last breaths for words and brush.
Holding his young daughter, frowning in distress,
pointing to Jì Bào, tears falling.
Breath rushing through his bosom with sobs,
tears streaming down his eyelashes, flowing freely.
Departing from the land to rest in eternal sleep,
containing boundless heaven within a single coffin.
Lamenting the loftiness of his grand measure,
admiring the flourishing of his great enterprise.
Reflecting on the end while caring for the beginning,
commanding at life's close to initiate glory.
Citing good and ill to warn against regret,
though within himself, nothing was hidden.
Regretting the lingering attachments within,
resenting the trivial details of final commands.
Entangling broad thoughts with silk ribbons,
soiling clear concerns with leftover incense.
Binding lingering affections, tender and loving—
how brief the life, yet how long the intent!
Displaying ceremonial robes before the curtained seat,
accompanying grace and beauty in jade chambers.
Presenting prepared items in empty vessels,
emitting mournful sounds from former singers.
Forcing sorrowful faces to keep rhythm,
hiding falling tears while offering wine.
Nothing so small it does not remain,
no form so kind it does not perish.
Hoping the sage's spirit may resonate,
imagining the dark deity's light restored.
If form and sound are obscured and lost,
even echoes and shadows must be hidden.
Strumming the clear strings in solo performance,
presenting dried meat and provisions—who will taste them?
Mourning the silent darkness of the fine silk canopy,
lamenting the vast expanse of Xīlíng.
Ascending the terrace, all are filled with grief;
gazing with beautiful eyes—what is there to see?
Having looked to antiquity to shed burdens,
truly simplifying rites and opting for modest burial.
Of what use are those robes and seals?
Leaving behind dust and slander for future kings.
Alas, where great attachments reside,
even the wise cannot forget.
Reading遗留 records with deep emotion,
offering this text with sorrow and grief.
At the Eastern Prefecture, while digging a moat north of the city wall,
they went down more than ten feet,
and discovered an ancient tomb.
It had no mound above ground,
and was not built with bricks.
The outer coffin was made of wood,
inside which were two inner coffins,
square in shape,
with no rounded ends.
Among the burial objects,
made of materials like wood, pottery, bronze, and lacquer,
there were several dozen types,
many of unusual forms,
impossible to fully identify.
Figures were carved from wood,
three feet tall,
perhaps more than twenty in number.
When first uncovered and seen,
they all appeared human-shaped,
but when touched with an object,
they turned to dust at the touch.
On the coffins were over a hundred Wǔzhū coins.
In the water were sugarcane joints, plum and plum-pit kernels, and melon rinds,
all floating up, not severely decayed.
No epitaph survived,
so the era could not be known.
The Duke ordered the city workers to rebury them at the eastern ridge,
offering a sacrifice of pig and wine.
Since their names and origins were unknown,
they were temporarily given the name Lord of the Silent Darkness.
On the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
the Minister Over the Masses' Assistant in Charge of the Guard, Commandant of the Direct Troops' Clerk,
Supervisor of the City Construction Records,
Magistrate of Línzhāng and Tinghóu, Zhū Lín,
prepared the sacrificial offering of pig and wine,
and respectfully presented it to the spirit of the Lord of the Silent Darkness:
Humbly overseeing the labor force,
in charge of the wall construction.
Digging springs to make a moat,
piling earth to form the foundation.
Once the outer coffin was opened,
twin coffins lay here.
Putting down baskets in sorrow,
laying aside spades with flowing tears.
The straw burial figures already destroyed,
the clay burial chariots already broken.
The mats and tables decayed,
the sacrificial vessels toppled low.
Plates held plums or plum kernels,
bowls held sauces or vinegars.
Sugarcane passed down its remaining joints,
melons displayed their leftover seeds.
Reflecting upon you, sir,
from which era were you born?
How many years did your radiant form exist?
How many years has your hidden spirit lain?
Was your life long or short?
Were you prominent or obscure?
The epitaph is obliterated,
your surname and name unpassed.
Who are your descendants now?
Who were your ancestors then?
Your merits and faults,
how are they utterly vanished?
A hundred walls are all being built,
seventy feet high, now even.
The wall cannot be shifted,
the moat cannot be turned back.
The yellow heartwood cypress already destroyed,
the side chamber already collapsed.
Following the inscription stirs thoughts,
stroking the figurines increases grief.
The Shooting General showed benevolence,
Guǎnghàn bestowed moist grace.
Sacrificing to bones at the prefecture's corner,
covering skeletons at the city's bend.
Admiring the ancient customs,
for you, sir, we change the burial site.
Moving the carriage to the northern moat,
the grave at the eastern foothills.
The pit is newly made,
the coffins are the original wood.
Joint burial is not ancient,
but what the Duke of Zhōu preserved.
Respectfully following the old principle,
we return and attach the twin souls.
With two pots of wine,
and a special pig as offering.
May your hidden spirit, vaguely present,
enjoy our sacrificial vessels.
Alas, how sorrowful!
On a certain day of a certain month in the fifth year of the Sòng,
the Governor of Xiāngzhōu, Zhāng Shào of Wújùn,
reverently receiving the emperor's command,
erected his banner in the old land of Chǔ.
Visiting the deep where Huáishā was composed,
finding the shore where the jade pendant was cast away.
Halting his carriage at Luó Pool,
mooring his boat at Mìzhǔ.
Then dispatched the Household Clerk So-and-so,
to respectfully sacrifice to the spirit of the former Chǔ Sānlǘ Dàfū, Lord Qū:
Orchids fragrant are broken,
jade fine is shattered.
Things dread firm fragrance,
people shun bright purity.
Ah, such as you, sir,
met an age of flaw.
Warm winds slackened in season,
flying frost hastened the node.
Yíng and Mǐ encountered strife,
Zhāo and Huái were not upright;
plans thwarted Yí and Shàng,
fidelity scorned Jiāo and Lán.
Your body severed from Yǐng's palace,
your traces all over Xiāng's shores.
Comparing to things, the fragrant herbs,
linking to kinds, the dragon and phoenix.
Your voice overflows metal and stone,
your will outshines sun and moon.
Like those planting fragrance,
truly bearing fruit, truly sprouting.
Gazing at Mì, heart sighs,
looking upon Luó, thoughts soar.
The mat used may gather dust,
but showing loyalty must not lack.
In the third year of Xiàojiàn of Sòng.
On the nineteenth day Xīnwèi, the first day being Guǐchǒu, of the ninth month,
Lord Wáng, with mountain delicacies and rustic wine,
respectfully sacrifices to the spirit of Lord Yán:
Alas, how sorrowful!
Virtue is built by the Way,
ritual is clarified by benevolence.
Only you, sir, in your excellence,
early years made your name soar.
In righteousness, exhausting the mysteries of the Yì,
in literature, overshadowing Bān and Yáng.
By nature stubbornly upright and pure,
in aspiration and measure, profound and outstanding.
Entering court, glorifying the state,
truly a flower of Sòng.
Talent matching Hàn and Wèi,
fame reaching Guīshā.
Holding rank according to imperial canon,
resting will among cloudy heights.
Pure friendships, simple companions,
sharing light, sharing waves.
Spirit higher than Shūyè,
stern as Zhòngjǔ.
Soaring alone with extraordinary wings,
solitary style, without peer.
Lingering in wine's virtue,
whistling and singing to the zither's themes.
Traveling and visiting over the years,
parting and meeting in quiet dwelling.
Spring wind, beginning of the season,
then we talked, then we composed.
Autumn dew not yet congealed,
your spirit returned to the Great Simplicity.
At dawn, the morning carriage departs,
gazing at your cottage, looking at the road.
Heart grieves, eyes brim,
feelings intertwine like clouds.
Cool shade covers the veranda,
the moon's beauty rests its glow.
Dim lamp casts moving light,
desk and writings, who illuminates?
Quilt and mat long dusty,
strings and pipes ceased their tunes.
Gathering sorrow in the orchid chamber,
shedding tears by the pine ridge.
Since ancient times, all meet their end,
at Niúshān, there were tears.
Not only the vast heaven,
destroys our bright excellence.
Bearing this grief,
respectfully presenting the sacrificial offering.
Offering wine with lasting remembrance,
looking back with sighs and sobs.
Alas, how sorrowful!
